But on the whole, I think this game is great. If you're at all analytical-minded, then give this a go.

A fun blend of RTS and RPG. The graphics feel very dated and there are some minor bugs at times. However, I really enjoyed it.
It is simple, and contains the usual resource gathering from RTS titles like AOE/Settlers/Starcraft etc.. But adds the dimension of having a hero who can level up and gain skills. The units of each faction are interesting, although I feel there could be one or two extra per faction.
A minor criticism is that, unlike more modern RTS, it does not make use of cover or terrain. This puts Spellforce 2 in the "old RTS" category.
If you can pick it up on a steam sale - good for fantasy RTS people. But don't expect AAA graphics or polish.

Dead Synchronicity: Tomorrow Comes Today is a very, awesome point and click game that takes place in the unknown, close future, after an apocalyptic event turned the world as we know upside down. Michael, our character finds himself in the middle of the happenings, but without memories about what happened, and explores the world after The Great Wave along with the player, while touching on the some topics on humanity, morals and ethics.
Personally I very much loved it - it's rare to find good quality point and clicks with serious topics, and this one only could have used a higher budget for some animations :)
Point and click with no moon-logic solutions, with relatively few hotspots (hold space to find interactive spots) ; I found the voiceacting pretty okay, while others criticized it as bad, so it's up for you to decide.  The animation of interaction is kind of lacking, but the storyline, the conveyed messages, and the general art style are top notch.
One important thing about the game: while it's about moving forward and not surrendering, it's very dark. It's not the popular, Fallout-type of postapocalyptic world, but a super miserable world of slavery, prostution, taking adventage of the weak, poverty, suicide and death - sometimes presented very visually for a point and click game.  It's not self-indulgant for the shock value, and all these topics used excellently - but they are there, be aware of it before your purchase. Also maybe you want to get it on a sale - 20€ is a lot for ~ 6-7 worth of P&C that ends with a huge "the rest is yet to come" cliffhanger, while the story is great it lacks the feeling of real closure because of this.

The game is quite flawed at launch. It's how I want to open this review. I've had the opening mission bug out on me near the end prompting a full restart, combat has frozen in certaint areas multiple times, leaving long delays before action resumes, and not only that, but the game seems very poorly optimized at this time. My GTX 780 is showing frequent (if small) frame spikes, and graphics are consistently not rendering properly. Please be advized that these issues exist at launch day.
That being said, what I have played of the game so far is... interesting. The story doesn't really seem to do anything new, in fact it is strikingly similar to Ezio's story. Stealth missions, while still plenty of fun, also don't seem to deviate from the tried and true format. Unfortunately, what could have been a huge reveal during the plot at the end of the prologue was quite underwhelming. I am also still very much in the dark as to who my present-day character is and how they fit into the story. This is something I would have liked to have been cleared up near the beginning before I was thrust into the past.
However, I have been enjoying playing the game and I do look forward to seeing how the game plays out. I am very fond of the downward parkour controls, and the obstacle maneuvering controls have been well-refined. I personally am happy to see the series return to Europe and to a busier city setting.
My verdict: If you're a big fan of the series and have played it all, my initial response is that there's enough here to keep you happy and comfortable, even if it doesn't sweep you off your feet. If you haven't played much, don't bother. As far as I can tell, the game down't hold up much on its own.

Pros

- Most items in-game are gotten from playing.
- DRAGONS
- HOVERBOARDS
- NEON MOTORCYCLES
- Allies that gives stats and collects gears.
- Switching classes on the fly
- Free stuff
- Compensation happens frequently
Cons
- Servers are abysmal
- Allot of bad Latency
- The servers seem unstable at times
- QUEUING
- Grindy like honestly just a grind fest
- Some classes are bugged
- This game doesn't understand the term "balance"
- Allot of things to obtain items can be bought with Credits - The game's cash currency

Dead Synchronicity is an engaging story-driven game that is well worth playing. The story is by far the best thing about the game, and it does draw you in. You really feel for Michael as he wakes up with no memory and discovers how unpleasant the world has become.
You have relatively little control over the actual path of the story and it does have a very abrupt ending, so if you like games with multiple paths through and decisive endings this game probably isn't for you (though even then I still recommend it if it is on sale!).
At about 6-8 hours for a first playthrough the game is quite short, and it isn't particularly difficult for a "point-and-click" style game.

As a fan of the Spellforce universe and the RTS genre, this edition was an easy purchase. After playing the Order of Dawn and the expansions several times; I got interested in the unique gameplay and the world of Eo.
However this game changed the mechanics of the gameplay and the way you play it, for example, you no longer play as a rune warrior in the campaign but instead you’re a Shaikan, possessing dragon blood with similar features to a rune warrior without the power of using the monuments.
The gameplay no longer uses the monuments as a headquarters for army and base building, but now you build small towns from which you build your armies, and although I preferred the old gameplay this was also fun. Your heroes now level up with you, allowing further customization.
Instead of managing the six nations like in the previous Spellforce, this one has 3 alliances in which you build armies, the Realm, the Pact and the Clans, the Dragon Storm campaign also adds the Shaikan faction.
The base building elements are fun to play like the previous game, but some aspects like the resources for the town and army management was superior in the Order of Dawn, they removed the buildings that doubled the resource income and the resources are on average very limited supply, this also presents more of a challenge because your enemies always possess huge amounts of resource deposits near their bases and you can use this to your advantage in some cases but also forces  you into more rushed tactics. The game also feature the Free game mode, allowing further gameplay and also a bit more challenging than the campaign.
I enjoyed the Rune warrior gameplay more than the Shaikan, but I still liked this game. There were some issues with the camera bugs in the Shadow Wars campaign, but fortunately the Dragon Storm expansion was free of them.
The soundtrack is beautiful and fitting to the Spellforce Universe. The graphics are also some of the most good looking of the real time strategy genre.
Overall, it is a good game and a fine sequel with some changes that might not please every gamer but it is a great addition to the universe.

I've played this game since closed beta, so it's much earlier than Steam release date, I should have much more hours than I have there. I have much experience with this game and I've seen it grow with some breaks until today.
This game is really great...
Pros:
+ Simple gameplay - kill, loot, upgrade, kill more, loot more, upgrade more...
+ Updates - they happen really often (once a week).
+ High amount of classes
+ Collector's dream - a HUUUGE amount of things to collect - weapons styles, mounts, wings, recipes for decorations and much, much more.
+ Unleashing the creativity - just like in Minecraft, you can build beatufiul buildings. You can make a portable house you can summon on an adventure world, also, you can make a club and build it's own island!
+ Community creates this game - dungeons, weapons, mounts, costumes, decorations, hats - most of them is made by community. Everyone can add something from themself into the game while getting rewarded with premium currency.
+ PvP - i think it's positive that it exists, it didn't use to.
+ Game depth - actually, you can find some depth, fe. upgrading equipment, choosing it's stats, strategies for fighting Shadow Tower (special dungeon) bosses, but remember - this game is simple, you won't have there WoW raiding experience.
...however, it also must have some flaws.
Cons:
- Grinding style - this can also be a Pro, but most people find doing the same thing over and over boring, and so leads to leaving the game. In my experience, most of my friends left the game just because of this.
- RNG - refers to a previous cons. Your progress with higher and higher diffculty worlds is limited by it. One will power up faster, other one slower. There's also timegated stuff that relay on RNG. It's cruel, but what are you going to do about it?
- High ping - as a Europe player, I find myself mostly at 120-200 ping. As of Mantle of Power, 300+ ping in newer worlds.
- Ranged classes attacks - you will often find yourself not hitting the enemy, although your projectile hit the enemy.
- No chat moderation
- Pay2Win? - you can buy items with real money from store, then sell them on market for a in-game the most used currency - Flux. With Flux you can buy everything you would need - the best equipment, mounts, wings, costumes etc, however, in my opinion, you can't win over other players in this game, you just speed up your proccess of getting good equipment, you can't be overally better than someone just because you pay money. A person, who hasn't bought anything with money, will never be worse than those, who pay.
(+ you can always enjoy this game without paying money)
(Mantle of Power update - spending A LOT of money has a chance to get you more power)
- PvP state - PvP is quite a new content and it's not balanced, I can say that. Matchmaking doesn't filter players and it doesn't punish AFKers. As I said earlier, ranged attacks are a real problem on PvP. It's really hard to hit someone who is jumping, especially for a ranged class.
Overall, in my opinion, the advantages cover the most of disadvantages (the same goes for grinding aspect, which can cover all of the advantages for some people). It's a really great game which you can fully enjoy as a free-to-play player (paid content can also be gained by f2p players). I highly recommend checking this title, one of the best free-to-play models on the market.

A cute, little point and click adventure, with somewhat simple but fitting and nice-looking pixelated graphics, and nice, calm minimalistic background music. The game has some minor faults that unfortunately detract from what could have been a better experience.
A lot of the riddles are tied to solving words and sentences by pushing the right notes/letters. My using a "/" is because the letters are shaped like notes, i.e. the font resembles musical notes. Although the letters are pretty enough (for the graphical style) and creatively done, they also have the drawback of confusing the player as to what letter the note is supposed to resemble.
Example: You're in progress of solving a riddle and it's nigh impossible to distiguish what is letter "e" from letter "t" because the "notey" font doesn't quite resemble a clear "e" or "t", causing you many times to press the wrong letter and having to try over and over until you get it right. Also, if you press the buttons to quick, the game will not register it, you have to take your time and wait for the game to "catch on" sometimes, registering the correct letters/notes. This makes some of the riddles frustrating for all the wrong reasons; it's not because you don't understand what the riddle is, and how you might solve it, it's because you are not able to distinguish the letters from each other.
I certainly don't want to slaughter the game, because I find the execution okay, but it needs some patching/cleaning up. If I have to recommend or not recommend it, I would say you could get more value for your money by buying another point and click adventure game, but give it a try if you're curious.
Kudos to the developer for trying something new.

So far I've played several hours so far over a few sittings and LOVE this game. To be fair, I like games that can, at times, vex me with their difficulty. Darkest Dungeon is meant to challenge your ability to manage your characters' health (including diseases), stress, money, supplies, equipment, traits and skills while balancing risk vs reward.
Folks complaining about RNG and difficulty level: It's possible this just isn't your kind of game. You've already heard the "cry moar, game is supposed to be hard" line from other reviewers, though, so here's some helpful advice if you ever want to give this game another try:
1. Don't start each quest with the mindset that you will absolutely win. You can run from battles and leave dungeons prematurely, and you should do these things whenever you think things are getting bleak.
2. Make sure you train up at least TWO full parties (4x2 = 8 characters) so you can trade off when the first party needs a rest. If you can avoid it, don't let any character go questing with more than 50 stress.
3. If you lose a higher level character, be willing to train the new one in lower level quests. Train multiple low level characters together if you're replacing multiples. This will also have the added bonus of earning you a surplus of gold.
4. Skip exploring whenever you can to maximize your chance of finishing a quest. This means:
- If you do a 90% scouting mission, remember you can skip one room guaranteed in a short quest, possibly more in longer quests. Choose wisely to skip rooms at a dead end to preserve health, resources and stress levels.
- If you do a 100% room battles mission, try to bring characters that have high scouting chance (pretty sure there are character/class specific traits that can ensure this). That way you can check whether particular hallways or rooms have battles and potentially bypass the ones that do not.
- If doing a quest that has a boss battle, skip as many unnecessary random chance events or battles as possible, and save your strength for the boss.
5. When provisioning, always buy a surplus of torches (the game says 4, but I bring a min of 10). Generally you want to keep radiant light level as much as possible because luck is generally better for you (particularly when it comes to surprise chance. Getting the jump on monsters is a huge plus.) Also don't ever leave without shovels (at least 3). As for food, 12 units at a minimum works for me (they can double as low-grade healing in a pinch).
6. Try to always have some sort of healer in your party. Vestal is generally the best right off the bat for this as they have access to both a group heal and a single target heal. Arbalest has a very handy healing skill, good in a pinch since they're also generally fast. Occultist's Wyrd Reconstruction has a large range and bleeds the target but is the best single target heal in the game. Crusader can heal both health and stress (and doubles as frontliner). Jester has one of the best stress heals, good to keep your party from going over the brink.
7. Ideally bring at least a couple of characters with group damage skills (hit more than one enemy at once). Some of my faves for this are Highwayman, Grave Robber and Arbalest.
8. Take advantage of status effects. Stun is great--keeps targets locked down until you can deal with them. Use party buffs that increase dodge chance. Use Mark to increase damage dealt on enemies or to make your tank a target.
9. To take out single threatening targets, make copious use of Bleed and Blight (for undead particularly) effects. I've noticed they stack from different sources, which can add up to incredible damage over time.
10. Besides treating your party's stress levels, keep up with treating their diseases and negative quirks at the Sanitarium. These give some annoying (and in the case of disease, HUGE) penalties that will make your characters easier to kill. There's also a whole bunch of negative quirks that can force your party members to interact with dungeon features, which is extremely inconvenient when you're trying to minimize stress in order to complete a quest.
11. This is a bit of a repeat of #1, but if you ever feel any sort of doubt your party can survive its current quest, retreat from combat. If you're absolutely desperate, abandon the quest. Yes, you won't get the quest reward, but you'll live to fight another day, and hopefully you've collected enough treasure and curios by then that abandoning isn't an total wash.
12. If the game is getting too frustrating despite your best efforts to be careful, e.g. you just lost a character you spent hours training in a cheap shot, or you've retreated from the fourth dungeon in a row and you're low on money, go play something else for a while. If after some time, you still feel revulsion and no urge to return to the game, then go ahead and leave that negative review.
I would still argue the game has done exactly what the devs set out to do, which is make a game where you're always stuck making the best of a terrible situation, but doing so doesn't necessarily translate to a game fun enough to be worth buying. So even if I disagree, I get it.

This is a game that has a interesting story and good visuals, then suffers terribly because of the gameplay.
~ Good ~
Story:
This bizarre, yet sometimes adorable story is told mostly without any dialogue. It reminds a lot about ”Alice in Wonderland” with a dark twist. A strange world where you meet both kind and aggressive creatures. As everything is so weird, you don't know what to expect around the corner. I love stories that can be told without words, which is rare to find nowadays.
~ Bad ~
Gameplay:
This is one of the most tedious games I have ever played. Most of it consists of walking around and backtracking to get one object you need for another area. Usually these objects are ridiculously easy to get (click once, get item. Done.) and often it takes more time to walk back. It unfortunately reminds me of ”Secret Files 3” where the main character is deliberately dumped back to the start, so that the game will become ”longer” as you waste time walking through non-interactive areas.
This also leads to dissapointments in the story, because most of the strange creatures interaction are redused to ”Fetch item. Give item.” It takes away the sense of fear and mystery about them. As everything about them is solved the same way, it leaves them all quite samey despite their different appearences.
Another tedious design of the game, which could have been brilliant and unique, is that some puzzles requires the character to sing notes that another character sings. All notes represent the alphabet (which is not brought up by the game for some reason) and you basically repeat a message. The problem is that you have so many notes and when you first play the game, none of them are displayed on your notebar. So unless you have a good ear for tones (I do.. a bit), great memory (definately not my thing) or great attention to things (nope), then these puzzles becomes frustrating.
The high pitched notes are not only irritating to listen to, but they are also hard to distinguish. Even with the background music off (which was overpowering the notes), it's still hard for me to make out the sound.
The notes are also not written in clear letters, instead they are in a font which makes them hard to destuingish. And there are some creatures which doesn't even show the notes you have to click, forcing you to have perfect sense of tone, memory, visuals and hearing.
This could easily have been the best part of the game, with a better choice of sounds (less earbleeding) and clearer visuals for the notes. And allowing them all to be displayed from the start. It would make the puzzles fun rather than frustrating.
Game bugs:
- Obviously the game is designed for something wider than a mouse cursor, as some doors won't activate unless you click very far off screen.
- The music in the start screen constantly glitches and skips.
- Sometimes when you try to interac with objects nearby a door or ladder, then the character will just walk out of the room, despite not clicking anywhere close to the exit.
- After I completed the game and tried to turn it off, the game crashed.
- Not every "room" in the game allows you to practice on the notes, despite that you can always bring out the noteboard to "sing". This leads to two problems.
1: There are only some rooms where you aren't "supposed" to sing. When you try to click certain notes, it will just click on the monsters in the background that will proceed to kill the character. How am I supposed to know she isn't supposed to sing in this room? Why can I click some notes while others clicks on the background?
2: When you want to practice next to the characters that only makes sounds and no notes, the game will make a loud "DING" sound, because you are technically clicking an area you aren't supposed to, which blocks out the notes sounds. Even when you have the notes screen up, the game makes that loud dinging noise as if you are missclicking.
Good expansion on the classic, could have stayed more true to the clunky retro nature of AoE 2. 7/10

I don't normally write game reviews, but after looking at the review page here I felt compelled to. I scrolled down for some time seeing nothing but negative 'reviews' from players (some of whom have hundreds upon hundreds of hours played) blantantly lying about the game, It's developers, or just in general looking for something to nitpick about so they can jump on the bandwagon.
Now It's not always the easiest stance to take, but when I see so many reviews of this nature I'm reminded of this quote:
"Right is right no matter how many people think It's wrong, and wrong is wrong no matter how many people think It's right"

I really hate to say this because I like Daedalic and I want to support smaller developers but . . I didn't like this game. Not just for the abrupt ending that other people have mentioned, although that was jarring. But I found it quite predictable; I had worked out most of the twists by the end of Chapter One. I also found the controls a bit fussy. I had to get my mouse in *exactly* the right spot to pick things up or exit a scene, so I missed things sometimes (and the palette is so dark that there aren't a lot of visual cues that there's something there). I also (and this is very subjective, of course) didn't much like the protagonist. His inner monologues tended to dive into purple prose quite often and, again, it was kind of predictable so I spent a lot of time frustrated that he was shocked at something because "Dude, we KNOW this! It was obvious an hour ago!".
On the positive side, the game has a nice grim atmosphere, the puzzles are relatively straightforward (with one very weird exception),  the locations are well done and the voice acting is solid all across the board so if that kind of thing is important to you, it might be worth picking this game up. I don't think I'm interested in the sequel, though.

On top of that what made me lose my heart to this adorable game the most was the art. The cute eyes of the droplet just make you fall in love instantly. It might just be my love for platformers in general but Drop Alive is one of the most adorable platformers I played and will probably have a special spot in my heart until the end of time.

TL;DR - Get this game . . . Get it . . . why are you still reading this . . . own this beautifully crafted piece of farming art.
Graphics - 10/10
Some people don't like pixel art.  To those people I say 'give this game a chance'.  It has beautiful night / day lighting.  Fireflies in the summer are my favorite.  They're a single pixel floating around with a halo of light around it lol
Gameplay - 10/10
Gameplay is semi-addictive.  One day calls for another day and another.  Not only is there farming, but there's also dungeon crawling and some exploration.  You can court a someone in Stardew and marry them.  You build, craft, farm, socialize, quest, explore, fight, loot, level up.  It's a harvest moon dream come true.
Sound - 10/10
You hear owls hoot at night alongside the sound of crickets chirping.  The sound of the ocean rushing and the seagulls squawking brings the beach to life.  Even when your dog beats his tail against the ground you hear it.  The sounds are so vivid.  The music is decent for the different seasons as well.  Summer can get repetitive and annoying tho lol.
Replayability is high.  This game can be addictive, and it draws me back all the time.  The creator of this game really put love into it.  The characters come to life,  there's so much to do.  Stardew really took me back to Nature ;)  I strongly recommend anyone to buy this game.  It is now and forevermore a  steam classic.  Enjoy.

I have spent about 40 hours in the game and just finally beaten it. I will have to say that this was not a great assassin's creed at all to me but a subpar B rated title.
The story of the game as you already know is about Arno who is a Frenchmen and son of an assassin, his father was killed and so he was adopted by a templar who was also killed. He blames himself and goes to join the brotherhood to rise the ranks and defeat the mastermind behind it.
The story felt very forced amd rushed. and so did the romance, it was a very dull plot from finish to end instead of being great like past assassin's creed that leaves players hungry for more. This game left me with a
sour taste as if I had accomplished nothing and wasted my time.  It was a complete letdown and
The maps and architecture in this game looks amazing and is very large, the buildings are very aesthetically detailed and for those that can experience it without performance hitches its very clear work and detail has been put into the game's design. Maps have tunnels underneath it and buildings that you can go in this time around.
The combat to the game this time is the same as the others with attack, parry, and roll except the kill streaks are taken out and is much harder, It needs more work because sometimes it can get clunky during battle due to possible bugs or fighting 5 stars enemy is such a pain. Best way of clearing enemies are using bombs smokes etc and just killing them all.
The parkour is improved with the ability to traverse up and down however can be quite buggy when it comes to climbing near windows. I felt like pressing directional in all different ways and solving a puzzle just to get past them.
The coop itself is very lacking, they took away the previous death match style games and replaced it with forced coops in certain places. There are coop missions you can do to earn unlock in armors and get more money with random mob generation which bugs out.  Most of the time people don't really try to stealth them, everyone rushes in kills accomplishes the mission or sometimes do escorts, rinse repeat and I can seriously see the replay value of this game dropping in a few weeks.
I love the fact that you can go over and over a mission to redo it again figuring out different routes in the game though it is limited in ways you can do them really but nevertheless the choice is there
The armor aspect of the game is a greay way to customize your assassin's but at the same time  quite silly because you can literally buy it all with helix points by paying which is such a silly and greedy system, You don't have to but you can do so.
Truly, I cannot recommend this game until things are fixed. The gameplay is by no mean horrible at all and by no mean very exciting but its the performance issues that really gets in the way.
When you turn down settings to tone it all down even to low and get the same fps problems its clearly an issue with the game not my rig. The game itself is having problems on consoles! If you do your research Everyone is having problems in this game even the higher end tier rigs with the fps and only a handful of people can run it. Overall the game itself was very sub par and introduces some nice new mechanics but also failed to really bring anything exciting to the table. At best for this triple A title it felt B rated and dissappointing, as a Fan I will have to thumb this one down and wait for them to pick themselves up.

Darkest Dungeon is a beautifully polished game filled with eldritch horrors alongside campy humor. Each of the bucketful of character classes plays differently, and finding combinations of types that work together is a joy. The art and animation is a clever use of low-budget (other "indie" gamemakers take note); it fits the game theme beautifully. The whole game is dark and difficult and weird.
Unfortunately, as others have mentioned, you are at the mercy of a RNG. The game itself has a disclaimer when you first start; it warns you that the game is never going to be easy, and will always be about managing terrible situations. Fine.
The trouble is, though, that the game is a mix of "perfect" strategy (each character class has best-in-slot items and abilities and positions and partners) and utter hands-off randomness. There's nothing you can do to respond to a situation; the dungeons are random, the combats are random, and the rolls are random. So even if you have a plan for addressing a certain type of situation, there's literally nothing you can do to react to a problem when it comes up. The perfect strategy is also frustrating - there's no point in trying a first-slot Vestal, for example. There's a use and pairing for each class. You'll need to get all of them, but it still won't matter.
Overall, this is a great start, but needed to go back to the drawing board on mechanics.

UPDATED:  Many of the technical problems have been addressed, the core fundimentals have not changed.  It now seems to run pretty well.
OLD REVIEW:  Despite the nummerous reports of a great PC version, this game is very much in need of a patch.  For me, the game was crashing frequently during chapters 12 and then 15.  Updating the NVIDIA driver provided a tempoary fix.  Right now I believe the checkpoint file is simply becoming corrupted.
If the crashing problem is addressed, this review will be revised.
As for the game itself,  it is stylish and visually captivating. The combat is generally satfying, with numerous combos and a frame-specific dodge move that will test your dexterity.  Much of your enjoyment will depend on whether you have the patience to master the game's mechanics.
However there are definitely problems, problems I believe many other reviewers gloss over for whatever reason.  Like many 3D hack 'n' slash games, the camera is abysmal.  Often it is not pointing in the direction of the enemies around you, so you can not see what they are doing.  With such fast-paced combat, this is most certainly a problem and often leads to unfair damage and cheap deaths.  Since you will be relying on the face buttons for all of your attacks, there is practically no time to adjust the camera with the right thumbstick.  To add to this frustration, some of the design choices in this game are plainly dated; turrets sections, vehicles sections, and quick-time events.  None of these gameplay elements are as refined as the combat.  The story is complete non-sense and very hard to follow, but at least it's sefl-aware enough to know ridiculous it is.  The main titular character is very appealing self-assured.  However the child character is incredibly irritating and tries tries way too hard to be cute.  The male characters are often silly and inconsiquential.  Jeanne, your nemesis, provides more waifu pandering in a game that already has plenty to begin with.
Overall Bayonetta is an at times enjoyable game that has a number of problems.  The technical ones for this port need to be addressed before I can give it a recommendation.

-Even though the challenge the game offers is nice, it is rage inducingly difficult. Some levels left me screaming at my screen as I tried it for the hundredth time over. Also, if you are a completionist like me, good luck getting those achievements.

If you're someone who has never touched the command line on a *nix system, then this will probably be a game that has a lot more milage for you.  It's a very simplified version of a terminal for a *nix system, and it's not easy to pick up the basic commands it requires you to learn.
On the other hand, if you have ever worked on the command line before, you'll find yourself being pretty frustrated that this game doesn't have a more advanced mode for navigation on the system.  You'll frequently find yourself dumbing down your navigation and wish you had things like:
find
sort
vim/nano -- why can't we manipulate logs in this game?
man (force of habit)
grep
Overall, not a bad game.  Feels a little slow if you have CLI experience, but generally fosters the good general detective work anyone would want to use when tracking something down on a system.

I've decided to reconsider my view on the BASE game Xcom 2.
The DLC that was released for the most part, was money-grabbing♥♥♥♥♥♥ that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me (and a lot of others) off, as no doubt easily seen when looking at the general consensus (negative) of the Season pass, and most of the DLC.
The Last Spark DLC is decent for what it adds, $10 for a reasonably decent new class and some story content, ultimately while not being the best content I would have liked (not enough customization options, not enough tactical options; fixed in War of the Chosen tactical wise), it was definitely the best post-release content they published.
I'd recommend looking into War of the Chosen if you intend to actually buy/play this game (do some shopping, reputable sites like GMG or Amazon are good alternatives, have decent discounts, Humble Bundle might have a good discount as well, and Steam might months after release). WoTC adds a lot of new content, and fixes a lot of issues in the base-game.
Now onto the base-game itself, my review is not based on the DLC policies (though I did mention part of it above to get my point clear and offer reasonable advice). The game functions moderately well, not completely stable, though significantly better than at-launch. The graphics are pretty great for this kind of game, though not as great as say Witcher 3 or similar AAA games (this is a strategy game however, with the graphics being an almost-afterthought.
There are both parts of the spectrum in this game, strategy and tactical, with the strategy layer being kind of minimalistic in design, and it's tactical layer being the major-gameplay focus. The strategy layer is where you go from point to point, gathering various objectives (which spawn partially based on RNG, partly based on date in game, later the date, more powerful the foes become), build facilities, items, do research to obtain better items/more options (usually started by killing foes, and disecting their bodies to study and learn), ultimately it is the place where you spend a minor amount of your time, but is somewhat crucial to your overall success, you have to choose which missions to take, which ones that you can't afford to take, which objectives to go for and which you can't, every day you spend somewhere is a day you can't elsewhere, and the enemies grow stronger as the days accumulate, so everything is an opportunity cost.
The tactical layer is, again, where the majority of your activity and playtime will occur. There are spanning maps in which you have to navigate the battlefield, usually starting in stealth to scout out and ambush, but sometimes you will be put into scenarios in which you are unable to do so (certain missions start you already revealed). This game has perma-death, meaning when a soldier dies, they die. Each character can equip armor, weapons, utility items, which include but are not limited to flashbangs (interrupt some abilities), lethal grenades like frags or plasma, medkits, smoke grenades, armor that increases health (not the same as armor armor), ammunitions that give various bonuses, and things that are situational, like mindshields that prevent psi powers from affecting that character's mind. Armor (the actual personal armor, not utility) can be replaced with various options, ones that allow you to run through walls, grapple, become cover for your allies, fire off rockets/flamethrowers, and also provide 'armor' that reduces damage taken by that amount, unless it is 'shredded' by certain attacks or explosions.
The tactical depth is pretty well-done, with characters having skill trees that allow for moderate amounts of customization, like improved swords or stealth even if group breaks stealth (or doesn't start in it), remote-healing or remote-damage dealing, etc. Flanking, suppression, cover removal, overwatch (reactionary shots to enemy movement typically), grenades, etc. are still featured in the game. Properly utilizing both the resources you have in the tactical and strategic layers will determine success or failure. The ability to provide equipment for your troops (which is always needed and wanted) requires you to properly manage the credits you have, the time it takes to get more, to build buildings, to train troops, or to have them recover from wounds. If you aren't careful, you could end up with a heavily-invested in soldier (high ranking, lots of abilities, extra stats, etc.) dying, and perhaps even their gear could be lost if you don't recover it. The two tie in together very well, if you fail on one, the other will no doubt suffer.
The ultimate goal of the campaign is to win before the 'Avatar Project' is completed, with you performing a multitude of actions in order to reduce their progress, make your troops more ready, improve your equipment, facilities, and/or income, before the final showdown. The more time you take, the better prepared your troops become, but you must also hurry as that means their forces will ramp up in intensity.
Ultimately, the game is somewhat challenging at times, and has moderate-decent customization options. The tactical layer is improved over the previous game, and the strategic layer isn't that bad either, better than the first game by far.
I'd price it's subjective value at about $30, with the new DLC being similarly priced at about $30 (I've watched 20-30 hours of the new content, from start to finish of a campaign).

An interesting mix between Uplink and Street Hacker, for the price of ~10 USD is definitely worth checking out.
The game is pretty fun, some things require attention to detail and logical thinking, and the humor is pretty good!
However, the game launched with a very bad bug which might make your save useless: if you try to make two missions at a time, you won't be able to complete the first one. This can simply kill your save.
Also, even though the presentation is well done and the interface looks pretty, I don't see much advance over what other Hacking games did before (Uplink was released in 2001), so you really should approach this with caution. The biggest difference here is being able to use both a GUI and a Console - which is good news.
This doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the game, of course. But it does dissapoint if you expected anything more than that.
I haven't finished the game yet, due to the bug that probably broke my savegame. But about the plot: it's decently intriguing and will make you want to uncover all the secrets, as a hacking game should.
So even though I ended up pretty disappointed - it's 2015, yet there's little news here. Even Street Hacker, which is a decade old and terribly programmed, had deeper features; and Uplink had a more compelling gameplay and story - there's still some fun to be had and some jokes/moments actually made me laugh or smile.
I do recommend waiting for a patch before playing it, though. So rush it on your own risk. :)
Thanks for reading!

Ok so you know what your getting with this, you should know by the screen shots, the description and indie price so on that part there are no excuses to dislike HackNet. I think it's great basically, it sort of gives me a nostalgic feel and I think  the devs at Team Fractal Alligator have done a cracking job in balancing everything out and maing it appeal not to just a specific set of people but a much wider audience than these types of games have before.
If you are a seasoned gamer then you'll remember a game a lot of reviewers are talking about called UpLink which was a very simular game from eons ago and was a huge cult hit, still is popular to this day. There have been a number of attempts over the years to create a modern day version, but getting the right mix of everything is the hardest part.
You don't want or need large rendering graphics, but obviously you do need some graphics I mean, just some kind of plain shell console throughout the entire game would really restrict the audience!  HackNet has got that just right in my opinion, there isn't too much, there isn't too little and the graphics that are used in modern developing are not that extensive.
Such a game has always really been targeted at a specific audience, namely the geeks and nerds and one thing that hasn't changed as much as it's not been completly dumbed down too much terminolgy wise. I mean I know other geeks and nerds and some of those know little about programming, but they can pretty much recite you the episode names for every stark trek series, in order. And HackNet appears to those people too because it has a point and click feature as well as a shell command prompt for those of who us are interesting more in that sense and have had previous exposure to a simular kind of environment over the years.
You can pretty much come into this game with generally no knowledge about hacking and have an enjoyable experience, and pinking up terminology whilst learning new things along the way. For some of you it could turn out to be a very educational experience. So all in all, I personally think it would be money well spent. Or if you are still cautious, it's worth the risk, you'll know in under two hours or not whether this is the game for you.

Overall, a great PnC game in the classic format of the genre, which I have been craving for ever!
I didnt even know that these are being made anymore until I happened upon it.
I'll give all the good points from my view first:
The visuals are bloody amazing, the artistic way in which the environment and the characters have been drawn and animated really pulls you into this world and envelops you.
Almost all the puzzles (i'll explain the "almost" in a minute) are very logical and realistic enough to be solved without too much banging your head against the desk with the occasional extra bit of strain on the brain to figure it out.  However, there are a small number of puzzles that were extremely irritating due not to being too tricky, but because they were just highly illogical (eg.  you need a light to be able to access a certain part of an area and even though there is a lamp available in a different location, the character refuses to take it for a silly reason, I understand where the dev's were coming from on this front, though, because you need to get through quite a few scenes in that area before you leave it for good, and if you are able to take the lamp away, that would be stupid because the room would end up in total darkness when you still need to get things done there, and allowing to take the lamp only later in the game would also look weird, but it still just feels unrealistic a problem. like I said there are a few frustrating bits like this but not many, I'm not ashamed to admit I used a walkthrough to get through these problem areas, and even when being given the solution from an outside source, I still stand that I wouldnt have found the solution through logical thinking, if I did find it would be by accident or chance)
The music is great, creates a very good accompaniment to what you are seeing and experiencing with the story line in each scene.  The composer did a sterling job on the soundtrack, if you read this, sir, I salute you.  From one composer to another ;)
The only real peave that ground my gears all the way through the game was the voice acting and the script.  Whenever there was dialogue, it always sounds like the actors were reading the script straight off the page for the first time and recording it right there.  Many of the accents sounded a little bit forced, as if the accent being spoken isnt the actor's native accent and they're trying too hard to get it right. I'm sure the company had a limited budget on the development but I think, if you're doing a game that is so story-driven, try put in a decent enough budget to hire professional actors to do the job, this was really the one aspect of the game that just kept me from being able to fully enjoy the storytelling.  For some reason, also, all the dialogue was extremely draggy, every character speaks really slowly for some reason.  Fortunately there is subtitles so I just read ahead while they took their sweet time talking and just clicked for the next bit of dialogue.  Also the script wasnt always the best, it was ok for the most part, but there were times that it really just didnt suit the character, like "Hunter" for example, ending almost every sentence with "dude" where it's obvious the man is not used to saying the word, sounded like an uncle meeting a teenager for the first time and trying, desperately, to sound cool, or "hip" as all the youngsters are calling it these days, dude...
A lot of people are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with the cliffhanger ending, but I think its all good as long as a sequel is produced in due course, which I believe it has so I'm really not bothered by that, sometimes it's a great way to prepare the audience for the next part of the story and to whet the appetite, keep em coming back for more.
All in all, Its a ♥♥♥♥ing great game guys!  if you look past the bad acting and one or two weird puzzles, its actually a beautiful piece of art, and a cool concept.  I love the Post-Apocalyptic vibe and time warpage.  And most of all the darkness of the game, I'd definitely recomment it.

I absolutely loved XCOM: EU and I'm a huge fan of tactial combat and strategy games. Not only did i sink quite a bit of time into XCOM: EU, but i actually bought the iOS version so i could play it when im away from my computer.
Like a lot of other fans of XCOM, when i saw XCOM 2 announced and i saw all the trailers for how the game looked and how much more stuff there was going to be in XCOM 2, I almost♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants in excitement. I preordered the game and I was so ♥♥♥♥ing ready to play this game. You can imagine how upset i was when the game launched and was practically unplayable because it ran like♥♥♥♥♥♥for so many people. I was willing to wait however, because i knew this game was going to be great.
Promptly after the Launch Day issues were resolved, a lot of people were saying that the game was unplayable, and to an extent, it still is. XCOM 2 is arguably one of the most difficult and punishing squad-based tactical combat strategy games on the market today. When the game first launched and everyone was talking about XCOM 2, i heard a lot of statements that followed the general idea of "XCOM 2 is the Dark Souls of combat strategy games".
Much like dark souls, XCOM 2 does not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about your precious little feelings. "Im sorry to hear that you missed with a 99% chance to hit, but you're still going to die here"  Clearly, there is a lot of XCOM:EU still reminiscent in XCOM 2, but there also isn't. This is why i feel so torn about giving this game a positive review, because i cant give it a neutral review, but i don't think it deserves a negative review. Let me run through the pros and cons real quick.
Pros:
+Excellent turn-based strategy that you know from XCOM:EU
+Abundant customization options (who wouldn't want to slice sectiods in half while wearing a top-hat and monocle?)
+DIVERSITY (good lord are there a lot of different enemy types in XCOM 2, which is something that i wish XCOM:EU had. I get that there are elite type enemies in XCOM:EU, but in the end theyre pretty much the same enemies, but stronger. XCOM 2 has a large variety of completely different enemies that have their own seperate abilities, armors, weapons, hopes, dreams, etc.)
+MELEE COMBAT (why wasn't this is the vanilla XCOM:EU?)
+Mod Support (idk about you guys, but if you arent saving the world as Guy Fieri, Shrek, John Cena, and Hatsune Miku, i think youre playing this game wrong)
~Unbalanced Gameplay (I love an uphill battle, and i totally understand that an uphill battle is exactly what the devs were going for when they made the game. After all, youre the resistance. You dont have military-grade stuff, so naturally the enemy will have better weapons and equipment. I put this as an iffy kind of thing as many people might be upset about the steep difficulty curve.)
~Lack of customization options (?) (honestly im not sure if this is the right way to put this, but i wish there were more basic styles for faces and hair. I kept getting recruits with the same faces, and i like to think that the resistance were only recruiting people from the same bloodline, but since those people kept dying, i dont think their bloodline would have lasted very long.)
Cons:
-HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥THIS GAME IS HARD (I like an uphill battle, but this game is unfairly difficult. There's the obvious 99% chance to hit situation, but there has been more than one time where i was directly adjacent to an enemy and i had a 35% chance to hit with a melee attack. Not a ranged attack, a MELEE attack. Honestly, the swords would do better to just be a decorative piece than an actual weapon.)
-Unoptimized (don't expect to be able to run this on any computer that could just barely run XCOM:EU)
-Unoriginal Story line (I really do want to like the story of XCOM 2, but i would have greatly prefered a situation where we did defend earth, but they came back in greater numbers, like the new independence day movie.)
-Less than (inter)Stellar voice acting (I didnt find Tygan or Lily to be super interesting characters. Like, i understand that  XCOM:EU's Dr.Shen would have taken a major stand against the alien forces and died doing such, but I find it a little odd that his daughter, who apparently would have been a little girl during the events of XCOM:EU, grew up to do the exact same thing as her father, with the exact same, if not more, skill as her father. Also, where the hell did Dr.Vahlen go? RIP(?))
I feel like a lot of the points I've made about the game's difficulty could be best sumarrized by the Best Friends Play XCOM 2 series. I believe there are 7 parts to the series, but im probably wrong about that. They do a great job of going into greater depth about a lot of the topics i've covered here, but then again, theyre considerably bigger losers than i am.
TL;DR
In the end i have to give this game a 7.5/10
If you like games with a 90 degree difficulty curve, smashing keyboards out of anger, and beating your head against a brick wall until you or the wall falls, then you will love this game.
Also it helps if youre a fan boy of XCOM:EU and Dark Souls like I am.

Darkest Dungeon is a beautifully polished game filled with eldritch horrors alongside campy humor. Each of the bucketful of character classes plays differently, and finding combinations of types that work together is a joy. The art and animation is a clever use of low-budget (other "indie" gamemakers take note); it fits the game theme beautifully. The whole game is dark and difficult and weird.
Unfortunately, as others have mentioned, you are at the mercy of a RNG. The game itself has a disclaimer when you first start; it warns you that the game is never going to be easy, and will always be about managing terrible situations. Fine.
The trouble is, though, that the game is a mix of "perfect" strategy (each character class has best-in-slot items and abilities and positions and partners) and utter hands-off randomness. There's nothing you can do to respond to a situation; the dungeons are random, the combats are random, and the rolls are random. So even if you have a plan for addressing a certain type of situation, there's literally nothing you can do to react to a problem when it comes up. The perfect strategy is also frustrating - there's no point in trying a first-slot Vestal, for example. There's a use and pairing for each class. You'll need to get all of them, but it still won't matter.
Overall, this is a great start, but needed to go back to the drawing board on mechanics.

The worst Bethesda RPG yet for a myriad of reasons, but most notably, because of its lack of soul. Everything -- from its characters, its open world, its towns, and its storylines are completely bland and boring. Characters spout obvious archetypes and obnoxious dialogue. Major hub cities are underwhelming, especially for a title coming out in the year of The Witcher 3. Gameplay becomes repetitive fast, partly because the game starts out handing you power armor and a deathclaw fight (two things that should have been more ceremoniously delivered in a fallout game) right at the very beginning. Weapon variety and armor variety is lacking. The gameplay still suffers from typical Bethesda wonkiness, but the main difference in Fallout 4, is that there is no engaging world and storyline surrounding that gameplay that encourages you to keep playing in spite of it. Considering Fallout 3 is my favorite game of all time, Fallout 4 is a massive dissappointment.

First let me say I do love this game. I like most everything about it. However, I just can't recommend it in it's current state. That being said, don't pass on this game completely! Once it updates and the bugs are fixed the game will be worth the full price easily.
As I write this, I have two seperate games that I have played that are frozen where they are in the storyline due to bugs. I can't go any further.
The major bug that plagues players right now is that you cannot accept any "jobs" while you have one active. The game will let you do so, but when you do it will render all previously accepted missions impossible to complete. One my first playthrough, I was not aware of this and got hours in before I encountered the bug. Second playthrough I was being careful- only sought out one mission at a time. The bug got me when I overlooked an email and took on another quest. That email that I overlooked was the main storyline calling, and because I didn't immediately perform it, I couldn't complete the mission. Game two over.
I hate to say this, but I just cant recommend it at this time. There are other issues involving savegame corruption as well. I look forward to the developer (who is highly active and responisve) fixing these problems and I will update my review to recommend at that time. Until then, I would pass on a purchase but put it on your wishlist for later.
UPDATE- The dev replied to this review directly, which you can see in the comments of this review. That speaks volumes to me that this is a good dev that cares about this game- the kind of dev that I feel that we (the Steam community) need to support. I anticipate changing this review from negative to positive soon.
SECOND UPDATE (07/08/16)- The bugs are now fixed, and this is a really good game highly recommed.

It is a bit sad to have to end up writing a "negative" review for this game. TL:DR : the game ends abruptly, there might be a second chapter, i guess? In its current condition the game is just not complete.
Plot wise...this is the most odd part. Aside of the amount of backtracking (it looks like as if each single puzzles requires you to get back each single time), you can sort of enjoy the usual sort of adventure with no major twist on the gameplay.
The story itself goes through a sort of apocalyptic "end of the world" theme: the entire world has been struck with an event (which is very generically described) and humanity is now plagued by a disease which renders ill people into dissolution, therefore making them the Dissolved. Your role sets a bit between trying to find out a cure and finding the truth about yourself, as you seem to be linked to it...
Some of the puzzles are pretty much non-sense...that kind of breaks the immersion you can have, although aside of them the overall story deserves to be played, despite of the major issue with it: basically, the game ends abruptly, cutting the story short of any end at all.
Visually, it is an outstanding looking game: the background images are drawn in a way that leaves little to imagination, it really shows how the concept was right there. And within its cruel and sharp desolation, it also has a sort of aesthetic value to itself...
The voice acting is truly accurate, well executed and on spot: each voice feels fitting to the character it is talking for, and each of the characters are well thought of, well characterized and truly set apart from each other.
On a sad note, the soundtrack sounds to me as if its not particularly (always) fitting to the atmosphere, and in particular the default volume balance (which is set to 100% for both the soundtrack and dialogues) makes it really overwhelming! I actually toned it down about to 70%. Anyhow, it feels a bit too exhaggerated most of the time, there are a couple of times when it truly feels fitting, but for the most part i felt like the rythm it uses is too fast in comparison to the scene its coupled with.

Drop Alive is OK. The concept is good but the poor mechanics were rage inducing.
- Visuals and music are nice.
- I really like the concept of this game. You're a water droplet that is slowly reducing in size. Water will bring you back to normal size, and the environment can change your form (steam/ice). It's simple, but clever.
- My main issue with this game are the controls. It feels sluggish and sometimes unresponsive, making precision jumping more difficult than it should be.
- Vertical movement when you are in steam form is annoying. You cannot move up faster, but you can press down (which moves you down a fixed distance). Every time you press down, you lose size, speeding up your death. If you pair this with the timing of the fire streams, it becomes a recipe for rage.
- Death is punishing. You start at the beginning of the level and must recollect any tokens you previously found. I usually don't consider this a negative aspect (games should be challenging), but the poor controls and unclear hitbox make deaths quite frustrating.
- The last two levels are long and frustrating to complete (especially if you want to collect all tokens). I found myself raging quite a bit in the process.
- I encountered a glitch where some of my collected tokens randomly disappeared in the level selection screen. Although I had collected some tokens (and completed the level) it did not register. I had to replay some levels to get the achievement.
Drop Alive is not bad, but it's not very well polished either. I wish there was a neutral recommendation option. In its current state, I cannot recommend this game. This surprisingly dark game has an interesting premise, that I won't spoil here, but that I quite enjoyed. It's basically a fairly standard grapic adventure gameplay  wise. Lots of conversations with NPC's, grab every item that isn't nailed down and then use them in iventory based puzzles.
Your character wakes up at the beginning of the game with no recollection of who they are (yeah, that old chestnut), and you will quickly discover that you are in a post apocalyptic hell hole and are effectively trapped in a facist run concentration camp. It does a very good job of creating a forboding sense of hopelessness and despair, and over the course of the game you will do some very dark things indeed. All of this is driven by the central mystery of what the hell happened. The end of the world came with something referred to as the "Wave", that laid waste to cities and populations. Over the course of the game you will set out to discover just what the Wave was and why it happened. Its pretty compelling stuff.
The game uses a very unusual graphic style that I really wasn't a fan of at first, but I'll admit had really grown on me by the end. Music is suitably ominous. Voice work is patchy, the main character is very good fortunately, but some of the supporting cast are pretty bad. It's kind of usual indie game on a budget syndrome with some people delivering a strong performance, while others just sound like whatever friends or family they could get to come to the office.
As a caveat there were a few annoying puzzles that I wouldn't have solved without a walkthrough. But honestly, that is not unusual for this genre. It just bears mentioning.
All up I recommend it to adventure fans who aren't afraid of a darked tale.

It's an interesting setting for what could be a good adventure game story, but sadly it falls short. It probably varies from person to person, whether or not the things I found to be problematic are bad in their eyes. So I will list them below, so it's easy to make your own decision.
I will keep it spoiler free.
Art style:
The art style is great and helps keep it easy to see all interactable items in the world, so you don't have to do the old adventure back-and-forth to make sure you didn't miss anything. It makes you concentrate on the story and the task at hand, which is good. Only a couple of times does the game hide things by making them virtually invisible -- that it is so infrequent makes it extra annoying, because you have no idea where you might have missed something.
All in all, this part is great.
Story:
The story starts out with the old "amnesia" trope (first seconds of the game, so not a spoiler), which is a trope, because it works. As part of the game you try to find out who you are, and at first it seems like this is done in a great way by letting you notice things on your own and piecing things together, but around mid-game it changes and you get force fed exposition in huge lumps. Often this exposition repeats itself by recapping things you learned 5 minutes earlier and at times painfully obvious things were explained to you as if you hadn't been paying any attention to the game up to that point.
It's bad storytelling and really makes the game worse since adventure games rely heavily on the story.
The story itself is ok, though I didn't really like the explanations it used for why things are as they are in the game. Especially the part where the game explains the games titular element feels painfully forced.
Puzzles:
The puzzles are for the most part very logical, so you almost never end up doing the inventory shuffle, where you combine everything with everything else. Great. There is even a good array of interesting achievements for fun combinations, which rewards the player for having fun. Double great. On top of that many combinations have semi-unique voice responses from the character and often give a hint to the use of the items, which all in all makes it fun to play around and helps you from being stuck.
Just great work in this department.
There are a couple of times where it makes no sense at all, what you have to combine, but when the rest is done so well, it didn't really bother me too much. Especially since it was with items you knew you needed to do something to and items you had not yet used -- so the combination will likely be one of the first you try even if it makes no sense.
You can argue that the repeated "I have used this super useful item, so now I will just throw it away" moments are annoying, but I can understand the need to clear out inventory even if I don't agree on this method.
Choices:
Not many adventure games give you any real choices. Some let you solve a puzzle in more than one way, thereby letting you feel a bit like you made a choice. This game does a whole third thing, which is really frustrating and the main reason that I didn't like it.
The story is extremely linear and at times it is directly railroaded.
You almost always only have one thing you need to do next -- one puzzle you have to solve. It may be personal preference whether or not this is something you like, but I don't like that. To me adventure games are better when you can go do other things while you think about how you can solve any specific puzzle. Yes, there are times where you need to do 2-3 things, but they are always linked, so you know that in order to do puzzle A, you know you have to do B which is obviously blocked by C, etc.
In conversations, you get to choose your replies. Or rather, no. You are presented with a list of things to say and often you are forced to click them all before you are allowed to stop talking to the person. This is very annoying especially since a lot of the lines are things you know are directly stupid things to say. But the game forces your hand.
Where the game directly railroads you is by again and again forcing your character to do some of the absolutely dumbest things you can think of. Either by you ending a conversation without revealing sensitive information to someone who absolutely shouldn't know it and then taking control of your character as you are about to leave. You character then returns to the conversation, reveals the information and only then are you allowed to leave. Forced and infuriating. Happens again and again and each time it just feels like you might as well just be watching a badly written movie because you really have no choice and the things the game forces you to do are so dumb that only lazy story writers use these elements to force the story to move on.
At the end I hated the game for doing this.
Voice acting:
Voice acting varies a lot. The main character does a good job with the material he has been given and it helps the game a lot. But many of the side characters -- especially the children -- are horrible actors. Don't get me wrong, there are also some good voice actors for the side characters, but the bad ones really are so bad, that it breaks the immersion. The kind that sound like they are just monotonically reading the lines.
Ending:
The game is super short.
The second you get to the point where you think the "real" game is about to begin, it ends abruptly. All up to that point feels a bit like you just getting to know the world and why you are integral to the story. I can only speculate, but it feels like they just didn't finish the game.
TL;DR:
A potentially good game marred by a lacklustre story force fed to you by a game that enjoys taking control of your character in order to make sure the story continues no matter how dumb the way it does so is. It is frustrating, because you can see the potential it has and that a lot of care has gone into the many other aspects of the game.

For a game with an eerie and unsettling atmosphere, Darkest Dungeon manages to be addicting in its own way.
When the player starts the game, a couple cutscenes will introduce players to the upcoming adventure, providing backstory for what seems to be a world ridden by horrors and a plethora of hardships.
The player will impersonate the heir of a distant relative, who went seeking glory and fortune in the undergrounds of his mansion. However, said relative opened a portal to a dimension of eldritch horrors and abominations, which once unleashed would spread around the world, bringing terror and desolation.
The player will hence enlist adventurers from around the globe to aid stop the spreading corruption at its core. Holy warriors, brigands and wizards will try to find redemption by taking part to quests varying in difficulty, longevity and objective.
The Hamlet will be the player's operations base, containing several buildings such as taverns, blacksmiths and guilds in order to help form a strong and resolute roster to employ in harder missions, preparing eventually for the final adventure in the Darkest Dungeon itself.
A peculiar feature about gameplay is the presence of a stress mechanic: during a quest your party of heroes, basing on several factors (light intensity, enemies with stress inducing skills etc.) will suffer an amount of fatigue which, upon reaching a certain cap, will change them for the rest of the quest. An hero can either become afflicted from stress, with its statistics changed towards a negative amount: the hero will also induce stress on others by discouraging them or being disrespectful.
There is also a smaller chance for the hero to become virtuous, which will largely decrease its stress value and the other heroes alike, as well as possibly buffing them.
The game's arts and soundtracks are polished and fit the depressing atmosphere really well. A narrator (voiced by Wayne June) will comment several times the player's choices and actions with cynical quotes, which greatly increase the immersion inside the game world.
Suggested to all RPG and management games fans.

Finding Teddy is a point n' click puzzle in which you play a little girls whose teddy-bear has been taken by a weird arm from the closet during your night.
What else would you do? Just go through the closet to get it back! Then, you find yourself in a wonderland.
There, there are "monters" which you need to help, and they help you in return. Otherwise they'll just eat you. That's life.
Point n' click games aren't really my kind of game, and this one doesn't change that. It has the aspects of those games that I don't like, such as very slow and little actual gameplay, and puzzles are sometimes too cryptic and turn into a click-fest.
But I certainly liked this game quite a bit, and it has certain aspects that make it unique.
First off, the artstyle. Despite very minimal, it's really well done. Every scenery looks very good, and the world seems alive because of it. You can see it from the screenshots, it almost gives me a Sword and Sworcery feel, but still stands on its own. Nothing to complain in this regard, and it's one of the aspects I liked the most.
Music didn't really standout to me, it was more ambience oriented, and that's ok, but I didn't find it particularly good. I wasn't bad either, but I barely payed notice to it. I'm talking about general music, and sound effects.
Then, there is a really cool mechanic with it, about which I'll talk further.
Gameplay is mostly standard point n' click. You click on the edges of the screen you want to go, or the item you want to pick up. Then, you click on yourself if you want to use items.
So, pretty standard, I'd say.
But, you eventually get a flute. With this flute, you can play different notes and pitches, and each note represents a letter of the alphabet.
With this, you can interact with some characters, and even try to translate what they're saying by finding which letter matches with a sound. This is something I've never seen before, and it works well, for the most part. Other times, you have to respond back, choosing the letter, and so creating a melody.
This gives a whole new aspect to both the mechanics and the world, and it's what makes it truly unique!
A big complaint I have with it, though, it that the background music sometimes overlaps with it, making it a bit too hard to figure out which sound you want. That's was really annoying at one point, but nothing you can't solve.
You go through 3 different stages, with different characters, and then you have a final "boss", which is all about communication, with a little easter egg in there.
In each stage, you have some optional monsters that may or may not be necessary to progress the story, and you should pay attention to them, because the Boss is mostly about things you've experienced before in the game.
Unfortunately, you can probably finish the game in a single hour, or so. Then comes NewGame+. I think this one was pretty bad, to be honest. The wonder and surprise from the first walkthrough is mostly gone, and you're left to "collect" Fireflies that appear on some areas. These aren't really hidden or anything, it's just about playing the game once again. Plus, it's a really cheap way to increase the game's longevity... why not give you the option the first time?
Aside from the fireflies, you can have a different look to your character, which could be cool... but whenever there is a scripted sequence, your character changes back during it. I don't know why this happens, but it feels very awkward. Would be nice to see it solved for future players. Nothing too bad, but an annoyance nonetheless.
Along with this, the achievements were mostly really bad, in my opinion. Half of them are to reward you for dying in each encounter. Instead of rewarding to figuring out things before hand, it rewards for failing. ... Why? It makes people purposefully failing if they want the achievement and have played well on their first time... It makes no sense to me, and it is the exact opposite purpose that achievements should have.
My final complaint is not being able to Alt Tab the game, or even changing options during gameplay. There are no sliders for the music and SFX, Alt-Tabbing doesn't work, there are a lot of annoying things about it in a technical level. These could be very easily solved, but the developers seemed to have taken the easier way out and just made something quick that worked... somewhat.
I've done everything there was to do in the game, it took my 2 and 1/2 hours, in 2 playthroughs, which is really short.
If you can withstand all the technical issues and annoyances, you'll actually find a really pretty game with some unique features to it.
I think it's worth playing once only, in my opinion. I'm interested what else can be done with this concept, and I'll be paying attention to you, "LookAtMyGames".
Go ahead and try it, it has its strenghts!

This is a surprisingly lively action puzzle combination that is easily one of my favorite indie game i've ever played. Only two hours long, and i spent the entire game highly entertained. WARNING: this game has a lot more puzzle than action. I see a lot of the reviews and it seems people who don't enjoy puzzle solving won't enjoy this game
The core of the game revolves around combining cubes. Different cube combinations can build towers that either attack enemies or support your attacking towers. You can also pull cubes through enemies to deal sizable damage, which is surprisingly effective when possible. Without cubes your player character has no offensive power to deal with enemies, which means you deal with the enemies almost entirely through building structures that fight for you.
I was surprised how smoothly the game played. Usually genre mixers tend to rely heavily on the first genre and include small elements from the second, but cubetractor makes an effort to blend the two and I personally found that it gave the player a lot of choice in how they can approach. You can start every level guns blazing combining as many cubes as possible and brute forcing the answer  but if you slow down you can find more efficient ways to complete a level. Most levels past the first three have 2-3 ways you can complete them and often sitting at the spawn point to plan out the level can be really enjoyable. One level i remember essentially having three different puzzles inside it, but you had to complete one puzzle in order to access the blocks to solve a second puzzle. Once you solve the second puzzle, you have to tear down buildings you had used for the first section to create a tower yet to be used in the level to hit some distant hard to reach enemies to unlock the exit.
The complicated levels and variety of strategies make for a more interactive world and you don't feel like you're solving puzzles as much as you are solving problems that happen to be in the way of you and your goal. I didn't get the sense i get with most puzzle games that rather than solving puzzles because i enjoyed solving puzzles I was solving the puzzles just to finish the game. Instead Cubetractor's level design was a lot of fun.
I only have two real complaints. Firstly, I did often found myself rushing to get the action going only to completely miss a cube in the corner that would make the level significantly easier. This happenned about three times before i noticed how often the developer seemed to put important cubes in corners, as if the devs were trying to teach the player to focus on their sourroundings. It's not really the developers fault that i wasn't paying attention, but it was very frusterating to fail a level multiple times only to notice how easy the solution was. Secondly the main story is somewhat confusing. You can choose to do the extra levels to get more of the story content, but even if you don't the game treats the story as if you had done all the side missions and learned all the characters quirks. Also don't bother trying to invest in the story. The characters can be cute in that Sesame Street sort of way where each character has a personality quirk or a gimmick, but pay too much attention and you notice how flat the writing is.
Overall a very positive experience. If you're a fan of puzzle games you will definately enjoy Cubetractor

I don't recall them trying to surround me). The RPG elements, mostly presented as perks, are ok, again, nothing noteworthy, with many being just percentage increments of something. The game also features a settlement system, that is rather barebones in the vanilla game, with very few lines of dialog and things to do with them.
Story: I won't go into detail on the story and it's merits,but my overall impressions are that it's not bad However it is affected because of two factors: a lack of either a defined backstory for your character, or the ability to mold it; and second, the dialog system. The first affects your ability to properly define your protagonist motivations and how you fit in the world. The second affects your ability to define your character as the story progesses, because the dialog feels contrived by the design decision of only and always having four options, with many times resulting in different flavors of "yes". Besides that, it lacks clear consequences for your actions, which differenciate clealry over different playthroughs. In that sense the story is rather linear, albeit just granting you the ability to do things in differnt orders.
Miscellaneous: the addition of the Creation Club certenly does no favors to this game, since it was a poor implementation of something different than your usual mods (either re-skins, or addition of some armor or weapon). As it is right now, it's presicely that, and to the consumer it's not a favorable desicion, and neither does it look like for the modders.
