As a young child losing something as seemingly trivial as a stuffed animal can be devastating. So imagine the shock of waking up in the middle of the night to see a monster climbing out of your wardrobe and making off with your teddy bear. Finding Teddy is the journey of a little girl off to reclaim what is most valuable to her, plunging headfirst into an uncanny dreamscape full of bizarre creatures and even stranger sounds in a lightweight point and click adventure.
Navigating the world by simple presses to the edge of the screen, you travel though nonlinear levels collecting items and solving basic puzzles. Many of these revolve around forming odd musical messages, in a bit of a call back to Close Encounters of the Third Kind, by which you communicate with the inhabitants of the strange world you find yourself in. As a musician I personally found these fun to solve and more original than the simple "bring object A to point B" that otherwise make up the bulk of the puzzles, but it should be noted that those with less of an ear for music or are even tone deaf will likely find them infuriating, perhaps even impossible. This is not to say only musicians and the like will be able to enjoy the game, but I feel it is wroth mentioning for those that find it difficult to pick out distinct notes, as this is likely not something for you.
Despite its initially dark appearance it is actually very sweet, with a charming cast and a fantastic ending that left me feeling warm and smiling through the credits. The pixel artstyle is quite lovely to look at despite a few jerky animations, and the soundtrack while generally just ambient noise is quite good when it decides to take more of a center role. The one thing that might turn people off is that it is very short, as I finished it in just under two and a half hours despite getting stuck at several areas. Veteran adventure game players will almost surely burn through it in even less, and aside from a few secret achievements there isn't any reason to return.
If you are not turned away by the somewhat frustrating musical puzzles and brief playtime, I would definitely recommend Finding Teddy to any fan of classic adventure games. It wasn't the least what I expected, but turned into something I grew quite fond of over my brief tour and expect many will find a relaxing and welcome change of pace to most modern gaming fare

is a strange and unique game where you play as Endroi, a robotic drone who seems to take strange delight in completing puzzles and frustrating the plans of his creators in a comically overblown fashion. Practically, the game is quite simple. You move your robot around the board and use the space bar to attract blocks toward your position. Once in motion, the blocks continue until they strike something causing damage, merge with another moving block to form a tower, or leave the screen. Cubes can be pulled only once (they will regenerate after a few seconds) and only in straight lines. The game is all about creating towers and striking enemies with moving cubes as you progress down the path toward freedom. The greatest advantage of this game is the story, you should read the entire contents during the game. On the other hand. the retro graphics of Cubetractor and the accompanying music start to bore very easily, although when it comes to music then you can always turn your own one. Worth buying during sales.

Finding Teddy reminded me of Superbrothers Sword & Sworcery EP. It's a point-and-click adventure, it's about the same length (just a couple of hours) and it has an amazing artstyle (even though Sword & Sworcery is just a tad more detailed). It's nicely animated, has a cute story and an unique way of solving puzzles, which rely mostly on sound. So you need a good ear to figure out how to imitate some of the tunes in it. After a while you'll figure out that the musical puzzles use a certain system. Once you figured that out the game will become a whole lot easier, believe me. I was impressed by the fact that the game was created in just a few months time. I have deep respect for that, because it's a polished game as far as I can tell.
Supposedly, there's also a New Game+, which should (could ?) give you a different ending and allows you to use a colored girl (instead of black and white) or use a mask that allows you find the fireflies hidden around the levels. I didn't feel like playing it a second time, but at least it's extra content.
Finding Teddy is a fine game, a game more people should play.

Finally, thank you, devs, for supporting Linux!

Spiral Knights is a chibi-style MMO dungeon crawler that encourages build building and gear engineering as the two things that will save your life against the monsters found in the Clockworks. The game was previously available as a standalone title but became Steam integrated, and has become one of the most popular free to play games to pioneer the genre.
The graphics are designed to be simple, stylistic, cute, and attractive. You'll find even the most monstrous of enemies to be some of the most adorable creatures in gaming, and the world itself to be heavily influenced by both steampunk and dungeon aesthetics. The game runs well due to its simplistic nature.
The balance of this game is based on a tier system, going from zero to five stars. In general, you can assume all weapons that fit into a single star level, ie one star, will be equal. There are some exceptions, most notably the bombs, but the situational effectiveness of these weapons outweighs their lack of general usefulness. You are encouraged to switch weapons at the start of every new level, to use your statuses and damage types to your advantage after learning the design of each level of the Clockworks.
The items system is based on a helmet and armor for defense, whilst offense includes two-four weapons depending on your buffs. The weapons can be swords (or hammers, maces, shovels, and machetes,) guns, or bombs. These items focus on one or two damage types, which will be more or less effective against enemies depending on their resistances. Some weapons also feature status effects, which in addition to doing extra damage, add even a second layer to effectiveness against only certain enemies. An additional tertiary type - trinkets - exists. These trinkets give small, varying bonuses such as defense, resistances, or health.
Most items in this game blend together in sets, giving you bonuses for combining certain items. This encourages owning multiple different sets, to properly fight everything the game has to offer. In addition, the four player coop allows you to fight with your friends where each person fills a specific niche role, combining to allow you to fight everything a level can offer.
The general 'idea' of this game is to make your way to a boss at your current tier. The world is split up into three tiers, and multiple different progressions down each tier. At the end of each progression through a tier, you fight a boss, which gives you exclusive loot and crowns (the game's currency.) Alternatively, you can use the relatively new missions feature to take a more story-based approach to the world, and fight everything the game has to offer at a good pace. After the fighting has cooled, you are brought to Haven, a public ground where you can do just about anything you expect from an MMO. Guild halls, an auction house, a training ground, and most importantly; vendors and crafting. Vendors sell items, sometimes exclusive for tokens or crowns. The crafting stations allow you to make items with a mixture of materials you find throughout the world, energy which you can purchase with crowns, and a recipe which you either earn from missions or purchase from the marketplace.
The progression of this game is wonderful, allowing you to slowly rank up and even engage in player versus player modes. You will slowly go from a weak, no star recruit to a five star knight of whatever specialization you choose to create. This truly engrosses you with your character, creating an attachment that can be tangible and real. You will truly come to love that cute little knight running around slaying cubes of grape jelly.
Servers are all official servers, as per usual with an MMO. The connection is good but unstable, where server disconnects are known to the playerbase but are relatively rare.
The story of this game is rather simple. You are a young knight in a seemingly desolate area who must help the army around you both rebuild and conquer the Clockworks. A simple premise, for sure, but an intriguing one. The missions system, which has not been a constant feature of the game, has added to this story and allowed it to blend seemlessly with progression.
The business model of this game is weak. A free to play game at its core, you can hop in and technically play the entire game in its entirety for free. Originally, to play more than ten levels a day you had to pay money to unlock more energy to keep going. This feature was removed, but with it, many prices were raised outside of that cost. This means that the game allows more grinding per day, but will take longer for that grind to be worth something. I would say this is a good thing as it encourages playing more per day than just playing for an hour a day. The prices are still definitely affordable.
Overall, this game can be fun for everyone; veterans of MMOs, young kids who enjoy the art and simplicity, or casual gamers looking for a cooperative experience. Stay for the cute art, the grinding and character building, or the engaging combat.
Overall Score: 87 - B+

So, I bought Dark Souls about 6 months after it came out on pc and well, I was not impressed. I initially didn’t have a controller, even after I picked one up I just wasn't into the movement of Dark Souls. It felt so clunky. . It just seemed like lame, slow combat with no sick moves haha.  At the time I was playing Kingdoms of Amalur or another action/rpg like that.
With my issues with the gameplay aside, I would have been down to stick it out and see what the game was about. However I quickly got frustrated with the so called difficulty of Dark Souls. The limiting bonfire system, no quest helper/tracker and the minimalist dialogue from the one npc at firelink made me just give up. I didn't see much of a story and what I did see was about as convoluted a story as I had seen.
With all of the frustration I had with Dark Souls I admit I still found it intriguing. I said to myself if they “fix” the movement and gameplay then I’ll give the series another shot. And so I waited, wanting to explore this acclaimed series but trying to find a more accessible entry point.
Dark Souls 2 came out and I was tempted but still apprehensive.
I bought Bloodborn on PS4 played it for 10 minutes and never played it again. My fault.
And then Dark Souls 3 came out, finally, the “modern” souls game I was looking for.
*********Spoilers**********************
Obviously, I waited for a Steam sale. I finally purchased Dark Souls 3. I was hoping that this would be a way for me to get into the Souls universe. I remembered the vague and cryptic story I had experienced and I was stoked to get into this.
So I started up Dark Souls 3 (again without a controller) and after 3 hours I got past Iudex, the first boss. I was excited by the movement being much smoother and also frustrated by the keyboard.  So I proceeded on with the game, moving onto Lothric Castle. I quickly became frustrated with the controls and I just could not progress, knight’s op versus keyboard. So I went out and bought an Xbone controller. I also started watching a let’s play on YouTube. I was determined to give this game all I had this time.
I slowly proceeded to get better and more comfortable with the game and the combat. I died to probably every single enemy in that castle.   My deaths, at that time, were far more stupendous than my kills. Die to the Dragon. Die to the skeletons next to the dragon. Die to the Knight after the skeletons. Die to the terrifying-possessed-zombie-thing next to the knight. I learned a valuable lesson with all that dying. Never underestimate an enemy.
A combination of fear and excitement made me slowly progress to the first REAL boss. As I finally encountered this beast I have to admit, I was awestruck. That thing is badass! And he proceeded to ground me into dust. He’s huge he’s strong and he’s fast? How do I kill this thing? I went in knowing this was gonna take a few tries.  Haha, after the tenth time I was ready. I knew this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s moves and he was going down! Popped an ember and… You Died.  Four more times and I finally owned that beast, the satisfaction was great, and, the relief of the bonfire was greater. Whew!
“So this is Dark Souls?” I thought.
“This is hard. But doable.”
I ventured forth looking to own some more heirs of fire. I rambled through the next areas trying to figure everything out as I went, but I would also be watching my trusty let’s play youtuber to share in my pain and triumphs. That really helped me as the Dark Souls mood can really creep you out!
As I slowly grew more powerful, I dabbled in pyromancy. I found my first Ultra Greatsword. I found side bosses and explored and learned about this tragic world.
Making my way through the middle of the game, I began to see some of the beauty of the world. There are some truly amazing sites in this game. Irithyll Valley. Anor Londo. So cool.
The bosses! Abyss Watchers. Pontiff Sulyvhan. The Dancer. Demons. DraGONS. GiANTS!!! Wow
So here I am now, just sitting in Archdragon Peak waiting to find the courage to beat the Nameless King.
And so now, coming full circle, Dark Souls 3 has made me decide to play Dark Souls again. Just to give it another shot. Now, I‘m a level 38 Pyromancer heading down to the catacombs. Been enjoying the hell out of it. Not as smooth as Dark Souls 3 but definitely great.
This game is one of the best gaming experiences I’ve ever had. I really can’t say enough about this game.
Thank you From Software!

Finding Teddy is a great cute little game, unfortunately a slew of glitches and poor design decisions makes me caution purchasing this game (ah, for want of a better scoring grade!)
The good: The art in this game is beautiful and atmospheric, both when it comes to backgrounds and to characters. There is little in the way of dialogue, but well-directed cutscenes do a great job of telling the (admittedly rather simple) story line. The protagonist is a girl looking for her kidnapped teddy in a strange dreamscape of monsters and spiders (arachnophobes beware). She comes across as very competent, and the game never overly sexualizes her or belittles her for being a girl, which is a huge plus for me. If I had kids I could definitely see myself playing this game with them.
The bad: The game is short, many of the high points are already given away in the trailer. Interface is somewhat lacking and difficult to navigate. New game+ switches to old art in animations. More damning, there being no option to save means it is easy to get stuck at some places in the game by advancing before solving puzzles vital to finishing the game. The inability to travel back to previous levels again means you can get stuck and be forced to replay the game from the start. This game requires a very good ear for pitch as most puzzles contains a step (or several) in which you must echo a sequence of high-pitched notes. This is a great gameplay element, but if you have less of an ear for music this game becomes a lot less enjoyable (this was the case for me) -- something that could easily be mitigated by giving players the option to show the letter-notes in every puzzle, and in any case ought to be better advertised before purchase. For the most part the music is great, but the high-pitched tunes can sometimes become a bit hard on your ear, which is a problem since the sound is too important to the solving of puzzles for turning the sound off for a bit to rest your ears to be an option.
In sum, this is a beautiful but short game with some innovative gameplay thet should have seen more work on the bugs and bottlenecks I mentioned above. I look forward to more games from this studio when they've found their proper sea legs.

The Spellforce series feels like a mish-mash of  Dungeon Seige and the original Warcraft: a shallow party based dungeon delve attached to a shallow strategy game.
You control a band of heroes, and sometimes you get a base to build an army of disposable red-shirts. The heroes level up with you and gain skills, the military units are cannon fodder. That's the crux of it; not much depth here. It does, however, create a nice hybrid game in that you don't have to live and die by either your hero build, or your micro-managing skills as a strategy gamer.
What Spellforce bills as a feature to make combat easy actually makes it tedious, but the amount of quick control it gives you is worth it. Once you're over the shock of having to click so many times to control your party, you'll find you can quickly dispatch many different units.
The story is on rails, so no replay value; but worth the pricetag if you like BOTH Baldur's and Warcraft.

A charming and sweet point-and-click adventure game that tells a beautifully sad story about a girl who enters a bizarre, Wonderland-esque world to track down her stolen teddy bear. The pleasant pixel-art visuals are a blend of Superbrothers: Sword & Sorcery meets Fez, with a vibrant color pallette more closely resembling that of the latter. Sound design is another strong point of the game; not only is there solid ambient music to help set a moody atmosphere, but sound also plays a prominent role when it comes to creating some of the more interesting and unique puzzles that Finding Teddy has to offer. I also really enjoyed the simplistic and traditional nature of the game. The interface is very minimalistic and there are practically no hints of any kind. The player is allowed to explore these dream-like environments on their own without any assistance and the game is better off because of this. The story is a short one (~90 minutes) but it doesn't overstay its welcome. It's the kind of adventure you can finish up in a single night and still be completely satisfied by the experience.
In all, I had quite a good time playing Finding Teddy. Nice art design, a minimalistic style, and an endearing story of friendship and loneliness. Recommended for those who are fans of the genre.

This game is almost great. It's a solid historical RTS game at its core. It is immensely satisfying to let loose a volley of musket fire or watch the simulated projectiles from field cannon ragdoll your opponent's troops. It borrows a lot from Age of Empires 2 in terms of mechanics, feeling, and ambience, which I certainly consider a plus. It makes gathering resources simpler and puts an end to annoyances like farm queuing. The game's few glaring flaws, though, affect it considerably.
I run into my first problem with the game when I run it. Having bought the "Complete Collection," I thought I would have one game to run with the campaigns and other content from the two expansions included, but when I start the game up, a prompt asks me whether I want to start the Complete Collection, the War Chiefs expansion, or the Asian Dynasties expansion. Bafflingly, running the Complete Collection only gives me the vanilla content; running the War Chiefs expansion gives me the vanilla content plus that expansion, and running Asian Dynasties gives me vanilla plus both expansions. This is confusing and it gives the impression that the Steam release was poorly done, like a rush job made by an intern in some outsourced office.
Next, I start up the game and I'm upset to see that my units have no formation orders. In AoE2, I could set the formation of my units, choosing to group them together, stagger them, or group them to defend weaker units, for example. I could also set units to be aggressive, defensive, to stand their ground, or to be completely inert. I couldn't do any of that in this game. Only after mentioning this problem to friends who have experience with the game did I learn that you CAN give formation and behavior orders--you just have to enable them from settings. Needless to say, that's poor game design. As far as I know, no in-game hints or tutorial lets you know you can turn formation settings on.
Finally, my biggest problem with the game is the home city and card systems. They are closely intertwined, and they suck. Here's the deal with home cities: In Age of Empires 2 (or really, any RTS that isn't garbage) you begin any game by choosing a civilization or faction. In those games, each civilization has its own strengths and weaknesses which make it unique, and the uniqueness of different civilizations is what keeps those games fun and interesting. In Age of Empires 3, however, you don't just pick a civilization--you pick a home city to go along with it. For example, if you want to play as the Germans, you have to pick your home city of Berlin, or Munich, or whatever (you can have multiple home cities per civilization, and level them up individually.) Playing as any home city lets you gain experience to level it up; experienced is gained when you do pretty much anything (build units, destroy units, find treasure on the game map, trade with civilizations native to the game map, and so on.) Leveling up your home city lets you pick new cards for it. Here's the deal with cards: earning XP in a game will cause a bar to fill up. When the bar is full, you can pick a "card" of your choice from your home city's deck to be shipped to a town center or other building. Cards are bonuses that can be one of a multitude of things, from extra villagers to crates of resources to town center wagons. So, basically, while playing any game, you can choose bonus units, buildings, or resources to materialize for you once every several minutes or so. Every civilization begins with a default deck but leveling up your home city lets you pick better cards. This sucks because it allows you to smooth out the flaws in any civilization and substantially changes what makes each one special. It lessens the consequences for screwing up; if you forget to mine gold, you can just wait until you can pick another card and get crates of hundreds of gold shipped express to your doorstep. No RTS, AoE3 included, could conceivably be improved by adding RPG elements and the ability to beef up a civilization. All civilizations should be on an equal playing field by default, and the ability to grind up the raw strength and adaptability of a civilization flies in the face of that basic fact of RTS design. The game would be vastly improved by having these awful systems removed so that I can just pick a civilization and have it work the same way every time, instead of being obliged to fine-tune it by grinding.
In summary, it sucks.

You are Gordon Freeman. A scientist who works for the Black Mesa facility. And an experiment you took part in has gone completely awry, unleashing an extraterestrial invasion, and now all hell has broken loose in Black Mesa. Your main goal is to survive and to stop the invasion, using the help of surviving Black Mesa employees, whatever you can get your hands on and your own bare wits.
Even if it is over a decade old, Half Life has aged very, very well. In fact it seems to do some things better than most Modern shooters - you can hold a heck of a lot of weapons for example, a great feature that barely has any presence in shooters nowadays. The gunplay is intense but fair, and you have a huge multitude of weapons to utilise - and they are all great and feel powerful. Enemy types are plentiful, varied and can get pretty darn tough as the game progresses. The enemy AI itself is intelligent and fierce - especially the soldiers who know how to flank well and work together. There are friendly NPC's as well, which are actually helpful: Security guards can help deliver covering fire and scientists can unlock doors and heal you if you are low on health. The game also takes good advantage of the environmental elements around it, technically making almost everything a threat or obstacle - some bridges can be destroyed which may require you to find another way around it, wet floors are obviously slippy so you need to be careful not to slide into an elevator shaft - Did I also mention that elevators in this game are barely ever safe? All of these great uses of particular stage elements called for some fantastically designed levels and puzzles that require a skilled gamer to complete.
Graphically, I will admit the game does look a bit blocky by today's standards and the character animations are pretty wooden, but each level within Half Life looks worlds apart from one another, especially the last part of the game, trust me, it's amazing, that's all I'm saying about it, I'm not gonna spoil it. The character and enemy designs themselves, most notably the aliens, are really creative, unique and varied. The real time cutscenes were cutting edge back in the day and even though the choppy and kinda unexistant character animations during these cutscenes are now dated in a sense, the fact that they are REAL TIME just makes them very immersive and makes you feel part of a great story.
When it comes to audio, the soundeffects are great and fits Half Life's sci-fi tone, and the guns are LOUD. The music tracks, although few and far between, are fantastic and give off great atmosphere. The voiceacting is also great, even if the recordings are a bit grainy.
If there was anything I thought that did detract from the overall quality from the game, is the fact that sometimes the player can get glitched in certain parts of the environment, so they can't move, therefore they would need to restart from the last save... but then again this barely ever happens.
Tl;dr Half Life is a groundbreaking FPS that has stood the test of time and I still consider it as one of the best shooters ever made, if not the best. An immersive, action packed, incredibly varied FPS that makes you feel like an action hero. Highly recommended to anyone who has at least an interest in videogames.

Seeing as the dev doesn't seem to give a damn anymore about providing the patches necessary to have the game work as advertised in a timely manner, I won't check on it or update the review any further.

Sadly, this has to be a
review.
The reason for this is the apparent lack of quality control before release. See details below.
First off, the concept is great. I really want to love this game for it's concept. It is basically a much better version of Uplink.
Now, is it realistic from a hacking point of view? No. But that's a good thing, because realistic hacking scenarios would be pretty boring for a game. The concepts are taken from the real world and simplified/modified to make an interesting game.
It is simple at first and doesn't get too difficult while still providing some challenges and a nice storyline.
That being said, while the game could be a 9/10, game-breaking bugs currently make it at most a 4/10.
Here are some that I've encountered so far:
- You are able to take multiple contracts at some point, but doing so will prevent further progression due to the quest completion system being bugged.
- Using multiple profiles is inconsistent, you can't be sure that your savegame remains the way it was
- Game supports windowed mode but crashes regularly if you focus on another window
- Loss of all savegames - this is a big one. The last time the aforementioned crash occured, I've lost all of my saves.
The last bug on this list is the main reason this review has come to a not recommended conclusion and the others severely contributed.
If any beta testing would've been done, such a list of game-breaking bugs wouldn't exist.
Update 1: After the most recent patch promised a solution  to "many issues that were causing people to lose save files" I've decided to start a new profile. Did some work, saved session and exited the game normally. And alas, as I started the game again today there were no accounts and my save_accountsMeta.xml was gone. Again. This is clearly getting ridiculous and I wouldn't expect a solution any time soon, the dev will probably need a few weeks to figure out the issues with Steam API/Cloud saves etc.
Update 2: Since apparently fixing the savegame issues within a reasonable amount of time isn't happening, I have to say this is close to false advertising. The game should be tagged early access if the amount of issues is still that extensive after two patches. This is the sort of behaviour I'd expect from large companies that simply don't give a sh*t anymore, not form an indie dev trying to make his name. I hope the dev learns some things from this failed release, one of them being that you shouldn't release a game full of bugs when you're too busy being at conventions after the release and don't have time to fix the issues.
Don't get me wrong: everyone makes mistakes and stuff like that can happen. But that doesn't change the fact that as a customer I kinda feel cheated, since there's a reason I don't buy early access and this time the product isn't of higher quality.
Again, once the major bugs are fixed and solutions for the existing issues are presented, I'll gladly give this game a recommendation.

Seeing that this game had no kind of formal review by anyone seemingly experienced. I decided I'd take it upon myself to do one. I don't know if you've noticed but I've put more than my fair share of time into this game.
To start the controls are as simple as they get, they typical moving, shoot by clicking the mouse (there is an autofire button if you're lazy.) and aiming. Simple enough right? Wrong.
The whole charm of this game is the fact that it is permadeath. You spend a lot of time with one character just to have him and all of your hard earned items flushed down the toilet as you look at the death screen with your jaw dropped. I cannot tell you how many times I have done this myself. Just because you made one little mistake. And in this game there are plenty of mistakes to be made. But the whole thing that makes it great it the fact that the better you are. The more time and resources you put into your character the more devastating it is.
But the whole point is the game doesn't baby you. It's quite comparable to Dark Souls or Demon Souls in this aspect. You run through a quick tutorial and are put in the middle of everything where you have no idea what to do or where to go from there.
People claim there are some pay to win elements in the game, which quite honestly yes is slightly true. But if you wait to get good at the game and enjoy a game that isn't babying you through it, you won't mind shelling out $10-20 for a few chests or character slots.
Skins, Items, Keys, and the newly added Mystery Box are a different story however. (I typically buy these with gold laying around after I buy chests and whatnot.)
Anyhow to sum it up. This is a great game. There is always something to do. Always something to challenge you. And nothing there to baby you. And please to avoid starting off bad with the veteran community. Don't beg for items. Good luck.

I am still optimistic that Starbound will be a great game, but I am starting to feel that I will not see that day for AT LEAST a year.  The current state of the game is not broken, but very far from feeling complete.  There are bits and pieces of brilliance and fun to be found while playing the game, but the game becomes a repetitive bore after exploring past the first couple of sectors.  "Bland randomness" is the phrase I would use to describe most aspects of this game that rely on the procedural generation.  The planets are randomly bland, the weapons are randomly bland, the monsters and NPCs are randomly bland, the unique structures and dungeons are randomly bland, etc.
The game seems to have spiraled into some kind of development hell for almost six months, with few updates, suspiciously vague promises of future content, and a fair deal of excuses to why development is going slowly.  Furthermore, I am appalled to see the overkill level of censorship that this company is now pushing against their fanbase: a justifiably angry fanbase that gave THEIR money to Chucklefish in order to help them expedite the development of this game.  At this point, I just I feel like I've been flim-flammed by a dubious indie game developer and payed far too much for far too little of actual substance.
Update (7/31/14): Tried the nightly build after a bit of messing with the files to stop the game from crashing... It's nice to actually see some of the features put into effect that they have been showcasing on their website, even if the gameplay is a buggy, discheveled mess.

Set in a dystopian world that was ravaged by an event known as The Great Wave, Dead Synchronicity: Tomorrow Comes Today is the first installment in a new post-apocalyptic point and click adventure. At this time, it is undetermined how many entries this series will have, or when the next one will arrive. Beware reviews that state that they were "uninformed" that this is an episodic point and click; that information is right on the store page.
The game revolves around a man named Michael, who is considered a "blankmind" since he woke in the new world with no recollection of his past. Throughout the story, you will uncover the details of what was significant in his past and you will also piece those together with what is going on in the present. As expected, being the initial entry into an episodic series, this title involves uncovering a lot of backstory. During the main timeline, an illness that turns people into "the Dissolved" is sweeping the land, and Michael is tasked with finding a cure for the son of the family who saved him. There are several plot twists, though the major one that comes at the end can easily be guessed during the early parts of the game; so it really comes as no huge surprise.
The dark expressionist artwork is exceedingly grim and blood soaked. There's a grand use of clashing warm and cool pastel colors that really sets off the dystopian vibe that this game has. The backgrounds are brilliantly drawn and painted, however I do feel that the characters, especially Michael, could have used a little more work. This latter point could also be due to the fact that I'm personally not a fan of the harsh, straight lines that expressionism is known for when it comes to homo-sapiens, but the characters seem much more bland in comparison to the world that they're roaming around in. Along with the fantastic artwork is an equally fantastic soundtrack. I'm not a big fan of indie music, but Kovalski did a great job of adding forlorn ambiance to the game. The music really brings out the overall mood of the title, although if you stay in an area too long the music will stop and it will fail to loop.
There are only a few gripes that anyone will have with Dead Synchronicity: Tomorrow Comes Today. For one, the game is $24.99 CAD, and it only lasts at best for 4 hours. Unlike many other Daedalic Entertainment point and clicks, the game isn't very complex or difficult to figure out either, so it's unlikely that it will provide a challenge for the seasoned point and click fan. Those who are not a fan of episodic games might as well wait until there's either a full collection available, or at least until we find out when the next title will come out. There's nothing exceptionally riveting in this initial installment, and especially not for the price point; the game has been terribly over-hyped. If you find it on sale for $5-10, it's definitely worth taking a look at, though.

To be clear; I LOVE XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within. I spent 200+ hours on that game alone, second in playtime only to Skyrim. But I have reasons for loving it; I love it because its combat makes sense (flanked enemies are easier to hit, explosives are guarunteed to hit at the cost of research material, always stay in cover, ect.), its research feels meaningful as opposed to grinding and moving on, the base building was cool (though a bit limited, but I was fine with that), there were ways to deal with crises and panic levels, the missions were engauging, and it had good pacing and story.
XCOM 2 is the total opposite. Its combat is RNG instead of strategy, which makes cover pointless. Also, melee enemies make cover even more useless since they just charge to an adjacent tile and slice your squad into cubes and/or stun them for two turns. Instead of getting materials from all enemies, there is a chance of getting loot from certain enemies. Of course, there is no way to determine who has loot and explosives always destroy it. With the Alien Hunters DLC, they give you new weapons, but one of them is very underpowered (the Bowcaster with a clip-size of one) and the rest are class-specific.
Its research is less rewarding and more grinding to get the next research objective to advance the game. Also, the projects take forever. It takes an entire month to research the tier-two weapons at the start to unlock magnetic weapons (aka still bullets, but a bit faster), while in EU/EW it took half as long without research credits, and you got LASERS! You could even research into laser shotguns! LASER SHOTGUNS (Thank you, Mr. Torgue!)! You could even get Grappling hooks in EU/EW, with an upgrade that lets you turn invisible.
The base building sucks. You need an engineer to clear out one room (which takes ten days), and the number of engineers you need increase every level you go down on your mobile HQ. Everything still costs power and resources to build and maintain and power stations offer way less power than they used to. Each generator produces three power units and each room requires three or more units to be built. In EU/EW, you build an access lift to gain another level of your base and excavate the ground of that level by spending money and five days (half as long as XCOM 2) per room. Each generator provides ten power units and the tier-two generators produce thirty power units.
There is no real way to deal with the Avatar Project (the equivalent of panic levels from EU/EW). Enemy research facilities randomly appear in the world and you need to establish contact with the region before you can attack it. The problem with that is you have to establish contact with a region adjacent to the one with the facility before you can make contact with that region and you can only make two contacts before you need to build a comm relay and wait ten days while your engineers build one and waste three power units. In EU/EW, you could reduce panic by launching satellites over the country, complete abduction missions in the country, shoot down and raid a UFO, or complete an alien terror mission when they appear.
The missions are bland and generic and repeat too often. The lack of maps and enemy variety make this particularly true. Its either protect relay, destroy relay, hack box, or escourt VIP. You start the mission concealed, but all of the missions are timed, which makes all possible strategery impossible. And these timers still count down while you are concealed. You get detected very easily and when that happens, all enemies instantly know exactly where all your squad-members are and one hit from an enemy (no matter what damage it is) hospitalizes your squad member for ten+ days or is a critical-hit-instant-kill. And if you don't finish the mission in time, then your entire squad is killed.
The story and pacing are stupid as well. XCOM 2 is about you losing the war against the aliens and they created a world government that is still abducting people for their DNA. The civilians are somehow fine with mutated alien creatures and fully-automated robot soldiers being the local police force along with human-alien hybrids. As far as pacing goes, psionics (mind powers) are introduced within the first two missions even thought they are supposed to be unlocked towards the end-game. They also made psionic soldiers into a seperate (underpowered) class which requires a psi-lab to be built (which needs five power, two engineers, and ten days to build), ten days to test the soldiers, two research topics, and a special engineering project.
This game takes so many steps away from the game before it and has no real strategy (or fun) to its gameplay. Just play EU/EW instead. Its cheaper, more fun, and doesn't require a super-computer to run properly (XCOM 2 refuses to run faster than 15 fps on the lowest graphics settings on my computer).

Spiral Knights is a chibi-style MMO dungeon crawler that encourages build building and gear engineering as the two things that will save your life against the monsters found in the Clockworks. The game was previously available as a standalone title but became Steam integrated, and has become one of the most popular free to play games to pioneer the genre.
The graphics are designed to be simple, stylistic, cute, and attractive. You'll find even the most monstrous of enemies to be some of the most adorable creatures in gaming, and the world itself to be heavily influenced by both steampunk and dungeon aesthetics. The game runs well due to its simplistic nature.
The balance of this game is based on a tier system, going from zero to five stars. In general, you can assume all weapons that fit into a single star level, ie one star, will be equal. There are some exceptions, most notably the bombs, but the situational effectiveness of these weapons outweighs their lack of general usefulness. You are encouraged to switch weapons at the start of every new level, to use your statuses and damage types to your advantage after learning the design of each level of the Clockworks.
The items system is based on a helmet and armor for defense, whilst offense includes two-four weapons depending on your buffs. The weapons can be swords (or hammers, maces, shovels, and machetes,) guns, or bombs. These items focus on one or two damage types, which will be more or less effective against enemies depending on their resistances. Some weapons also feature status effects, which in addition to doing extra damage, add even a second layer to effectiveness against only certain enemies. An additional tertiary type - trinkets - exists. These trinkets give small, varying bonuses such as defense, resistances, or health.
Most items in this game blend together in sets, giving you bonuses for combining certain items. This encourages owning multiple different sets, to properly fight everything the game has to offer. In addition, the four player coop allows you to fight with your friends where each person fills a specific niche role, combining to allow you to fight everything a level can offer.
The general 'idea' of this game is to make your way to a boss at your current tier. The world is split up into three tiers, and multiple different progressions down each tier. At the end of each progression through a tier, you fight a boss, which gives you exclusive loot and crowns (the game's currency.) Alternatively, you can use the relatively new missions feature to take a more story-based approach to the world, and fight everything the game has to offer at a good pace. After the fighting has cooled, you are brought to Haven, a public ground where you can do just about anything you expect from an MMO. Guild halls, an auction house, a training ground, and most importantly; vendors and crafting. Vendors sell items, sometimes exclusive for tokens or crowns. The crafting stations allow you to make items with a mixture of materials you find throughout the world, energy which you can purchase with crowns, and a recipe which you either earn from missions or purchase from the marketplace.
The progression of this game is wonderful, allowing you to slowly rank up and even engage in player versus player modes. You will slowly go from a weak, no star recruit to a five star knight of whatever specialization you choose to create. This truly engrosses you with your character, creating an attachment that can be tangible and real. You will truly come to love that cute little knight running around slaying cubes of grape jelly.
Servers are all official servers, as per usual with an MMO. The connection is good but unstable, where server disconnects are known to the playerbase but are relatively rare.
The story of this game is rather simple. You are a young knight in a seemingly desolate area who must help the army around you both rebuild and conquer the Clockworks. A simple premise, for sure, but an intriguing one. The missions system, which has not been a constant feature of the game, has added to this story and allowed it to blend seemlessly with progression.
The business model of this game is weak. A free to play game at its core, you can hop in and technically play the entire game in its entirety for free. Originally, to play more than ten levels a day you had to pay money to unlock more energy to keep going. This feature was removed, but with it, many prices were raised outside of that cost. This means that the game allows more grinding per day, but will take longer for that grind to be worth something. I would say this is a good thing as it encourages playing more per day than just playing for an hour a day. The prices are still definitely affordable.
Overall, this game can be fun for everyone; veterans of MMOs, young kids who enjoy the art and simplicity, or casual gamers looking for a cooperative experience. Stay for the cute art, the grinding and character building, or the engaging combat.

To be honest. I like this game. I really do. Rather than go on an incoherent rant I'll just make my points:
Pros:
*Story; the story is enough to have kept me invested for quite a while and I started back when there was no story. But it's not really too much to write about. It's more the lore of the planet than the actual plot that is where I take the most interest.
*Atmosphere; With the setting being multiple layers of different planets you would think chibified cuteness would be the right look, but it suprising works well here. Not to mention things don't look so cuddly the farther down you go.
*Mechanics; I had to change up from the default key settings personally, just made things easier for me. The dungeon crawling and combat is very reminiscent of top-down Legend of Zelda games, particularly Four Swords when(or if) you can get a full party. It sparked up a sort of feeling of nostalgia for me.
Cons:
*Near-dead community: Over the years the community seems....lacking. Not sure if I'm logging in at the wrong times to catch people or what, but it's pretty hard to even get one teammate. Let alone three. With how much of a bullet hell the lower levels are, having it all aimed directly at you doesn't make things easy.
*Grinding; Not my first rodeo being at the endgame of an MMO and just working at building a good arsenal. But the sheer amount of effort needed to do so is insane. The crafting system requires you do find items in the deepest and hardest depths of the planet, which usually are only found in the last level. With the lack of people even around, this task is nearly impossible. Plus, if you don't have another hard-to-find item you're screwed if you die, as you have to start all the way from the last checkpoint. If you're doing a mission, got to start from the beginning of the mission you were on.
*Pay-to-win; This is the big one for me. Those super-rare items mentioned above, can easily be bought in the store. Or you could skip the crafting altogether and just buy the item you're looking for. I understand that the developers have to make some profit, heck I even bought the DLC. But this is blatantly pandering to anyone willing to pay while leaving people who are here for a good free-to-play experience in the dust. There is an exchange market for in-game currency to paid-for currency, but the rate is so high that you could easily waste weeks, even months, trying to get the amount just to buy what you're looking to get. To me this is sadly the biggest flaw in the whole game and is exactly how free-to-play should NOT be done. Sadly enough it wasn't always like this. The change really came when they introduced the current crafting system.
All in all, I do like this game, and I will still play it as a timewaster. But I have to give it a thumb down until there are some approvements done to actually make it viable as a progressive free-to-play MMO.

To be honest....I want to like this game. I really do. However, there are more issues with it, than are reasonable for an IP.
Pros:
Art - The art style is very cartoony, invoking a feeling of childlike wonder. The short stature of the characters, cute designs of the battlesprites, weapons, even the enemies feels less like a dangerous delve through the depths of a world, and more like a child on a playground. The bullets seem like pingpong balls, the blades like nerf swords, and the enemies even feel like silly critters in a childs imagination.
Music - The music score is wonderful. When it works. But when it works, it works perfectly, and typically suits the intensity of the situation. Playful music for common exploring and time spent at the Haven, yet intense during fights.
Aesthetic Design - A great core design of ever changing levels, and shifting templates. While not varied, the layout of enemies and items are often random enough to give most tilesets a feeling of randomness.
Cons:
Art - The art and writing don't fit each other. The art feels like a child on a playground, yet the writing invokes a sense of danger and hostility. Yet, with the lack of any kind of lethality, intense artistic design, or abrupt scene shift, the entire art dynamic feels as though its a child trying to sound like an adult. Even the business of the game, industry (Gremlins), and office workers (Devilites) seem like a childish attempt to call adult jobs evil.
Music - It never works. The track will play, then suddenly cut out. Intense music will play with only one enemy remaining. Calm music will play, cut out, then skip in place on the same 20 second loop. There's only about 4 tracks in the game, and all of them grow tedious and repetitive after the 5th hour of listening.
Difficulty Curve - The game spikes its difficulty without reason or warning. The game is divided into 3 Tiers. Tier 1, with all the enemies doing 1 basic ability, and being fairly weak. Tier 2, where enemies often do 2 actions, have greater health and damage, and sometimes a shield. Then Tier 3. Where all bets are off. Enemies attack without warning at times, the attack indicator sometimes doesn't work, the damage is obscene (to the point where 4 star and 5 star rated gear will barely cut it, even against its prefered damage type), your health rarely stands out for more than one to two hits. At Tier 2, you start to see a dependency on Energy for revives, Crowns for literally everything, and even rare orbs called Orbs of Alchemy.
Drops - Item tables are so scarce, that you can see Tier 1 loot drop on Tier 3 loot tables. Meaning even if you play on Elite difficulty (where enemies have 3X all stats, including damage, resistance, and health), the chance of getting the loot drop you need to advance, is less than 1%. The dependency on a rare item called Orb of Alchemy (coming in several flavors), becomes so great, that simply advancing 1 rank or 2 stages in the arcade, becomes entirely reliant on your luck. But fear not, you can purchase them for an exorbent amount of energy. At the current going rate, you can buy most gear, items, and resources for energy. The issue lies in the pricing of energy trade.
Energy - Energy is the lifeblood of this game. Want to buy something? Minimum of 50 energy. At the curent going rate, that's 9.5K Crowns. What's the issue, right? Well, to buy energy, it's 100 for 9.5K crowns. How many crowns do you earn, on average during a 45 minutes trek through the Arcade? About 3K, if you're playing on Elite difficulty. Meaning the average grind takes around 2 hours, for enough crowns to purchase 100 energy. That's enough for 6 of the most basic orb of alchemy, or 2 free revives if you inevitably die. How much does stuff require at the higher end, you might ask? Oh, just a meager 3500 energy, per item. Meaning you'd better start grinding. But never fret. You can always just buy 3500 energy for a meager 20$USD.
Auction House - Due to the standard trade rate of Energy for Crowns, or Crowns for Energy, it essentially means there is little to no leeway in stock pricing. Everything has a minimum price, before you're simply losing out on energy, and wasting your time. But, if something is a rarity, people will price their supplies at the thousands. The average price of an item is always thought of, meaning there is never a decrease in price, only an icrease based on supply and demand.
Connectivity - Connection drops, excessive lag, and phantom damage that sticks through. If you want a game that revolves around sticking you in a mandatory fight arena that's too small for the number of enemies inside, against foes with too much damage, suddenly losing connection for 2 seconds, dying, and having the game decide that it's
fault, then look no further. 90% of the damage you'll take in this game, will come from enemies missing you, the game deciding you were still in their attack radius, dealing damage to you, and not taking it back when it realizes the error. Expect a lot of deaths and wasted time on damage that didn't, or shouldn't have hit you.
Mandatory Arenas - Every 2 floors has a mandatory arena. Sometimes it has 2 or even 3. Certain missions have upwards of 5. In these arenas, you're pitted against upwards of 10+ enemies, in a space too small for that many foes, many of which have excessive mobility, the ability to target while winding up an attack, and very large hitboxes on their attacks. These mandatory arenas simply suck the life out of the game. In the lower tiers, they're comical and fun to do. Little bit of kiting, some dashing, and a bit of damage is all you'll ever suffer. But after Tier 2 kicks in they immediately become more bother than they're worth. Enemies will never drop enough hearts for you to survive, you'll take needless damage, many enemies will corner you and bodyblock you until your shield is broken, then beat you to death. Overall, an unneeded experience, especially on higher difficulty areas with spam-happy enemies like Mechaknights, Devilites, and Howlitzers.
Enemy Types - There are so few variations of enemies, that it becomes tedious to fight the same opponents over, and over, and over.
Status Effects - There's only 5 status effects in the game, and all of them affect you to a greater degree than your enemies. If you get sleep, you stay asleep for an unnaturally long period of time. Meanwhile, enemies will awaken after 1 hit. If you get frozen, it lasts up to 10 seconds, whilst enemies will break free after 2. Shock will deal large chunks of your health, and stun you for a second, whilst enemies will just take a small amount of damage and keep moving (save for mechaknights who freeze in place for 1 second). Fire will do an absurd amount of damage to you, yet very little to enemies. Poison hurts you initially, and makes it so you can't heal, whilst enemies just can't heal.
Damage Types - There's 3 types of damage. Shadow, Elemental (fire, shock, stun, freeze), and Normal. Normal does little damage, but consistently. Elemental does increased damage to those weak to it, but becomes lackluster against normal and shadow enemies. There are even enemies who are weak to elemental, yet resist it as well. And Shadow, which does well against most enemies, but not enough to be useful mid to late game.
Weapons - The weapons make no sense. Melee have to stand still to attack, whilst guns can fire accurately while moving. Bombs take an extended period of time to charge, then must charge again before exploding. And can not be picked up or thrown once placed. Some guns require you to remain stationary for lackluster damage and aim. Overall, the weapons feel almost scatterbrained in design, with no consistency or coherence.
Overall, the game feels like it had the potential to be something great, but lost track of what it wanted to be, and became a sub-par attempt at something amazing. If it had proper funding and design structure, it could be amazing.

As a great Fan of the Souls Series (except Demon Souls because i didn't have a PS3) i can say that Dark Souls 3 is one of the best games i have played in a long long time. Why you ask? Well there are a few Reasons:
1. Graphics look gorgeous. They also looked pretty well in DS1 and even in DS2 but this part is a true gem in that regard. When you get to the first Bonfire and you gaze into the far distance...that was one of the first moments i had Goosebumps in this Game.
2. This game would never be so good as it is without the Soundtrack it comes with. Every boss feels so more epic because of it. A true Symphony.
3. The Story. As always in the Souls Series the Story doesn't tell itself through cutscenes like in any other game, but more through the dialogues with the NPC's you are encountering and for the most part through the weapons/items you can find/transpose.
4. The DLC's are definetly worth it, and if you don't want them, it is still a very good game that can entertain you hundreds of hours.
But there are still some things i want to point out before you consider buying this gem.
- If you want to play with your mouse and keyboard you will have a hard time. This game plays best with a controller. Period. The DS1 port for PC was terrible and even after two more parts it still feels "wrong".
- PVP is mediocre. And thats because there are a online cheaters. And if that wasn't enough Fromsoft punishes you if you encounter one. I myself was invaded multiple times in an area that is like an open PVP arena itself (won't say where, you will see if you get there and i don't want to spoil anything) and the next time i log in i get a warning from FROMSOFT that i cheated and am now softbanned. WTF?! I was really really mad when i got that message because the Servers can obviously not distinguish between the persons who play fair und who invade while hacking the game. If you don't have this problem, good for you. But if you have it, just play offline. PVP is just crap at this point.
Still i highly recommend this game.

Reviewing a 15 year old game is really challenging, considering the fact that everything about gaming has changed ever since, BUT if I say that this 15 year old game is what single handedly paved the way for what shooters are today its bold statement. HALF-LIFE needs no introduction, out in 1998 it had a very powerful impact in the industry, back in a time when FPS was all about running and gunning through narrow corridors HALF-LIFE single handedly changed that trend, it was a revolution of its time and was a direction for game developers.
The story is very simple, you are a scientist who works for a top secret research facility, one day an experiment goes horribly wrong and it rips open a portal to another dimension, the base is riddled with alien life forms and in order to confront the situation the govt. dispatches soldiers, their mission is not only to wipe out the threat but also the evidence which includes the entire Black Mesa science team including you, it’s all about survival. Simple story but the game has a very powerful sense of narration, story-telling and presentation.
Its crafted so well that it stands the test of time even today, the ones who played this game when it was released know why HALF-LIFE is praised so much, the ones who play it today find it stale, I don’t blame them but fact is that this was the first game to implement narration and ingame story telling without the player leaving control, no cut scenes or anything that takes you away from the player, even levels have a cohesive transition, they are merged by loading screens so the game feels like a smooth flow. Games today lack that kind of flow. The premise of the game is so well designed it feels like a living breathing world with an ecosystem.
It’s the game that merges old school shooters with new or lets just say it brings shooters to a whole new direction. there is a wide variety of weapons at your disposal, each one of them behaves so perfect that shooting is very satisfactory, also there is a wide variety of foes who have different behavior, today these things are very common but imagine all of these things in 1998, it bagged more than 60 GOTY awards.
The level design, the sound design, the atmosphere, the feel of claustrophobe and isolation, the desperation of survival are some of the attributes that make HALF-LIFE.
If there was no HALF-LIFE, there wouldn’t have been VALVE, this is the game that made them, gave them this legendary stature.
For the love of gaming play this. You owe it to yourself.

To be clear; I LOVE XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within. I spent 200+ hours on that game alone, second in playtime only to Skyrim. But I have reasons for loving it; I love it because its combat makes sense (flanked enemies are easier to hit, explosives are guarunteed to hit at the cost of research material, always stay in cover, ect.), its research feels meaningful as opposed to grinding and moving on, the base building was cool (though a bit limited, but I was fine with that), there were ways to deal with crises and panic levels, the missions were engauging, and it had good pacing and story.
XCOM 2 is the total opposite. Its combat is RNG instead of strategy, which makes cover pointless. Also, melee enemies make cover even more useless since they just charge to an adjacent tile and slice your squad into cubes and/or stun them for two turns. Instead of getting materials from all enemies, there is a chance of getting loot from certain enemies. Of course, there is no way to determine who has loot and explosives always destroy it. With the Alien Hunters DLC, they give you new weapons, but one of them is very underpowered (the Bowcaster with a clip-size of one) and the rest are class-specific.
Its research is less rewarding and more grinding to get the next research objective to advance the game. Also, the projects take forever. It takes an entire month to research the tier-two weapons at the start to unlock magnetic weapons (aka still bullets, but a bit faster), while in EU/EW it took half as long without research credits, and you got LASERS! You could even research into laser shotguns! LASER SHOTGUNS (Thank you, Mr. Torgue!)! You could even get Grappling hooks in EU/EW, with an upgrade that lets you turn invisible.
The base building sucks. You need an engineer to clear out one room (which takes ten days), and the number of engineers you need increase every level you go down on your mobile HQ. Everything still costs power and resources to build and maintain and power stations offer way less power than they used to. Each generator produces three power units and each room requires three or more units to be built. In EU/EW, you build an access lift to gain another level of your base and excavate the ground of that level by spending money and five days (half as long as XCOM 2) per room. Each generator provides ten power units and the tier-two generators produce thirty power units.
There is no real way to deal with the Avatar Project (the equivalent of panic levels from EU/EW). Enemy research facilities randomly appear in the world and you need to establish contact with the region before you can attack it. The problem with that is you have to establish contact with a region adjacent to the one with the facility before you can make contact with that region and you can only make two contacts before you need to build a comm relay and wait ten days while your engineers build one and waste three power units. In EU/EW, you could reduce panic by launching satellites over the country, complete abduction missions in the country, shoot down and raid a UFO, or complete an alien terror mission when they appear.
The missions are bland and generic and repeat too often. The lack of maps and enemy variety make this particularly true. Its either protect relay, destroy relay, hack box, or escourt VIP. You start the mission concealed, but all of the missions are timed, which makes all possible strategery impossible. And these timers still count down while you are concealed. You get detected very easily and when that happens, all enemies instantly know exactly where all your squad-members are and one hit from an enemy (no matter what damage it is) hospitalizes your squad member for ten+ days or is a critical-hit-instant-kill. And if you don't finish the mission in time, then your entire squad is killed.
The story and pacing are stupid as well. XCOM 2 is about you losing the war against the aliens and they created a world government that is still abducting people for their DNA. The civilians are somehow fine with mutated alien creatures and fully-automated robot soldiers being the local police force along with human-alien hybrids. As far as pacing goes, psionics (mind powers) are introduced within the first two missions even thought they are supposed to be unlocked towards the end-game. They also made psionic soldiers into a seperate (underpowered) class which requires a psi-lab to be built (which needs five power, two engineers, and ten days to build), ten days to test the soldiers, two research topics, and a special engineering project.
This game takes so many steps away from the game before it and has no real strategy (or fun) to its gameplay. Just play EU/EW instead. Its cheaper, more fun, and doesn't require a super-computer to run properly (XCOM 2 refuses to run faster than 15 fps on the lowest graphics settings on my computer).

Combined with the low stats and equipment of your rookie soldiers, this makes it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play those missions.
The game has improved in all other aspects, the story is amazing and it feels home on the computer. I would have wished for an option to deactivate some (not all) of the turn limitations in order to get the option to take some more turns to cope with the enemy.
Very sad that they limit you so much and for me it adds a lot of difficulty in the early game that is just frustrating and unnecessary.
I will keep playing and adapt my tactics but non the less it's a thumbs down for the game. :(

Everything besides skins are earned with ingame currency that you gain by playing and logging in. 2-3 days of play per weapon has been my average. Blacksquad also has a major advantage that other F2P FPS don't have. It has a Thriving competitive edition in South Korea. This game is a port from that game with a few western twists and it is obvious that the devs are experienced with how smooth their weekly balance and skin updates are. Battleeye anti-cheat is amazing and in 80 hours I have experienced 2 cheaters.
Overall if you want to get in on the ground floor of the next thriving competitive F2P games start practicing now. 7k avg players will skyrocket once more people try it out.

I bet someone's saying 'Oh well you probably have tons of different items right?'. Wrong. I have tons of items with the same skins that are either hyper-futuristic, or somewhat realistic. Those same people from earlier might be saying 'Oh well, they must have different stats, right?'. Wrong again. They all have nearly the same stats for each level, and the ones that are different are really splitting hairs on the difference levels. For example "63 stability" as compared to "64 stability". I dont need this.
I'm just going to say this now, nearly everything in this game is either
1. Very Ugly.
2. Floating because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ world generation.
3. Doesn't any make physical sense.
4. Has some idiot crawling over it trying to harvest block from something that doesn't drop any.
5. All of the above.
I may be the only one who dosent like this, but seeing gigantic floating Minecraft plot world builds scattered accross an otherwise barren wasteland with ugly monsters, is realy unappealing to the eyes. Also this games insane color pallete makes my eyes nearly bleed. Some of the dungeons are so colorful in a lackluster enviorment, or the enviorment is passable and the dungeon is a solid chunk of brown with no supports. Biomes are interesting, but when I'm trying to have a nice sit down it my ugly house with terrible colors, I dont want to be ambushed by a gingerbread man from accross the map because I entered his general airspace.
On the topic of mob targeting, I think this game put a cat with a laser tied to its head in an all white room, and then tried to program something off of the result. Sometimes you'l be fighting a fierce dragon thats drooling lava, and it will suddenly just get bored and walk away. Where's the action man? Another interesting thing is mobs will walk around peacefully when your ready for them, then decide to attack you when you turn away. Got a little SCP-173 spice I see.
Another great thing about this game is that is has random and wierd lag spikes. Alone in the plains? Lag! Adventurning with buddys, all killing mobs? Not a drop of it! Then theres the more predictable lag, like the hub world. But than again, it's predictable, not acceptable. You will have a casual framerate of around 10 fps in the hub world, which is really the most important places besides acctually being in a world. But then again, you need the hub world to get to any and every world, and lots of things (Such as quests, battle modes) require you to go there.
To top it all off, the game has micro transactions and pay to win features such as:
Pets that give you boosts
Vehicles that make you move faster
Skins
Memberships
Gear that gives you an advantage over casual FTPs
Here's another thing, theres NO POINT WHATSOEVER for any of this. The story is generic, and my opening cutscene was spent fixing myself a cup of tea, so I had to rewatch it later. Pretty much happieness, then a darkness comes, things are bad now. You're fighting that darkness, yatta yatta so origional. The game could live somewhat without story, but not when the only thing you ever do in the game is raiding the same dungeons over and over again. Then you take the loot, turn it in, get some material to craft rings which makes it easier to raid those same dungeons and the cycle repeats. There is no goal. The only real progression is your level bar and the difference between having and not having shouder pads on your armor after 10 levels. Mind you that's cosmetic.
And my finishing move, this game is more buggy than a stray cat behind a dive resturaunt. Here's a quick list of my bugs so far (MInd you, I'm 7 hours in!):
1. Crashing when turning on the game.
2. Crashing when turning off the game.
3. Crashing when joining a world.
4. Crashing when leaving a world.
5. Avatar spazzing around the map like a fruit fly in a waste bin.
6. Unkillable mobs thanks to them having insanely high heal stats. (Not sure if that's a bug, but It caused me to be unable to complete a dungeon so I guess that counts.)
7. Mobs attacking me through walls.
8. Mobs being invisible.
9. Mobs that can't teleport normally teleporting.
10. Hitboxes are the worst.
Thats 7 hours of game time, and those first 4 have happened an uncountable amount of times. It feels like they just said the game was no longer early access so people would invest money in it.
Despite all of this, the game
be fun. The art style is charming and it has a simplicity to it. Despite the pallet in my opinion is really gross, I assume some people could like it. Discrediting everything I've said, the game is definitly worth a try, but I wouldn't say the game is good, much less great.
But hey, it's a trove full of possibility.

Just beat the game at 67 hours on the normal Darkest mode.
Pros:
-Beautiful art and atmosphere, using minimal frames but converys action perfectly
-Challenging but fair.  Some people think that it's unfair because of all the RNG or it's too hard.  In my opinion, although there is RNG, you can plan ahead and mitigate a lot of it with strategy.  For example, putting on stun chance trinkets, if you're missing your stuns, or using blight trinkets if you can't seem to apply your blights.  Or putting on bleed resist trinkets or bringing bandages when questing in a zone with lots of bleeds.  Only 3 of my heroes died during my first playthrough, including *spoiler* the 2 required for the last boss.
-Lots of different classes that synergize with each other
-Quirks and stress system make every hero unique
-Feeling of progression.  Always upgrading town/leveling heroes/getting new trinkets
-Pick up and play.  I find myself fitting in a dungeon whenever I have a 15 mins break or something.  Especially good for my PS Vita on the go.
-Excellent writing.  Slowly learn the dark secrets of your ancestors, which I find very interesting
-Interesting boss mechanics.  4 zones with 2 bosses in each zone.  Another 2 bosses from town events.  And 2 more you can encounter randomly from dungeons.  The final dungeon has 4 levels each with their own bosses as well.
Cons:
-Can be grindy at times.  You are either in town upgrading stuff or in a dungeon.  Have to do multiple runs to level up your roster for the final dungeons.  Max hero level is 6 and you require 2-3 dungeons to level up depending on the dungeon length
-Have to beat each boss 3 times and they pretty much play out the same way, with only tiny changes.

From the same developers who made Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance comes Bayonetta with a Devil May Cry gameplay an overdose of crazy and over sexualization of females. Bayonetta is a stylish action game where you play as a witch that consorts with demons to fuel her magic powers, she has been sealed inside a coffin for 500 years where she slumbered until someone freed her. Without any memories of her past she fights against countless angelic enemies that try to kill her. The game is harder to play then Devil May Cry since it requires that the player uses witch time to slow down time to a fraction of its normal pace. This allows the user to bypass the opponents defenses and execute combinations of attacks and other feats that would otherwise be impossible (some enemies can only be killed during witch time). Witch time is activated by dodging an enemy attack just before getting hit and that is rather hard to master.
Unlike in Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance and Devil May Cry where u kill enemies and destroy environment objects to get hp back in Bayonetta u will find that hp orbs are very rare to get from enemies and environment objects, the amount of hp received from hp orbs is too low.
PRO:
+ devil may cry gameplay
+ overdose of crazy
+ over the top action sequences
+ platforming
+ racing
+ arcade shoot em up
+ huge variety of weapons which can be equiped in the hands & feet slots (each weapon has its          own properties, combos and types of wicked weave attaks that do increased dmg and use up magic)
+ accessories that provide an added effect or modify a technique (you have 3 slots)
+ crafting: lollipops which give you increased attack, hp, shield, magic and magic flutes that cause heavy damage to any nearby angels
+ epic boss battles (some bosses you can climb and fight on them)
+ elite enemies drop their weapons which can be used by the player
+ finishers (just like in mortal kombat x u get to finish off a boss when his hp is low, perform an instant kill attack on low enemies or deal huge dmg to elites using your magic)
+ collectibles: journals, umbran tears of blood, broken witch heart hp upgrade, broken moon pearl magic upgrade, angelic hymns gold LP (broken or full records of music that unlock weapons)
+ good AI (enemies gang up on you and hit you one after another or a few at once, in higher lvl difficulty the enemies are very aggressive)
+ good game optimization
+ decent graphics
+ decent story
+ good soundtrack
+ replayability
CON:
- dodging an enemy attack just before getting hit is hard to master (it is necessary in order to slow down time)
- elite enemies can combo attack, stun or stunlock the player just how the player can do
- frustrating action sequences with split second time buton input
- fights can get disorienting at times (some areas rotate the camera 360 deg horizontal or vertical around the character, other areas have u fighting on the walls, ceiling and floor while switching between them as you jump, bad camera angles, enemies to big to fit on the screen which hide your character as you move around them)
- very rare and very low hp orbs drop from enemies and environment objects
- very huge requirements for crafting items
- game to short

Xcom 2 is a turned based RPG with decent production values. I love turn based RPGs and strategy games like this, but I can only recommend this game to people like myself, but not everyone. The game's overall production values are only average in my opinion, as a lot was recycled from X-Com 1. Also, I feel as though the story is not as strong as the origional. The game is harder than the orginal as well (at first), but then gets easier as your people get better armor and abilities.
They cut some good things out from the original like shooting down UFOs, but they added some cool new weapons and powers. I also did care for maps with turn limits (you can get mods to fix that though) as sometimes because the maps are randomly generated, you could get a map that is huge in a bad starting spot and have it be near impossible to finish. Overall a good game, but it won't be everyone's cup of tea.

Hacknet is a game where player takes the role of a hacker in search of the mysterious story of Bit, another hacker.
The game requires the use of the terminal, but GUI is available too for convenience.
For those that came looking for an experience similar to Uplink, I would say for the experience you get in Uplink, Hacknet definitely nailed it. Differences being that Hacknet is more terminal oriented and is more story oriented.
Instead of comparing the game to Uplink, Hacknet can be compared to "Digital: A Love Story", which is also a hacker, story driven game.
Another strong point of Hacknet is the story. The story drives the entire game. It starts slowly, but gets progressively more and more tense, starting to put your abilities to the limit, especially at the end *wink wink*
Do I recommend it? Of course.
