A very solid first adventure game from Fictiorama studios. The subject matter (the eventual temporal death of everything) gives this game a much darker storyline than is common in this genre and in fact I was genuinely shocked by one or two set pieces.
I played through a press copy of the game, and found the puzzles to be generally on point, except for one part where the solution was really subtle and I missed i completely for about an hour. The logic of the puzzles make sense for the most part.
Voice acting is present throughout, there are a few characters which are 'misses' but in general it is very well done, and breathes life into the surroundings, and makes you care about the characters a lot more than if it was just text. The music is pretty cool too, a prog rock style that just about meshes with the surroundings, and the art style is very fresh, and unlike anything I've seen before.
If you're looking for a new, dark point and click that has obviously been made with a lot of love, you couldn't do much better than checking out Dead Synchronicity.

The support team is also quick in answering issues you have. i submitted a ticket and 4 hours later a GM replied and managed to fix my issue (cant cash in a sale in the market). As of writing this review they are about to undergo a major database transfer, which should fix the latency issues that other reviews are talking of
Overall this is a fantastic game that you should atleast give a go before passing it off as another lame voxel game. Trust me you wont regret it, unless of course you regret losing more than a hundred hours of your life to a game.

I started to play Unturned due to me looking for a zombie survival game with multiplayer support and PvP elements. And I did get that when I first started. Unfortunately, the dev decided that it'll be a good idea to create the game in the image of its fanbase. Especially when 80% of the people that play this game are immature little boys and the other 19% are immature teenage boys above the age of 15. I doubt wanna discriminate against the entire fanbase so I'm gonna pretend there's a 1% that's chill and you'll actually enjoy playing with if you've never known or talked to them before. Of course, creating a game in the image of little kids isn't the best for the game nor the rest of fanbase. The kids constantly beg for RP content and for an increase in the intensity of PvP and the dev grants it to them. That's not a good idea at all.
Developer: At first I thought that this dev was an amazing dev cause he's always talking to the players and outputing weekly updates and he was only 16 when he starts to work on Unturned too. But after a while, I see why it's not wise to have someone so young spearhead a single MMO game with over 20 million downloads. The game is completely broken, a lot of the items and concepts have balancing issues and he completely ignores them to work on 4.0, a version that's not gonna be out any time soon, while having his loyal fans struggle with the difficults of the current version. A trend that's been happening as of late is that he's adding more useless and uncalled for content which have server breaking implications.
Broken Items: There are a lot of "OP" and unbalanced weapons, vehicles and concepts in the game. The fact that there's something called a Horde Beacon which can be crafted in less than 5 minutes and done in less than 10 which gives you enough equipment (according to how many members you have doing that horde beacon) which can be used to raid an entire server. There's also a glitch where you can effortlessly enter a base without even having to break in. Exploited by many players and Youtubers yet there is no fix for it. Pistols are essentially useless unless you can get the drop on your opponent at a very close range. Melee is such a disappointing feature that it's not even used unless you can't find a gun. And in most cases, even if you do have a melee weapon, it'll be best for you not to rush in and try to kill a guy with a gun cause it simply will not work unless he's really bad or distracted. Third person is the worst feature ever added in that game. It's so broken and easily abusable that it's not even fun.
Terrible Playerbase: The playerbase in Unturned is enough to give you every type of fatal disease known to man. This game is riddled with little kids that make it very hard for you to even want to talk in world chat. There's also some of those who think that because they've killed you or your team; they're automatically a god at PvP or something. I'd say the biggest turn off for me is the playerbase. It gets to a point where all you seem to encounter are those cancer kiddies that ruin your experience in everyway. A prime example of this is an 11 year old that seems to be the meme of Unturned. His name is Minikillz. If you're ever invited to a PvP clan then that's where they commonly flock and I highly suggest you talk to a psychiatrist if you made the mistake of actually joining.
Survival Content: Straight up, the survival aspect of Unturned is gone. A lot of people use the argument that there are still Vanilla servers so survival is not dead yet. That's a flat out lie. An easy vanilla server will never be considered a survival server in my eyes. Due to the lack of difficulty and most people only use it for PvP. You never find bases on easy Vanilla servers anymore because it's just too easy to grab gear and raid it. No matter where you place your base, the next day it'll be raided. I played with some people that when they did play vanilla, all they would do is look for a gun and kill. No more, no less. The PvE element is basically non-existant. Now, I enjoyed "Normal Mode Vanilla" a lot on big maps. And it's all that I played for at least 400 of my hours. It's honestly the only thing I enjoyed. However, all the normal mode servers are either empty or no longer around. Unturned is now a run and gun sim. And that's not enjoyable whatsoever.
Mods: One word...D E A D.
Simply put, unless you're into a broken game with a nasty fanbase, broken content and absolutely no survival aspect at all and a brain dead developer...
THEN THIS IS THE GAME FOR YOU!

X-Com 2 is better and worse at the same time as its predecessor.   I personally enjoyed having mech troopers and genetically enhanced abilities to help personalize my squads.  X-Com 2 doesn't have those.  But it does have quite a few other things.  Below I will go through both negatives of the game and positives.  And I will try to add any differences if they come to mind.
+ Very good storyline with the game.  (both games)
+ Ability to create and grow each soldier. (both games)
+ Ability to change/create character appearance.
+ Mod supported to really add depth to the game.  (I only used appearance and voice mods up to this point)
+ Turn based.  (always a bonus for me as I prefer more strategy than action)
+ Relatively simple to play and yet enough to make it seem complex.  (good tutorial)  (both games)
+ Downloadable contect was good and at good prices.
+ Can add storyline to your own troops creating my personalization to them.
+ Plenty of variety for weapons and things of such nature.  Like penetrating rounds, or flame bombs/grenades.  (both games)
+ The base classes (not modded) are good.  You can streamline your troops for a specific roll or broaden them out to handle various rolls with a bit less efficiency.  (both games)
+ Graphics are good.  But you may need an updated computer to play even on the lowest settings...
- Graphics are good.  But you may need an updated computer to play even on the lowest settings...
- No more Mech troopers or genetically enhanced troopers.
- Can get redundant for gameplay.  So don't kill it doing an all weekend thing.  Play occasionally and it will keep.  (both games)
- Make sure you read the feedbacks on mods.  If you are unfamiliar with them and they get "glitched", you may have difficulty in removing them (even if you uninstall the game and re-install).  SO READ THE FEEDBACKS BEFORE SUBBING!!!  Or be prepared to do your homework to get rid of them.
+ They do have something to help you to do mods as well as the programs and such.  Just beware that it does take a tremendous amount of memory to install.  But could very well be worth it.
+ With mods, personalizing your soldiers and crew adds a great deal of imangination for character depth.  Can't emphasize how good this is.  Makes for some extremely fun RPG with friends.
+/- Newest DLC is hard.  Adds flavor to the game, but keep in mind that its really hard.  About half enjoy the difficulty and the other half cry...
+ At the time of this review, the devs are still involved into the game.  Although I haven't seen much from them, they still launched a few DLC's since it's release.
+ Big community board.  Lots of helpful players willing to assist you with ideas and information.  (naturally there is always those few♥♥♥♥♥clowns, but ignore them and you will be fine)
If you are still unsure of buying this product, feel free to check out Mr. Odd's (or ChristopherOdd) gameplay videos on youtube.  He is well-known for gameplay stuff with various games and is getting more popular as time goes on.

The devs decided to move themselves all into an office and that was pretty much the last we had heard from them. By April, I stopped paying for the server. No new content meant nobody wanted to play it, and I'm not paying for an empty server. The game is still in Alpha. It's barebones. There are bosses, there are planets, theres a way to cheaply duplicate thousands of sentry guns. Then there was an article talking about all these planned upcoming changes, like farming progression and an actual story. This game is garbage right now in it's current state. Don't buy into the hype. Don't give the devs another cent until they finish the game. Starbound is just another example of why Early Access games should be avoided at all costs, which is a shame because there are many Early Access games out there that are shining examples of what we want in an early access game, like Broforce and Hack n Slash and Contagion.

Wonderful game. Ton of fun, active developer support, Lobbies fill up quickly regardless of region VERY easy to get a match going pretty much any time of day. It may take a few minutes to get started, but that's even true of player-count juggernauts like Call of Duty.
Fractured Space has interesting and fairly balanced gameplay. Every ship is relevant in some way, but choosing the right ship for the task always matters. Ping is almost irrelevant in matches - I've experienced no difference in gameplay between 40 and 350 ping. It's in early alpha, so there are a few problems that are typical of that sort of thing, but they're mostly addressed quickly and effectively.
There's one final progression wipe coming on the 21st of January, so playing before then might suck a bit if you don't want the exclusive skins they give as a reward for high-levels prior to the wipe. But the game itself is a lot of fun regardless, and definitely worth your time and the rather minor $10 investment it takes to get it.

All in all, not a game for most people, but for that small percentage of people it is for, its good.

- Token tracker

Cons

This game could be further improved by:-

2) Resizing the level select (because you need to click the arrow keys multiple times in order to repeat the desired level). Certainly, the devs can fit all 12 levels in one screen,

Overall, this could be one of my free favourite games if its not for the difficultness for I need to repeat certain levels more than 10 times and 4 hours to complete it. Perhaps, I am not good in platformer games.
However, you should give it a try and challenge yourself. It can be frustrating but satisfying.

I saw an article about this game on Kotaku about a month ago and it's been on my wishlist ever since. As soon as it was released today, I picked it up and I have to say I'm really enjoying it.
Overall, the game has a simple layout and there's not much too look at, but that shouldn't be a turn off for anyone who's thinking about picking this game up. The game offers a good balance of navigating systems via a GUI or via command prompt, which operates quite a lot like the real thing, albiet a lot more simply.
The story is pretty engaging as well, and while I've only played about 2 hours of it, I've already been tasked with quite a few contracts that vary in style, including proving myself to a 'hacktivist' group. I'm also blown away by the amount of junk files that can be found on the computers that I've hacked, which include a lot of messages and emails which make the game feel more 'alive'.
I'd have to say the most enjoyable part of this game some far [SPOILERS] was failing to hack into another hacker's proxy server and subsequently getting hacked, which resulted in me having to track down a file to get my system back up and running. The game even included a BSOD, which made me laugh. After obtaining the file I needed and rebooting my system, I found the GUI to be completely different, like I was using another PC's OS, which goes to show how much thought went into this game by the developer.
If you're looking for an entertaining game that's fairly cheap, I couldn't recommend this enough.

It's hard to call this a game, really. It's more like a slot machine with a few interactable parts. Yes, I've got quite a lot of hours on it, and I'll probably play it again, at some point, but only once I've installed plenty of mods. You see, the 'difficulty' in this game relies on RNG, and on RNG alone. Without that, there'd be nothing. Now, it is a turn-based RPG, and those generally work on RNG, but it is hard to figure out so many of the systems in this goddamned game. See, I thought, going in, that there would be plenty of systems to make the game all about risk vs reward. The torchlight system for example, makes it so that your party has a lower chance of being caught off-guard as well as much lower enemy bonuses to hit chance, all at the cost of lower chances for better loot. Going in with a low light torch or no torch at all is supposed to do the opposite. Now, perhaps it's just my own bad luck, but I never had that experience. No matter the torch light level, my party would get surprised frequently, and hit with critical attacks much more often. The speed system as well makes little to no sense. Sometimes an enemy will go three times in a row before you, other times only once.
Sure, you're not commanding a company of heroes, more like a group of has-beens and failures looking to make a name for themselves or at least some money, but after constant party-wipe after party-wipe, I just gave up and turned to mods. Generally to help me in terms of RNG, and at least make it feel like my higher leveled heroes were actually a higher level than the idiots I constantly had to bring in on the coach. Now, to be fair, there are already ways to push the RNG slightly in your favor. Certain damage types are better in certain zones, while others are useless in the rest, but that doesn't help when your Plague Doctor gets critted on five times in the beginning of the catacombs and dies instantly, leaving the rest of your party teetering on the edge of insanity or already flung off. Buffs in this game are nearly useless, in my experience, leaving classes such as the Man-At-Arms and Jester in the dirt for much more pratical heroes that can dish out damage or pump out heals.
Grinding is the name of the game, and that is a 'feature' in games that I hate with a passion. It artificially extends game time while cutting back on the amount of work the dev team has to do. You'll have to send group after group of heroes into the same zones over and over in hopes that some will level up and accumulate enough trinkets to actually be good at something. Unfortunately, higher leveled heroes refuse to go into lower leveled dungeons, meaning you can't have one veteran guide a bunch of newbies to help them level up. You'll also find that the only way to actually keep some heroes still useable  you'll need to spend extreme amounts of money on them to keep their sanity low and to get rid of the occassional, crippling negative quirk. This leaves you questioning whether it's better to get rid of a hero, or keep them around. In the end, it's usually better to just throw them out, as they'll likely die in one of their first attempts on a higher leveled dungeon.
I want to give this game a positive review, I really do, but unfortunately, I can't. The art is beautiful, the voicework is professional, even if the lines happen to be cringe-worthy at times, as the game tends to be incredibly edgy, but those can't make up for a game that isn't a game so much as it is a roulette wheel that you often have no control over. With mods to give your heroes a few more edges over the nigh-unkillable beasties they often find themselves up against, this game is very enjoyable, otherwise, it feels like I'm just sticking my hand into a blender.

Finally a Souls game with a decent budget and at the peak of it's popularity. Unfortunately, I think this may be the end. There is a fairly limited amount gameplay you can do with the way they approach their games and sooner or later it just feels like more of the same. I started back in the day and played the hell out of Demon's Souls on PS3 before it had a US release (had to import the Chinese version, which was in English.)
Frankly, by the time they got around the releasing DS1 I was already feeling burnt out and felt that maybe the changes were not enough to keep me. Eventually I played through it and even got into DS2 (because it WAS fairly different, but alas this was the reason the mainstream bandwaggoners/meme kids hated it.)
Here we are many years later and Im not sure what to say about it. Yes, it's more polished than ever and better graphics than ever and the old callbacks and the eeryie atmosphere is all here. But at the same time , I feel that maybe From has gotten too big for their own good and are struggling with the inexperience of handling a mainstream audience, trying to please too many people at once and ultimately pleasing no one.
While the newer fans will swear by this game and it is quite good, after 3 other games just like it I personally found it kind of a slog and way too easy. PVP has been thrown out almost entirely and we are left with something like a pointless gankfest and some hackers. No longer is there any room for advanced technique in game and any hope of comparing it to something like fighting game (which admittedly was a stretch even back when) is all but disappeared and what we are left with is kind of a Souls-flavored, clunky glorified God of War button masher without any story or presentation or 3d breast.
Souls as a whole got by on being kind of almost anti-mainstream, do as we please charm and the bugs and the lack of polish actually created a lot of the more memorable moments in the games. Once we're in full swing full budget mainstream territory like in DS3 and the bugs are there intentionally to try and fabricate some of that charm, it all feels a bit empty and there is no reason to actually continue to support this game as it doesnt really need it. The corporate of Sony have noted the series popularity and have placed some full time money experts to see how they can extract the most out of the poor saps that jumped on the bandwagon too late.
It's a bit like that local band that became big. You were there when they played small clubs and you want to be happy for them now that they are selling out stadiums and even want to buy those 80$ overpriced tickets because its personal to you and you were there with them on the come up, but at the same time you dont really want to go and the songs are a little too clean now and you dont recognize anyone in the crowd and cant help to feel like this thing you once were a fan of is dead and it's corpse is just being passed around for the subhuman denziens to feast upon while you are left to think back fondly on the days of old when this series was good. When you could tell a friend about this game by explaining that "skeletons take less damage from pierce weapons because they are bone" and not "it has cool graphics and memes."
I understand that the original concept of every Souls game is overly ambitious and From has always fallen short of greatness, but this kept a certain hope within the fanbase that maybe they will one day make it big and do every more if they just had a little more success. But we are through the looking glass now and it is clear that they are simply fairly mediocre programmers/designers/artists that are not overly creative and DS3 is probably the first Souls game that has no aspiration or vision behind it other than getting a hit in the safest way possible from a business perspective.
After playing DS1 I was left wondering, what would happen if more developers tried something ambitious and original and actually made games focused on the things they loved and not the things that sell well. After DS3 I am left wondering why this series has any fans at all anymore and maybe it could have been a better game as a whole if they never hit it big with Bloodborne.
Souls is dead, long live Souls.

What to say about Darkest Dungeon. I've never played a game before that seemed so determined to kill you, and worse, is actually very good at it until you start to understand the nuances of how it works. That didn't happen for me until my third attempt at playing through.
Once you get there, though, the frustration gives way to pure joy as you start manhandling enemies in the dungeon. Your A-Team will do more and more work. The dungeons begin to seem trivial, the outcome guarenteed before you even enter them.
Until suddenly they stop being trivial. Complacency will be their downfall. Fresh off a decisive run in which your heroes didn't even seem to get stressed much, you venture into a new dungeon or a new difficulty. That's when it all goes to hell and you'll be happy to escape with any of your prized team.
At the end of the day, this game is just a delight. You should figure out the basics on your own, take a few playthroughs to do it. Don't google for any shortcuts or tricks until you get to that point I mentioned. When your heroes are level 5 or so and you're hitting higger level dungeons, knowing what heroes to bring (particularly in boss fights) is very helpful.
I can't recommend this game any more than I have, it's worth absolutely every penny and then some. You'll curse the gods of random number generation, but you'll keep coming back for more.

This game is awful in every sense of the word.
Best way to describe it? A contentless Terraria.
I really cannot think of many positive things to say about this game. It has terrible bosses (both looks and difficulty wise). Who thought it would be oh so funny to make the first boss be a penguin in a flying saucer? Whos humour is so bad that they actually found that funny? Why wasn't the boss simply an alien in the flying saucer, that spawns more aliens on the surface instead of penguins?
Then we have the second boss, which is a robot that you build yourself. You build it, just to kill it. This boss also looks idiotic too. How hard can it be to make a threatening looking robot? That's one of the main problems with the few bosses in this game. They don't look threatening at all. They're also way too easy.
At least the dragon is somewhat decent.
Anyway, the game has been casualized to hell and back too. At first we had threat levels for each sector. For example, in the alpha sector, the threat level went from 1-10, beta sector 10-20, and so on upto threat level 100. You could immediately see the difference in difficulty between a threat level 1 planet, to a threat level 4+.
Now we have 10 threat levels maximum. Alpha sector has nothing but threat level 1 planets, beta nothing but threat level 2. Chucklefish claim that the difficulty is still just the same, but that is a flat out lie. The monsters apparently get stronger the further you dig down into the planet, but I never noticed any difference, even when I reached the planets core. Speaking of which, you have next to no reason to dig past the surface in this game. Terraria was filled with sprawling caves which had many neat things to find. Starbound caves are devoid of anything besides a few enemies. You might as well stay on the surface.
Oh and once you reach a certain depth, the music cuts off. Some may argue that this creates atmosphere, but since the caves are so dull I don't see how it adds to anything. Instead it comes across as lazy. There could have easily been some cave themes that actually added to the "creepy" atmosphere that they were trying to go for.
Now onto the monsters. They look awful. They sound awful. Seriously, half of them make horse sounds, the other half make sheep sounds. It's so irritating to listen too. What's the matter? Couldn't even take some time out to give the enemies some decent, unique sound effects? Again, lazy.
I think it was advertised at some point "never see the same enemy twice!". Well I have seen the same exact enemy multiple times over. I've also seen that same enemy, except coloured green, instead of purple.
Do chucklefish not know how to make things look threatening? Well, they sort of do since I have seen a few enemies that actually look good, but most of the time the enemies look goofy as ♥♥♥♥. Why must chucklefish insist on taking the goofy route? Is that their plan? To make the games comedy be aimed at morons that find an enemy with a mohawk funny?
I could go on and on about this games shortcomings, but I'm going to cut it short here.
The bottom line is, Terraria, which took a few months to create (granted it was still a little rough around the edges when it first came out too) is a far and away better game than Starbound which has taken years and is still in alpha, which the devs are calling beta. The updates are few and far between. It's been like what? 4 months now without an update?
Talk about taking the money and running. I had the game bought for me thankfully, or I'd actually be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off if I payed money for this crap.
So remember kids, don't buy incomplete games, because this happens. The devs have no incentive to work on it now that you gave them 3 million for a barebone skeleton of a game.

Ok, so im revising my views on this game. I have put nearly 400 hours into it and can tell you: SKIP THIS GAME. Buy Terraria instead. Seriously. Starbound sucks.
Starbound was pitched as Terraria in SPACE! by Tiyuri (the head guy of Chucklefish) years ago.
When it first hit Early Acces, it was most definatly looking to be exactly that. And then, Tiy decided that the game needed some Dark Souls style mechanics. No one quite understood what he meant and to this day, we cant figure it out. The only thing many players understand is that Tiy decided that "Fun" was something that was not needed for "his" game.
5 years of development, and the devs still have no real idea what the game is supposed to be. They kept toting ideas like Metroidvanias, Symphony of the Night, and Dark Souls as the basis for their changes and slowly the game became less of what was pitched and more of a "Welp, its what it is." With no real defined game in there. It has no identity. Its not a sandbox, its not a story driven game. Its in a wierd in-between that sucks the fun out of playing it. Everything is gated behind terrible walls. Its bad.
Pros: The planets. They are neat to go out and explore. The dungeons are neat. The Pixel Art is amazing.
Cons: The game is the very definition of "Repetative."
Basically, the ENTIRE game boils down to this formula in terms of your armor and weapons
Amor/weapon tier at same level as planet: Die in 3 or 4 hits, kill in 4 to 6 hits
Armor/weapon below tier of planet: die in 1 to 2 hits, takes 10+ hits to kill things.
Note: This hit to kill stat is based on melee weapons only becuase Tiyuri decided years ago that Ranged weapons are not worth using. He believes they cheapen combat and instead of going the route of Terraria and making interesting ranged and melee, he thought Ranged shouldnt be worthwhile.
The monsters are not a challange. The combat is terrible. All ranged weapons are absolutely worthless. They use your suits "Energy Bar" which is the same energy used for your techs like double jump and dash. Ranged weapons deal absolutely miniscule amounts of damage and you can expect to spend your entire energy bar to MAYBE kill 1 monster of equal tier. Sniper Rifles can be OK but the shot reload times make them a niche use at best.
TL:DR Skip Starbound. Its not fun. What could have been a fun Sandbox or a fun Terraria in Space has been Tiy'd up to the point of being awful.
Also note: The devopers used to actively talk to the community, but often became offended when anyone had VALID CRITICISMS. Im not talking about "Your game is SUCK AND BAD", but rather legitimate issues like "Ranged weapons arent worth using. Melee is vastly better and heres an idea that might balance out Ranged a bit". Valid Criticisms were often met with name calling and comments of "You arent a part of our team and therefor dont know the direction we are going."
The entire dev team now actively avoids any place that doesnt allow them to ban people for voicing concerns.

A nice sendoff to a series that had started to show repetitiveness; while it borrows more than it probably should from its previous entries as well as its mechanical spinoff Bloodborne, the game still packs enough challenge, compelling boss fights, amazing environments and tidbits of lore that any fan of the series must play it.
The difficulty is a heavily discussed aspect of these games that receives more attention than it should for the wrong reasons. There is no slider; instead, the game lets you build your own difficulty through your choices in starting class, weapons, armor, items and spells. Additionally you can summon other players or NPCs to aid (or hinder) you, which again lets you take control of the difficulty.
That being said, Dark Souls III does feature several small improvements in many aspects that streamline the core experience while changing others that may not resonate well with experienced players; this includes weapon arts (skills), armor no longer requiring reinforcement, less restrictive covenant allegiance, more multiplayer items and covenant interactions, among others.
In regards to DLC, if possible try to buy both for the full narrative experience as they play into each other but otherwise The Ringed City is the better value proposition, with more expansive areas, intriguing boss fights and a more satisfying finale for the series as a whole. Ashes of Ariandel is not bad  but is definitely lacking in content, with the PvP matchmaking the only remarkable feature it has to offer.
New players can start with this title but playing at least the original game first since the world, like its combat, does not hold your hand while you try to understand its lore and characters. Wait for a nice discount on the DLC or the complete edition for the full experience; otherwise stick to the base game and the 2nd DLC.

XCOM 2 is a turn based tactics game with strategy and base building elements. The basic mechanics are solid, easy to deal with, and have a depth that belies the ease of learning the basics.
Having just beaten the game after a hiatus, I can come back and definitely give an unabashed recommendation for this game: This is a true sequel to XCOM, not a map pack like Terror From the Deep, or a complete genre bender like Apocolypse. If you liked XCOM it has all of the same things, and some added twists to keep things interesting. The simplicity sharpens the conflict and research to a razor edge of engagement.
On another note, this is Terror From the Deep except not. More difficult, different mechanics, terrifying enemies, etc. Just lacking the lovecraftian undersea motif.
As for the difficulty, it starts off difficult, gets really difficult, then - if you survive - it gets much easier and you can usually coast through the endgame. Be prepared to lose your troops, work on flanking and tactics, and try your best to keep your squad intact.
A fun, enjoyable game. High on stress at the beginning, high on enjoyment once you've mastered your group.

Players new to the game, coming from AoE 1 and/or 2 should be warned that it has a generally different graphical style and generally fosters a more dynamic and fastpaced playstyle.

This game is quite a classic RTS from the glory days of AOE, Warcraft, Starcraft, Dawn of War, Red Alert etc. The game features 40+ hours of singleplayer campaign missions for all the expansions, covering several story arcs that are both fictional and historical aswell as multiplayer. The game has aged very well and is still enjoyable and pleasing to the eye after all these years.
Age of Empires allows you to play as many kingdoms from history, ranging from China, The Netherlands, Great Britain and many more. Each country has several unique buildings and units that give all countries a different playstyle. On top of that you are able to unlock 'cards' for your deck by gathering experience. As you build things, destroy enemies etc in the game you will earn experience that can be used for shipments. The shipments you have available are based on which cards you choose in your deck, each one providing a different bonus or group of units. By earning experience while in a battle you'll unlock points, where every point can be used to use one of your shipment cards.
Another feature Age of Empires has is the Age system, starting at Age 1 you are able to build limited amounts of buildings and units and use limited amounts of shipments. As you upgrade your town hall you'll be able to use better shipments that you can only use at more modern ages aswell as new units, unit upgrades and buildings.
One of the fun things to do in the game is using the walls and gates to construct a protective barrier around your buildings and placing strategic cannon towers or artillery to defend your base from enemy armies. It's a great game to fool around in against the AI or with and against friends. You can also play with random people if you don't know anyone that has the game, but given the quality of the game it should be possible to convince a friend to get the game aswell ;)
I highly recommend this game, definetely a 4.5/5.

Advertised as an RPG when really it's a first person shooter type game with a bizarre 3rd person view controlled by artfully manipulating 2 joysticks and numerous buttons simultaneously.  The PC-Keyboard Mouse support is so horrendous it’s virtually unplayable (Badly ported console game?) and the controller interface (I went and bought a dualshock4 just for this game) seems designed to be useable only by people with exceptional hand eye coordination. I have well below average hand eye coordination so I play classic RPG titles like Skyrim and the AD&D games.  They're too easy so I bought this one thinking it was a harder RPG. Big mistake.  Couldn't return it because I had given it 10 hours in the tutorial area just so I was confident I could never play it.
Issues:
Belligerently designed control setup to separate the exceptionally coordinated from normal people.  (Who won’t be able to play.) (RPGs use the characters dexterity, not the players.) Reminds me of that crane game you try to get a prize by trying to use a joystick to pick things up but the movement is somewhat hinky.
No first person view.
Not really playable with Keyboard and Mouse, Need a controller.
Controller interface is flakey. Buttons randomly drop out, joystick axis reverts to default, etc. only fixed by restarting DS3.  Audio also comes and goes with the controller hooked up.
Steam’s controller configuration is poor.  Lot’s of things I’d never use and missing things that could be useful. Spent a whole day to get the controller working “reasonably” because I had to exit and restart DS3 with each change to be able to test it.
Conclusion:
Would be a fun game if it had a reasonable interface and, perhaps, a first person view.

Bayonetta is easily one of the best games I've ever played. This is one of few games I've played where I legitimately have no real complaints. The graphics are fine, even quite good because of this port. The soundtrack is fantastic. The story is over-the-top absurdity and spectacle in a truly wonderful way, sporting one of my favorite endings of any game I've played. The gameplay, by far the most important part of a game in this genre, is so good that playing Bayonetta first legitimately ruined my ability to enjoy Devil May Cry games.
Bayonetta makes Devil May Cry 3 and 4 (the ones I've played) feel extremely stiff and limited by comparison. Only having one attack button with maybe 3 main strings while on the ground, 3 in the air and a basic launcher, only being able to dodge while locked on, etc--those things all feel archaic and downright bad in comparison to Bayonetta's huge set of combo strings and freedom to dodge. Because of this freedom to dodge, enemies are allowed to be faster and more aggressive than Devil May Cry enemies, keeping things challenging. The game is really well balanced across difficulties, such that a player new to the genre (as I once was) will find Normal to be an enjoyable challenge. Hard asks the player to step up their game and start to learn to play for real with faster, more aggressive enemies from the beginning. The final difficulty takes away Witch Time, an ability in lower difficulties that causes time to slow down around you for a few seconds when you dodge an enemy attack at the right moment. In a lesser game, taking away such a seemingly essential mechanic as Witch Time would make enemies potentially feel unfair. In Bayonetta, taking away Witch Time is more like taking off the training wheels--it's still completely functional and balanced without it, you just have less of a huge advantage over your enemies.
Bayonetta is also extremely replayable due to the depth of the combat and the quality of the difficulty tuning. Before playing on Steam, I had played some 80 hours on 360 and I'm not even close to feeling like I'm done with the game as I continue to improve and find new uses for combo strings and new ways to chain them together.
One of the only games I would rate 10/10. If you like action games, particularly of the character-action genre pioneered by Devil May Cry, it's hard to imagine how or why you wouldn't like this. Nintendo, please have mercy on the masses and bring Bayonetta 2 to Steam and/or other consoles, I need more of this glorious franchise.

XCOM 2 is a turn based tactics game with strategy and base building elements. The basic mechanics are solid, easy to deal with, and have a depth that belies the ease of learning the basics.
Having just beaten the game after a hiatus, I can come back and definitely give an unabashed recommendation for this game: This is a true sequel to XCOM, not a map pack like Terror From the Deep, or a complete genre bender like Apocolypse. If you liked XCOM it has all of the same things, and some added twists to keep things interesting. The simplicity sharpens the conflict and research to a razor edge of engagement.
On another note, this is Terror From the Deep except not. More difficult, different mechanics, terrifying enemies, etc. Just lacking the lovecraftian undersea motif.
As for the difficulty, it starts off difficult, gets really difficult, then - if you survive - it gets much easier and you can usually coast through the endgame. Be prepared to lose your troops, work on flanking and tactics, and try your best to keep your squad intact.
A fun, enjoyable game. High on stress at the beginning, high on enjoyment once you've mastered your group.

Visuals and audio are stunningly superb, but the gameplay is so confusing that I absolutely have no idea what's going on. :)
It seems that I need to recruit adventurers, whom I have to send on quests to explore dungeons. This exploration is pretty linear, and enemies, traps, obstacles and treasure chests show up in a queue. If there's any kind of considerations to be made or tactics to employ while, well, going down these tunnels to deal with the next random encounter, it remains hidden from me.
During combat there seems to be an initative dice roll which determines which hero or enemy takes their turn to act. Each actor has a set of "special powers" that only affect certain position slots. Most powers can only be activated when the hero is in a particular position slot, so switching places with a comrade is also an action which can only be made once per turn. As the consequence of actions a number of modifier flags may appear attached to an actor, but since combats are quite short (and so are the lives of my heroes) I'm not convinced that these matter too much -- because the heroes will start bleeding and go mad quite soon, then suffer a heart attack, and usually that's the end of their story.
I know that nowadays "permadeath" is in the fashion, but there's just too many things going on in this game, yet because there's no attachment or sense of continuity, the experience isn't very immersive.
I'd only recommend buying this game for its visuals and audio -- as a technology demo or as a showreel of the artists --, but to me it has practically no value as a game.

I've got a few hours into this now and so far I love the fluid way that the interface works. It's a perfect blend of GUI and CLI and you can seamlessly use either. The "hacking" does not seem cheesy at all.
It's more about exploring and adventure than trying to replace real hacking skills with a puzzle. The missions are unique, clever, and humorous. Unlike other hacking games where each mission seems to just blur into the same 4-5 types of tasks, Hacknet makes each mission unique with elements of the basic "hacking" skills strung together in different and more challenging ways.
The way that new skills, tools, and techniques are introduce via the missions is really satisfying. For example, when I gained access to the decypher tool, I still had the file laying around from an earlier mission that was encrypted. When I decrypted the file, it completed a part of narrative for the earlier mission that was implied but not explicitly stated.
If you enjoy these types of games, you'll definitely love this one.

I tried this for some hours. But I must agree with some of the negative reviews, this game is missing some heart! It just don't gives you that awesome-space-factor that you could expect from something like this, despite it's graphics. True this is early access and most things will probably improve, more content added etc. For the moment it's more of a proof of concept than a playable game.
For a moba/Worldoftank-ish combination in space it's not having nearly enough game mecanics or variety:
*Mobas in general have LOTS of abilities, playable units and combinations of equipment. Which adds a lot to overall variety and unique playstyles. This game is lacking in all three.
*Games like world of tanks have unique features like module/compartment damage that makes you angle your unit to deflect and protect your vulnerabilities. This game is lacking here as well. If the game would've had this feature; i.e weapons, engine, warp engine and abilities talking damage/getting disabled it would've added a lot to the game!
And what's with the level system? Why does the whole team share levels in this game? Not that the leveling system adds much to the game, as it's more like a multiplier for your space ships's speed/health/damage  (more or less exactly the same as in robocraft's moba feature) rather than something that increases your ships abilities. (blink range, boost's speed/duration, detection range etc). Many of the different ships feels like they have similar health and damage which isn't really helping.
The graphics are cool from time to time. Some effects, like the sniper weapon's firing are missing, (at least when spectating) as I haven't played with that particular ship myself. (While I watched the sniper ship shooting, without the sound effect I wouldn't have noticed the ship shooting at all). And damage effects aren't that spectacular, only some fire particles here and there. If chunks of my ship would've been missing instead, that would've been cool!
High ping. While I played my ping were around 100-250 most of the time. This didn't really affect the game though, so it's
as all orders you give your ship are instant. (I still hit the enemies without any problem. Sometimes a slight rubber-band effect appeared on the enemy ship (my own being still unaffected)). This is one of the problems with the game that I can see getting fixed easiest.
So basically some mayor rework and added features is required on most gameplay elements for this to become a great game. Graphics whise some improvments could be made, but nothing is really lacking.
So as it is now I would not recommend this game.

This game is awful in every sense of the word.
Best way to describe it? A contentless Terraria.
I really cannot think of many positive things to say about this game. It has terrible bosses (both looks and difficulty wise). Who thought it would be oh so funny to make the first boss be a penguin in a flying saucer? Whos humour is so bad that they actually found that funny? Why wasn't the boss simply an alien in the flying saucer, that spawns more aliens on the surface instead of penguins?
Then we have the second boss, which is a robot that you build yourself. You build it, just to kill it. This boss also looks idiotic too. How hard can it be to make a threatening looking robot? That's one of the main problems with the few bosses in this game. They don't look threatening at all. They're also way too easy.
At least the dragon is somewhat decent.
Anyway, the game has been casualized to hell and back too. At first we had threat levels for each sector. For example, in the alpha sector, the threat level went from 1-10, beta sector 10-20, and so on upto threat level 100. You could immediately see the difference in difficulty between a threat level 1 planet, to a threat level 4+.
Now we have 10 threat levels maximum. Alpha sector has nothing but threat level 1 planets, beta nothing but threat level 2. Chucklefish claim that the difficulty is still just the same, but that is a flat out lie. The monsters apparently get stronger the further you dig down into the planet, but I never noticed any difference, even when I reached the planets core. Speaking of which, you have next to no reason to dig past the surface in this game. Terraria was filled with sprawling caves which had many neat things to find. Starbound caves are devoid of anything besides a few enemies. You might as well stay on the surface.
Oh and once you reach a certain depth, the music cuts off. Some may argue that this creates atmosphere, but since the caves are so dull I don't see how it adds to anything. Instead it comes across as lazy. There could have easily been some cave themes that actually added to the "creepy" atmosphere that they were trying to go for.
Now onto the monsters. They look awful. They sound awful. Seriously, half of them make horse sounds, the other half make sheep sounds. It's so irritating to listen too. What's the matter? Couldn't even take some time out to give the enemies some decent, unique sound effects? Again, lazy.
I think it was advertised at some point "never see the same enemy twice!". Well I have seen the same exact enemy multiple times over. I've also seen that same enemy, except coloured green, instead of purple.
Do chucklefish not know how to make things look threatening? Well, they sort of do since I have seen a few enemies that actually look good, but most of the time the enemies look goofy as ♥♥♥♥. Why must chucklefish insist on taking the goofy route? Is that their plan? To make the games comedy be aimed at morons that find an enemy with a mohawk funny?
I could go on and on about this games shortcomings, but I'm going to cut it short here.
The bottom line is, Terraria, which took a few months to create (granted it was still a little rough around the edges when it first came out too) is a far and away better game than Starbound which has taken years and is still in alpha, which the devs are calling beta. The updates are few and far between. It's been like what? 4 months now without an update?
Talk about taking the money and running. I had the game bought for me thankfully, or I'd actually be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off if I payed money for this crap.
So remember kids, don't buy incomplete games, because this happens. The devs have no incentive to work on it now that you gave them 3 million for a barebone skeleton of a game.

Ok, so im revising my views on this game. I have put nearly 400 hours into it and can tell you: SKIP THIS GAME. Buy Terraria instead. Seriously. Starbound sucks.
Starbound was pitched as Terraria in SPACE! by Tiyuri (the head guy of Chucklefish) years ago.
When it first hit Early Acces, it was most definatly looking to be exactly that. And then, Tiy decided that the game needed some Dark Souls style mechanics. No one quite understood what he meant and to this day, we cant figure it out. The only thing many players understand is that Tiy decided that "Fun" was something that was not needed for "his" game.
5 years of development, and the devs still have no real idea what the game is supposed to be. They kept toting ideas like Metroidvanias, Symphony of the Night, and Dark Souls as the basis for their changes and slowly the game became less of what was pitched and more of a "Welp, its what it is." With no real defined game in there. It has no identity. Its not a sandbox, its not a story driven game. Its in a wierd in-between that sucks the fun out of playing it. Everything is gated behind terrible walls. Its bad.
Pros: The planets. They are neat to go out and explore. The dungeons are neat. The Pixel Art is amazing.
Cons: The game is the very definition of "Repetative."
Basically, the ENTIRE game boils down to this formula in terms of your armor and weapons
Amor/weapon tier at same level as planet: Die in 3 or 4 hits, kill in 4 to 6 hits
Armor/weapon below tier of planet: die in 1 to 2 hits, takes 10+ hits to kill things.
Note: This hit to kill stat is based on melee weapons only becuase Tiyuri decided years ago that Ranged weapons are not worth using. He believes they cheapen combat and instead of going the route of Terraria and making interesting ranged and melee, he thought Ranged shouldnt be worthwhile.
The monsters are not a challange. The combat is terrible. All ranged weapons are absolutely worthless. They use your suits "Energy Bar" which is the same energy used for your techs like double jump and dash. Ranged weapons deal absolutely miniscule amounts of damage and you can expect to spend your entire energy bar to MAYBE kill 1 monster of equal tier. Sniper Rifles can be OK but the shot reload times make them a niche use at best.
TL:DR Skip Starbound. Its not fun. What could have been a fun Sandbox or a fun Terraria in Space has been Tiy'd up to the point of being awful.
Also note: The devopers used to actively talk to the community, but often became offended when anyone had VALID CRITICISMS. Im not talking about "Your game is SUCK AND BAD", but rather legitimate issues like "Ranged weapons arent worth using. Melee is vastly better and heres an idea that might balance out Ranged a bit". Valid Criticisms were often met with name calling and comments of "You arent a part of our team and therefor dont know the direction we are going."
The entire dev team now actively avoids any place that doesnt allow them to ban people for voicing concerns.

I highly recommend this game. In a way, it has a better implementation of the squad-building in xcom. Whereas xcom has you gravitating towards your favourite squaddies that you use repeatedly, Darkest Dungeon has mechanics that oblige you to rotate troops in-and-out of active duty.
Another way to describe it is that you are running a company of mercenaries, and you are continuously sending in teams that are *not* all-powerful, *nor* perfectly equipped, though *perhaps* emotionally challenged. You are giving orders to a work force, and if you aren't progressively advancing them at different levels, then you are handicapping your enterprise.
Before writing this review, I skimmed some of the recent reviews that other steam gamers have posted. So many negative reviews! And for each negative review, I could see that, fundamentally, the person did not understand how to leverage the game mechanics.
I've heard so many dumb things about how players try to exploit the game mechanics. Let me give an example: 1) hire a bunch of level-0 mercenaries, 2) send them into a dungeon and grab whatver loot they can, 3) have them retreat back to town with that loot, and 4) fire the mercenaries that survived. And this is *their* strategy for accumulating money that will pay to support their favourite 4-person team. This is inefficient and wasteful.
Don't listen to anyone that says the RNG is to blame, for again this denotes someone that does not know the game mechanics. Let me be clear. There is not going to be an encounter where you are completely safe from the enemies. This is not a traditional swords and sorcery dungeon crawler, where a healer will keep you in perfect health. You will *not* be able to out-heal the enemy attacks. Instead, you must leverage all of each team's abilities to minimize the number of attacks that are incoming (i.e., kill them quickly and efficiently).
Another thing to understand about this game is that HEALTH is not important at the end of a quest. Your guys will fully heal. But what you need to be concerned about is minimizing STRESS. For this reason, you absolutely need to be killing enemies quickly to reduce their attacks (which cause stress), and you need to prioritize enemies that specifically have stressful attacks (that cause *high* stress).
If you are continuously returning to town with guys that have 100+ stress, then you are doing something wrong. And letting your guys get stressed is expensive because that requires you to spend money to de-stress.
Okay, I've written too much here. Suffice to say, there is thoughtful strategy in this game, there is subtle humour, there is continuous tension, and there is satisfaction from advancing your guys' abilities (not to mention getting success with different team configurations).

Short: The game seems out of control.Technically a mess and the intent to bring action into a strategy failed this time. Like a house built on top of a house does not work either.
Long:
After having high hopes, especially on the fresh scenario i was disappointed, and as mentioned by many here the game has three kinds of flaws:
Those that can be corrected. (all those minor glitches and crashes)
Those that could be corrected but arent. (custom character creation , balance, big bugs)
Those that can not be corrected without making a complete different game. (overloaded gameplay and how the concept was realized)
The game is full of bugs and the support is horrible. Although the engine has already been used in a previous game it seems now, months after the original release there is still lot of patching neccesary and that the game is technically ruined to an extent the developers are not able to control it.
Yet they bring out a DLC in the meantime, great!
So now i have this green banana, waiting for it to mature, maybe with help of the long war team, which should not be their job. They take mature bananas and put ice cream and toppings on them (hard mean and tough toppings though).
The major flaw is that for a strategy game there is no strategy or tactics, everything changes all the time. Thats a nice concept to keep the challenge high and increase the "action". But if everything changes all the time, often within the same turn, you have no opportunity to adapt to the new situation and change, except by reload&luck. My feeling while playing can be described like this:
While hoping to get things done in the avenger some event pops in, go to fight.
Dont waste energy on the sneaky stuff, you can only get one or two enemies before they start hiding, and because they will move again in the alien turn any plans you had beforehand are meaningless.
Create and do your supersmart plan "A", sudden changes, but you cannot move anymore, turn ends, aliens do stuff, something explodes because it was shot a turn ago, maybe hurting your key units, your turn begins, make a plan "B", move the wrong soldier first, triggers some sudden event, fail, reload savegame, follow plan "B" with different soldier first, repeat until outcome is the least worst to end the turn, alien turn full of movements and mean superpowers that mess you up, reload, make a plan "C" and see if alien turn does not mess it up that bad. Else go back to plan "B" and accept your fate, give up on thinking even 2 steps ahead, sudden event, end turn, alien turn, something bad happens again, turn limit near, rush in and sacrifice for the mission goal. Be happy if even two movements had the feeling of being tactical and you felt smart with a nice overwatch and had a nice cover-hopping-combo with a special skill use.
Enough whining. I dont like it because, as we germans say: Its neither meat nor fish! That is not action, that is not tactics.
The nerfing and tweaks done also dont solve the problem but create flaws on other situations. The XCOM 1 gameplay cannot be expanded endlessly.

Bayonetta is the king of the stylish action genre for a reason. It works on every level, from truly  terrible play who doesn't understand the basics up to master level play. It is an excellent game and the core combat is some of the absolute best in the genre if not THE best. Not enough can be said about what a true delight Bayonetta's combat is.
That said, some of these level gimmicks are absolute garbage. I detested DMC4's awful campaign and at least Bayonetta levels are straightforward. Just then you get hit with a big fat boss with like six QTE segments who spends half the boss fight underwater and then a really terrible Space Harrier minigame that lasts about 30 minutes. And then finding all the collectibles practically requires a guide. (You have to shoot all the benches in the area. You have to backtrack all the way to the start of the level after beating the last fight before finishing the mission and the bonus will magically appear.) Most players won't notice these problems because they only grate on repeat plays, which is what THIS WHOLE GENRE IS MADE FOR.
There are times this makes me nostalgic for Transformers Devastation, which was nearly but not quite as good as Bayonetta at combat, but at least the levels were straightforward and the gimmicks not so awful.
Still, this is an absolute must play if you love stylish action at all. It was a perfect antidote to the disappointment of DMC4 when it first came out and is STILL the champ of the genre today.

In short this game is more or less XCOM 1.5. Though that is not necessarily a bad thing as the great gameplay from the previous one is still in there, the bad thing is that it feels as if many of the assets such as animations have been re-used from the previous game so it does not feel entirely fresh. And the graphics look sleek without being too good.
Many of the new additions are great and since you are now on the offensive most of the time it means that many missions have timers, so you have to get your objectives done and then get out as soon as possible which creates tension and forces you to adopt new tactics compared to what you were used to previously. Though some of the missions have timers that either are too short or does not make much sense in relation to the objective. Such as the missions where you have to secure a supply stash, and even though you start the mission in stealth the enemy will still destroy the supplies if you take too long even if you were never detected.
The endgame also feel a bit too easy, as there are no elite versions of many of the enemies, ADVENT soldiers of all kinds seem to level up and develop as time goes on, but many of the units such as the Vipers don't. Meaning that a once feared enemy no longer is a threat at all. So the pacing feels a bit off later on.
Customization is really great, with many new ways to customize your soldiers, from a wide selection of hats and armours, even weapons and character personality animations can be changed to make your own squad more unique. Many of the classes also have been a bit more streamlined as well, and many skills feel a bit more useful and distinct. The specialist for example can now go down the skill path to become a medic or combat hacker. Both are useful so it is up to you how you mix and match character skills and builds.
All in all I enjoyed XCOM 2, but I feel that they could have done more, it feels like a large expansion rather than a full new game. But if you liked XCOM: Enemy unknown, then you will probably enjoy this one, just be prepared that they are fairly similar while at the same time have enough differences. If nothing else there is always a steam sale later on.
One thing is the same still though, RNG is still a ♥♥♥♥♥.

What would happen if you gamified the idea that you found a copy of an OS which was so dead-simple to use, anyone with basic computer and investigative skills could hack into
? You'd get Hacknet, an excellent hacking game designed to be the spiritual successor to Uplink. Slick graphics, a sliding difficulty designed to get you introduced to the game's mechancis one-by-one, and an in-the-background story which is surprisingly pointient and explores not only how insecure computers really are to a dedicated hacker, but the ramifications, both practical and mornal, of an OS designed to hack anything.
It's a short, satisfying hacking game which, despite how complicated it seems at the outset, eases you into its mechanics, world, and story, and gives you the surprising, satisfying feeling of being both a master hacker and Sherlock Holmes at the same time.
For the mandatory "Is this Uplink 2.0" part of the review: no. This is
the spiritual successor hardcore fans of Uplink have been looking for because:
If none of the above scared you off, then read on because this spiritual sequel is, in spite of the above, a worthy one IMO...
As mentioned above, Hacknet uses its command-line for much of the hacking, with a few GUI helpers for those tasks too cumbersome to exclusively do in the GUI, like keeping track of all the known IPs and keeping notes. Despite this, there are only a few core commands, and are remarkably easy-to-remember with repeated use - and the game is
careful to ensure you do - and often relate to what they do. For example, to crack an in-game computer's SSH port, run SSHcrack [insert port number here]. This is further helped by the addition of command auto-completion - something the game teaches you how to use very quickly. So, that SSHcrack command I just mentioned? All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a
easier.
The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old.
Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end.
You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter.
All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time.
Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles.
I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean
- is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with.
The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you.
I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

This is my first XCOM game. I've read a lot of good things about this franchise but didn't really give it a try.
XCOM 2 is having excellent squad / turn based tactics. Once the fight starts, it gets really intense on how you use tactics to surround and defeat the alien forces. Sometimes everything will go according to your plan, you will advance your squad, position them and set up an overwatch to cover your other squad members during their movement. But sometimes, the enemy will surprise you, your squad will be flanked resulting in casualties or even loss of your squad member(s), that's the time you switch your tactics to minimize the damage.
Weapon / gear upgrades are also cool. The level of customization on your squad members is also nifty, presents a lot of options. Once your squad starts getting promoted after successful missions, you will start to care for your squad leading on to choosing your best squad members for the most difficult missions.
Graphically the game is also good, nice animations, workable engine with occasional FPS drops, but everything looks good on the battle map.
Back in the HQ, you have a lot of technologies to research, which help you in developing new gear / weapons for your squad. New facilities can be built which add up to your prowess. That can be a little confusing but trial and error will eventually make you understand the ins and outs.
Solid strategy game, i would say, solid tactical strategy game!

This game is worth every single penny. It's a classic RTS game. It's fairly easy to get the jist of. Hell, even I got the hang of it quickly. That really speaks volumes to me.
This game is even better when you have someone to play with or against. On occasion, the online service will run into problems and people may not be able to join your game and/or you won't be able to join theirs. I have only recently started to notice this problem (10/31/15) so I am not sure how common it will become. It usually just takes a bit of time to fix itself though.
As mentioned before, it's real-time strategy. You get to pick the Civilization that you like the most. These include the Germans, Spanish, British, Asian civs,  Native American civs, and a lot more. Each have their own strategies. In the game, you are pitted against another Civ(s), whether it be an AI or an actual player. Your civilization's economy relies on 3 things: food, wood, and coin. Your villagers, or workers, must work to gather these resources and build your colony. You can use the resources to create buildings, buy improvements, and train an army.
Eventually, you'll need an army. There are infantry, calvalry, and artillery units. You can also have naval battles with various ships if there is a body of water on the map. As mentioned before, there are numerous strategies for victory. I'd recommend trying out all the Civilizations and see which one you feel most comfortable with.
Overall, this game is godly. It will stand the test of time, and I hope that the online service will remain available for years to come (after all, it still has a sizable community).
P.S. There is a fort called Het Huys de Hoop

I was a fan of Uplink back in the day, but it is certainly time for a modern quality release! I streamed Hacknet for 5 hours the other night and we had a great time experiencing what the world had to offer. You would think I rocketed through the game faster, but honestly much of the time was spent messing around in servers and poking around. The intuitive gameplay, explorable content, and the way the game handles failure made for a really enjoyable experience.
One thing I enjoyed was how intiutive everything was. This isn't linux, this isn't MS-DOS, this isn't even hacking per se. It's an adventure game with a command line interface. Hacking concepts and tools are abstracted for playablilty though it should be noted that there are some real hacking suites out there that are scarily easier to use then what you find in the game.
I'd love to go into details about the exciting things I found, but half of the fun is exploring. One big suggestion I have is to read through the help command in your OS - all 3 pages. Your HacknetOS has a lot of functionality that you wouldn't normally expect. The commands can also let you have a lot of fun! I had a ball changing some IRC logs and websites to include my viewers names to much embarassment and laughs.
An aspect I appreciated is that the punishment for making mistakes is firm but fair. Going into too much detail would be spoiling, but suffice it to say don't just get cozy clicking on the GUI for everything you do. Know your commands and they will treat you well in return.
I did encounter a few minor bugs, some graphic glitches dealing with text, however none were game breaking and I documented this information back to the company. At the stage I'm at in the game there were no hardware upgrades, but I have uncovered a number of hacking tools to provide alternate forms of entry into more difficult servers.
I'm happy to share more of my experience with you, or if you'd like just stop by the channel to see it in action.
DISCLAIMER: I was provided a pre-relase copy of the game by Surprise Attack Games with no additional compensation or influence. Heck I like the game so much I'm picking up a copy to give away to my viewers. :)
EDIT:  After a few more streams of the game, and now about 15 more hours spent with Hacknet I'm still loving the experience  The universe is solid, with some very interesting servers you encounter that make homages to pop culture and game references in some instances.  The banter logs are proabably my favorite things to hunt down as it makes it feel a little more real that people are using these boxes.
As for those miffed about me talking about my stream?  I respect your thumbs down, but potential buyers got to see Hacknet in action and it helped them make a purchasing decision (lots of YES!).  Totally worth it.

A cut above the rest in the FTP MMO environment, a surprise hit, a casual environment. Two thumbs up!
GOOD: Trove is a lightweight MMO with a number of options and flexibility in what you would want to focus on, and isn't particularly difficult at any point, compared to most MMOs. Nothing in the game takes a larger commitment than 30 minutes, and can easily and comfortably be played intoxicated. Personally, I love this game. It's everything I've wanted in an MMO: An easy to understand massively multiplayer environment without signing up for a full-time job or a two-week training course on the wiki. There's a heavy emphasis on vanity and personal creativity, and makes it very difficult to grief other players. Hot-swappable classes put an emphasis on the player's "mastery level" over your class level, giving you a tremendous amount of freedom and flexibility. The end-game content is still challenging enough for purists to pursue, or you could just spend all of your time building your own world, unlocking crafting recipies, or getting dragon souls attunement. The game is super relaxing and the community isn't perfect, but better than most.
BAD: Some players may not like the cutesy voxel imagery. Some hardcore players will find the cavalier attitude toward class balance and lack of depth in character stat development to be frustrating. The music and sound effects can get a tad repetitive. Some players find it boring, and the game is kinda front-loaded. Specifically, getting your first class or two to max level is much more time-consuming than others - because you can put end-game gear on mid-level classes and player's mastery level (gotten from advancing anything in any class) gives passive buffs to all classes. Additionally, at the time of writing this, Trove wasn't expected to be as popular as it is and as such is plagued by understaffing and server limitations. There is supposed to be a big improved hardware migration next week, but at this point it's been a year of what seems to be like 1/5th downtime. PvP is newly introduced and horrendously unbalanced, even for an MMO. User-created content is what the PvE is made of and yet it still somehow gets repetitive. There is a limited number of biomes and PvE can get very grindy.

The goal of this review is to objectively oppose people claiming the game is RNG-based, insanely difficult and grindy (all positive sides of DD are described very well by others).
1. RNG. Yes, as everybody else who completed the game I had some of my top heroes suddenly wiped by unfortunate series of crits/stuns/whatever. Yes, it felt bad. Yes, at first I was furious and wanted to blame somebody (game creators) or something (dishonest RNG) for this. But then I realised it would be so childish and stupid to do so.
Lots of different games use random and sometimes your win or lose is determined by it - but only sometimes. Consider the poker. Random? Definitely! Still, there are great players and there are unskilled ones.
Here it's just the same -  if you run like 90 weeks in DD, of course even if you play well there would be situations in which random will punish you. But also there would be situations when random will save your heroes (dodges/crits/great heals and so on).
You can't guarantee the success with 100% probability-that is true. But for a good player this probability would be much higher than for a bad player. It's just too tempting to blame random instead of your poor game decisions.
2. Grind. Yes, the game loop does not change too much throughout the game. I would consider it one of the biggest issues of DD. But most of reviewers pointing at grind say that you will spend hours training new heroes to replace the ones who got killed by hideous RNG. After recent patches it is just wrong - now you can replace fallen heroes pretty quickly especially if you have completed at least one level of darkest dungeon.
Also, It is obvious that you just have to somehow feel the loss of your heroes - otherwise the game would be just too forgiving. People who want to complete the game faster now can choose the newly added Radiant version of the game.
3. Difficulty. Yes, DD is not easy - it's turn-based strategy after all. If you want to free your mind and relax, go play something else. You will need to understand how the game is played, invent your strategies based on that hard-earned knowledge and test them in dungeons risking lives of your heroes - and this is exactly why the game is so compelling. If you don't want to analyse your mistakes and always blame RNG instead, you won't be able to make significant progress.
For me it was one of the most challenging strategies I've ever played; it was a great pleasure to overcome all the difficulties and complete it.
I would greatly enjoy any meaningful comments (especially if your opinion is the opposite to mine!)
