Bayonetta is the king of the stylish action genre for a reason. It works on every level, from truly  terrible play who doesn't understand the basics up to master level play. It is an excellent game and the core combat is some of the absolute best in the genre if not THE best. Not enough can be said about what a true delight Bayonetta's combat is.
That said, some of these level gimmicks are absolute garbage. I detested DMC4's awful campaign and at least Bayonetta levels are straightforward. Just then you get hit with a big fat boss with like six QTE segments who spends half the boss fight underwater and then a really terrible Space Harrier minigame that lasts about 30 minutes. And then finding all the collectibles practically requires a guide. (You have to shoot all the benches in the area. You have to backtrack all the way to the start of the level after beating the last fight before finishing the mission and the bonus will magically appear.) Most players won't notice these problems because they only grate on repeat plays, which is what THIS WHOLE GENRE IS MADE FOR.
There are times this makes me nostalgic for Transformers Devastation, which was nearly but not quite as good as Bayonetta at combat, but at least the levels were straightforward and the gimmicks not so awful.
Still, this is an absolute must play if you love stylish action at all. It was a perfect antidote to the disappointment of DMC4 when it first came out and is STILL the champ of the genre today.

This game has a great graphic style, and the narration adds so much to the gloomy mood of the game. Really good atmosphere. However the gameplay is both difficult and tedious because of the way your party can be affected by the RNG.
With a little bad RNG luck it's possible for your heroes to permadie which sets you back for many hours of grind. Grinding is what you do throughout 90% of the game, but only RNG can be somewhat mitigated by mastering the mechanics. There's never any relief from the grinding for gold and for leveling up your characters.
The core gameplay loop is interesting at first (assemble a party, adventure in a dungeon, fix up your party's stress, change skills/trinkets according to the next dungeon you plan to visit, and repeat) and even the combat is pretty cool, but it's so hard to advance in the game that it becomes boring after 10-15 hours when you've seen the mechanics the game has to offer. If one hero dies it feels like it's three steps forward, two steps back. If a hero doesn't die and you successfully complete your objective, the progress made is still pretty small.
If you wince when you hear unfair RNG or grind then this game is not for you. But if you like a slow-burning experience with a focus on RNG and overwhelming odds, you might enjoy Darkest Dungeon.

What would happen if you gamified the idea that you found a copy of an OS which was so dead-simple to use, anyone with basic computer and investigative skills could hack into
? You'd get Hacknet, an excellent hacking game designed to be the spiritual successor to Uplink. Slick graphics, a sliding difficulty designed to get you introduced to the game's mechancis one-by-one, and an in-the-background story which is surprisingly pointient and explores not only how insecure computers really are to a dedicated hacker, but the ramifications, both practical and mornal, of an OS designed to hack anything.
It's a short, satisfying hacking game which, despite how complicated it seems at the outset, eases you into its mechanics, world, and story, and gives you the surprising, satisfying feeling of being both a master hacker and Sherlock Holmes at the same time.
For the mandatory "Is this Uplink 2.0" part of the review: no. This is
the spiritual successor hardcore fans of Uplink have been looking for because:
If none of the above scared you off, then read on because this spiritual sequel is, in spite of the above, a worthy one IMO...
As mentioned above, Hacknet uses its command-line for much of the hacking, with a few GUI helpers for those tasks too cumbersome to exclusively do in the GUI, like keeping track of all the known IPs and keeping notes. Despite this, there are only a few core commands, and are remarkably easy-to-remember with repeated use - and the game is
careful to ensure you do - and often relate to what they do. For example, to crack an in-game computer's SSH port, run SSHcrack [insert port number here]. This is further helped by the addition of command auto-completion - something the game teaches you how to use very quickly. So, that SSHcrack command I just mentioned? All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a
easier.
The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old.
Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end.
You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter.
All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time.
Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles.
I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean
- is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with.
The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you.
I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

I was a fan of Uplink back in the day, but it is certainly time for a modern quality release! I streamed Hacknet for 5 hours the other night and we had a great time experiencing what the world had to offer. You would think I rocketed through the game faster, but honestly much of the time was spent messing around in servers and poking around. The intuitive gameplay, explorable content, and the way the game handles failure made for a really enjoyable experience.
One thing I enjoyed was how intiutive everything was. This isn't linux, this isn't MS-DOS, this isn't even hacking per se. It's an adventure game with a command line interface. Hacking concepts and tools are abstracted for playablilty though it should be noted that there are some real hacking suites out there that are scarily easier to use then what you find in the game.
I'd love to go into details about the exciting things I found, but half of the fun is exploring. One big suggestion I have is to read through the help command in your OS - all 3 pages. Your HacknetOS has a lot of functionality that you wouldn't normally expect. The commands can also let you have a lot of fun! I had a ball changing some IRC logs and websites to include my viewers names to much embarassment and laughs.
An aspect I appreciated is that the punishment for making mistakes is firm but fair. Going into too much detail would be spoiling, but suffice it to say don't just get cozy clicking on the GUI for everything you do. Know your commands and they will treat you well in return.
I did encounter a few minor bugs, some graphic glitches dealing with text, however none were game breaking and I documented this information back to the company. At the stage I'm at in the game there were no hardware upgrades, but I have uncovered a number of hacking tools to provide alternate forms of entry into more difficult servers.
I'm happy to share more of my experience with you, or if you'd like just stop by the channel to see it in action.
DISCLAIMER: I was provided a pre-relase copy of the game by Surprise Attack Games with no additional compensation or influence. Heck I like the game so much I'm picking up a copy to give away to my viewers. :)
EDIT:  After a few more streams of the game, and now about 15 more hours spent with Hacknet I'm still loving the experience  The universe is solid, with some very interesting servers you encounter that make homages to pop culture and game references in some instances.  The banter logs are proabably my favorite things to hunt down as it makes it feel a little more real that people are using these boxes.
As for those miffed about me talking about my stream?  I respect your thumbs down, but potential buyers got to see Hacknet in action and it helped them make a purchasing decision (lots of YES!).  Totally worth it.

This game is awful in every sense of the word.
Best way to describe it? A contentless Terraria.
I really cannot think of many positive things to say about this game. It has terrible bosses (both looks and difficulty wise). Who thought it would be oh so funny to make the first boss be a penguin in a flying saucer? Whos humour is so bad that they actually found that funny? Why wasn't the boss simply an alien in the flying saucer, that spawns more aliens on the surface instead of penguins?
Then we have the second boss, which is a robot that you build yourself. You build it, just to kill it. This boss also looks idiotic too. How hard can it be to make a threatening looking robot? That's one of the main problems with the few bosses in this game. They don't look threatening at all. They're also way too easy.
At least the dragon is somewhat decent.
Anyway, the game has been casualized to hell and back too. At first we had threat levels for each sector. For example, in the alpha sector, the threat level went from 1-10, beta sector 10-20, and so on upto threat level 100. You could immediately see the difference in difficulty between a threat level 1 planet, to a threat level 4+.
Now we have 10 threat levels maximum. Alpha sector has nothing but threat level 1 planets, beta nothing but threat level 2. Chucklefish claim that the difficulty is still just the same, but that is a flat out lie. The monsters apparently get stronger the further you dig down into the planet, but I never noticed any difference, even when I reached the planets core. Speaking of which, you have next to no reason to dig past the surface in this game. Terraria was filled with sprawling caves which had many neat things to find. Starbound caves are devoid of anything besides a few enemies. You might as well stay on the surface.
Oh and once you reach a certain depth, the music cuts off. Some may argue that this creates atmosphere, but since the caves are so dull I don't see how it adds to anything. Instead it comes across as lazy. There could have easily been some cave themes that actually added to the "creepy" atmosphere that they were trying to go for.
Now onto the monsters. They look awful. They sound awful. Seriously, half of them make horse sounds, the other half make sheep sounds. It's so irritating to listen too. What's the matter? Couldn't even take some time out to give the enemies some decent, unique sound effects? Again, lazy.
I think it was advertised at some point "never see the same enemy twice!". Well I have seen the same exact enemy multiple times over. I've also seen that same enemy, except coloured green, instead of purple.
Do chucklefish not know how to make things look threatening? Well, they sort of do since I have seen a few enemies that actually look good, but most of the time the enemies look goofy as ♥♥♥♥. Why must chucklefish insist on taking the goofy route? Is that their plan? To make the games comedy be aimed at morons that find an enemy with a mohawk funny?
I could go on and on about this games shortcomings, but I'm going to cut it short here.
The bottom line is, Terraria, which took a few months to create (granted it was still a little rough around the edges when it first came out too) is a far and away better game than Starbound which has taken years and is still in alpha, which the devs are calling beta. The updates are few and far between. It's been like what? 4 months now without an update?
Talk about taking the money and running. I had the game bought for me thankfully, or I'd actually be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off if I payed money for this crap.
So remember kids, don't buy incomplete games, because this happens. The devs have no incentive to work on it now that you gave them 3 million for a barebone skeleton of a game.

Ok, so im revising my views on this game. I have put nearly 400 hours into it and can tell you: SKIP THIS GAME. Buy Terraria instead. Seriously. Starbound sucks.
Starbound was pitched as Terraria in SPACE! by Tiyuri (the head guy of Chucklefish) years ago.
When it first hit Early Acces, it was most definatly looking to be exactly that. And then, Tiy decided that the game needed some Dark Souls style mechanics. No one quite understood what he meant and to this day, we cant figure it out. The only thing many players understand is that Tiy decided that "Fun" was something that was not needed for "his" game.
5 years of development, and the devs still have no real idea what the game is supposed to be. They kept toting ideas like Metroidvanias, Symphony of the Night, and Dark Souls as the basis for their changes and slowly the game became less of what was pitched and more of a "Welp, its what it is." With no real defined game in there. It has no identity. Its not a sandbox, its not a story driven game. Its in a wierd in-between that sucks the fun out of playing it. Everything is gated behind terrible walls. Its bad.
Pros: The planets. They are neat to go out and explore. The dungeons are neat. The Pixel Art is amazing.
Cons: The game is the very definition of "Repetative."
Basically, the ENTIRE game boils down to this formula in terms of your armor and weapons
Amor/weapon tier at same level as planet: Die in 3 or 4 hits, kill in 4 to 6 hits
Armor/weapon below tier of planet: die in 1 to 2 hits, takes 10+ hits to kill things.
Note: This hit to kill stat is based on melee weapons only becuase Tiyuri decided years ago that Ranged weapons are not worth using. He believes they cheapen combat and instead of going the route of Terraria and making interesting ranged and melee, he thought Ranged shouldnt be worthwhile.
The monsters are not a challange. The combat is terrible. All ranged weapons are absolutely worthless. They use your suits "Energy Bar" which is the same energy used for your techs like double jump and dash. Ranged weapons deal absolutely miniscule amounts of damage and you can expect to spend your entire energy bar to MAYBE kill 1 monster of equal tier. Sniper Rifles can be OK but the shot reload times make them a niche use at best.
TL:DR Skip Starbound. Its not fun. What could have been a fun Sandbox or a fun Terraria in Space has been Tiy'd up to the point of being awful.
Also note: The devopers used to actively talk to the community, but often became offended when anyone had VALID CRITICISMS. Im not talking about "Your game is SUCK AND BAD", but rather legitimate issues like "Ranged weapons arent worth using. Melee is vastly better and heres an idea that might balance out Ranged a bit". Valid Criticisms were often met with name calling and comments of "You arent a part of our team and therefor dont know the direction we are going."
The entire dev team now actively avoids any place that doesnt allow them to ban people for voicing concerns.

A cut above the rest in the FTP MMO environment, a surprise hit, a casual environment. Two thumbs up!
GOOD: Trove is a lightweight MMO with a number of options and flexibility in what you would want to focus on, and isn't particularly difficult at any point, compared to most MMOs. Nothing in the game takes a larger commitment than 30 minutes, and can easily and comfortably be played intoxicated. Personally, I love this game. It's everything I've wanted in an MMO: An easy to understand massively multiplayer environment without signing up for a full-time job or a two-week training course on the wiki. There's a heavy emphasis on vanity and personal creativity, and makes it very difficult to grief other players. Hot-swappable classes put an emphasis on the player's "mastery level" over your class level, giving you a tremendous amount of freedom and flexibility. The end-game content is still challenging enough for purists to pursue, or you could just spend all of your time building your own world, unlocking crafting recipies, or getting dragon souls attunement. The game is super relaxing and the community isn't perfect, but better than most.
BAD: Some players may not like the cutesy voxel imagery. Some hardcore players will find the cavalier attitude toward class balance and lack of depth in character stat development to be frustrating. The music and sound effects can get a tad repetitive. Some players find it boring, and the game is kinda front-loaded. Specifically, getting your first class or two to max level is much more time-consuming than others - because you can put end-game gear on mid-level classes and player's mastery level (gotten from advancing anything in any class) gives passive buffs to all classes. Additionally, at the time of writing this, Trove wasn't expected to be as popular as it is and as such is plagued by understaffing and server limitations. There is supposed to be a big improved hardware migration next week, but at this point it's been a year of what seems to be like 1/5th downtime. PvP is newly introduced and horrendously unbalanced, even for an MMO. User-created content is what the PvE is made of and yet it still somehow gets repetitive. There is a limited number of biomes and PvE can get very grindy.

The goal of this review is to objectively oppose people claiming the game is RNG-based, insanely difficult and grindy (all positive sides of DD are described very well by others).
1. RNG. Yes, as everybody else who completed the game I had some of my top heroes suddenly wiped by unfortunate series of crits/stuns/whatever. Yes, it felt bad. Yes, at first I was furious and wanted to blame somebody (game creators) or something (dishonest RNG) for this. But then I realised it would be so childish and stupid to do so.
Lots of different games use random and sometimes your win or lose is determined by it - but only sometimes. Consider the poker. Random? Definitely! Still, there are great players and there are unskilled ones.
Here it's just the same -  if you run like 90 weeks in DD, of course even if you play well there would be situations in which random will punish you. But also there would be situations when random will save your heroes (dodges/crits/great heals and so on).
You can't guarantee the success with 100% probability-that is true. But for a good player this probability would be much higher than for a bad player. It's just too tempting to blame random instead of your poor game decisions.
2. Grind. Yes, the game loop does not change too much throughout the game. I would consider it one of the biggest issues of DD. But most of reviewers pointing at grind say that you will spend hours training new heroes to replace the ones who got killed by hideous RNG. After recent patches it is just wrong - now you can replace fallen heroes pretty quickly especially if you have completed at least one level of darkest dungeon.
Also, It is obvious that you just have to somehow feel the loss of your heroes - otherwise the game would be just too forgiving. People who want to complete the game faster now can choose the newly added Radiant version of the game.
3. Difficulty. Yes, DD is not easy - it's turn-based strategy after all. If you want to free your mind and relax, go play something else. You will need to understand how the game is played, invent your strategies based on that hard-earned knowledge and test them in dungeons risking lives of your heroes - and this is exactly why the game is so compelling. If you don't want to analyse your mistakes and always blame RNG instead, you won't be able to make significant progress.
For me it was one of the most challenging strategies I've ever played; it was a great pleasure to overcome all the difficulties and complete it.
I would greatly enjoy any meaningful comments (especially if your opinion is the opposite to mine!)

This game has a great graphic style, and the narration adds so much to the gloomy mood of the game. Really good atmosphere. However the gameplay is both difficult and tedious because of the way your party can be affected by the RNG.
With a little bad RNG luck it's possible for your heroes to permadie which sets you back for many hours of grind. Grinding is what you do throughout 90% of the game, but only RNG can be somewhat mitigated by mastering the mechanics. There's never any relief from the grinding for gold and for leveling up your characters.
The core gameplay loop is interesting at first (assemble a party, adventure in a dungeon, fix up your party's stress, change skills/trinkets according to the next dungeon you plan to visit, and repeat) and even the combat is pretty cool, but it's so hard to advance in the game that it becomes boring after 10-15 hours when you've seen the mechanics the game has to offer. If one hero dies it feels like it's three steps forward, two steps back. If a hero doesn't die and you successfully complete your objective, the progress made is still pretty small.
If you wince when you hear unfair RNG or grind then this game is not for you. But if you like a slow-burning experience with a focus on RNG and overwhelming odds, you might enjoy Darkest Dungeon.

This is a truly beautiful game. The level of detail each ship has is stunning. It's a joy seeing your turrents pivot and track your pointer. Your orientation is important, different ships have different fields of fire, some favor broadside action, others at the fore, others have smart guns that fire inderectly, and so on. It's a joy to see each turret open up depending where you are aiming.
No ship feels more powerful than the other, nor is one loadout better than the next, they just give you more options and choices, and the chance to really personalize some ships and find your own style.
In terms of gameplay, the 10 player matches are very intense, but newbie friendly. You can have veterans and newbies in the same team and not feel like you're babysitting anyone or the other way arround. The controls and mechanics are very intuitive, making the game easy to master. That doesn't make it boring though! The magic is in the slugging matches between crafts, and that never gets old.
It's very close to a perfect information game, you almost always know what the enemy is doing, and he knows what you're doing too. That means that strategy is key here, knowing when to split your team, or stay together takes a while to sink in, but seeing an impromptu party of strangers work together as a well oiled machine is worth it.
The company is very active and constantly adding stuff, with a new ship appearing in an almost monthly basis. This is a very solid and underappreciated game, and it's pretty unique in what it has to offer. It's less of a moba in space, and more of chess in space. Less about using complex abilities and gear and more about anticipating your enemy and cooperating with your ally. Worth your money and your time.

However, there are some considerations before you buy this:
1. Your system specs and health, this is important, like any modern video game, first check if your computer meets the specs for playing this game, and of course if your computer healthy enough to run it. There are many bitter complains because of this.
2. DLCs and patches, since there are a couple of DLC out, there have been patches that change the balance and gameplay, so be prepared to start a new Legend/ironman/100deadsoldiers run every time a new patch is out, otherwise better wait for the last patch DLC, which could be at the end of this year.

Now that you've taken such considerations, the brilliant thing of this game:

Drop Alive is a plarformer game in which you control a water drop and clear levels in order to get from a house to a pond. The idea is quite simple. Actually, everything about this game is simple, beginning from the visuals, though the music, sound, and controls. The graphics look done by hand, which is quite unique in video games. Only one button for jumping is used alongside the analog/d-pad movement. The game is also not too long, but not too short either. It is simple, but it is this simpliness that is its biggest charm and selling point.
Each level is different, which is nice. New elements show up. The game do not bore the player. There are three types of the drop: normal water, steam when heated and ice when frozen. It surprised me at first when the drop turned into steam when it touched a heated metal pipe. I was expecting a far more simple game. It turned out to be better than I expected. There are even small touches like that a sponge sink in the water from the drop!
I really liked playing it. It felt like good old times came back, when people made games more for sharing the fun than for the money. It has ‘this thing’ in it than a lot of games today do not have.
The biggest problem with Drop Alive are bugs. They destroy the good and fun atmosphere the game brings.

Since I first played Half-Life 2 before playing its predecessor, Half-Life, I expected the game to be low-res, boring, and nearly impossible due to game glitches like most games created around the time. Needless to say, I was completely wrong. Half-Life is just as good as Half-Life 2, if not better. I had a blast playing its campaign on its most difficult setting. Remember: Fast Save is F6. The game is challenging enough that you will not get annoyed by its simplicity, but you also won't give up in frustration due to its complexity. I recommend this game 8/10 for anyone that plays FPS's, enjoys a good story, and won't go deaf from a large amount of amazing dialogue.

If you like games about positioning and strategy, this game is great. A lot of the negative reviews are out of date, so they're not so reliable. One thing I don't like is that the while the game is about flying capital ships, their firepower seems underwhelming compared to what you see in other sci-fi media.
Graphics:
Ships look great.
Stations and asteroids look kinda bland, but the game is still in alpha, so I hope they're just placeholders.
Effects are hit and miss, as some are much better than others. Likely due to the game's alpha status.
Gameplay:
On the surface it seems kinda dull, but spend a little time learning what each ship can do and a whole lot of possibilities open up. Deployment of ships can win or lose games, as an ambush on a ship or a station at the right time can tip the balance. The game encourages teamwork as each ship type has a role to play.
Sound:
It's your average pew pew in space sounds. Nothing bad, but nothing outstanding.
The ship's crew talks to you in game, providing tips disguised as immersive voice acting. A nice touch.
Longevity:
There's a bunch of ships available, but only a few game modes and maps. In it's current state, I reckon I could get 10-15 hours enjoyment from it. However, as I've mentioned, the game is still in alpha so there will be more content to come.
I got the game for free, but I wouldn't buy it in its current state. Luckily the game will be available as a free to play/pay game when it leaves early access. So definitely give it a go once it reaches that stage.

I bought this game on sale based on Totalbiscuit's recommendation and I was not disappointed. After playing for over 70 hours I am just now starting to get bored of it. For less than $20 I would consider that a good deal. It's worth noting that I mostly play shooter and stealth games so I wasn't expecting to fall in love with this game the way I did.
So why do I like this game so much? I would say it's mainly because the gameplay "loop" is rather addictive! This loop has three main components to it. First you must recuit people who have arrived to your little Hamlet off the stage coach. There are fifteen different types of characters you can recruit, each type having different strengths and weaknesses. Then you must go fight and explore in the four (five if you count the darkest dungeon) dungeons surrounding the hamlet. In these dungeons your team will endure stress, illness and often death. But with each successful mission you are rewarded with treasure, experience, trinkets, etc. After each mission you return to the hamlet to heal the characters who just returned and prepare another group for the next mission.
In addition to all of that, Darkest Dungeon also has a rather nice visual style, an excellent narrator and an intense sountrack that WILL stick with you long after you're done playing.
The main issue I have with Darkest Dungeon is that it could give the player more information about each dungeon before   they start their mission. It would be especially helpful to know what sort of enemies you will be encountering, as each kind has their own set of strenghts and weaknesses. Instead you will probably have to keep the Darkest Dungeon wiki up on your phone or second monitor as you play unless you're a complete masochist.
While this may all sound very straightforward to you I promise the game is deeper than my silly little review could cover. I strongly encourage you to buy the game and give it a shot.

I put this game to my 3 day test and I can't put it down. While I recommend the game, I'm going to pick some bones with it because some of the biggest issues with the game are the kinds that turn 15 minutes into 10 hours.
Being that I recommend this, I will start the negatives. People are more likely to listen to a recommendation when it isn't blind worshop, but tempered.
Starting out, know what you're getting into. The game defaults to a setting called "Deck-Based Stage Coach." This setting should be disabled immediately. For 50 in-game weeks, I got the same 4 classes, over and over. Classes that could not viably be used as a cohesive unit. And since your heroes level up, and cannot return to dungeons beneath their level, I wound up using team after team after team of support only units that don't mix at all to try and grind gold to send out the better team to make real progress. Upon disabling Deck-Based Stage Coach, I immediately got 3 of the classes I could have used over the past year and was able to start making progress again instead of scrounging by on a thousand gold or less every other mission. So turn that off, because it can leave you picking the exact same classes every week regardless how far you upgrade the coach.
Second, accept that sometimes RNG will just♥♥♥♥♥♥on you. I've seen a few rounds where a character went to 100 stress in no time due to stress-stacking by the enemy. And at 40 stress per enchantress (minus resistences) plus additional stress anytime any character gets critted, you can EASILY have a unit at 0 stress top out at his 100, get afflicted, and then drag your whole team down by giving each of them 10 stress per move (40 per round) from your own team, on top of the 100+ the enemy can throw your way when your luck gets bad. Don't listen to the meta guys, they probably never played this game: When your luck goes south, tactics alone will not save you. If RNGesus hates you, you won't be able to retreat, your jester won't help in the least, and you'll be screwed. All because a near-0 stress unit lost their mind in the worst ♥♥♥♥ing luck you think you'll ever have.
Between those 2 issues, if you lost a hero to bad luck, you might not even see another of that class (or even relatively similar combat role) for an in-game YEAR.
So turn off that deck-based stage coach by going to Options>Gameplay Options once you've loaded a save, and you'll find the heroes get randomized again, which is good.
So, you'll still lose some guys to really bad groupings of back to back crits. Sorry. But now it won't take you 20 hours and a hair loss treatment to get them back. In fact, it might be 2 hours and you've worked a new one back to fill that slot. Never identical, but acceptable. Sometimes better.
One thing I love about this game is
One of my biggest gripes in gaming is the meta whoring: Do it this very linear way or it won't work well. Not here, another title that actually allows a degree of freedom in your apporach. Those troll elitists arguing in YouTube comments about "OP should've used..." are usually always wrong. Because you can switch many types of groups and use them interchangeably. Not EVERY type, but many. I rarely roll jesters because I find that their stress relief is next to nothing compared to a good grave robber (critting will destress your team- doing it often is better than a skill that does it on command), but many will swear by jesters: Truth is you can use either and many alternatives. The potential to mix and match is great, though not entirely unlimited.
The atmosphere is lovely. I don't really use that word, but it is. It's ♥♥♥♥ing perfect to be honest.
The boss fights are about rage inducing your first time. Some, anyways. But it's because they have a very special set of conditions. And you'll find yourself retreating once or twice until you understand their tricks. Then you'll roll in again and wipe the floor with them. Absolutely love this game!
Completed Veteran. 44 hours.
Completed Legend. 57 hours.
+ Sniper is my MVP. From early missions all the way to final mission. Highest damage, highest kills, lowest injury. KillZone and Serial are important for getting out multiple shots in one round. AP round equipped to help bypassing armor. Wraith armor - Hook is extremely important. Free action to get to high ground. One mission, I had 2 snipers with KillZone, and initiated with a grenade. Most spectacular bloodbath~!
+ Psi is useful for late game. Domination for mind-control. Most other abilities for guaranteed damage. Stasis for emergency. Inspire is frequently useful to activate another squad member who is in a better position.
+ 2 Grenadiers. Bomb everything to wipe out cover and armor. Without cover, the rest of squad can take kills easily. Especially for Sniper.
- Specialist. Played entire game with 1 main Specialist and 1 backup in case the main is injured. However, I wonder often if another Ranger, Sniper or Grenadier is better. Specialist is needed for the missions that require you to *hack*. Often reaching the objective on the last round... Having one specialist makes it much easier. Haywire doesn't work well in early missions (Legend), and late game, some of the "lamppost" hacks are not worth sacrificing one action point. Someone said to combo Repeater (% chance to execute), with Guardian overwatch Specialist. At the end of my campaign, my specialist did a grand total of 17 executes. Not very impressive. But during the missions, I was always thankful when it triggered on a big nasty enemy.
+ Ranger. Sometimes 1, sometimes 2. They do not trigger overwatch. At close range, deals tons of damage. Rapid fire helps to secure missions where I need to destroy an objective. Several times running short on timer, a Ranger dashes forward (Run N Gun) to save the day. Rotates different armor based on missions. They are my tanks against Chryssalid. I.e. equip the armor that ignores Poison. On other missions, equip the healing armor.
What most of the Internet says is true about getting your squad size up.
*** Guerilla Training School - Squad size upgrade. Get it fast!
** Advanced Warfare Center - Faster recovery.
** Proving Grounds - Get special rounds fast.
* Laboratory - After all other facilities are done (e.g. Power Relay, Resistance Comms, Psi Lab) to help research faster.
* Defense Matrix - Helps significantly in that one mission. Not sure if I can do without, but in Legend, I'm not taking chances.
- Shadow Chamber - Not that important. Just needed to advance the story.
I used mods to speed up game play, and to display more information, like flanking, LOS, kill counts, injured days, black market items uses, etc.
The earlier missions are the hardest.
Especially the first mission! Try to get high grounds with full cover. Lure enemies into rest of your squad in high grounds and full cover. Rotate members with grenade to the front. Don't take chances. You can die in one shot. If you survive one shot you are lucky. Mission is not timed, so take your time!
Don't give up. Once you get Squad size (5) upgrade, things become better significantly. Then the weapon upgrades. Then the Squad size (6) upgrade.
(small amount of spoiler)
The easiest way to win Final mission, I found, is to camp at the section before the final room. There is a narrow bridge leading into the final room. I have the 1 Sniper camp on the building facing that narrow bridge. Rest of my squad scattered around.
Leading towards the final room, I try to dominate/mind-control 1 or 2 enemies. Gatekeeper is absolutely the best enemy to mind control. Archon the second best. Once mind-controlled, with the rest of the squad waiting in the previous room, I'd move the mind-controlled enemy into final room, agrro the enemies pack, and run back. A few turns later, the *most important enemy* (not to reveal spoiler) will come into your room. Take it out in 1 round (or 2)! It is very possible! Since *the most important enemy* will T******* around each time you hit it, it is important to spread your squad evenly across the room.
Repeat.
Win.

Starbound is a game very similar to Terraria. It is a 2D sidescrolling Minecraft-like. However, I was never able to get very much into Terraria, despite how fun it sounded in theory. Starbound takes Terraria's theoretical fun, fixes all the issues it had, adds tons of cool features, and plops you down on a random planet in a random star system in a random galaxy ...
The variety of planets accessible via your spaceship is practically infinite, as is the variety of flora and fauna found on them. Exploration is huge, combat is satisfying, and progression is clear. Multiplayer is a blast, and cooperative monster fighting and base building are mostly better than they are solo.
As of this review, the game is currently in beta and missing a great deal of content, and for testing purposes, progression is extremely quick and easy. Lots of content is slowly but steadily being added, and progression will eventually be appropriately extended and fleshed out.
Starbound will definitely keep me coming back for more, particularly as updates are released. 8/10, pending final content.

Alright, where to start?
Well, i am going to just state all the new features of the game so that way you can see what exactly what you might like or hate. Why? Because something i hate may be something you love ( vice versa) and i'll limit my opinion as it shouldn't really stop you from buying this game as it truly needs to be experienced rather than read upon or watched.
FEATURES:
•	Multiplayer and Campaign.
•	Weapon customization (attachments and camouflage).
•	More character customization.
•	More enemies .
•	Newly designed old ones.
•	Melee weapons.
•	New classes (duh..!).
•	New income mechanic . ( It isn't automatically provided, you must sacrifice time to collect it )
•	A wide array of mods.
•	Enhanced graphics ( you already know that :P).
•	An armor mechanic . ( both you and enemies have armor which makes both more difficult to kill)
•	Different Ammo types. ( helps with armor and special enemies )
•	A lot more utilities for your troops.
•	No MECs. ( there's an EXO-suit which i find similar)
•	Same weapon tiers ( only 3)
•	Different command system (goodbye satellites).
•	Different buildings and rooms to make .
•	No more jets and spaceships.
•	Loot system ( weapon attachments, soldier upgrades and resources which can be picked up in the battlefield)
•	Timed campaign.
•	More timed missions.
•	A character pool outside the campaign where you can design your own troops and share them with the community.
And of course a different set of characters.
I think those are the most significant features but if i forgot any i will replay and edit it. If you feel spectacle about any of the features such as the timed missions then don't worry as i've mentioned, there are mods available which do provide various ways to remove or improves some or all of the features. Hell, theres alot of new interesting ones too!
In terms of story, we lost the war. Sucks i know. However, we're now insurgents which provides a different approach to the game. We're the ones in the shadows, not them. We're the ones who ambush. I honestly love it as it gives me a reason to return to the previous game as they're quite different.
I personally completed my first playthrough in roughly 30 hours ( i did spend like an hour or 2 to customize some soldiers). A second one? I doubt it for now as i'm busy however i can see someone getting a good 100 hours with the vanilla game and its available mods. Personally, i'll wait until it releases an expansion like XCOM did with "Enemy within". For the dlc, i haven't purchased any with the exception of the pre-order bonus which only adds cosmetic features. Don't feel left out as there are mods which add even better ones.

Lovely game, and it's barely in freaking alpha. I would really recommend the developers just embrace the MOBA theme just as they do the space theme, it would make for a pleasureable experience and also attract an already humongous MOBA community.
The sectors idea is very nice and creative, but adding more of a lane feature like constant influx of computer NPC's that the capital ships can farm can generate a better "farming" instance besides the capturing of mines. The lanes could kind of interfere with how the mines are placed in the map, but a good way to counter this is maybe just having the lanes go straight through the middle of the three mines in the sector, therefore creating the "NPC lane" of a traditional MOBA.  The lanes would consist of small fighters and the occasional sisge-like small patrol cruiser. In most MOBA's they would be the creeps and the occasional siege catapult or engine. These NPC units would serve to finally give the player capital ships their real scale of masiveness. The capital ships are supposed to be impending flying space fortresses. This is definetely nailed in the Star Wars game Empire at War which has amazing space battles that ended up with me looking for something similar in Fractured Space. The varying types of ships serve to give the Mon Calamari and Star Destroyers the scale they deserve. This might be an excellent example since I know this studio was partially inspired on their previous game, Zero Suit, by the tremendous universe that is Star Wars. The varying scales of the ships fighting in Empire at War space battles added a way more epic feeling not only for the scale, but also the complexity of the conflict, the firepower and chaos.
The Gamma sector is definetely very cool, serves in what in LoL would be the Baron and in Dota Roshan to gain extra bonuses for your team.
Upgrades could be diversified a lot, maybe creating a sort of shopping list in forward and main bases to upgrade a ship better. For instance, upgrades that you want to choose to adapt to a situation. Armor agaisnt sniper-like overseer ships would be interesting for a Heavy class capital ship and therefore serve in balancing out any problems their might be with balancing ship classes in game. This would definetely be an area to do a lot of work and thinking on, there exist many possibilities which the developers should definetely take advantage on and expand.
Overall, great game, would gladly play waaaaaaay more from now on, and I love the dedication it is recieving. Pretty looking and on an alpha state is a very good sign.

Half-Life is a classic. It was my first "true" FPS (my only other games prior being Minecraft and the Portal franchise) Admitedly, the graphics technology is... outdated, to say the least, but what it lacks in tech, it makes up for in every other regard. The design is spot on, and it has a natural learning curve and is great for both those who want to get into FPSs or veterans who have been around since the days of Wolfenstein. The story line is great in the fact that it is... the best adjective for this would be transparent. I do not mean that it is easy to see what comes next, and in fact it throws you several curveballs which mix up the gameplay even more. What I mean by transparent is that if all you care about is blasting aliens, the story will fade into the background and the dialouge will bother you no more than a blast from your shotgun straight into a zombie's face. Conversly, however, if you enjoy deep narratives with mysteries and solutions around every turn, Half-Life will delight you as well as you catch sight of some graffiti on a wall, overhear your enemies talking about your activities or even catch a rare glimpse of an odd man in a dark suit. Half-Life truly has something for everyone, form varied gameplay to an imersive story with both blended seamlessly together in a ride you'll be unlikely to forget.

Absolutely love this game!
Completed Veteran. 44 hours.
Completed Legend. 57 hours.
+ Sniper is my MVP. From early missions all the way to final mission. Highest damage, highest kills, lowest injury. KillZone and Serial are important for getting out multiple shots in one round. AP round equipped to help bypassing armor. Wraith armor - Hook is extremely important. Free action to get to high ground. One mission, I had 2 snipers with KillZone, and initiated with a grenade. Most spectacular bloodbath~!
+ Psi is useful for late game. Domination for mind-control. Most other abilities for guaranteed damage. Stasis for emergency. Inspire is frequently useful to activate another squad member who is in a better position.
+ 2 Grenadiers. Bomb everything to wipe out cover and armor. Without cover, the rest of squad can take kills easily. Especially for Sniper.
- Specialist. Played entire game with 1 main Specialist and 1 backup in case the main is injured. However, I wonder often if another Ranger, Sniper or Grenadier is better. Specialist is needed for the missions that require you to *hack*. Often reaching the objective on the last round... Having one specialist makes it much easier. Haywire doesn't work well in early missions (Legend), and late game, some of the "lamppost" hacks are not worth sacrificing one action point. Someone said to combo Repeater (% chance to execute), with Guardian overwatch Specialist. At the end of my campaign, my specialist did a grand total of 17 executes. Not very impressive. But during the missions, I was always thankful when it triggered on a big nasty enemy.
+ Ranger. Sometimes 1, sometimes 2. They do not trigger overwatch. At close range, deals tons of damage. Rapid fire helps to secure missions where I need to destroy an objective. Several times running short on timer, a Ranger dashes forward (Run N Gun) to save the day. Rotates different armor based on missions. They are my tanks against Chryssalid. I.e. equip the armor that ignores Poison. On other missions, equip the healing armor.
What most of the Internet says is true about getting your squad size up.
*** Guerilla Training School - Squad size upgrade. Get it fast!
** Advanced Warfare Center - Faster recovery.
** Proving Grounds - Get special rounds fast.
* Laboratory - After all other facilities are done (e.g. Power Relay, Resistance Comms, Psi Lab) to help research faster.
* Defense Matrix - Helps significantly in that one mission. Not sure if I can do without, but in Legend, I'm not taking chances.
- Shadow Chamber - Not that important. Just needed to advance the story.
I used mods to speed up game play, and to display more information, like flanking, LOS, kill counts, injured days, black market items uses, etc.
The earlier missions are the hardest.
Especially the first mission! Try to get high grounds with full cover. Lure enemies into rest of your squad in high grounds and full cover. Rotate members with grenade to the front. Don't take chances. You can die in one shot. If you survive one shot you are lucky. Mission is not timed, so take your time!
Don't give up. Once you get Squad size (5) upgrade, things become better significantly. Then the weapon upgrades. Then the Squad size (6) upgrade.
(small amount of spoiler)
The easiest way to win Final mission, I found, is to camp at the section before the final room. There is a narrow bridge leading into the final room. I have the 1 Sniper camp on the building facing that narrow bridge. Rest of my squad scattered around.
Leading towards the final room, I try to dominate/mind-control 1 or 2 enemies. Gatekeeper is absolutely the best enemy to mind control. Archon the second best. Once mind-controlled, with the rest of the squad waiting in the previous room, I'd move the mind-controlled enemy into final room, agrro the enemies pack, and run back. A few turns later, the *most important enemy* (not to reveal spoiler) will come into your room. Take it out in 1 round (or 2)! It is very possible! Since *the most important enemy* will T******* around each time you hit it, it is important to spread your squad evenly across the room.
Repeat.
Win.

Alright, where to start?
Well, i am going to just state all the new features of the game so that way you can see what exactly what you might like or hate. Why? Because something i hate may be something you love ( vice versa) and i'll limit my opinion as it shouldn't really stop you from buying this game as it truly needs to be experienced rather than read upon or watched.
FEATURES:
•	Multiplayer and Campaign.
•	Weapon customization (attachments and camouflage).
•	More character customization.
•	More enemies .
•	Newly designed old ones.
•	Melee weapons.
•	New classes (duh..!).
•	New income mechanic . ( It isn't automatically provided, you must sacrifice time to collect it )
•	A wide array of mods.
•	Enhanced graphics ( you already know that :P).
•	An armor mechanic . ( both you and enemies have armor which makes both more difficult to kill)
•	Different Ammo types. ( helps with armor and special enemies )
•	A lot more utilities for your troops.
•	No MECs. ( there's an EXO-suit which i find similar)
•	Same weapon tiers ( only 3)
•	Different command system (goodbye satellites).
•	Different buildings and rooms to make .
•	No more jets and spaceships.
•	Loot system ( weapon attachments, soldier upgrades and resources which can be picked up in the battlefield)
•	Timed campaign.
•	More timed missions.
•	A character pool outside the campaign where you can design your own troops and share them with the community.
And of course a different set of characters.
I think those are the most significant features but if i forgot any i will replay and edit it. If you feel spectacle about any of the features such as the timed missions then don't worry as i've mentioned, there are mods available which do provide various ways to remove or improves some or all of the features. Hell, theres alot of new interesting ones too!
In terms of story, we lost the war. Sucks i know. However, we're now insurgents which provides a different approach to the game. We're the ones in the shadows, not them. We're the ones who ambush. I honestly love it as it gives me a reason to return to the previous game as they're quite different.
I personally completed my first playthrough in roughly 30 hours ( i did spend like an hour or 2 to customize some soldiers). A second one? I doubt it for now as i'm busy however i can see someone getting a good 100 hours with the vanilla game and its available mods. Personally, i'll wait until it releases an expansion like XCOM did with "Enemy within". For the dlc, i haven't purchased any with the exception of the pre-order bonus which only adds cosmetic features. Don't feel left out as there are mods which add even better ones.
For those unfamiliar with the X-COM games: its a Sci-fi turn-based strategy game featuring the titular fictional organization tasked with countering alien invasions of Earth.
I suggest watching the trailer of both games. Also try to buy the previous installment as it was amazing and i feel it prepares you for this one ( i think this one is more challenging).
Personally i haven't had any performance issues. The game didn't crash at all for me during my playing hours. However sometimes ( like 3 total ) the game which fps lag or screen tear. I don't know exactly but i would become really slow so i just restarted it. I should mention that i feel the saving system is ALOT better as you can go back to a previous turn incase you mess up :p I can't remember it being in the first game, regardless its great to see it here.
I hope you found this some what helpful.

Dark Souls 1 - After a journey of misteries and many lifes wasted in
failure, like Artorias, the knights of the White Path, Knights of
Catarina, and many than others, all the knights that followed the Great
Lord of Sun, Gwyn, into the kiln of the first flame fighting the curse
and the end of the Age of Fire. We kinda felt the duty to accomplish our
mission and sacrifice ourself in order to not make their past vain,
becoming nothing but a puppet in the hands of gods.
Later, we discover that everything was useless.
Dark Souls 2 - Nobody remember anymore of the Four Lords, just their
souls remained in this corrupted world, Drangleic, four powerfull souls
from the Lands of Lordran.
King Vendrick is looking for a way in order to win the curse, and it
seems he managed a way to stop it, but not to heal it. In the meanwhile
his brother Aldia, scholar of the First Sin, discover the real cause of
the curse: a seal created from Gwyn in order to keep the first flame
alive. This is the First Sin of the Gods, their want not to die.
After we "kill" Aldia, he tells us the most important thing of the
series:
"But the question remains.. What do you want, truly? Light, Dark, or
something else entirely?"
Dark Souls 3 - The flame is now fading in a way that never been before.
Lothric refused to link the Fire, that's why bells called for us,
champion of Ashes, the resemblance of all the failures of the past. We
must find the Lords of Cinder and make them linking the fire, no cares
how we manage to do it. During our journey, someone is looking after us:
the black church of Londor, descendant of Kaathe's will. We discover
that we can usurp the First Fire and give it to the Real Darkness,
becoming the Lord of the new age of Humanity.
The path of the big betraial, where we cover all the past with ashes in
order to break the cycle of the Fire and creating something completely
new, an age without Gods, only humans, and gentil darkness..
So here we are, at the real Kiln of the First Flame once again, fighting
the manifestation of all the cursed ones who decided to sacrifice for
the Age of Fire, for their Gods.
A fight beetwen the traitors and the serves of Gods, the last fight.
Once we manage to win the Soul of Cinder, here something happens.
He revives.
Nor his body, just His will to not be forgotten.
Lord Gwyn, the first lord of Cinder. His soul is still here, fighting
for the last time trying to keep the Fire alive.
But everything is useless, 'cause every fire will turn to Ashes.
And so the flame will fade, and so the world will be merged from grey,
silent ashes.
Meanwhile, a strange painter is making his last paint, imaging a new
cold, dark and gentle world. A world painted with the blood of the Dark
Soul, the same souls that tried to emerge all this time, the same caotic
soul that wanted freedom from the seal of Light, the seal of Fire.
A new, dark world, where Dark Souls could be free.
That's the story of many of us, the story of choices, different paths
who converged into the same, peacefull end, 'cause everything will
vanish, every flame will fade.
Thanks Miyazaki, and all the working team.
Thanks From Software, and absolutely thanks to all the players who lived
in this trilogy.

This game... it looks awesome on the covers, screenshots and videos, but once you've played it, man...
The fatal flaw is the control. It's stiff, awkward and unresponsive. In a game that relies hugely on your combat skills, having slippery controls is your doom. That, in combination with the fact this is largely a trial and error game, makes for a bad time. Not just trial and error, but doing the exact same battle(s) over and over again until you win.
Not my idea of fun trial and error, which would be a game which relies more on your strategy instead of building up a muscle memory against each enemy and boss.
There's no redeeming quality, it's like a beat 'em up where you die a lot until you get it right. There's no alternate path but forward.
I get that you can't just walk up to every enemy and expect to down them without ever getting hit, but this game took it way too far up its alley. Even in the beginning it's relentless. A very,
basic introduction/explanation to the core gameplay and that's it. They'll toss you in the ring with a boss that kills you in 2 consecutive hits.
No chance of retaliation, nothing. Then when I happen to come across another boss which was a bit more manageable, when it was down to half health, it grew into a much larger, stronger boss of which the attacks were even more dangerous and impossible to dodge. There is no mercy or an opportunity to learn.
Another thing which grinds my gears is that this game sort of forces you to use a controller. I'm a PC gamer in heart and soul but I do have a controller which I bought solely for Rocket League. Why am I telling that? Because Rocket League seems to be the
game in which a controller is (debatably) better than mouse and keyboard. But in thr long run, controllers will never ever win it from mouse and keyboard, not on any area maybe except comfort. It's much faster and accurate than controllers will ever be. This game is not an exception either. With the controller you have to manually aim your camera around with a second stick whereas with the mouse you can just look around freely and have your attacks ready at the same time. Any PC game should have default PC controls, mouse and keyboard that is, as a standard. Not even Rocket League had that sort of pushy feel.
What an awful disappointment this game was based on what I expected from it, and I am not ashamed to share that with anyone reading this, not everyone has to like this overhyped game still being sold for the full price of a whopping 60 euros (buy 2 nice whiskeys for it instead). I'm turning a deaf ear to the ridiculous amount of positive ratings this game has since my experience with this game was just poor to the very absolute. What I expected was a fairly difficult game with open-world elements. What I got was a half-broken chivalry game that relies on lots of trial and error, the not-fun kind of trial and error like I described.
It being difficult is not an excuse to wave away negative reviews since it's a crucial factor in enjoying the game. There's difficulty done right and difficulty that could use some finetuning. This game would be a perfect example of the latter.
I'm just gonna remove the "git gud" comments and the likes, I've played roguelikes and games on hardest difficulties before so I'm not unfamiliar with high difficulty in a game. The only difference is that the games in question were a lot better than this frothy game so naturally I'd sink in more time to acquire skill.

Half-Life is a classic. It was my first "true" FPS (my only other games prior being Minecraft and the Portal franchise) Admitedly, the graphics technology is... outdated, to say the least, but what it lacks in tech, it makes up for in every other regard. The design is spot on, and it has a natural learning curve and is great for both those who want to get into FPSs or veterans who have been around since the days of Wolfenstein. The story line is great in the fact that it is... the best adjective for this would be transparent. I do not mean that it is easy to see what comes next, and in fact it throws you several curveballs which mix up the gameplay even more. What I mean by transparent is that if all you care about is blasting aliens, the story will fade into the background and the dialouge will bother you no more than a blast from your shotgun straight into a zombie's face. Conversly, however, if you enjoy deep narratives with mysteries and solutions around every turn, Half-Life will delight you as well as you catch sight of some graffiti on a wall, overhear your enemies talking about your activities or even catch a rare glimpse of an odd man in a dark suit. Half-Life truly has something for everyone, form varied gameplay to an imersive story with both blended seamlessly together in a ride you'll be unlikely to forget.

Heartily Recommended.

It's incredibly much like its predecessor, adding very little and mildly remixing or removing a lot of aspects that made Enemy Within such a balanced spread of fun and depth of strategy.  The ship's room-building strategy feels incomplete and profoundly unrewarding, basically a chore.  One room type seems to exist for the sake of a single mission (ship defense), without a clue that it's a one-off, so you can easily waste time and money building it in anticipation of a repeat which never comes.
The story is PURE face-palm.  I was transfixed by the generic awfulness of the ending, I thought perhaps it was a parody of some kind, but the game takes itself far too seriously.
Bugs also abound - enemies that do nothing except watch you shoot at them turn after turn until they're dead, and soldiers that sometimes can't move.  I'd swear one or two of the soldier advanced skills basically do nothing.
Graphically it's mediocre and not much of a step up from its predecessor.  Outside of cutscenes, character lips don't move even if they're talking and looking right at you.  Creature designs are weak, partly being meh variations on its predecessor, partly being super-generic (sectopod!), and in one or two cases completely laughable (hi, breasty-snake!).
Pick up Enemy Within for a cheaper, extremely similar but superior strategy experience.  Skip this one and wait for the inevitable XCOM 3.

***NOTE**** --  CONTRARY to what other reviews say...purchasing gold is NOT "necessary" in this game and you can indeed unlock every class without paying a cent (just hover over the class in the character creation menu to see how...it's always "reach level 20 with 'x' class". :)
Very simple and highly addictive gameplay! Plays like a mini-rogue-like-mmo. :) Yes, permadeath is a feature, but even if you don't care for that like I didn't I would still suggest you give the game a try. I mean, hey, it's free! Plus the max level cap which does not take long at ALL to reach (45 minutes if you're really effecient, in my experience) is 20, and you have a chest to store extra loot in so you can pass on some of the goodies you find to your next character.
Yes, you should expect to die, but there are classes to unlock from reaching max level with other classes and other neat-o-stuffs. :) Micro-transactions exist in the game, but they are not in any way necessary. The best things, imo, that you can get with them are character slots and extra chests for loot storage. Buying actual loot, in my mind, somewhat defeats the purpose of the whole game (to max out your character).
It's a great game that you can pick up and play for 5 minutes at a time to have a bit of fun. It's ALSO a game that you can invest hundreds of hours into one character maxing them out if you wanted to (farming the gods for stat pots...you can learn about those from google if you wish)!! Casual and hardcore gamers alike can find a ton of fun here, and I highly recommend it. :)

Where should I start with this game?! It's such a fantastic game, with so many positive elements scattered throughout. Even if there are some negative aspects, the positives easily outweigh them. They're so lengthy that I have to list them all.
Easily the most obvious strength of the game. It is a simple yet adorable art style, and it translates very well into the 3D models used throughout the game. The detail of the battle area is very profound, and you can even tell the differences in the Clockworks background when it comes to different levels. It's simple, but it works, and it works amazingly.
Another aesthetic positive of this game is the overwhelmingly good character design. It was pretty obvious from the start that the designers wanted each knight to look different from each other by giving basic customization in the form of color, height, and eye shape, but despite its simplicity, there are a large amount of options on how to customize your knight. Even the NPC knights can be easily distinguished by just looking at their colors. Same goes for the battle sprites, where your color determines their eye color and harness color.
The enemies of the game, however, is where the designs really show. The Kats and Gremlins especially, in my opinion. The Kats have this ability of immediately scaring you, despite the adorable aesthetic of the game. For the Gremlins, you could easily tell which class is higher than another is by simply checking their size. It was a very trivial note, but it definitely stood out for me, and adds some depth to the way of living of the Gremlins.
This game has a battle system that has been done before, but it does have its quirks. Instead of making an eighteen types and what it damages more effectively, less effectively, and is completely resistant to, like Pokemon (an amazing game franchise), the developers decided to go for the simple Rock, Paper, Scissors formula. However, instead of using three of the four elements or just lazily using rock, paper, and scissors, the game uses Elemental, Piercing, and Shadow, three very unique names for the formula. Elemental also has its fair subcategories, but all three affect a certain monster type the same. The status elements are also considerably different from your typical game, especially Poison, where instead of slow damage, you cannot be healed. The weapons and armor are also amazing, and each one must be carefully chosen to create a strong knight. All in all, the battle system is amazing, and the only real flaws are the Sparks of Life and the nightmare level that is Emerald Axis.
I don't have much to say on Heat and the Forge system, except for the fact that it is a unique leveling system, but the Heat gap from levels 1 and 2 is just absurd, in my opinion.
The story of Spiral Knight so far is relatively above average than most RPGs that use a medieval setting, but that's mainly because of the futuristic elements found within the lore of the game. Other than that, the story is cohesive and straightforward. Can't really say much without spoiling anything.

I think it's time to give this game a proper review:
I have since developed a love-hate relationship with this game.  When you die, you lose everything that character had equipped, in the Inventory, and the Backpack and anything in it.  In short, you have to start from square one.  Now, this is where the microtransactions come in: there are a lot, and this is an extreme understatement.  Any given user has a total of 50 Chests available to them in their Vault.  You start out with 1, and purchasing any additional Chest is 500 Gold, which equates to $5 USD.  I've purchased every single one; yep, that's $150 into this game, and a large portion of that was BEFORE trading cards were added.  And that's just counting the money I used to buy Chests; even more has gone to feeding my Pets and buying Backpacks.
But, it was ROTMG that first introduced me to the social gaming atmosphere that is Steam.  I had never used Steam before, and really had only downloaded this game due to the Steam Holiday 2013 Sale.  The community, both through Steam and the larger browser community, is generally very kind and generous, and as long as you treat your fellow gamer with the respect you hope to receive, you'll get it.  Y'know, just don't be a jerk, and your gaming experience will be that much more fun.
However, if you're scared by the microtransactions, then it is with a heavy heart that I do not recommend this game.  There's really no way to progress in the game without putting money into it.  How much you do put in is entirely up to you, of course; just be careful.  I would say, avoid buying any sort of Weaponry, Armor, Abillities, or eggs from the Nexus.  Once you become comfortable enough with the game, more than likely you'll be able to find those Items on your own in the more dangerous areas, or trade for them in the Nexus.  Don't be afraid to ask questions: as long as the answer isn't blurted out in all Caps and ends with an expletive or 'n00b!', it's likely a good, honest, correct answer.
Another thing: death, as aggravating as it is, is actually integral to the game.  When you die, you receive a tally screen showing you how much Fame you received, which is another form of pseudo-currency in the game.  Fame allows you to feed your Pets and upgrade your Guild Hall (if you're part of a Guild).
I've put a lot of time (and money) into this game.  It's got a place in my heart.  Maybe it'll earn a place in yours, too.

Coming after XCOM: EU, this game had large shoes to fill. Especially given the previous title's excellent DLC that added some excellent features to the core game.
The one thing I was most nervous for, was content. After playing XCOM EU with all the DLC I figured XCOM 2 may feel diluted, kind of like the feeling of going from The Sims 2 with all DLC to 3 with zero DLC.  Turns out, there's actually a lot of content in this game. They managed to keep augmenting soldiers in the form of personal combat sims, and even kept psionic powers for your troops.
The best part of this game is easily the tension it creates by having permadeath on your squad members in battle. Deciding whether to leave a man behind or risk more of your team is a tough decision to make, but makes the victory so much sweeter when it works. But be ready for heartbreak when you're star ranger goes in for the kill only to miss the swing of his sword point blank. Ironman mode is how this game should be played, but maybe not until you've given it one good playthrough
My largest gripe with the game has to be the timers. Between the overall doomsday timer and the mission turn counters, it hurts the game. They add in a nice feature of starting in cover where you can sneak up on your enemy, but then they add in timers on nearly every mission making it a necessity to rush forward. Meld from EU was a much better solution to this. You had timers, but it was only for a bonus, not to fail the mission.
Pros:
- Permadeath
- Great leap in graphical fidelity
- Polished and nearly bug free
- Excellent replayability due to randomly generated maps (even different starting missions)
- Challenging
Cons:
- Performance issues (though has gotten significantly better since all the patches)
- Timers, timers, timers

Some good ideas, rather weak implementation. High points are offset by extreme frustration with the design choices and game balance.
Campaign:
Campaign pacing can be annoying. You're constantly interrupted and forced to fly around the world on missions that can be skipped in theory but not in practice due to the negative consequences. You feel like you're being led on a leash instead of leading the resistance. It's a wasted opportunity more than anything, since the story is a perfect setup for a Jagged Alliance 2 -type guerilla strategy game where YOU decide exactly how to fight back.
Tactical battles:
Tactical battles are very formulaic. The big problem is that you never get more than 6 soldiers on the field while the strength and number of enemies keeps growing. The battles are balanced by dividing enemies into several small autonomous groups that only "wake up" when you walk within their range. This brings an artificial quality to the combat: you have to be careful not to step in the wrong direction when you're fighting an enemy group, so as not to wake up another group that's just idling close-by.
Most missions are easy and you can go 10 missions without losing a single soldier. Then you may e.g. run into a Sectopod that kills two of your full-health officers in one turn, paniciking the rest of the team, making it impossible for you to finish the mission in time and causing you to lose the entire team. Or you may run into 3 enemy groups that happen to be next to each other.
Now and then there's some genuine fair challenge, but it's overshadowed by the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tty ways that can cause you to lose your entire squad in just 2 turns without a chance. Add to that the negative effects of failing a mission, and you'll be looking to start a new game if it happens more than once. Unless, of course, you're not on iron man and are willing to save/load.
Bugs:
The game engine has several graphical, audio and gameplay bugs. I lost my colonel when I couldn't pick her up when she fell unconscious next to a wall (destroying the wall with grenades didn't help). I had to end an iron man game because it kept freezing on a post-misson screen. A bug causes audio samples to loop infinitely. The camera can freeze in 3rd person view in battle, making it impossible for you to play your turn.
UI and graphics:
All UI transitions are animated and the game has a lot of inserted delays. They'll drive you mad but can luckily be removed with a few quality of life mods. There's no option to entirely turn off the VO box though, so you'll have to get used to a lot of repetitive complaints for this and that. At least you can turn voice volume to zero.

This game is worth $15, but don't expect it to ever become anything more.
Starbound is a 2D sci-fi sandbox building game.  It's pretty much Terraria in space, really.
However, the actual gameplay consists entirely of this:
1. Beam down to planet
2. Laugh at planet's goofy-looking monsters and tentacle trees
3. Spend 9 hours grinding the goofy monsters for crafting currency
4. Get pushed off a cliff by a pink, fire-breathing seagull and lose 30% of the crafting currency
5. Use crafting currency to build device that summons boss.
6. Slowly wear down boss's health while wedged into a tiny, impenetrable corner
7. Use loot from boss to make device allowing you to go to more planets
8. Marvel at really cool spaceflight animation
9. Repeat from step 1
That said, it is worth the $14.99 that it currently costs.  The combat is pretty bad and the resource gathering is mind-numbingly grindy, but the goofy monster part alone (the part that actually worked) is probably worth the price of the game.
It should also be noted that this game will realistically never leave Early Access, hasn't been updated in 5 months, and the developers spent $4,000,000 of Kickstarter money on booze, drugs, and roguelike pirate games.
But still, it's only $15.  And it's worth it for what you get.  But don't expect to ever get anything else.
