The spiritual successor of Harvest Moon that captures what Harvest Moon is by heart
Could be better, could be worse. It's definitely a beautifully designed pixelated world, but the people itself sometimes looks weird, especially with that bow leg and all. I'm also not a fan of the more western artstyle, but each to their own. After all, that's what the mods are for~
Any complain that you have over the graphics (other than it's pixelated) could potentially be fixed by the mods, since the modding community have been growing and churning out mods every so often, and the dev often welcomes the mods, and implemented some of the mods into the base game.
Perfectly captures what Harvest Moon is all about. This DOESN'T mean that the game is exciting for everyone. If you find the Harvest Moon series boring with all it's repetition and monotone everyday life, then you might not be into Stardew Valley either. The game does bring in it's own unique twist to the game, mainly the mine is now a dungeon crawler section and there's a fishing minigame, where you now have to play a minigame, instead of your usual 'throw the bait and wait till it bites and pull it', but i don't quite like it either.
I am a fan of Harvest Moon, so this might comes from a place of bias, but so far, Stardew Valley captures what made Harvest Moon great, and improves on it but without overshadowing the original intention.
Really could be better. I like the song and overall sound effects, but me, along with several other people, plays with the music turned off, or with a mod. Problem lies in the fact that the music doesn't repeat/have a long delay before it repeats. So you'll be plowing the fields, and all of the sudden the music just stops.
The music quality is good, but with that jarring problem, i can't actually give it a higher score
To be perfectly honest, i don't like the story, but i don't hate it. It's the usual Harvest Moon story, you inherit a farm, you move out from the city, and now here's your new life. It's been done, it doesn't need a change (i guess?), and it's just a segway to the actual meat of the game, which is the gameplay.
Sure, not everyone plays Harvest Moon for the story, they play it for the characters. While the villager offers quite the diverse cast of characters with all sort of personality, it's quite a, well, cliche. My main gripe would be with the bachelor and bacholerettes. Their character at first is sooooooooo one dimensional, like for real, it's almost like the dev just picked a personality and only develop the characters from that one personality. You have the basic girl, the jock, the nerd, the bookworm, the hippie, and the emo.
Granted, once you start knowing them, their personality does develop into something more of a human being, but some characters was treated diffferently from the others. For example, (rant ahead)
All in all, most of the characters could be better, but it's hobbled down by the limitation of how much they can say. Again, there's a mod for that
Definitely a good Harvest Moon spiritual successor, but not without it's flaw. It doesn't last as long as some Harvest Moon game does, but it's definitely worth the shot if you like this type of game

The game that reassigned the life goals of thousands of angry real-time strategy nerds who relentlessly blasted death metal out of their sterephones while molesting the taunt buttons when it first came back - is still alive and well. That is, perhaps not so much as when it first premiered, but AoE 3 still attracts a considerable amount of gamers which is impressive given how the strategy gaming industry was completely dwarfed with upsurge of other games is latter years.
There's not much of a gripe you can hold against this now-classic: the texture and gameplay is focused and realistic, in startling contrast to the puerile graphics of the prequel (although I won't hold back that Age 2 also rocked) as well as the addition of the home city, which granted a completely new dynamic to the game. As is the problem with most strategy games, the inherently incoherent AI (some kind of stratagem devised by evil game planners to render games inconsistent and all puddy) is a bit problematic, but it's still something that can be coped with. The Online could definitely use some revitalizations, though. Yeah, everyone knows Ensemble Studios called it quits years ago, but still... can't someone do something to add some color to the online community and gameplay? The lack of updates is unnerving.
However, AoE retains its place as one of the best RTS games, ever. Even the two expansion packs kicked♥♥♥♥♥ Asian Dynasties in particular added an exotic and 'colonial' palette to the game that made it even more memorable for me. The addition of three new factions (China, India, Japan) certainly made the game the well-nigh perfect, multinational, multi-tactical strategy delight.

One of my favourite games of the year so far.
I did my first playthrough on the easy difficulty (because I didn't play 2012's XCOM reboot and so haven't played any of the series since the 1990s!) and never really struggled with it, especially later in the game when you've researched the advanced weapons. By the end my squad was pretty OP and could take out almost any opposition without much trouble. But even so, it was hugely enjoyable, and definitely has replay value - I'm playing again (and again) on harder difficulty levels. With careful management of resources and building the right facilities your squad still gets pretty strong once you get past the early stages, but it doesn't stop being highly addictive. I always think I'll just play one more turn before I stop ... and end up stopping four missions later.
You can already customize your team of soldiers, to add a personal touch so you get attached to them and don't want them to die, and you can add even more flair to their appearance with various cool mods. I also liked the weapon upgrades, although the options available are a bit limited. There are some great mods in the Steam Workshop that tweak the UI in useful ways.
I played the Linux version and found the graphics and performance to be fine, and it's very stable (I've had a couple of issues in hours and hours of play, but nothing that wasn't solved by re-loading a save game). The framerate only struggled when my PC was busy running a dozen other CPU intensive tasks in the background at the same time as the game, which is to be expected!

This is a decent improvement upon EU/EW, decent enough to justify the "2" in it's name.

The new mechanics reflect that, especially all the timers. Thankfully, you can mod them or even remove them completely (not recommended). These bring a sense of urgency into a TBS game, which is not unique to XCOM 2, but it's a great thing nonetheless.
The difficulty went up considerably (even higher with the Alien Hunters DLC, hate the Rulers), but again, you can mod a lot of it. You can pretty much mod everything you want and play the way you like. The community really shines here and will keep the game alive for a long time, fingers crossed.
As for the technical side of things, the only bugs I've encountered so far (shortly after AH DLC release) had been mod related. My PC is detailed in my profile and using the GF Experience settings the game is always smooth and looks great.

I bought two copies of this game before it even came out. I gave into the hype because I loved terraria so much and I loved space so much. I've learned the hard way to never buy a game that is not out yet.
This game has many many small cool aesthetic features. There's already more furniture and different blocks in this game than all of terraria. The torches flicker. There's villages and the npcs talk to each other and say "I'll get you for killing Billy" and what not. There are monsters that make fart noises.
All in all though, the game is just an amature mess. The real meat of the game is boring and incredibly uninspired and it makes me so sad to say that since I was probably hyped for this game for years. Pixels are the in game currency and pretty much used only for crafting and I do not understand why. Say you want to make iron armor. It takes like 10 iron armor and 500 pixels. Why? Why do you need money. It should be enough that you grinded the materials for it.
Ontop of all that, you lose 25 percent of your pixels on death and can't get them back even if you go to where you died. There does not seem to be a sell feature either yet. (game has been out about 6 months now) and there is no way to trade pixels with friends either.
The monsters and planets are all randomly generated which sounds like an amazing idea. till you get to a few different planets and realize everything is exactly the same as the other planet. sure the enemies look slightly different but they act almost completely the same. It's much more exciting to find the non-randomized enemies around but they're rare.
The music is great and relaxing. That is until you come up upon a level 1 bird and suddenly you are assaulted with this strange epic boss fight music. It's unbelievably jarring and really takes away from the mood. When you actually find a cave and go underground there is just flat out no music at all. I found a nice flesh biome underground but it was made completely dull and uninteresting as there was no music no sounds or anything to make it sound like it was hell.
There is also an unbelievable ungodly amount of grinding. I have already mentioned that with pixels before, but it actually does get worse. Even with a diamond pick axe, going down into say the heck/flesh biome? The blocks will take about 5 or 10 seconds to break. Sure in this game you break 9 blocks at a time but it feels so incredibly boring to sit there holding down left mouse button in complete silence while you break some flesh blocks that have copper ore in them. The second boss summon took about a total of 100 steel bars. (thats 200 iron ore and 100 coal ore.) Thats not even counting the thousands of pixels spent or the armor and weapons you absolutely need to progress. The boss itself was bland and took about 3 minutes to kill and had only 2 attacks. on its death, it dropped a key which let me progress to the "harder" levels.
I went to the third galaxy set and just couldn't take it. Every planet is essentially the same. Gather the resources in complete silence, fight the random monsters that all do the same thing, and then summon a boss and repeat.
Ah, I forgot to mention. Building in this game is great. It's well thought out and extremely easy to do. However, there is no reason to. It's incredibly depressing. In Terraria you build houses and homes for yourself and other villagers and you see your home flourish into a village depending on how you build it.
In this game? There's no benefit to making a single house. You have a spaceship. You put your crafting materials and chests in it. Whats the point in building a home on a planet when you're just going to leave it and go exploring tons of other planets? You can spawn villagers and guards, but its all aesthetic and does nothing to benefit you besides being cute. It's actually a pain to go back to any home you make on a planet since you have to go to your ship and then use your precious fuel to return back. All for what? A chance to look at a shiny castle you made? A place to find all the different colors of dirt you stored?
I just can't reccommend this game right now. I thought 6 months would be enough to make the game at least a little better but i guess its not. Maybe in 2-3 more years this game will be amazing. I really hope it is. But right now it's only good intentions that are not implemented well.

I've played ROTMG for a couple years now ever since the game was created from the TIG Assemblee Competition. The game has drained hundreds of hours of my life (outside of the steam client hence little time recorded via steam). This game started as a simple and addicting bullet hell online game by Wild Shadow Studios. The artwork was created by a guy who goes by the alias, Oryx. Interestingly, you can buy the Sprites from Oryx's website if you google it. Like I said it started via a competiton I was there to see it grow and thrive into the beast it is now. I leveled and maxed a couple classes and spend hours on their old forums and wiki. I loved this game.However, not all good things are meant to last and the main dev for Wild Shadow got burnt out with this and sold it to the social media gaming company, Kabam. This is where my review for choice goes negative.
Kabam began as one of those Facebook Social "Gaming" companies. I just logged into Realm of the Mad God, this is what I saw: Beginners Package: +2 Character Slots, +3 Vault Chests, +1 Pet, +2600 Gold - how much money you ask? $20 dollars (but a $60 value). Everything wrong with micro-transactions Kabam has accomplished. And I completely understand that a company needs to make money off their product and free-to-play's use the micro-transaction model. But I think there is a right way and a wrong way. This way is in our face - the Nexus you start in is surrounded by purchasable items with real money. High Level Items, Pets for (almost 2600 Gold each), a Gambling "mysterious box" vendor, and More. Go ahead and buy a high level item only to perma-death in your first hour and losing the item permanently as well. These are things you didn't see before Kabam got their Facebook gaming hands on it. If you can ignore this than you'll quickly see your client's chat fill the entire screen with spammers to what appears dozens and dozens of 3rd party chinese websites to buy items and stat pots...
Luckily, the core of ROTMG it remands uncorrupted for the most part. Leveling is fun and addicting - late game you farm Stat Pots which turn your hero into a true destroyer. High level items are nice and can add some interesting new mechanics to existing classes. ROTMG does perma-death right - once you get a feel for late game enemies, dungeons, and bosses - you can live quite a while if you play safely. Perma-Death in this game is also kind of soul crushing (but it doesn't receive any negative score from me for that). Imagine playing a character for dozens or hundreds of hours if you're careful enough. Imagine slowly capping all of your stats and getting great high level items. Then you die to lag, to a mistake, to a shotgun spray of a boss... All that time, the items, that character - gone forever. You might question why you play this game in the first place, but once you mentally recover -- you'll be back for more and more.
GREAT GAME --- POOR COMPANY.
NOTE: I do give credit for Kabam for continually releasing additional content like new dungeons, items, etc. You are probably a better man than me if you can ignore the in-your-face micro transactions and advertisements for micro-tranactions from the character selection screen to the main ingame hub.

I had to many "wtf" moments (wtf is happening, wtf just hit me, wtf just killed me, how the f did this happen) to find the experience enjoyable.

To make this an actual review, I've got a really good  chocolate browine recipe:
Ingredients
250g unsalted butter
200g	good-quality dark chocolate (70% cocoa solids), broken up
75g dried sour cherries, optional
50g chopped nuts, optional
80g cocoa powder, sifted
65g plain flour, sifted
1 teaspoon baking powder
360g	caster sugar
4 large free-range eggs
zest of 1 orange, optional
250ml crème fraîche, optional
Preheat your oven to 180°C/350°F/gas 4. Line a 24cm square baking tin with greaseproof paper. In a large bowl over some simmering water, melt the butter and the chocolate and mix until smooth. Add the cherries and nuts, if you’re using them, and stir together.
In a separate bowl, mix together the cocoa powder, flour, baking powder and sugar, then add this to the chocolate, cherry and nut mixture. Stir together well. Beat the eggs and mix in until you have a silky consistency.
Pour your brownie mix into the baking tray, and place in the oven for around 25 minutes. You don’t want to overcook them so, unlike cakes, you don’t want a skewer to come out all clean. The brownies should be slightly springy on the outside but still gooey in the middle.
Allow to cool in the tray, then carefully transfer to a large chopping board and cut into chunky squares. These make a fantastic dessert served with a dollop of crème fraîche mixed with some orange zest.

I was drawn to a 3D MOBA and I got one.  I honestly can't imagine a better way to implement the "lane" MOBA mechanic in 3D space.  The ships look super cool and sitting in hangar looking at my ship is one of the most enjoyable parts of the game.
A MOBA thrives on its characters though, and these characters (the capitol ships) are NOT fun to play.  For most ships the control is cumbersome.  There is no effective diversity of roles.  The game tries to designate roles to certain ships, but the tanks are not tanks, the supports can't support, and the meta favors snipers and brawlers to the exclusion of everything else.
This problem is compounded by the small group of highly passionate people who ONLY play to the brawler/sniper meta currently controling the matchmaking.  MOBA players like to think there is a counterplay to everything, but this game simply does not allow that.  Certain ships are just better, and if you don't have those ships you will be punished.
One change I recommend to this game is to build stronger tanks.  That would slow the meta and help the support ships define their role.   Longer range support would also help players to not feel like they risk instant death just to heal the tanky ship.
Until the meta changes and the core player base has some strategic diversity, I do not recommend this game-
-unless you just want to look at pretty space ships.

This game is worth $15, but don't expect it to ever become anything more.
Starbound is a 2D sci-fi sandbox building game.  It's pretty much Terraria in space, really.
However, the actual gameplay consists entirely of this:
1. Beam down to planet
2. Laugh at planet's goofy-looking monsters and tentacle trees
3. Spend 9 hours grinding the goofy monsters for crafting currency
4. Get pushed off a cliff by a pink, fire-breathing seagull and lose 30% of the crafting currency
5. Use crafting currency to build device that summons boss.
6. Slowly wear down boss's health while wedged into a tiny, impenetrable corner
7. Use loot from boss to make device allowing you to go to more planets
8. Marvel at really cool spaceflight animation
9. Repeat from step 1
That said, it is worth the $14.99 that it currently costs.  The combat is pretty bad and the resource gathering is mind-numbingly grindy, but the goofy monster part alone (the part that actually worked) is probably worth the price of the game.
It should also be noted that this game will realistically never leave Early Access, hasn't been updated in 5 months, and the developers spent $4,000,000 of Kickstarter money on booze, drugs, and roguelike pirate games.
But still, it's only $15.  And it's worth it for what you get.  But don't expect to ever get anything else.

For the longest time, I vehemently hated on the Dark Souls series.  I had tried Dark Souls 1, Demon Souls and Bloodborne and just was frustrated with what felt like an artificially difficult and cheap experience.  I insulted the series fans and wrote them off as attention seeking elitist with too much free time on their hands.
When Dark Souls 3 was released, it was given the same treatment and for a year or so, I ignored it despite the overwhelming amount of people recommending I play through it.  However, after playing through the literal pile of triple A sand box, third person action adventure games from the likes of Ubisoft and EA, I had run out of games to play and my idle hands turned toward this game.  Not with an open mind but only to play and prove to myself it was nothing more than a re-release of the same experience as before.
Just as before I booted up the game, created a semi-human looking character and set out for disappointment.  After playing for what seemed like only half an hour or so, I found myself stuck at Lothric knights present before the fight with Vordt. But instead of wanting to call it there and chalk it up as me being right.  I began throwing myself again and again at the enemies, experimenting with new tactics each time, getting a feeling of exhilaration as I learned to dodge their attacks perfectly and take them out one by one without taking a hit.  It was exciting, so much more fun than I had had from the past 2 years of video games.  I marched into the boss fight feeling like a champion, and died. But unlike previous souls games, I now felt that I just needed to keep at it, learn the motions of the enemy, experiment and eventually, I would crush that icy fat man beast.  I ended up killing him on my second try. When I finally checked my actual play time, I had been playing for 6 hours straight.  I was hooked. Since then, I've gone back and finished as many souls games as I can and am hungering for more.
My personal feelings aside, this game improves on so many things from its predecessors, making it one of the most beginner friendly entries into the series.  Tight precise controls, faster and more responsive combat and a more open and accessible world to go back through to explore and toughen up from.  The game runs in flawless 60fps at 1080p with, online pvp connection issues aside, fewer bugs and crashes than any triple A title I can think of.  The game has massive replay value.  The thing I love most about this game is that it does not feel artificially difficult.  When you die, it does not feel like being cheated out of a victory due to some unforeseen or overtly ridiculous one shot attack.  When you die, you learn from it, you see where you messed up, and it provides motivation to go at it again and again.  This is present in the earlier souls games but non more fair, in my opinion, than Dark Souls 3.  I highly recommend any action adventure/RPG fan give this game a try.  It will pleasantly surprise most, if not all.

I bought two copies of this game before it even came out. I gave into the hype because I loved terraria so much and I loved space so much. I've learned the hard way to never buy a game that is not out yet.
This game has many many small cool aesthetic features. There's already more furniture and different blocks in this game than all of terraria. The torches flicker. There's villages and the npcs talk to each other and say "I'll get you for killing Billy" and what not. There are monsters that make fart noises.
All in all though, the game is just an amature mess. The real meat of the game is boring and incredibly uninspired and it makes me so sad to say that since I was probably hyped for this game for years. Pixels are the in game currency and pretty much used only for crafting and I do not understand why. Say you want to make iron armor. It takes like 10 iron armor and 500 pixels. Why? Why do you need money. It should be enough that you grinded the materials for it.
Ontop of all that, you lose 25 percent of your pixels on death and can't get them back even if you go to where you died. There does not seem to be a sell feature either yet. (game has been out about 6 months now) and there is no way to trade pixels with friends either.
The monsters and planets are all randomly generated which sounds like an amazing idea. till you get to a few different planets and realize everything is exactly the same as the other planet. sure the enemies look slightly different but they act almost completely the same. It's much more exciting to find the non-randomized enemies around but they're rare.
The music is great and relaxing. That is until you come up upon a level 1 bird and suddenly you are assaulted with this strange epic boss fight music. It's unbelievably jarring and really takes away from the mood. When you actually find a cave and go underground there is just flat out no music at all. I found a nice flesh biome underground but it was made completely dull and uninteresting as there was no music no sounds or anything to make it sound like it was hell.
There is also an unbelievable ungodly amount of grinding. I have already mentioned that with pixels before, but it actually does get worse. Even with a diamond pick axe, going down into say the heck/flesh biome? The blocks will take about 5 or 10 seconds to break. Sure in this game you break 9 blocks at a time but it feels so incredibly boring to sit there holding down left mouse button in complete silence while you break some flesh blocks that have copper ore in them. The second boss summon took about a total of 100 steel bars. (thats 200 iron ore and 100 coal ore.) Thats not even counting the thousands of pixels spent or the armor and weapons you absolutely need to progress. The boss itself was bland and took about 3 minutes to kill and had only 2 attacks. on its death, it dropped a key which let me progress to the "harder" levels.
I went to the third galaxy set and just couldn't take it. Every planet is essentially the same. Gather the resources in complete silence, fight the random monsters that all do the same thing, and then summon a boss and repeat.
Ah, I forgot to mention. Building in this game is great. It's well thought out and extremely easy to do. However, there is no reason to. It's incredibly depressing. In Terraria you build houses and homes for yourself and other villagers and you see your home flourish into a village depending on how you build it.
In this game? There's no benefit to making a single house. You have a spaceship. You put your crafting materials and chests in it. Whats the point in building a home on a planet when you're just going to leave it and go exploring tons of other planets? You can spawn villagers and guards, but its all aesthetic and does nothing to benefit you besides being cute. It's actually a pain to go back to any home you make on a planet since you have to go to your ship and then use your precious fuel to return back. All for what? A chance to look at a shiny castle you made? A place to find all the different colors of dirt you stored?
I just can't reccommend this game right now. I thought 6 months would be enough to make the game at least a little better but i guess its not. Maybe in 2-3 more years this game will be amazing. I really hope it is. But right now it's only good intentions that are not implemented well.

This has to be one of the my favourite top 5 games. This is an exceedingly well-made, well-balanced game. The art is awesomely gruesome and simply a joy to view. As gross as it is, the art instilled a morbid desire to see more daunting images of stretched facial skin over the Swine Drummer’s drum, disfigured mermen such as the Pelagic Guardian, and putrid decease-spitting Sea Maggots.
I am fairy new to the game at the time of writing. I've only played around 14 or so hours, and feel I have barely scratched the surface. I struggled to make any advance or inroad into the game. Continually failed missions and dead heroes plagued the first 10 hours or so. But you soon learn that this game is not at all about success. It is more about being disappointed by gruellingly failure and yet trying to dig your way out of challengingly gloomy situations.
There is also definitely an element of luck to this game. You may find that heroes are unwilling to come away from the bar and fight with you because they are too busy enjoying a drink. They may misplace your gear and it goes missing from your inventory. I even had a Bounty Hunter in my party that was a nymphomaniac, which means he recovers more at the Brothel, only to be told later that he had been banned from the brothel for reasons best left unsaid. One can only imagine….
However, it is definitely this up-and-down sense of luck that creates the illusion of ‘hope’, which in turn pulled me deeper into the core gameplay and kept me coming back to it even after the disappointment of constantly failing missions. You do sometimes win one or two as well, you know.
One such example occurred this evening. I have just defeated the Swine Prince in the Warrens - my first victory over a boss character. I had previously fought a Wizened Hag and lost very convincingly, having been boiled and melted in her cauldron. Good times! Sufficed it to say, there was certainly no expectation at all of even coming close to victory, but I was intrigued by the introduction and art for the Swine Prince. I went ahead anyway and figured I could always leave the battle, abandon the mission and keep the loot I had gained. As the battle proceeded, I felt a slight glimmer of hope in a gore festering dungeon I had previously considered hastily departing. The sense of elation upon striking the killing blow was simple one I have not felt since beating the final boss in FTL. I jumped out of my chair grinning, waving my fist in the air!
This game is so good! I don't usually write reviews, but this game is most certainly 'executed with impunity’, and I just had to write something about it.

Black Squad is a good FPS game.
The graphics are fairly good, even on lowest settings the guns all have a good feel to them, like they are actually made of metal. The character models all have a good realism to them, the cloth looks like cloth and the metal looks like metal (duh). The environments all have a very nice realism to them, such as light flare from looking at the sun, and trees swaying as if actualy wind is in the game. The maps themselves are pretty impressive. They are well rendered and there is enough tactical positions that they allow you to feel like a sneaky player. The maps also are very varied, such as in Deathmatch there is a Cruiseship, Middle Eastern dusty place, an oil rig, and Tallin (capital of Estonia) to name as many as I can remember. All the maps have good lighting for the most part, and player models do not get lost in the scenery or in props, which helps for general visibility.
The gameplay is pretty good to be honest. It feels like a hybrid of CS:GO and S.K.I.L.L Special Force 2. There is Deathmatch which is pretty much the most fun of the modes for a casual player, such as myself, as i can just jump into a game and shoot some people. There is a more competitive version which is a 5v5 or 8v8 Bomb Defusal mission, which feels more CS:GO like, but is a decent enough mode with exclusive maps. There is currently no mode(as far as i am aware) which can give the player a solo rank, like Global Elite etc in CS:GO, but their is one for a clan ranked match, where you earn points for your clan to get a rank for the clan as a whole.
As the tagline of the game said, this game is not Pay to Win in anyway. There is no advantage to spending money, as guns, armour and grenades can all be bought for credits, the ingame currency. The only reason you would spend real money is if you wanted skins(the skins all look very clean and nice), and an added bonus is that the sallest money transaction is $1 or £0.75. You are given enough to buy 1 gun anyway as a starting present, but all gun can be claimed for 15 days from the DLC page at the top of this page. They expre after 15 days, but you will have sufficient time to use them all in that time to see which you like, and will probably then buy.
The only real problem I have with the game is the UI, which is very small and clustered at the bottom of the screen, when there is plenty of space around the edge of the main menu etc which is in the middle. I don't think this is a major problem for most other people, but maybe i'm just fussy or something. Also, every 1 in 10 times i log in, it resets my keybinding, which I find annoying.
Black Squad is a good game, especially since it doesn't cost any money. This is a game i would expect to be around £6/$10 normally to buy, so the fact it is free makes it even nicer. The graphics are good, the guns are very varied with 50+ types, the gameplay is fun and the community isn't overly toxic.

Overall a great game:
The style of the game in terms of graphics, audio, voice over, writing, is excellent.
There is a large variety of enemies and heroes, and the tactics of the battles are relevant and interesting, allowing you to combine different heroes and their skills for different strategies.
The game is definitely punishing in many regards. The permadeth/autosave and the random nature of some battles mean things can go bad quickly. That's both frustrating and rewarding: I've certianly rage quit upon losing heroes, but at the same time, it gives a lot more adrenaline to the battles (and makes decisions like push on our retreat a lot more relevant).
The game also gets pretty grindy (which is it's explicit point). After an initial burst of play, now I'll basically play about 30 minutes a day after work (i.e. complete maybe one dungeon level), which is good pace for me to enjoy the game without it feeling too repetitive.

Bayonetta is a fond throwback to the days of 3-D action games, not unlike Devil May Cry or God Of War. A majority of the game involves running around fairly linear paths, having the path close off, and having to defeat enemies to progress. Nothing too special. Fortunately, though, the combat is absolute gold. Bayonetta has all of the moves Dante had back in Devil May Cry, like jumping, melee, and shooting attacks, among a few unique traits as well. For example, holding down the punch or kick button lets Bayonetta use the guns strapped to her hands and feet. Rotating the movement analog stick and pressing the attack button lets Bayonetta go into an odd shooting sequence where players blast enemies with repeated gunfire. The most interesting inclusion to combat, and generally the most profitable, is Witch Time. By dodging enemy attacks at the very last second, Bayonetta can slow down time and attack enemies for extra damage and points. These skills are the tip of the iceberg and once more abilities are added to Bayonetta's arsenal, the game shifts into overdrive. It just never stops.
Pros
+ Fantastic combat system is stylish, diverse, and unquestionably visceral
+ Incredible graphics make combat flashy and intense
+ Multiple difficulties and game medals will keep you coming back
+Excellent style and overall game design
+Quirky characters and story
Cons
- Storyline delivery can be pretty cheesy
- Not a huge penalty for dying
-No WQHD support
Now before I start, I'll mention that I'm a big DMC fan, as well as a moderate God of War fan, but I think it's safe to say that Platinum Games have made an action game on par with DMC 3 and GoW 2 (which are my favourite games in the 2 series gameplay wise).
Unlike DMC and GoW, there is no “Devil Trigger/Rage “ mode in this game. Instead, magic is used for Torture Attacks, which are powerful (sometimes 1-hit-KO) attacks that vary per enemy, you can continuously push the marked button to get extra Halos (Halos are the currency for the game, where you can buy healing items, accessories (more on them later) and techniques, amongst other things). Magic is also used for special abilities from techniques or accessories.
The enemies start off simple, not unlike Devil May Cry, but they slowly grow in size and stature. New weapons from fallen enemies change up the gameplay considerably, especially when switching items on the fly. The bosses are absolutely tremendous, some of the best ever seen in the genre. Leviathan angels and monstrous demons appear and dynamically change the way the boss fight is made. If taking out a monster over a pit of lava isn't big enough for you, try attacking a beast while in a free-falling stone temple. Yeah, Bayonetta doesn't skip on the showmanship, resulting in an absolutely unforgettable rollercoaster ride of an action game.
The familiarities to Devil May Cry don't end there. Bayonetta can rack up points with stylish and diverse combat, while also earning medals throughout depending on time, defense, and combat style (a kind homage to another Clover Studios title, Viewtiful Joe). Bayonetta can also earn Halos to spend on new weapons and skills in the Gates of Hell, or find hidden items to trade for more powerful stats. Aside from the combat, things can slow down considerably, especially when solving simple puzzles or avoiding environmental hazards. The combat still takes serious precedence in Bayonetta and the fact that it's so powerfully satisfying makes the minor problems disappear almost entirely. One minor issue is the lack of any serious penalty for dying. The worst that happens is a point deduction, but fans of the genre will push their skills to their limits. If you're aiming for high scores and awards (and unlockable difficulty settings), Bayonetta is definitely challenging. However, if you're after a simple run-through of the story (for shame!), Bayonetta can feel a bit forgiving.
The levels are pretty linear, with a set number of encounters in each one. After you finish battling in each separate encounter, you are given a medal ranking based on your performance. One thing that I found strange is that if you go through the level and even find all the “off the path” areas, you still won't engage in every battle. You have to back track to find them. Problem is, there is really no reason to back track except to find these extra battles. In some levels, I still haven't found every encounter (maybe I need an accessory I haven't bought?). This is odd to me, but doesn't hurt the gameplay unless you yearn to get every medal.
To mix things up, Bayonetta's most original feature is its dodging system. In order to defeat enemies easier and avoid hazardous obstacles, you must master the right trigger. You have to pull the trigger just before you are about to take damage, and you will go into Witch Time. This is a slow-motion segment that allows you to attack your enemies with little to no chance of them hitting you. It's highly useful, and also comes into play in puzzle situations, so it doesn't feel just like a gimmicky gameplay mechanic and actually feels like a fleshed out feature in the game.
Enemy variety also becomes an issue. The game tends to repeat bosses way too much, and without the added thrill of seeing them and defeating them like you get when you face them originally, it just feels like you are treading old ground. The people behind this game have created some of the most iconic video game monsters in history; there is no reason they couldn't have been more original with their enemy design.
On the bright side, the sometimes repetitive gameplay is broken up with vehicular segments that are high-octane and thrilling. These require a ton of skill to beat on the more difficult gameplay modes and yield pretty awesome moments. However, they go on for too long and lose a bit of their impact. It would have made more sense to separate out these gameplay segments over the game instead of just having a few long segments.
Grading
GRAPHICS: Excellent- Not the best graphics 3.7/5
SOUND: Great- Good voice work through out, 3.5/5
CONTROLS: Great- Fantastic fighting controls, a ton of moves can be combo-ed into any other move. 4.8/5
GAMEPLAY: Excellent- One of the few triple A actions games out there. Dante and Kratos have new competition. 4.7/5
Play Time/Replayability-The game is a standard 8-12 hours for an action game, but because of the great combat mechanics, the game is sure to keep on giving after the first playthrough.  4/5
Final Verdict 4.3/5

One of my favourite games of the year so far.
I did my first playthrough on the easy difficulty (because I didn't play 2012's XCOM reboot and so haven't played any of the series since the 1990s!) and never really struggled with it, especially later in the game when you've researched the advanced weapons. By the end my squad was pretty OP and could take out almost any opposition without much trouble. But even so, it was hugely enjoyable, and definitely has replay value - I'm playing again (and again) on harder difficulty levels. With careful management of resources and building the right facilities your squad still gets pretty strong once you get past the early stages, but it doesn't stop being highly addictive. I always think I'll just play one more turn before I stop ... and end up stopping four missions later.
You can already customize your team of soldiers, to add a personal touch so you get attached to them and don't want them to die, and you can add even more flair to their appearance with various cool mods. I also liked the weapon upgrades, although the options available are a bit limited. There are some great mods in the Steam Workshop that tweak the UI in useful ways.
I played the Linux version and found the graphics and performance to be fine, and it's very stable (I've had a couple of issues in hours and hours of play, but nothing that wasn't solved by re-loading a save game). The framerate only struggled when my PC was busy running a dozen other CPU intensive tasks in the background at the same time as the game, which is to be expected!

This is a decent improvement upon EU/EW, decent enough to justify the "2" in it's name.
In true old-school UFO fashion it's assumed that you lost the first game and now the tables have turned. You're no longer desperately defending yourself, you're now desperately attacking and chipping away at the great alien system put in place.
The new mechanics reflect that, especially all the timers. Thankfully, you can mod them or even remove them completely (not recommended). These bring a sense of urgency into a TBS game, which is not unique to XCOM 2, but it's a great thing nonetheless.
The difficulty went up considerably (even higher with the Alien Hunters DLC, hate the Rulers), but again, you can mod a lot of it. You can pretty much mod everything you want and play the way you like. The community really shines here and will keep the game alive for a long time, fingers crossed.
As for the technical side of things, the only bugs I've encountered so far (shortly after AH DLC release) had been mod related. My PC is detailed in my profile and using the GF Experience settings the game is always smooth and looks great.

There are a few ships in the game that are insanely OP. Back when the game was first released everyone was complaining about the Assassin class with plasma cannons being OP because it could almost destroy a flagship in a single run, but people didn't realize that it was really hard to move across the entire map with the cloak on, and then back away once the cloak was gone and you were taking hits.
But now they have a 'sniper' type ship that fires a steady beam and rips through any ships health in seconds. And ontop of that, the weapon has almost no cooldown period and stupid insane range. So basically you can hit someone from across the map and never have to really move...
There are a lot of balance issues that need to be worked out with the ships and their respective loadsout/damages/speeds/etc. Once those are done I have no doubt that the game will be as fun as it used to be, but until then I won't recommend the game to anyone. It's basically a 1-sided battle in every single match. You're either going to completely dominate because your team is all using the OP ships, or you're going to be completely destroyed because your team is trying play fair without the OP ships.

XCOM 2 is by FAR my favorite Turn-Based game.
Heres why:
XCOM 2 takes place after the war, and the game assumes that we lost. Earth is now under alien rule, but we do live peacefully, or so we think.
Until it is revealed that the Advent Corporation (the Corporation that rules the world) is working on a project that could end the world. So, as commander, it is your job to prevent that.
BTW: XCOM 2's tutorial is a lot simpler than Enemy Unknowns tutorial (the prequel) in my opinion.
But i am rambling, let's get into core gameplay.
New things:
-Classes have been revamped and are a lot more interesting (Ranger, Specialist, Grenadier, and Sharpshooter)
-New mechanics such as: Concealment, fire spreading, more world destruction, PTSD (as I call is when it is actually called being "shaken"), and many more!
-Mostly random maps
-New aliens (SCREW YOU CODEX!)
-Things you build like weapons and armor are applied to all soldiers, even ones you recruit one later on, so you don't need to spend a whole ♥♥♥♥♥on of money building stuff
-Dark events
-There is no longer a council to babysit (thank god!!!!)
-Melee attacks (swords used by Ranger class)
-(insert more stuff I forgot here)
Bad things
-Camera angles can be wonky sometimes
And that's really it!
Overall, XCOM 2 is amazing and I love to play it, even though it's challenging.

Realm Of The Mad God brings a seemingly boring concept to life through simple textures and gameplay. Band together with other players, level up and eventually die in the endless cycle of this bullet hell mmo. "The sin is not in being outmatched, but in failing to recognize it."
This game is challenging and enjoyable for its difficulty, among other factors. The narrator and the art style set the atmosphere of a dark game, as you might expect from the title. Darkest dungeon is a game of tactics and narrative. As you explore the locations around your ancestor's manor, you must make decisions on your preparations then in your pathing and combat. The game is rewarding through progressing the narrative and in the same way that is satisfying to a complete something.
"Seize this momentum! Push on to the task's end!"
This game is worth playing through until its end, at the time of this review I'm still not there yet (I'm stuck on the last area). Did I mention that the game is difficult? The fun is overcoming the challenges presented, which usually involves failing, once or a few times, and trying new strategies (party composition, skill sets, etc.) until you find something that is really cool or actually works.
The game is repetitive. The game is repetitive. The game is... (you get the point). The normal encounters of the dungeons will often blur together, especially in the same area, but the bosses stand out. The bosses are unique, flavorful, and supplemented by the game's wonderful narrator, Wayne June. At times in life, not just in the game, the quotes spoken by him will resonate in your mind, making even minor events more enjoyable. Out for a hike in the woods, yet forgot to bring water? ("Overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer")
"Injury and despondence set the stage for heroism... or cowardice."
The choice is yours, buy the game and conquer it or don't. Darkest Dungeon broke my expectations for the genre and has left other games feeling lack-luster by comparision. An intriguing story, tactical combat, great atmosphere, and consistent updates. Darkest Dungeon is worth buying for a many hours of entertainment.

Bayonetta is a fond throwback to the days of 3-D action games, not unlike Devil May Cry or God Of War. A majority of the game involves running around fairly linear paths, having the path close off, and having to defeat enemies to progress. Nothing too special. Fortunately, though, the combat is absolute gold. Bayonetta has all of the moves Dante had back in Devil May Cry, like jumping, melee, and shooting attacks, among a few unique traits as well. For example, holding down the punch or kick button lets Bayonetta use the guns strapped to her hands and feet. Rotating the movement analog stick and pressing the attack button lets Bayonetta go into an odd shooting sequence where players blast enemies with repeated gunfire. The most interesting inclusion to combat, and generally the most profitable, is Witch Time. By dodging enemy attacks at the very last second, Bayonetta can slow down time and attack enemies for extra damage and points. These skills are the tip of the iceberg and once more abilities are added to Bayonetta's arsenal, the game shifts into overdrive. It just never stops.
Pros
+ Fantastic combat system is stylish, diverse, and unquestionably visceral
+ Incredible graphics make combat flashy and intense
+ Multiple difficulties and game medals will keep you coming back
+Excellent style and overall game design
+Quirky characters and story
Cons
- Storyline delivery can be pretty cheesy
- Not a huge penalty for dying
-No WQHD support
Now before I start, I'll mention that I'm a big DMC fan, as well as a moderate God of War fan, but I think it's safe to say that Platinum Games have made an action game on par with DMC 3 and GoW 2 (which are my favourite games in the 2 series gameplay wise).
Unlike DMC and GoW, there is no “Devil Trigger/Rage “ mode in this game. Instead, magic is used for Torture Attacks, which are powerful (sometimes 1-hit-KO) attacks that vary per enemy, you can continuously push the marked button to get extra Halos (Halos are the currency for the game, where you can buy healing items, accessories (more on them later) and techniques, amongst other things). Magic is also used for special abilities from techniques or accessories.
The enemies start off simple, not unlike Devil May Cry, but they slowly grow in size and stature. New weapons from fallen enemies change up the gameplay considerably, especially when switching items on the fly. The bosses are absolutely tremendous, some of the best ever seen in the genre. Leviathan angels and monstrous demons appear and dynamically change the way the boss fight is made. If taking out a monster over a pit of lava isn't big enough for you, try attacking a beast while in a free-falling stone temple. Yeah, Bayonetta doesn't skip on the showmanship, resulting in an absolutely unforgettable rollercoaster ride of an action game.
The familiarities to Devil May Cry don't end there. Bayonetta can rack up points with stylish and diverse combat, while also earning medals throughout depending on time, defense, and combat style (a kind homage to another Clover Studios title, Viewtiful Joe). Bayonetta can also earn Halos to spend on new weapons and skills in the Gates of Hell, or find hidden items to trade for more powerful stats. Aside from the combat, things can slow down considerably, especially when solving simple puzzles or avoiding environmental hazards. The combat still takes serious precedence in Bayonetta and the fact that it's so powerfully satisfying makes the minor problems disappear almost entirely. One minor issue is the lack of any serious penalty for dying. The worst that happens is a point deduction, but fans of the genre will push their skills to their limits. If you're aiming for high scores and awards (and unlockable difficulty settings), Bayonetta is definitely challenging. However, if you're after a simple run-through of the story (for shame!), Bayonetta can feel a bit forgiving.
The levels are pretty linear, with a set number of encounters in each one. After you finish battling in each separate encounter, you are given a medal ranking based on your performance. One thing that I found strange is that if you go through the level and even find all the “off the path” areas, you still won't engage in every battle. You have to back track to find them. Problem is, there is really no reason to back track except to find these extra battles. In some levels, I still haven't found every encounter (maybe I need an accessory I haven't bought?). This is odd to me, but doesn't hurt the gameplay unless you yearn to get every medal.
To mix things up, Bayonetta's most original feature is its dodging system. In order to defeat enemies easier and avoid hazardous obstacles, you must master the right trigger. You have to pull the trigger just before you are about to take damage, and you will go into Witch Time. This is a slow-motion segment that allows you to attack your enemies with little to no chance of them hitting you. It's highly useful, and also comes into play in puzzle situations, so it doesn't feel just like a gimmicky gameplay mechanic and actually feels like a fleshed out feature in the game.
Enemy variety also becomes an issue. The game tends to repeat bosses way too much, and without the added thrill of seeing them and defeating them like you get when you face them originally, it just feels like you are treading old ground. The people behind this game have created some of the most iconic video game monsters in history; there is no reason they couldn't have been more original with their enemy design.
On the bright side, the sometimes repetitive gameplay is broken up with vehicular segments that are high-octane and thrilling. These require a ton of skill to beat on the more difficult gameplay modes and yield pretty awesome moments. However, they go on for too long and lose a bit of their impact. It would have made more sense to separate out these gameplay segments over the game instead of just having a few long segments.
Grading
GRAPHICS: Excellent- Not the best graphics 3.7/5
SOUND: Great- Good voice work through out, 3.5/5
CONTROLS: Great- Fantastic fighting controls, a ton of moves can be combo-ed into any other move. 4.8/5
GAMEPLAY: Excellent- One of the few triple A actions games out there. Dante and Kratos have new competition. 4.7/5
Play Time/Replayability-The game is a standard 8-12 hours for an action game, but because of the great combat mechanics, the game is sure to keep on giving after the first playthrough.  4/5
Final Verdict 4.3/5

I updated this review and changed my recommendation to no since I'm not really recommending the game until things get fixed and more polished.
Gear Progression and Difficulty
Gear progression is interesting, but fails to keep pace with player. You can jump to the next tier too quickly and the difficulty doesn’t scale well at all. This is due to the fact that the bosses drop unique items needed to progress to the next tier. It's a great concept, kill boss, gear up, explore and progress to the next boss, rinse repeat. What you get isn't implemented very well at all; the fights are dull and lack the challenge of bosses in similar games like Terraria. On top of that they can be easily exploited simply by building some blocks as a barrier.  This leads to my next point.
Combat
Combat is very cumbersome and becomes boring rather quickly. While it's awesome to have futuristic weapons like plasma rifles/laser guns most of the crafted melee weapons are exactly the same with the only difference being swing speed. Most creatures can be killed with one or two hits from a melee weapon of the same tier and that’s basically it for almost every creature with the exception of some NPCs. Sure you can find awesome weapons, but they don’t feel powerful, you just keep clicking and whatever is in front of you dies. There’s never any sense of diversity with enemies and the AI combat is basically just jump attacks with some decently powerful ranged attacks from flyers. NPCs could be a challenge due to their weapons and armor, but the AI is too limited. The NPCs never work together and basically become cannon fodder. The system isn’t broken, but it definitely needs tweaking with a lot more weapon and AI diversity, especially mobs of NPCs.
Space Travel
I’ve played MineCraft, Terraria, Cube World and many other sandbox games, but it was the space travel which drew me to this game in the first place. Having basically unlimited planets to explore seems like a great idea, but again it needs work and balancing. There’s “sectors” that get progressively harder and have more diverse “biomes”. That makes it fun to jump from solar system to solar system to discover new planets and find weapons, tech, dungeons, towns, etc. While the biomes are interesting, I like the asteroids and moons, they still don’t feel that much different from each other. Again the enemies in the biomes are basically all the same with the same AI but different skins, it’s a blue slime instead of a yellow slime. That would be OK if they AI acted differently but you’re basically fighting the same stuff over and over.
Building
Building stuff is easy, fun and there a ton of objects to acquire throughout the universe, but again things need adjustment like some materials take way too long to break if you made a mistake building your structure or simply want to make a change to an existing structure.
There’s a lot to love about Starbound and I still have fun playing it, but there’s a lot of work to be done. I’m not going to get into any comments about the Devs or Chucklefish, but I will say they have a hit on their hands if they concentrate on getting core mechanics, AI and combat working.

They also adopted a puppy and have used the backers money not to fund Starbound, but each take up work on individual projects and then publishing other's games.
Should be good if/when it's finished. Slated for release in 2013 - that's officially moved to 2015 and will probably be moved again.
If you like repetitive grinding you should buy this game, but do not buy it to support or follow development. Chucklefish has already made over $15 million from Starbound and owning the game doesn't give you any extra idea of how development is going.
If you want to support this game not buying it is the better option - falling sales is the only thing that may get Chucklefish to buckle down.

I've been playing this game on and off for a while now, and have to admit it's one of my favorite turn based RPGs of all time. As others have mentioned it strikes a good balance of management style activities with turn based adventures.  The gameplay mechanics are interesting and varied if a little intimidating when you first start off, but before you know it you will be min/maxing your team and gear to try and survive the next dungeon.  Kind of reminds me of a turn based version of FTL on steroids.
Some of the reviews have bashed the difficulty / RNG factor, but personally I find this a big draw for the game.  Yes, the RNG can be punishing at times but for me that adds a layer of replayability to the whole experience.  Not to mention the fact that the difficulty synergizes really well with the art and sound direction of the game.  It's mean to be dark, gritty, and damn near impossible.
Overall a very unique and well executed game which promises many hours of fun for those who can handle the challenge.

Fractured space has been a very enjoyable game so far.
The game is still in alpha, and under constant development. In the last couple of months the developers have released an additional 5 ships, all with unique abilities and gameplay styles. Expanding on an already impressive collection of ships.
With over 20 ships you can choose a gameplay style to suit your character, mood, and opposing team, for example:
**Edit**: Some of these ships have been renamed, or had abilities tweaked ***Edit***
If they don't sound like fun, then you can play as some of the more traditional ships like the flagship, destroyer, carrier, or leviathan, variations on the battle cruiser class ship, each with its own pros and cons.
The gameplay is heavily team and objective based. While a lot of games are played just using the in game communication, the real fun starts once you communicate with your team mates using voice. While the game lacks a voice system at the moment, the developers provide a teamspeak server, and a number of clans run their own.
That said, there are a number of issues with the game. Since the developers are constantly adding new features, and ships, the game is a constant state of needing rebalancing. While this is an ongoing process, there are some weeks where you find some ships are over powered, or your favourite strategy has become unviable. In the past few months, we have seen the carrier ship flop between being overpowered, and underpowered as the dev's fail to get the balance just right. This is more than acceptable throughout the alpha and beta stages of any game. Some of the other bugs that have shown up throughout the alpha have been worse, but as it stands, the game is massively playable, and I've put in a large number of hours, trying out new strategies and the gameplay mutates.

Let me just start this review by saying that I love the XCOM franchise.
I loved watching my dad play UFO defence when I was about 5 or 6, I loved playing it and it's sequel myself once I found the game again in my teen years (although it was tough as hell), I loved playing the Firaxis reboot and I am happy... oh so very VERY happy to be able to say that I absolutely ADORE this game!
The setting is flipped on it's head as you take charge of the remainder of what was once XCOM. Starting out as little more than an underfunded freedom fighter movement, that just happens to have a spaceship. Right from the start the pressure is on and the feeling every time you whitness a new enemy type is aprehensive to say the least. It improves vastly on the soldier customization of the previous game and the mod support is insane.
If you liked any of the previous XCOM strategy games I strongly advice you to buy this one. It's a new take on the setting but it's still XCOM in all it's tactical, turn based, unforgiving, frustrating and customizeable glory!

First off, at the time of writing this game is in alpha, hopefully my criticisms will be distant memories by the time it's fully released.
This is a game I WANT to love.  I'm not even a MOBA gamer usually, nor do I play a lot of online pvp at all, but the setting and theme of this game draw me in and make me wish it was better then it is just now.  Capital ship combat in space, big weapons, teamwork oriented, beautiful graphics, sounds awesome!
But!  At the time of writing I rarely enjoy a matchup.  I'm by no means an expert player, still just experimenting with the various ships to get a feel for what they can do, but about 75% of the matches I join up are totatlly unbalanced in terms of player skill, whether in my favour or against it.  I liken it to gambling, every time you join a match you're rolling that die hoping for a good matchup thats fair and challenging for everyone involved, but the majority of the time I'm not getting that.  There is apparently a matchmaking function in the works, but it's not available yet, hopefully they sort this out as soon as possible.
There is essentially no tutorial other then a short video, as a new player you're thrown into a live match with relentless opponents who'll happily curbstomp you until you disconnect in frustration.  I would say on average any match with beginner players has a very high chance of them disconnecting after a few minutes.  Different players will fill those slots to keep the teams even usually, but my point is for people trying out it's pretty punishing.  I've heard the developers are planning to fix this, but at the time of writing the game is missing this feature.
Overall I feel the game has a ton of potential, and I understand it's not complete, I sincerely hope the developers resolve those two glaring deficiencies soon or I fear this is another game that could have been great that gets passed over for its flaws.

Short Version - XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within are vastly superior to this game. Go buy them instead, or if you have them and want more Firaxis XCOM, install and play the Long War mod.
I wanted to like this game so bad. Hundreds of hours into Enemy Unknown and I was ready and raring to go for the next step. And there are certainly next steps in XCOM 2, the Starting concealment, the changes to Psionics, different enemy types, those were all really good ideas. On the other hand, there's simply too many things that can make your game go sideways through literally no fault of your own. In EU, I usually knew when I made a mistake. Sometimes things go poorly one turn, and that's the way it is, and it usually doesn't happen too often unless you're just committed to riding the bullet train of bad decisions. XCOM 2 just is the bullet train of failure, and there's no brakes on that train.
Barring the DLC, the art is slick and totally on point, a really good iteration of Enemy Unknown's style. Tygen is cool, but lacks the personality and interest of Vahlen. He's 24/7 cool as a cucumber, and is just constantly aloof, where Vahlen had a proper forward face, but there were plenty of hints through dialogue that at any given time she was basically 2 seconds away from dissecting the nearest thing to her, living or dead, while singing opera. Lily Shen's interest basically drops right after her introduction, she never develops even though she's got the most opportunity to do so. On top of that, she looks EXACTLY like Jackie Ma from Sleeping Dogs, right down to the hairdo and freckles, so that's wierd.
The soldier base models are all basically flat, they have zero silhouette and really wierd proportions. Even though there's more customization, somehow it feels more constrained, and I think it's due to there just being less interesting faces and hairdos available.
And, once again (see: Batman: Arkham Knight), XCOM 2 has massive performance issues by trying to ship a "next-gen" game on a decade-old engine.
Like Rocksteady, they bolted too many custom tools and rendering software onto Unreal Engine 3, and while Unreal is a fantastic engine, they both were trying to do rendering that the engine was just not meant to do. So, came the litany of "I have a top-end machine and I get 20 FPS" and "Game crashes at launch" on forums, and while I only had catastrophic issues once or twice, the load times and frame chug just inside the Skyranger are simply unforgivable.
The story of XCOM losing was a bitter pill to swallow, but it gave a good start to why there's more aliens in the future. But beyond that, the presentation just lacks the same punch as Enemy Unknown. It lacks tension and a sense of urgency, even though that's what XCOM 2 is supposed to be completely centered around.
I'll go watch the intro cinematic to Enemy Unknown just to watch it, because it gets me totally jazzed up to save the world. Michael McCann kills it with the music, and that stutter cut with the Skyranger gets me giddier than a schoolgirl to go shoot some aliens. On the other hand,the intro to XCOM 2 has scenes that should arguably be even more intense, but the lackluster directing, the totally midtone soundwork, it all made it feel so.... ordinary. Like blowing up ADVENT checkpoints is just what you do on a Tuesday afternoon. Though, Bradford jumping through a window was pretty sweet.
The sense of tedium never goes away, as you're constantly shifting back and forth across zones because everything takes too long. You'll rarely finish one activity before you have to go do a guerilla op, oh did you happen to notice, ADVENT's  putting the boots to some hippies in a commune that happen to be our friends, hey you should go look at this wierd spot we found, oh by the way, you need to go pick up your monthly cheque from this spot because we couldn't be arsed to mail it to you direct, and there's a 3 day processing wait, did you want to sell stuff, well you gotta go fly there too, because apparently there's only ONE Black Market bazaar on the planet.
There's a nice balance that Enemy Unknown struck between the Strategy and Tactical layers of their game, The Tactical portion was an overt stress-fest of playing hide-and-seek with bullets, doing Hail Marys behind the tiny log that is your only available cover, and hoping to Sweet Baby Ray's that the Meld canister you're after isn't just a total pod-fest of X-rays. The Strategy layer was much more subtle, and the contrast makes the game actually playable. The Strategy layer gives you time to think, to manage your resources and marshal your thoughts on your game plan. It can be a good 10 minutes before another mission crops up, which is good downtime for the player so they aren't keyed up for too long.
XCOM 2 learned nothing from its predecessor. The constantly running around, the Doom Ticker front and center, everything takes too long, and missions pop up with an annoying frequency to how much you can actually get done in the Strategy layer before "Hey, you gotta pop half-way round the world to go save those dirty hippies again" There's really never time to rest in XCOM 2 and it's frankly exhausting even thinking about booting the game up.
The last sticking point, and really the final straw for me, is really how screwed the game balance was, and continues to be. Instead of say, fixing the fact that missions play like a round of "Whose Line is it Anyway?", where the shot percentages are made up and the aiming angles don't matter, they decide a good idea is to heavily nerf one of the only options for consistent damage, and taking away the biggest reason you pick Volatile Mix (increased grenade radius). Not even mentioning removing the only means of stopping "Run-n-Gun" Chrysallids and Stun Lancers. And there was obviously decisions that were made akin to those bouts of insanity throughout its development. Tons of enemies have armour (DR in EU) and Shieldbearers can give anyone in a huge radius armour, fine. But they took out Shredder rounds, so the only ways are, Psyhic attacks on non-robotic enemies (which bypasses armour, so the rest of your squad is still stuck in DR hell), an extremely high-level perk for Rangers, and the aforementioned nerfed grenades. Thin Men made a new appearance as the Vipers, and they can strangle you from a distance, great! But, (up until a patch a couple weeks ago, where they can't dodge 100% shots anymore), they have a high chance to straight-up ignore half of incoming damage from any weapon that rolls to hit. Your squad starts most missions Concealed, which allows you to try and get the jump on your enemy by (potentially) setting up kill zones to obliterate a pod before they can shoot back, Awesome! But why is there a 10, or even better, a FIVE (yes, five) turn timer on the mission? It completely nullifies the concept of Concealment and geurilla warfare if your only option to succeed in the mission is to dash forward non-stop until you reach the objective, because you WILL run into a pod, you WILL lose Concealment, and after that, you can't hope to just keep running and expect to win.
There's things to like in XCOM 2, but it's just such an unfun, buggy mess.

I decided to leave a review due to recent changes by Bethesda.
I have played Fallout, Fallout 2, Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas, so I think I know enough about the series to judge them (from my humble point of view at least).
This is no longer a fallout RPG and more of a post-nuclear shooter. It lacks almost everywhere compared to it's predecessors. And it has micro-transactions to boot.
The game itself is OK.
*The graphics are good.
*The world is big with lots of locations.
*Guns feel nice in combat.
*Power Armor change was a step in the right direction.
*Added settlements system was interesting too.
Now the bad things.
*This is no longer an RPG. The dialog was dumbed down. Like many reviews already stated, you have only the following options: yes, sarcastic yes, negative attitude (but still yes), and a question. On multiple occasions I saw something in the dialog that I wanted to say, but the character ended up with a different tone with other wording. There are no skill checks (since there are no skills). You can max out all stats and you can no longer specialize in something.
*The story is bad. Without spoilers, I would say that I had more fun replaying the story of Gothic 2 than this. There are some cool moments that really impress, but they just can't fill the story holes and are such more due to the graphics rather than the story itself.
*The difficulty balance is off. Hello my raider friend who will die only after half a clip to the head (this is subjective, but I never liked this Bethesdays' difficulty system). Also I would imagine that good weapons should be scarse and not all over the world that no longer can produce them.
*Power Armor is no longer hard to get. Remember how you used to go through the whole BOS recruitment process and training? Not anymore. Special weapons no longer feel rare. Wish they could have a quest like in Fallout where you had to find a plasma gun and then find a gun smith who could make it even better.
*Characters are OK, but no longer as good as previously. To me they don't feel special anymore, not like in F:NV where you travel with a companion, learn about him/her, about his/her problems, start to feel for him/her and just then set out on his/her quest to right the wrongs and make the world a better place.
*The generic quests are annoying (insert "I'll mark it on your map" joke). It's fine to have generic quests, but I don't like them being shoved in my face all the time. And you cannot decline them.
*Settlement system feels incomplete. It's fun to start building around, but you learn fast that it is more than a bit clumsy.
Some other thoughts:
*Weapons and armor mods are cool, but in the end you just go for the best mod you can craft.
*Lots of location, but most of the time it feels empty. There are really good locations with NPCs and lore and loot, but overall you will be just going from point A to point B killing and looting all in the way.
*DLCs are a mixed blessing. On one hand they offer something more, but on the other - it doesn't feel worth the price.
About Creation Club.
I fully support the idea of paying the mod makers. It would be nice to have a place, supported by the developers of the game to integrate the mods into the game with proper testing. It would be nice for good mod makers to be advertised. The problem is, CC is not that. It will download mods you don;t own to your PC. It can (and most likely will) break your mods (read about F4SE). It has ridiculously high prices that Bethesda will keep for them self (mod makers do get paid, but not from sales). And on top of that I do not support micro-transactions in a single-player full priced AAA game.
I will not recommend this game. There are games with better world, story, RPG elements and combat for a less price.
If you really have to buy this game, wait for a huge discount.

I have seen many, many bad reviews of this game. To sum it up:
- It can be grindy if you go for Darkest or Stygian difficulty, but there are strategies to overcome this (people can beat the game in 21 weeks in Stygian). You need to be smart. You can also play Radiant (which it doesn't make the game any less easier — just shorter).
- It is a dificult game. You need to play this game differently to other games: troops are disposable, objectives clear, and there are tricks to maximise effectiveness. This isn't Final Fantasy Tactics.
- RNG can be devastating. This is why you need to train your troops. To try and even things out.
- You will fail. This is part of the game. You need to learn from your mistakes.
Just like in Dark Souls, you need to treat this game differently to what you're used to. Then, and only then, you will succeed...
... if you don't have a stress-induced heart attack first.

Half-Life is a game for which so much can be said but so little need be spoken. Following the path of scientist Gordon Freeman, Half-Life takes the player on a journey to put a stop to a scientific experiment turn catastrophy in the form of an alien invasion. The occasional let down from awqward platforming and limited problem does little to dent the brilliance of Half-Life.
To all gamers, you are obliged to experience this piece of gaming heritage.
