There are a lot of things about this game that bug the crap out of me. The timed missions, the Avatar project which basically puts a timer on the campaign itself, the scarcity of elerium cores which makes outfitting your squad kind of hard, the same old six person squad size, the needless delays that make the game seem to grind to a halt at the worst possible times...the list goes on and on...
But there is a mod for every one of those complaints. Every. Single. One.
For everything about this game I din't like, someone else didn't like it either and made a mod to fix it. Then all of these truly amazing modders came along and created wonderful content that took an already impressively open game and expanded it even further. I have no idea how many mods I am currently subscribed to at this point, but every complaint I had about the game when I first bought it has been addressed by the community and my games are much more diverse due to all of the options unlocked through user created content. I'd also like to add that despite having an absurd number of mods active the game is VERY stable. This many mods on something like Fallout New Vegas? Forget about it.
So if you enjoyed XCOM and were on the fence about this one you should consider giving it a try. If there is something you heard about it that made you hesitant about picking it up, wait for it to go on sale. I am glad I bought it, though, and it is even better than the previous iteration.

The thing about this game is that theres a huge element of surprise. You'll find out what I mean when you play the game.

This is, what I would call an action-adventure FPS. This game really set the standard for the genre.
There's a fair assortment of weapons. Speaking of weapons, you're going to need ammo. Alot of it.
That's not necessarily a bad thing - it's everywhere. Or atleast, it's not very hard to find ammo.
The other thing with this game is that, you, the player needs to be very patient. This game has backtracking.
of it.

There is music in this game. Although, they only really play during intense parts, it's still quite well composed.
If you look past the backtracking and constant dying, you'll
this game. Trust me.
It's absolutely fantastic, and really set the standards for the FPS genre after 1998.
That's not all I have to say about Half-Life, but if I did, you and I would be here all day.

Though I played some CS years ago, I've almost totally skipped Half-Life before. And finally the time has come to remedy that problem. Even though HL already celebrated its 15th birthday, it still is a fresh experience. I'm not a big fan of most FPS, mainly because they rarely give a unique experience, not even with the great graphics of these days. They often lack story, likeable characters or special atmosphere, and consist solely of shooting everything.
In some respect, HL also suffers from these problems, the story itself isn't really elaborated (though much more is hinted at) or unique and there is little character development (I quite like Gordon, however :). But as for the atmosphere: HL is somehow very charming. The layout of Black Mesa facility is quite silly sometimes, but it's really enjoyable to roam it's endless corridors. I also like most of the enemies, and alternating alien and human foes gives much variety to gameplay. Scripted events are great, as well and the pacing is just excellent (especially in the first half).
The "jumping puzzle" parts of the game are not common in contemporary titles, but had been present in the past and, to be honest, fighting off enemies while standing on flying platforms and hopping from one to the other is quite exciting. The use of space and room in the game is usually clever, you have to concentrate quite hard not to  fall off the edge of a small floating island while shooting and finding an adequate hiding spot is vital in many situations. Some issues arise from this however, firing from behind shelter, using the alien gun with the enemy-seeker darts for example, makes some foes easier to kill than probably intended by the creators. The physics of the game has its own problems as well.......
All in all, I highly recommend this game, I think it lives up to its fame, even today!
And now, it's time to install Half-Life 2... :)

This game won't stop giving me tragic stories that would end up being major motion pictures.
Had a five man squad, affectionatly named Roughneck squad, sent in to extract data from an advent computer. Lead by Lt "Smash" Rodgers, "Rose" York the Grenadier, "Carbon" Takiban the Assault, "Gambler" Hendrick the Gunslinger, and "Inferno" Soto the Technical. The mission was rated light-medium so I figured with some careful leap-frogging and ambush tactics the leam would be more than fine.
Start out in a delapitated neighborhood with no contacts in sight, good sign. The squad starts making a slow approach through backyards and a bunt out playground towards the house storing the computer. Seeing a good holding point for extraction, with a clear line of sight to the objective, the leam takes up positions and Smash sends his gremlin through the window to grab the data. As per usual this tips Advent off that there are operatives in play and causes them to send in the works. Gambler pops a flair and the first bad news comes up '8 turns til evac'. I'm floored, how can it be that long? I haven't touched any of the pods, so it's not like they were sending reinforcements in already. We're professionals though and this should be within our wheelhouse, or so I thought. Second piece of bad news comes up in the corner 'reinforcement imminent' in all red, which means next turn. The team makes a hasty set up for overwatch and we hope we can ride it out. As the reinforements drop in, it's a full dropship, big trouble with two mecs. After dealing medium damage to the reinforcements the real terror show begins. Four pods activate around our evac zone, mecs, snakes, at least a dozen troopers of different classes, sectoids, it's now five vs seventeen and our cover can't protect from all the flanks. Smash was the first to go down, his cover pulverized by mec artillery and sniped by a snake to put him down. Rose ended up taking a stunner shot from a drone and being taken out of the fight for the moment, leaving Gambler, Carbon, and Inferno to try and salvage this operation. What proceeded was a daring hit and run campaign that saw Gambler gunning down the snake that killed Smash as well as a few troopers, Carbon scrapping the mecs with the help of his arc thrower, and Inferno managing to scatter some of the troops with a well placed rocket and some super heated napalm. Sadly, their luck wouldn't hold out. Rose finally woke up in time for a dual drop pod and the return of a few of the scattered pods seeking vengence. The entire team had been severly injured at this point (no one above 3 pips of health) so Carbon made the hard call. Mary had been the one to grab the intel off of Smash's body before being tazed and Carbon knew that as long as the intel got back to base, it would technically be a win. After Rose smashed some of the Advents cover with a well palced grenade, Carbon hooked a fulton extraction pack to her and extarcted her, along with the intel. As if knowing their secrets we gone, the remining mecs bombed Carbon until he was nothing but paste spattered against the disused power station. Inferno and Gambler silently mourned their friends passing, but would not go quietly and proceeded to reap a heavy tally of advent. Inferno caught a stray shot from sectoid and went down, leaving Gambler alone, but one last ray of hope shone through, the extraction smoke finally popped. One more onslaught and Gambler can leave this hell hole. Almost two straight minutes of fire and this brave gunslinger and no positive hits, he can do it...he can make it! Shame the last snake on the field had other plans though, his tongue snaring Gambler and yanking him from his near freedom...and a second later the coils crushing the life from him and ending his death defying career as a pistolero.
After this mission all I could do was hang my head and think "I failed them..."

There are a few things i dislike about Realm of The Mad God, though. For example, when you die you literally lose everything you were carrying; and sometimes, its not even your fault that you died! Maybe you were a bit laggy, maybe you got distracted, maybe somebody else was stupid, the point is, just one slip up and you can lose everything, and that can be really maddening. Also, it may be free to play, but its definately not "free to win", to gain good items you have to fork up quite a lot of money, considering. I recomend that you don't play a lot of ROTMG, because it can get seriously addicting and maddening. Watch yourself and it can be a fun game.

The Creation Club could have worked if it just consisted of high-quality DLC-sized add-ons that were fully voice-acted and offered hours of additional content. Instead, we got overpriced cosmetic items, some of which already have similar (often superior) versions available for free on the Nexus.
As for the game itself, it's alright, though the stripping down of dialogue options and alternate paths (besides the major faction choice) really limits replayability. It feels more like Star Wars: The Old Republic than a single player RPG. There is also a lack of interesting characters and side quests, as well as few memorable decisions. This is partially recompensed by  positive changes to power armor, gunplay, weapon modding, and followers. The bobbleheads and magazines were also more fun to collect as they gave perks instead of just stats. The settlement system is a bit hit-or-miss, but it's not a bad inclusion. It just makes towns outside the main hubs a bit dull.
Would have still recommended prior to the Creation Club, but that nonsense doesn't belong in a Bethesda RPG with an extensive modding community.

Though I played some CS years ago, I've almost totally skipped Half-Life before. And finally the time has come to remedy that problem. Even though HL already celebrated its 15th birthday, it still is a fresh experience. I'm not a big fan of most FPS, mainly because they rarely give a unique experience, not even with the great graphics of these days. They often lack story, likeable characters or special atmosphere, and consist solely of shooting everything.
In some respect, HL also suffers from these problems, the story itself isn't really elaborated (though much more is hinted at) or unique and there is little character development (I quite like Gordon, however :). But as for the atmosphere: HL is somehow very charming. The layout of Black Mesa facility is quite silly sometimes, but it's really enjoyable to roam it's endless corridors. I also like most of the enemies, and alternating alien and human foes gives much variety to gameplay. Scripted events are great, as well and the pacing is just excellent (especially in the first half).
The "jumping puzzle" parts of the game are not common in contemporary titles, but had been present in the past and, to be honest, fighting off enemies while standing on flying platforms and hopping from one to the other is quite exciting. The use of space and room in the game is usually clever, you have to concentrate quite hard not to  fall off the edge of a small floating island while shooting and finding an adequate hiding spot is vital in many situations. Some issues arise from this however, firing from behind shelter, using the alien gun with the enemy-seeker darts for example, makes some foes easier to kill than probably intended by the creators. The physics of the game has its own problems as well.......
All in all, I highly recommend this game, I think it lives up to its fame, even today!
And now, it's time to install Half-Life 2... :)

I love the X-Com series, loved the original title back in 1994 and love it's sequel. I even have a fondness for the reboot of the series, of which, to some extent...I would recommend. This title however, though it has some great mechanics in place and could be quite enjoyable, has you suffering through so many peformance issues that you really have to wonder what the hell they were playing this game on while in development. They MUST have seen these issues that literally every one of their customers has witnessed, yet they just didn't bother to fix them.
More often than not I sit around 50fps, then at times I will drop down to 40fps in retaliation sites. On an i7, 16GB RAM and a GTX970...that is far from acceptable for this type of game. Character customisation is great, you can set up some great plays and feel like you are being quite sneaky. In the end though, performance becomes your biggest enemy and the RNG regarding your soldiers shots cuts down any tactics you had in place.
I want to play it, and I want to enjoy it...but they messed up so damn hard. Sorry, Firaxis, fix it before releasing any more DLC and we might see a change.

The biggest improvement over EU is presentation. The story and connection to your soldiers is fantastic. You will feel like you are truly running a resistance movement. And with that being said, fighting a superior enemy is no easy task. This game encourages planning and tactics. Any deviation from this approach and you will be punished.
That being said, I truly dislike the timers. Occasionally this would be a good way to create some variation like in EU. The first few months are complete hell due to the progression curve. This can be due to unlucky RNG or mistakes in planning. Sometimes I would find myself having to make a mad dash across a map just to make it to the evacuation site on time. Fortunately if this isn’t your way of playing, mods can fix it. I have played both ways. Each style has its own merits.
The graphics have been improved over the original. This isn’t just a reskin job from Enemy Unknown. Aliens look more realistic and sometimes just plain creepy. Music and sound effects are also implemented well.  It’s the subtle things like alien voices or the eerie glow of the gatekeeper as it opens up. Environment physics are a fantastic improvement over EU. You will understand the first time you get blown up from underneath a roof.

Let's get a few things straight before I begin.
1st: Realm of the Mad God is a free to play. You do not have to pay, in order to find out if you really enjoy the game or not. So dont hesitate to download this very small, low storage game.
2nd: If you aren't one who enjoys any of the following concepts: "Multiplayer, Team Effort, Dungeon Crawler, Minimalized Graphics, Classes, Permadeath, In-Game Economy and Trade Systems, In-Game Purchases...etc" then you might as well back the hell out.
3rd: In-Game Purchases aren't necessary to fit the games bill. You don't need to throw any amount of currency in, to get the best experience this game has to offer.
Realm of the Mad God has been with us for several years, though it may not have been on Steam for that long. We could find it as an online game, playable through certain browsers and flash plug-ins. Just recently, about a year and a half ago, coming up to two years ago, this game was released on Steam.
With its pixelated graphics, good ratings, and thorough trailers I thought I might as well give it a shot.
Gameplay Experience: Not once was I disappointed in the games efforts to give me the best enviroment for gameplay. I never ran into a bug, or glitch for that matter. Its cross-platform multiplayer experience gave me several oppurtunites to meet friends, and join in many events.
Permadeath: This game IS set-up with a permadeath system. Though it is hard to believe so, your account does gain perks with every death. The longer you survive with each character or class, and the more bosses you kill, the more "Fame" you obtain. With this fame, you can purchase different items, or unlock separate classes. So all-in-all, Permadeath isn't all too bad.
Graphics: Now, let's talk about these graphics. Many players like their graphics smooth, or realistic. You need to expect several visible PIXELS before actually getting into the game. The whole game is made from pixels. From its font, to the spells you cast, everything is made of pixels. Don't get sassy with me in saying everything is made of pixels, everywhere. You get what I'm trying to say. These pixels make the game unique, and provide smooth, not-so-hard-to-run gameplay.
Multiplayer: The whole game is multiplayer. There is no singleplayer, but you can choose to level up and defeat bosses on your own, which does get harder as your character progresses, require the help of others. Everywhere you go, there will be somewhere nearby. But this isnt always a bad thing, as you can chat with them, teleport to them, trade with them, follow them, and several other actvities.
I seem to have covered the main areas of complaint, and overall feel of the game. I hope this review helped in aiding in your decision.

Really awesome game, mix of a classic 'Counter Strike', 'Call of Duty 4' and 'Battlefield: Bad Company 2' with some unique features. Game code well written, had zero lags and freezes within six hours of straight play in different modes.
Overall graphics and animations quality on a decent level, everything looks smooth and well-detailed.
Gameplay itself consist of team only modes - classic 'team deathmatch', 'demolition' and 'assassination' similar to a bomb defuse and VIP-escort from a CS1.6 and 'destruction', similar to  a 'rush' from BF:BC2. Plus, theres few optional rulesets, such as 'rifles/shotguns/knives only' or a 'survival' version of TD with disabled respawns.
Game modes, maps and inventory balanced nearly perfectly, comparing to a similar games. Most maps are symmetrical in terms of walkable path (but not in terms of textures, theres no copy-paste of same buildings, roads and static things) and key objects  in 'destruction' mode.
The only asymmetrical maps are made for  a 'demolition' and 'assassination' modes and Id like to point that maps for a local 'bomb defuse' mode created with higher quality comparing to Counter Strike: Source or even Global Offence maps, and feeling much more accurate and tactically rich, reminding best maps from CS1.6.
Each gun have unique stats (within 0-100 range). Theres no uber 'pay2win' guns at all, every gun have own strengths and weaknesses. For example you can pick very accurate or fast-shooting rifle, but with a small overall damage, few powerful rifles with nearly twice as much damage, but with an awful recoil as well.
The only weird thing is that all grenades (HE, smoke and flash) are temporary and require periodical repurchase, while all guns you can buy - always permament, requiring one-time purchase only. Luckily this is not a problem at all, since 15000 free coins being given every day, and this sum more than enough to buy all types of grenades.
Immediately after registering a nickname (no e-mail, date of birth and other info needed) youll recieve 200000 coins plus 15000 within daily event. This money is more than enough to buy 1-2 new guns (which are being sold for in-game currency and real money).
Moreover, theres no hardcore money grind like in a similar 'f2p' games, youll recieve coins and medals for a daily and weeky events (daily check-ins and total played time for a whole week respectively), level ups as well as for every finished match.
Additional advantage of a 'Black Squad' - game being protected by a 'BattleEye', really effective anti-cheat tool comparing to an awful 'PunkBuster' or a passive 'VAC'.
The only problem that can occur - awfully bad or selfish teammates on your side, since theres only quantity autobalancer, not a skills-based autobalancer. For a 'team deathmatch' and 'demolition' this is not a real problem, since everything depends on your sole skills and due to a lagless servers (at least european one) and proper hitboxes its possible to outsmart and outplay even few enemies, paving the headshots road to victory.
The only mode, in which success depends on luck and random than on skills - 'destruction'. This mode looks alike 'CoD4' and 'BF:BC2' combo in terms of gameplay, with four different classes, possiblity to accamulate special points for each portion of damage you was able to inflict, which later might be traded on different one-time abilities, such as mines and grenade launchers, healing and ammopacks, fieldscan and bombardments. The one and the only objective - to get rid of all enemy command posts, which is impossible without decent team play.
In conclusion Id like to say that I tried many 'F2P' games such as 'Operation7', 'Crossfire', 'Counter Strike: Nexus', 'Tactical Intervention', but 'Black Squad' was the only properly made and properly balanced grindless game among those I have played. Thus, I highly recommend to play this game.

Before I write this review, let me give you a disclaimer. I've been playing this game a whole bunch and as a whole, I actually kind of liked it. Though it wasn't stellar as a Fallout game, it was a decent game in it's own right and could stand on it's merits.
This was before bethesda introduced it's horrendous "Creation Club" system.
The Creation Club is bethesda's way of trying to tap into the micro transaction market.
When it was introduced, the creation club promised curated premium mod content, painting a picture of high quality community made mods that were very close to DLC's in terms of scope. It was exciting because having a spot in the creation club meant that you had access to the tallent at bethesda during different phases of the development process. This was an unprecidented opportunity that was meant to push the modding community of not just fallout 4, but also skyrim, to new limits of content creation.
Fastfoward to the actual implementation of creation club. Do we get amazing DLC-esque quest content? Do we get loads of new and wacky gameplay systems, like changing seasons, moving dungeon platforms, and working spear combat?
No. We get cosmetic items. We get literal horse armor. We get the option to change our pipboys color scheme. What a letdown.
Also, to add injury to insult, my F4SE is broken. And it will keep breaking. Over and over again. because EVERY TIME BETHESDA WANTS TO UPDATE THE CREATION CLUB CONTENT, THEY WILL PATCH ALL OF IT TO YOUR COMPUTER, AND FORCE YOU TO DOWNLOAD 600+ MB's of DATA WITHOUT YOUR CONSENT.
They do this because, again, they want to cash in on microtransactions. They know that in order to circumvent the limitations of the PS4 and XBONE CONSOLES, they need to introduce these micrtransactions as a patch (official game), so that the people will have the opportunity to pay them a dollar to let them change their pip boys black. And they're too lazy to change it for the PC.
TL;DR
In Bethesda's latest iteration of their "Paid Mods" scheme, they somehow manage to turn a game into literal malware while simultaneously managing to completely destroy a large component of it's community modding tools (F4SE)

This game is a little gem a bit rough around the edges. I am not a Roguelike fan, but while the grinding is more or less unavoidable, knowing a couple of things can clearly make your runs easier, and having a large stable of mercenaries also reduces the impact of a bad run.
My two main issues with the game:
- having the same bosses at each difficulty level is less than completely fun. Sure, you cannot use the exact same tactic since damage output is not the be all, end all at higher levels, but a little variation would have gone a long way.
- the hunger mechanism is a bit *too* random, and stacking on food is almost mandatory.
Beyond that, the atmosphere is excellent I just love the artwork, the game does a good job at making you try different mercenary combos, and having to manage your mental quirks carefully gives a bit of life to your pack of soldiers of fortune - proving once again that heroes are defined by their flaws more than anything else (and who in their right mind would NOT send the Vestal to the brothel for stress relief ? :)).
A big thumbs up - a trifle less grindy would have make it a must have, but it is still quite enjoyable as it is - as long as you do not rage-quit on the occasional unlucky spell that can happen in all similar games.

The biggest improvement over EU is presentation. The story and connection to your soldiers is fantastic. You will feel like you are truly running a resistance movement. And with that being said, fighting a superior enemy is no easy task. This game encourages planning and tactics. Any deviation from this approach and you will be punished.
That being said, I truly dislike the timers. Occasionally this would be a good way to create some variation like in EU. The first few months are complete hell due to the progression curve. This can be due to unlucky RNG or mistakes in planning. Sometimes I would find myself having to make a mad dash across a map just to make it to the evacuation site on time. Fortunately if this isn’t your way of playing, mods can fix it. I have played both ways. Each style has its own merits.
The graphics have been improved over the original. This isn’t just a reskin job from Enemy Unknown. Aliens look more realistic and sometimes just plain creepy. Music and sound effects are also implemented well.  It’s the subtle things like alien voices or the eerie glow of the gatekeeper as it opens up. Environment physics are a fantastic improvement over EU. You will understand the first time you get blown up from underneath a roof.
This is a fantastic strategy game that deserves high praise. Firaxis listened to the people that wanted a real PC strategy game. Needless to say, I am happy with how the franchise has been treated this time around. I most certainly will be ordering the inevitable expansion in the near future.

I did enjoy the game sometimes, but for the most part I ended up yelling at the screen when the rng♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me for various reasons.
My first game I lost a hero on what I considered the tutorial mission. I knew then I would probably end up unistalling the game.
The heros are somewhat dispoable. I do understand that. You need to understand that. Every week/mission more come in so they can be replaced. With the rng, they can drop like flies on any difficulty if you don't play smart. My problem is I was trying to play safe and the heals make that a bad idea. You can play safe and heal or play for damage and pray you outdo them before they kill you.
Safe is a problem because you can not normally heal outside of combat. Some characters can self heal or heal others, but only in combat. If nnot in comabt, You can eat food for 1 point hp per item or camp and use skills to heal. Other then that. your health when combat ends is the health you have for the next battle. I have played no other game with this concept. Yes, it is risk vs reward and tactics. I would normally enjoy that, but not here.
If you manage to survive missions, you can slowly build up your heros. Armor, weapons, abilities levels  can be upgraded with heirlooms at the shops then gold to pay for said upgrade for the characters. You get the heirlooms as you go through the levels or complete the quests.
Now, you can abandoned a quest/level and keep whatever loot you've found. the problem is the heros gain a large amount of stress. When stress hits 100, you hero generally gains a negative quirk. They may start saying random things, hurt themselves, go berserk and not listen, refuse heals, etc.
You have to decide if the mission is worth the risk of losing a hero you've built up or running and gaining stress.
Stress can be removed. It costs gold. Negative quirks can be removed. It costs gold or a lot of gold if you let the quirk become permanat. Same with diseases.
Sometimes a "stress out" will give a postivie quirk but that is very very rare in my playthroughs.
I haven't played the game very long. I don't deny that. It just pisses me off so much the game isn't fun anymore.

Let's get a few things straight before I begin.
1st: Realm of the Mad God is a free to play. You do not have to pay, in order to find out if you really enjoy the game or not. So dont hesitate to download this very small, low storage game.
2nd: If you aren't one who enjoys any of the following concepts: "Multiplayer, Team Effort, Dungeon Crawler, Minimalized Graphics, Classes, Permadeath, In-Game Economy and Trade Systems, In-Game Purchases...etc" then you might as well back the hell out.
3rd: In-Game Purchases aren't necessary to fit the games bill. You don't need to throw any amount of currency in, to get the best experience this game has to offer.
Realm of the Mad God has been with us for several years, though it may not have been on Steam for that long. We could find it as an online game, playable through certain browsers and flash plug-ins. Just recently, about a year and a half ago, coming up to two years ago, this game was released on Steam.
With its pixelated graphics, good ratings, and thorough trailers I thought I might as well give it a shot.
Gameplay Experience: Not once was I disappointed in the games efforts to give me the best enviroment for gameplay. I never ran into a bug, or glitch for that matter. Its cross-platform multiplayer experience gave me several oppurtunites to meet friends, and join in many events.
Permadeath: This game IS set-up with a permadeath system. Though it is hard to believe so, your account does gain perks with every death. The longer you survive with each character or class, and the more bosses you kill, the more "Fame" you obtain. With this fame, you can purchase different items, or unlock separate classes. So all-in-all, Permadeath isn't all too bad.
Graphics: Now, let's talk about these graphics. Many players like their graphics smooth, or realistic. You need to expect several visible PIXELS before actually getting into the game. The whole game is made from pixels. From its font, to the spells you cast, everything is made of pixels. Don't get sassy with me in saying everything is made of pixels, everywhere. You get what I'm trying to say. These pixels make the game unique, and provide smooth, not-so-hard-to-run gameplay.
Multiplayer: The whole game is multiplayer. There is no singleplayer, but you can choose to level up and defeat bosses on your own, which does get harder as your character progresses, require the help of others. Everywhere you go, there will be somewhere nearby. But this isnt always a bad thing, as you can chat with them, teleport to them, trade with them, follow them, and several other actvities.
I seem to have covered the main areas of complaint, and overall feel of the game. I hope this review helped in aiding in your decision.

I bought it because of the overwhelmingly positive reviews on Steam. Plus I saw the Bayonetta 2 review and thought that looked good. While the gameplay is OK for combat generally, the boss battles are beyond stupid and way too plentiful though. The story is horrendously bad. And it doesn't end (at least it feels that way). Near the end, the bad guy monologuing was absurd, and terribly long.
I am all for divorcing myself from reality to a decent degree, but this game goes too far. The stroy is a disjointed nightmare. I mean you can somewhat follow it, but it is far too cliche', and nonsensical. Remember the guy you just killed? Well he is back, and none the worse for wear. Remember all the bosses you killed? Well, they are all back, and in one piece.
And they throw stupid new ideas at you near the end of the game, like: I never did it before, but all of a sudden I am steering a bullit. Also, there are terribly long sections where you are riding a motorcycle, or a missle, that just feels like an unnecessary minigame to steer and shoot on a rail. On the ground: Oh, you can turn into a raven. Cool. But we ( the Devs) do not want you going that way so here is a nice invisible wall for you. And in between combat many times, they abuse the cliche' bridge falling to pieces as you run across it gag.
I wanted to like it. I tried to like it. And while it has some good combat (about 20% of the game is good), it has frustrating and illogical (according to the rest of what you learned in the game) fixed camera boss battles (20%). The walking and looking around is OK, but you are fighting the camera all the time. Another 30-40% is suffering through the story and the terrible motorcycle missle sequences.
I changed my review to recommend with the qualifier of skipping the story.
Edit: I have been playing through the battles again, and skipping the terrible cutscenes, and the combat is fun and deep, and takes time and practice to get it right. I give the combat of general villians, and minibosses a thumbs up. Still do not like the major bosses but they are tolerable. And I still absolutely hate the motorcycle, missle sections and the entire story. I can't skip the cutscenes fast enough.

Starbound has a great concept: copy "Terraria" but do it in space, with multiple character races plus more of a story. Unfortunately, we're now at around 4 1/2 months without a stable update. I expect there eventually will be a fairly complete version of the game, and it'll probably be good, but stay away until that happens. I mistakenly convinced three of my friends to chip in for a 4-pack of the game because of the devs' promise of a "Beta" in "2013". That promise turned out to mean "a very incomplete alpha in 2013 December, followed by getting so wrapped up in moving offices to England that we go from stable updates, to rare unstable updates, to nightly builds that we literally said might blow up your computer and kill your dog". What's really annoying is that the company has devoted repeated effort to advertising other games instead of putting full effort into this one. (Admittedly some of those don't involve the same dev team members, but it's still bad form.)
In short, what you're getting if you buy now is a very incomplete "Terraria" prototype and a vague promise that you'll have a complete game whenever the devs can be bothered to finish it.
2014.12.4: We're now at nearly a year past the first "beta" with no noteworthy stable updates since February. Basic features like quests remain very incomplete even in the nightly builds that are the devs' excuse for not producing a professional quality release (they had millions of dollars of initial funding) in nearly a year.

THE BREAKDOWN:
THE GOOD - I absolutely love this game and think of it as one of my all time favorite turn-based RPGs w/ a hearty Lovecraftian seasoning to make the flavor all the better. The art style is amazing and the sound design and narrative are a wonderful backdrop to this oh so twisted, hopeless journey into the darkest of dungeons; a journey you soon won't forget, assuming you can complete it, which leads me into 'The Bad' and why I would have preferred to go with a nuetral review if Steam had that option).
THE BAD (or why I came to hate this game, despite my love for it) - essentially, this is the last quarter of the game, or I should more specifically state the Darkest Dungeon quests. The staggering difference between your team's skillbase and the level of attack damage/damage absorbtion that they possess versus that of the enemies you'll face in the latter portion of the game was so poorly conceived and executed on the part of the developers that it nearly defies all logic and comprehension.
Chance and luck; the probability of getting in crit hits and heals; the percentage of these and other occurrences, etc. have all always been a large part of what make turn-based RPGs so challenging yet fun. Darkest Dungeon, sadly, was apparently not tested or balanced properly so as to allow it to be completed by conventional means (again referring to the latter portion of the game, the first 3/4 or so was fantastic). Regular enemies and bosses alike in the DD quests will dodge so frequently and follow up with attacks vastly more times than your roster of characters will, not to mention the fact that their crit hit chance seems to be boosted far beyond what it should be, which isn't saying too much considering that your painstakingly lv. 6 grinded character(s) will likely get 1 or 2 hitted in no short period of time and if not die outright from those hits, then they'll likely become irrational, fearful, selfish, etc. as they so often do which will further complicate things and possibly inflict upon them a chain of heart attacks until they are finally killed.
I had a wonderful time killing nearly all the bosses and leveling my characters up until trying my hand at the DD quests. From that point forward I had no choice but to make backup saves so that I could have a starting point prior to a battle and then if successful, a save made after the battle (you'll notice that the game will pick up where you left off mid battle or dungeon if you have to exit the game, so it's entirely possible to do this). The final 2 quests (currently, I'm on the final boss) left me no choice but to literally have backup saves for more backup saves for mid battle points and even then it took me nearly 18+ hours just to get through the first 3 DD quests and try my hand at the final one (there are 4 total if you play on Radiant mode).
Knowing what I now know about this game, it is literally a physical impossibility to complete these last quests by conventional means. Love everything there is to love about this game through the first 3/4 or so. After that, and even when making backup saves, prepare to have both your resolve and sanity tested to the breaking point; an ironic mimicry of the anguishing grind and mental state of the heroes throughout this game.

This is one great game by Platinum. Glad them and Sega decided to port it here. Also, this is one nice port with few errors and decent additions.
To describe the combat, it's fast, fluid and hard. Even normal can make quite a few people die a bunch of times before perfecting the combat motions, despite having near infinite dodge. There's a lot of combos to practice from a bunch of weapon and weapon combinations. Your character, the titular Bayonetta can hold 4 guns. One for each limb. There's also a two handed sword and other things. Also, enemies can drop weapons you can use for a limited time. Plus there, other maneuvers like finishers and even a taunt.
Visuals haven't dated much since the initial release, and with higher possible resolutions and other eye candy, it now looks very gorgeous. At higher settings the game may push lower tier computers to their knees but this game in low settings still looks rather nice and doesn't demand that much. Sounds are very good as well and there's English and Japanese voice tracks. As a rarity, the English voice is very nice on this one. The English voice over has as much soul as the Japanese version this time around, so that's a great plus.
In the end, this is a great port for a great game. This is pretty much how ports should be.

When this game was release I was just turning 2, so I never got to play it.
I've played for almost 10 hours so far and loved every second of it, you're always doing something; I haven't experienced any boring sections yet, every section has something to do, enemies to kill, somewhat puzzle-ish scenarios, or an objective you must figure out.
The game gives you information from generic scientist surviors you meet, security personell (which you can also request that they help you fight, although the AI for them is terrible by today's standards, they can prove useful at times) and what seems to a army loudspeaker. Other times you figure it out on your own.
Graphically it's nothing compared to today's standards but Valve has made HD textures, which are on by default. You can also get another out there on the internet although it may not be worth your time. There isn't anything that is going to improve the visuals drastically, but honestly the game is fine without, it's still very playable and it's in no way going to hinder your enjoyment.
Gameplay is enjoyable and satisfying, the simple first person gunplay is great; pick up ammo, shoot, reload and stand behind cover, and reload whenever you can. Shooting alien crabs and those who they have taken over is relativley easy but a lot of fun. Shooting soldiers is a huge amount of fun, and it's where you have to think more about what you are doing and use the more varied weapons you have in your arsenal; they can be simple hand guns, revolvers, machine guns, shot guns, cross bows, grenades, etc.
It's an enjoyable classic game, you shouldn't miss this out in your life.

You'll see quite a few negative reviews, those are mostly filled with mis-placed anger and hyperbole.  Often by dudes who played for barely two handfuls of hours.  I have played for 165 hours at the writing of this review, take that for what it is worth.
Anyways, I will not bother to describe what XCOM 2 is, you likely know or have heard enough about it to either want to check it out it or not.  The question is not what you know of it, but is it good?  The answer is yes, though it is far from a perfect or completely satisfying game too.
Having played XCOM since it was a box filled with floppy disks I was looking forward to XCOM 2 and for the most part I have been happy with the result.  There is enough new stuff and changes that it feels like a new game, but just barely.
The Good
-----------------------
Destructable environment (which has saved my squaddies more than once... and mauled them once ina while)
Story: While the story is a bit of a railroad, the adventure is getting there.  The choices you have to make and sacrifices from those choices are excellent.  An alien raid late game becomes interesting.
Missions:  The timed missions are tough at times (mostly due to environment), most I found to be fairly challenging but not impossible if you use good tactics (over watch is still very much your friend).
The environment:  With a procedurally generated environment maps are a lot less predictable and difficulty can vary wildly as terrainm goals and enemies are not always where you think.  That said sometimes the mission is impossible because of these placements.
Upgrades:  The ability to upgrade weapons with components is cool and makes for some fun choices.  Not every class has the same needs for upgrades which makes most of the gear useable for someone.
Character customization:  With the first DLC, there are lots and lots of options for your soldiers.  That said the initial choice the program makes seems to be less diverse at times.
Modding:  There are a lot of really good mods chunked out and like Civ 5, there is probably something there that will really pique your interest.
The Ok
----------------------
Classes:  I think the classes are just a bit off, there really needed to be one more that was combat focused.  That said there are mods and DLC coming...
Aliens:  The aliens are a good mix and present interesting challenges, that said the developers went with the bullet sponge philosophy rather than more aliens.
Iterative Design:  This is nearly a bad thing, what XCOM is... is not something new.  It is ultimately the same basic game as the last XCOM particularly if you look at the game as a whole and play it through the end game.  The formula works, but it could have been more.  Perhaps DLC will address some of this, but if XCOM 3 is the same way I will call shenanigans.
Difficulty: There have been some harping on this, the game gets very difficult if you aggro more than one squad.  If you take on two alien squads it is a little sticky.  Three squads and you are likely toast.  I have been playing wargames with toy soldiers for a very long time, I know tactics and those tactics are do not be overly agressive and use over watch whenever possible.  So the winning formula is a bit predictable, but timed missions will throw that into the wringer at times which shifts this from bad to ok.
The Bad
------------------------
Cover:  I still dislike that you cannot have a character go prone or kneel like the old XCOM games.  When physical cover is the only modifier that feels like a kind of lazy choice.
Nationalities:  A great mod for this exists, but there should have been more out of the box.   As well, more voice work for languages would have been welcome even were it a couple more per language type (e.g. Chinese, Japanese, Indian, Dutch, etc).  For a AAA title, this is really lacking.
Strategic Game:  The base management feels mostly like an after thought.  There are no real choices to be made as far as what you build.  For example defences, this will not help shoot down an attacking saucer it will help defent you after the aliens raid your ship that has been forced down.  As well some of the tech tree choices are very linear too, though the random enhancements do mitigate this slightly.
Synopsis:
----------------------------------------
The end result is XCOM 2 is very good and bordering on great.  I wish it had been a slightly more different game when you look on the story arch as a whole, but the getting to the end has some new and different choices that mitigate this.  I maybe wanted a little more out of the game, but maybe DLC and mods will (over time) address this.
I picked up XCOM 2 on release day and do not regret it.  If you like this kind of game generally and XCOM specifically this will be a worthwhile addition to your library.

Hours feel like minutes in this top-down 8-bit styled adventure game. This fantastically fun experience of owning a farm, fishing, connecting with the town, fighting through mines, and adventuring harkens back to series like Animal Crossing and Harvest Moon. From the beginning of the game, you are left to your own devices and can choose to focus on whatever you like. However, unlike some other games that offer this, there is not a lack of direction and it is easy to jump from one activity to the next. When you start, managing your farm will be a full-time job. Do not let this discourage you, though, because as you make more money and progress through the game, it will become easier and less time and effort will be required. Whatever you may like, this game will likely have something for you to enjoy.

My First Playthrough:
Week 1 - Reynauld and Dismas successfully escort me to the Hamlet.
Week 7 - Neville's party leaves to scout the Darkest Dungeon. They do not return.
Week 14 - Reynauld strikes down the Necromancer Apprentice in the Ruins.
Week 19 - Crevecoeur bleeds to death while battling Cultists.
Week 29 - Dismas recovers the Ancestor's relics from the Cove.
Week 39 - Gournai's group slays the evil Hag in the Weald.
Week 55 - Griffin and his comrades are killed while defending the Hamlet from Brigands.
Week 73 - Cardonell finds the Ancestor's resting ground in the Darkest Dungeon.
Week 80 - Gournai returns from the Darkest Dungeon after opening the portal.
Week 93 - Reynauld, Dismas, Ide and Erquemboure step into the portal of the Darkest Dungeon.
Week 94 - Only Dismas returns from the darkness to tell his tale...
Darkest Dungeon is one of the best roguelike RPGs available on Steam today. Lead a team of heroes as they explore abandoned ruins, battle vicious monsters and disarm deadly traps. But don't forget that their minds can only take so much before stress drives them into despair and (literal) insanity.
The game has a beautiful hand-drawn art style, a great soundtrack and a narrator that really sets the atmosphere of a Lovecraftian horror film. It definitely doesn't handhold the player for very long as you could have casualties even in the very first "tutorial" level. But despite the initially steep learning curve, the gameplay is very well-polished and painstakingly tuned to keep you on your toes at all times.
Overall, I recommend the game primarily to experienced gamers who are looking for a challenging new dungeon crawler or roguelike. Note that the recently released "Radiant Mode" may also be a good option for gamers who are new to the genre and/or those who would prefer to reduce some of the grind required in the mid-late game.

Half-Life. Holy crap. Half-Life has not only revolutionized the FPS genre, but it is also singlehandedly responsible for Steam's creation/Valve's success, and is the reason that PC is the best gaming platform on the market. When I played this a few years ago, I got stuck on chapter 4 and didn't go back to it. But recently I decided to not let the game win like that and I passed the chapter. What I found past that was the best shooter game I have ever played, a HUGE immersive story that keeps you guessing what will happen next, a variety of levels and puzzles that keep you hooked, and all around a brilliantly crafted and impossible to put down game. There are a few sections I did not like. Chapter 8: On A Rail and Chapter 17: Interloper seemed to drag on, and Chapter 12: Surface Tension has a few bits I did not care for. But don't let that fool you. There is a reason that fans are constantly crying out for Half-Life 3. And that reason is because these are the best damn games you're going to get on Steam.

BUY AT YOUR OWN RISK. After a string of missed promises, mismanagement and spending of the long invested money of both Steam customers and Kickstarter backers, Starbound development is effecitvely dead in the water. There is little to no hope of significant updates in the near future due to the total fracas of bad business decisions made by the developing firm Chucklefish. The details of such events can be found with a few rudimentary searches.
In its current state the game has a very low level of progression or content, you have a small variety of biomes with pre-generated dungeons scattered and recycled through them, arbitrary grinding walls that simulate game progression but are really just time sinks to give you the illusion of gameplay. There is little to do with the items you collect and few items or avenues to explore in game. Combat is somehow more simplistic and blase then Minecraft or Terraria given SNES style AI of walk towards the player and attack and mininmal sprite based hit detection. As far as matching to the promised scope of the game the current iteration is no where close and has little hope of ever reaching there. It is doubtful it will ever lose its "Early Access" moniker.
You are better off purchasing Terraria or some other sandbox game as this project has unfortunately fell victim to a classic case of business failiure, I can only stress my empathy for those who unlike a traditional investment model, must watch their money be wasted. I hope any dissatisfied customers find proper avenues to retain their 15$ or more after such a mess caused by incompetence and marketing hype.

Ok, I'll try to be serious with this one.
Xcom2 is the sequel to Xcom: Enemy Unknown and assumes that humanity lost the war against the aliens. Most people live in Alien-run cities, under the constant vigilance of ADVENT, the Alien Peacekeeping force. Your job is to lead the remmants of the Xcom project against the Alien Overlords via tactical strike missions, which yield rewards like new personel, additional resources or minor buffs. Soon enough, the stage is set as the Aliens commence the AVATAR project (which does not filter the world in a red and blue hue, unfortunately). It's a race against the clock as you can't stop their progress, only delay it.
Xcom2 brings back the famous (or infamous, depending on your views of it) RNG-based accuracy system, and further expands on it with new game mechanics like hacking (which can yield rewards, complete objectives or increase the mission difficulty, depending on the RNG). It also introduces a Dodge mechanic, meaning that units with a high Dodge stat have a chance to cut incoming damage by half.
Now as for how well these mechanics mesh into the gameplay, Xcom's RNG-based accuracy offers you a chance to increase your odds of a successful shot with various abilities and items, for example, scopes, Holo-targeting, height advantage and others, meaning that it's possible to ensure that you never miss your target. Unfortunately with the hacking mechanic, you are completely reliant on RNG, even after you research better gear, as the hacking protocols for more powerful enemies are, naturally, more difficult. A specialised ammo can help lower their defenses, but for the most part, it's all down to how the RNG decides to play. Fortunately, the game can be complete without ever using this mechanic, barring objective hacking which can never fail, so you aren't forced to subject yourself to it.
Now the Dodge mechanic, on the other hand, adds another layer of frustration to the game, as perfect positioning and flanking angles can result in an otherwise dead enemy to live by reducing incoming damage. This is especially frustrating when there are multiple threats with the ability to dodge. Explosive damage from grenades is undodgeable, but this forces the player to rely heavily on grenades, often dictating the squad you will field beforehand, rather than allowing the player the freedom to experiment with different items and units.
Grenades themselves are a tremendous asset in this game, as opposed to the first, as they can destroy the environment and relieve enemies of their cover.  They can also create new pathes to priority objectives, useful when the objective is in a building. They shred armor and deal unavoidable damage and cannot miss, unlike rockets in Xcom: EU. However, as great as grenades are, unfortunately, their reliability makes them a must in a squad as opposed to a luxury, because why rely on RNG when you can guarantee damage? Nobody, in a practical sense, would choose RNG. And Xcom punishes those who can't make practical decisions, further cementing their place in the game as the go-to weapon of choice. There are better weapons, to be sure, but the grenade's reliability gives it the edge for best weapon in the game.
Sightlines in this game seem to perform worse than before, often resulting in your support characters activating a pod while the majority of your squad is already out of moves. It's so bad that a unit standing directly next to another with vision might NOT have vision of the same enemy. Enemies will often spot you directly through walls as well, like they all have Xray vision. There are mods to help deal with this massive oversight (heh), but the fact that this made it into the final product is a real shame.
The game also has its share of bugs and errors, crashes are still common, though luckily, autosave is turned on by default, so if you're like me and don't save until you're done playing, you don't have to worry about your progress.
Nitpicking:
This is just my personal opinion on certain game mechanics that shouldn't be present but don't adversely affect the game.
1. Central Officer Bradford acts as your military advisor, and unfortunately, has gotten much more vocal since EU. Even when you turn off Beginner VO, he often repeats the same advice multiple times during a mission, which can take its toll on your patience, especially if a mission is going poorly (the last thing anybody needs after missing 3 90% shots is to be nagged at). Basically Bradford is Navi from LoZ:OoT but with better chest hair (let's see who's done their research).
2. Pacing: Despite the sense of urgency implemented by the AVATAR project, the game itself feels slow, slower than EU which had no timetable. There are far too many camera swings (what is with Firaxis and cameras?), pauses in gameplay to hover over something for the sake of dialogue, and the slowmo overwatch shots, which can result in a bug where the slowmo plays for the entirety of the animation, rather than just the shot. It makes the game at times feel tedious and slow, the opposite of how a quick Guerilla Op should feel.
Despite everything, however, I still recommend this game. The modding community is pretty great, and the feeling of pulling off a flawless mission just never gets old. The game may be a little rough around the edges, but it's still a great (albeit frustrating) experience.

A decent enough, if not buggy, game that has a Fallout paintjob. Too bad it's a Bethesda game that's only "decent". If this game was anything other than Fallout, I'm certain people would be a bit more forgiving towards it. But as it stands, it's a run-of-the-mill shooter with some RPG elements and tons of crafting.
The combat has been greatly improved from the earlier entries in the franchise, and that is a huge plus. You don't need to rely on VATS to play the game well and effectively as long as you're not playing with a steering wheel. The weapons look and feel alright, but nothing about them is truly stellar. The sound effects are fairly wimpy, and on higher difficulties the enemies have a tendency to shrug off an alarming amount of bullets without perks and upgrades.
Speaking of perks and upgrades, those are really the only RPG elements you'll find in this thing. No skills, no meaningful speech options, only 4 speech options at all times, regardless if that makes sense or not, and extremely linear weapon upgrades dumb down the series. Without skills, perks have to do all the heavy lifting and dirty work (do 20% extra damage with X weapon type ehmergerd) and rarely do anything actually interesting. You need perks to lockpick and hack, you need perks to craft, you need perks to do damage, to heal, to carry more. You need all those perks because they are objectively the best available and necessary if you want to remain competetive with the NPCs.
Upgrades are also extremely linear. I bought into Todd's little "we have hundreds of weapons" lie and was disappointed beyond belief. What he meant is that there's like a dozen weapons and all of them have an X amount of linear upgrades. It's not about "customizing" the weapon or "making it yours". It's about do you want to do 10 damage or 15 damage, or do you want to be more accurate or not, or do you want more ammo in a mag or not. When you get your highest tier crafting perks, there is no choice or options. You always want the upgrades with the biggest numbers. Same thing with upgrading power armor.
The story is absolute garbage, your character is a predetermined one, there is next to no roleplaying to be done, you can't be anything but concerned goody-two-shoes parent. There's no karma, no faction reputation, no nothing. The "evil" acts you can do is mostly limited to saying "screw you pay me" or shooting people in the face. That's not really roleplaying.
So, what is there in this game that's worth it? Well, it looks pretty when the textures load properly, and maybe when you get some mods. It plays okay whenever you're not bogged down in bugs. The game is a love letter to loot w-h-o-r-e-s like myself who want to take everything that isn't bolted down with them. Building settlements is quite fun, if not ultimately pointless and finnicky.
The game is also riddled with bugs, some of which aren't fixed without community patches or the DLCs. My most recent playthrough of the game was stopped by a bug that was somehow related to memory or save game size issues, which caused the game to freeze every few seconds and on saves, making the whole affair completely unplayable beyond that point. This problem has not occoured over at my friend's place, who has all the DLCs installed and an equal number of mods to what I had.
Speaking of mods, the mods really do make the game more enjoyable, as is the case with any Bethsoft title. That is, when you're not told "screw you pay me" when you want a mod.
If you like either farming, 2d games, a relaxing game give this a try, you won't regret it.

Ok, I'll try to be serious with this one.
Xcom2 is the sequel to Xcom: Enemy Unknown and assumes that humanity lost the war against the aliens. Most people live in Alien-run cities, under the constant vigilance of ADVENT, the Alien Peacekeeping force. Your job is to lead the remmants of the Xcom project against the Alien Overlords via tactical strike missions, which yield rewards like new personel, additional resources or minor buffs. Soon enough, the stage is set as the Aliens commence the AVATAR project (which does not filter the world in a red and blue hue, unfortunately). It's a race against the clock as you can't stop their progress, only delay it.
Xcom2 brings back the famous (or infamous, depending on your views of it) RNG-based accuracy system, and further expands on it with new game mechanics like hacking (which can yield rewards, complete objectives or increase the mission difficulty, depending on the RNG). It also introduces a Dodge mechanic, meaning that units with a high Dodge stat have a chance to cut incoming damage by half.
Now as for how well these mechanics mesh into the gameplay, Xcom's RNG-based accuracy offers you a chance to increase your odds of a successful shot with various abilities and items, for example, scopes, Holo-targeting, height advantage and others, meaning that it's possible to ensure that you never miss your target. Unfortunately with the hacking mechanic, you are completely reliant on RNG, even after you research better gear, as the hacking protocols for more powerful enemies are, naturally, more difficult. A specialised ammo can help lower their defenses, but for the most part, it's all down to how the RNG decides to play. Fortunately, the game can be complete without ever using this mechanic, barring objective hacking which can never fail, so you aren't forced to subject yourself to it.
Now the Dodge mechanic, on the other hand, adds another layer of frustration to the game, as perfect positioning and flanking angles can result in an otherwise dead enemy to live by reducing incoming damage. This is especially frustrating when there are multiple threats with the ability to dodge. Explosive damage from grenades is undodgeable, but this forces the player to rely heavily on grenades, often dictating the squad you will field beforehand, rather than allowing the player the freedom to experiment with different items and units.
Grenades themselves are a tremendous asset in this game, as opposed to the first, as they can destroy the environment and relieve enemies of their cover.  They can also create new pathes to priority objectives, useful when the objective is in a building. They shred armor and deal unavoidable damage and cannot miss, unlike rockets in Xcom: EU. However, as great as grenades are, unfortunately, their reliability makes them a must in a squad as opposed to a luxury, because why rely on RNG when you can guarantee damage? Nobody, in a practical sense, would choose RNG. And Xcom punishes those who can't make practical decisions, further cementing their place in the game as the go-to weapon of choice. There are better weapons, to be sure, but the grenade's reliability gives it the edge for best weapon in the game.
Sightlines in this game seem to perform worse than before, often resulting in your support characters activating a pod while the majority of your squad is already out of moves. It's so bad that a unit standing directly next to another with vision might NOT have vision of the same enemy. Enemies will often spot you directly through walls as well, like they all have Xray vision. There are mods to help deal with this massive oversight (heh), but the fact that this made it into the final product is a real shame.
The game also has its share of bugs and errors, crashes are still common, though luckily, autosave is turned on by default, so if you're like me and don't save until you're done playing, you don't have to worry about your progress.
Nitpicking:
This is just my personal opinion on certain game mechanics that shouldn't be present but don't adversely affect the game.
1. Central Officer Bradford acts as your military advisor, and unfortunately, has gotten much more vocal since EU. Even when you turn off Beginner VO, he often repeats the same advice multiple times during a mission, which can take its toll on your patience, especially if a mission is going poorly (the last thing anybody needs after missing 3 90% shots is to be nagged at). Basically Bradford is Navi from LoZ:OoT but with better chest hair (let's see who's done their research).
2. Pacing: Despite the sense of urgency implemented by the AVATAR project, the game itself feels slow, slower than EU which had no timetable. There are far too many camera swings (what is with Firaxis and cameras?), pauses in gameplay to hover over something for the sake of dialogue, and the slowmo overwatch shots, which can result in a bug where the slowmo plays for the entirety of the animation, rather than just the shot. It makes the game at times feel tedious and slow, the opposite of how a quick Guerilla Op should feel.
Despite everything, however, I still recommend this game. The modding community is pretty great, and the feeling of pulling off a flawless mission just never gets old. The game may be a little rough around the edges, but it's still a great (albeit frustrating) experience.

This game is remarkably well polished for an Alpha, the game is rather good looking, well balanced and huge fun! The core of the game is simple to understand – capture the bases to upgrade your ships and open jump points to the opponents base.  If you ever played a Tabletop naval or space war-game the fleet tactics required will feel familiar however as the captain of just one ship its teamwork that wins games.
The tactical options are really good and the ships feel right to fly.  The really big ones turn and move at a nice stately pace packing good hull strength and effective weaponry. While smaller ships generally really shift and manoeuvre well. Making them harder to hit and more able to use the asteroids as cover.
All ships have some unique features that shift the tactics greatly from ship to ship. The Carrier for example has some potent close range beams, good hull and of course 3 wings to command. Used right these wings can get some good flanking damage or damage a target hiding in the rocks -Making it a ship that can effectively harass multiple opponents from relative safety.  While my favourites of the big ships have more powerful weaponry and better hulls both have issues. The Destroyer has long range deadly weapons which awful accuracy on the move and serious firing arch restrictions – Optimal is a broadside the shots also have a serious flight time making aiming a challenge particularly on the a small ship that knows you are there.  The Leviathan moves slower while its guns are firing and can’t track targets as quickly as the carrier, and if you stop shooting you then have a fairly long cool down before the guns can be activated again. The leviathan also has a tactically interesting skill – it can drop jump points so the team can jump straight to it. However its defenceless while creating the point, and the jump point does not last very long. So it takes good communication and tactics to make the most of this skill.
With so many ships already in the game I won’t go on further on them all except to say that all ships have their uses in game. I personally very much enjoy playing the Corvette – might not get any kills in the whole game, but its fast and can put out a reasonable amount of damage for a support craft that specialises in disabling the opponent and healing allies.  A good Corvette can really boost a team, keeping the biggest ships at the frontlines longer.
There are of course some issues in the game. But so far I have not come across a game breaking one. And the quality of game is such that if it had a few more maps (perhaps for smaller and bigger teams?) you could call the game finished.

XCOM: EU is like space chess.
XCOM 2 is like space tabletop wargaming.
XCOM: EU is well-balanced, polished to a mirror shine, and stands the test of time thanks to its visual cohesiveness and the depth of its tactical gameplay, where aliens' skills have been carefully balanced against XCOM's skills, and, while situations can occasionally get dire at higher difficulties, the overall game is challenging but fair, feeling like a battle between nonsymmetric equals.
XCOM 2 is an unbalanced, unpolished, visual cluster-♥♥♥♥, where the abilities are made up and the stats don't matter. A lot of new abilities feel like they were thrown in because they sounded cool, but they all are either tactically inferior to the game's previously established options (Psi-reanimation is dumb), or so overpowered that the first turn you see the unit you focus fire their owners into oblivion (Shieldbearers, Gatekeepers, Sectopods, etc.). The randomized maps just make each area completely non-distinctive (seen one ugly desert resistance haven, seen them all), and overall, gameplay consists of ambushing and killing off pods on the turn you contact them, over and over again. The increased ability diversity, the increased amount of item abilities, all of these theoretical contributors to "tactical flexibility" just end up contributing to the feeling that this is a clunky, unbalanced mess of a game, the product of dozens of conflicting codexes as opposed to XCOM: EU, which felt like it had been sanded down from a clunky forebear to a smooth, incredibly enjoyable strategy game.
That being said... I like it a lot.
Call me a sucker, but I have fun dressing up my troops, installing mods to screw with the balancing even further, liberally blowing up buildings, experimenting with more radical soldier builds, and just generally loosening up a lot more than I did with XCOM: EU. It's a fun game, as long as you don't think about it too much, which makes it a game I love playing and hate watching, unlike XCOM: EU, which I'll admit is a game I love watching much more than I love playing. Watching XCOM 2 makes me see the balancing issues, it annoys me that the game isn't punishing bad play, but then playing it makes me happy that my Imperial Guard themed troop didn't get a plasma bolt to the face this turn, removing the rage-quitting element that was omnipresent in my time with XCOM: EU and making for a much more enjoyable Friday night experience.
It's the strategic equivalent of a giant bag of Cheetohs, in comparison to the filet mignon of XCOM: EU. There will always be a place for both, and as easy as it is for some to say XCOM 2 is inferior, I find myself crawling back to it for my fix every weekend.
Is it worth sixty bucks? Depends on your income bracket, but probably not.
Is it worth thirty bucks? Probably, that's what I got it for, and I'm not the slightest bit salty about the purchase...

TLDR: Paid mod system broke free mods altogether. Nuff Said. That being said, details below.
I used to really enjoy this game. It is pretty decent as a standalone game. However, it was GREAT with mods. Yesterday or so a new update went out that enabled Bethesda's paid mods system, Creation Club. It sounds pretty decent and all, as it allows modders to essentially freelance to release mods for a price. As long as it wasn't stepping on the toes of the modding comunity that was fine. Unfortunately, this is not how it works. CC does a few things that entirely breaks free modding for all of us. First, it resets the load order of mods. This is a big problem as carefully tunes load orders are ESSENTIAL for funtional modpacks. Second, some of the paid mods seem to be fundamentally incompatible with the free mods. Finally, it breaks support for F4SE, which is a script extender that allows most of the more complex mods to function. Another big issue, is that even if you buy NONE of the paid mods, CC requires your machine to download the entire set of paid mod data files. Right now, at inception it is 2+ GB. Imagine what that will be in a years time? I cannot support the path that Bethesda has taken in this regard. I will be rolling back my game version, backing up a clean copy, disabling updates, and washing my hands of this utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I can only hope that this does not kill the modding comunity. Remeber Bethesda, many of us bought your games knowing that we could mod your lackluster, outdated games to make them kickass adventures. Your games simply are not that good b themselves. They are, however, decent modding platforms. Please reconsider your actions. I will update this review if the situation changes.

updated as of 20170731 - finally uninstalling this:
tl;dr: not recommended. Grey Havens finally provided some new content on the levels, but the major flaw here is the grindfest and bad economy.
Gameplay is fun at start but gets repetitive - this itself is not that bad but the system punishes casual players too much. Late game (including PvP) requires massive grinding and/or microtransactions.
500+ hours were back in 2011 days where it was fun and I had friends to play with. Got busy eventually and quitted.
Coming back in 2017, the changes since 6 years are basically these:
- forging (additional crafting materials required to level up gears: very bad design that forces everyone to grind for it; lots of feedbacks from players in forum to improve it but to no avail)
- crafting/alchemy (additional crafting material required to craft gears: also bad but not as grindy; most likely a way to stop people from mass crafting to get the UVs they want, making it even more grindy overall to keep up with game)
- battle sprites (companion with some helpful skills - this is okay)
PvP
- P2W oriented - you need to have really high end gears with UVs of (very) high bonus to excel at it (either dumping loads of cash or grind 24/7 for months.
- connectivity issues - very bad latency for everyone except those in US because there are only 2 servers: US / EU, where pvp is dead in the latter. Hoping there'd ever be an asian server is also not very viable because there's not enough player base to get the PvP started (not a lot of people want to get their♥♥♥♥♥kicked by people with epic gears).
- There is option to play in the lower tiers i.e. beginners' gears, but not very popular; I reckon the community mostly want to be able to use their shinies.
* UV = unique variants, bonus stats applicable to your equipment at different levels (low to very high bonuses); for the riches
