*Note, I wont be putting anything of the story in here, but I will have points on certain aspects of the game that some people may want to reveal themselves.  Also might be a bit lengthly so if you prefer just skip to the bottom.
Darkest Dungeon is a roguelike, turn based RPG game that is based in a lovecraftian inspired, gothic victorian.  The basic premis of the game is that your ancestor was the owner of a vast estate, but after hearing rumour of ancient eldritch powers being hidden beneath the manor, he sought out to uncover this unfathomable and ancient secret.  To say the least, this goes poorly, and it is up to you to send waves of heroes into the corrupted and twisted regions to strike back against the evil that has claimed your family's home.
Now onto the game itself.  Darkest Dungeon overall is, in my opinion, a game that reflects the idea that no matter how much you plan, failure is always an option.  The game itself is heavily based off RNG, much like games such as XCOM, except in this it seems to reflect moreso.  Curios laid across the map, randomized traps and monster spawns, all of which can cause a make or break in any expedition.  The main highlight of the game though is stress, which is gained from characters interacting with certain objects, being struck by certain enemy abilities, recieving critical hits, or even exploring a dungeon.  This will eventually cause your heroes resolve to be tested and will either cause a positive or negative affliction.  The effects of these varies, but naturally negative afflictions are extremely hampering on the party while positives are a boon.  Stress is then recovered by killing enemies, landing critical blows, or healed at the tavern/church using stress healing.  Another aspect of the game is light, something that works on two extremes.  When above 75 light, your party gains an increased chance to surprise enemies and scout the dungeon,  The lower the light level goes, the more your heroes will become stressed.  However, when the light level drops, loot becomes far more exceeding and criticals become much more prominent.  But this applies to enemies as well, so it is a large gamble whether you chose to fight in darkness or in light.
The heroes in Darkest Dungeon are the main aspect of the game, however.  These are the individuals you will send on each expedition, ranging in a wide array of abilities on functions.  The classes are Arbalest, Bounty Hunter, Crusader, Grave Robber, Hellion, Highwayman, Houndmaster, Jester, Leper, Man-at-Arms, Occultist, Plague Doctor, and finally Vestal.  Each of these classes function very differently, and often will require experimenting to find which classes work best with which.  As you progress through the floors on each dungeon, heroes will become either lifted or burderned by quirks.  Things like doing more damage in bright light or becoming obsessed with killing, all things that will either be a boon or bane to them in expeditions to come.  Heroes are also upgraded using the guild and armoursmith, improving skills as well as their weapons and armour is essential to progressing.  That being said, I will move on to my final point, the dungeons themselves.
Currently there are five areas you can explore;  The Warrens, Weald, Ruins, Cove, and the Darkest Dungeon.  All of these locations share some common enemies, however vary in every other regard.  Each contain their own set of traps, interactable objects, and enemies, all with their own abilities.  Therefore its worth note that some party builds may work in certain areas better than others, and is something often to consider.  Most importantly with these areas are the bosses, each varies as much as the enemies but will put a much more difficult fight.  Every boss has their own set of abilities like every other enemy, and can each inflict havoc in their own way.  As you fight through each area, missions will become harder, and heroes of higher level cannot do dungeons beneath them.  What this means is that heroes of resolve level 3 cannot do dungeons that resolve level 0-2 heroes can, same with Resolve level 5 heroes not able to do 3.  This is something that must be considered, as you must be able to progress heroes while also being able to handle the lower level dungeons.
As I said earlier, Darkest Dungeon is a game that is heavily relies on RNG, and this means that its not a matter of if you will lose, but when.  Heroes will die, expeditions will fail, and sometimes individuals will have to be disbanded.  There will be times when heroes will miss every strike, and enemies hit with critical blows frequently.  This is, at its core, what Darkest Dungeon is.  It is a game which holds you and the enemies on the same board, and while the enemy or you may have the advantage, a single blow can change the outcome entirely.  But it isnt impossible, and while the game can certainly give you a much harder time, it is making the best of a bad situation.  So expect to fall, pick yourself up, and keep cracking at it.  There may be no game winning formula, at least in my experience, but learning through experience will eventually allow you to push on.
TL;DR To sum up, Darkest Dungeon is a game that doesnt hold punches, but it does so in a way that you may still trudge forward. The array of heroes and their own unique abilities makes expeditions something like an art, finding the perfect fit to smash aside enemies. It is also holds a very unique aura and style that makes it stand out on its own, and even with its flaws, still makes it a game that I will reccomend.

Dark souls is one of the most rewarding games i have ever played, the feeling when you kill a boss, is the greatest, and thats the point.
The difficulty was never in mind when Hidetaka Miyazaki designed dark souls, it was just about overcoming your challenges and get better, everyone fails at their 1 attempt, 2 attempt, 3 attempt...40 attempt, and thats how dark souls is, just like any other thing in life, drawing, math, football, or just being artist maybe, after a while things start to get easier and easier, and you start to become more comfortable with yourself, thats exact how dark souls work. And thats how more games should be. Im not saying every game should be like that, of couse we need a variety of how games are. And im not saying that games should be more souls-like.
The gameplay is great, the combat is great, the camera can be a little weird sometimes and you can end up fighting that more than your enemies, so i recommend not to only rely on it, but dont worry most of the time its great.
The story are just like any other souls game, you dont understand anything so you go to youtube too find explanations, but thats what i like about dark souls games. They drop you down in this dark grim world, with not much of an explanation who you are fighting, where you are, who anyone are, and more, of course you can try to find it out yourself if u have the time.
The atmosphere is great every place you go, it gives you the feeling that this is not your normal fantasy story, this is a corrupted world with no hero, only one they call the choosen undead or champion of ash, who has existed many times, and can be anyone.
There are much more to be said about dark souls 3, the weapons, the combat, how you level up your character, and more.
Of course no games are perfect. The bonfires can be a little too close sometimes, the graphics are not the greatest, i still think the pc port could have been better, and more smaller problems.

BUY AT YOUR OWN RISK. After a string of missed promises, mismanagement and spending of the long invested money of both Steam customers and Kickstarter backers, Starbound development is effecitvely dead in the water. There is little to no hope of significant updates in the near future due to the total fracas of bad business decisions made by the developing firm Chucklefish. The details of such events can be found with a few rudimentary searches.
In its current state the game has a very low level of progression or content, you have a small variety of biomes with pre-generated dungeons scattered and recycled through them, arbitrary grinding walls that simulate game progression but are really just time sinks to give you the illusion of gameplay. There is little to do with the items you collect and few items or avenues to explore in game. Combat is somehow more simplistic and blase then Minecraft or Terraria given SNES style AI of walk towards the player and attack and mininmal sprite based hit detection. As far as matching to the promised scope of the game the current iteration is no where close and has little hope of ever reaching there. It is doubtful it will ever lose its "Early Access" moniker.
You are better off purchasing Terraria or some other sandbox game as this project has unfortunately fell victim to a classic case of business failiure, I can only stress my empathy for those who unlike a traditional investment model, must watch their money be wasted. I hope any dissatisfied customers find proper avenues to retain their 15$ or more after such a mess caused by incompetence and marketing hype.

They should call this Age of Empires Not. I've always liked Microsoft Games Division because they made quality games. I've been an AoE player as long as I can remember, but this is not AoE. Here's why.
Someone in a meeting during the development of this game, who has obviously never played the game,  must have raised their hand and said these 10 Things;
1. Hey, you know that scenario creator thing? No one really uses that, and the ones that do really don't like it being so easy to use. So let's make one that's much harder to use.
2. Let's don't let them save game when testing a scenario so it can be played as a game later. No one does that.
3. And those random maps? Ah, you know they don't use that so let's take that out too.
4. When selecting an AI, instead of just selecting one for the computer, let's make them also place objects in the game to make it actually work.
5. And here's something really fun to them. When they create a scenario and choose human for player 1, computer for all the other empires, and select AI's for the computer players, here comes the fun part; When they go to play the scenario, we'll switch them from player 1 to another player instead. They'll find that really funny!
6. And you know those formations that you could use in older versions of AoE? I don't think anyone uses that. Let's remove that.
7. Patrols? Why would they want their troops to patrol? Nah. Take that out too.
8. And you know those towers? People build way too many of them. No one needs more than 7, so let's put a limit on them. Even if one player gathers more resources, they shouldn't be allowed to build unlimited towers. No one should ever build more than 7 in my opinion and people should play it the way I would play it, not just any way they want to.
9. Same with Ships. They shouldn't build so many, so let's limit that too.
10. Oh and this one is real important. Players used to have the ability to place waypoints from their barracks, stables, etc. at an enemy location and fill the queue with 15 troops from each one and if it was more than the population limit, they wouldn't be made until the pop fell below the limit. Instead, in the new AoE, let's not let them schedule those troops in advance. If they want reinforcements, make them go back and do that during the attack so the other player gets a break.
Those aren't all of the problems with the new AoE compared to the excellent older AoE versions, so other people who never played the game must have also raised their hands too.

Honestly I thought Enemy Unknown was a 10/10, so I guess that makes this an 11/10.

For early access, this is a great game. If you are even slightly interested in spaceship fighting games, get this.
Pros:
Great graphics
Balanced, Team based, Moba type matches
Good number of ships for such an early game
Constant updates with new balancing and content
Cons:
matchmaking is still haphazard
player base is still small (will continue to grow)
Lots of DPS ships, could use a few more Support types (hopefully added in future updates)
Difficult learning curve (although some actually like this struggle)
Only one map and match type (for now)

In a nutshell this game follows similiar rules to the likes of World of Tanks, Star Conflict and Warthunder etc.  The main difference being that its set in space with 6 degrees of freedom and you fly bloody huge capital ships!
Unlike the previously mentioned games Fractured Space has done a great job of making each ship unique with totally different weapons and special abilities making every new ship unlocked a new experience and as of now there is no "tier" system whereas a tier 1 ship will get totally outclassed by a tier 10 ship etc.  This means that if you like one of the early ships then you are not forced to stop using it when you unlock other ships which i think is a great idea!
Ontop of this there is no forcing you to play a ship you dont like to unlock the next ship as all experince gained goes to the faction as a whole so in my eyes another big plus to the game.
The current content in the game is pretty small but they add new ships about every month or two and there is enough people playing it to never struggle to find a game and the latency so far during games is fantastic for me personally.
I have always been a fan of huge spacships and the idea of the slow moving monsters firing devestating broadsides at each other from 50km away and if you want that then its here!  If you want smaller, nimble craft then they are also here.  If you want snipers then you have them and if you want sneaky cloaky ships then its all here.
The game is great and is improving constantly and plays just fine on my pretty low end laptop on low to medium graphics and still looks great!
If you are a fan of small team based combat games such as WoT and Warthunder and also a fan of huge spaceships then look no further!

I initially gave this game a negative review. This was purely based on issues with the stability and performance of the game. It took me a few days and more drivers than I can count, but I finally managed to get the game to work without crashing and actually play through it.
While I still have some reservations because of the stability issues, I think that the game, from the game-play point, does deserve a positive review,
If you haven't played the first XCOM or XCOM Enemy Within, I recommend playing Enemy Within first, because that is a great game that is absolutely worth playing, and it will make you appreciate XCOM 2 even more. You don't have to, but you'd be missing out.
The game's story starts 20 years after the events of the original game and under the assumption that XCOM lost the battle and aliens took over. The game is still very much XCOM one knows from the previous installment, but it manages to successfully turn things upside down and make the game fresh, different and exciting. Basic concepts like movement and cover remain the same but things quickly get different beyond that point. There are new weapons, new soldier classes with mostly new abilities, there are a few that are same or similar to XCOM, and of course there are new aliens.
They took basic principals from various XCOM missions and made them new and fresh again. Still, if you have played XCOM you will quickly recognize what missions those were and will appreciate the creativity with which they were changed. I especially like how they remade the “Panic” missions.
Graphics were updated and look great, when they work. UI was revamped and takes some getting used to. It is different, but I don't think that it is better than the one in XCOM which I still prefer.
My favorite thing about XCOM 2 is that the difficulty is much more balanced for the duration of the game than XCOM was. It is a bit harder but if you played the previous XCOM game that is a welcome change. There are a number of missions that have a limited number of turns for winning the mission and that makes the game more interesting. While some players my not like this change, it fits my dash happy play style just right.
To conclude, the game is every bit as enjoyable as the previous installment but it does have stability and performance issues. If you are willing to work through them, you will be rewarded with hours of entertainment.
Very good storytelling throughout the game. Mechanics are a bit dated and some controls are hard to rememeber to use in certain situations. Overall 9/10

I bought this game way back when it first released as EA. The game was a shadow of the game it is now and it still enthralled me. The final product, which continues to be supported with love and care, is unquestionably one of the best games I have ever played. Darkest Dungeon is a game that pulls no punches and sparingly shows mercy, but it's all the more fulfilling for it.
Not unlike XCOM, it utilizes two levels of strategy. The Hamlet, your base of operations, must be upgraded and maintained, as must your ever changing roster of heroes. Preparation is the name of the game. Once a party and mission have been selected, you will be thrown into the dungeon proper. The dungeon crawling mechanics are where this game really shines. Stress and health serve as your two measures of a character's well-being, and both will be strained time and again as your party faces dangers both mundane and otherwordly.
That brings me to the atmosphere. This game paints a haunting picture from start to finish, in no small part thanks to the impeccable voice work of Mr. Wayne June. Red Hook picked the perfect person to narrate their game, and his smooth yet sinister voice strikes the perfect balance of comforting and creepy. The Hamlet itself reflects the state of the world, slowly growing stronger over time, yet never quite reaching a true state of nobility or peace. The sound design further reinforces the Lovecraftian aesthetic, with both dramatic battle themes and haunting noises in the dark.
The art is a beautiful expression of the power of minimalism. Animations utilize a shockingly low number of different frames, but the impact is not at all lessened. Certain enemies embody horror even without detailed movements. The art depicts just what it needs to and is never insufficient.
Darkest Dungeon is a game of loss and grief. Heroes will die. Missions will fail. Some moments will be bleak. But the moments of triumph are all the brighter for penetrating that suffocating darkness. Some may be turned away by the crushing weight of inevitable loss, but this is a game that teaches determination in the face of adversity.
I have purchased this game a second time through PSN, and I look forward to any and all future projects from Red Hook. Any fans of RPGs, dungeon crawlers, crushingly difficult games, Lovecraft, or all of the above owe it to themselves to play this game. I could not recommend this game more highly and I am eagerly awaiting (at the time of writing) the upcoming DLC for this game.
And remember, there can be no bravery... without madness.

Darkest Dungeon is a rare treasure of a game that defies the outwardly unappealing nature of some of its mechanics. I intially passed it up because I am not normally a fan of turn-based games, especially dungeon crawers. I do like roguelikes, though. DD has a level of quality and design that elevates it far above other dungeon crawlers, but is also among the meaner roguelikes out there, and ultimately, the survival of your characters may be left to chance. I somewhat dreaded the prospect of playing a game where my heroes can, and to hear it told, WILL die, though you do have the rare opportunity to ressurect them. I was nonetheless inspired to play it based on what else I'd heard, and I am damn glad I did. It has a truly masterful and haunting score and sound design, a great, heavily-lined art style and my favorite sort of dark fantasy setting, a huge and diverse cast of character classes and a truly awesome narrator in Wayne June, who I discovered is known for his narrations of Lovecraft and Poe, making him perfect for DD's tale of an ancient, eldritch horror unleashed beneath the manor house of a once-prominent nobleman.
You play the role of this nobleman's heir, implored by him to return to their estate, claim the family fortune, and stop the clutching shadows before they can spread. To that end, you can hire a colorful cast of misfit rogues, pilgrims, thieves, outcasts and weirdos to send in to the four major areas surrounding the Hamlet, your base of operations. Parties of four venture into the Ruins, Weald, Warrens or Coves in search of treasure and the horrific bosses. Interestingly, you may enter the final, titular dungeon from the very beginning... but as I understand it, doing so with an inexperienced party will go about as well as you might expect. I'd love to go into greater detail about the classes here but that would greatly pad out the length of this review. They're worth reading up on- a lot of them don't function entirely as you might expect. My personal favorite would have to be the Grave Robber: With her throwing knives and mixed bag of dirty tricks, she can perform well in a variety of parties and from virtually any combat position. Combat is very simple to pick up but mastering it will take many hours, though it uses relatively small damage numbers. There are also a lot of custom classes and other mods out there, and it is also a simple matter to go in to the game's files and manipulate them using a text editor if you so desire, though doing so may seriously disrupt the game balance, if you're a purist about it.
In the finest tradition of works based on or derived from Lovecraftian lore, not only is your party's health in question, but their sanity as well. Everything from losing a bit of torchlight to being forced to endure the mad ravings of an escaped sanitarium patient or worse, facing nameless horrors from the outer spheres, takes a toll of stress on your heroes, as does tripping a trap you didn't know was there, running out of food, or even being around an Abomination when he goes beast mode. If a hero reaches 100 stress, they may become afflicted with dispair, paranoia or other conditions, seriously impacting their combat performance. Sometimes they may instead overcome their stress, becoming Virtuous and gaining bonuses. But if a character reaches 200 stress, they suffer a heart attack and are immediately sent to "Death's Door", as if they had lost their health. A character at Death's Door is not dead, but any further damage suffered may kill them- and you have no way of knowing which hit will do it. For me, Darkest Dungeon has been the sort of game where things will usually go well if you are paying absolute attention and prepare adequately, in particular, there are specific strategies against the bosses that can allow you to avoid the majority of problems, for example, using the Arbalest's flare to clear Marks from your party in the fight against the Swine Prince, thus avoiding a lot of his potential damage. But how quickly the tide may turn... I nearly lost poor Dismas in the opening tutorial and I had an Abomination die in what should have been a simple apprentice Weald scouting run. Never take any battle for granted: Check your party composition, the map, your skills, your trinkets, your provisions, and then check them again.
The deciding factor for me getting the game was a recent major update that added "Radiant Mode", which, while not actually making the game's combat easier, instead shortens what was often described as major mid-to-late game grind, increasing gold and xp gains, and shortening the number of runs necessary to face a dungeon's bosses. I highly advise against going into Darkest Dungeon blind. There is an extensive array of guides available both on steam and elsewhere. Moreso then even other dungeon crawlers, Darkest Dungeon is tactically and strategically complex, and not understanding things like party composition and positioning, skill setups, crowd control and damage over time effects, enemy composition and abilities, proper allocation of provisions, weaknesses and resistances, and prioritizing character and town upgrades will likely lead to party wipes and empty coffers. Your only saving grace is that hiring new heroes is always free, and you get more of them at once by upgrading your Stagecoach.
If you are not as concerned as me about losing people (you monster), Darkest Dungeon is one of the better RPG titles of the past decade or so, and absolutely worth purchasing. Just be advised that it is no cakewalk.

Der Themepark für Masochisten...
...und solche die es werden wollen! Mit dem dritten Ableger der Soulsborn Reihe (Demon´s Souls und Bloodborne ausgeklammert) leitet From Software also den vermeintlichen Abschluss der Trilogie ein. Und verdammt, was für einer! Eine Odyssee die nachhaltig Spuren hinterlassen hat.
Ich bin ein Spätzünder was diese Spielereihe betrifft, der Hypetrain ist komplett an mir vorbei gerast. Ich bin alles andere als ein Casual-Gamer, ein absoluter RPG-Fan und das weit über zwei Jahrzehnte hinweg. Ich hätte mich mit dem heutigen Wissen in den Allerwertesten gebissen wären diese Spiele an mir vorbei gezogen.
Es grenzt schon an eklatanter Selbstherrlichkeit mit der das Entwicklerstudio auf sämtliche modernen Konventionen und Komfortfunktionen der Spieleindustrie pfeift. Tutorial? Ein paar Textnachrichten und der erste Boss werden dir schon zeigen was du kannst und was nicht! Questmarker, Map, hilfsbereite NPC´s? Bwahaha! Vorgekaute Geschichte? Geh zu Bioware! Herrlich, denn nur so kann sich die einzigartige Atmosphäre aufbauen.
Der Weg ist das Ziel, wie eine Motte in ewiger Dunkelheit, auf der Suche nach diesem einen Leuchtfeuer am Horizont. Praise the Sun!
Die Atmosphäre...
...ist ein Strudel aus Melancholie, Verzweiflung, düsterer Schönheit und Hoffnung. Die Spielewelt ist fantastisch gestaltet, wenn auch streckenweise deutlich "heller" als noch in Dark Souls 1, so transportiert sie dennoch das Dark-Fantasy Setting hervorragend. In Verbindung mit dem erstklassigen Soundtrack und der allgegenwärtigen Bedrohung des eigenen Wohles ergibt sich hier ein Sog an Atmosphäre wie ich ihn selten erlebt habe.
Die Grafik...
...ist die wohl offensichtlichste Weiterentwicklung von Dark Soul 3 zu seinen Vorgängern. Kurzum, man darf jetzt auch in visueller Eleganz sterben. Sehen wir davon ab, dass völlig egal wie ich die Regler im Charaktereditor stelle, man seinem Charakter in der Regel freiwillig einen Helm aufsetzt, ist die Spielewelt zu großen Teilen eine Augenweide. Hier lohnt es sich stehen zu bleiben und einfach die Kulisse wirken zu lassen! Allem voran möchte ich aber die Animationen und das allgemeine Design der Bosskämpfe hervorheben. Bis auf wenige Ausnahmen wird man hier in einer opulenten Aufmachung nach Strich und Faden verdroschen, die ihresgleichen sucht. Liebe Spieleentwickler, DAS ist ganz großes Kino!
Der Soundtrack ist...
...wie oben bereits erwähnt, fantastisch gelungen. Er glänzt sehr oft mit Abwesenheit, über weite Strecken ist er einfach nicht existent. Ein Fehler, schlechtes Sounddesign? Oh nein, die Ruhe vor dem Sturm! Keine Sorge, da wo der Sound passende Dramaturgie erzeugt ist er auch anwesend und das so konsequent und vehement dass das Adrenalin in ungeahnte Höhen aufkocht. Die Komposition aus absoluter Stille und bombastischem Orchester ist intelligentes Sounddesign vom Feinsten!
Das Kampfsystem...
...ist der Grundpfeiler der Souls Reihe und wurde (meiner Meinung nach) von Teil zu Teil immer ausgefeilter. Es mündet in Dark Souls 3 in das mit Abstand beste Kampfsystem was ich aus dem Genre der Action-RPG´s kenne, selbst mein bisheriges Steckenpferd Dragon´s Dogma (auch sehr empfehlenswert) sieht hier schlichtweg kein Land. Hat man einmal die Möglichkeiten verstanden die einem das Spiel an die Hand gibt, fühlt sich der Kampf unfassbar intensiv an und der Gegner ist jederzeit kontrollierbar, auch wenn so einige das Gegenteil behaupten, das liegt aber nicht an der Spielmechanik sondern am Spieler selbst.
Das Feedback ist wuchtig, der Impact gegnerischer Treffer sehr gut umgesetzt. Wenn ein haushoher Boss seine meterlange Klinge in meinem Schild vergräbt, dann ist nicht nur die Ausdauer leer und der Charakter benommen, nein man glaubt ohne zu zweifeln das dieser Schlag ungeblockt dem virtuellen Ego die Lichter ausgeblasen hätte. Einziger Wehrmutstropfen bleiben die Caster-Klassen bzw. Skillungen, diese spielen sich aufgrund ihrer Fernkampf-Natur eher langweilig, aber auch das ist nur meine subjektive Meinung.
Der Schwierigkeitsgrad...
...der Souls-Reihe polarisiert, auch der dritte Teil ist hier keine Ausnahme. Ein Phänomen fällt mir immer wieder auf, Spieler die mit dem ersten Teil begannen empfinden den dritten Teil als "leichter", bei Spielern die erst mit dem dritten einstiegen und anschließend den ersten spielten war es genau umgekehrt. Kaum jemand scheint zu erkennen, das hier ganz eindeutig der Lerneffekt reinspielt. Hat man einmal verstanden um was es geht wird das Spiel deutlich "machbarer". Ganz konkret ist es bei mir so gelaufen. Dark Souls 3 war mein Einstieg und ich musste viel erlernen. Es ist heut nicht mehr selbstverständlich dass ein Spiel den Spieler herausfordert. Dark Souls 1 war mein nächster Ritt und er fiel mir spürbar leichter, Dark Souls 2 ist dann noch einmal eine andere Geschichte, dort ist mir regelmäßig das Gesicht eingeschlafen O_o
Aber wie schwer ist es denn nun? Ordentlich, hier wird einem nichts geschenkt! Button-Smasher und Lernresistente werden entgeistert aufgeben. Mangelnde Konzentration und Lernbereitschaft werden hier konsequent bestraft. Ist es deshalb unfair? Nein, zu keinem Zeitpunkt. Beobachten, den eigenen Charakterbuild beherrschen, Movesets der Bosse lernen und entsprechend reagieren, that´s it. Tatsächlich versetzt mich dieses Spiel in die Zeiten progressiver Raids diverser MMORPG´s zurück, man wird mit jedem Versuch besser. Auf ähnlichem Niveau fällt dann auch die Belohnung aus wenn der Hassgegner endlich auf die Bretter geht. Nein nicht in Form von fettem Loot, sondern dem Gefühl tatsächlich was geleistet zu haben, wenn auch "nur" in digitaler Form.
Gibt es eigentlich auch negative Punkte zu berichten?
Öhm...für mich persönlich nicht wirklich, aus objektiver Sicht kann man sich aber wahrscheinlich ein paar Dinge aus den Fingern saugen. Ich könnte mir vorstellen das sich DS1-Veteranen an der etwas schlauchigeren Spielewelt stören, sowie an der nicht mehr so ausgeprägten Vertikalität dieser. Auch ist das Balancing der verschiedenen Kampfschulen manchmal etwas fragwürdig (zumindest im PvE), während man sich beispielsweise an so manchem Boss als Nahkämpfer seiner Wahl die Zähne ausbeist, legt man diesen als hauptberuflicher Pyromane..äh Pyromant schon in den Dreck bevor er sich vorgestellt hat. Dieses dezent überzogene Beispiel diente nur der Veranschaulichung.
Alles in Allem ist mein Fazit klar. Ich schreibe hier über ein Spiel was es ohne Umschweife in meine persönliche Top 5 auf Lebenszeit geschafft hat. Um auf die eingangs erwähnten hinterlassenen Spuren zurück zu kommen: Danke From Soft, ihr habt mir mit dieser Trilogie ein unvergessliches Spielevergnügen bereitet und mich nachhaltig für jedes kommende Action-RPG versaut!

A good game even at the Alpha stage.
It is a MOBA-style game: 5v5 teams, class-based charaacters (or rather, ships), lanes BUT no creeps, no towers and no "jungle".
It uses a twitch/simulator style of control where you move your ship with WASD keys and aim your weapons (and abilities) with your mouse, instead of clicking somewhere on the screen where you want the ship to go.
Instead of travelling with your teams creeps down a lane that is protected by turrets - there are two bases and several capture points in each of two lanes which give your side advantages (in the form of automatic upgrades for your ships) as well as access to the teams base (via capture of the two bases in a lane.
Rather than winning by destroying the enemy defenses and ultimately torching their "ancient" (like in DOTA...or any other fantasy MOBA) you actually have to CAPTURE the enemy base to win. Think of capture points in Team Fortress 2, where a superior number of the enemy will cause the capture point to slowly turn to your side and a superior number of defenders will halt that capture. The capture % does not go down, so once you've made some progress in capturing the enemy base, that progress will not be lost...and the same applies to your base being captured as well.
That's the basic overview of the game "rules".
As for the actual gameplay, as I've mentioned you manually control your ship, and there are various ships fulfilling various roles for the team. Tanks, close range damage dealer, long range damage dealer, interceptor, support/healer, etc. There are only a few ship classes avaliable from the start and the more you use a class the more research points you gain to unlock further variations/classes.
Since its a MOBA, there will be an element of customisation, of course. In Fractured Space, that element is the actual ships Crew, as well as the ships abilities.Various crew members give various attributes to your ship, allowing you to fine tune how you want to play with your chosen ship. You can have more than one crew set and swap them around prior to starting a game. You start with two pre-made crew sets; The Renegades and The Mercenaries. You can change the crew set's names as well as the crew members. To get new/other crew members, you have to purchase them in game.
You can further customise the ship by changing the main weapons it uses as well as its core abilities. These are more "change of flavour" types of customisation rather than outright completely different weapons/abilities making the various classes more predictable in terms of gameplay. For example, you can trade speed for damage on your main cannons, while changing your Flagship's drone swarm to do more slowing rather than damaging to the enemy ship, etc.
The devs play with other players every Thursday and the game is CONSTANTLY updated, meaning that you must give thought to how old a video is if you're looking for gameplay footage. You will notice differences in the UI, new ships, etc depending on how old a video is - so don't watch something that's a year old and expect it to be how the game is at the moment.
As for the game packs, they aren't necessary but are worth while.
My 2c.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
My reply to Holy Athena's comment:
Actually, there are aspects of MOBA in this game, except you have to interpret them more openly than just going "nah, you're wrong, get ♥♥♥♥ed".
The territories that your team's ships have to go through are akin to lanes in other MOBA games - you have to choose a path to go to in engaging your enemy. Simply because you have to warp to them does not divorce them from being similar to lanes.
There are no creeps, as I've obviously said at the very top of my review. One absent aspect does not make Fractured Space a completely original and inspired-by-nothing game.
There is equipment to buy, but it is bought outside of the match, in the main menu instead of having you rush back to base and then spending precious time going through a shopping list. Again, just because it’s done differently does not mean it isn't there at all.
There are no towers to destroy or attack the opposing team, but there are outposts that need to be captured and provide a barrier to the enemy from advancing AS WELL AS gaining resources that ultimately upgrade the entire team's ships on a whole. Again, you fail to make the connection simply because you’re approaching this black on white, as narrow as possible.
Lastly, considering all of the above, it is very much a type of MOBA game and the fact that it does things different actually works in its favour - it is a fresh take on the genre and translates into intense ship-to-ship battles and rewards team coordination immensely.

I've been trying out various MMOs as of recent (I figured I should probably play something a bit less toxic than your popular MOBAs for now). World of Chorecraft - uh- Warcraft, a few of the countless mobile MMOs, even Wizard101 and none of them really rang with me.
That was, until I started playing Spiral Knights.
My original intention of playing this game was to see why everyone made mention of my League main looking like a Spiral Knight. Now, I can't stop playing and I don't want to stop playing anytime soon!
With a pace that doesn't bore you from how easy it is and doesn't work you up from how hard it is (I have enough Dark Souls in my life, thank you), it's actually fun to play this MMO! The graphics are both charming and have aged very well despite how old this game is. The missions aren't all exactly the same (Kill 12 boars... Again) and the rewards are actually satisfying (a flaming sword is always better than potions I never bother to use). Throw in the fact that the community is friendly, everyone gets the same rewards, and there's no need for a class that everyone needs but nobody wants to play (cough, healer, cough) then you get a recipe for the best multiplayer to have ever graced an MMO!
My only regret to this game is that I didn't start playing it six years ago.

At first I thought I wouldn't enjoy it, the game having been released in 1998 and all, but after playing about an hour (the game is aprox. 9 hours long) I realised: this game has truly managed to stand the tests of time and remain an amazing game regardless of its problems.

I initially gave this game a negative review. This was purely based on issues with the stability and performance of the game. It took me a few days and more drivers than I can count, but I finally managed to get the game to work without crashing and actually play through it.
While I still have some reservations because of the stability issues, I think that the game, from the game-play point, does deserve a positive review,
If you haven't played the first XCOM or XCOM Enemy Within, I recommend playing Enemy Within first, because that is a great game that is absolutely worth playing, and it will make you appreciate XCOM 2 even more. You don't have to, but you'd be missing out.
The game's story starts 20 years after the events of the original game and under the assumption that XCOM lost the battle and aliens took over. The game is still very much XCOM one knows from the previous installment, but it manages to successfully turn things upside down and make the game fresh, different and exciting. Basic concepts like movement and cover remain the same but things quickly get different beyond that point. There are new weapons, new soldier classes with mostly new abilities, there are a few that are same or similar to XCOM, and of course there are new aliens.
They took basic principals from various XCOM missions and made them new and fresh again. Still, if you have played XCOM you will quickly recognize what missions those were and will appreciate the creativity with which they were changed. I especially like how they remade the “Panic” missions.
Graphics were updated and look great, when they work. UI was revamped and takes some getting used to. It is different, but I don't think that it is better than the one in XCOM which I still prefer.
My favorite thing about XCOM 2 is that the difficulty is much more balanced for the duration of the game than XCOM was. It is a bit harder but if you played the previous XCOM game that is a welcome change. There are a number of missions that have a limited number of turns for winning the mission and that makes the game more interesting. While some players my not like this change, it fits my dash happy play style just right.
To conclude, the game is every bit as enjoyable as the previous installment but it does have stability and performance issues. If you are willing to work through them, you will be rewarded with hours of entertainment.

Okay, onto the technical aspects of the game..
The level design sucks. The stages are very constrictive, almost claustrophobic. The gameplay sucks. The game is very linear, requiring you to follow specific strategies to advance and you need patience to get through the game with your sanity intact. The game is supposed to have an auto-save feature but if you leave the game before finishing a level, even after it "autosaved", you will always have to restart the level from the beginning, only saving your stats and halos. If you like shoot'em ups like Devil May Cry then you may enjoy this but be prepared for crappy level design and sloppy gameplay and clear your schedule before you resume playing. Don't start a level unless you're prepared to finish it or else you'll be doing it over again from the beginning.

Promises don't mean anything.
Announced in 2012, Beta released in 2013. Officially claimed to be "fully released" by 2013, this game was pushed back in development because it was not properly finished. Through many updates at first, the game's difficulty was scaled down drastically, and was turned into something equally easy as Minecraft. Originally being made by the Developer's views, the game was changed drastically by community requests and incorporating user-created mods. Originally promised to have "thick and fast" updates, the game met a stagnant halt, only to be given a beta-beta release by the name of [Unstable]. This is where the small updates were to be shown, and for a time, they were. A very short time, at that. After a few small patches and one moderately average sized patch, stagnant development once more arrived. The crew behind the game moved out of the country over to Europe, and set up shop where everyone was close together. Surely the updates would be fast now, you'd think. The biggest update since March 2014 is that they have a small dog at the office.
The game had such a booming and viral start. It was a game of promises, dreams, and a great pixel game; something incredibly rare nowadays. The game had a somewhat rocky start, being a cleverly disguised alpha instead of the stated beta release, but it was playable. Many features felt nice, and the gameplay fit well with the atmosphere and music. Then it got boring because nothing was new. Through lost promises and hilariously bad customer support on the official forums, many people believe this game is dead. It pretty much is, when the developers are spending little time developing as they once did.
At first, we had developer streams. We could talk to the developers for HOURS, talking about everything down to the color of the kitchen sink. Then we had some streams of gameplay with less discussion. Then we had preorder bonuses, including some really lame things like a statue of "you" in the game. Then we had promises of fast updates, which has so far been a lie. It's been months since the last real update as of this post time, and there's no real sign of progress. There were people who donated HUNDREDS to this game, only to be shafted so far. By definition, as of the game's current and past iterations, this game is a scam.
I still hold hopes that the developers will EVENTUALLY do something for the game's betterment, but I will definitely not expect them. It's obvious they ran with the money. If you want this game, look up youtube videos first. If it looks like something you'd want to play, then by all means buy it, but just remember that it's a buggy, unfinished game with no hope in the nearby future of completion. Other Early Access games are more likely to be fully released ten times over before this is out of the current be- I'm sorry, ALPHA release.

This game is just great. I remember playing it on my 360 when it first came out, and having such a fun time. It's no different here. I feel like I don't have to explain what Bayonetta is, as most people already know and many have already explained. So I figured I'd post what is missing from this game.
First, the OST that comes with the game doesn't include "Fly Me To the Moon" which is a great rendition of Frank Sinatra's classic song; and most people who would want the OST of this game would want that song. What is included is: One of a Kind, Riders of the Light, Battle for the Umbra Throne, Theme of Bayonetta, The Old City of Vingrid, and The Gates of Hell. It's not a big deal, since you can listen to the song with ease, but it would have been a nice addition.
Second is that MSAA doesn't seem to work. I have tried all the settings for MSAA, and I can't see any difference in looks or resources used, and I've seen other users reporting this too. A prime example of why people should stay away from Early Access, when this game is complete it might be truly fun however in this state its a definitive DO NOT BUY. Some games are capable of being fun in unfinished states but Starbound is not, what is currently offered is a sandbox, a very dull sandbox. It's great if you want to build or just stare at the same procedural environments over and over. Sadly even the core feature of the current alpha is lacking, the combat.
The vision for this game is sweet, however it's far beyond the horizon and I don't get how the game could be finished in even a year at the current rate of development, I think perhaps 2 updates in total so far have come out, ones which didnt add content but rather just remixed the barest progression system ever. There might be some turn around with this due to the recent restructing of Chucklefish, I have seen some interesting progress in their daily updates (showing us what they're working on, not actually playable).
I have seen some negatives of the game just from this alpha and they don't bode well for the final release. If you are a fan of Terraria's tight controls and graphics they are not to be found in Starbound. The graphics are fluffy as well as player movement and combat.To elaborate I feel as if all movement in the game is slow, from the velocity of bullets to fall speed, as well as the hitboxes of monsters being somewhat strange, probably in part to their procedural generation. I have a hard time believing the game will have a high difficulty lacking of frustrations, whereas in Terraria due to its good performance it can ask much of the player in it's boss fights. My current outlook is that more fun will be gotten from the noncombat experiences of the game. Those experiences however apart from building are nonexistant in the current build, features such as trading, questing, farming (plants are in but the full extent of the system is missing), and storylines are still in development.

I'm a fan of the Classic UFO Defense (and Terror from the Deep). I have played the Enemy Unknown Reboot - which was a nice game, with new ideas and great gameplay/graphics.
However, in XCOM:EU I started seeing problems. Unfair difficulty and glitches being the worst. However, for the most part I enjoyed the ride.
Then I bought XCOM 2 on presale. I played it for 170+ hours. I wanted to like it. A lot.
I thought the graphics would be better than the ones from the previous game. They weren't. The models and animations looked old, lacked polish. Maybe the levels looked better, mainly because of their semi-random nature with more variation.
The character customisation is extensive, but the random characters start looking all the same after some time. I'd rather focus more on other features for the soldier face/build than caring about my weapon camouflage. I feel that I need to invest too much time creating custom soldier if I don't want generic ones.
What about difficulty? Good, if you enjoy being a masochistic. The game uses unfair mechanics with the excuse of making it old-school. Really? Please stop spawning aliens on unfair positions and in unfair quantities. I struggled to finish the game on EASY mode! I'm sure I'm not THIS bad. I realise that the old XCOM was hard, but it seems that you went too far and feels unbalanced, to say the least.
But what really destroyed the game for me was the performance. I have a good PC for 2016 standards (i5 4460 + GTX 970) but I kept seeing performance dips, staggering and hiccups. That's not a good experience. To make things worse, I started seeing artifacts (possibly after the final mission became a glitchfest). Even when I started another game, the glitches were still there. Now either the game fried my GPU (I hope not... I haven't experienced glitches in other games) or this is one of the worst optimized games I ever played.
Nice try Firaxis, but please focus on quality and polish next time.

Darkest Dungeon is a game about risk management. The RNG and turn-based format are critical to this, as actions are assessed by their intended effects and the odds of succeeding in each of those checks. Do you bank on a high roll for an attack to finish off an enemy, or do you attempt to stun the enemy to focus your party's attacks on other targets? Do you spend a turn healing off damage, or do you attempt to finish off a weaker enemy to get the battle over with quicker? Do you explore a dungeon in bright light for easier enemy encounters, or do you wander around in the darkness to scavenge for more of the loot and heirlooms needed to upgrade the Hamlet and your heroes? The game's opening text states clearly that this is a game about making the best out of a bad situation, and although it's easier to remember the failings of past expeditions, the successes far outweigh the failures with proper preparation and execution.
My mileage on this game came from this constant stream of thoughtful decision-making, ever-present in just about every click I made. In spite of the game being nothing else but hallway crawls, I never got tired of it thanks to how engaged I became with the rules and systems within the game. The added tension stemming from uncertainty, as well as the game's woodcut aesthetic and eerie sound design, sells a slight chance of hope within a dungeon of despair which I cannot help but try and seek out for myself.

the good:
+ it's a pretty decent game at base, definitely worth the $20 less than its launch price i paid for it
+ there's a nice variety of missions, at least initially, so you're only likely to get terribly bored of the game with extensive playthroughs or second runs (but even then, the game being substantially harder on my second go 'round has mitigated this somewhat)

- the game's plot didn't really grab me, though the unique Plot Maps™ were pretty neat - YMMV of course

My one critisism is that it feels really unbalanced at times. Some missions seem super difficult when it seems  like they shouldn't be. Then there are the missions that are supposed to be hard,  but sometimes seem fairly easy. Usually it's the former.  I hope the balance gets worked out in further updates, or with mods. Many missions are timed in the number of terms you can have to successfully compleye the mission, and that can compond the difficulty. For clarification, I've been playing the game on the 'normal' difficulty, one above the easiest setting.
EDIT 5/15/2016: I completed the game to the end. Some of the balance concerns worked its self out as I got to get better at the game and got upgraded weapons and armor. I'm going through a second playthrough and I found that upgrading the armor and weapons as soon as I can to the second tier makes a big diffrence. If anyone is having trouble with the difficulty I recommend these upgrades (research then building in engineering) as soon as possible, or at least before you start to get into the midgame. The timers still are a bit annoying sometimes, imo. The late-game I found sometimes should be more difficult. Once you're fully upgraded it's significantly easier to survive and defeat the enemies.
Comments on the story: One thing that isn't completely clear is how XCOM lost the first war. It isn't really specified if it happens part way through the first game or if it was after the first game's ending, where the ending was just a setback. Most people say it's the former, but it's never clarified out in-game. Maybe it's explained later than I am at and managed to avoild spoilers.
The graphics and audio are excellent. You need a decent video card to handle the game on its highest settings, however. With my 670 I sometimes get slowdowns during the loading screen and sometimes in the avenger, but while it's not always at 60 fps, it generally runs well in the missions.
XCOM 2 has good mod support. I look forward to seeing what some people come up with.
EDIT 5/15/2016: I've been trying a few mods. It's still early days for modding XCOM 2, but they are coming in. Some of the voice packs are very amusing. I recommend trying the characters from Saints Row 3 and 4.

I find this game to pretty fun and enjoyable. It has its flaws in terms of business model and progression. If you are willing to grind your way to unlock new and more powerful ships, then you will be fine. As you play you CAN unlock new equipment for old or new ships, if you can afford it and if you saved up enough points/coins. It takes a lot of time to unlock the more ships or unbalanced ships such as assassin and sniper.
If you ignore the grind, progression time and business model you will still find the game enjoyable once you get used to the different ships, their abilities and how to counter other ships. As you go 5vs5 in a capture the base kind of arena game.
All in all a fun game considering it is still on "Alpha" and "Early Access".
If you are like me you might get annoyed with the fact that the progression of the ships, make no sense. As the ships do not get stronger, they just unlock new ships. And a lot of the ships you start with are not your primary choice, so you are forced to play a ship to unlock a new ship of your preference and playstyle.
You could argue that the 3 factions each have a starting ship that is different from the others, one is faster, other is slower and third might have a more damaged based ship. But it is still a problem in this design and unlock due to the fact that it takes a lot of time to unlock, level up and upgrade each ship.
Anyway, I think you will still enjoy the game but you might find it frustrating in many areas such as business model, pay 2 win model, premium model, speed of progression, how you gain points and credits, how you spend it and how the game forces you to grind a lot if you make mistakes in your choices.
The core game is fun though.

Darkest Dungeon is a game about risk management. The RNG and turn-based format are critical to this, as actions are assessed by their intended effects and the odds of succeeding in each of those checks. Do you bank on a high roll for an attack to finish off an enemy, or do you attempt to stun the enemy to focus your party's attacks on other targets? Do you spend a turn healing off damage, or do you attempt to finish off a weaker enemy to get the battle over with quicker? Do you explore a dungeon in bright light for easier enemy encounters, or do you wander around in the darkness to scavenge for more of the loot and heirlooms needed to upgrade the Hamlet and your heroes? The game's opening text states clearly that this is a game about making the best out of a bad situation, and although it's easier to remember the failings of past expeditions, the successes far outweigh the failures with proper preparation and execution.
My mileage on this game came from this constant stream of thoughtful decision-making, ever-present in just about every click I made. In spite of the game being nothing else but hallway crawls, I never got tired of it thanks to how engaged I became with the rules and systems within the game. The added tension stemming from uncertainty, as well as the game's woodcut aesthetic and eerie sound design, sells a slight chance of hope within a dungeon of despair which I cannot help but try and seek out for myself.

Age of Empires III: Complete Collection is a real-time strategy game from Ensemble Studios and published by to what now Microsoft Studios. It is a sequel to the Age of Empires franchise. Age of Empires III: Complete Collection also contains both expansion packs from Age of Empire III.
Age of Empires III saw many improvements and feature upgrades in term of gameplay while retaining the unique play of Age of Empires series. Many new features included are the new home city and card deck. Card deck allows you to call many abilities such as reinforcements of units, resources delivery, unique upgrades delivery and many more from home city to your new colony. Age of Empires III takes place in the new world of America. You will be seeing units such as the Musketeer, Dragoon, Minuteman and many cannons. Another new features added here is a trade post. Trade post can be built on trade routes or local tribes such as the Aztec to gain their allegiance and lets you train their unique units.
Graphics in Age of Empires III is definitely far better improved and upgraded than the previous Age of Empires, far better effects, models and textures, shaders, everything is beautiful and fully detailed in this game. Performance is also great, no issues that can ruin your play.
Seeing that many Microsoft games such as the Age of Empires II or Age of Mythology has been upgraded with Steamworks feature, Age of Empire III should see that support too, since this is the latest Age of Empire series.
Age of Empire III: Complete Collection is a great game to play, I recommend this.

It should be known by now that I've been a fan of the Age games from way back. There's just something about the historical nature of the games that appeals to me. To be fair, I think elves and space marines are neat too, but I think it's more exciting to explore the what ifs of real, historical situations. Though not quite as faithful to "reality" as some strategy games, the first two Age games offered us exciting sojourns into the worlds of "capital A" Ancient and Medieval strategy. The third title, Age of Mythology, proved that the mechanics were just as solid even if the historical inspiration was a little loose.
Now Ensemble is back on the history train with the third official Age of Empires game. Age of Empires III moves the action to the New World, letting players lead a variety of European nations from the Age of Discovery through the Industrial Age. Eight playable nations battle across a wide variety of geographies -- from the swamps of Florida to the snowy passes of the Rocky Mountains. Players can recruit different Native American tribes and seize control of various trade routes. Material and technological support will be offered by the player's home city back in Europe.
The 24-mission campaign is very well designed. Divided into three large acts, it tells the story of three generations of the Black family. First Morgan Black, a Knight of St. John races to the New World to stop the Spanish from seizing a powerful natural wonder. Next, Morgan's grandson John and his Native American allies find themselves in the Seven Year's War. The final act shows John's granddaughter Amelia as the head of a railroad company making their way west.
I won't spoil the particulars of the story here but a common quest and a common enemy unite all three acts. The connections aren't always clear at first, but the associations start to build as the game goes on. Putting the pieces together isn't terribly hard but it gives a nice sense of purpose to the whole game and keeps you invested in the action.
While we're talking about the game's story, it's refreshing to see a game that covers this era of warfare without referencing either Napoleon or the American Revolution. While both are fertile ground for strategy game developers, it's nice to get something a little different this time around. Meeting Washington and Bolivar and taking part in the Seven Year's War adds a little authenticity as well as variety. On the other hand, some of the choices -- like finding Russians in Colorado -- may leave gamers scratching their heads in wonder.
The range of missions is pretty broad. There are plenty of defense missions where you have to protect a given structure or a whole town from enemy assault. In other cases you'll have to destroy or capture key structures. Along the way there are plenty of other objectives: rescuing captured settlers, seizing trading posts, liberating Native American settlements and a whole host of other tasks. Better still, many missions combine a variety of these objectives at once. While most of the missions let you build a base and start collecting resources, there are some missions where you have to make do with a set number of troops.
Outside of the single player campaign, Age of Empires III benefits from a very soild multiplayer interface. A few simple clicks take you to ESO2, Ensemble's online matchmaking service. Finding and joining games is remarkably easy and there are a wide variety of options to choose from. Different starting eras and resource levels will let players jump into as advanced a game as they want. The AI offers up a few taunts from time to time to (sort of) replicate the personality of a human player. It's a nice trick honestly.
In general the AI is very strong. You can find some exploits here and there but, for the most part, the AI knows how to make a good army and how to lead it. While the computer opponents in some RTS games send out trickles of units from time to time in order to keep things interesting, the AI in Age of Empires III tends to rely more on groups of units and will hardly ever use them in pointless, suicide attacks. In my games the AI has had a good handle on when to press an attack and when to retreat. The only real weak point in the AI is its tendency to leave some of its settlers too isolated. (Since there are no resource dropsites anymore, it's also hard for human players to keep tabs on where all their settlers are.)
The range of technologies and units is relatively broad here. In the early ages, players will have to make do with troops that are very similar to the medieval set from Age of Empires II. Crossbows eventually give way to muskets as the ages pass by. Soon players will be fielding long lines of musketeers and using mortars to bombard enemy towers. While it may seem that some of the unit types are redundant, you'll find that each type has a specific role to play on the battlefield. Like the other Age games you'll have a variety of ranged and melee-focused cavalry and infantry as well as a nice range of artillery units. Identifying the counter units and building a balanced force is just as important as knowing where and when to strike the enemy.
Like the rest of the games in the Age series, the naval element is merely there to support the land battles. The handful of ships and maritime technologies don't offer many options. You will find that the naval side of the game is fairly compelling early on while you're dealing with pirates and chasing your enemies across the Atlantic. Once you start fighting in the interior of the American continent, you won't really miss the naval aspect of the game as much.
Pathfinding seems to be a bit of a problem here and there. Huge formations can easily find their way through the most densely packed settlements but my one hero unit can't seem to find his way out of the middle of a line of infantry. There are cases where the pathfinding is a little too good. Units are able to predict the best routes through a maze even when large parts of that maze haven't been uncovered yet. This is most telling during missions where you're leading a small force through a series of winding canyons. As long as you click on their eventual destination, they'll make their way through the labyrinth with nary a wrong turn.
While we're on the subject, it seems odd that you can't select a single unit out of a group by clicking on their portrait at the bottom of the screen. Trying to grab a specific hero unit out of a large formation should be easier than this. Luckily, there's an option in the game to disregard any non-combat units when you click and drag to select a group. This helps to keep your settlers from marching out with your soldiers.
Age of Empires III also introduces some new elements -- home cities, native tribes, trade routes and such. Taken individually none of these are profound innovations but their cumulative effect makes the game feel fresh and strengthens the appeal of the core design. So in total of this review, I recommend this game to anyone who loves RTS Games.

.
A standard game is 20 - 40 minutes of blasting your opponents into the next galaxy while trying to take over their forward stations giving you access to the enemy home base which you must capture. To get your team an advantage you must control mining stations in the lane that will allow you to upgrade your ships to the point you can survive the home bases defensive weapon platforms and crush your opponents.
The tag MOBA in the description should not worry people who don't like MOBAs. It does not feel overwhelming like one despite using the core design principles of them.
I cannot say the developers have not made mistakes in the time I have played. What they have done is admitted their mistakes and done their best to fix them. Based on this I hope they will continue to make good decisions and improve the game. They also do a reasonable job of being transparent with regular streams, being present on the forums and doing interviews with a few of the youtubers and streamers who play this game.
At this moment there is a massive grind to get to some ships. Thankfully this should be improving with the next up date with a change from a misguiding tier system to a cost based on how recently the ship was released. The ships are in theory balanced against each other with some ships being more specialised. The starter ships are competitive jack-of-some-trades but will lose out to a specialist if the situation is right. I personally recommend the Pioneer as a simple to use good all rounder.
The business model allows for "pay to skip" with platinum, the premium currency, which unfortunately can only be purchased in set amounts that will leave you in situations where you have a small random amount of currency you can't use to buy anything.
You can however obtain premium currency in the daily reward system, admittedly in small amounts. The developers have said they plan to add more uses for small amounts of currency so hopefully committed money will not go to waste.
As well as unlocking ships faster, platinum is used for buying skins. These range from recolours to versions with new models and visual effects.
Hopefully you have found this useful and once again try it for yourself!

I will sum up this game by telling you my first Dark Souls experience...
I got dark souls 3 and played it yesterday because it was on sale. Never have played a Dark Souls game before, I was vastly under-prepared.
I considered picking deprived for my class at first thinking it would be an easy game and that it would make it a bit more challenging, in hindsight it’s a good thing I ended up going with assassin.
My friend got the game too and we wanted to play with each other but found out we had to solo the first level to be able to summon another player so I go at that.
Going through it the game seems really easy and I consider restarting with a harder class. That didn’t last long as I came up to the boss for the tutorial level.
First I try some sneaky stuff and going around him, that didn’t work as you can’t open the door till he is dead. Next I try just rushing him and swinging my sword around, that didn’t work either since I found out I didn’t even start the fight and had to pull a sword out of him to be able to damage him.
I pull the sword out and kinda just stand there not know what to expect. He then precedes to hit me, pick me up, throw me across the field, and kill me.
I’m slightly irritated but realize that I had no clue what to do and think I’ll do better this time. I go back in there and frantically run around trying to get back to my Souls to recover them. I’m kinda a completionist so I’m not gonna let myself lose any souls. When I finally get my souls back I try fighting him but he’s already gotten me low and I e had to pop a potion or two so I die quite quickly.
I repeat this and start getting stuff down, I’m actually able to get to the boss without taking damage consistently. I still get rekt by the boss though.
After a hour or so of this grind I’m starting to get the hang of it. Until I realize that’s just not true as he turns into some giant tar monster thing after half health and recks me.
I kept going at it for a long while but then something happened. I failed to retrieve me Souls before he killed me. I was furious. I threw my controller and went to make some pizza rolls.
When I come back I considered restarting as like a knight since I already lost all my souls and have seen in most Dark Souls clips they are a knight. I ended up deciding against it as my friend reminded me that I have been getting items from the guys I kill leading up to the boss that will give me Souls. My friend had beaten this boss on his third or fourth attempt and was just farming everything before the boss whilst waiting for me so we can do stuff together.
I continue to try this fight attempt after attempt and I’ve gotten to the point where I can do the first half of his health bar flawlessly but keep getting killed by the second part. I’m starting to get the hang of it, at least I think I am but in actuality probably still suck. I’m not really used to this type of game since I normally play games like CS:GO, PUBG, overwatch, and Osu!.
After about another three or four hours of trying this I’m finally able to do it. I kill him. It’s over. Then I see the bonfire that spawns after killing him and I’m so relieved. I continue on and can finally meet up with my friend.
Some of the time I spent failing at that boss my friend spent looking up how to do co-op stuff so he had it all ready. He joins my world and I sigh a sigh of relief as I think I’ll finally have a good chance at doing stuff. Then someone invaded my world, kills us both, and we go to bed.

TLDR: Paid mod system broke free mods altogether. Nuff Said. That being said, details below.
I used to really enjoy this game. It is pretty decent as a standalone game. However, it was GREAT with mods. Yesterday or so a new update went out that enabled Bethesda's paid mods system, Creation Club. It sounds pretty decent and all, as it allows modders to essentially freelance to release mods for a price. As long as it wasn't stepping on the toes of the modding comunity that was fine. Unfortunately, this is not how it works. CC does a few things that entirely breaks free modding for all of us. First, it resets the load order of mods. This is a big problem as carefully tunes load orders are ESSENTIAL for funtional modpacks. Second, some of the paid mods seem to be fundamentally incompatible with the free mods. Finally, it breaks support for F4SE, which is a script extender that allows most of the more complex mods to function. Another big issue, is that even if you buy NONE of the paid mods, CC requires your machine to download the entire set of paid mod data files. Right now, at inception it is 2+ GB. Imagine what that will be in a years time? I cannot support the path that Bethesda has taken in this regard. I will be rolling back my game version, backing up a clean copy, disabling updates, and washing my hands of this utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I can only hope that this does not kill the modding comunity. Remeber Bethesda, many of us bought your games knowing that we could mod your lackluster, outdated games to make them kickass adventures. Your games simply are not that good b themselves. They are, however, decent modding platforms. Please reconsider your actions. I will update this review if the situation changes.

If you are interested in this game, then you are hoping for the simple kind of silliness that comes from making a piece of bread struggle to be toast but nothing so referential or random as dressing it up in armor while a patsy follows you clacking coconuts on your quest to the Holy Grille. That is mostly what you get. It's hard being bread, but you're bread, and that's funny.
There are two main caveats. The camera sucks, and you have no information.
The camera is as clunky as your movement, but not what you paid to experience. I suspect skill with the camera is similarly acquired as the movement but your initial experience will vastly differ from the perfectly framed trailers and quickly adaptive let's players. And when frustrated from the gradually decreasing grip meter giving out the camera becomes the thing to blame. It also nigh breaks the bagel racing mode.
Aside from that, this game desperately needs some sort of Detective Mode that shows you exact areas of dirtiness and heat. One of the games merits is discovery for the player of different heat sources, but these almost always have a switch. Let's take a 90s era CRT tv, if you owned one you won't know if the developers made the top also hot like a real one or if you'll just have to press against the screen. The iron will seem like the most obvious heat source, but can you still use it if it isn't glowing red like activated hot things? Trial and error necessitates repetition, which will quickly sour the humor of it all.
However if you don't care about scores eventually story levels give you 'Magic Marmalade' which allows you invincibility and unlimited grip. So you'll always be able to see every level.

I am Bread may strike people as a novelty game, but it has some real meat behind its fluffy appearance. The amazingly weird premise is bolstered by an intriguing control scheme and physics-based gameplay.  Though it has some crusty edges around its soft center, it has more than enough freshness to warrant a recommendation at its whole sale value.
As an autonomous piece of bread, your main objective is to move from the rest of the stilted loaves to a place in the same room where you can become toasted. Environmental hazards like used band-aids and dirt reduce your edibility, forcing you to find different pathways as you jitter and flip your way around the house with the shoulder buttons and the left analog stick. The variety is surprising, as you'll find multiple ways to flip, toss, and jiggle your bread with the shoulder buttons.
It might be weirdly unintuitive at first, but with practice, the controls become quite natural. It ultimately becomes a key part of the game from easily becoming a stale novelty. Suffice it to say though, a controller is a must. The keyboard and mouse combo would only wreck your hands.
The crusty parts eluded to earlier involve a camera that can sometimes work against you. The angle can change quickly, altering the way the controls and forcing you to compensate for it. It happens infrequently, but leaves an irritating impression when it does happen. The environment could also use some life to it, as aside from the multiple ways to become toasted, there isn't much else to do in it. Some challenging trigger events like turning on the TV (which I found disappointingly unresponsive in the second level), or even a combo of related actions could have added much more value.
Nonetheless, I am Bread provides fresh, delicious scent to an indie landscape overstuffed with me-too first-person shooter and rogue-lite games. Highly recommended for those looking for a new, action-oriented game and recommended still for everyone else.

I played most of the way through the main plot, in the sort of meandering, totally-ignoring-most-plot-missions way that Bethesda games let you do so well. I enjoyed playing it and was excited to get the DLC and get a fun mod setup going.
I finally bought all the DLC during Steam's Quakecon Week sale, got ready to play, and now I have to wait while 2GB of mods I don't want get downloaded, waiting for me to pay for them? Seriously, Bethesda, mods are optional; don't force people to download files they have not specifically requested. I could even forgive the in-game paid mods (sorry - "content you must exchange credits for") as an attempt to get polished mods into the limelight and give a little (probably a very little) to the mod authors, but this execution is beyond botched (just how botched? They released all the .bsa files in such a way that anyone with a modicum of modding knowledge and a few free programs will be able to add all the paid content into their game for free, with the modders who did the work never seeing a penny).
Seriously, with all the backlash last time a paid modding system was released, how could Bethesda not do this with more care? If the paid mods (oops, sorry, content)  change to a decent delivery system - something totally optional, ideally separate, with no force-updated features - I may remember to change my recommendation.

Bayonetta (and Bayonetta 2) are simply the best games in their respective genre.  It takes the incredible enemy design and AI of the Devil May Cry series along with it's combo-centric player freedom and blends it with the enemy aggression and tenacity of the Ninja Gaiden series.  Operating the way most action games operate that combination would be impossible to manage as hyper aggressive enemies restrict player freedom to move and perform lengthy combos.  But Bayonetta twists the formula with a grace not found in any character action game before it.
By removing the traditional animation locks found in the genre and giving you the incredible ability to dodge without loosing your combo (dodge offset, look up how to perform it immediately) it combines your offensive actions and defensive actions into every frame of the game loop.  You're always attacking and always defending simultaneously in a dance-like display when you master the game's rhythm.  No other game quite like it.  It's a thrill to master; if you have ever liked a game in this genre Bayonetta is a no-brainer.

Fractured Space is a rare gem among Early Access/Alpha games, in that it has both replayability and enjoyable gameplay. At its core, it's a lane-based capital ship MOBA, with a combination of great graphics and interesting ships. Each ship is very different in how it plays, and (right now) it doesn't take much work to get a new one. The devs add new ships with every update, along with other features, helping keep the game fresh.
Coming from Counterstrike, I was impressed at the amount of teamplay already necessary to win, even if everyone only uses the text chat. Teamwork makes the difference between victory and defeat, and as the community is pretty small still, you will often run into the same players multiple times in a playsession.
As an alpha, the gameplay is very well done, but other parts of the overall experience are lacking. It is difficult to play with a group of friends, as there is no party or matchmaking (yet), and the main menu buttons are sometimes clunky. This is certainly made up for by the quality of the gameplay, which is the most important aspect of a game anyways.
Overall, Fractured Space is a game I would suggest to people who enjoy MOBAs or space sims, but it's a good enough game anyone can try it out.

Get Bayonetta, it's a great game and I enjoyed this game so much that I am about to head out to the store and buy a new wireless dongle after this review.
