I have always wondered if Aliens have nipples, and due to the graphic models in ths game, I have found out. This game is a testimony to how awesome strategy games can be, and without it my view of gaming in this era would be tragic.  I didn't see a lot of difference in gameplay however from the first XCOM.  I can understand the concept of "Why mess with success?", and I certainly agree with that sentiment, but I would have liked to have seen some innovation done with the same fundamental game design.
PROS:
1. It is an awesome strategy game where even the environment is effected by your actions in combat. It is turned based and fairly immersive.
2. The graphics are very good. I see a lot of games updating their graphics and giving no substance. Well, this game delievers you a great experience with graphics to match.
3. Permadeath, capture, mentally incapacitating, and mind controlling your troops are a few things that the aliens use to frustrate you and keep you on your toes. It is challenging and complex because of this.
Cons:
1. All of the missions I have played so far have a timer. That pisses me off beyond pissoffity. There are a lot of escort missions, missions to capture or destroy relays, and just generally destroy everything within a limited amount of time. I don't want to have to hurry to implement my strategy. This is the worse change that I have seen in this game so far. It even deters me from playing it over some of the other titles that I have recently purchased.
2. The game still has issues with environment. For isntance, aliens are shooting me through walls etc...
3. The percentages don't really seem to be truly accurate in combat ie, Having a 90% chance to hit, but you miss. This has been a kind of an annoyance in this series.  They haven't improved on it yet. I mean, if you are going to have stats in a game make them accurate to the strategy, otherwise the games seems unfinished and unrealistic.
In conclusion, yes, I would by this game if you are a fan of the series, but don't expect leaps and bounds over the original. It is almost identical in every way except for the storyline, which is pretty awesome to say the least.

There's a lot to be implemented but depending on the kind of gamer you are, I say there's more positives than negatives.  If you are playing for story and exploration, you'll exaust all there is to do fairly quickly, regardless of the nigh infinite number of planets to explore.  However, there'll always be that one obscure new instrument, costume, or piece of furniture that's out there if you want to spend hours and hours scouring planets.  That said, if you use a cheat program then you'll cut down on the interestingness of this aspect by more than half.  As a building game, I think this a lot more robust than people have been giving it credit for.  The multitude of furniture, items, wiring devices and unique biome blocks make the game feel like an endless crate of legos.  If you don't want to play with legos, well maybe you'll be bored more quickly than others playing Starbound.  The combat is a joke by endgame.  The large variety of melee weapons, guns, and throwing weapons are fun to look at once, just like the monsters.  Then all it becomes the same.
I haven't spend much time playing multiplayer, but I can't recommend spending too much time playing with anyone either exploring or building.  It might be fun during your first playthrough, finding weapons, building shelter, slaying bosses, finding quirky instruments and sharing resources.  Yet after that, there's not much fun, unless you want to make your own fun and create your own games.  There is a surprisingly active mod scene, which adds to every facet of this game and might be enough to polish off anything I've criticized of the game before.
At the end of it all, I personally spend an hour or two a day just gathering resources and expanding my home-planet's city.  That's approaching 500 hours.  I think that alone speaks more than any praise I could give this game.

Somehow I managed to avoid playing any of the Half-Life series over the last 15 years. I decided it was time to end this drought when I saw a sale on the Valve Collection and purchased 26 titles for €45.
It can sometimes be tough to get into a very old game if you haven’t played it before, mainly due to the nostalgic factor being absent. Half-Life surprised me though. I enjoyed the entire adventure, bar one or two extremely frustrating parts that you wouldn’t see in modern games. Still, I was happy to overlook these flaws considering it’s age.
There isn’t much of a story, but there doesn’t need to be. Something bad has happened and you have to do something about it to survive. The game does a great job with pushing you along without making it extremely obvious what you have to do next. Everything is subtle, and it is easy to miss a few paths or tunnels that lead you to next chapter.
Graphically, its pleasant enough, although some textures are pretty low res which is to be expected. The audio quality is quite poor too, but it does just enough to be acceptable. I found the AI pretty good, with some enemies proving a real challenge. The scientists and guards that you must interact with also behave quite well when you need them to do something. It’s all very basic stuff but it just works.
The map does a very good job of making you feel like you aren’t on rails, even though you literally are for one chapter of the game. The game took longer to play through than I expected with some really cool challenging puzzles, but still nothing that would blow your mind by todays standards.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone. 15 years on it’s still a lot better than many games in it’s genre, both in terms of gameplay and feel. It is challenging and at times frustrating, but I believe it is essential to experience this piece of gaming history.

One of the best games I've had the pleasure to play.
Intense combat, interesting boss battles, plethor of good weapons and armor, interesting and useful spells, really nice graphics (just try it with a ReShade preset. You're welcome.)...
But it doesn't stop there. Just try to look at the lore. Everything, and I mean everything, is well made. Whether it is inside the game world itself, or just mentionned by NPCs. or even just suggested by a simple piece of rock at the right place, everything makes sense. Cudos.
PvP is great, even if tremendously frustrating at the beginning. Once you grasp some basic range and timing concepts, you start to get better, and boy is that satisfying.
The ennemies aren't very smart on their own, but sufficiently so that you have to pay attention, time your moves correctly, and not waste anything. Bosses are all very different and interesting to fight.
You can pretty much go for any build that seems good to you / fits your playstyle. With enough tweaks here and there, the right weapon and spell combination, and a good knowledge of the different skills / movesets (Oh Friede Great Scythe :3 ) your weapon has, everything will work.
Please, give us more of this. Even if it's not a Souls game (which makes me really sad), do your best.

(Keep in mind I posted this just after I started playing) Fractured space is a very enthralling masterpiece, that has some flaws which most certainly need to be worked upon.
The great parts about Fractured space are as follows: It's unique concept. Fractured space at first just seems like a nerd's wet dream with collosal spaceship battles, lasers, and missiles. But the further you delve unto it's depths you realize it is much more. It has ties to common FPS, MOBA, and startegy games that will bring in just about anyone that likes the styles of any game in those genres.
Fractured space has a good art style, by creating beautiful and haphazard looking spaceships. However these are not your average spaceship, as these are the motherships that you would typically deploy from in most other space dogfighting games. Aditionally they are greatly balanced, and allow you to work amazingly together in teams.
A couple of Fractured space's flaws: Lack of a playerbase to properly enforce the developers to work regularily and on more core gameplay features.
Additionally there is little to no balancing when joining a server. For example it is very common to be teamed against several very high levelled people.
Overall, in it's current st8 I would r8 a l8 8/12. Could use some work, but very well established in it's current state already.

This game is supposed to be Terraria in Space. It looks like Terraria in Space. It is not Terraria in Space.
Starbound is clearly an early access game, yet it's been on sale for over half a year. There has been little progress made in the development, even though the developers have received $4 million on Kickstarter and countless sales on Steam.
Whatever. The game itself is what matters. It's very boring. There are fundamental issues with the movement, combat, and progression. Movement is clunky, and getting around on planets never gets particularly fast. Combat is incredibly bland. There are only 2 boring enemy types, and some ridiculously overpowered bosses. Progression is bizarrely linear for what is supposed to be a sandbox game. It essentially boils down to : grind for way too many resources, cheese a boss to death, craft a new workbench, fly to next area, repeat. Every tier is not much different than the last, and there's very little reason to revisit previous areas. You'll spend most of your time gathering some resources, then quickly checking lots of random planets for their dungeon loot. Sometimes the dungeons are interesting, at least. Too bad finding them is a huge chore.
Yes, these concerns could be resolved in due time. However, these are fundamental gameplay issues. Starbound looks great, and it has lots of toys. The problem is that the devs keep focusing on superficial elements, instead of fixing the game itself.
Don't waste your money or time. I doubt this game will get any better. The developers have clammed up, and now they refuse to listen to any criticism. That's a sure sign this game won't see any real changes.

Essentially, the game's concept is MOBA + FPS session game + spaceships.
Combat is 3-dimensional. Your ship has armor on 6 sides, and it can be damaged or destroyed. Your firing arc varies from ship to ship. Some ships have more turrets on the sides, some have strong frontal missiles etc. You must understand which ship can do what to win.
The ship classes are all nice. Some, in my opinion, still need balancing and polishing, but they're all unqiue and have strengths and weaknesses. Massive Destroyer has long-range broadside batteries that tear smaller ships apart, and can take a beating, but its turrets are re-e-eally slow at tracking, so if somebody is attacking from behind it's going to die in 5 seconds. Hunter is one of the smallest ships, and its armor is lacking, but it can use short-range teleportation, and its frontal cannons, if aimed properly, can hit hard. Assassin can use stealth mode, Carrier can launch swarms of fighters, Sniper can deal massive damage at long range etc.
There's no "pay 2 win" ships or options. "Premium" ships are just variants of existing ships with different subsystems and look. Whatever you fly, it's impossible to win without teamwork and coordination.
The game is still in alpha, though it's already interesting to play. 80% of battles I played were back-and-forth, with all-out base attacks, last stands that turn the tide of the game, and sudden flanking maneuvers. I never regretted paying for it, as it has already earned its 10$.
If you don't want to pay for an Early Access game (which is a common sentiment), it's going to be free-to-play when it's out of alpha state, and people who purchased it will get some exclusive stuff - a win-win situation in my book.

You want a free-to-play without a catch and you enjoy cute hack-and-slash titles that are easy to get into but have sufficient depth of customisation to keep its content rich later on.
One of the original 5 Steam Free-to-Plays. It was brilliant then and still quite formidable now. It's strength is that nothing is ultimately hidden behind a paywall and you're not bombarded with constant advertising. All of the content is (to my knowledge) available... you just have to work for it. You can spend real money to speed things up and get goodies more frequently - but it's entirely optional.
The game itself is a simple Zelda-esque hack-and-slash where you take control of a knight, armed with a shield and 2 weapons of your choice from swords, pistols or bombs. It's elegantly simple but with sufficient skill required to master it. You navigate random, procedurally generated levels (or scripted missions) taking out a variety of foes - descending further into the game, where harder enemies, better loot and bosses lurk... All the while learning and crafting better kit (with plenty of room to really specialise later on). It's very easy to get into and is delightfully warm and charming; both in its cute aesthetics and fun music.
You can play solo or form a team of up to 4 knights for an expedition - luckily, the enemies strengthen accordingly, so it doesn't necessarily make things easier  (i.e. you're not penalised if you want some solo runs).
My only qualm is that, since its inception, some of the updates have made the game a tad overcomplicated. The crafting gets a bit puzzling where, in addition to normal recipe items, you now need fire to level up your kit (where before it levelled up as you played), alchemy orbs to craft new kit, special food to feed your pet and rare items to evolve them... All of which are found in different ways. You can get the hang of it - but it's a bit much upfront.
But it's nice to see Spiral Knights still getting some love and updates since 2011. Whilst the new inability to revive teammates is a shame - the trade-off is that they've removed the previous limit on how many levels a player could enjoy in a day (without spending in-game currency) - so you can at least play a lot more now.
... oh, and it's free which, all things considering, it's pretty phenomenal for the content.

Let me first say that I've never played a Bayonetta game before this one, & while this game is a great PC port it's still not perfect. I do however recommend the game, since it is by Platinum Games & nearly all of their games are a jolly good time.
-Bayonetta is FINALLY on PC
-Fun action Based Combat
-Fun & Lovable Characters
-Lots of unlockables
-QTE Segments
-Minor Camera Issues
-Can be Repetitive
The gameplay itself is pretty basic when it comes to similar games in the genre, but this hack & slash is almost anything but basic.  You attack with B/Y buttons to perform various combos. RT is your dodge & if you dodge at the last moment you enter Witch Time, which makes everything in slow motion & gives you a major edge on your enemies.  As you play through the game, you unlock a shop to buy upgrades, items, & weapons.  Most of the time, I found myself buying health items, as this game is no push over, even on normal.
If you perform the right combos they will end in a finisher, where Bayonetta uses her hair to summon a demon to attack her foes, & if you max out your magic, you can instantly finish off one enemy.  Your magic charges by attacking & dodging enemies, but also drains when you get hit.  There are items & collectibles to be found throughout the game, some of which can be traded to a vendor to unlock more items.  There are also challenges in the game in each level that I think are meant to be done when you've gotten a few upgrades, as I've not been able to beat a single one yet, but I probly just suck.
My main complaint with the game is the QTE's.  They happen too quickly & are super easy to fail & when you do it's instant death.  It's also hard to tell when the game wants you to push the dang button, cause 3 out of 4 times I fail, even though I swear I pressed it at the right moment.
There's also some slight camera issues.  It's relatively easy to be attacked by an enemy off screen & sometimes the camera seems to disorient itself to auto-face certain angles, when I'd be much happier just positioning it myself & having it stay where I put it.
This game is worth buying for the full price of $20.  The game itself is an instant classic & I couldn't be more thrilled to have it on PC.  Now if only we could get Bayonetta 2 on here, but that probably won't happen anytime soon.  At least we're getting Vanquish!

I waited until I'd played this game for more than 50 hours, over a span of more than two months, to write this review. Because this game is "under development", a necessary part of any review would have to include the way the game is developing in order to be accurate.
I would have written a very different review had I done this a month ago. I loved this game; I was very very excited to see where it was going.
But now I can definitively say that this game is a
game, and that it is going to remain a bad game. The developers are plowing this one straight into the ground. They are basically milking the early-access sales revenue to over-develop certain aspects of it unnecessarily, while ignoring the game's critical flaws. This is one of those "endlessly developed" games that is never going to survive the development stage. One day, this game will disappear, and everyone who's spent money on it is going to lose out.
It's definitely attractive enough to catch your interest at first; after the steep learning curve, you get to a point where there are some great gameplay moments, but over time they are overshadowed by a few massive flaws in the game design that make the overall experience more frustrating than anything.
Imagine a multiplayer team-based battle and strategy game where you can't pick your own teams, communicate well with ANYONE (whether on your team or not), create private lobbies, customize your key mapping, or kick AFK players. Now imagine that game is a fast-paced space-battle game where you need to earn experience to unlock ships and ship abilities, and where everything depends on strategy, ship type selection,  and communication (which, as previously mentioned, can't be done well at all). Now add to that f**king nightmare the fact that the auto-team-selection process ignores experience rankings, and will penalize you if you quit a game.
Now, imagine that the developers do nothing but endlessly d*ck with ship designs and capabilities FOR NO F*CKING REASON WHATSOEVER, instead of addressing the game's major flaws. Imagine that they overdevelop ship design so much that it actually backfires and makes the game less fun to play.
That's f**king Fractured Space in a nutshell.
There are 5 players on each team. The map is divided up into 5 smaller maps, which are accessed via hyperspace jump. Each map contains stations, some of which are assigned to each team at the start, and some of which are neutral. All stations are able to be captured by occupying them long enough. Capturing stations is necessary to do things like enable jump points, heal ships, and accelerate the capture of additional stations. Each team has a home base, which occupies its own map and must be accesed via jump. The game is won when one team occupies the other's home base long enough to capture it. All stations except the home base can be captured and re-captured without limit.
The five maps include each team's home base, a middle map called Gamma, and two larger, long maps on each side called alpha and beta. Gamma has just one station in the middle of it. At certain intervals, Gamma will become available for capture for a limited time. Capturing Gamma confers powerups that increase ship capabilities like speed and defense.
Alpha and Beta are the big maps on either side. Each team has a base in both Alpha and Beta, on their side of the map. Between each team's base are three stations that are neutral at the start of the game. Capturing these neutral bases will allow you to capture the other team's Alpha or Beta base faster. You need to capture the other team's Alpha or Beta base to open up jump access to the opposing team's home map. Once you've done that, any of your teammates who are in the same map can jump to the enemy's home base, to capture it and thus win the game. However, you have
bases to defend while doing so, and only five players on your team, including you. While you are trying to get their base, they can very easily be getting yours, so strategy is necessary. However, there's no voice communication in this game, and the controls for typing are awkwardly placed, and you can't re-map them! And even if you did, you'd
, while also managing the very complicated controls of your ship, and possibly defending against attack.
Each home base has a small station on either side of it that you can capture to make it easier to take the main base. There are complicated rules regarding base captures that I'm not going to explain here; this game has taken enough of my time already.
The ships are really complicated to control, and you can't re-map the controls to make it easier on yourself. Each ship has specific capabilities, and specific sets of controls that come with it, and these must be re-learned each time, for each ship. Then, once you've learned a ship, often you have to re-learn it, because the developers have "balanced" it yet again, because that's all they do.
In addition, you have to start out with very rudimentary ships, and purchase new ships and abilities with experience points. You get experience points by doing things like winning battles, but that's pretty hard to do when you're new and using the clumsy and weak beginning ships. So expect to spend some long hours getting the snot beat out of you while you are fumbling to learn this game with the sh*tty beginner's equipment. It has to be done, or you can't get to the good ships, or even unlock the better abilities of the beginner ships. And if you have to quit a game, or if you crash out (which happens a lot), or the server fails? You lose any experience you may have earned, even if you've spent the past 40 minutes racking it up in a match.
Abilities like jumping, weapons, special defenses, and exclusive ship class abilities all are limited by cool-down periods, which, like everything else that it takes so long to learn about each ship, are subject to sudden, inexplicable "balancing" that will require you to adjust the way you play, or give up on the ship altogether.
That is the sum and total of this game's "development" strategy: to endlessly d*ck around with ship design. They keep adding ships, adding or removing abilities, changing the parameters of the existing abilities, and the like, without addressing any of the serious flaws that make this game frustrating. It took 4 months of steady complaints for them to add a woefully-inadequate AFK auto-kick feature that doesn't solve the problem at all, and in that time, there were near-daily updates to ship design and capabilities instead. Scroll back through the Steam news for this game and read it for yourself.
The game has a very small community, mostly because of the steep learning curve, and the flaws in the overall design. Therefore, you will wait a while on off-nights to collect enough players in lobby for a game that isn't in Europe. There are brief floods of new players during the times when they are doing special-access deals, but they mostly just flail around and ruin a lot of games for the steady players, then get sick of it, quit, and uninstall the game.
This game is probably going to die, which makes me sad.
So don't get it. Even if you find enough in this game to love, like I did, it will just break your heart in the end. F*ck these guys.

This game is similar to CoD and CSGO, without the toxicity (so far) in online competitive games, mainly due to the fact that most of the game modes do not confer you a competitive rank, besides changes to your K/D, unless you're playing clan ranked games, for which you don't get stuck with randoms trying to derank anyways.
My first impression of this game reminds me of the days playing Alliance of Valiant Arms, similar types of graphics and settings, and game modes even, except the battle mode which is something unique.
The game features skins similar to the CSGO system, though not tradable so mainly just cosmetics to show your skins off, and does not offer any material benefits such as stats unlike the capsule guns in A.V.A. It isn't hard "grinding" for the guns either, you win 10 games per day and you will get about 100 medals, every 2 or so hours gives you $15k which stacks 5 times per week. Daily login reward comes with $15k and on every 7th day you earn 500 Medals. On average if you play 2-3 hours a day and win 10 games, chances are you get to buy 2 new permanent guns every week ($ Shop and Medal shop respectively).
The game also offers DLC Try-before-you-buy system, you get to try new weapons out for 15 days just to get the feel of it before deciding on which weapon you want to buy with your hard grind cash.
This game is still being developed, and for a free to play game, I'd say the pay to win element isn't there (yet), and that the devs do listen to the community and make appropriate changes and steering of this game's direction. Although that's pretty much the same with every other game during its early project life. So about this paragraph here, I've yet to comment anything more than that until in a few more months time when this game matures a little more.
I do hope seeing some larger maps in the future, some of the maps are too small with about 30 odd people getting tightly packed which turns even long-range sniping into CQB sometimes.

Why I bought the game: Wishlist game / -66% off coupon. Researching more RTS games I took a chance on this one, and do not regret it.
What I liked about the game: I was 5 years late playing this game, but I am an avid RTS fan. It has all the elements of a great RTS, unique buildings to each ruler, gathering and maintaining resources, upgrading units, and strategizing your victory. It reminded me of the old school Command and Conquer games, having a Special unit, and unique to each ruler, or province. The graphics for a dated game are pleasing to the eye, I recommend if you're using an up to date monitor to set the game to use minimal UI, and also adjust your zoom out for further away.
You start with Settlers, you build a town, you set up trade routes with local natives, you build defensive structures, and walls. You gather supply, and experience to unlock more upgrades, you conquer your opponite via land, or sea. What sets it apart is the sense of exploration you get on the maps, finding treasure, and fighting for trade areas can be a whole other strategy.
What i've completed of the campaign I am enjoying, I am playing on medium and have had to restart a few times, the game is not forgiving of mistakes, but learning and adapting is why i love RTS.
What I didn't like about the game: There is quite a bit of noise notification as default in the game, during battle it can sound like a trumpet battle.
Would I buy at current asking price of 39.99? No, and I waited forever for this to go on sale, it was awesome to unlock a badge and get the -66% off coupon, today I see it is on sale -75% off for spring sale, very worth it, and I will be keeping this one installed!

Half Life is one of the best games I have had the privalege of playing, and one of the best first person shooters of its time. The combination of first person shooter action with intricate (and crafty) puzzle elements makes for great pacing as well as lethal entertainment.

It's signficantly better than the X-COM re-make from a couple years ago. And that re-make was, at least in my opinion, a pretty good game.
------
Here are the notable improvements:
+ Much, much more choice in missions and strategy on the geo-view. In the game from a few years ago (which I will just call X-COM from here on out), you had basically a linear path. You could skip missions, sure, but otherwise, the geo-view was just a place to go to when you were ready for the next mission. In X-Com2, there is so much more in terms of options, though: want to scan a location for supplies? Want to complete a mission to reduce Avatar? Want to do a story mission? All three tend to be options at once, virtually all game long. So, a lot more to decide on.
+ It's a sort of smaller thing, but the concealment mechanic speeds up gameplay a good deal. In X-COM, I sat inching up with my 4-6 soldiers, trying to just trip one pod at a time even from the very start of the mission. Concealment addes a bit more tactical diversity to the missions where you have it, but if nothing else, it simply let's me move quickly until I see the warning zone, which means less creeping forward in those first turns of untimed missions.
+ Soldiers now have an ability choice at every level-up except the first. This, too, is a small thing, but in X-COM, there were a couple level-up points where there was a single ability given without any choice. Having a few more choices to make does help.
+ Missions themselves offer more decision-making, now. Choosing an extraction point, which occurs on a small number of mission types, is just one more layer of thinking out your movements.
+ Special event missions work better, now. No more "sudden-attack-on-base-with-no-chance-to-re-equip" non-sense. Can't say much more than that, though.
+ Regions don't just leave the council because of an arbitrary timer, now. You can lose -- and win back -- regions, now, meaning, again, there's more flexibility in the missions you skip or take.
+ No training airplanes to fight with against mini-game toy UFOs.
--------------------
It's not perfect, though. I won't do individual points for this part, but, there are a few gripes still to be had. For one, too many enemies stun, disorient, mind-control, bound, or 'insert-loss-of-control-over-soldier-ability-name-here'. It gets to be a bit much, especially in the late game, and there isn't always a reasonable counter (mind-shield covers some, but not all, of the issues). Another gripe is that the early-game is still too lacking in toys and tactics to play with. Like X-COM, it's a little annoying that there aren't more decisions to make for basic weapons right away. Why not let the shotgun be used by more units, if they want? Why not add one more basic weapon type (a SMG, maybe?) that can be used in place of the Assault Rifle? It's a small gripe, but for a sequal, it would have been reasonable to expect maybe just a little more for basic weapons?
--------------
Overall, though, a significant improvement over an already good game that came before it.

To start off, as far as problems with framerate are concerned, when I first booted up the game and played the Prologue, it was so choppy to the point I couldn't time my dodges properly. I went to look in the discussions a few hours later and found someone had posted a fix. The solution was to go to the NVIDIA control panel, click on Manage 3D Settings, go to the Program Settings tab, add Bayonetta.exe as a program to customise, and then select High-performance NVIDIA processor as the preferred graphics processor. Now I am able to play the game on full graphic settings with silky framerates and seldom a hitch. I'm well above the recommended specs, so the initial problems were quite a concern for me. Hopefully they work for others just as well.
Now, as far as the game itself, it's absolutely brilliant. I first played this game back in 2010 a short while after it was initially released, and I spent that entire summer playing the living hell out of this game on Xbox 360. It takes a while for it to get old as it is designed to be played through over and over and so on.
Probably the only actual weakness Bayonetta possesses is the plot that is so far up it's own♥♥♥♥♥that I still can't completely grasp it 7 years after originally playing through it (for further exposition and a better understanding of what the hell is going on, I suggest watching the anime Bayonetta: Bloody Fate. It's essentially a rehash of the game's story, but with a noticeably streamlined plot that makes you go "Oh! I get what that means now!") It's a minor gripe in my opinion; I enjoy the story and writing, it's just hard to understand, especially on your first playthrough.
Apart from that, combat is still exhilarating as ever, replete with a versatile arsenal of infernal weaponry and nifty accessories, some of which yield satisfactory reward if you master them, i.g. The Moon of Mahaa-Kalaa, a bracer that gives you the ability to parry and, with perfect timing, counter an enemy attack, no matter if it's against a lowly Affinity or a boss angel. Aside from a decent selection of special techniques, the combo list in general is insane, each weapon having it's own full list of attacks. And just because it's a button mashy action game does NOT mean it doesn't require skill, especially on higher difficulties. Your reflexes and choice of weaponry are crucial in getting as high of a rank as possible, doubly and even triply so if you are on Infinity Climax or doing a simple challenge (the really good ones of which I shan't spoil, but when you find them they are SICK.). Also, I recommend staying away from the easy difficulty settings as they will hinder your learning of timing and combos thanks to the automatically equipped Immortal Marionette, which only serves to enable pure brain-dead button mashing of the highest order.
This game is an absolute gem, tied with Final Fantasy X/X-2 as my favourite game of all time, and I am so happy it's on Steam for new players to experience and even long time fans like me to revisit and appreciate with higher performance fidelity once you fix any issues that may be present upon startup. I'm proud to say this is a fantastic game and I highly recommend it to fans of action games and over-the-top fun overall.
TL;DR - Read the first paragraph if you have performance problems (for users of NVIDIA chips, this should help you). This game is brilliant and a must-have for players who enjoy nonsensical fun, convoluted story, and innurendos. Pick this up, you won't be sorry!

XCOM EU/EW was one of the best games I ever played, and I think this lives up to it and even exceeds it in several respects. The diversity of the combat, the way the timed missions pushes you to be play more riskily and offensively are all great, and in particular the more extensive customisation available on the soldiers is great. The full playthrough experience somehow seems less rich than the previous incarnation, but I guess that's because I'm comparing it to the fully expanded XCOM EW, with EXALT, meld, the extra missions, plus the whole slingshot mission series. If we get a similar load of expansions for XCOM 2 then it will end up being awesome.
The real reason for this review though is to make a suggestion, that would make it even more awesome. I think it would be great if your soldiers developed traits and negative/positive abilities that are triggered by events in mission and over which you have no control (like for characters in some of the Total War games). I thin this would really add to the narrative drive of each playthrough, and also the degree to which you get attached to your squad. What if specific squad members developed close friendships for one another that granted them tactical bonuses if deployed on the same mission, or some kind of "grief" penalty for the surviving one if one died? What if certain squad members developed hatreds for one another? What if they lost limbs and had to get bionic arms and stuff that also changed their combat abilities?
On a related note, while the visual customisation of soldiers is obviously much better than in XCOM EU/EW, the range in their stats seems to be less, and in effect makes them less unique in a combat context. The hacking skill, for example, levels up in the same way for each soldier, and Will maxes out at 100, which means basically any colonel level soldier or mid level psi-trooper will always end up getting to 100, at which point Will becomes irrelevant. There should be a greater range in base stats and more random stat progression to allow for that occasional hacking genius/deadeye etc who comes along every few campaigns.
I'm sure there are some mods addressing some of this stuff, so if anyone sees them please let me know.

UNTURNED is told entirely within a closed world. That’s why we sympathize with characters who are essentially evil. The story by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola is a brilliant conjuring act, inviting us to consider the Mafia entirely on its own terms. Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) emerges as a sympathetic and even admirable character; during the entire film, this lifelong professional criminal does nothing of which we can really disapprove.
During the movie we see not a single actual civilian victim of organized crime. No women trapped into prostitution. No lives wrecked by gambling. No victims of theft, fraud or protection rackets. The only police officer with a significant speaking role is corrupt.
The story views the Mafia from the inside. That is its secret, its charm, its spell; in a way, it has shaped the public perception of the Mafia ever since. The real world is replaced by an authoritarian patriarchy where power and justice flow from the Godfather, and the only villains are traitors. There is one commandment, spoken by Michael (Al Pacino): “Don’t ever take sides against the family.”
It is significant that the first shot is inside a dark, shuttered room. It is the wedding day of Vito Corleone’s daughter, and on such a day a Sicilian must grant any reasonable request. A man has come to ask for punishment for his daughter’s♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don Vito asks why he did not come to him immediately.
“I went to the police, like a good American,” the man says. The Godfather’s reply will underpin the entire movie: “Why did you go to the police? Why didn’t you come to me first? What have I ever done to make you treat me so disrespectfully? If you’d come to me in friendship, then this scum that ruined your daughter would be suffering this very day. And if, by chance, an honest man like yourself should make enemies . . . then they would become my enemies. And then they would fear you.”
As the day continues, there are two more scenes in the Godfather’s darkened study, intercut with scenes from the wedding outside. By the end of the wedding sequence, most of the main characters will have been introduced, and we will know essential things about their personalities. It is a virtuoso stretch of filmmaking: Coppola brings his large cast onstage so artfully that we are drawn at once into the Godfather’s world.
The screenplay of “The Godfather” follows no formulas except for the classic structure in which power passes between the generations. The writing is subtly constructed to set up events later in the film. Notice how the request by Johnny Fontane, the failing singer, pays off in the Hollywood scenes; how his tears set up the shocking moment when a mogul wakes up in bed with what is left of his racehorse. Notice how the undertaker is told “someday, and that day may never come, I will ask a favor of you. . .” and how when the day comes the favor is not violence (as in a conventional movie) but Don Vito’s desire to spare his wife the sight of their son’s maimed body. And notice how a woman’s “mistaken” phone call sets up the trap in which Sonny (James Caan) is murdered: It’s done so neatly that you have to think back through the events to figure it out.

Terrible, frustrating, and unfair are the words that come to mind most when I think of XCOM 2. I loved XCOM Enemy Within and have several play throughs logged yetI loathe the sequel: XCOM 2. The game lacks the charm and novelty of the first. The premise that you are a Guerilla makes the Command Center portion of the game annoyingly tedious. The game literally won't let you finish doing anything in one go. It'll send you to a region to "investigate" and you won't even get to finish your investigation before it throws a time sensitive event at you.  You're going to be juggling a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥instead of having a straight forward experience.
Enemies are too powerful and have too many abilities. Mutliple enemies have the ability to perform several attacks in one go. Advent Stun Lancers can take out multiple soldiers by yielding them unconcious even though your troops have 3/4th health left. Tongues from Vipers literally travel through multiple walls to snag one of your soldiers away from your group. This is pure LAZINESS from the developer. Line of sight defintely affects your own hit chances but apparently does not effect the AI. Not to mention that hit chances for the most part are made much more predictably unpredictable. I've never missed so many 70% or more shots before, and this is a regular thing. You might miss these at crucial times and the FREQUENCY of missing these high percentage shots is incredibly high.  Also the route your soldier takes to get to an assigned destination is bizzare. For example your soldier could go around a building and up a ladder to get to a particular destination. Yet instead of using a logical route your soldier will smash through two glass windows, alert a group of enemies to reach that same destination.
This game is literally the most frustrating thing ever. For the most part, I really enjoy challenging and tough games. Yet this game doesn't reward you AT ALL for your tactics, caution, or experience. I'm over 20 hours in and I've started a new play through with my new knowledge of the game. I've made no progress in improving my mission performance as the game doesn't reward you tactics. It's just a random pile of ♥♥♥♥ YOU. I wish I could get a refund and I don't recommend this game.

A lovely RTS for those with an eye for that kind of genre, there's a lot to be found in this game. Firstly, the DLC's continue to add a fresh take on the game, introducing 3 civilizations each (for a total of 6) into the game, with half sharing the same general premise as the others (Asian Dynasties Civs introduce Daimyos/ Shoguns while the Warchiefs introduce war dances, and that's just scratching the surface). By far my most favorite part is the concept of 'Home Cities' introduced in the game. These centers of your civilization (Like if you're the German Civ, your home city is Berlin, though it can be whatever you want) can send shipments of units, resources, or upgrades your way for use in your conquests. Really livens up the pace and makes it feel different from other cookie cutter RTS games. Haven't played much of the campaign, since I was more fascinated with my own home city to bother.

This game could easily had been another brilliant Xcom title, but unfortunatly (in my opinion) fell short for the following reasons.
1. Timed missions
The many timed missions in this game where probably made to give the player an element of suspense and take more risks as time is of the essense. But really it causes more fustration since in many cases the small amount of turns before mission fail is down right unreasonable. That is unless you want to sacrifice some of your soldiers stupidly and let mostly RNG decide how the mission will go from there. And even if you do it sill might fail for reasons I will list as well. You will usually not have time to make use of any sound tactics. Just push through and hope luck will spare your men.
2. Line of sight problems
Spotting and shooting enemies, or even worse, enemies shooting you through walls when they could not even have seen you is a problem that has presistet through all of Firaxis Xcom titles. I don't remember being that plagued by it in Xcom EW, but this game really does it alot. It feels cheap when you kill enemies and really shouldn't be able to but to have one of your top soldiers die because of something like this is infuriating and it's just not acceptable. Why is this still a problem?
3. Clipping issues
I experienced a few times that some enemies just went through walls as if it was not there and also through roofs. I once had a guy atop of a roof and then a viper who was in the floor underneath pull him too her through the roof is if it was not there. These are things that can really ruin your mission. It's "fine" when you can save and load but as with the other Xcoms people might want to play in "ironman mode" and then these things happen???
On the final mission there were several cases where I had problems tossing granades because the path of my granade would go through the floor and into the empty void underneath.
4. Another line of sight issue...
You can be in the midst of a fight against a group of aliens and then move one of your soldiers just ONE tile and then all of a sudden a new group of aliens are triggered who you should have seen because they were in line of sight but didn't. In other words it is nearly imposible to prevent being overrun by aliens randomly. And in timed missions this can really ruin your day. Yes this game is supose to be hard, but this is just silly and unfair.
5. Crashes
Had the game crash on me several times. Thankfully vertifying the integrity of game files solved that and some other problems I had.
6. Sound out of sync in cut scenes
7. Mediocre voice acting
8. Boring and forgetable soundtrack
To be fair I will also mention the positive things about this game
1. The classes and their new skills
The different classes and the many new skills that has been added in this title are great and let's the player find some quite creative and fun ways to fight back at the aliens and to get out of sticky situations.
2. The graphics
It is not super but it looks good for what type of game this is. I still wish the aliens where a bit less feral and more "alien" in both looks and animation, to help create a more sense of dread and mystique. And also some of the facial hair that you can customize on your soldiers look hilariously bad   ...atleast you can just change that.
3. The loading screen artwork
I really liked them ^^
4. Map variations
This time around all maps are procedurally generated and no two maps are the same. Of course there where many SIMILAR maps, but there was enough variation of both layout and biomes to not feel like you were playing the same maps over and over, as were more of a problem in the previous titles.
5. Mod suport
There has already been made mods that fixes some of the many problems this game has. But sadly some I doubt can't be fixed by mods. And of course it is great that they made it easier for moders to add new things to this title.
Final thoughts:
All in all playing this game was more a fustrating experience than it was fun. This IS xcom so I expected it to be hard. And it was but for all the wrong reasons.
It was hard mostly because of glitches and bugs and faulty game mechanics that screws you over in often completely random and unfair ways. It seems as though the devs tried to cater to the harcore gamers and made this game even harder than the last, which is good but it helps little when you feel like the biggest enemy is not the aliens but the game itself.
You don't feel like you are responsible for your own losses, just like you don't feel like your responisble for your own victories. You feel lucky or unlucky.
Xcom EW was difficult too and also had some timed missions. But it was done in a better way even though I was not too fond of them there either, they were more reasonable.
I played EW in "ironman mode" and later in the game suffered some highly significant losses.
But they were FAIR losses. Not some random imposible shot through a wall. So I got over it pushed through and beat the aliens.
It felt amazing because I felt that I was responisble for that victory.
I could not have said the same for Xcom 2 really. And I would NEVER want to play it in ironman mode. Atleast not the state that it's in now.
I was very happy when I finnished this game. Not because I won but because it finally ended.

Fractured Space is an ARTS/MOBA that's dressed up in a space game theme.  It's alright, but it's not wonderful.  Each ship has a number of abilities, but unlocking new ships is slow.  The game itself is alright, but everywhere feels very empty.  Unlike most ARTS games, Fractured Space has no minion waves, no small ships being set out by bases to fight over.  This means that it plays more like a domination game mode in an FPS, but with experience and money to snowball matters.
Outgame customisation is interesting: You get to choose lead crew members for certain roles on your ship, which all give small statistic bonuses, such as 2-5% capture rate, or a slight increase to turning speed.  What's interesting is that each crew member has a unique voice and portrait and will make relevant comments as you play; such as the pilot telling you when you are charging for warp.  I think this is a great facet of the game, and will get better as more content/options are added.
Fractured space might be a great game when it's out, but I don't think it's worth buying yet.

There is a reason why this game is so widely praised and so notorious that people have categorized FPSes into pre-Half-Life and post Half-Life. This was one of the first FPS games where the story and the environments actually matter.
Story: You play as Gordon Freeman a scientist working for an Area 51 like scientific facility called Black Mesa. From the first scene where you are on a tram you see the parts of the underground Black Mesa facility that make you feel like a tiny rat in a big place. An accident occurs that causes dimensional rifts to open up to hostile aliens. You must escape from Black Mesa. But the story is not divided up into cut scenes with unredeemable villains and sinless heroes. As you explore the facility you find out that the people you trust: your government, fellow scientists, etc. are not telling you everything.
Gameplay: The facility itself has interesting parts including a freezer, a rail tram system where you have to be cautious and stop to eliminate enemies, a nuclear reactor, and more. The environments and level design are very good. You get a large arsenal of weaponry that grows as you progress through the game. Interesting weapons include the Tau Cannon (chargeable cannon), the crossbow, and some alien weapons like killer bugs called Snarks. You are free to play how you want as the game gives you ammo for all your weapons on a regular basis. You have two types of enemies: the aliens and the HCEU (human soldiers). The latter might be a spoiler but it’s a trope anyways. As I said earlier the game makes you feel like a rat in a big place. You have to vault ladders, go through vents, scale mountains and more.
Ever since Half Life came out FPSes have gone the way of story driven gameplay rather than gameplay only. Some people might blame this game for that whenever they play a game where the gameplay is boring and is divided by cutscenes that you skip the second time around. Many of those games are great but one usually comes out that makes everyone say "Games were better before." What I can say is that Half Life is a great game and you should definitely pick it up.

A very underrated game, a very underappreciated game. This game feels heavy and slow-paced, but it is meant to be like that. You're piloting a capital ship in space. A capital ship with thousands of people on board, and every capital ship is different. A very team-based game, you cannot get away with simply having really good players on the team. There has to be some sort of coordination.
The game feels amazing, looks great, and has plenty of ships to unlock in its current state. Once it is released, it will have many more ships to unlock. And it's only ten dollars! What can go wrong with that? You should buy this game, I guarantee you will enjoy it (especially if you are a space combat fan)!

To boot, it's some weird spaceship MOBA with a few elements from FPS games. (Aiming, leading targets, beautiful explosions and sassy crews.) The fact that I feed off space sims and worship the Homeworld series probably biases me a bit, but oh well. Here we go.
I'd have to say it's pretty fun, surprisingly. But there's a few points to keep in mind, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.
We can start with visuals. It's not bad in the looks department, but you don't have a huge selection for what you want on or off. (I'd love to turn off blur, but alas..) The only thing I find overwhelmingly cheesy is the Reaper's side-shield aesthetic. The maps are pretty simplistic, the bases even painfully moreso- It's upsetting seeing such pretty ships fly past such ugly stations.
Another pain is the camera positioning. Some may like it, some may not, I personally find it workable but a little bit chaotic- It can toy with your situational awareness and clips with nearby objects on occassion, and the secondary view with zoom is fixated on a sphere outside of the ship, so using it up close isn't ideal. You do get to look at that awfully pretty ship from third person, though. Even if it takes up more of your screen than is ideal.
What makes up for this is the gameplay. No fight is the same, and they range from slow to fast and in-your-face. It's incredibly unique that it nearly makes up for there only being one map. Forgive me if I sound a little passionate- I really enjoy the combat in this game.
Gameplay is really straightforwards- Five ships head against eachother for resources to improve their ships (Done automatically at the larger bases & home) and ultimately to capture the enemy base to secure victory. You've got five zones, pushing up through the outer two and hitting the middle when 'gas' pops up. (Capture the point to gain a boost to your firing, not always worth it mind you)
Because of how that works, kills aren't overly important until later in the game when respawning has increased from ~10 seconds to ~50+. You'll still want them though, since you get bonus XP/Credits for them, but your team can win a game with a nasty negative team K/D ratio.
Advancement is simple. You earn manufacturer points + credits from playing, and spend them to unlock + purchase ships or upgrades. (There aren't a lot of them yet.) In four rounds playing a certain manufacturer's ship, you should have enough to buy another ship.
Their to-do list looks pretty honest and leaves me hopeful that they'll stay true to their development. FOV sliders, new ships, a friends list, yes please and all in planned development. (Ideally.)

X-Com 2 is unlike Enemy Unkown, which held your hand all the way to the point where you blew up the enemy mothership. After that, it's up to you how to figure out a way to dry your clothes off, clean your face and hair, and un♥♥♥♥ your thoroughly moistened English paper that was due last week. 10/10 would cry myself to sleep again.

It's a memorable game and experience, but not quite like CXOM:EU, and probably is memorable mostly due to XCOM:EU. And there's essentially only one reason for it, timed battles.
I get the hunch that Firaxis attempted to take the step even more towards the mainstream appeal by adding a bit of "speed" and extra adrenaline into the game through that system. In a sense it works, but at the cost of being overly annoying. Added adrenaline at the cost of suspense, guns blazing at the cost of careful strategy.
There's still a lot of strategy and tough decisions though of course, due to the fact that the timer will more often than not force land you into e.x.t.r.e.m.e.l.y tough situations, and I mean e.x.t.r.e.m.e.l.y tough, especially during legendary ironman. And by e.x.t.r.e.m.e.l.y I mean some pretty messed up odds and circumstances with everything to loose, everything hanging on everything, and everything tethering on the edge, countless of hours tethering on the edge of everything, countless of times over and over again. Add in quite a few frequent invisible wall enemy LOS bugs, and a patrol AI that calculates it's movements based on your position so as to always strike you at the (for you) worst of possible moments, and you have a game that you generally get the sense of as messing around with you and being genuinely and completely unfair.
I'd written the exact details for just one example of these fights but the type limit of 8000 characters forces me to remove it, but lets just say getting surrounded by 10 (with 3 to follow) non-trivial enemies in a surpise ambush out of nowhere when you are only at the level of magnetic weapons and no armor, well if you're familiar to XCOM you probably know just what kind of a mess that could result in.
So what do you do to combat this on legendary ironman, and show that piece of whatever what it really means to mess around with someone? You save scum, though only possible at most to the start of the turn, so everything up until then is final. And even then, you get into situations after which you sometimes do wonder how in heaven these 6 or so, by now legendary and possibly even having been infused with a soul, group of hardened warriors, with blood, sweat, tears, pain, despair, anger, courage, brilliance, heroism, patience and struggle ever got out of those situations not only alive but with victory.
At the end, having beat it, I felt not the least bit of guilt for the save scumming. I felt it was totally fair. And the horrors that this team had to go through compared to the team from XCOM:EU on ironman impossible, were by far many times worse. I never had to save scum on EU, but then again, I never had to be forced into out of this world crazy definition of insanity situations as I had to in this installment. You could pick your fights and engage the enemy on your own terms in EU. On CXOM2 instead you get it handed to you and then have it say "here, take it, good luck getting out of this one now".
But what can I say, Fatma Inanir, Mustafa Hizmetci, Yusuf Israil, Muhammad Abd-Al Rahman, Rashid Salman and Farook Yahiah, will deservedly forever be inscribed in the terrorist branded freedomfighter soldier rebels hall of fame in history. Their names remaining more memorable than their EU fellow brothers in arms, remember all their names and looks even with 2 months passed since last running the game. It's just that this time, things got to level where divine intervention became duly justified and established. And these six were the ones to have the honors of nailing the final blow on this fiendish monstrosity. Justice, after struggle, with patience, becomes inevitably served.
8/10,
for a fiendish game, with bugs, punishing design decisions, tough in-game decisions, tactical brilliance potential, memorable moments, bond creation to your soldiers, having a more fluid feel and a wider tactical repository than EU, but in general being a step to further become more mainstream by appealing to the casual player who can get a bit more of a thrill by the timed missions in normal difficulty with no ironman. For anything else, this game becomes your sworn enemy and nemesis whom your sole purpose in gaming life becomes to obliterate it because you know it deserves to be put down and then burn in hell kicking and screaming for all the ill intent it showed in its prior life before that.

Well, a third part for Age of Empires. What to expect of it?
If you have never played the first two parts of AoE, here you'll get a little summary: Age of Empires I and II were defining new standards for the RTS-genre when they came out. Not as fast-paced as Starcraft or WarCraft, but with more strategical Depth and more focus on the organization of your camp and with a build-in history-part wich made the game even a little educational without decreasing the fun of the gameplay. You always could choose from many different cultures which had some units and technology in common, but some unique units and cultural advantages and disadvantages.
Now, what is different in AoE III?
First of all, after AoE I playing in antique times and AoE II playing in Medieval times up to the discovery of the new world, AoE III consequently plays in times of the colonization of America and the civil war. Like AoE I & II, AoE III contains many true historical events, locations and persons, but unlike both prequels, the main storyline of the campaigns is highly fictional so that it might be difficult to tell which events in the game truely happend and which are made up. The main storyline of the campaign is about a sect which tries to find and conquer the fountain of youth in the new world and a family which is bound by fate to stop them. On their journeys they encounter many historical persons like Georg Washington or Bolivar, but most of the game is about hunting down the sect. So the game is far less educational then the previous ones.
The second big difference is that the cultures do not longer have most techs and units in common but every nation has their own tech tree. Some things of course still are open to every culture but the differences between the cultures are far bigger then before. This isn't much of a problem because you can still tell the strengths and weaknesses of an unfimilar unit very fast, but it is more difficult then before to play a new nation.
And the there are the RPG-elements. Not only do you have imortal hero-units (like in Age of Mythology) which can only be knocked unconscious and stand up again if no more enemy units are around, you will also play random maps with a "hometown" which can level up between games and send you support if you collect enough experience by surviving a certain time, killing enemy units or building your camp. Although this may increase the motivation to play more random maps they removed the option to play a random culture, which I really loved in AoE I & II.
The AIs are weaker then in AoE II which is good for beginners but a little disappointing for more expert players. The balancing is also worse. There are some strategies to break the game. A pack of at least 20 osman heavy bombards, for example, is almost invincible. No AI-player ever was able to beat me if I got that far.
With the complete Collection, you will also get the two Add-Ons: The War Chiefs and Asian Dynasties.
The War Chiefs adds playable Native American Tribes (Without this Add-On they are only available as some sort of mercenaries if you build trading posts near their villages witch appear randomly on random maps). Although playing a native american culture is a very wellcome change and a challenge, it is clearly unbalanced. Those cultures are given many new and unique techniques like sending settlers to a totem and dance to do rites which give you advantages like faster ressources or stronger soldiers, they still desperatly lack heavy siege weaponary. Native american soldiers are only strong in large nummers and will have to attack early to not get overwhelmed by superior firepower of other nations.
The Add-On also adds two campaigns which complete the storyline of the original game campaign by filling gaps and finishing the somehow open story. The focus, of course, is more on the war of the native americans against the europeans and so it is no true surprise that you will have to face general Custer at wounded Knee. Still the two new campaigns are much more shallow...
The Asian Dynasties finally adds some civilizations from Asia like the Indians and the Chinese. The storyline of the new campaigns has nothing to do with the story of the original campaign. The Indian campaign for example takes place around the fight for independence in India and the chinese campaign describes the discovery of the american continent by a chinese admiral which might have taken place (or maybe not) long before Columbus was born.
Overall AoE III: Complete Collection is a decent RTS game with some unique features, but if you were a big fan of AoE I & II you might be disappointed because it is a really different game then what you are used to. Still it is worth a try.
If you have never played AoE I or II, but you like RTS games, you should definitly try this one.

Fractured Space: An Early Access Review - 20th June 2015
I don't usually buy Early Access games. In fact, I've been burned several times before and swore to never buy another, yet Fractured Space looked so beautiful in the videos and screenshots I saw, that I couldn't resist picking it up in the Steam Summer Sale. Because this review is Early Access, please bear in mind it's likely to become obsolete as the devs continue to work on the title.
Fractured Space is a 5v5 multiplayer game, in which two teams start at opposing sides of a 'map' set in space. There are two routes down the map (Alpha and Beta), and the goal of the game is to control the various fixed outposts down these routes to gain access to the Enemy base. Once the enemy base is captured, the game is won. As both teams have the same objective, clashes within Alpha and Beta force players to think carefully; playing offensively or defensively depending on the enemy's position.
When your ship dies, you respawn back in your base and so need to weigh up which side is strategically best; whether to move down an already dominated side, or defend the other from approaching enemy ships. Quite often I've seen badly coordinated teams all move down one side and miss the enemy capturing all the points down the other; a move which usually results in the main base losing some capture points.
The visuals are beautiful and the ship models are very nicely rendered. Plasma fires ripple down your hull as a barrage of laser shots, from some unseen foe, strikes you suddenly, catching you unawares. The audio is impressive too, with the occasional comment from your AI crew, the immersive thudding of flak fire from the Flagship, or even lightning fast laser fire from a Brawler class.
Now on to the bad points (which, as the title is Early Access, will possibly/probably be ironed out in future updates). Firstly, in running an EVE Online group, I have several players that want to play Fractured Space with me. Although we can join the game together, there is no guarantee that you'll be on the same side. You can elect to switch sides at the beginning, but this often fails to work as the game auto-balances the teams before the action begins. Whilst I can appreciate the reason behind this, it often results in frustration as friends go up against each other, instead of being able to work together.
Each ship has a role, and the roles are all varied. There are snipers, brawlers, destroyers, carriers, corvettes, etc. As you earn experience from each fight, you can unlock more advanced ships and better equipment to install on them. At present there are three tiers of ships, from three different factions, but the upgrade options are a little sparse on the tier two and three ships. Some are just stock loadouts, with no further upgrade possibilities. I suspect, however, that the game devs are working to implement further ships and fittings in future updates, so I wouldn't be too concerned about this for the moment. That said, even without an update to this, it takes little away from the base gameplay, which can often be very intense. The grind for these tier two and three ships isn't too bad either, and I've managed to unlock most in just 16 hours of play.
The game lasts until the enemy base is captured, as previously stated, be that 5 minutes, 10, 15, 20... Getting a quick game in before bed isn't always a wise move, as leaving a game before the end results in a reward of negative 'honorable conduct' - a move, I dare say, introduced to prevent people leaving games once one team has a distinct advantage over another. In the last two days, I've occasionally found myself on a team fighting 4v5 because someone left the game early. With the teams only consisiting of 5 players per side, the loss of a 5th player makes a great deal of difference to the dynamic of a team - especially with sometimes lengthy respawn timers.
In conclusion, my friends and I have had a great deal of fun from this game thus far. There are naturally things that the game devs could work on to further improve the game, but as it remains Early Access, it gives the devs the opportunity to do just that.
Should the devs read this review, I would suggest that allowing players the opportunity to work on the same team should be something they spend time investigating as a matter of priority. I would also consider the merits of allowing players to change out their ship choice once a battle has started, as often an enemy team consisting of a Brawler and Sniper combination is often hard to counter, and if you pick your ship class poorly, any battle is just an inevitable waste of time as you slog towards the foregone conclusion of defeat.

I do like space battles, space strategies and everything about space. But I cant recommend this game in its current state.
First, it is a 5v5 battles. Well, it doesn't sound impressive. The map  ("the" because there is only one (!) map in current version) is divided into 5 sectors, 2 for base, 1 for special gas station and 2 main battle areas. So we have 5 ships fighting in 2 areas. 2v2+3v3 or any combination. And that is not only unimpressive, that is really poor. Vast space to battle and only a few ships in fray?
Well, ok, lets move on to the ships themselves. You have 3 shiplines and you are forced to play with the first one unlocked in order to advance on techtree. Noone cares if you want to be a sniper, you will have to go in close fight as a heavy ship first. Want that fast killer-ship? Ok, go play 5-6 games on a support one (and XP is awarded for kills, not healing, so you will need like 15-20 games). You think techtree is big? Nope, 3-7 ships. Not great at all. You want customisation? Bad for you, some ships have none, some have small "more damage-less speed" or "longer radius-lesser damage" tweaks.
The only real strenght of the game right now is its graphics, it looks really good. But if you want gameplay for the money you pay, you should wait for more content.

I am overall disappointed with the game, being an XCOM enthusiast. I've played XCOM1 for 255 hours, but I do not feel like giving XCOM2 more than the 55ish hours I gave it so far
XCOM2 follows the same pattern the previous games did: start with rookies, study alien tech, build some armors and weapons, learn psionics, find a way to the aliens' base and destroy it, and have your base attacked at least once in the process. There's even pretty much the same tech development - assault rifles into magnetic guns (laser guns) and then plasma. Only 3 armor tech levels too. Sure, there are modifications and some fancy variations of weapons and armors, but that's still underwhelming. This is hardly an improvement on XCOM1:EW. I expected XCOM2 to be much more developed than EW, but it's merely on par. It's not even longer than XCOM1.
The final mission is also an insult to the player. I don't want to spoil the surprise here, but it was not just difficult, the designers made it simply unfair. I was about to prevail against the odds, when the crucial enemy I needed to kill teleported away to the other end of the gigantic map leaving me sorrounded by a dozen enemies.
The game is a bit glitchy and unstable - hopefully there will be patches in the future to fix that. Fortunately, not everything is gamebreaking, but I had to restart the game and steam several times in my playthrough. Frozen cutscenes, cutscenes displayed more than once, disappearing/stuttering/looped audio. Currently, it is not worth its full price - I recommend waiting for discounts.
What is perhaps the most puzzling is the poor design of gameplay. Sometimes I would roar in frustration because I had to listen to the same dialogues over and over again after restarting a mission and there was no way to skip it - the apogeum of frustration are the terror missions. The game still hijacks the camera away from you (I think I know better what I want to look at, thanks). Also, does the cam really have to center on the soldier I switch to every time? Lots of your time will be wasted for no reason at all (I recommend getting some mods to fix that - they don't change any balance, such as Quiet Bradford) because apparently you need full 10-15 seconds to be told that there has been progress on the Avatar project.
There are several improvements though: waypoint soldier movement, reloading does not end the turn anymore, more class balance, diversified enemies, diversified terrain, soldier customization, simplified base build-up, melee attacks (finally!!!). I might have forgotten some things, but they certainly do not change my opinion of the game.

My main criticism are missions whereby you have to save npcs, as the game forces you to take great risk and it becomes a game of luck.  Generally I let a few npcs die while getting into position as it was the only way to complete without losing a few soldiers.  Personally I don't like being rushed in turn based games, but whatever.
Overall a great game and I hope an expansion comes out soon.  Could have been longer as once I got the pacing right and kept my best troops from dying it didn't take long to finish.  Hardest modes are stupidly difficult as it generally comes down to (mostly) luck.

If you haven't heard of Age of Empires, then say hello to one of the most iconic RTS franchises. With the release of Age of Empires 2 HD Edition, there's quite a bit to go around for fans of the franchise. But enough about that, how is Age of Empire 3?
Well it really depends on what you're after. Visually, it's still pretty freaking gorgeous, and it holds up quite well, though it does show its age a bit (what do you expect for an 9 year old game). the lighting effects are great, and the smoke and particle effects, especially the destructible debris that falls of buildings is a nice visual treat, and I remember how amazing it looked back in 2005, and to me it still looks great.
In terms of gameplay, it feels more in line with Age of Mythology, Ensemble's previous entry, rather than Age of Empires. From the way you choose a leader each age (mirrors choosing minor deities in Age of Mythology) to general UI layout and control schemes, AoE3 feels much like a spiritual successor to Age of Mythology, with a focus on historics rather than mythos.
Though with this iteration of the series,  there are new, much needed improvements. Gone is the need for a drop off point for your workers; like the Atlantean race in AoM:TT (Age of Mythology: The Titans), your workers only need to mine from the resource to generate that resource. This makes macromangement considerably less fiddly.
Another change is how Caravans work in AoE3; instead of building a market, creating some caravans, and sending them to a Town Centre, there are now neutral Trading Posts that need to capture, which provide a steady steam of either Wood, Gold, Food or Experience. There are other neutral buildings the map, such as native settlements, or saloons which give you access to new units.
But by far the biggest addition to the series is the Home City. The Home City has a deck of shipment cards which can be sent to you during the game, depending on how many levels you gain through experience (gained by fighting, find treasure, building or from aforementioned trade caravans). The shipments can range from dozens of cavalry soldiers, supplies of wood/gold/food,  to permanent improvements to military, defense, economy and so on. It can change how you play, and it's an interesting additon to the game.
The singleplayer in the Complete Collection offers up plenty of content, with about 8 campaigns, ranging from 15th/16th Century colonials to Battle at Little Bighorn, to the Indian Revolution, and even a little bit in Japan during the Sengoku period. It has plenty of nicely realised characters, interesting stories for each campaign, and enough content for each campaign so they don't feel short. This along with the 14 civilizations you can play in singleplayer (and multiplayer, though there isnt much of a population) skirmishes means plenty of content for your money's worth.
If you're new to the Age of Empires franchise or if you enjoyed Age of Mythology, then Age of Empires 3 will be a fun ride through some events through history. If you preferred Age of Empires 2, then you might not like Age of Empires 3 quite as much. For me though, its a hearty recommendation.

The opening intro plays, I have no idea what's happening.

female characters fighting on a watchtower that is falling from the ♥♥♥♥ing sky, while earth-quaking orchestral soundtrack with choral chants blast my speakers and a narrator gives speech about what I assume is some background lore.
While trying to get the hold of the game's controls and trying to pay attention what is going on,
So that scene ends as fast as it started and now I see some kind of a graveyard. There's a comedy-relief character that acts like a retard, dancing around the graveyard rambling about things I don't understand. Then theres a nun that is giving some blessings or some♥♥♥♥♥♥to a dead person, I assume. As my brain is trying to understand all the input it has received in the last 5 minutes, some angels arrive from the sky and the nun starts to beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them. Then the ♥♥♥♥ing coffin blast's open and some giant black guy who wears
at midnight emerges from his slumber and starts throwing handguns to the nun that is spinning in the air with moves that break the laws of physics and space-time continuum. All this with oddly catching soundtrack.
As my brain is having meltdown from all the physical manifestation of modern japanese pop-culture I have witnessed, I realise that I have fallen in love with this game. Then the game proceeds to actually teach me it's mechanics and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is this game's combat deeper than the cold abyss of Mariana Trench. Now, with a huge grin on my face, I take control of some unstoppable, over-powered sexy witch and proceed to kick♥♥♥♥♥with the power of a thousand big bangs.
What an emotional rollercoaster, and that was only the first half an hour or so.
So yeah, I can absolutely recommend this game for someone that hasn't played Bayonetta before.
So, the game gets pretty challenging as it goes on, though it is entirely possible for everyone to beat the game, if you have the will to keep trying. In the last few chapters they re-use the old bosses as common enemies and that got pretty tiring.
