Just to get this straight this game is just like freaking Minecraft! But positively like Minecraft. The game starts off as a tutorial and when your in the tutorial you get to pick between a variety of classes. Originally, the main classes you got to pick in the beta of the game when it first started was a Knight, a Gunslinger, a Candy Barbarian, or a Dracolyte.
Classes
Knight- Mainly used for tanking. Can withstand many enemies. Great damage. Close range. Has a passive skill that when hit your next attack deals more damage. The great thing about Knight it is good for soloing but damage is not that great.
Gunslinger - Has an advantage at range. Uses a gun. Good for damage. Has a passive skill that when shooting in the air while attacking an enemy in the air while airborne your next charged shot will be instantly charged without cost.
Candy Barbarian - Mainly uses melee weapons as an advantage. Close range. Can withstand many enemies. Skills provide healing and can hit multiple targets. Good for damage or for soloing.
Dracolyte- This is most likely a overrated class in my opinion but I'm not saying the other three classes are bad but this class has just got more advantages and it's just so overpowered to use. Uses a staff and the freaking skill is a flamethrower that lasts forever until the enemy dies. The most awesome thing about the last or ultimate skill of this class is that you get to transform into a fire- breathing dragon that is most powerful than your flamethrower and it can literally annihilate everything well I'm just exaggerating if you know what gear to equip.
Also in Trove you get to build your own house and make cool pixels like Pokemon, and other stuff which are like the things you need to build in Minecraft but your going to have to mine for blocks just to build stuff.
In that case, the game is fun, building is enjoyable, and having a fire - breathing dragon is the most coolest thing I've ever seen in my life.

Its not F2P game anymore when you have to buy revives with ingame currency (energy).
Pros:
+ Family friendly
+ Controller support
+ Elemental damage system
+ well designed maps/platform
+ There are 2 ways to play the game, simple one being going all normal dmg weapons which kids can understand easily, and other way is understanding elemental system + enemy elemental resistance/ vulnerability which could take some time to get used to.
+ The game is not dead as people say, there are still enough people playing it, the game was released 2011, ofcourse it has to die sometime.
Cons:
- Asian server not available
- Enemies are not balanced when playing solo (it is fixed on 4 player difficulty, it doesn't change when only 1 player is available). In short, you can't play this game solo.
- More grind = less fun, for example: Orbs of Alchemy droprate is horrible (I am not against the grind system, but in this game its not balanced).
- You have to buy revives with ingame currency. Thats a big no for a F2P game. Warframe used to have this system, they removed it and added xp loss + 4 revives system, which everybody liked. In spiral knights you loose ingame currency + xp/heat, so its just useless. Want to revive teammates? yeah you have to use the ingame currency for that.

I am overall disappointed with the game, being an XCOM enthusiast. I've played XCOM1 for 255 hours, but I do not feel like giving XCOM2 more than the 55ish hours I gave it so far
XCOM2 follows the same pattern the previous games did: start with rookies, study alien tech, build some armors and weapons, learn psionics, find a way to the aliens' base and destroy it, and have your base attacked at least once in the process. There's even pretty much the same tech development - assault rifles into magnetic guns (laser guns) and then plasma. Only 3 armor tech levels too. Sure, there are modifications and some fancy variations of weapons and armors, but that's still underwhelming. This is hardly an improvement on XCOM1:EW. I expected XCOM2 to be much more developed than EW, but it's merely on par. It's not even longer than XCOM1.
The final mission is also an insult to the player. I don't want to spoil the surprise here, but it was not just difficult, the designers made it simply unfair. I was about to prevail against the odds, when the crucial enemy I needed to kill teleported away to the other end of the gigantic map leaving me sorrounded by a dozen enemies.
The game is a bit glitchy and unstable - hopefully there will be patches in the future to fix that. Fortunately, not everything is gamebreaking, but I had to restart the game and steam several times in my playthrough. Frozen cutscenes, cutscenes displayed more than once, disappearing/stuttering/looped audio. Currently, it is not worth its full price - I recommend waiting for discounts.
What is perhaps the most puzzling is the poor design of gameplay. Sometimes I would roar in frustration because I had to listen to the same dialogues over and over again after restarting a mission and there was no way to skip it - the apogeum of frustration are the terror missions. The game still hijacks the camera away from you (I think I know better what I want to look at, thanks). Also, does the cam really have to center on the soldier I switch to every time? Lots of your time will be wasted for no reason at all (I recommend getting some mods to fix that - they don't change any balance, such as Quiet Bradford) because apparently you need full 10-15 seconds to be told that there has been progress on the Avatar project.
There are several improvements though: waypoint soldier movement, reloading does not end the turn anymore, more class balance, diversified enemies, diversified terrain, soldier customization, simplified base build-up, melee attacks (finally!!!). I might have forgotten some things, but they certainly do not change my opinion of the game.

Darkest Dungeon is one of my favourite games I have ever played, along with being one of the most unique. Thus, this review will be a little biased, but I will do my best to be as impartial and even as I possibly can. Red Hook have really done something special in this game, and I love how involved they are with the community, and the small additions they make such as the new content and patches, the extra artworks and pieces to the character's past that are posted on the forums, and the great interactions I see by the Red Hook staff.
The Narrator: I cannot stress enough how amazing the Narrator, or the Ancestor is in this game. He does an incredible job at setting the tone and the atmosphere of the game, and has a great voice all around. This is aided by the fact that Darkest Dungeon has some amazing writing, and choice quotes.
The Music and the Sounds of the Game: The music and sounds of the game are excellent, aiding the narrator in making the game's atmosphere as great as it is.
The Characters: The characters in Darkest Dungeon are written very well, and Red Hook do a great job of developing the characters with the small amount of time that they use. The afflicted and virtuous quotes really add to them.
The Overall Art Style: Another great thing the game does is the art theme. Something that you may notice is that you will never see any of the character's eyes, they are either obsured by a helmet or a hat, or just shadowed. This really conveys the hopelessness of the characters and the hellishness of their experience.
The combat: Ironically, the combat is not my favourite thing about the game, it's good don't get me wrong, and there are some really unique things you can do with the compositions.
No Varience of the higher levels of bosses: This is a weakness, there are 3 levels of bosses in the game, yet they don't change in look or combat, purely just hitting harder. This is dissapointing, and a simple reskin would have done wonders.
A little grindy/repitive: Darkest Dungeon kinda falls into the pitfall of grinding. Whether it's for money, levels or unlocking a boss, the game sometimes feels repitive.
Difficult: This is a borderline one, as it is less of an issue to some people (like me) The game is purposely hard, and when characters die, they stay dead. If you cannot handle a set back, this game might be a little much for you. Also you get screwed over by RNG a lot, but sometimes it goes in your favour as well.
All in all, I believe Darkest Dungeon is an incredible game, not only in the gameplay, but in the atmosphere and overall innovation, and I heavily reccommend the game.

Positives: Beautiful artwork and sound, engrossing turn-based adventuring in procedurally generated maps with equally random enemies and choices, limited resources forcing innovative decision-making from players, and no bugs or programming flaws that I've managed to locate in over eighty hours of play.
Negatives: Large margin RNG for player and enemy combat that can reduce even carefully built situations to nothing, lack of player-motivated saves to prevent replaying of situations in the hope of a better outcome, (practical) permadeath aspect of characters, repetitive feeling to play even with procedurally generated levels (though that might be because I've played it as much as I have).
Recommendation: Do not buy if you get frustrated at losing progress through random events and/or do not enjoy turn-based side-scrolling dungeon crawlers. Do buy if those aspects please you and you want a story steeped in horror, solid gameplay that is fair but punishing, and having to think carefully about your choices instead of just reacting.

This is a punishing, cruel, and vicious game. It can and will reduce you to swearing at it and declaring that the developers wanted nothing more than to torture players with unwinnable gameplay.
I accepted this when I bought it. And I have revelled in that torture ever since.
I'll admit, I might be a bit masochistic but the atmosphere created by this game, the delicious richness of the artwork and the intricate working of its turn-based mechanics coupled with a generous helping of RNG make victory very hard to attain but oh so very satisfying when you finally grasp it.
The one moment when a Man-At-Arms brings down his mace and destroys a nigh-unbreakable cannon. The meaty rip of a broken blade tearing through a tentacled horror, vivisecting it before it has a chance to react. The rush of watching an archer wrestle with her inner demons, then take on a look of determination that banishes fear and demands evil flee lest it be riddled with crossbow bolts. Those moments are the ones I treasure when playing Darkest Dungeon.
You won't need eye-hand coordination here but you will need careful planning, a willingness to persist despite losing carefully crafted characters to a run of bad luck or a single crippling blow that forces you to withdraw and leave them to the monsters you have tried to drive out of your ancestral home.
But just as folks sit at slot machines for hours on end, waiting for that one moment, that single time when all the symbols are just right, so too do I stack the odds in my own favour as much as I can, then push into the claustrophobic corridors and gore-spattered rooms to see if this time will be different. If this time, I can at last rid the world of a shambling horror, a failed experiment in flesh-manipulation, a cannibalistic wretch, or things that don't belong anywhere save in nightmares.
The game is very easy to learn, has plenty of guides and information to assist the beginner, while keeping statistics and mechanics tucked away to keep even veteran players guessing. If I dig into that pile of corpses, will there be something of value within or will it just give a crippling infection? When the strain of dealing with unspeakable horrors becomes too much, will the adventurers bond together in their resolve or turn against one another?
I like that uncertainty, that feeling of creeping doom that comes of wondering if I'm going to turn a corner and bump into something I hadn't planned on and really do not want to face. Because it can happen and does happen with just enough frequency that it becomes unnerving. I wander through a dungeon and watch my party mop the floors with the inhabitants, then stare in awe as a tentacled monstrosity rips through them as if they were made of tissue paper.
But I'll be back. And I'll keep coming back because I love this world and this game. I started playing because I like saving the world from nightmares.
Now? Now I'm playing for that and one thing more: to prove that, despite dealing with recalcitrant heroes, devastating battles that turned against me due to a single critcal hit, and watching my graveyard fill with the hopeful and the hopeless alike, I WILL one day obliterate the slavering things that dwell in the very nadir...of the Darkest Dungeon.

Retrieve this, save that, kill this. There is no wacky adventure like the Super heroes in Fallout 3 or the creepy vault crawl of the parasitic plants in Fallout: New Vegas.
Every side quest is forgettable and the main quest is a rehash of Fallout 3. Despite all of the improvements, they neglicted the real thing that Fallout so great: The Story.
Fallout 4 is gonna go down as a regrettable installment to the series, a game that should of been handed over to another company that cares. The real story is in the DLC, which you have to buy if you want an actual Fallout experience. Not worth it.

-Great customization
-Improved gameplay
-no story
-repetitive
-linear despite being a RPG
If you want a fun game, I recommend Witcher 3 or the older Fallouts. There is nothing here but a shooter set in the Fallout universe.

I want to like this game. It's highly stylized, and I love turn-based RPGs. This turned out to be a mediocre example of the genre, though.
There are numerous problems with the game I have that other people probably love. Here's my issues with it:
-Characters going insane happens way too fast (enemies in the first area can raise it by 20 party-wide), making the game even more luck based than it already is.
-The squishy characters die so quickly. If the enemies want your squishy dead, it's dead. The bots aren't stupid and won't attack your frontliner unless they have to. I would applaud this A.I. if it didn't devolve the game into a tank meta.
-It's slow and boring. With a game like Fire Emblem (Let's be real, it's the best comparison), it tries to keep you involved. With Darkest Dungeon, you select your most powerful move on every guy and click the enemy a bunch. It stays selected for you so all you do is spam the enemy. Granted, it didn't bother me when I started but around the two hour mark I felt so uninvolved I decided to get a refund.
tl;dr It's like Fire Emblem with less variety, less involvement, and less fun.

Old game that I can still recommend. It's good to go back to it after a long while. Sure, it has this massive grind if you don't want to fork up cash, but there's enough mindless roaming game in here to forget about it. And I never feel pushed to the grind to get to higher end content.
I usually play solo, but as with any multiplayer game, this one shines when playing with others. Sure, you will have to strategize a little when playing with a friend, as your attacks and theirs can push enemies around and make other players miss their attacks. So plan ahead or pick other enemies. Speaking of attacks, this game has a little bit of difficulty spike near the end levels, even if you select the stage's easiest difficulty. So you will have to either become very good playing solo, or go along with others to the deeper parts of the game.
I like the combat mechanics even though sword and gun play feel slow and clunky compared to other action RPGs. What I liked most was the bomb weapons. You get to be a literal bomberman when using this weapon. See. In this game, bombs are actually infinite. You equip them like any other weapon. They are slower to use than the other weapons, but they cover a big area and allow you to zip into a boss attack range, set a bomb at their feet and be on the other side of the stage well before he finishes his attack.
As grind and real money goes, you can choose to either grind for things or buy some gear with real money. Unlike some other games, this one sells you straight out gear of all tiers in the shop. That gear won't make you much stronger though. It just makes you eligible to enter the deeper levels. Most of the game play is based on player skill after all. With some gear combinations making it just a little bit easier to deal with the mobs. And you will be fighting a lot of mobs as the game tosses them in droves at you in some areas.
Visuals are rather dated but they are still extremely cute. You can dress up your character with many outfits and armors scattered throughout the game. You can dress it with even other armor (added to a dedicated costume slot that grants no stats), so you don't have to drop your preferred look even if you change armor.
All in all, this is a good time killer game that you can play, leave and come back later and can be enjoyed casually or in a more hardcore way.

Darkest Dungeon is one of my favourite games I have ever played, along with being one of the most unique. Thus, this review will be a little biased, but I will do my best to be as impartial and even as I possibly can. Red Hook have really done something special in this game, and I love how involved they are with the community, and the small additions they make such as the new content and patches, the extra artworks and pieces to the character's past that are posted on the forums, and the great interactions I see by the Red Hook staff.
The Narrator: I cannot stress enough how amazing the Narrator, or the Ancestor is in this game. He does an incredible job at setting the tone and the atmosphere of the game, and has a great voice all around. This is aided by the fact that Darkest Dungeon has some amazing writing, and choice quotes.
The Music and the Sounds of the Game: The music and sounds of the game are excellent, aiding the narrator in making the game's atmosphere as great as it is.
The Characters: The characters in Darkest Dungeon are written very well, and Red Hook do a great job of developing the characters with the small amount of time that they use. The afflicted and virtuous quotes really add to them.
The Overall Art Style: Another great thing the game does is the art theme. Something that you may notice is that you will never see any of the character's eyes, they are either obsured by a helmet or a hat, or just shadowed. This really conveys the hopelessness of the characters and the hellishness of their experience.
The combat: Ironically, the combat is not my favourite thing about the game, it's good don't get me wrong, and there are some really unique things you can do with the compositions.
No Varience of the higher levels of bosses: This is a weakness, there are 3 levels of bosses in the game, yet they don't change in look or combat, purely just hitting harder. This is dissapointing, and a simple reskin would have done wonders.
A little grindy/repitive: Darkest Dungeon kinda falls into the pitfall of grinding. Whether it's for money, levels or unlocking a boss, the game sometimes feels repitive.
Difficult: This is a borderline one, as it is less of an issue to some people (like me) The game is purposely hard, and when characters die, they stay dead. If you cannot handle a set back, this game might be a little much for you. Also you get screwed over by RNG a lot, but sometimes it goes in your favour as well.
All in all, I believe Darkest Dungeon is an incredible game, not only in the gameplay, but in the atmosphere and overall innovation, and I heavily reccommend the game.

Positives: Beautiful artwork and sound, engrossing turn-based adventuring in procedurally generated maps with equally random enemies and choices, limited resources forcing innovative decision-making from players, and no bugs or programming flaws that I've managed to locate in over eighty hours of play.
Negatives: Large margin RNG for player and enemy combat that can reduce even carefully built situations to nothing, lack of player-motivated saves to prevent replaying of situations in the hope of a better outcome, (practical) permadeath aspect of characters, repetitive feeling to play even with procedurally generated levels (though that might be because I've played it as much as I have).
Recommendation: Do not buy if you get frustrated at losing progress through random events and/or do not enjoy turn-based side-scrolling dungeon crawlers. This is a punishing, cruel, and vicious game. It can and will reduce you to swearing at it and declaring that the developers wanted nothing more than to torture players with unwinnable gameplay.
I accepted this when I bought it. And I have revelled in that torture ever since.
I'll admit, I might be a bit masochistic but the atmosphere created by this game, the delicious richness of the artwork and the intricate working of its turn-based mechanics coupled with a generous helping of RNG make victory very hard to attain but oh so very satisfying when you finally grasp it.
The one moment when a Man-At-Arms brings down his mace and destroys a nigh-unbreakable cannon. The meaty rip of a broken blade tearing through a tentacled horror, vivisecting it before it has a chance to react. The rush of watching an archer wrestle with her inner demons, then take on a look of determination that banishes fear and demands evil flee lest it be riddled with crossbow bolts. Those moments are the ones I treasure when playing Darkest Dungeon.
You won't need eye-hand coordination here but you will need careful planning, a willingness to persist despite losing carefully crafted characters to a run of bad luck or a single crippling blow that forces you to withdraw and leave them to the monsters you have tried to drive out of your ancestral home.
But just as folks sit at slot machines for hours on end, waiting for that one moment, that single time when all the symbols are just right, so too do I stack the odds in my own favour as much as I can, then push into the claustrophobic corridors and gore-spattered rooms to see if this time will be different. If this time, I can at last rid the world of a shambling horror, a failed experiment in flesh-manipulation, a cannibalistic wretch, or things that don't belong anywhere save in nightmares.
The game is very easy to learn, has plenty of guides and information to assist the beginner, while keeping statistics and mechanics tucked away to keep even veteran players guessing. If I dig into that pile of corpses, will there be something of value within or will it just give a crippling infection? When the strain of dealing with unspeakable horrors becomes too much, will the adventurers bond together in their resolve or turn against one another?
I like that uncertainty, that feeling of creeping doom that comes of wondering if I'm going to turn a corner and bump into something I hadn't planned on and really do not want to face. Because it can happen and does happen with just enough frequency that it becomes unnerving. I wander through a dungeon and watch my party mop the floors with the inhabitants, then stare in awe as a tentacled monstrosity rips through them as if they were made of tissue paper.
But I'll be back. And I'll keep coming back because I love this world and this game. I started playing because I like saving the world from nightmares.

XCOM 2 is a turn based tactical strategy game, releasing on PC in February 2016. The game is a direct sequel to XCOM Enemy Unknown which was released in 2012. XCOM 2 was developed by 2K Games and Firaxis Games.
Like the first game, game play is separated into two. A management style simulator of controlling your base, and technologies inside it, whether it be through engineering or scientific research – allowing you to advance certain aspects of your base how you choose. Along with the base management side of the game, there is also a map style function which is where you move your ship around the world to different locations, or hubs of activity. Whilst on the map you will see side missions, your main missions, scrap piles to explore for extra money, along with a plethora of other activities to take part in.
The main mechanic in XCOM is of course the tactical squad based game play.  This squad of soldiers can consist of five different classes, which again can be specialized even further by using the skills tree which you earn points in through promoting your squad members. To begin with the classes start out very much the same apart from the weapons that they use. After you have gained a few promotions with the characters you will start to differentiate the classes quite a bit with the abilities they will gain. The actual in game mechanics are very much the same as the previous version of XCOM, but just with general improvements. The game’s cover base system works really well, with some handy UI enhancements that make it easier to see how the cover affects you.  What I wasn’t too keen on was the aiming mechanic. On countless occasions I found myself face-to-face with a foe, and still my percentage chance to hit them with my gun would be around 30%. I know there is always going to be a chance anyone will miss a target, but c’mon, these are trained soldiers in point blank range, it shouldn’t be that low. This became increasingly annoying as you progress through the game onto harder enemies which make a habit of getting up close and personal with you.  Overall I found the game play in XCOM to be really intuitive and very addictive with that “oh one more turn” feel to it.
Graphically, XCOM 2 is a really stellar looking title. Absolutely crisp animations of anything that moves, right the way down to the rag doll effect of bodies when they get shot (or blown apart). It just looks so fluid that it feels real. The textures and character models are also really high quality too. Normally in tactical games like this the graphical element is more skinned down on to allow for more focus on the game play but not XCOM 2. It is one of the best looking games to come out in the past 12 months and one that will really challenge your rig if you want to push out max settings.  The voice acting is top notch too; I was a little disappointed that all of the enemies have the same kind of voice, but given that there is plenty of different enemies in the game to begin with, this can be forgiven a bit. I would have liked to have seen a little extra depth used with sound in the game mechanics; there is an element of stealth to the game play, at least at the start of missions. It would have been nice to have some sort of sound meter that would trigger alarms for the enemies if you made too much sound – again just a small improvement which would of made the immersion all that more deeper.
The game has varying levels of difficulty for the overall campaign – this of course is down to how hard you want the game to be.  After you have finished one play through of the game you will unlock “Ironman” mode which essentially saves your game after every action you take, meaning you cannot jump back a few saves if you messed something up. You have one chance to succeed and that is it. Given that the side missions in the campaign can make a real impact on how the rest of the game pans out, I see this as a really interesting game mode that has the potential to have endless amounts of replay ability. I have been playing for roughly 15 hours so far and I have just about finished my first play through. I will for sure be trying out the Ironman mode personally to see how hard it really can be. Where you start on the world map, and the in game maps are all randomly generated, so whilst the actual objectives of missions may stay the same, where you carry out those objectives will differ from play through to play through.
Technically, I had a couple of issues. The main one being I did get random crashes. A few of these caused my graphics drivers to crash. This stopped when I configured an SLI profile for my two 970s and helped with the overall performance of the game too thankfully.  I was happy enough playing on 1080p given the high quality of the graphics on show to begin with. My rig was not capable of playing at 4k, and to be honest I think you would struggle to find a rig to play any of today’s recent releases on 4k.  Whack you’re AA up to max and you won’t really notice a difference though.
XCOM 2 is by far the best game in the series so far; the graphical enhancement of the game, as well as the improvements made on the already core game play mechanics makes this a tactical turn based player’s wet dream. Apart from the technical issues I had, I have struggled to find anything major wrong with this release.  The game’s regular price tag of £34, 99 is the mark of this being a AAA release; the sceptics amongst us will want to wait for this to drop into the sales market but if you are keen to pick up where Enemy Unknown left off, XCOM 2 will definitely keep you entertained for plenty more hours with a greater gaming experience.

EDIT:
I loved Enemy Unknown. I loved Enemy Within (although the multiplayer started to plummet downhill at that point). Despite having to switch to pc for this game, I sincerely wanted to love it too. I was thoroughly caught up in the pre-launch hype.
I initially wrote the review, below, when the game was only a few months old. Now that all the DLCs are out (I didn't buy them) and the game's been patched to somehwere close to completion, I've come back to change my review from positive to negative.
I am back playing again, after abandoning this game in apathy, several months ago, but I'm not playing the game that Firaxis designed; I'm playing the game that Long War studios designed, Long War 2.
And I love it, although I haven't got far in about 30 hours as the game still takes forever to play on my pc despite minimum settings. What Long War 2 has highlighted for me, is just how poorly designed the vaniilla game was. While I can give Firaxis some credit for the procedural maps (although I liked the old maps too), the new character pool design and a decent enough plot, the actual game they designed, and I'm talking about both the strategy layer and the tactical battles, is awful. Scanning for missions was irritating due to the constant interuptions; most of the rooms you build in the avenger have little point in being there, the classes were perfunctory clones of the EU/EW classes at best with one in particular being OP at the start of a campaign and another blatantly OP at the end. But worst of all were the way the battles were plagued by the woeful pod mechanics which caused the alien pods to home in your squad even before leaving stealth. Which, combined with the punishing mission timers, took all the joy out of the battles, and most of the tactical options too. You either blow everything up and rush through it, or you lose. that's it.
Frankly, there's barely any part of the vanilla game that hasn't been improved by modders, which just shows how little thought, how little love, these developers actually put into their game. They did enough to market it to the masses, make their money and then move on. Meanwhile the modders work for free to design a good game, leaving the players themselves to try and balance the game to their preference, knowing all along while they do it that their efforts could be ruined by Firaxis's patches (but only when they have DLC to sell) that break mods and corrupt save files, leaving more work for modders and players in their wake. A very lengthy procedure. And one the modders and players shouldn't have had to do.
Thank god for the Long War studios. Now, in a single mod, most of that effort has been taken away and players can finally just sit down and enjoy a game without first having to design their own.
By the way, I've stopped trying to use the steam controller with this game. The bugs which Firaxis introduced with their very first patch have still not been fixed and I have no faith that they ever will be. The double click bug still persists. I'm not sure about the other bug, which ended your turn prematurely.
So, in summry, I don't recommend this game. But, if you can pick it up cheap (and don't bother with the DLCs), then the Long War 2 mod is definitely worth your time. And, despite having only been out for about a fortnight at this point, it's already been patched and improved more than the vanilla game has been since release.
Original review:
The basic, vanilla, game is good. Just good. It's a well thought out concept but it lacks any depth. If you play this game without modding it then, you'll probably enjoy it but, it won't leave anywhere near as lasting an impression as the previous versions (EU/EW). Where Firaxis have been clever is in embracing the modding community because they've now given themselves, and you and me, access to an army of talented, altruistic modders, working for free to add depth to the vanilla game and make it incredible.
After only a few months, there are already an incredible amount of mods that add cosmetic features, voice packs, quality of life improvements (many of which should really have been in the vanilla game anyway - 'evac all', for example, is a glaring omission), extra map content, extra advent/alien units, extra missions and added meaning to the strategy layer by tweaking the parts that, on reflection, don't make much sense (scientists>engineers for staffing the lab, for example, or the horrible way in which you can level up completely overpowered psi units) and even an upgraded launcher is available with which to manage your mods because, yet again, the one Firaxis actually provided is parsimonious and lazy.
The only problem with all this, is the time and dedication you'll need to experiemnt with mods and difficulty settings in order to find the balance of play that suits you best. I'm nearly 200 hours in and I haven't found mine yet. Mind, that wasn't helped by UI difficulties. As an ex-console player of EU/EW (ie I like to sit on my couch ;-P), the transition to keyboard/mouse is not easy and I tried to get the best of both worlds by using a steam controller. Almost my first 20 hours was spent configuring this to my liking (I had hundreds of hours of console, muscle-memory telling me that the left trigger is the camera zoom and now I'm supposed to use it as the move/shoot button! Fat chance!).
And then they patched the game to coincide with the first DLC and, unfortunately introduced bugs to the steam controller UI (I get an unwanted double click in the menus and can sometimes end my turn on the battlefield prematurely simply by pressing the move/shoot button after a left click). These aren't game breaking but, nonetheless, are annoying and will hopefully be patched out.
So, if you don't have this sort of time or dedication available, you could try watching some youtubers (there are seemingly hundreds of them crawling out of the woodwork now) and copying the mods they've used. Let someone else balance it for you, leaving you only to fine tune it, at the end, to yourself.
The multiplayer is tagged on and uncared for. It badly needs a points rebalancing. Tier 3 advent officers are currently only 400 pts, for example, so you'll be seeing a lot of them. I'd recommend you only play against friends as the rankings system is still a toxic playground for disconnecters and is haunted by one particularly obsessive and abusive individual who's learned to hide behind a never ending series of pseudonyms in order to get people to play him more than once. You may get the feeling that there's an army of arseh@les playing this game. There's not, it's just one. I'd suggest you treat this as a single player game only, it's not worth the hassle, right now, of playing strangers competitively.
TL/DR: I heartily recommend it. But it's a modded version I'm really recommending, and we're all likely to end up playing a slightly different game to eachother. The vanilla game is just a shell on which to build.

The controls aren't meerly challenging as they are unpredictable. It's often difficult to tell what pressing forward will cause the bread to do; sometimes flopping one way or the other. The degree of motion is also somewhat confusing. Throwing the stick in a direction  can send the bread in a flying leap or have it just limply flop over. This sounds minor, until you factor in rediculous time limits and surfaces that can rapidly drain your health from a momentary touch.
The physics engine can't behave itself (check the community page, it's like 60% gifs of the physics bugging out). Which again, is cute to see happen, but when you've spent 5 minutes making your way across a level, only to be thrown across the room by a bug, it quickly turns from cute to controller snapping frustrating.
If you can pick it up for a couple of bucks the wackiness is certainly charming and distracting, but ultimatly the frustrating lack of agency in the game play will probably have you giving up long before you've explored most of the content.

Dr. Gordon Freeman arrives late for work at 8:47 am in the Black Mesa Research Facility, using the advanced Black Mesa tram system that leads through the facility. He arrives at the Anomalous Materials Lab, his work place, and he is informed by the security officer that the scientists have a special experiment today, so he goes to the locker room and puts on the hazard suit. He goes to the lab's lower levels, and arrives at the Anti-Mass Chamber, where he is instructed that the specimen to be used that day is the rarest and also the most unstable specimen the lab has ever worked with. He is tasked with pushing the specimen into the scanning beam of the Anti-Mass Spectrometer for analysis. players enlist the help of traumatized scientists and trigger-happy security guards to get through high-security zones, sneaking and fighting your way through ruined missile silos and Cold War cafeterias, through darkened airducts and subterranean railways. When you finally come in sight of the surface, you realize that the inhuman monsters aren't your only enemies-for the government has sent in ruthless troops and stealthy assassins. There are no levels in Half-Life, or, more specifically, it lacks the concept of levels and episodes we've come to expect. The game is a continual stream of locations from beginning to end. You can move back and forth at will (with only a few exceptions), as can those who are pursuing you. And though the brief loading time between zones is the one artifact that breaks the flow of the game, the transitions are thankfully brief.
Weapon, ammunition, and health placement follows the same philosophy. You'll hardly ever come across an item that is just bobbing and spinning in place like some gift from the heavens. Valve has done a good job of justifying the typical health and armor meters. Freeman is wearing a hazard suit, used by researchers involved in dangerous experiments. To regain health and armor energy, you must fill up at power stations. These are almost always located in logical places, usually near areas where dangerous work would be performed. There are no power-ups to be found. Weapons and ammo are taken from supply closets or the corpses of fallen security guards and soldiers. Even the more experimental weapons have their proper place - in the weapons research department of the facility. And late in the game, once you've left the research facility, the supply of ammo and first aid kits is believably scarce.
The only problems with Half-Life are the results of it being so ambitious. The fact that all of the humans in the game look like clones takes from the otherwise realistic atmosphere. The diversity of the levels and puzzles will undoubtedly leave you thinking some areas were better than others. But complaints that arise are simply a reaction to the fact that the game is so close to ideal. Half-Life is an exceptional single-player game and a solid multiplayer game.

Darkest Dungeon is one of my favourite games I have ever played, along with being one of the most unique. Thus, this review will be a little biased, but I will do my best to be as impartial and even as I possibly can. Red Hook have really done something special in this game, and I love how involved they are with the community, and the small additions they make such as the new content and patches, the extra artworks and pieces to the character's past that are posted on the forums, and the great interactions I see by the Red Hook staff.
The Narrator: I cannot stress enough how amazing the Narrator, or the Ancestor is in this game. He does an incredible job at setting the tone and the atmosphere of the game, and has a great voice all around. This is aided by the fact that Darkest Dungeon has some amazing writing, and choice quotes.
The Music and the Sounds of the Game: The music and sounds of the game are excellent, aiding the narrator in making the game's atmosphere as great as it is.
The Characters: The characters in Darkest Dungeon are written very well, and Red Hook do a great job of developing the characters with the small amount of time that they use. The afflicted and virtuous quotes really add to them.
The Overall Art Style: Another great thing the game does is the art theme. Something that you may notice is that you will never see any of the character's eyes, they are either obsured by a helmet or a hat, or just shadowed. This really conveys the hopelessness of the characters and the hellishness of their experience.
The combat: Ironically, the combat is not my favourite thing about the game, it's good don't get me wrong, and there are some really unique things you can do with the compositions.
No Varience of the higher levels of bosses: This is a weakness, there are 3 levels of bosses in the game, yet they don't change in look or combat, purely just hitting harder. This is dissapointing, and a simple reskin would have done wonders.
A little grindy/repitive: Darkest Dungeon kinda falls into the pitfall of grinding. Whether it's for money, levels or unlocking a boss, the game sometimes feels repitive.
Difficult: This is a borderline one, as it is less of an issue to some people (like me) The game is purposely hard, and when characters die, they stay dead. If you cannot handle a set back, this game might be a little much for you. Also you get screwed over by RNG a lot, but sometimes it goes in your favour as well.
All in all, I believe Darkest Dungeon is an incredible game, not only in the gameplay, but in the atmosphere and overall innovation, and I heavily reccommend the game.

From the initial marketing I was overwhelmingly excited for this game to launch, with the previous fallout games being masterpieces of gaming for their genre I instinctively had the highest hopes for Fallout 4.
That's why this review has to be written, because I've never been so disappointed in a game like this before.
Initially the game is set up quite well and there's a sense of excitement and wonder uncovering the truth of the institute and the fate of your son. I personally enjoyed the main story and can't find thinks to pick at.
One of the things I didn't like about Fallout 4 was the dullness of the side quests.
!SPOILER ALERT!
For example the hole in the wall quest, the vault dwellers had no personality and story that I could integrate with to make me care about the decisions gor that quest. In other fallout games most people atleast give you some back story or let you help out with petty problems. As far as I was concerned the vault dwellers were about as interactive as raiders :/
I also think the way the wasteland is set out initially is horrible, first off all of the proper settlements are either faction settlements or diamond city (I say proper referring to "I can fully interact with the ai there") and the other settlements are full of people of raider level intelligence who spit randomly generated quests for me. One of my biggest complaints is how concord sets up the world, giving you access to both power armor and a minigun (both end game equipment - to some degree) while facing off against a deathclaw (an end game enemy) just feels so wrong at the beginning of a game... It really nullifies the rest of the experience imo, which is why I steer clear of it every new game.
I don't think I need to repeat this in detail, but the perk system and talking stuff is just♥♥♥♥♥♥..
The game also performs rather crap in a lot of areas, I initially played the full game on medium - low on my old 780 ti and when I got my new pc with a 1080 I expected a huge boost in fps, but I really didn't see any change which was more then a little disappointing.
Finally we reach post game content. I was happy with Fallout 4 once I had finished it, it was an average game but a pretty terrible fallout game. I got entertainment out of that and that's all that mattered.
I was expecting Fallout 4's dlc to be of the same size and quantity of atleast Fallout : New Vegas. Unfortunately we ended up with two moderately sized expansions that didn't contain much (I really liked far harbour, even though it was more or less a copy and paste from Fallout 3's point lookout) and a bunch of smaller additions that should've been in the game at launch (the vault expansion I'm not including as a large expansion because it mimics the same stuff that's present in the game and adds the same value as the smaller expansions.
I just feel like all the dlc was half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ If they added two more larger expansions I would've been happier but I doubt it would've raised the quality of the game beyond average.
Now with the addition of the creation club... It's like I was holding Fallout 4 in my arms with chewing gun and cement being the only thing stopping it from falling apart, believeing it was still the game i wanted it to be, now Bethesda comes along and smacks Fallout 4 out of my arms and it's just left it in ruins.
It will take huge effort for my faith to be restored. For now, I do not recommend buying this game unless you've never played a Fallout game before and you lower your expectations greatly :(

This is a punishing, cruel, and vicious game. It can and will reduce you to swearing at it and declaring that the developers wanted nothing more than to torture players with unwinnable gameplay.
I accepted this when I bought it. And I have revelled in that torture ever since.
I'll admit, I might be a bit masochistic but the atmosphere created by this game, the delicious richness of the artwork and the intricate working of its turn-based mechanics coupled with a generous helping of RNG make victory very hard to attain but oh so very satisfying when you finally grasp it.
The one moment when a Man-At-Arms brings down his mace and destroys a nigh-unbreakable cannon. The meaty rip of a broken blade tearing through a tentacled horror, vivisecting it before it has a chance to react. The rush of watching an archer wrestle with her inner demons, then take on a look of determination that banishes fear and demands evil flee lest it be riddled with crossbow bolts. Those moments are the ones I treasure when playing Darkest Dungeon.
You won't need eye-hand coordination here but you will need careful planning, a willingness to persist despite losing carefully crafted characters to a run of bad luck or a single crippling blow that forces you to withdraw and leave them to the monsters you have tried to drive out of your ancestral home.
But just as folks sit at slot machines for hours on end, waiting for that one moment, that single time when all the symbols are just right, so too do I stack the odds in my own favour as much as I can, then push into the claustrophobic corridors and gore-spattered rooms to see if this time will be different. If this time, I can at last rid the world of a shambling horror, a failed experiment in flesh-manipulation, a cannibalistic wretch, or things that don't belong anywhere save in nightmares.
The game is very easy to learn, has plenty of guides and information to assist the beginner, while keeping statistics and mechanics tucked away to keep even veteran players guessing. If I dig into that pile of corpses, will there be something of value within or will it just give a crippling infection? When the strain of dealing with unspeakable horrors becomes too much, will the adventurers bond together in their resolve or turn against one another?
I like that uncertainty, that feeling of creeping doom that comes of wondering if I'm going to turn a corner and bump into something I hadn't planned on and really do not want to face. Because it can happen and does happen with just enough frequency that it becomes unnerving. I wander through a dungeon and watch my party mop the floors with the inhabitants, then stare in awe as a tentacled monstrosity rips through them as if they were made of tissue paper.
But I'll be back. And I'll keep coming back because I love this world and this game. I started playing because I like saving the world from nightmares.
Now? Now I'm playing for that and one thing more: to prove that, despite dealing with recalcitrant heroes, devastating battles that turned against me due to a single critcal hit, and watching my graveyard fill with the hopeful and the hopeless alike, I WILL one day obliterate the slavering things that dwell in the very nadir...of the Darkest Dungeon.

So, two years ago I would have whole-heartedly reccommended this game. Hell, three days ago, I'd still have thought of it in it's vanilla form as a solid time sink, as buggy and uninpired as it was. But given the complications that have arisen with the creation club, this is not a game that you should even have on your hard drive. After sinking hundreds of hours into this (Modded, obviously) I'm going to have to uninstall it.
So, paid mods are bogus, as we already know. I'm happy to donate to good mod authors, and I'm happy to pay for real DLC, but we have several serious issues with this part on it's own, and they aren't even why I'm uninstalling the game. The first is the obvious "Why would I pay for this if I can get it better for free?". The second is that I can't just pay with money. I have to buy credits that don't match up with mod prices so I always overpay. And the third is thatr we're relying on Bethesda to make sure the mods are functional. That last one really gets me, as the modding community is almost a necessity because Bethesda games are so buggy to begin with. Why would I trust the creators of a broken product to give me something that works?
This also seems to be something of an effort to eliminate free mods to some degree, since every time the creation club updates, so to does Fallout 4, which makes F4SE no longer work properly. Which turns your game into a crash-fest, if it runs at all. Given how much content should be flowing through the creation club, if they truely want to allow players to mod the game in any meaningful way, this means daily updates for Fallout 4, and by extension F4SE, which is a ♥♥♥♥ing headache at the end of the day when I just want to unwind and play video games.
But those things are actually pretty minor to the now redundant final nail in the coffin of Fallout 4. For some reason, every single mod on the creation club is automatically downloaded on to your hard drive wether or not you've paid for it. You pay to unlock it basically. This is stupid on the developers part, because now I can get those mods for free (if they were worth the effort to steal, but they're not), but the big downside to this is that as more mods are added to the creation club, the more room it's going to take up on your hard drive. Right now, there are 12 mods on the creation club, with those files alone totalling around 600 Mb and the update totalling 2Gb, somehow. What the creation club has done is turn Fallout 4 into a $100 bloatware virus. So, because I run fallout 4 on an SSD, that's gonna fill up pretty damn quick, given just how many mods are out there. So, that game has got to go.

I've put plenty of time into Fallout 4, and let me tell you it's pry one of the weakest games I've ever played from Bethesda.
First off, it's highly insulting to the player. You really think your dialogue choices matter? Nope, for some baffling reason there's a voiced protagonist now so don't expect much deviation in conversations. But hey, at least the number of lines recorded is really really high!
Hours and hours of content?! If you think a poorly designed and implemented radiant quest system is content that's always fun and engaging instead of filler... then I suppose that it's true?
A well written and branching narrative that will hook you right in? Let's see if you can guess the act two twist based on the first 15 minutes of the story: Your wife/husband is killed and strange men have taken your baby, but not before refreezing you for an indeterminable amount of time which no one ever seems to realize until said twist. Also this game has one of the dumbest plot holes I have ever seen. You didn't pick up the friendly dog as a companion weeks ago when you first emerged from the Vault? Here allow me to whistle so that this one specific dog, that is miles away and outside the city, runs literally the same path that took you hours to get through in a matter of seconds. Truly some of the most laughably bad plots I've ever seen.
Oh and don't forget the "Creation Club" which is supposed to provide only simple reskins (Mind you all this is at the time of writing, so hopefully they've removed all traces where you are in the future). Think there will be any quests that you can pay hard working modders for? Nope, seeing as there is a file size limit that renders quests near impossible. It's a genuinely awful system that has sucked most, if not all, the good will I had towards Bethesda.
TL;DR

When I read the Kickstarter I was pretty hyped, not to mention a community I was in hyping it up as well. While I did enjoy it for the first 50 hours or so, it just got...boring (this is coming from someone who has 290+ hours in Terraria). No matter how much I tried I just could not get back into it. The game has several problems, but I'll just list what I think are the biggest ones:
-The generated monsters. The creators described the creatures of Starbound as "infinite", however they all look like Pokemon rejects. They're only 2 types (ones who stay on the ground and the ones who fly) and only around 3 types of attacks (charging at you, spitting fire at you, and one I'm forgetting). Some are neutral, some are aggressive. They still have a major lack in variety.
-Performance. The game is just not optimized. I may have a♥♥♥♥♥♥PC but I've heard of people with high-end PCs having trouble running the game. I mean come on, the game doesn't even look that good. This is unacceptable.
-Bugs. While you may not notice them at first, the game is crawling with them.
-Races. There is simply no need to play as ANY race, because races do not have special abilities, rather their armor does. This is a problem when the developers boast their races and how they are special and unique when in reality they're not.
-Planets. The game's planets are not randomly generated from person to person. This means that a person could share coordinates to a planet where it may have great loot which effectively kills exploration except if you're the one who is adding on to that list, which most people are not.
-Content. I hear a lot of people say that this game is loaded with content, even more so than Terraria. This is simply false, and anyone you hear say this is delusional. Starbound's content consists mostly of useless♥♥♥♥♥♥and randomly generated weapons and creatures. There are more ACTUAL weapons and creatures (no, taking 2 types with 3 attack types and splicing colors and forms does NOT count as a seperate creature) in Terraria that are not randomly generated (sans their modifier, which can be reforged). They may be equal on cosmetics and building material, but that's not the main game.
Overall, this game is a mess. It does nothing special and WILL get old.

Joseph Vissarionovich Stalin[a] (18 December 1878 – 5 March 1953) was a Georgian-born Soviet revolutionary and political leader. Governing the Soviet Union as its dictator from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953, he served as General Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1952 and as Premier of the Soviet Union from 1941 to 1953. Ideologically a Marxist and a Leninist, Stalin helped to formalise these ideas as Marxism–Leninism while his own policies became known as Stalinism.
Born to a poor family in Gori, Russian Empire, as a youth Stalin joined the Marxist Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. He edited the party newspaper Pravda and raised funds for Vladimir Lenin's Bolshevik faction via robberies, kidnappings, and protection rackets. Repeatedly arrested, he underwent several internal exiles. After the Bolsheviks gained power in the October Revolution of 1917 and established the Russian Soviet Republic, Stalin sat on the governing Politburo during the Russian Civil War and helped form the Soviet Union in 1922. Despite Lenin's opposition, Stalin consolidated power following the former's death in 1924. During Stalin's tenure, "Socialism in One Country" became a central concept in Soviet society, and Lenin's New Economic Policy was replaced with a centralised command economy, industrialisation and collectivisation. These rapidly transformed the country into an industrial power, but disrupted food production and contributed to the famine of 1932–33, particularly affecting Ukraine. To eradicate those regarded as "enemies of the working class", from 1934 to 1939 Stalin organised the "Great Purge" in which hundreds of thousands—including senior political and military figures—were interned in prison camps, exiled, or executed.
Stalin's government promoted Marxism–Leninism abroad through the Communist International and supported anti-fascist movements throughout Europe during the 1930s, particularly in the Spanish Civil War. However, in 1939 they signed a non-aggression pact with Nazi Germany, resulting in their joint invasion of Poland. Germany ended the pact by invading the Soviet Union in 1941. Despite initial setbacks, the Soviet Red Army halted the German incursion and captured Berlin in May 1945, ending World War II in Europe. The Soviets annexed the Baltic states and helped establish pro-Soviet Marxist–Leninist governments throughout Eastern Europe. The Soviet Union and the United States emerged as the two world superpowers, and a period of tensions began between the Soviet-backed Eastern Bloc and U.S.-backed Western Bloc known as the Cold War. Stalin led his country through its post-war reconstruction, during which it developed a nuclear weapon. In these years, the country experienced another major famine and a period of antisemitism, which reached its peak in the 1952–1953 Doctors' plot. Stalin died in 1953 and was succeeded by Nikita Khrushchev, who denounced his predecessor and initiated a de-Stalinisation process throughout Soviet society.
Widely considered one of the 20th century's most significant figures, Stalin was the subject of a pervasive personality cult within the world Marxist–Leninist movement, for whom Stalin was a champion of socialism and the working class. Since the fall of the Soviet Union, Stalin has retained popularity in Russia and Georgia as a victorious wartime leader who established the Soviet Union as a major world power. Conversely, his autocratic government has been widely denounced for overseeing mass repressions, hundreds of thousands of executions and millions of non-combatant deaths through his policies.

Half life 1, well were to begin, everybody and their long lost relatives know what half life is and they also know how much it raised the "FPS" genre onto its feet and pushed the bar high. A lot of modern day shooters fail to provide the atmosphere and the fluid simple controls of this great title, There have been so many people reviewing this game so I'm finding it quite hard to start so i guess i shall start by telling you what the game is about.
-----SPOILERS----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Dr. Gordon Freeman arrives late for work at 8:47 am in the Black Mesa Research Facility, using the advanced Black Mesa tram system that leads through the facility. He arrives at the Anomalous Materials Lab, his work place, and he is informed by the security officer that the scientists have a special experiment today, so he goes to the locker room and puts on the hazard suit. He goes to the lab's lower levels, and arrives at the Anti-Mass Chamber, where he is instructed that the specimen to be used that day is the rarest and also the most unstable specimen the lab has ever worked with. He is tasked with pushing the specimen into the scanning beam of the Anti-Mass Spectrometer for analysis. However as soon as he pushes it, it explodes, and creates a sudden catastrophe called a "resonance cascade"
-----SPOILERS----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The story is really good, its actually quite funny, modern games often spend massive amounts of money on spectacular scenes and explosions and deep heart felt commentary in order to set the mood......But How does half life do it that right with a 8-10 minute opening "TRAM RIDE" into the Black Mesa facility, and all it really is, is Mr. freeman going into work that day, and that scene alone provides one of the most enigmatic experiences i have ever felt in the prologue of a game.
players enlist the help of traumatized scientists and trigger-happy security guards to get through high-security zones, sneaking and fighting your way through ruined missile silos and Cold War cafeterias, through darkened airducts and subterranean railways. When you finally come in sight of the surface, you realize that the inhuman monsters aren't your only enemies-for the government has sent in ruthless troops and stealthy assassins. Their orders seem to be that when it comes to the Black Mesa, nothing gets out alive... and especially not you.
That said the journy would be nothing without great enemys with complex ways to kill them like the headcrabs, and nothing would kill them better than the coverted crowbar that "Freeman" Wields. The weapons apart from that are nothing special, exept maybe the laser designated RPG launch
There are no levels in Half-Life, or, more specifically, it lacks the concept of levels and episodes we've come to expect. The game is a continual stream of locations from beginning to end. You can move back and forth at will (with only a few exceptions), as can those who are pursuing you. And though the brief loading time between zones is the one artifact that breaks the flow of the game, the transitions are thankfully brief.
Weapon, ammunition, and health placement follows the same philosophy. You'll hardly ever come across an item that is just bobbing and spinning in place like some gift from the heavens. Valve has done a good job of justifying the typical health and armor meters. Freeman is wearing a hazard suit, used by researchers involved in dangerous experiments. To regain health and armor energy, you must fill up at power stations. These are almost always located in logical places, usually near areas where dangerous work would be performed. There are no power-ups to be found. Weapons and ammo are taken from supply closets or the corpses of fallen security guards and soldiers. Even the more experimental weapons have their proper place - in the weapons research department of the facility. And late in the game, once you've left the research facility, the supply of ammo and first aid kits is believably scarce.
The only problems with Half-Life are the results of it being so ambitious. The fact that all of the humans in the game look like clones takes from the otherwise realistic atmosphere. The diversity of the levels and puzzles will undoubtedly leave you thinking some areas were better than others. But complaints that arise are simply a reaction to the fact that the game is so close to ideal. Half-Life is an exceptional single-player game and a solid multiplayer game.

I would often try new weapons or items, say "oh, that's how that works" and then have to reload from an earlier save to use it correctly.
As far as game stability: I am playing on a 3-year-old iMac at 1080p and the game never once glitched or crashed. Animation was quite smooth, too.
In regards to the timed missions, I don't have a particular problem with that as it adds a layer of interest by forcing the player to try different tactics, squad assignments, and loadouts to solve the tactical problem. On the other hand, these missions are quite unforgiving and I relied heavily on reloading earlier saves when missions went FUBAR.
A complaint I have is that a lot of the more interesting items you can build are not that valuable in most missions so they end up not worth using. For example, by the time you are able to build the flamethrower and gas grenades, most of the enemies you encounter are immune to fire and poison and so there is no incentive to equip these items.
In regards to game difficulty, about 1/3 of the way through the game is really tough due to a lack of intel and supplies. I was on the verge of losing the macro game several times as the Avatar meter filled all the way up. However, once you push past that point the game gets much easier as your weapons and armor finally begin to match and then overmatch your oppenents.
So highly recommended as a tactical, turn-based wargame; but I will say that if I didn't have the ability to reload game saves as often as I wanted, I probably would not rate it nearly as high as that would ratchet up the difficultly considerably.

Having the fanboy hype at a maximum, I "thought" I was having a blast. 10 hours in, you realize that the side quests seem a little repetitive and the dialogue is literally Yes, No, or Yes but with sass. 15 hours in, you know that it's the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over. Retrieve this, save that, kill this. There is no wacky adventure like the Super heroes in Fallout 3 or the creepy vault crawl of the parasitic plants in Fallout: New Vegas.
Every side quest is forgettable and the main quest is a rehash of Fallout 3. Despite all of the improvements, they neglicted the real thing that Fallout so great: The Story.
Fallout 4 is gonna go down as a regrettable installment to the series, a game that should of been handed over to another company that cares. The real story is in the DLC, which you have to buy if you want an actual Fallout experience. Not worth it.
So for the score, I would have to give it a 4 out of 10.
-Great customization
-Improved gameplay
-no story
-repetitive
-linear despite being a RPG
If you want a fun game, I recommend Witcher 3 or the older Fallouts. There is nothing here but a shooter set in the Fallout universe.

first off, i must note I am a very impatient fellow.
That being said, I hate all that is this game. This is a trial and error sort of game, the trouble being every trial can last about 15 minutes or longer.  the first hour of the game is spent trying to get used to the controls. Then you blunder along trying not to touch the floor or other various things through each room. Apparently the controls are better with a controller, but after trying it with my steam controller, they were even worse. I am using a keyboard and mouse, and while I got the controls down pretty good finally, some things are just random and uncontrollable.
When you are not figthing the controls, you are fighting the camera and it is very hard to navigate up a wall with limited grip time while having to adjust the camera as well and trying to squish yourself up between two tight spaces.
It took me like 20 minutes just to fit inside a toaster thanks to flaily bread controls.
Anyway, the gameplay itself is unique and clever, but not very fun. It is just repeating the same thing over again until you figure something out to get you further along in your helpless search for a heat source.
When you miraculously reach a heat source, good luck trying to find the place where it actually would heat you up. I am not sure if there are certain spots only that are hot, or if the game just isn't working correctly. For example, I was climbing all over a space heater, but only one tiny spot on the whole thing heated me up. As you scramble around the heat source trying to get toasted, you will likely fall off and die. Not very fun.
If you are a more patient human being than I and enjoy doing long repetitions of bread flopping over everything, then buy it. I personally find it very boring, slow moving and frustrating because you never feel truly in control.
The game does give people like me some help though. If you fail twice on a given level, some super butter or something comes and gives you unlimited life and grip. This makes beating the levels much easier, but it makes a boring game even more boring.
One good thing I can say about "I Am Bread" is that there is a rather large amount of content. Too bad the game is too horrible to play through it all. I usually force myself to beat terrible games, but for the second time in memory, I have had enough after 5 levels.

Most of the missions have turn limits for objectives, so you can't always just move/oversee/move/oversee your way through every map.  Sometimes you have to play it more fast and loose.
The bad: 30gigs was a bit large for my SSD, so load times were slow off of my 7200RPM disk.  Once a mission is loaded though they generally run well.  Some animation issues here and there where they may forget to play in combat.  A couple of odd sound buggs.  In my first play through, I only had one actual crash.  The interface isn't always obvious if you'll have Line-Of-Site to a target when you move.
Overall:  If you liked X-Com 1, this is more delicious X-Com goodness.  If you didn't like the first, skip it.

The good:
-Great soundtrack and use of instrument items.
-Randomly-generated enemies get amusing designs sometimes, with those in higher tiers gaining new abilities (curse you barb spray).
-Backstory behind all the races can influence how they interact with eachother, though only in dialogue currently.
-Randomly generated, but consistently so, allowing coordinates to be shared between players to find cool stuff.
-Pokemon.
The bad:
-Bosses can be cheesed pretty easily, sometimes by accident.
-In fact, the entire game can be cheesed, really. Between burrowing just under the surface, walling myself off from enemies, and using a movement tech to fly over stuff, I soloed the game all the way to the final tier, crafted endgame armor, and found a tier-ten legendary sword without ever crafting a chestpiece, which means I had 1/2 the armor and 1/5 the health I should have had for the entire game and still managed to complete it. Shouldn't something prevent that?
-Gameplay gets repetitive. There are different planetary and underground biomes, but even the tentacle and heck biomes still play the same as the others, just with cosmetic changes, and any biome-specific loot is fairly inconsequential.
-There are STILL dungeon/NPC instances I have yet to encounter, but I don't really need to, because they're all roughly the same (except the Portal-based one, that's pretty neat, but finding it without coordinates can be a chore, and it lags like hell even in singleplayer).
-Lackluster tutorial only briefly mentions some critical gameplay elements without actually showing them to you (Cooking? Bed healing? Pickaxe? Anvil? Nah, you don't need any of those, you'll be fine).
-Players in multiplayer can destroy your ship decorations and steal your locker items unless you build your base on an asteroid far above the planet's surface.
Conclusion:
If you like building stuff, play Minecraft.
If you like fighting stuff, play Terraria.
If you like exploring stuff, play Starbound.

I bought this game just before their first “free weekend”, and found quickly that it is a challenging game that is constantly in the process of evolving. As an early-access Alpha, the growing community had direct input into how the game evolves, the feedback of the players directly impacting the direction of the game developers. This process proves that the game developers care about what their players have to say, and are building the game around the community, instead of trying to build a community around the game.
The game itself does have a small learning curve as there are numerous ships and play styles, along with more complicated tactics and strategies that are always evolving, but it’s well worth it to put in the time and effort necessary to master these skills. With more than 40 hours invested in this game, I still feel like I’m learning new things and tweaking my playstyle constantly in order to find new competitive edges.
Buyers keep in mind that the game is early-access, so not everything is perfect and polished yet, it is only an Alpha build, but its on a good track. What is currently available looks good, sounds good, and plays well. I’d recommend buying and buying now.

pros:
-> if you're a fan of top down fighting and dungeon crawling, this game can suck up your free time like a sponge
-> it's also a lot of fun to play with friends, up to a party of 4 players, from real life or haven
-> art style isn't shabby and pretty easy on the eyes, fun for any age range in the whole family
-> this game is already pretty old, but there's still a lot to do for newcomers and old pros alike
---> combat is very flush, with tons of flashy weapons and even more bad guys to use them on
---> there's plenty of background lore and tidbits like that hidden in this game if you're into that
---> feeling fabulous? theres lots of armor and accessories to help you look fly, and thats pretty fun
---> join or create a guild to form a small community with more than just 3 other players
cons:
-> there's a lot of incredibly useful hidden mechanics that the game really should teach you, like using your shield to cancel attack animations and increasing reaction time
-> a lot of the better weapons and armor can only be achieved through unconventional ways or buying it at an inflamed price, which can throw a wrench in your plans for your perfect arsenal
-> the game makes you grind a lot for ingame currency to be able to pass through a lot of the game
---> a remedy to this is if you do your homework and plan out what arsenal you want by the end of the game so that you dont make stupid descisions too early on in the game

-> there's not really any recent updates at all anymore, and the community is slowly shrinking...
conclusion:
i think this game won't last that much longer anymore,
but you should still get it and play if you like top down shooters and dungeon crawlers;

I really enjoyed this game, as I did the original Xcom. The character customization adds a lot more to the fun than I would have expected. In regards to gameplay, it is pretty much the same as the original Xcom, if you are familiar with that. My biggest complaint is that the game does not give much guidance on how weapons, items, and abilities function so you have to figure them out by trial and error. I would often try new weapons or items, say "oh, that's how that works" and then have to reload from an earlier save to use it correctly.
As far as game stability: I am playing on a 3-year-old iMac at 1080p and the game never once glitched or crashed. Animation was quite smooth, too.
In regards to the timed missions, I don't have a particular problem with that as it adds a layer of interest by forcing the player to try different tactics, squad assignments, and loadouts to solve the tactical problem. On the other hand, these missions are quite unforgiving and I relied heavily on reloading earlier saves when missions went FUBAR.
A complaint I have is that a lot of the more interesting items you can build are not that valuable in most missions so they end up not worth using. For example, by the time you are able to build the flamethrower and gas grenades, most of the enemies you encounter are immune to fire and poison and so there is no incentive to equip these items.
In regards to game difficulty, about 1/3 of the way through the game is really tough due to a lack of intel and supplies. I was on the verge of losing the macro game several times as the Avatar meter filled all the way up. However, once you push past that point the game gets much easier as your weapons and armor finally begin to match and then overmatch your oppenents.
So highly recommended as a tactical, turn-based wargame; but I will say that if I didn't have the ability to reload game saves as often as I wanted, I probably would not rate it nearly as high as that would ratchet up the difficultly considerably.

Completed my first run of the game the other day, Veteran difficulty.  This game rocked.  Great strategic play, I loved the randomized maps, research felt a lot clearner than the last game.  The revamped classes kick♥♥♥♥♥ although certain skill still seem to be no-brainers for Snipers.  Heavies are probably the most ballanced with some really hard choices.
Gameplay is still as brutal as ever.  Missing a shot can really hurt your team bad.  Expect to regularly bring home injured crews.  Most of the missions have turn limits for objectives, so you can't always just move/oversee/move/oversee your way through every map.  Sometimes you have to play it more fast and loose.
The bad: 30gigs was a bit large for my SSD, so load times were slow off of my 7200RPM disk.  Once a mission is loaded though they generally run well.  Some animation issues here and there where they may forget to play in combat.  A couple of odd sound buggs.  In my first play through, I only had one actual crash.  The interface isn't always obvious if you'll have Line-Of-Site to a target when you move.
Overall:  If you liked X-Com 1, this is more delicious X-Com goodness.  If you didn't like the first, skip it.
