From the initial marketing I was overwhelmingly excited for this game to launch, with the previous fallout games being masterpieces of gaming for their genre I instinctively had the highest hopes for Fallout 4.
That's why this review has to be written, because I've never been so disappointed in a game like this before.
Initially the game is set up quite well and there's a sense of excitement and wonder uncovering the truth of the institute and the fate of your son. I personally enjoyed the main story and can't find thinks to pick at.
One of the things I didn't like about Fallout 4 was the dullness of the side quests.
!SPOILER ALERT!
For example the hole in the wall quest, the vault dwellers had no personality and story that I could integrate with to make me care about the decisions gor that quest. In other fallout games most people atleast give you some back story or let you help out with petty problems. As far as I was concerned the vault dwellers were about as interactive as raiders :/
I also think the way the wasteland is set out initially is horrible, first off all of the proper settlements are either faction settlements or diamond city (I say proper referring to "I can fully interact with the ai there") and the other settlements are full of people of raider level intelligence who spit randomly generated quests for me. One of my biggest complaints is how concord sets up the world, giving you access to both power armor and a minigun (both end game equipment - to some degree) while facing off against a deathclaw (an end game enemy) just feels so wrong at the beginning of a game... It really nullifies the rest of the experience imo, which is why I steer clear of it every new game.
I don't think I need to repeat this in detail, but the perk system and talking stuff is just♥♥♥♥♥♥..
The game also performs rather crap in a lot of areas, I initially played the full game on medium - low on my old 780 ti and when I got my new pc with a 1080 I expected a huge boost in fps, but I really didn't see any change which was more then a little disappointing.
Finally we reach post game content. I was happy with Fallout 4 once I had finished it, it was an average game but a pretty terrible fallout game. I got entertainment out of that and that's all that mattered.
I was expecting Fallout 4's dlc to be of the same size and quantity of atleast Fallout : New Vegas. Unfortunately we ended up with two moderately sized expansions that didn't contain much (I really liked far harbour, even though it was more or less a copy and paste from Fallout 3's point lookout) and a bunch of smaller additions that should've been in the game at launch (the vault expansion I'm not including as a large expansion because it mimics the same stuff that's present in the game and adds the same value as the smaller expansions.
I just feel like all the dlc was half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ If they added two more larger expansions I would've been happier but I doubt it would've raised the quality of the game beyond average.
Now with the addition of the creation club... It's like I was holding Fallout 4 in my arms with chewing gun and cement being the only thing stopping it from falling apart, believeing it was still the game i wanted it to be, now Bethesda comes along and smacks Fallout 4 out of my arms and it's just left it in ruins.
It will take huge effort for my faith to be restored. For now, I do not recommend buying this game unless you've never played a Fallout game before and you lower your expectations greatly :(

So, two years ago I would have whole-heartedly reccommended this game. Hell, three days ago, I'd still have thought of it in it's vanilla form as a solid time sink, as buggy and uninpired as it was. But given the complications that have arisen with the creation club, this is not a game that you should even have on your hard drive. After sinking hundreds of hours into this (Modded, obviously) I'm going to have to uninstall it.
So, paid mods are bogus, as we already know. I'm happy to donate to good mod authors, and I'm happy to pay for real DLC, but we have several serious issues with this part on it's own, and they aren't even why I'm uninstalling the game. The first is the obvious "Why would I pay for this if I can get it better for free?". The second is that I can't just pay with money. I have to buy credits that don't match up with mod prices so I always overpay. And the third is thatr we're relying on Bethesda to make sure the mods are functional. That last one really gets me, as the modding community is almost a necessity because Bethesda games are so buggy to begin with. Why would I trust the creators of a broken product to give me something that works?
This also seems to be something of an effort to eliminate free mods to some degree, since every time the creation club updates, so to does Fallout 4, which makes F4SE no longer work properly. Which turns your game into a crash-fest, if it runs at all. Given how much content should be flowing through the creation club, if they truely want to allow players to mod the game in any meaningful way, this means daily updates for Fallout 4, and by extension F4SE, which is a ♥♥♥♥ing headache at the end of the day when I just want to unwind and play video games.
But those things are actually pretty minor to the now redundant final nail in the coffin of Fallout 4. For some reason, every single mod on the creation club is automatically downloaded on to your hard drive wether or not you've paid for it. You pay to unlock it basically. This is stupid on the developers part, because now I can get those mods for free (if they were worth the effort to steal, but they're not), but the big downside to this is that as more mods are added to the creation club, the more room it's going to take up on your hard drive. Right now, there are 12 mods on the creation club, with those files alone totalling around 600 Mb and the update totalling 2Gb, somehow. What the creation club has done is turn Fallout 4 into a $100 bloatware virus. So, because I run fallout 4 on an SSD, that's gonna fill up pretty damn quick, given just how many mods are out there. So, that game has got to go.

We were all told not to play with our food.  Now, our food plays... with us.
Straight out, it's clear this is not a game for everyone.  Expecting a silly Bread 'Simulator' Youtube-sensation smash-em-up?  Look elsewhere.  I AM BREAD needs *surprising* amounts of skill and puzzle solving.  Surprising unless you've played Surgeon Simulator, Bossa's previous game, which likewise required you to train your brain to learn what keys WON'T hurl spoons and scalpels all over the theatre.  This'll sound scathing but some reviewers prefer the Bagel Racing because it's a lot more straight forward and not at all punishing.  If you're interested enough to read this, you'll laugh plenty while you play, yet I AM BREAD will make you feel like your mild-mannered alter-ego has been bashed around the head with a baguette.
Yes, story mode about living bread.  The other modes are a very fun distraction but Story Mode hooked me in.  It's a surgeon simulator prequel!  As surreal and daft as that is, it works. You're taken on an adventure and the world really does become all about one thing: You aren't just bread; you must become TOAST.  You play through as a loaf possessed with life, each slice seeking any and all ways to become everyone's favourite morning accompaniment.  Story Mode takes place over the course of a week.  One of the joys is how the mission at hand engages you completely, and before long the escalating impact of your toasty obsession becomes deadly clear.  This loaf will stop at nothing, slowly pushing its owner into a frenzy while the world (or his therapist and security guards, at least) thinks him insane.
You have complete control of every corner and every movement of your wholesome slice, and you will have to learn how not just to grip, but how to flip, how to leap, how to swing and hurl things about to get through the levels.  The levels aren't just kitchens and lounges and petrol stations, because there is an increasing requirement to learn what you've tried out in previous levels to get through the next.  This is one thing that makes I AM BREAD much more of a game than I think a lot of players give it credit for.  It takes timing and practice and a lot of patience - with yourself more than anything!! You'll totally flop on some key manoeuvre and curse your aching fingers, but you'll try again and figure it out.  The only difference between limping across a kitchen surface or crawling painfully up the side of a bin, and flipping across car bonnets or leaping across chasms and flipping gracefully over petrol station shelving, is YOU.
Over the course of a week, you'll have to find heat sources, of which there are a few even in the same level, while avoiding anything that'll render you inedible.  Later you'll have to be a bit more creative (and destructive?) in your mission to toast yourself.  It requires level exploration until you spot something, it clicks, or you have that "I wonder if..." moment.  The levels are littered with everyday objects and I adored how everything seemed to move right, from bin lids to swinging petrol station signs, to individual piles of books and rolling gas tanks.  Some things break physics conveniently without going anywhere near the stupidity of something like goat simulator - switches move easily at a stroke, bread is surprisingly strong enough to hurl bricks at cars, and lighters will flick just by touching them.  These breaks are convenient and welcome!  If things get too difficult too often, you are offered a way to become edible no matter what you land on, but I recommend avoiding this.  Staying edible is half the game!
Thanks to Bossa's intent on providing banquets rather than just the one offering (surgeon simulator had several modes by the time they were done), the other modes add content to this game each with its own brilliant twist.  Bagel Racing is easy to get to grips with, though I did initially expect to race other bagels and multiplayer bagels would have been fantastic.  Starch Wars is pretty epic in which you'll take on an evil ironing board and its Rye Fighters.  Rampage puts you in control of a very angry baguette intent on smashing everything, swinging itself about like a baseball bat.  Cheese hunt sees you take on a quest for several pieces of cheese in a room as a piece of Rye, but isn't so interesting.  Zero-G is surprisingly addictive and very nicely done.  I haven't completed the Team Fortress mode but its a quirky version of the same thing and looks a lot of fun as you interact with familiar objects and weapons from comatose Heavy Weapons Guy's world.
It's not a long game, over with in a couple of evenings or maybe 4-6 hours (depending on what you do with the other modes).  It's very silly, great to play with mates or family around, it's got a nice dark glint in its eye, it's easy to play and difficult to master, but your patience and determination will be rewarded.  Remember this is a game in a true sense and you'll be ready - YOU
BE TOAST.  I am a fan.  If you've even read this far, just get it on offer and have a great time.

I've put plenty of time into Fallout 4, and let me tell you it's pry one of the weakest games I've ever played from Bethesda.
First off, it's highly insulting to the player. You really think your dialogue choices matter? Nope, for some baffling reason there's a voiced protagonist now so don't expect much deviation in conversations. But hey, at least the number of lines recorded is really really high!
Hours and hours of content?! If you think a poorly designed and implemented radiant quest system is content that's always fun and engaging instead of filler... then I suppose that it's true?
A well written and branching narrative that will hook you right in? Let's see if you can guess the act two twist based on the first 15 minutes of the story: Your wife/husband is killed and strange men have taken your baby, but not before refreezing you for an indeterminable amount of time which no one ever seems to realize until said twist. Also this game has one of the dumbest plot holes I have ever seen. You didn't pick up the friendly dog as a companion weeks ago when you first emerged from the Vault? Here allow me to whistle so that this one specific dog, that is miles away and outside the city, runs literally the same path that took you hours to get through in a matter of seconds. Truly some of the most laughably bad plots I've ever seen.
Oh and don't forget the "Creation Club" which is supposed to provide only simple reskins (Mind you all this is at the time of writing, so hopefully they've removed all traces where you are in the future). Think there will be any quests that you can pay hard working modders for? Nope, seeing as there is a file size limit that renders quests near impossible. It's a genuinely awful system that has sucked most, if not all, the good will I had towards Bethesda.
TL;DR
This game doesn't deserve the tag "RPG," but if you don't mind lack luster and predictable story that is almost entirely trite and a game cycle that starts to wear thin after a while... I guess pick it up when it's really cheap.

Completed my first run of the game the other day, Veteran difficulty.  This game rocked.  Great strategic play, I loved the randomized maps, research felt a lot clearner than the last game.  The revamped classes kick♥♥♥♥♥ although certain skill still seem to be no-brainers for Snipers.  Heavies are probably the most ballanced with some really hard choices.
Gameplay is still as brutal as ever.  Missing a shot can really hurt your team bad.  Expect to regularly bring home injured crews.  Most of the missions have turn limits for objectives, so you can't always just move/oversee/move/oversee your way through every map.  Sometimes you have to play it more fast and loose.
The bad: 30gigs was a bit large for my SSD, so load times were slow off of my 7200RPM disk.  Once a mission is loaded though they generally run well.  Some animation issues here and there where they may forget to play in combat.  A couple of odd sound buggs.  In my first play through, I only had one actual crash.  The interface isn't always obvious if you'll have Line-Of-Site to a target when you move.
Overall:  If you liked X-Com 1, this is more delicious X-Com goodness.  If you didn't like the first, skip it.

The game is good; it's pretty, it sounds amazing, and it improves on everything from the first game.
However at the same time it also slips up in a couple places. Regardless, it's still a fantastic game that I recommend if you've played the first game, or if you're just a tactic/strategy nut like me.
Pros:
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Crisp audio and sound effects
+ Interesting story that keeps building
+ Tough difficulty that keeps pace with you
+ Character customization adds a personal element
+ Destructible environment allowing for different ways to get where you need to
+ Different classes with many talents to pick from, customizing them further
+ Various tools and attachments allow you to tweak your weapons and soldiers to apply to your game style
+ Easy to learn, always a challenge
Cons:
- Graphical glitches
- Long load times inbetween turns
- Many of the missions are timed, taking away from the careful consideration of strategy
- Difficulty can be unforgiving in the beginning
- Avatar Status on the main map grows quickly; no real way to stop it
- Difficult to acquire staff or resources for research, buying staff or soldiers
- Forgettable main characters; no real connection to anyone
I enjoyed this game at the beginning; actually thought it was better than the first XCOM. The game was beautiful, the story (albeit confusing at first considering how the first one ended) was interesting and kept me wanting to move it along and build my team to fight back.
However as I got further, there were few things that begun to annoy me about it. One of my biggest gripes being the whole timed missions where things are heavily skewed against you. Regardless despite these cons, the pros outweigh it.
The game is visually pretty, nothing really special but crisp and suitably light and dark when it needs to be. One thing that really stuck out for me was the sound effects, the machine gun fire ripping from the guns, the plasma burning through the air, the grenades shunting from the launchers only to land somewhere and explode with a boom, breaking apart buildings and cover, blowing people away left right and center. You really feel the audio, and it's awesome. Everything feels dangerous and lethal; what you'd expect when you're shooting at someone and being shot at. Coupled with the possibility of death, you get real sweaty real fast when you hear someone raining fire down on you.
I'm a guy who loves to add his friends into the game, and the game actually comes with a Character Pool that you can completely customize your buddies and recruit them in the game. The customization options are a little limited but you can get the gist of it, and it makes it real personal real fast. I felt pretty attached to my guys, and now I was way more invested in making sure everyone got out alive.
The difficulty was a little tough in the beginning, and the recovery times were long and tough, but as you start to get farther in the game, it evens out. The ability to mix and match with utility tools, and augment weaponry allows you to fine tune your character to deal with a specific situation (pure fighting ability) or various ones (soldier support, or scouting). Add on specific talents in a talent tree system to add more variety skills to your character, and you have a specialized solider who you created.
Another cool thing about the game is the maps, there isn't a linear way to get somewhere. You can go through the streets, atop the roofs, or even through a building and blast through a wall to surprise the enemies from their flank. The new concealed system allows for this to be quite effective; something I was pleased to see implemented in XCOM 2.
Now, the shoddy bits. The game was great, but there were a few things that made me frustrated and disgruntled. The graphics were shaky sometimes, not loading properly or at all, or sometimes having effects that just continued to exist for no good reason (fires or objects that had been blown up, still existing, not providing cover). It wasn't always there, but when it was, it was just a tad annoying. The loading times for movements sometimes took excessive periods of time to load, or when the aliens had all moved, it would still say its their turn for a good 15-30 seconds before finally allowing you to move. Not a game breaker, but definitely a problem when it resulted in the game slowing down considerably.
One of my BIGGEST issues with this game was the absurd amount of time limit stuff. Now as a gamer, I hate time limit stuff but I know it's an integral part of gaming. But in XCOM 2? It's literally in at least 70% of the missions. You have to stop this thing from detonating in 8 turns. You have to kill this guy in 8 turns. You have to protect this device (which is in the middle of all the enemies) in 8 turns. It's frustrating. Considering the game is already tough on you with getting shot, the healing times between missions and just surviving, and now you have to abandon almost all tactics to just get to the objective in time? That's one key thing I was not happy with.
Another in conjuction with that, was the Avatar system in the main menu that was like the panic meter in the first game. I found there was no way to just be able to sit around and do missions, everything counted as a marker against me at until I started doing the main missions, my meter was already almost full. It's like it was forcing me to finish the game.
All in all, it was a solid game that I'd recommend to people regardless of the crazy time limits imposed upon you for every mission you do. I would not say it's better than the first one mechanic wise, but it definitely carries on the game and kept me interested right up until the end. If you like strategy and tactics and don't mind being put through the wringer sometimes; get this game.

"The graphics and unit designs are pretty great" (+)

This game is an extremely well made game. I'd recommend it for a number of reasons. The gameplay is great and has a ton of variety with the different nations. If you're a huge RTS buff, this game has the potential to be something great for you(including that this version has the DLC nations which can be a ton of fun). I mean, it already wins praise for one that that I've already brought up: IT'S AN RTS WHERE YOU CAN BUILD WALLS AND WALL DEFENCES. I mean, that is already reason enough to play it because so many RTS games would benefit from that but never think to add it. When a RTS game has a huge focus on base creation and development, it's almost insulting to not see walls involved. The DLC nations that are added in are also extremely fun and add some freshness to the game. The base nations have some variety to them but the 2 DLC nation sets add so much more with new types of explorers with new abilities and just new everything.
All the praise aside, there are still some issues with the game. Firstly, the pricing is HORRIBLE. I enjoyed the game a lot with both playing alone and with a friend but $40 is not worth it(I bought it on sale). I'd recommend keeping an eye out for it being on sale, especially if you have friends to play with. The game can get really fun with you play with people you can talk to. One of the first times I played, my friend built a ton of howitzers and placed them around my main base, telling me that I was being taken over as a commonwealth and that I'd have to pay taxes...with the lives of my soldiers! It was funny but if I had payed $40 for the experience, I'd had felt a little cheated through the enjoyment. Because while it does give a lot, I wouldn't say it was enough with the pricing. Another big issue is when trying to set up a custom match, you have no idea how the map is going to look. The game shows an old fashioned looking map type thing that has the name of the location on it instead of how the map is going to look/work. It may be a cool idea but I swear that many of the maps with coasts in the photo were all land and the ones that had no water at all had huge lakes or coast lines. It was really annoying whenever I wanted to have a naval empire.
But all and all, it's a really good game. I'd recomend it if you're an RTS lover and/or you have a friend who wants to try it with you(when it's on sale!)

I have waited a long time for this to hit PC. 100% Bayonetta on Xbox, though I doubt I'll ever be able to do that again.
Plain and simple, it's a Hack'N'Slash. Basically Devil May Cry without a complicated button sequence for dodging. If you loved the legacy DMC games, you might jump right into Bayonetta. After all, it's nearly the same devs.
Combat is again, Hack'N'Slashy. You have combos make you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ and nice finishers to give angels a bad day. Then you have climactic beatdowns to make these golden wretches regret they ever existed.
Story is interesting. There is no moral direction of who is good or bad like in DMC. A conflict without a sense of who is good or evil.
Music is unique, and just plain awesome. Sampler comes with 6 tracks, which is less than I expected. But no complaints for 20 bucks.
Also, realize that this has been designed as an arcade game. I have read that many people hate it for cutscenes, and combat being "interrupted". Which it's not being interrupted, it's in stages, or verses in this case. It's designed with the intention of being played in an arcade.

Not only that, but I found the mini-puzzles to be quite entertaining. All in all, this is one heck of a game, and there's no wonder it's been established as a masterpiece.

Cast a debuff --> Mob resists

You play as a piece of bread with a singular goal: stop at nothing to become toast!  But wait, you must also be edible, so no crawling around on the floor as you complete your quest for a toaster.
You can individually control each of the four corners of your slice of bread, and each corner can be used to grab something.  The bread flops around with ragdoll physics as you strategically alternate between corners in order to flip your way to a suitable toaster.  Controlling the bread is unbelievably difficult, and made worse by poor camera movement, but you do get the hang of it after a few hours of severe frustration.  Thankfully, repeatedly failing every level allows you to optionally become invincible and complete the level without worrying about your edibility.
Each level has multiple methods that will allow you to become toast. You can turn on the radiator, break the tv, use the iron, light the grill... the list goes on.  There are also several possible paths to reach each, so you can play each level several times.
The game has quite a bit of humor in it.  Story mode allows you to watch as your owner slowly goes insane.  Starch Wars mode allows you to fly around in a spaceship made from a slice of bread in order to save a baguette.  Team Fortress 2 mode requires you to become a Sandvich.  Other modes have you race around as a bagel, break things as a baguette, find cheese as a cracker, etc.  My personal favorite is Zero Gravity where you can soar through the house.
I think the game is worth a shot, despite the incredibly difficult controls.  Just remember,

When I read the Kickstarter I was pretty hyped, not to mention a community I was in hyping it up as well. While I did enjoy it for the first 50 hours or so, it just got...boring (this is coming from someone who has 290+ hours in Terraria). No matter how much I tried I just could not get back into it. The game has several problems, but I'll just list what I think are the biggest ones:
-The generated monsters. The creators described the creatures of Starbound as "infinite", however they all look like Pokemon rejects. They're only 2 types (ones who stay on the ground and the ones who fly) and only around 3 types of attacks (charging at you, spitting fire at you, and one I'm forgetting). Some are neutral, some are aggressive. They still have a major lack in variety.
-Performance. The game is just not optimized. I may have a♥♥♥♥♥♥PC but I've heard of people with high-end PCs having trouble running the game. I mean come on, the game doesn't even look that good. This is unacceptable.
-Bugs. While you may not notice them at first, the game is crawling with them.
-Races. There is simply no need to play as ANY race, because races do not have special abilities, rather their armor does. This is a problem when the developers boast their races and how they are special and unique when in reality they're not.
-Planets. The game's planets are not randomly generated from person to person. This means that a person could share coordinates to a planet where it may have great loot which effectively kills exploration except if you're the one who is adding on to that list, which most people are not.
-Content. I hear a lot of people say that this game is loaded with content, even more so than Terraria. This is simply false, and anyone you hear say this is delusional. Starbound's content consists mostly of useless♥♥♥♥♥♥and randomly generated weapons and creatures. There are more ACTUAL weapons and creatures (no, taking 2 types with 3 attack types and splicing colors and forms does NOT count as a seperate creature) in Terraria that are not randomly generated (sans their modifier, which can be reforged). They may be equal on cosmetics and building material, but that's not the main game.
Overall, this game is a mess. It does nothing special and WILL get old.

Has some nice weapon and player models, decent performance, and an accessible FtP model, but plagued by lag and what I can only describe as Dancing Idiot Syndrome. No fun, especially when coupled with the massive disconnect that high ping players bring. You will find a lot of them, because apparently the Asian players get better pings to the NA servers than to the Asian servers.
Time to kill is absurdly low, but also very inconsistent. Weapon balance is questionable, with some being outright useless or redundant in the face of other guns. Map design is pretty much only narrow corridors with one or two angles in on them, barely any open space to speak of. Long sight lines are quite rare. Some elements of the maps are also notably unbalanced toward one team or the other.
Cannot recommend until there are more servers and ping limits, as well as weapon balance passes, maybe some movement nerfs. As it is, it's more frustrating than fun.

Darkest Dungeon as most of us know is a very challenging rpg in which you recruit heroes and train them up to tackle the Darkest Dungeon to correct your Ancestor's wrongs.  The more I play it, the more I love it, and that continues to occur for myself.  Now, a lot of people really don't like this game, mostly because of how rng oriented they think it is. The thing is, it's not.  Not to be rude, If you see someone complaining that it's the game's fault that they got screwed by a random crit, they're right, but they are also wrong at the same time.  As for the recent release for the DLC, the Crimson Court, even more people complain about the game's absurd dificulty.  My opinion of the game is positive actually, not negative.  Sure, there are a few things that get me sometimes, but you just have to learn that the game is about making the best of a bad situaltion, not planning to get really lucky with random crits and not get hit.  I have edited my old review because I feel that I've played the game long enough to truly see into what I like and dislike, expecially after completing my Stygian campaign.
Why I like this game:
1. Probably the best rpg battle system of all time.
Sure, I may be biased, but admit it.  It's genius.  The fact that you can only use certain skills from certain positions is a really creative game mechanic, in fact, I've never seen any other game that does this.  It adds a layer of melted cheese on the plain patty that has existed for decades.
2. Great artstyle.
This game not only has some fun gameplay, but it has some great graphics.  The artstyle not only looks nice, but compliments the theme of the game being about the downsides of adventuring, especially the Darkest Dungeon quests.
3. Building upgrade system (Hamlet)
I always thought that the idea of being able to upgrade buildings outside of quests to help you in later quests is a great idea.  It really gives you a sense of progression, and I'm always looking forward to doing quests to get more heirlooms to upgrade them.
4. Boss designs
The bosses in this game are great in the fact that it rewards you for being prepared.  Many may argue against this idea, because they say "You're not supposed to have to be prepared.  You have to be able to beat the boss without knowing what it is."  No.  If you fail, you fail. You will learn from your failiures, and most people reject that idea, which is why they quit and give the game a bad review.
5. Area mechanics
Each area has it's own challenge.  Like how most enemies in the ruins are immume to bleed, and in the Warrens enemies are resistant to blight.  This mechanic allows you to create interesting party compositions in order to tackle each area.
6. Wayne June
Seriously.  Isn't he such a great narrator?
Although this game has a few problems (stun glitch), the positives outweigh the negatives and it's overall more fair and balanced than most people may think.

From the initial marketing I was overwhelmingly excited for this game to launch, with the previous fallout games being masterpieces of gaming for their genre I instinctively had the highest hopes for Fallout 4.
That's why this review has to be written, because I've never been so disappointed in a game like this before.
Initially the game is set up quite well and there's a sense of excitement and wonder uncovering the truth of the institute and the fate of your son. I personally enjoyed the main story and can't find thinks to pick at.
One of the things I didn't like about Fallout 4 was the dullness of the side quests.
!SPOILER ALERT!
For example the hole in the wall quest, the vault dwellers had no personality and story that I could integrate with to make me care about the decisions gor that quest. In other fallout games most people atleast give you some back story or let you help out with petty problems. As far as I was concerned the vault dwellers were about as interactive as raiders :/
I also think the way the wasteland is set out initially is horrible, first off all of the proper settlements are either faction settlements or diamond city (I say proper referring to "I can fully interact with the ai there") and the other settlements are full of people of raider level intelligence who spit randomly generated quests for me. One of my biggest complaints is how concord sets up the world, giving you access to both power armor and a minigun (both end game equipment - to some degree) while facing off against a deathclaw (an end game enemy) just feels so wrong at the beginning of a game... It really nullifies the rest of the experience imo, which is why I steer clear of it every new game.
I don't think I need to repeat this in detail, but the perk system and talking stuff is just♥♥♥♥♥♥..
The game also performs rather crap in a lot of areas, I initially played the full game on medium - low on my old 780 ti and when I got my new pc with a 1080 I expected a huge boost in fps, but I really didn't see any change which was more then a little disappointing.
Finally we reach post game content. I was happy with Fallout 4 once I had finished it, it was an average game but a pretty terrible fallout game. I got entertainment out of that and that's all that mattered.
I was expecting Fallout 4's dlc to be of the same size and quantity of atleast Fallout : New Vegas. Unfortunately we ended up with two moderately sized expansions that didn't contain much (I really liked far harbour, even though it was more or less a copy and paste from Fallout 3's point lookout) and a bunch of smaller additions that should've been in the game at launch (the vault expansion I'm not including as a large expansion because it mimics the same stuff that's present in the game and adds the same value as the smaller expansions.
I just feel like all the dlc was half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ If they added two more larger expansions I would've been happier but I doubt it would've raised the quality of the game beyond average.
Now with the addition of the creation club... It's like I was holding Fallout 4 in my arms with chewing gun and cement being the only thing stopping it from falling apart, believeing it was still the game i wanted it to be, now Bethesda comes along and smacks Fallout 4 out of my arms and it's just left it in ruins.
It will take huge effort for my faith to be restored. For now, I do not recommend buying this game unless you've never played a Fallout game before and you lower your expectations greatly :(

So, two years ago I would have whole-heartedly reccommended this game. Hell, three days ago, I'd still have thought of it in it's vanilla form as a solid time sink, as buggy and uninpired as it was. But given the complications that have arisen with the creation club, this is not a game that you should even have on your hard drive. After sinking hundreds of hours into this (Modded, obviously) I'm going to have to uninstall it.
So, paid mods are bogus, as we already know. I'm happy to donate to good mod authors, and I'm happy to pay for real DLC, but we have several serious issues with this part on it's own, and they aren't even why I'm uninstalling the game. The first is the obvious "Why would I pay for this if I can get it better for free?". The second is that I can't just pay with money. I have to buy credits that don't match up with mod prices so I always overpay. And the third is thatr we're relying on Bethesda to make sure the mods are functional. That last one really gets me, as the modding community is almost a necessity because Bethesda games are so buggy to begin with. Why would I trust the creators of a broken product to give me something that works?
This also seems to be something of an effort to eliminate free mods to some degree, since every time the creation club updates, so to does Fallout 4, which makes F4SE no longer work properly. Which turns your game into a crash-fest, if it runs at all. Given how much content should be flowing through the creation club, if they truely want to allow players to mod the game in any meaningful way, this means daily updates for Fallout 4, and by extension F4SE, which is a ♥♥♥♥ing headache at the end of the day when I just want to unwind and play video games.
But those things are actually pretty minor to the now redundant final nail in the coffin of Fallout 4. For some reason, every single mod on the creation club is automatically downloaded on to your hard drive wether or not you've paid for it. You pay to unlock it basically. This is stupid on the developers part, because now I can get those mods for free (if they were worth the effort to steal, but they're not), but the big downside to this is that as more mods are added to the creation club, the more room it's going to take up on your hard drive. Right now, there are 12 mods on the creation club, with those files alone totalling around 600 Mb and the update totalling 2Gb, somehow. What the creation club has done is turn Fallout 4 into a $100 bloatware virus. So, because I run fallout 4 on an SSD, that's gonna fill up pretty damn quick, given just how many mods are out there. So, that game has got to go.

I've put plenty of time into Fallout 4, and let me tell you it's pry one of the weakest games I've ever played from Bethesda.
First off, it's highly insulting to the player. You really think your dialogue choices matter? Nope, for some baffling reason there's a voiced protagonist now so don't expect much deviation in conversations. But hey, at least the number of lines recorded is really really high!
Hours and hours of content?! If you think a poorly designed and implemented radiant quest system is content that's always fun and engaging instead of filler... then I suppose that it's true?
A well written and branching narrative that will hook you right in? Let's see if you can guess the act two twist based on the first 15 minutes of the story: Your wife/husband is killed and strange men have taken your baby, but not before refreezing you for an indeterminable amount of time which no one ever seems to realize until said twist. Also this game has one of the dumbest plot holes I have ever seen. You didn't pick up the friendly dog as a companion weeks ago when you first emerged from the Vault? Here allow me to whistle so that this one specific dog, that is miles away and outside the city, runs literally the same path that took you hours to get through in a matter of seconds. Truly some of the most laughably bad plots I've ever seen.
Oh and don't forget the "Creation Club" which is supposed to provide only simple reskins (Mind you all this is at the time of writing, so hopefully they've removed all traces where you are in the future). Think there will be any quests that you can pay hard working modders for? Nope, seeing as there is a file size limit that renders quests near impossible. It's a genuinely awful system that has sucked most, if not all, the good will I had towards Bethesda.
TL;DR
This game doesn't deserve the tag "RPG," but if you don't mind lack luster and predictable story that is almost entirely trite and a game cycle that starts to wear thin after a while... I guess pick it up when it's really cheap.
IF YOU DO BUY THIS GAME:
A bit of advice, I find this game doesn't stand up well to multiple playthroughs when you start to see pass everything.

This is my first, and, currently, only review.
I may only have a few hours logged on Steam (at time of writing), but in reality, between the Xbox 360 and Wii U versions of this game, I have about 200 hours of playtime logged, and I feel as though I've barely scratched the surface. The game has three playable characters; I've only played as one. I've beaten the game on Normal, Hard, and Non-Stop Climax, but I've never done a full platinum run (here's hoping for a QoL patch to facilitate that!). I've unlocked all of the weapons and accessories, but I haven't used them all. I haven't bought all the costumes. I haven't fought the secret boss. Despite this, I don't mind starting my quest to do all of those things from square 1 for the third time.
That's because this game is simply fun to play.
Your skill level is irrelevant. Even if you're a complete novice, you can just jump into Very Easy mode and use the Immortal Marionette to help you do awesome combos. After you beat the game, you unlock its use in other difficulties, so if you want to use it the entire time, that's up to you. Or, you can stop using it at any point, and take full control of the character. In this way, the game sort of eases you into it at your own pace. It can be as easy or as difficult as you want it to be.
And like any great single-player game, it has a scoring system, which grades you on how long you take, how stylish your combos are, and how much damage you take.
Hideki Kamiya created this game's genre, whatever you want to call it, with Devil May Cry. He then perfected it with Bayonetta. The action in this game is second to none.
The design philosophy is top notch. When you complete the game, you unlock Handguns, which are strictly weaker than the starting weapons, Scarborough Fair, because you, as the player, want a greater challenge upon finishing the game, not a lesser one. And Kamiya knows this.
There is a very deep combat system on play here. If you can, try to find the strategy guide Future Press produced. If you can't find it, tell FP (on social media) that you would buy a reprint if you could. If you're wondering why you should get the strategy guide, find
for it on YouTube.
Another thing worth pointing out is that this game was designed to be a self-contained product. The original Xbox 360 (lead platform; the bad PS3 port wasn't done by PlatinumGames) release was never patched, because it didn't need a patch (Lt.-Col. Kilgore glitch notwithstanding, but it's on you if you wanna abuse that glitch). Bayonetta has no DLC because it needs no DLC. There are hundreds of hours of value in this game right out of the box, and it's polished to near-perfection.

In short: In principle XCom 2 is a good game with a few minor improvements over XCom: Enemy Unknown/Within and plagued by a truckload of bad design decisions that were quite clearly rushed into the game without proper evaluation or testing (although Firaxis has proven before that they don't test their games properly before releasing them). It's obvious that Firaxis wanted to try some new things, but the changes are all over the place (some good, most bad) and it's obvious that they didn't thoroughly consider how the game is affected by the changes.
Add to that the game is super buggy, runs like crap, and you wonder why Firaxis charges full price for a game that is clearly years from being ready for release. It is obvious that they at no time actually played through the game as the performance problems and bugs are noticeable immediately on the first menu screen before even starting the game. Even the very first tutorial mission likes to bug out, with dead soldiers flying all over the screen while the terrible framerate is laughable.
First off, I don't mind a challenge, but what Firaxis has done with XCom 2 is plain and simply daft. They cranked up the difficulty so high that the lowest difficulty is harder than the hardest in Enemy Unknown, thereby making it a game that appeals only to a minority of players (and not me). It also means that if you have other things to do than playing this game it will become extra frustrating as you can't just jump in and play a few levels and expect to progress. You will have to redo missions over and over, and fail at nauseum.
Per the story it's been 20 years since the first game. In that time all human soldiers etc. have forgotten how to shoot a gun, meaning they cannot aim at or even hit a wall and even at at 98% chance to hit they will miss 7 of 10 times (which should statistically be impossible). For the most part you're lucky if your soldiers have a hit chance around 30-50% even when flanking an enemy at short range, but for the most part they will have a hit chance far below that, which makes the early levels very tough to beat - borderline impossible. At the same time the aliens are almost guaranteed to hit with every single shot and quite often they will crit your guys through obstacles, thus often one-shotting half your squad on turn 2 while you're still setting up.
You also still have the issue of not being able to whack an alien in the face with your gun despite the alien being in the square next to your soldier. All soldiers, except for snipers, no longer have a pistol, which means they have no close range abilities whatsoever (excluding the ranger who more often than not only does half the damage they should), which again means that if an alien gets within 5 squares of your soldier, then you're soldier is dead. Combined with your soldiers' inability to hit anything at any range, this adds to the needless increase in difficulty.
That you have to evacuate your dead soldiers in order to recover their equipment is okay in principle, but the problem becomes that if you lose a squad with modded weapons a bit ways into the game it will be near impossible to progress as you need the mods to stand any chance against the aliens. Now, that wouldn't be a major problem if you could at least make the mods (or even just slightly inferior versions), but you can't. You have to loot them from aliens. That is bad design. Finding awesome weapon mods on aliens is good. Not being able to make mediocre mods yourself is bad and makes no sense.
Arbitrary short turn limits effectively removes all tactical aspects of the game because you can't use overwatch and you can't take your time and scout out the map to find the safest route. You're forced to rush on nealy all missions which goes against the fundamental concept of XCom, namely that of it being turn-based and highly tactical. With the turn limits the turn based system becomes pointless and any ability that relies on you not using all the action points become irrelevant. Short turn limits belong on the higher difficulties, or even in challenge modes, but not on the normal difficulty. If Firaxis had bothered thinking before implementing this terrible idea, then the turn limit would be an optional difficulty setting (as in custom difficulty), or better yet a bonus objective for extra rewards. Forcing you to rush at all times really does nothing good for the game.
A lot of the game's features aren't explained properly (and may be difficult to figure out if you haven't played the previous game), like the black market. You start off with very little money and that money is quickly spent, at which point the game tells you to visit the black market to sell some junk. Only you can't. Yet. The black market is much further into the story and the game doesn't even tell you that, at all, until you've done the mission that unlocks it - as in you have to secure the area before the game tells you that the black market is there. How did you get your equipment in the first place, if not through the black market? The game never explains that.
The geoscape is bothersome at best, annoying most often, and directly frustrating for far too much of the game. You're constantly handed missions you HAVE to deal with, which is okay, sort of. Except it means you constantly don't have enough time to gather resources or set up radio towers etc, and then have to constantly go back and forth across the map because you get interrupted as soon as you get where you want to go. It makes everything take much longer than it really should and again, does nothing other than arbitrarilty lengthen the game.
There are tons of customization options for your soldiers this time around, but it's obvious that Firaxis spent most their time perfecting that instead of paying attention to the rest of the game. The customization system works (for the most part) flawlessly, but nothing else does in the game. Performance is atrocious and no amount of changes to the graphics settings makes any difference. Lowering the graphics quality (like reducing lighting quality and turning off heavy features) actually lowers the framerate, which shouldn't be possible. Occasionally the game will reach 60+ fps, but for the most part it will chug along at 30-50 fps while absolutely hammering the GPU (on my heavily overclocked GTX 960) - and the graphics are not remotely good enough to justify the terrible framerate or the GPU load. When there's LESS to draw (like on the mission results screen) the frame rate goes to complete crap for no other reason that Firaxis clearly never intended the game to run at a playable framerate.

Hmmmm........... Just finished XCOM 2 (finally) and i'm asking myself;
Was it really worth it?
I'd like to start of with the negatives of the game as there aren't very many if i'm honest (spoilers on the above question i guess XD) Well, first off i think the most glaring problem is the performance which is pretty bad for a game like this. Firaxis hasn't exactly bent over backwards to release updates however which is pretty frustrating to say the least. The Introduction of timers is mixed for me but sometimes really frustrates me, making me wish they were not in the game but there are mods for this so that issue can easily be sorted. Finally, i feel the geoscape area of the campaign (overall strategy section, not battle tactics) can sometimes be a little linear as some 'multiple' choice operations  can easily be narrowed down due to an obvious benefit to picking a certain OP over another.
With the bad stuff outa' the way, lets look at the stuff it gets right and there's a lot so i'm gonna bullet point it:
. Crazy soldier customisation
. Better strategic campaign design
. Huge variety of Alien enemies
. Game is a challenge- a good one
. Story is actually very interesting, i was thinking about the ending long after i finished the game itself
. Graphics are superb for this type of game
. Music soundtrack is awesome
. Good variety of missions
. MODS!!!!!!!!!!
. Good rate of new enemies throughout the game
. Map design is excellent, even though most are randomly generated so you are going to see a huge variety of maps!

So yes, yes this game is worth the £35-40 price tag so do yourself a favour and join the fight to free earth! FOR XCOM, VIGILO CONFIDO!

*Input same voice lines in and out*
Jokes aside, I picked this game up to try it for a casual, primary TDM based game, and for what it stands for being non-pay to win game that is also free to play, the only thing it has going for it, is that concept and decent gameplay.
Gameplay is quite reminiscent to a combination of Call of Duty and Counter Strike, and quite nostalgic to Combat Arms style gameplay. The EXP and Money earned per game is quite miniscule, so prepare to grind to gain new weapons to use on your loadout. Three loadouts are given to customize, and the game starts you with starter weapons that are subpar to other guns in the game.
Once you start to get used to the aim and mechanics of the game, is where the game’s ideation starts come into play, being a pure skill reliant gameplay, where no factors of paid weaponry can dictate who wins a gunfight. Other reviews will also touch base on the region lock, and playing in NA servers, be prepared to face people from other regions with 100+ ping.
From the start of the game, you can see a lot of obnoxious things to nitpick, which a few comes to mind is that during the tutorial, they force you to use default sensitivity and settings, which comes with deafening audio of headshots and the same death cry used repeatedly, which results in annoyance (yet seemingly funny) experience as a player of many titles of the FPS genre. Guns have a missing a single shot in their magazine, hit reg could sometimes be buggy, and other times it becomes a cluster♥♥♥♥ of nades and dead bodies, wreathing in agonizing pain of the same voice line. Sometimes I feel this game takes itself a bit too serious, or is clearly making fun of certain themes of other iconic FPS games.
But giving the benefit of the doubt, it is still in Early Access, so a lot of things can be changed to develop this game into a rather enjoyable game that both sides of FPS gamers, serious or casual, can both enjoy. Until then however, I will be enjoying this game on an ironic standpoint, playing this game only when bored or wanting to have a giggle.

Great survival-crafting sandbox games that is better with friends. I played this when it first came out on Early Access so here's my two cents on it.
-
. You get your own spaceship which you can use to travel between galaxies/cluster/whatever you call it. The universe is so big that you probably won't be able to discover everything on it (also just want to add in that typing in coordinates on the spaceship console feels so satisfying hearing that audible click). You can also hire crew members to your ship and upgrade your ship as it gets bigger (Check out the Ship Upgrade page on the Starbound wiki, they have gifs of all the ships upgrades which is really cool).
-
. You start out on a peaceful planet that poses no harm to you but as you yearn for more, you start to face the need to upgrade your armor, find stronger weapons and craft better equipment to help you progress further.
-
. Finding a planet and running around finding out what it contains is pretty exciting. I've spent 300 hours on this gaame and there are still things that I've yet to discover.
-
. As someone who hates port-forwarding/using Hamachi just to play with friends, I was surprised and happy to come back to a much simpler multiplayer setup where you only need to start your game and invite anyone on your friends list to play. It's that easy.
-
. Not much to say here. The more choices the better.
-
. I think this is what turns me off from the game at times. Sure, there are different types of monsters on different biomes/planets but they all feel the same. It's either the ones on the ground that charge towards you/shoot something at you or the flying ones that do the same thing. I remember back in Early Access they had a mini-boss on each planet that you can discover while exploring which I think is something they should add; maybe a hidden dungeon for each planet with a boss.
-
. The quest department is very lackluster as there are only a few formulas to how the quests work (fetching & escorting). Besides that, the main quests' purpose is only to build the player up to the endgame dungeons called Vaults so don't expect much of a story there. I recently saw some wiki links that showed that they had some pretty interesting quests that were removed so I hope they're still working on it.

In the short amount of time that I have been playing this game I have come to see some pro's and con's to it. Some of the ships are way over powered and used most often. The main ships used are the Assassin, the Enforcer, and the Frigate. The Frigate is over powered due to its shield ability which people have been abusing to an extent, and the Enforcer has a high damage ratio, ranging in the thousands to ten thousands, the assassin people have been using the cloak ability in the enemy base to hide, randomly going in for a small percentage of capture, and hiding again. Among the weaker ships is the sniper. the sniper has a limited range of fire, but the main problem with it is that if anyone gets behind it you have no defensive abilities other than your missiles, which fire every once in a while. essentially if someone gets behind you, you are dead. you might as well just sit there and let it happen.
The overall game play is very well done, the map is simple and it allows for a wide variety of tactics. One of my favorite tactics was with the hunter. I would blink to the topmost part of the field that i could and head to the enemy station. when i got close enough i would blink down into it and capture it. then i would jump to the enemy base and blink around until i died. Big fan of the premise. This is probably as close as we'll get to ID4: The Game. The problem isn't the concept, it's the execution.
Ultimately, if you want just a carbon copy of XCOM1's gameplay elements -- top-down view, 2 moves per soldier, etc. -- then you'll love this game. If you want some innovative design ideas and a gripping story, you need to look elsewhere.
They somehow managed to make the story even more boring and shallow than in XCOM1, which is particularly evident as you dig deeper. Once you get past all the mystic mumbo jumbo garbage, it's a bunch of nothing under the guise of ambiguity. I would've preferred a giant, glowing brain-in-a-jar kicking in humanity's front door to steal all their water or whatever than what XCOM2 hands you. At least the brain thing would've been fun.
Gameplay is more of the same except now it's "resistance" flavor. Which is fine because XCOM1's chess match style gameplay was great. Except that there's a new concealment 'feature.' There's no explanation or tutorial on how to best use this. Initially, I thought you could complete objectives and missions concealed, then disappear into the shadows. That's not the case. If you don't attack the first group of enemies you see, you eventually reveal all the enemy groups the deeper you go into the map. When you reach the objective, there are permanently stationed enemies around it. By then revealing yourself, you activate each group of enemies until you're surrounded.
It's a waste of a great concept. Stealthy resistance tactics diluted down to a free overwatch shot.
Character customization options are a little bit better in places but also worse in places than the previous game. Most facial hair looks terrible, and there simply aren't that many options. They managed to add a few more accents -- such as British and Australian English -- but removed other languages entirely, which is a shame.
tl;dr: Great concept, terrible execution. Regret blowing $60 on this, probably worth more like $20-30.

*Note: I have very little time played on my Steam version of this game, but have played around 80 - 100 hours on the disc version.*
Age of Empires III incorporates an awesome New England settings rendered in amazing graphics. The combat is more intense, more diverse, and much more realistic than that of the original two Age of Empires games, which were already great. The interface has been updated and greatly improved (only three resources allow for a smoother process of building and running your civilation).
The game has many great new features, including:
-use of a "home city", a city you customize and level up through battle, that serves as your main menu and gives rewards
-ability to train troops in groups of five, instead of individually
-random capturable treasures scattered around the map that give unique bonuses
-more realistic battle (soldiers burn buildings instead of hit them, cannonballs knock down trees, ships sink, etc)
-awesome revamped naval combat. Limited fleet size allow more tactical fighting strategies
-unit special abilities. these vary greatly, providing a single powerful shot, treasure gaurdian taming, stealth, etc.
-ability to build trade posts to ally with native americans, providing unique/powerful upgrades and native units
-use of limited and highly-profitable trade posts along a railroad, which are visciously fought over
-unique use of ability cards, picked outside of battle, and used during game for special advantages
-highly diverse wild animals to fight, hunt, and tame. Tamable ones includes wolves, coyotes, bears, cougars, and more.
-interesting and useful incorporation of time-period features, including minute-men, trains, native allies, and more.
-addition of artillery units (various cannons) that add a unique element to combat
-(with Asian Dynasties expansion) ability to play as one of three native American tribes (Sioux, Aztec, and one other)
Things I do not like about this game:
-population size still limited to 200 units
-artillery is a bit overpowered (specifically anti-infantry artillery, though it is more realistic that way)
In short, if you are a fan of the original two AoE games, love historical time period-set war games, like strategy combat, or just want to have some great fun on an amazingly underrated and easy-to-learn game, buy Age of Empires III now. And while you're at it, the expansions are great and well worth the money.

I do kind of wish there was a "Neutral" option for this review.
This game falls under the category of games such as Goat Simulator that expects you to find it funny on premise alone, and sadly it's one joke that lands for very few and even if it does land for you it's unlikely you'll find it funny for several hours.
So... Why is this a recommendation?
-Unlike Goat Simulator, there isn't a grand total of one joke per level. It's ridiculous how many puns are packed into the game and some of the more subtle ones actually made me chuckle. There are no shortage of bread puns in this game.
-This game succeeds in the same way Surgeon Simulator succeeded- It actually has merit above just being a game with bad controls. Both this and Surgeon Sim are games with actual learning curves and the potential of mastery- Games where you can actually get better and better at them and earn your A++ rank.
-Actually really, really hard. I'm not even joking, this game is pretty tough especially if you want high rankings.
-Surprisingly open levels. Your goal is to become toast, but there are many different ways to do that- Making your way to a toaster is one, but you could also toast yourself inside an oven or on a BBQ. How you get to something that can make you into toast is also completely up to you, as long as it doesn't consist of crawling along dirty surfaces such as the floor- But even then, skilful play can get you across the floor with minimal damage, too.
But there's a lot of things that drag this game down, too, unfortunately.
-Like Surgeon Simulator's A&E Edition it outstays its welcome. The campaign mode is at a pretty good length, but if you want 100% completion in this game it will be an incredibly painful and boring experience. They mix it up with different kinds of bread but it isn't really different enough to work particularly well. Especially with all the extra stuff they've added through updates. It's very unlikely you'll actually have the interest to play every extra level at least once.
-The controls are actually TOO bad. Surgeon Sim is a game that appears to have bad controls to the uninitiated, but all you need to do is actually learn the controls and the controls will no longer be an obstacle to your play. I Am Bread, on the other hand, doesn't appear to have that quality- No matter how good you get the game's physics engine will still screw you over at times because your very movement is dependent on the game's physics engine. This may have been because of the fact I didn't use a controller but I still feel like even movement felt more difficult than it needed to be.
-Once again, it may be because I didn't use a controller, but those zero-gravity levels... UGH.
-There didn't appear to be any secrets or secret levels like there were in Surgeon Simulator. Surgeon Sim had this titanic number of easter eggs and so on that were pieced together in order to discover an amazing secret level- I Am Bread doesn't have anything like that.
Overall I Am Bread is IMO not as good as Surgeon Simulator was. It still manages to do what games of its type consistently fail to do but it's a downgrade to what Surgeon Sim was. It's not exactly a game I can muster up a "Not Recommended" rating for because it does have merit especially if this kind of game is what you're looking for, but I'd still recommend you pick up Surgeon Sim instead of this.

If, like me, you played Xcom Enemy Unknown (or its expansion, Enemy Within), you probably remember defeating the aliens who were trying to invade Earth. Unfortunately Commander, there's some bad news.
Earth's citizens have been living under a "peaceful" alien rule for 20 years, and you're now part of an underground resistance force, trying to stop the aliens' secret, sinister plan, before its too late.
Just like the previous game, Xcom2 is divided into two distinct areas of gameplay: the base, and the missions. During the base phase you can research new technologies, build better weapons, armours and equipment, recruit and train your soldiers and manage your economy. Missions involve taking a squad of upto 6 soldiers to achieve objectives such as protecting some civilians, stealing some intel, recovering an item or destroying an alien base. Combat is the same turn based style as before.
Although Xcom 2 is a good game, it didn't quite excite me as much as the previous game did, and I can't quite put my finger on why. I think it might just be because I've played Enemy Unknown/Within for a combined 122 hours across 5 successful campaigns, so although Xcom 2 is bigger and better, there's also an element of "more of the same".
The Good
•	Your soldiers have a fantastic range of abilities. I found every class of soldier to be extremely useful.
•	Large variety of aliens with unique abilities including mind control, stun, poison, disable weapons, area of effect attacks, shield allies, teleport, clone, shapeshift ... and probably more that I'm forgetting.
•	The combination of above two points results in lots of tactical depth. I often spent a few minutes on my turn just analysing the situation and considering all my options.
•	You can upgrade your soldiers' weapons with mods recovered during missions that give special abilities, including reloading the weapon without it costing a turn, bigger clip size, a percentage chance to attack multiple times on your turn, and a percentage chance to get an instant kill no matter how much health the alien has (I actually killed the most powerful robotic enemy in one shot thanks to this, which was a really cool moment).
•	The campaign is longer than the previous game. It took me 40 hours to finish, compared to 25 for EU/EW.
•	More visual customisation options for your soldiers.
The Bad
•	The story is fairly generic and none of the characters are particularly interesting. It doesn't help that the player character never speaks. If there's another sequel, I'd like to see a bit of Mass Effect style banter in between missions with the guys back at your base, to add a bit of personality.
•	Poor technical performance. I saw several examples of the action camera not actually showing me the action because my view was obscured by scenery (walls, trees, etc). I saw countless occasions of both the aliens and my soldiers attacking through solid walls (both shooting and melee). And the framerate stutters horrendously when loading into and out of a mission.
•	Frustratingly high number of missions where there is an extremely tight turn limit to achieve the objective. For example, hack a data relay before it shuts down in 8 turns. The data relay is so far away from your starting point that it takes 3 turns to get there moving full distance each turn. And of course there are 2 groups of aliens between you and the objective, which will probably take 2 turns each to kill if you do everything perfectly. These kind of missions feel like there's zero room for error, but at the same time, you just have to rush forward, abandoning any kind of intelligent tactics. The absolute worst missions are when you have to stop the aliens from destroying a data relay, which is on the other side of the map, and the aliens are already shooting it on turn 1.
•	"Concealment" is a wasted mechanic. Your squad starts most missions in stealth mode, and the aliens don't attack you until you are "revealed", which happens if you open fire, or enter their line of sight. But its pretty much impossible to stealth an entire mission because there are always aliens next to the objective, and so the few times I tried to sneak past a group of aliens, I actually ended up in a bad situation because when I was inevitably seen, I'd find myself surrounded. I quickly figured out that it was safer to ignore concealment, and just attack immediately.
•	There are occasions where you have to choose between 3 missions that have different rewards (and penalties for the ones you ignore), and just like EU/EW, you can still only do 1 mission, even if you have enough healthy soldiers for 2 or more full squads. All those resources, all that fancy tech, and we still can't build a second dropship, or at least capture one of the aliens' dropships?
The Recommendation
Whilst its not quite as amazing as I hoped, Xcom 2 is still a good game that is worth playing. You'll get good value for money from a full price purchase. If you've never played Xcom before, you don't need to play the previous games first because the story has essentially been reset, so you could start with Xcom 2 without a problem.

Don't buy this game for it's name. Actually, it's a shame for the outstanding AoE franchise.
AoE III is a wonderful game, with good graphics and enough in-game possibilities (i'm talking about buildings and characters), but it lacks the supremacy of AoE II and AoE.
This game looks like the developers wanted to make a game that would ressemble the very first Empire Earth. Well, it doesn't.
- Remember that awesome feeling in AoE II and EE when changing the map size to 'gigantic' and you had no idea where to start exploring first? You won't find it here. According to me, this game stands or falls with the scale of its maps.
- Also a big fail is the building-aspect. You don't have the feeling, when building your houses and military buildings, that you're constructing a city. After putting your, let's say 20, buildings close to each other and in an structurised manner, it looks like a mismatched slum of the 14th century which you want to put on fire. I know, some of you will say: 'Oy, AoE isn't about building, it's the fighting that counts!' And i'll even say they're correct. But be honest with yourselves, it's the whole that counts, isn't it?
- Another, rather 'stupid', improvement is the fact that in-game you have the possibility to make your homecountry deliver supplies (troops, food and villagers). Seriously, who gives a damn for this? This makes you feel incompetent for playing this game, since you'll have to 'beg' for help. Not a nice feeling, not?

So, two years ago I would have whole-heartedly reccommended this game. Hell, three days ago, I'd still have thought of it in it's vanilla form as a solid time sink, as buggy and uninpired as it was. But given the complications that have arisen with the creation club, this is not a game that you should even have on your hard drive. After sinking hundreds of hours into this (Modded, obviously) I'm going to have to uninstall it.
So, paid mods are bogus, as we already know. I'm happy to donate to good mod authors, and I'm happy to pay for real DLC, but we have several serious issues with this part on it's own, and they aren't even why I'm uninstalling the game. The first is the obvious "Why would I pay for this if I can get it better for free?". The second is that I can't just pay with money. I have to buy credits that don't match up with mod prices so I always overpay. And the third is thatr we're relying on Bethesda to make sure the mods are functional. That last one really gets me, as the modding community is almost a necessity because Bethesda games are so buggy to begin with. Why would I trust the creators of a broken product to give me something that works?
This also seems to be something of an effort to eliminate free mods to some degree, since every time the creation club updates, so to does Fallout 4, which makes F4SE no longer work properly. Which turns your game into a crash-fest, if it runs at all. Given how much content should be flowing through the creation club, if they truely want to allow players to mod the game in any meaningful way, this means daily updates for Fallout 4, and by extension F4SE, which is a ♥♥♥♥ing headache at the end of the day when I just want to unwind and play video games.
But those things are actually pretty minor to the now redundant final nail in the coffin of Fallout 4. For some reason, every single mod on the creation club is automatically downloaded on to your hard drive wether or not you've paid for it. You pay to unlock it basically. This is stupid on the developers part, because now I can get those mods for free (if they were worth the effort to steal, but they're not), but the big downside to this is that as more mods are added to the creation club, the more room it's going to take up on your hard drive. Right now, there are 12 mods on the creation club, with those files alone totalling around 600 Mb and the update totalling 2Gb, somehow. What the creation club has done is turn Fallout 4 into a $100 bloatware virus. So, because I run fallout 4 on an SSD, that's gonna fill up pretty damn quick, given just how many mods are out there. So, that game has got to go.

If, like me, you played Xcom Enemy Unknown (or its expansion, Enemy Within), you probably remember defeating the aliens who were trying to invade Earth. Unfortunately Commander, there's some bad news.
Earth's citizens have been living under a "peaceful" alien rule for 20 years, and you're now part of an underground resistance force, trying to stop the aliens' secret, sinister plan, before its too late.
Just like the previous game, Xcom2 is divided into two distinct areas of gameplay: the base, and the missions. During the base phase you can research new technologies, build better weapons, armours and equipment, recruit and train your soldiers and manage your economy. Missions involve taking a squad of upto 6 soldiers to achieve objectives such as protecting some civilians, stealing some intel, recovering an item or destroying an alien base. Combat is the same turn based style as before.
Although Xcom 2 is a good game, it didn't quite excite me as much as the previous game did, and I can't quite put my finger on why. I think it might just be because I've played Enemy Unknown/Within for a combined 122 hours across 5 successful campaigns, so although Xcom 2 is bigger and better, there's also an element of "more of the same".
The Good
•	Your soldiers have a fantastic range of abilities. I found every class of soldier to be extremely useful.
•	Large variety of aliens with unique abilities including mind control, stun, poison, disable weapons, area of effect attacks, shield allies, teleport, clone, shapeshift ... and probably more that I'm forgetting.
•	The combination of above two points results in lots of tactical depth. I often spent a few minutes on my turn just analysing the situation and considering all my options.
•	You can upgrade your soldiers' weapons with mods recovered during missions that give special abilities, including reloading the weapon without it costing a turn, bigger clip size, a percentage chance to attack multiple times on your turn, and a percentage chance to get an instant kill no matter how much health the alien has (I actually killed the most powerful robotic enemy in one shot thanks to this, which was a really cool moment).
•	The campaign is longer than the previous game. It took me 40 hours to finish, compared to 25 for EU/EW.
•	More visual customisation options for your soldiers.
The Bad
•	The story is fairly generic and none of the characters are particularly interesting. It doesn't help that the player character never speaks. If there's another sequel, I'd like to see a bit of Mass Effect style banter in between missions with the guys back at your base, to add a bit of personality.
•	Poor technical performance. I saw several examples of the action camera not actually showing me the action because my view was obscured by scenery (walls, trees, etc). I saw countless occasions of both the aliens and my soldiers attacking through solid walls (both shooting and melee). And the framerate stutters horrendously when loading into and out of a mission.
•	Frustratingly high number of missions where there is an extremely tight turn limit to achieve the objective. For example, hack a data relay before it shuts down in 8 turns. The data relay is so far away from your starting point that it takes 3 turns to get there moving full distance each turn. And of course there are 2 groups of aliens between you and the objective, which will probably take 2 turns each to kill if you do everything perfectly. These kind of missions feel like there's zero room for error, but at the same time, you just have to rush forward, abandoning any kind of intelligent tactics. The absolute worst missions are when you have to stop the aliens from destroying a data relay, which is on the other side of the map, and the aliens are already shooting it on turn 1.
•	"Concealment" is a wasted mechanic. Your squad starts most missions in stealth mode, and the aliens don't attack you until you are "revealed", which happens if you open fire, or enter their line of sight. But its pretty much impossible to stealth an entire mission because there are always aliens next to the objective, and so the few times I tried to sneak past a group of aliens, I actually ended up in a bad situation because when I was inevitably seen, I'd find myself surrounded. I quickly figured out that it was safer to ignore concealment, and just attack immediately.
•	There are occasions where you have to choose between 3 missions that have different rewards (and penalties for the ones you ignore), and just like EU/EW, you can still only do 1 mission, even if you have enough healthy soldiers for 2 or more full squads. All those resources, all that fancy tech, and we still can't build a second dropship, or at least capture one of the aliens' dropships?
The Recommendation
Whilst its not quite as amazing as I hoped, Xcom 2 is still a good game that is worth playing. You'll get good value for money from a full price purchase. If you've never played Xcom before, you don't need to play the previous games first because the story has essentially been reset, so you could start with Xcom 2 without a problem.
