To me,
will always be a proper example of how Early Access should look like: started with a solid working beta build, continued with relentless support and regular updates, released within a reasonable amount of time, while not losing player base and maintaining the final vision of the game.
I won't go deep into describing how Darkest Dungeon functions exactly (it would take me hours), I'll just list some of the basic info you need to know before buying it:
* This is crucially important: gameplay is somewhat grindy. You will have to run through the same dungeons over and over again. Though, enemy composition, traps, items and encounters inside always change, as well as the level composition. And even though there is a story behind this whole thing, main thing to enjoy in this game is exactly this grindy gameplay. Be sure to check out a few videos before you decide to buy it or not.
* Aesthetically game is amazing. Graphics, voice-over, sounds and music create a perfect grim atmosphere that fits game like a glove. This is how proper dark dungeon should look like!
* Game is *very* hardcore. You will lose heroes frequently, you will earn negative perks a lot, you will be always low on gold and items. But that's how the game works, so don't be discouraged by that.
* Battles are very challenging and it's going to take significant time before you'll be successful at fighting foes. You'll have to try a lot of different team compositions, get to know all the classes, level up a few skills and buy a few items. But when you'll do, you'll start enjoying the game significantly more.
Overall, you can not skip this game if you're a fan of hardcore, punishing, grim squad-based RPGs with zero tolerance for even the smallest mistakes. I've been playing this game since June, 2015, and even though I didn't spend hundreds of hours, as some other reviewers here, I utterly enjoyed this experience, and will be definitely looking out for more to come.

QWOP with toast.
If you aren't familiar with QWOP, it is a game where you have to control someone's individual joints to make them run/walk. It is incredibly awkward as a control scheme and is basically a joke game.
I Am Bread is basically that, except instead of controlling a person, you control a piece of toast. You can stick one or more of the corners of the bread to a surface in order to move, flipping over and over again to get around the level. You can stick to anything, and ultimately, the game is a bit of a physics puzzle.
The problem is that the incredibly awkward controls are endlessly frustrating. Getting into the toaster in the first level is an arduous, unpleasant task which takes an enormous amount of work. The toast flops around freely and almost uncontrollably, and while it is not that hard to simply move around large, flat surfaces, any sort of specific positioning is an awful, awful chore.
And that's just the first level.
This game is endlessly frustrating and unless you actually, genuinely enjoyed QWOP, this game will drive you batty.

I will start this review off by stressing the fact that this game is not for everyone.
The game lacks the direction of most modern games. There is no checklist, telling the player to plant a certain amount of seeds in a specific area on their farm. There is no narrative and the quests that are distributed to the player are rather repetitive. These quests, however, do not hinder the player's experience. In fact they urge the player to explore the small world allotted to them. These quests will introduce mechanics that the player might previously have been unaware of. That being said, having to catch a certain kind of fish within 2 days inorder to earn a quick buck can be somewhat of a pain, despite these tasks being optional.
But the strength of this game isn't in its quests, rather in the atmosphere it builds. Whenever I load my save up, all of the stress that builds up on a day-to-day basis gets washed away. The game provides a feeling of Zen whenever I play. It's a very pleasant game. The graphics are vibrant and full of color. There is almost no conflict to be found. But, again, this might turn some players off from buying this game. Perhaps to another player, this game would seem boring, and perhaps said player can find more catharsis in some other game.
I love this game, but if you aren't a fan of games like Minecraft or Terraria, in which the point of the game is rather unclear, then I doubt you will share my sentiment. It's a great little game, and in a world of looming corporations (that currently make up the gaming industry) trying to stick it to the little guy, these great little games are a godsend
tl;dr - It's a wholesome game that relaxes me, but it is definitely not for everyone.

Half-life is a pretty well-known game, it's got that old PC game feel, which could be considered good or bad, on one hand, yes, older games often offered a very powerful challenge, but on the downside, this was mostly caused by the fact that game design was something that had to be learned solely through hands-on experience, due to it being a new concept for people to work with. You play as Gordon Freeman, a mute scientist, majored in Theoretical Physics. You start off entering the Black Mesa facility for an experiment, which, naturally, goes horribly wrong, afterwards, Gordon finds himself trapped in the facility, surrounded by bizarre creatures you would NOT find on our planet. Your goal is to escape from the facility while combatting the many creatures that have invaded, as well as some marines, who have been given orders to kill the scientists to cover up the incident. The majority of the challenge in the game comes from utilizing your resources, because unlike other games there are no areas where you can heal and reload, instead you'll find various ammunition located across the game, but none of it is durable, and the only weapons in the game that don't use ammo are the melee crowbar, and this hornet firing weapon you get rather late in the game. The only places you can heal up infinitely are these small pools that only begin to show up VERY late in the game. So basically you have to find out how to dispatch various enemies while utilizing as few resources as possible. This is a very nice challenge, but sometimes it just comes down to you saving before attempting something, and simply experimenting to see how little of your resources you can expend. The game was significantly longer than I had expected, and is very challenging, I got this game when it was on sale for 75% off, for 2.25$, I ended up getting the Half-Life pack for 75% off, for an overall 10$, since you can get the whole package for the same price as you can get this game alone when it's on sale, I'd recommend waiting for it to go on sale, overall I'm glad I got this game, and I do recommend it.

I enjoy really playing XCOM 2 up to a point and that point comes at around the 2/3rd mark on Legendary Ironman. Before this the game is a very challenging squad based strategy with fairly balanced enemies and extremely tough time pressure on missions. After this point XCOM seems to fall back on overpowered units to try to make the late game tougher than XCOM:EW, however I think they have got the balance wrong and it slows the game down into one where you just pound the same enemy unit again and again while popping mimic beacons and hoping his mates don't turn up. If they do - alas, there goes your campaign!
Added to this the game does suffer from some very irritating bugs and quirks. Civilians popping doors your soldiers are standing behind, a ton of LOS issues, massive units destroying scenery while on patrol, split pods, a whole train vanishing from one turn to the next and exposing my squad! An objective with 40 health catching fire instantly blowing up.
I love the Xcom series, I put around 600 hours into the last game and almost 100 into this one but if like me you find ironman impossible your preferred way to play Xcom then I cannot recommend you try this until the late game balance is changed and some of the more glaring bugs are fixed. It will drive you insane and make you as bitter as I am.
On the positive side the mods in the workshop are the best thing to happen to Xcom in ages, voicepacks and costumes can really make even the most horrible mission a laugh and you can add in a ton of gameplay elements. Firaxis did a great job in making this available to the community.
I'm not going to stop playing this game, however I have handily completed classic ironman twice then lost at more of less the same point in impossible runs three times in a row. So I think I am going to delve into some gameplay mods instead.

This is an amazing game. Coming from someone who loves games like Harvest Moon, this game is spectacular. The ability to farm and grow your farm how you want, whether it be by raising animals, growing plants, building tree orchards, etc, just gives you so many options. And if you don't want to farm, you can go out an explore! Go mining, fight monsters, go down to the beach and fish, talk with the towns people.
The towns people are what really make this game special too. The fact that each character has their own routine that they follow, their own likes and dislikes, their own stories, it feels amazing to spend time learning about them and just having fun.
That's what the game is all about in the end. It's about having fun and relaxing, and this is the perfect game to do it in. If you are looking for a game to spend the whole day playing, or only want to put in just a few minutes in each day, this is the game. This game is not for everyone, that is true, but there is something here that everyone can enjoy.

If you've ever wondered what would happen if you mashed QWOP and OctoDad together I Am Bread is it. You play a piece of bread on a quest to get toasted in each level, using various items such as irons or radiators or frying pans. Touching the floor or any other dirty surface will reduce your edibility percentage and once that hits 0% you lose.
Unfortunately, the game’s engine and programming also mean you will have to battle with the camera randomly adjusting itself on certain angles and the bread ragdolling around spastically from time to time. You can alleviate this to some degree by predicting which corner will contact next during a flip and hold that corner’s respective button down but even that can be a guessing game. Keeping in mind, your grip meter is counting down the entire time you are holding any buttons down so you’re on a time limit until you reach stable ground. After a few rounds of flailing and failure the game will throw you a bone by giving you an invincibility power up although using it basically removes any challenge from the game.
I Am Bread is one of those games where you either love the concept or hate it, and I couldn’t find anything to love about it. Maybe it’s just me, but I would rather spend time fighting bad guys than my own controller.

DD has something that is missing from the current generation of sandbox style games - a really satisfying loop. Off to the depths with your party to kill some monsters, grab some loot, get sick, go insane, and stress out, then back to town to recover, heal, relax and level. The town portion has a relaxed sports management game vibe, while the dungeon crawls can be tense and challenging. Each phase is short enough though that there's always interesting strategic decisions to make.
Unlike XCom style games though, even a party wipe doesn't crush your progress, because there's always more characters on the development mill. Sooner or later something WILL go wrong - that's RNG. ;) It is a grind, but a fun interesting grind which ensures you shift focus at regular intervals, and it is nice to play a game full of neurotic characters who's best option may well be to run away to fight another day. For the first hour it will punish you and you will hate it, but soon morbid fascination will seduce you to its bleak and withering charms. :)
Edit: Ps. If you don't like games with punishing RNG (e.g, you hate Blood Bowl), you don't like games with strict loops (eg. Stardew Valley) or get bored with procedurally generated Rogue inspired games then you won't like this.

I should have written something a long, long time ago. I've been playing this since Beta.
Reasons I love this game:
+ The Atmosphere of the game is perfect. The writing and Narrator tell a great story and the Narrator quotes in battles, interacting with curios, and other cutscenes (Boss battles, town events) is well done. The soundtrack is phenomenal, and the dungeon themes descend, with your characters, into madness as the light wanes.
+ You get a very real sense that your characters grow, suffer, and die. As their stress increases they let you know. They inform you whether they feel up to another run or whether they want to go on a drunken bender. Some of them will ONLY go on drunken benders and do not care if you want them to gamble or go pray. And it makes sense that the guy with Deviant Tastes is no longer allowed in the Brothel so, yes, you do have to address this issue.
+ The upgrades to the Stage Coach allow for characters to show up at Level 3, which save alot of time and money on levelling and upgrades. Which makes sense because as your Hamlet grows, people are better trained when they arrive and no longer run into the darkness unprepared.
+ Red Hook is still updating the game. Want to jump right into a harder difficulty? Stygian Mode is arriving soon. Want a shorter game experience because you don't want to farm out 100+ Deeds to fully upgrade The Blacksmith? Radiant Mode is here. And you can customize your experience as well. Don't like the corpses feature? You can disable it. Don't like enemy crits for ridiculous amounts? You can edit that in the options. Want more Town Events? Increase their number. Did you lose an entire party in a boss battle and lose trinkets? There's a special mission to help lessen the complete loss now.
+ The 'Wolves at the Door' plot mission.
+ DLC is planned for the future.
Regarding Criticisms:
- Yes, the game is difficult. However,
. This game teaches you to learn from your failures. I've put more hours into this than the 129 showed because of Offline play, but I still get party-wiped on occasion. Sometimes the enemy just gets lucky and rolls a strong crit. Some things can be planned for: you can bring provisions for interacting with Curios, you can Reinforce positive quirks and remove negative ones. There are 15 classes which all excel in certain areas. Skeletons don't bleed, but the entirety of the Warrens does. Some of the more recent reviews are going on about how difficult/unforgiving the game can be. Again, the game is difficult. But if you are willing to learn from your failures and plan effectively then you can mitigate some of the threats facing you. If you want an easy experience where you walk through the game, this isn't for you.
- Yes, negative effects from Curios are strong. If you don't learn from mistakes and insist of repeating them you will have a bad time. Learn what works and what doesn't. If you're into guides there are many great guides on the forums that explain Curio interactions. If you want to go in Blind then take notes.
- Rebuilding the town feels like it will take forever in a Non-Radiant Game Mode. Spreading out your resources is a bad idea. Focus on what you need most and really invest in that.
If you're interested in a solid RPG with good combat mechanics, a solid story and atmosphere, and understand that there can be no bravery without madness (and enemy stress-crits), this game is probably for you.
If you're interested in a game where you can plow through in a quick time and be able to ignore your mistakes, then this game is probably not for you.
Hope this helps.

No in-game voice comms.
Overall: Fantastic game, especially now it's free.

I am at the crossroads, and decided that games should be enjoyable and not require trauma-crisis management the entire playthrough.
If you aave a heatlhy positive party with no quirks or other illneseses, doesn't matter. O Age of Empires 3 é um jogo para Windows que faz parte da famosa série Age of Empires. O game se tornou a principal referência quando o assunto é jogos de raciocínio e estratégia. Seu objetivo é administrar as construções da cidade, as tecnologias que estão surgindo e a expansão da sociedade, de forma a fazer com que ela cresça da maneira mais organizada possível. O título faz você viajar pelos séculos e é diversão garantida.
Ao iniciar a partida, você volta no tempo e vive como pessoas de outra época. Existem oito civilizações, entre elas: Britânicos, Espanhóis, Portugueses e Franceses. Neste contexto, é possível encontrar minérios, madeira e ouro. Além de comercializar produtos e conseguir comida de qualquer maneira.
Nesta versão, mudar o status e evoluir acontece de um jeito diferente das outras versões. A experiência é mais importante e dá mais pontos do que conseguir novas tecnologias. Por isso, não é necessário somente avançar no tempo para adquirir novas ferramentas.

Ah, yet another entry into the already incredible Age of Empires franchise.  There are few RTS franchises that can boast about having as much success as AoE has had, and there is good reason behind that.  After putting in nearly 100 hours into the game I can easily say, this one does not disappoint for the most part.  It's no AoE II, but it's close.  That puts this game head and shoulders above most other strategy games.  Ensemble Studios really did an incredible job on their final entry into this series, and they will be greatly missed.
The gameplay of this entry in the AoE series is very similar to the previous two.  Build a base/town, build an economy, raise an army, destroy your enemies.  While it might be a simple straightforward process, it's a hell of a lot of fun.  The combat is visceral, the interface is simplistic enough for even brand new strategy game players to get a grasp on it in just a few short minutes, and the payoff is worth it, for the most part.  The only part that seems to have gotten worse in this entry, is the unit path-finding.  I don't know why or how this particular area got worse, but it definitely did.  Units will seemingly go completely out of there way to get to where you want them to go.  And villagers will CONSTANTLY lose track of what they are supposed to be doing.  The Idle Villager button was nice in AoE II, but it wasn't a necessity.  But in AoE III, you will be clicking it every minute.
There are several modes of gameplay in this version including but not limited to: Campaign, Single-player Random Maps, Multiplayer Standard, etc.  But all of them hold the same general process of base building and conquering your enemies.  The campaigns are lengthy, but slightly repetitive and the characters are not really that engaging, even in the expansions.  The real gem is the multiplayer.  There are several different civilizations to choose from, each one with incredibly unique units that have completely different capabilities.  So while the units are different, this forces different strategies depending on the civilization you have chosen. This creates a unique experience and feel to each civilization and keeps the gameplay fresh while extending it's longevity.
Of course when it comes to multiplayer strategy games, balancing is key.  ESO did a pretty good job of balancing units and civs to begin with, but there were a few missteps in the original that were fixed in the expansions.  So of course the final expansion, The Asian Dynasties, is the definitive AoE III multiplayer experience.  (I don't think you can even play the Warchiefs multiplayer anymore)  I do not wish to go much further in depth with gameplay simply because this is a strategy game and can literally be talked and discussed about forever.  So I'll just finish with this:  The gameplay is really incredible and enjoyable, while also being long-lasting.
This game was released in 2005.  2005.  I'll say that one more time.  This game was released in 2005.  And it STILL looks better than a ton of games being released these days.  The new physics engine that was put into place for AoE III is incredible and might be the best looking one in strategy games.  Buildings fall apart completely differently depending on what they are being attacked by and how.  Fire two cannons at two different houses, and they will be blown apart in completely different ways, even from the same angles.  This game was WAY ahead of it's time in terms of graphics.  You will often find yourself just sitting and staring in wonderment at the action that is taking place on the screen (when really you should probably be taking care of other things in the game).
The audio is perfectly matched for this game.  All the way from the muskets firing, to armies being demolished by elephants, and to cannons thundering over everything else.  And you will hear those cannons from very far away.  Just this small addition, brings in a massive level of tension to the game (especially when playing with Fog of War on).  You can hear the artillery slowly encroaching on your base, and depending on your level of readiness, you are either swarming around trying to prepare or silently waiting for the first shot to be fired in a battle that will determine the fate of your town.
As for the music, it's OK.  I'm a big fan of the soundtracks in the AoE series as they have always meshed ever so perfectly with the gameplay and visuals.  This entry probably has the weakest soundtrack of all three games.  But it's not terrible.  Just OK.
This game has tremendous lasting appeal.  And ESO specifically built it that way.  By implementing the new Home City system into this entry, your City can earn experience and level up after almost every match, which unlocks new cards that you can put into your City's deck that provide bonuses that can be called upon during the match.  Anything from a passive bonus to resource gathering rates, to massive extra reinforcement troops.  The servers are still packed with players ready to fight and try to demolish you so don't be afraid of dwindling player base.
This game is definitely an 8/10.  Superb gameplay, fantastic graphics, awesome audio, and great lasting appeal.  Is it worth $40?  Probably not.  That's a lot of asking money for a game that came out in 2005.  I think $30 is much more reasonable.

DD has something that is missing from the current generation of sandbox style games - a really satisfying loop. Off to the depths with your party to kill some monsters, grab some loot, get sick, go insane, and stress out, then back to town to recover, heal, relax and level. The town portion has a relaxed sports management game vibe, while the dungeon crawls can be tense and challenging. Each phase is short enough though that there's always interesting strategic decisions to make.
Unlike XCom style games though, even a party wipe doesn't crush your progress, because there's always more characters on the development mill. Sooner or later something WILL go wrong - that's RNG. ;) It is a grind, but a fun interesting grind which ensures you shift focus at regular intervals, and it is nice to play a game full of neurotic characters who's best option may well be to run away to fight another day. For the first hour it will punish you and you will hate it, but soon morbid fascination will seduce you to its bleak and withering charms. :)
Edit: Ps. If you don't like games with punishing RNG (e.g, you hate Blood Bowl), you don't like games with strict loops (eg. Stardew Valley) or get bored with procedurally generated Rogue inspired games then you won't like this.

I should have written something a long, long time ago. I've been playing this since Beta.
Reasons I love this game:
+ The Atmosphere of the game is perfect. The writing and Narrator tell a great story and the Narrator quotes in battles, interacting with curios, and other cutscenes (Boss battles, town events) is well done. The soundtrack is phenomenal, and the dungeon themes descend, with your characters, into madness as the light wanes.
+ You get a very real sense that your characters grow, suffer, and die. As their stress increases they let you know. They inform you whether they feel up to another run or whether they want to go on a drunken bender. Some of them will ONLY go on drunken benders and do not care if you want them to gamble or go pray. And it makes sense that the guy with Deviant Tastes is no longer allowed in the Brothel so, yes, you do have to address this issue.
+ The upgrades to the Stage Coach allow for characters to show up at Level 3, which save alot of time and money on levelling and upgrades. Which makes sense because as your Hamlet grows, people are better trained when they arrive and no longer run into the darkness unprepared.
+ Red Hook is still updating the game. Want to jump right into a harder difficulty? Stygian Mode is arriving soon. Want a shorter game experience because you don't want to farm out 100+ Deeds to fully upgrade The Blacksmith? Radiant Mode is here. And you can customize your experience as well. Don't like the corpses feature? You can disable it. Don't like enemy crits for ridiculous amounts? You can edit that in the options. Want more Town Events? Increase their number. Did you lose an entire party in a boss battle and lose trinkets? There's a special mission to help lessen the complete loss now.
+ The 'Wolves at the Door' plot mission.
+ DLC is planned for the future.
Regarding Criticisms:
- Yes, the game is difficult. However,
. This game teaches you to learn from your failures. I've put more hours into this than the 129 showed because of Offline play, but I still get party-wiped on occasion. Sometimes the enemy just gets lucky and rolls a strong crit. Some things can be planned for: you can bring provisions for interacting with Curios, you can Reinforce positive quirks and remove negative ones. There are 15 classes which all excel in certain areas. Skeletons don't bleed, but the entirety of the Warrens does. Some of the more recent reviews are going on about how difficult/unforgiving the game can be. Again, the game is difficult. But if you are willing to learn from your failures and plan effectively then you can mitigate some of the threats facing you. If you want an easy experience where you walk through the game, this isn't for you.
- Yes, negative effects from Curios are strong. If you don't learn from mistakes and insist of repeating them you will have a bad time. Learn what works and what doesn't. If you're into guides there are many great guides on the forums that explain Curio interactions. If you want to go in Blind then take notes.
- Rebuilding the town feels like it will take forever in a Non-Radiant Game Mode. Spreading out your resources is a bad idea. Focus on what you need most and really invest in that.
If you're interested in a solid RPG with good combat mechanics, a solid story and atmosphere, and understand that there can be no bravery without madness (and enemy stress-crits), this game is probably for you.
If you're interested in a game where you can plow through in a quick time and be able to ignore your mistakes, then this game is probably not for you.
Hope this helps.

This game is one of my favorites. It is one of the best strategy games that I know of. I am not a big fan of the campaign, but that isn't where the fun really is at. The fun is with managing your economy, building an army, and working together with your friends to take down the enemy.
There are not as many civilizations as in the previous games, (Spanish, British, French, Portugese, Dutch, German, Russian, and Ottoman for the core game. Iroquois, Sioux, and Aztec for the War Chiefs Expansion. Japanese, Chinese, and Indian for the Asian Dynasties Expansion) but each civilization is very unique. The more you use a Home City (Civilization), the more you can customize with it. Leveling up grants you new Home City Shipment Cards to better bolster your economy, military, or navy.
There are many different maps to choose from, along with the option to design your own (the Scenario Editor has tons of customization options. It takes a while for my powerful laptop to load it all).
There are not many different game modes, but really, you don't need them. Every game is unique. One game, your enemy could build a powerful Navy. Another, he or she could build a grand army. Part of the fun comes from predicting your enemy's movements and developng strategies to counter them.
The graphics are kind of choppy compared to the next-gen triple A games, but the gameplay is really what makes the game great.
I would highly suggest this game to everyone, but I would advise them to wait to purchase it until there is a big sale on Steam (I got mine for $10. The regular price is $40). I give this game a 10/10. I look forward to meeting those who follow my advice on the battlefield.

holds up!

Speaking of blasts, despite being a war game, it has real time physics and ragdolls so when you shoot someone with a cannon they actually and believably go flying! DD has something that is missing from the current generation of sandbox style games - a really satisfying loop. Off to the depths with your party to kill some monsters, grab some loot, get sick, go insane, and stress out, then back to town to recover, heal, relax and level. The town portion has a relaxed sports management game vibe, while the dungeon crawls can be tense and challenging. Each phase is short enough though that there's always interesting strategic decisions to make.
Unlike XCom style games though, even a party wipe doesn't crush your progress, because there's always more characters on the development mill. Sooner or later something WILL go wrong - that's RNG. ;) It is a grind, but a fun interesting grind which ensures you shift focus at regular intervals, and it is nice to play a game full of neurotic characters who's best option may well be to run away to fight another day. For the first hour it will punish you and you will hate it, but soon morbid fascination will seduce you to its bleak and withering charms. :)
Edit: Ps. If you don't like games with punishing RNG (e.g, you hate Blood Bowl), you don't like games with strict loops (eg. Stardew Valley) or get bored with procedurally generated Rogue inspired games then you won't like this.

Fallout 4 is a good game with a lot to offer, made a even better thanks to mods. Free mods that you can get at the nexus especially if you are running it on PC. However, the negative review is due to the publisher's desperate (and repeated) attempts at milking the modding community, even though the modding community has already helped them sell their games way longer than they would usually do. As such instead of rewarding modders with more tools and changes to the game without a cost, they implement the "creation club". A service that currently offers primarily inferior versions of free mods and one mod that is actually good, but sadly not worth the price to get it. Why? Well even if that one mod might be worth it, is it worth the price you will have to pay when you have to spend at least 8 bucks (euro or dollar) to get it, thanks to the "credits system". Credits mind you that the terms of condition states that you have no rights when you buy, and can be removed, changed or whatever at any time. It also removes your lawful protection for purchases, such as refunds. In addition, while they claim to test content, they do not take any responsibility for the mods in any way (Again you can find this info in term of service).
Bethesda did implement one helpful feature to support the paid skins for you pipboy, but when you can get hundreds of better looking and free alternatives, why bother?
Creation club in its currency form offers nothing to customers except those stuck on a console where these paid mods are the only option. For the rest of us, this is a clear anti-consumer move, where you are forced to enjoy extra unwanted content on your pc.
The biggest problem is the simple fact that you get nothing for paying. No safety, no insurances that the content works, no rights and the joy of being forced to purchase more credits than you need.

A serious dissapointment compared to every other recent Fallout Game, as well as the originals. This has been my favorite series since the 90s, but if Bethesda continues their anti-consumer tactics then I will not be purchasing another game from them. The choice to do player-character voice acting was a horrible one, and essentially removes the RP in RPG from this game. Your speech choices are almost always limited to 3 versions of yes, and a no. The main plot is extremely weak and uninteresting, and is really just a poorly executed copy of what was masterfully done in Fallout: New Vegas - which was not written by Bethesda.
As a massive fan of building in most games, I was incredibly excited about the settlement building aspect of this game. It is decent, but horribly poorly executed and acts like it was a mod forced into the game, rather than a base part of the game. Never the less I found is enjoyable - but many many others don't. It can be very much redeemed with mods, as much of the game can. But you shouldn't have to buy a crappy game to play a good mod.
Speaking of Mods, Bethesda is once again trying to monetize them. Even after the massive backlash of their first attempt for paid mods, they've reskinned it into their "Creation Club" so that you can buy all those weapon skins you were previously getting completely free! Oh, but they say that with the creation club, they guarantee all the mods will work! You don't get that guarantee just downloading from Nexus or another mod site do you? Well, no you don't. But don't be tricked into thinking you'll get that with Bethesda either. When was the last time they released a stable game on PC? It takes them a year to get games into a remotely stable place, and then when they're done you'll still randomly crash every few hours unless you install mods to fix those things. Mods have been free to PC gamers for years, and while I am all for supporting modders who make great content financially, I don't support Bethesda cheaply trying to cash in on mods that have been free for decades to PC gamers. It is extremely unlikely I will be purchasing another Bethesda game unless they change these ridiculous policies.

I read some of the lower played hours and the people are wrong. The game is super fun and addicting. It is a mix of CoD 2 and CS:GO. But don't go into this game expecting 100% counter-strike because it is not that. The meta right now is AK 47 and deagle. Both of these guns you can unlock for free. The maps are really good, I enjoy em. I have over 1k hours on CSGO, and been playing counter-strike for years now, going back to 1.5. This game feels like maybe Call of duty pro mod. You get rewards as you log into the game everyday, and on the 7th? day you get a bunch of medals, which you can buy weapons for. The weapons you can buy are not a 14 day trial, you will have them forever. It does not take long to grind the weapons either. They have matchmaking and it works well. I'm a huge CS:GO fan, and you can easily matchmake for a 5v5 bomb & defuse match.
They do have random box skins, and they are hard to get just like in CSGO. The only thing is that you can't trade them with other people.
I have seen some reviews about hitboxes being bad, but there is a mode where you can test them yourself, and to me, they seem fine. Not sure how they are when the person is moving though. I have been playing a bit so far, and it seems solid to me (when someone is moving). This is a korea shooter / call of duty ISH type of game, so you can get some random running head shots.
I said earlier how I do like the maps. The maps usually have a 3 lane, sometimes they do split off, which is nice. You got your standard path to A and B with a mid for sniping.
They do have a clan system, which can be leveled up and you will get a cool emblem.
If you like CS:GO, and find some korean shooters fun to play, I would recommend this one. I been enjoying it a lot. It has that "one more match" feeling like CS:GO, and maybe that's why I keep playing it. Plus, it would be nice to get some of the sick looking knife skins :) .
Lastly, the devs do check the discord and steam forums as well. They always do streams on twitch and talk about the things they see the community chatting. They are close to the communication like Blizzard does with their games. They are VERY open with answering all kinds of questions as well.

Don't be fooled by what everyone is saying about this game. But, Darkest Dungeon is NOT for everyone.
This game is notoriously hard, especially with its seemingly broken RNG. But, that doesn't mean its impossible.
This game requires patience, tatics, and preparation. Don't expect this game to be an easy train ride and expect it to be a run through an opposite facing highway. This game will be unfair at times, but so is life.
You will grind a lot, and will have to create and remember multiple strategies for every area, enemy, and enemy parties. You will not get what you want all the time. Even the simplest missions can become overwhelming. You will lose your best heroes and may have to abandon missions if you wish to keep your best men alive.
This may sound a lot to ask from the player, but that is what the game is about. No hero is supposed to come out of every fight with health and mind intact. This game delivers the true experience ragtag teamwork in horrific setting.
So, do you think you have what it takes to delve the Darkest Dugeon?

I recieved this game for free back on the first free weekend well before it went F2P.
As this game gets updated quite frequently my previous review was out of date so i figured i would update it so here goes.
Whilst i do recommend this game mainly due to the fact its F2P i would warn you like many F2P games it is now incredibly grindy. In the time it took for me to unlock a tier 2 relativly cheap ship the brawler i could have pre tech tree update unlocked at least 2-3 ships. The grind is now incredibly long. Although the Xp grind isnt too bad the credit grind sucks (Ships must be unlocked with manufacturer specific XP and then bought with general currency). For me the grind has been a major turn off for the game. Also as part of the tech tree update my previous ships were all reset so i have to grind ships now.
Pros:
Gameplay is really solid. Capital ships feel slow and heavy like they should more games really should do this style of gameplay. Ships also feel unique like MOBA heroes each with specific roles and playstyles.
Graphics the graphics are pretty good the ships for the most part look really good with each of the 3 manufacturers(Think countries in War thunder or WOT) having a specific style of ship design e.g. The Zarek have got a boxy design continued through there ships. However the environment could do with work aside from the bases which are massivly improved now.
Variety. Theres a lot of variety in ships theres over 20 ships in game now i think. Each one plays differently and has unique abilites. Some include the basiliks black hole. Or the Leviathans fusion  beam. Whilst other abilites carry over to other ships e.g. Missiles and strike craft are seen on a lot of ships. Also whilst there are several cloaking ships (Assasins e.g. Infiltrator, Ghost, Basilisk) Each one plays differently with the basilisk being a support ship in comparison to the offensive styles of the others.
Cons:
Grind. Its pretty ridiculous imo. XP grind comes first and is over pretty quick. Then you need the credits and say youre grinding your first ship you will often find yourself with all the XP and half of the credits meaning youre now grinding a 2nd ship to afford the next which means by the time you have the XP for the 2nd youre massivly behind in creds. Some ships are also outrageously exspensive. Also anyone wanting to play a cloaker now has to wait an age and the easiest to get is the basilisk and the Widow one of which sucks as its too easy to counter and the other is good but doesnt really play much like an assasin. Also the grind forces you into playing certain ships repeatedly e.g. When i was grinding for the brawler i only had the pioneer starting USR ship which i hated to begin with. Now i am grinding for the basilisk and i would be forced into playing the sentinel which is a ship i hate due to my hatred of autoaim guns. Also its just boring for me. Fortunatly i have the revenant a limited time ship given away a while ago so i at least have got a good ship to play in that tree but repeatedly playing it still bores me
Ship designs. Imo the ships vary from being really awesome e.g. Colossus to being fairly lackluster the new superlifter looks like a box. As does the gladiator. Or the interceptor which looks spookily similar to a reaper or paladin. I get manufacturer ships should look similar but a bit more variety is nice.
Of note a lot of people complain about the paragon (Carrier) being removed i dont really mind the ship was a major irritation when it was around had too much health imo and didnt really acomplish all that much. But my opinion on it is if the devs felt it shouldnt be in the game thats there decision and i agree with them it wasnt working and wasnt functioning as a carrier should but i look forward to a future one.
Again to sum up its a cautious recommend if you like battlestar galactica or various other sci-fi stuff then this is pretty awesome but if you have a job and dont want another then the grind might be too much for you.

This is a terrific game--but now the bad news. The difficulty is way off balance and makes the early game super hard. Devs want to convince players that losing soldiers is "not catastrophic," yet it is completely catastrophic. Skipping early missions not as much of an option as it should be. With mission timers and "Doomsday Timer", you have to really have your high ranking soldiers survive, otherwise you won't have the ranks to get the extra attacks to survive when you REALLY need to. A couple of key promotion upgrades and item upgrades come too late, and when they arrive, you are on easy street, and the mid-game, end-game is a cake walk. Psi arrives too late. I found this to be the case on two play throughs at two difficulty levels.
Also, as others have said, the storyline favors an excessively linear approach, especially in early and mid-game. I would expect all this to be ironed out with patches, but in the meantime I would reccomend mods that help out the early game.
That said, the devs have really listened to every last complaint and have made an exceptionally fun game.

Age Of Empires III is one of the best strategy games I have ever played in all my years of strategy gaming. It combines the exciting and fast paced elements of Starcraft with the slightly slower and more strategic elements traditional to the Age Of Empires franchise. The graphics are phenomenal, especially when it comes to building destruction. Unlike games such as Starcraft 2, where they suddnely start burning in strange places after being mauled by melee units, the buildings in Age Of Empires show exactly how your units are doing damage.
There is just something very satisfying about watching your artiller fire into a crowd of infantry, leaving a trough of blood and bodies. Or even better, watching your mortars fire a volley, smashing in the roof of the enemy townhall.
The campaign is mediocre, although the Asian Dynasy campaings were in my opinion extraordinary. My favorite being the Indian campaign. One of the challenges using artillery is the time it takes for the cannons to switch from transport mode to fire mode, which is more than enough time for cavalry to ride in and decimate your heavy weapons. The Indians don't have that problem, as their cannon are mounted on freaking elephants. ELEPHANTS. That basically means you can pull some Lord Of The Rings style action, with your cannon-armed elephants charging into an enemy city and blowing them apart. Keep in mind, Western firepower is stronger, so don't expect to win an allout fight of cannon with the British if you're playing as the Indians.
The Asian DLC also throws in a unique third element, which is exports. As I said earlier, Western artillery is vastly superior to that of the Asian countries. So basically, if you get your exports up, you can bring in some deadly fire support for your armies.
My only complaint with Age Of Empires is that the combat AI seems to get confused. When you attempt to move your entire army somewhere, you have three options. You can just plain right cliick, which will set your units to Move, in which they will single-mindedly go to their destination. They will NOT attack the enemy. Your second option is to right click on an enemy unit or building, which would mean they would target that one object, and ignore all others. Now the third option is what needs work. You can click Attack Move, but here's where the problem comes in. You can only attack move on terrain you can see. If you try and send your army to attack where you KNOW the enemy is, they will not move. Late game, when you are controlling multiple armies, this can get confusing. When you would prefer to send one army to take out an enemy stronghold, and then control a second army in a flanking manuever on the enemy support, before moving in to reinforce the assault, you may find yourself unpleasantly surprised to discover that your reinforcements stopped. There is very little that as depressing as seeing an army brought down by rifle volley after rifle volley, while the cavarly that would have saved them is too far away to help.
TL;DR: This game is excellent. Well worth the full price, although I would suggest waiting for it to go on sale. I got it for about 3 cents on the Humble Bundle (give or take) and at the same time it was on a massive sale here on Steam. Keep an eye out for when that happens, and you will find yourself with hours of fun. Just remember to keep your eye on your armies at all time to be sure they are coming in to support you!

A very sadistic turbased combat game that has excellent artstyle and audio especially the narration of Wayne June. Gameplay offers complex builds depending on the team/groups. Each class is unique and has its own strengths and weaknesses.
It can be quite punishing but it can be done if you take the time and patience to learn the game. The smallest mistakes will kill your group.
RNG can be be diabolical against you or hilariously lucky for you. It goes BOTH ways, no one complains when their heroes are landging crits and dodging blows. You can expect from both ends of the spectrums as either your heroes getting crit and stressed to insanity or you get lucky and one or two of your heroes passes a resolve test and slaughters the entire dungeon by themselves. That's the extremes though and most of the time a well supplied and carefully built group can endure most dungeons especially when adding specific heroes that excel in specific dungeons. This game is about the Risk and Reward movement. A wrong turn can cost you dearly.
Don't let the vindictive and immature people patrolling and downvoting positive reviews dissuade you. If you enjoy actual challenging games then this might grab your attention for a while.
Again, only purchase if you're willing to take the time to learn the game and deal with challenging situations. Only major downside I can think of is the grinding for heirlooms to upgrade buildings but otherwise it's a great game.
It's not perfect and can be brutal at times but still challengingly fun and the atmosphere is deliciously grim.

This game is a mixed bag.
It's not a Role Playing Game, there is little story as such in the game. It's also not a rougelike game albeit there are some random elements like special encounters of sort of wandering monsters.
This is a fully turn-based game - battles are turn based, town phase is turn based even moving in the dungeon is turn based. You can see animation of characters walking but still the party is an object moving on the map tile by tile. There are some bugs or designer choices that mix turn based character with dexterity based gameplay - if your character has a quirk that forces him or her to use some curio on the map then you have like about 3 seconds to use an item on that curio before the character uses it. But that't the only place that I've seen such dexterity based element.
Graphics are really beautiful if you're into Mike Mignola style of art, but graphics alone don't make game great. This is mostly an inventory & party management dungeon crawler with a bit of settlement upgrades based on 6 resources:
- gold to buy stuff
- four different types of heirlooms to upgrade your buildings
- heroes to be sent to die... I mean loot stuff from dungeon runs
Upgrades are rather expensive, dungeon runs are rather long and time consuming, levelling up may take ages sometimes.
This game has a huge RNG factor entwined into the game. Like you can have an almost perfect run where you aren't really wounded and stressed and hit one party of enemies like wild rabid dogs or other killer oozes with 12 Hitpoints that may mop the floor with your party because of killer super powerful critical hits all the while you're trying to hit them and miss most of the times.
Somewhere on Reddit there is a post about a guy who got all of his party wiped by like three rabid dogs that all of a sudden started to critically hit party members. That's all true, RNG can be a pain sometimes but I guess that's all of the charm in this game.
Pros:
- graphics
- overall dark and gloomy mood that's very immersive
- original character classes - after all those characters are murderers, weirdos, madmen and other unsavory lot
- RNG after all, it makes the game interesting and unpredictable
- titular dungeon is absolutely hardcore - expect very powerful enemies with many hitpoints, strong attacks and high resistances. Even high level heroes can die with ease there. Like in Demise: Rise of Ku'utan.
Cons:
- RNG doesn't make this game rougelike, come on, there aren't that many variables after all
- repeatable dungeon runs - after about five hours into the game you'll see most of enemies and encounters out there
- experience and resources grinding - really, what's the point of those heirlooms? Couldn't upgrades be purchased in gold?
- backtracking in dungeons is boring, it's like walking simulator
- slow animations that can't be turned off or made faster
- there is some semblance of plot in this game but after one hour of listening to mister Received Pronunciation Narrator I've had enough of this voice. To me it's like listening to someone trying to speak something to you in a deep voice while having his mouth full of marshmallows. Aaargh.
After all I can recommend this game for those players who like turn-based games of dungeon crawling and party management with beautiful graphics and who can look over some flaws like repetitive gameplay, resources grind and sometimes unfair RNG.

Everything that was ho-hum about the first has been improved. More angles, movement, weapons, enemies. More creativity of combat tactics. Much better game aesthetic over the cartoonish first. Beam weapons satisfying to see go off. Great map and country-control system. Incentive to take other tactical approaches, excellent mission variety, you name it, it's better.
This is a terrific game--but now the bad news. The difficulty is way off balance and makes the early game super hard. Devs want to convince players that losing soldiers is "not catastrophic," yet it is completely catastrophic. Skipping early missions not as much of an option as it should be. With mission timers and "Doomsday Timer", you have to really have your high ranking soldiers survive, otherwise you won't have the ranks to get the extra attacks to survive when you REALLY need to. A couple of key promotion upgrades and item upgrades come too late, and when they arrive, you are on easy street, and the mid-game, end-game is a cake walk. Psi arrives too late. I found this to be the case on two play throughs at two difficulty levels.
Also, as others have said, the storyline favors an excessively linear approach, especially in early and mid-game. I would expect all this to be ironed out with patches, but in the meantime I would reccomend mods that help out the early game.
That said, the devs have really listened to every last complaint and have made an exceptionally fun game.

Don't be fooled by what everyone is saying about this game. But, Darkest Dungeon is NOT for everyone.
This game is notoriously hard, especially with its seemingly broken RNG. But, that doesn't mean its impossible.
This game requires patience, tatics, and preparation. Don't expect this game to be an easy train ride and expect it to be a run through an opposite facing highway. This game will be unfair at times, but so is life.
You will grind a lot, and will have to create and remember multiple strategies for every area, enemy, and enemy parties. You will not get what you want all the time. Even the simplest missions can become overwhelming. You will lose your best heroes and may have to abandon missions if you wish to keep your best men alive.
This may sound a lot to ask from the player, but that is what the game is about. No hero is supposed to come out of every fight with health and mind intact. This game delivers the true experience ragtag teamwork in horrific setting.
So, do you think you have what it takes to delve the Darkest Dugeon?

A very sadistic turbased combat game that has excellent artstyle and audio especially the narration of Wayne June. Gameplay offers complex builds depending on the team/groups. Each class is unique and has its own strengths and weaknesses.
It can be quite punishing but it can be done if you take the time and patience to learn the game. The smallest mistakes will kill your group.
RNG can be be diabolical against you or hilariously lucky for you. It goes BOTH ways, no one complains when their heroes are landging crits and dodging blows. You can expect from both ends of the spectrums as either your heroes getting crit and stressed to insanity or you get lucky and one or two of your heroes passes a resolve test and slaughters the entire dungeon by themselves. That's the extremes though and most of the time a well supplied and carefully built group can endure most dungeons especially when adding specific heroes that excel in specific dungeons. This game is about the Risk and Reward movement. A wrong turn can cost you dearly.
Don't let the vindictive and immature people patrolling and downvoting positive reviews dissuade you. If you enjoy actual challenging games then this might grab your attention for a while.
Again, only purchase if you're willing to take the time to learn the game and deal with challenging situations. Only major downside I can think of is the grinding for heirlooms to upgrade buildings but otherwise it's a great game.
It's not perfect and can be brutal at times but still challengingly fun and the atmosphere is deliciously grim.

Review from 2015:
This is essentially what Mechwarrior Online should have been.
A skill based, tactical shooter with various roles. It still has "enough twitch"-aspect so the player skill plays a major role. A single skilled player can somewhat dominate the game as there aren't many "instant hit" weapons that you couldn't avoid with proper movement and positioning. The few lasers in the game are pretty limited in effective range. Some of the weapons also have firing arcs, which means that if you aren't positioned well, you might be only to fire eg. one out of four main weapons.
+Looks and specially SOUNDS suberb
+Not just a hitscan shooter, moving plays a HUGE role. Plenty of weapons that will require timing.
+Extremely playable, controls are silky smooth and responsive as you get hang of the intertia and mass of your ship
+Different ships and builds REALLY impact gameplay
+Although team based, a single player skill matters MUCH more than in a typical MOBA
+Although there is currently just one map, I think the asteroids are procedially generated, meaning gameplay changes a lot from round to round
+Avg. game lasts only 15-20 minutes
-No real leaver penalty yet (this isn't really that much of a problem as people can join games that have already started)
-Armor mechanics aren't properly explained (damage multiplies if you break armor)

Run around aimlessly, stumble upon a dungeon, button mash your way through it, pick up your generic loot, throw away the dozens of worthless trash you just got, rinse, repeat.
That's as far as this game goes in terms of progression and depth. It was a nice distraction for an hour, then it quickly degraded into a bore. The classes in this game are incredulously shallow. I'm not at all exaggerating when I say that you've seen all that a class has to offer within the first few levels. I've played a good amount of MMOs, but nothing could have prepared me for the sheer nothingness that is Trove's classes. Each class only has 3 skills. Yes, 3 skills. So, after you've played one for a few minutes, that is it. The sense of progression other MMOs provide by steadily unlocking new abilities as you level is painfully absent in Trove, because there are only 3 abilities anyway. The entertainment provided by the classes of an MMO is extremely important, so even if this game did everything else right, it likely still wouldn't be worth your time. Sadly, it doesn't do anything else right either, mostly because there isn't really much else to this game to begin with. After you've completed a few dungeons, they will all start to feel the same. They provide no real challenge and if you run through them button mashing you'll still win. Anyone with half a brain and some decent gear could beat a boss fight with their eyes closed. When you complete the dungeon, you will be showered with an insane amount of items, which sounds good in theory, but 90% of it is useless. Because of this, you'll end up spending a lot of time cycling through your inventory, throwing away the massive amount of useless garbage the game forces in your face. It's a repetitive, shallow, and unenjoyable grindfest of an MMO that I would never recommend to even my worst enemy.

This game is a mixed bag.
It's not a Role Playing Game, there is little story as such in the game. It's also not a rougelike game albeit there are some random elements like special encounters of sort of wandering monsters.
This is a fully turn-based game - battles are turn based, town phase is turn based even moving in the dungeon is turn based. You can see animation of characters walking but still the party is an object moving on the map tile by tile. There are some bugs or designer choices that mix turn based character with dexterity based gameplay - if your character has a quirk that forces him or her to use some curio on the map then you have like about 3 seconds to use an item on that curio before the character uses it. But that't the only place that I've seen such dexterity based element.
Graphics are really beautiful if you're into Mike Mignola style of art, but graphics alone don't make game great. This is mostly an inventory & party management dungeon crawler with a bit of settlement upgrades based on 6 resources:
- gold to buy stuff
- four different types of heirlooms to upgrade your buildings
- heroes to be sent to die... I mean loot stuff from dungeon runs
Upgrades are rather expensive, dungeon runs are rather long and time consuming, levelling up may take ages sometimes.
This game has a huge RNG factor entwined into the game. Like you can have an almost perfect run where you aren't really wounded and stressed and hit one party of enemies like wild rabid dogs or other killer oozes with 12 Hitpoints that may mop the floor with your party because of killer super powerful critical hits all the while you're trying to hit them and miss most of the times.
Somewhere on Reddit there is a post about a guy who got all of his party wiped by like three rabid dogs that all of a sudden started to critically hit party members. That's all true, RNG can be a pain sometimes but I guess that's all of the charm in this game.
Pros:
- graphics
- overall dark and gloomy mood that's very immersive
- original character classes - after all those characters are murderers, weirdos, madmen and other unsavory lot
- RNG after all, it makes the game interesting and unpredictable
- titular dungeon is absolutely hardcore - expect very powerful enemies with many hitpoints, strong attacks and high resistances. Even high level heroes can die with ease there. Like in Demise: Rise of Ku'utan.
Cons:
- RNG doesn't make this game rougelike, come on, there aren't that many variables after all
- repeatable dungeon runs - after about five hours into the game you'll see most of enemies and encounters out there
- experience and resources grinding - really, what's the point of those heirlooms? Couldn't upgrades be purchased in gold?
- backtracking in dungeons is boring, it's like walking simulator
- slow animations that can't be turned off or made faster
- there is some semblance of plot in this game but after one hour of listening to mister Received Pronunciation Narrator I've had enough of this voice. To me it's like listening to someone trying to speak something to you in a deep voice while having his mouth full of marshmallows. Aaargh.
After all I can recommend this game for those players who like turn-based games of dungeon crawling and party management with beautiful graphics and who can look over some flaws like repetitive gameplay, resources grind and sometimes unfair RNG.

Let me start by saying as I played through the game, I started out loving it and enjoyed it less and less every passing moment. Also, I am a diehard XCOM fan and have played every game from the original through the expansions, Xenonauts, XCOM:EU and EW, The Bureau, and now XCOM 2. I also believe Ironman is the only way to go, otherwaise you can just negate every bad thing that happens. Now to the review:
The start of the game is fantastic, and Firaxis has made some awesome refinements to the combat systems from XCOM:EU/EW. The textures, animations, and overall polish are crisp. The game started out hard, as an XCOM game should, but not unfair. I then found myself constantly interrupted by ceaseless side missions and events that interrupted the flow of the game back at base, while I was able to quickly field a force that was unstoppable and never lost a soldier after upgrading to Mag weapons. By the time I got plasma's, it was no contest. The game quickly turned into a tedious affair, but I had high hopes for the final mission. The second to last mission, which I won't ruin was phenomenal and I found myself re-invigorated and ready to finish the game on a high note and write a stunning review. The last mission was going awesome until the final battle. I suffered innumerable bugs, the worst of which was that when I moved my soldiers across a certain point ont he bridge, which if you've played you know what I'm talking about, a cutscene triggers. This cutscene locked the camera on the final position the camera was in when the cutscene ended, and I could not issue any commands to my troops. I had to save and exit then reload for every single soldier, which took about 30 minutes to just get through that position. Then the final battle occured. For the first time in any XCOM game or XCOM spinoff, I felt cheated. It was not just difficult, it was blatently unfair. There seems to have been no creative process behind this battle and in order to make an epic final challenge, the developers decided to throw endless waves of troops at the player, while supporting that with several of the most powerful alien forces in the game. This might seem like a a fun challenge, but an ability with a four turn cooldown, meaning there is only ever a one turn break between attacks, takes off half a soldiers health and is AOE that spand half the room. You have a similar attack, but it also forces a position change, which there is almost only half cover throughout the room, which is equivalent to no cover. I felt cheated. I was destroyed on my Normal/Ironman game with no hope of winning whatsoever. I could have employed some cheap tactics, like hiding out back on the bridge and mowing the enemy down one by one until I fulfilled the objective, but that would be an exploit of the AI system and would not have felt fair.
TL;DR First XCOM game to botch the insanely difficult but always fair feeling of the game. Cheap tricks employed by the developers at the expense of a clever but difficult final challenge result in frustration. Bugs abound, even after multiple patches that break gameplay and ruin the core experience during the most critical levels and dramatic moments. Save yourself the headache, get XCOM:EU/EW and Xenonauts unless you feel that exploiting AI systems instead of tactically challenging gameplay is fun.

As I grew up, my favorite game was Age of Empires II, the first strategy game I played. The first game I
played.
It focused on growing your nation from the darkness of early Middle Ages, with your troops still using clubs and such, all the way to the Renaissance with cannons, mighty castles and wonders to build and hold.
But then the third game changed its ways.
AoE III Starts where it left off, only a bit further. It's Colonial age, and many nations build their ships in order to claim the newly discovered America. So, you're free to choose one of the 8 nations, each with its own gimmick. The Dutch get Banks to build, which generate money, Russians train their troops very quickly, French have more powerfull villagers, etc.
This is an incredible improvement over the previous game, where each nation only had some buildings, units and techs locked from them, alongside with a diffrent special unit and technology to make in castles.
The problem comes in, when you acknowledge that some Nations are simply unstoppable if they get just the right things, which can be just near them in some maps. For example, letting Dutch build a lot of their banks, can make them nearly unstoppable, because they get enough coin to support large armies with a lot of upgrades. And this can happen if the map has a lot of food and/or wood near starting places.
While the game has many maps, you'll have a bit of trouble finding out what kind of it will it be if you don't know US states well, as almost every map has is named like that: "Orinoco" "New England" "Carolina" etc. Thankfully, you won't be bored. Islands, Deserts, Plains, Woods, Taigas, if you can name it, it's probably here.
When you first choose your nation, you'll be treated to your Home City (Which name can be changed before confirming your choice), Which is the main feature of the game. Here you can unlock "cards" which you can add to your "deck", up to 21 cards can be in your deck. But don't worry, it's not the main game.
Cards are simply shipments from your HC that are sent to your colony: from a few villagers and resource crates, through military units, special technologies and carts with enough materials to build an enormous fort to the powerful mercenaries and upgrades.
Each card is locked to a certain age, so if you want to get more powerful ones, you have to advance. You also need to gain XP points which represent your growing might. When you get enough, you can send a new shipment, or wait a bit if you want something diffrent.
XP is gained through killing enemies, building, winning matches, and simply being good at the game. Reaching enough XP also levels up your Home City, which allows you to unlock new cards and new items to change the looks of it.
BUT; You will most likely die before you fully expand your city. Really. It takes more time than you can imagine, even with long matches and a lot of tactics.
When it comes to fightin', collectin' and buildin', AoE III does it with more BANG.
The matches are much faster than in the previous game, and fights are more juicy.
Villagers collect resources much quicker, without a long walk to the nearest drop-off point. Even building is fast and training large armies in short time is a achiveable goal. The problem is, you have no fun in doing that.
In AoE II you could make your units form a box in order to protect weaker units inside, or spread apart to make flanking easier.
In III, the most complicated thing to do for your "Imperial" musketeers is to spread apart slightly, so the splash damage won't be so bad. The units can be simply spammed without knowledge, and it'll be a good tactic. Only sometimes making for example; some Halberdiers is a good idea, and I don't like that.
Thankfully there are also other things to take care of: Treasures await in the maps, which grant many things, from resources to rare units and upgrades. You can meet native tribes and make alliances with them. You can control a Trade Route which will be generating resources for you. And with every nation having it's own way in things, every match is great fun, even though you won't be caring about your army much.
When it comes to the graphics and sounds, the game still looks great and sounds fantastic (apart from the a bit narmy and hammy voice actors).
The buildings fall apart when damaged, and turn into a pile of rubble. Explosions leave behind a column of dirt and smoke, every musket has it's own puff and flash. The water and forage look really nice, and you'll feel the power of your Bombards, muskets and ships just by listening.
Some textures are a bit outdated, and when zoomed in, the models do look a bit primitive, but since you're playing zoomed out to get as much view as possible, this won't be a problem.
The biggest problem I have with this game, is the campaign, which is passable at best.
The storyline is very easy to predict and characters aren't that great. While some missions are engaging, there are some that will end before you manage to get your plan together, or will make you sputter curses untill the next one (Act 2 Mission 2).
You can try it out if you want something different, but don't expect anything groundbreaking.
With the Complete Collection, you also get
and
expansion packs.
Each gives you 3 new nations, 2 new campaigns and many, many changes.
expand the native tribes, and even lets you play as some, while
gives you control over Japanese, Chineese and Indians (duh) and again, each with their own gimmicks.
Expansion packs also give you new maps, game modes and changes to some things.
In conclusion, AoE III CC is a certainly good RTS that may lack some things, but will be a great addition to your game library if you like the older AoEs, strategies or simply want to spam IM IN UR BASE KILLIN UR DOODZ in chat during multiplayer games.
Even though it doesn't support achievements, or the Workshop, it doesn't mean that the game is bad. Those things could make the game even better, but so far with everything you got here, they won't be needed for now.
# Good variety of maps to choose.
# Each Nation brings something new to the game.
# Good Graphics and Sounds.
# Home City and Shipment cards system.
# Expansion packs extend the already rich gameplay.
# Simply enjoyable RTS experience.
# Campaign isn't that great.
# Voices "smell of cheese and ham".
# Less control over your armies.

I have always been following Unturned way before it even released on steam, way before it even gained fame. This game was regularly updated and as of now, it seems that way. Back then, there used to be another version of this which I was looking forward to more than what we have now but I suppose it's time will never come. Regardless, it never occurred to me that the time for the game to even reach steam would come and knowing that it did, it literally came as a big thing for me and for the players who have been with the game and have been keeping up-to-date with it. I've honestly lost track of how long this game has been in development, but never did it occur to me that during it's development it would reach higher than it could have seemed to.
I am simply proud of how far this game has come to, and if something, i'd give the Developer more than a cookie for getting so far with the game. In short, I
.
+ The gameplay. If you're new to this game let alone the survival-genre, you will definitely love not only the gameplay but the game itself for the experience it provides to the player, which can be quite unique.

Honestly, it has been a while since I last played Unturned. Since I had already spent most of my time playing the game before it's release in Steam. That is how much I can recommend Unturned.

Well the Paid Mod update made me finally do my first EVER Steam review on what is ultimately a very dissapointing game even before this happened. I was lucky and got it cheap a couple of weeks ago.
Cons:
1) Controls - First I would like to point out that playing this on mouse and keyboard is horrific. There is a 1-2 second delay (doesn't sound a lot but when your playing it is) when you have gone back on a menu in your pipboy and you try to select another item. You can see the screen but another item is selected and you click too quickly and bam you've selected the other item meaning you have to go back again. Basically use a controller...that's right in a first person rpg shooter on the PC I'm telling you to use a controller...
2) Paid Mods - downloading unwanted software and putting it behind a pay wall
3) Settlements - The most innovative part of this game is the base building. However unless you download SIM Settlements, a FREE mod by Kinggath, it is the most annoying, finicky and unforgiving part of the game. I thought at first this was because of me using the controller (see above) so i tried to switch to mouse and keyboard and it was worse. I may be wrong however and Bethesda maybe intended you to use mats to place objects? Seriously get Sim Settlements and save yourself the pain.
4) VATS - Basically bullet-time. My first gripe with this system is immersion as I believed the VATS system was an extension to the Pipboy (maybe I'm wrong) but low and behold before you even pick up a pipboy you can go into VATS. My second gripe is that it's a well documented how bad the FPS part of the Fallout series is. Why are they still using this system instead of improving the actual real-time combat?
Pros:
1) Gun/Armour Smithing - Really nice system definately the best part of the game in my opinion. Now we just need to be able to use the items you craft outside of the current combat system.
2) Settlers - If you manage to get past the building of your settlement you will start recruiting Settlers. Now the awesome part of this is you can equip these settlers with all your crap you pick up.
3) The Free Mods...?
4) Nope can't think of anymore pro's

I have 400 hours in this game. While this does not make my opinion any more than
, it does make my opinion an
opinion. Much of the negative feedback for the game comes from people with around 20 hours of gameplay, often much less. I'm not telling you how to think, but I implore you to keep these things in mind when reading my review, and others' reviews. Most importantly, use critical thinking. Do not make your purchase decision just because I like the game, or just because somebody else does not like the game. Take the objective facts from every review you find, corroborate and verify their validity, and use those facts to decide if the game is the right fit for you.
With all that said, I think this is a phenomenal game. It's a difficult RPG where position and strategy are important. There is a small but important town management mechanic, allowing you to upgrade your heroes, as well as treat their stress and disorders. The game explores the more cynical, realistic aspects of a militia journeying into an underground dungeon of horrors. Your heroes are flawed, they are not 'heroes'. They can become stressed, and eventually afflicted. Everything is held together by a captivating Lovecraftian theme and story, that I will not spoil for you.
The Crimson Court DLC will set you back 10 USD, 10 EUR, or 7 GBP. It adds a new area, a Crimson Curse mechanic, infestations, and a bunch of new enemies and bosses. I'm not going to spoil the intricacies of the new mechanics, because it's really amazing discovering it on your own. I will tell you that the DLC's mechanics can be difficult to manage, especially with a new playthrough, and
for a new player. Please do not enable Crimson Court at the start of your first playthrough. I recommend winning the campaign once, or getting up to hero levels 4-5 on your first playthrough before giving it a shot.
Reading the negative reviews for this game frustrates me. Every single one is some variation on "This game is too hard! It has RNG!". Yes, it is hard, sometimes crushingly so. It is supposed to mop the floor with you, so you can learn the hard way how the game works, to subsequently stand up and conquer. If this sounds
, it's not a flaw in the game's design. You may have picked the wrong game. To counter the RNG complaints... Really? You're complaining about entropy in an RPG? Allow me to point out that you dodge and crit
than the enemy does, yet you fail to notice your own luck because you're too busy fuming about that last time your Leper missed.
To anybody that's complaining about game crashes or similar, don't worry, Red Hook is easy to get ahold of. The first place I'd try is on Reddit:
Don't be afraid to ask for help!
The grind is a bit monotonous, especially in the first part of the game where you have not many heroes, all with rank 1 equipment, stressed, and not enough resources to deal with it. I've restarted several saves a few weeks in.
. Red Hook has tried to address this, with the recently added
, which aims to reduce the grind. I admit I haven't tried it myself, because I refuse to play games on 'easy' ;P
Do I think you should buy this game? Yes, absolutely. Without repeating myself too much, I do implore you to read other reviews and gather together if this game is right for you. Thank you for reading this entire thing, and I wish you luck with your possible purchase.
