The sequel to my favourite game is here. Xcom give it to ya, baby!
So what's new? Better graphics, more customization, procedural levels, timed objectives, hacking, meele attacks, ambush mode, and finally, mod support.
Quirks and bugs are present just like in the original, but the game is very much playable and beatable.
Failing/ignoring missions is no longer as severe as it once was and the game is balanced better toward the harder difficulties than in EU. (I hated the insane aim bonuses in Xcom EU on Impossible difficulty, this game is more fair in this regard)
However, the hardest difficulty is still a huge jump from the penultimate one. Suddenly, you'll be stuck for three turns on a sectoid that retreats to full cover and laughs its a$$ off at your 30 percent shots. (you'll need 3 hits on average to kill it by the way) Problem is, you don't have time to wait for an opportunity and flanking it will only alert more enemies. There are ALOT of enemies on legendary and they sure as hell don't care that you're on the clock.
I wish there were a difficulty level between the  two hardest ones. It would be the sweetspot for me. Enemy Unknown had the same problem. Oh well, can't have everything.
I bought the game at full price and it deserves every penny.
It's a unique, deep, satisfying experience with high replay value. I heartily recommend it.

There are multiple unlockables are rewarding to find, including new weapons to experiment with.

The only problem now is that even after completing all of it you'll be left wanting more and that will mean keeping your fingers crossed that they will bring the sequel over to PC.

This should have been done a long time ago.
However I'm glad they did eventually port it to PC. If I had known that this port was in the making I would never have bought the PS3 verions of Bayonetta 2 weeks ago.
This port is very well done, the textures look so much better than the PS3/360 version, and the game runs at a smooth 60 FPS. Shadows and effects look better and also no more jagged edges, especially with 16xAA.
I would recommend using custom settings, that way you can max everything manually. This is a very good port, controllers work flawlessly, and there are no issues so far.
The only thing people may compain about is that it's locked at 60FPS, which I don't see as a problem since it doesn't affect gameplay, and it runs pretty smooth regardless.
I am using a 144Hz monitor freesync monitor, and it runs really, really smoothly.
My RX 480 is even able to run this game at 4K using VSR (Virtual Super Resolution) and scales it down to 1080p, still at a solid 60FPS.
This is how Bayonetta is meant to be played. A great game, and at a reasonable price. Unlike DMC 4 Special Edition upon release.

It is just a matter of how will you continue the game. This game is definetley punishing to those not willing to play it strategically as certain classes or parties work better with one another.
This game is a turn-based rpg where you usually control a party of 4. Not only can your party memebers die from losing all their health but they can also succumb to madness if the their stress bars increase from either taking damage, enemy spells, certain negative traits, and etc.
Many of the enemies you encounter can be either easy to overcome or can you leave you in distraught. Either way, any enemy can be challenging if not taken serious. The challenge in this game is defenitley nice and I think it feels like an accomplishment when i overcome a difficult dungeon or boss.
What I really loved about this game was the artstyle and it's dark and sinister appeal. Also I really think the narrator is so eerie, but badass to hear especially with his extensive vocabulary.
Overall, this is a great game for those that like turned based rpgs with a challenge to them. Would recommend buying it ASAP but waiting for a sale ins't bad too.

Despite the significantly lower player base and also my recent inactivity on the game, I still feel that I'm obliged to provide my own insight into this game that I've invested quite a bit of time into.
To start off, Spiral Knights is basically a hack-and-slash multiplayer RPG that enables players to explore the depths of the Clockworks, fight monsters, play through a story(-ish) mission mode and engage in player-versus-player minigames. Boss battles, swarms of enemies, hazardous environments, the like. However, there's more than just combat when it comes to player-player interactions as the game. The game's other features include:
- Item trading between players, and an Auction House system that enables players to buy/sell their items for in-game currency.
- Guilds and Guild Halls where players can get together, share items such as weapons and materials, access most shops within short distances from each other, and craft trophies using materials dropped from bosses. Guild halls have a required upkeep that guild members need to pay weekly. Teamwork!
- Sword/Gun/Armour/Bomb crafting system which allows players to equip their arsenal to suit their battle needs.
- Upgrades to gear called Unique Variants that add bonuses to the gear and have a chance of being obtained during crafting or can be randomly applied to gear for a fee.
- Costumes/Accessories that players can use to add their own artistic touch to their armour, with the large number of items and colour schemes available, the possibilities are almost endless!
- Events that go in rotations throughout the year, as well as annual holiday events that give players the chance to obtain items and gear that are related to the event's theme, some of which have special characteristics that no other items have!
- An alternate currency (Energy) that can be purchased using real money and can be used to purchase items and gear directly from an in-game store (Supply Depot) or even converted to the regular in-game currency.
I think there are more features but those are what I came up with off the top of my head. Personally, the game can be quite fun, especially for people who love slashing, smashing and blasting monsters in a cute, anime-style fashion. There are three weapon classes, swords, guns, and bombs, and none are necessarily better than the other. The game's battle mechanics may seem simple since most of the time since spamming attacks usually does the job. This makes the learning curve easy because learning to incorporate movement with one's attacks makes a pretty solid player, however the skill ceiling is a little higher due to techniques such as shield-canceling, shield-bashing, charge attacks and using status effects to one's advantage. Upgrading your gear up to 5-star isn't very difficult but it does need some time.
I understand that some of the people reading this may be (or may have been at some point) regular SK players and might think that this combat stuff is a little pointless, but that's just because we do it so much that it just becomes a habit and that it's "easy peasy" and that makes it a little more difficult to look at these things objectively.
The player base and community are mostly very laid back, very chill, and I've met some pretty awesome people on my journey (You know who you are :P). Most people would be more than happy to give you a hand on a mission or on a Clockworks raid, either for completion purposes or just to help you make some cash. Yes, there may be a couple of rude players or scammers here and there but I prefer to look at the big picture and say that they won't totally ruin your experience of the game itself.
Summary:
- The game looks neat and simple, it's not overdone for the most part, however when it comes to costumes and accessories it can be a little tiring to have the same items released but in a different colour scheme. The NPC artwork is cool. Overall quite pleasing to look at.
- Combat mechanics are easy to learn, whether using swords, guns, or bombs. Weapons have different attack speeds and damage types. Monsters have resistances and weaknesses to certain damage types and makes weapon choice important. PvP has quite a high skill ceiling, but weapons with 'Attack Speed Increase' or 'Charge Time Reduction' Unique Variants, armour with 'Defense Increase' Unique Variants, and trinkets with health or attack speed boosts certainly do help. But I guess the main enemy in PvP is lag. :P
- Helpful and nice player base, the game is more fun when played with others, also allows for coordinated gameplay (most of the time).

I recently reviewed this game for my game review blog, Five Penny Review. If you enjoy this review, please visit my page:
(As a note: I have played this game longer than the listed time before I had Steam.)
What sets this game apart?
Half-Life was an influential milestone in gaming and has been considered one of the best games of all time by various magazines and critics. The main reasons for its acclaim and success deal with the way the game is presented, completely through the eyes of its protagonist, who is unseen and unheard except for his hands. This full immersion into Gordon Freeman's perspective means that there are no virtually no cut scenes or text boxes, leaving the player in control and learning the story through observation and conversation. Progression through the game is often not completely linear, featuring puzzles and exploration that had not been featured in earlier first-person shooters. Half-Life also utilizes aspects from the survival horror genre, both atmospheric and mechanical, from jump scenes to limited ammunition. Half-Life was a unique entity on the first-person shooter market, and a milestone for PC gaming in general. In addition to its contributions as its own entity, several expansions were released and Valve Software encouraged outside developers to create third-party mods.
What is the difficulty factor?
The introduction to the game is amazing in its simplicity. To teach you how to move about and to introduce you to the Black Mesa complex, the game begins with Gordon Freeman is running late for work and you must hurry to the lab. From here, new information is displayed as it becomes necessary, although anyone familiar with PC first-person shooters should be able to pick things up quickly.
As a whole, Half-Life tends to be a fairly difficult game, however the difficulty rarely comes from the same place as first-person shooters that came before it. The puzzles and three-dimensional platforming make up the core of the game, and the survival horror elements like limited ammunition and unique enemy AI and detection make Half-Life a thinking game. Rushing and running and gunning will be less successful than a patient and thoughtful strategy.
Does it use media effectively?
Half-Life looks great and it has aged fairly well. The environments are detailed and diverse, exploring the full range of the Black Mesa complex, inside and out. The creatures and alien weapons are creative, drawing on similar creatures from science fiction and putting a unique twist on them. The horror aspects of the game are well set up with plenty of jump scenes and tense moments. The soundtrack helps add to the suspense at times, while adding to the adrenaline of the actions scenes at others. The voice acting left a bit to be desired, even when the game came out, but the croaking computerized voice is a recognizable relic of Half-Life that you won't soon forget.
Best moment in the game?
Half-Life has a lot of great moments, several of which involve blowing up helicopters, trains, or giant monsters. Half-Life also has a lot of great quiet moments, even the train ride to work at the beginning of the game is impressive in its own way. When I sat down to think about the best moment in the game, for me, one scene popped immediately to my mind. During the chapter Apprehension, you encounter your first Ichthyosaur, a giant fish rivaled only by the Boss Bass in Mario 3 in virtual-fish-frustration. The Ichthyosaur grabs a scientist in a flash when you first enter his domain, and soon you find yourself dangling over his pond in a cage, forced to confront the force of nature before you run out of oxygen. I remember this sequence as the one that made me jump the most during my first play through, and it holds up now. It is also when you receive the crossbow, and I'm a bit of a sucker for sniping weapons, but the scene is still really memorable with that fact aside.
Who needs to play this game?
You mean you haven't played this game? Shame on you! Half-Life is a classic game and is often considered among the best in the history of gaming. Even 15 years later, it holds up extremely well. Even if you are not normally a fan of first-person shooters, this is not the action dredged game that you might expect; it has its moments, but they do not define the game. It plays closer to a faster paced survival horror game, full of atmosphere and puzzles and monsters. Half-Life is available on Steam and is frequently on sale during their sales. If you pick it up, I would highly suggest getting the pack that includes Opposing Force and Blue Shift, the two expansion games released by Valve.

The graphics are good, the music is really great (although a bit repetitive), the general art style and animations are really good. I love to modify my soldiers, equip them with stuff, and level them up.
So long for the good; now the bad. This is a console game kind of looking like a PC game. The user interface and controls are really bad. This game is basically a giant random number generator. It is torturing you with 98% chance-to-hit misses and soldiers ducked behind high cover dying instantly from critical hits. It feels like tactics, but it is actually mostly luck. You are never getting an edge because each time your soldiers level up or you finally have that new loot, a bigger alien shows up and trashes everything again. Some people might find this challenging or funny, however I do not find it enoyable. My sessions end up and save-and-reload grinds because I don't like loosing soldiers. I just want to get to the next story point, but then there is yet another (inter)mission with meaningless aliens randomly thrown at your poor soldiers. The whole game feels like you are trapped in a hamster wheel.
In addition to that they just charged $40 for an expansion (War of the Chosen)? The game is overall better than before, but the price point is really out of proportion for what you get.

While the idea of controlling a bread that desperately wants to be toasted is neat, the game itself is a letdown.
The leveldesign is poor, and I found it hard to want to play more.
The controls are a novelty at best, and likely take a long time to execute right.
All in all, I didn't have much fun playing it.

I've wanted to play this for a long time and am so happy to finally get my grubby hands on it.  Bayonetta feels and plays like a cooky spin-off to the Capcom Devil May Cry games, while borrowing parts of God of War and generally turning all amps to 11 .  Its silly, stylish, bat-sh*t insane and thoroughly Japanese through and through.  If you don't like these kind of games, I doubt Bayonetta will change your mind.  It should be borne in mind that Bayonetta is pretty much a straight up brawler, with hardly any puzzles or exloration to break up the combat.
For me, Bayonetta was a great game in parts, but widlely frustrating and annoying in others.  Overall, the combat is simply amazing, with so much scope for interesting combos and challenging your twitch reactions for those perfect dodges you need. I also enjoyed the hammy B-movie plot and bad acting - it all lends to that quirky charm.  Howeever, at other times, this was the most frustrating game i had played in forever - the awful camera, the instakill quicktime events in the middle of a frickin boss fight, the repetition of enemies (HOW MANY FRICKIN TIMES DO I NEED TO FIGHT GRACE AND GLORY???)  the nausea enducing dodges in the rocket level, and the fact that some of the games bosses are just not fun ot fight (like the reused bosses in the tower level)
But what other game lets you spank angels, wear shoe-guns or turn your hair into a screen filling demon?  Despite its (some considerable) flaws, Bayonetta is a gem, but a gem that's not above inducing a lot of rage quits.  PC port ain't bad either.
All in all, fans of this type of game should check it out.  I must say i do prefer hack n slashers with some good environmental puzzles or exploration to break up the fighting (Devil May Cry 3, Darksiders, God of War etc) so i can't give Bayonetta the 'best in class' rating a lot of people seem to give it, but it is worth playing for sure!
P.s dear Sega thank you. please bring Vanquish next!

Well the Paid Mod update made me finally do my first EVER Steam review on what is ultimately a very dissapointing game even before this happened. I was lucky and got it cheap a couple of weeks ago.
Cons:
1) Controls - First I would like to point out that playing this on mouse and keyboard is horrific. There is a 1-2 second delay (doesn't sound a lot but when your playing it is) when you have gone back on a menu in your pipboy and you try to select another item. You can see the screen but another item is selected and you click too quickly and bam you've selected the other item meaning you have to go back again. Basically use a controller...that's right in a first person rpg shooter on the PC I'm telling you to use a controller...
2) Paid Mods - downloading unwanted software and putting it behind a pay wall
3) Settlements - The most innovative part of this game is the base building. However unless you download SIM Settlements, a FREE mod by Kinggath, it is the most annoying, finicky and unforgiving part of the game. I thought at first this was because of me using the controller (see above) so i tried to switch to mouse and keyboard and it was worse. I may be wrong however and Bethesda maybe intended you to use mats to place objects? Seriously get Sim Settlements and save yourself the pain.
4) VATS - Basically bullet-time. My first gripe with this system is immersion as I believed the VATS system was an extension to the Pipboy (maybe I'm wrong) but low and behold before you even pick up a pipboy you can go into VATS. My second gripe is that it's a well documented how bad the FPS part of the Fallout series is. Why are they still using this system instead of improving the actual real-time combat?
Pros:
1) Gun/Armour Smithing - Really nice system definately the best part of the game in my opinion. Now we just need to be able to use the items you craft outside of the current combat system.
2) Settlers - If you manage to get past the building of your settlement you will start recruiting Settlers. Now the awesome part of this is you can equip these settlers with all your crap you pick up.
3) The Free Mods...?
4) Nope can't think of anymore pro's

Before we begin, I have a bunch more hours into this game, but just played off of steam. (400-something)
Bragging about my low amount of hours ingame aside, this game is kind of like TF2. Not in the sense of gameplay, but in the sense of new content. That is, there isn't much new stuff happening. The last new weapons were added in 2014. Since the players control energy prices, energy has gone up to around 11K crowns, which is very difficult for newer players to obtain. Heck, the original developers of the game aren't even there anymore.
That being said, I sincerely enjoy and recommend this game. Why? Read on...
Graphics are good, especially for a 2011 700MB game.  The enemies are designed to have clearly choreographed attacks, not to make it easy, but so you can learn how to dodge, time, and intercept attacks. The enemies get harder the farther you go, so learning those moves early on can save you a bunch of sparks of life later on. The point is that this game isn't just a point-and-click fiesta, but has decent amount of skill involved. I have never encountered a cheater or hacker, and the community, in my biased opinion, is one of the better ones out there. Grinding is a large part of the game, but the arcade levels are random and always different. (Unless you replay the same one 6 times because the treasure vault is right th-oops) This grinding does take a long time, and if you go to the recipie vendor, and he doesn't have your recipie, tough luck. gotta do the levels again. But you obtain loot and shinies along the way, so at least you get those should your recipie not be there.
Another thing this game has is character. The weapons are cool, there's a ton of different armors, shields, and weapons, AND HATS. The levels are fun, and not too repetitive, and finally finding that Sacred Grizzly Pathfinder helm recipie is... well, I don't know. I'm still looking for that one. :) But crafting weapons after finding the recipie and leveling it up makes you feel pretty good, and getting that new sprite perk is always cool.
Remember how I said new content was slow? It is. not gonna lie. However, it has been inproving. Grey Havens, the new guys, have been doing a pretty good job fixing stuff and adding small new things into the game. (I spent far too many crowns at the Slime Casino) Now would be the time to try the game out rather than 2 years ago, in terms of content. They have yet to add new levels, or anything big to the game yet, but I think they're gonna do fine. Once you complete the campaign (which is fairly long, including required grinding for stuff) you still have guilds, acades, and more to do.
In summary, Spiral Knights is a fun 3rd person MMO that's free to play, has a good community, and will certainly keep you busy for a while. While there isn't an incredible amount of new stuff to the game, it's slowly getting there, and Grey Havens does care about the game. AND THERE'S HATS!

You've just spent 15 minutes climbing up walls, carefully edging your way around bookshelves, deliberately nudging yet another expensive ornament to the floor far below.  Just across the room - your holy grail, your final destination: a source of heat.  But between you and toasty nirvana, a colossal THREE FOOT gap.  It feels like a mile. You grab onto the bookshelf with one of your corners, and catapult yourself across the gap as hard as a piece of bread possibly can.  With this final leap of faith, time seems to slow down from the exhiliration as you pirouette through the air.  Just as you slam into the opposite surface you desperately cling on with every corner that makes contact like a tiny, wheaten spider-man.  You only have a few moments to hold on, and with sheer panic you begin to flail your way towards the heat source.
Except, it was a lamp, and your impact knocked it over.  You're now vertical, holding on for dear life with one corner, hoping against hope that you can just maintain your grip long enough to finally become toast.  50%.  70%. 90%!  You flip around to toast the other side, feeling your grip begin to weaken.  "NO! I WAS SO CLOSE!" you scream inside, as you feel your victory slipping away, and finally you fall.  You now lay on the floor, in a pile of toenail clippings, inedible and unwanted - nobody likes toejam toast.
You start again, yet another slice from the same loaf.  This time, you anticipate the situation and stay on the side of the lamp, so when it finally lands, you're on top.  The feeling of accomplishment growing inside you as you watch that bread slowly turn golden-brown is unlike anything else in modern gaming. You are a genius! You are a champion! You are TOAST!

Half Life is a game that shocked the gaming industry back in 1998. It might've not been the first of its kind, but it was certainly one of the best. The graphics, inferior compared to today's photorealistic games, were still amazing when it came out.
You play as Doctor Gordon Freeman, a scientist working for the mysterious Black Mesa corporation. After discovering an alien planet known as Xen, several experiments are conducted to bring back specimens from this new world. As you come to work one day, everything is normal- except for a test involving a teleportation to Xen, and a suspicious man in a suit warning about unforseen consequences. The team ignores this, and it would cost them nearly everything. The experiment fails, and all hell breaks loose as Xen creatures teleport into the Black Mesa facility, killing anyone and anything. You wake up, during the aftermath of this event. Determined to escape, you fight your way through the facility, all the way to Xen. To find out the rest, you have to play the game. And believe me, every single second of this game is worth it.

A new world, new adventures, and a new beginning...
Following the successful Age of Empires franchise is AOE III, now wonderfully remastered into one complete pack on Steam. This is a must-get for not just AOE fans, but fans of strategy games in general. Age of Empires III is a strong example of what makes the AOE series a classic in RTS games. From micro to macro-management, housekeeping to empire building, the game is easy to learn yet difficult to master.
The game is set in the 17th thru 19th centuries when European nations expanded their dominions and colonies across the world. On the other side of the globe, Native American civilizations fight to survive or adapt to European incursion, and Asian civilizations cautiously open their borders to a foreign and strange culture. From large musketeer battles to cavalry charges, and artillery blasting away at mortar and brick, the game is a visual delight to relish.

Quite possibly one of the best Action games ever made, now for PC! The port has unlocked resolution and runs at a nice rock-steady 60fps during gameplay (on my GTX970 and i7-4790). Xcom 2 is alot like Xcom 1...
Does it mean it's good you ask? Well yes and no
First and foremost let me tell you I had a blast playing this game, it was a lot of fun, it was rather addictive, especially in the beginning and I am sure that anyone who enjoys turn based games is going to enojy this one. But when making comparison to previous titles (Xcom and Xcom EU) there doesn't seem to be that much of a difference and sometimes you may find game even lacking content-wise especially with Xcom EU. So without any further adue let's get into review.
Right of the bat, probably the most important aspect of the game. Xcom 2 in comparison to Xcom one had gone through some changes, this in my opinion serves the game well and was a right decision, but generally speaking it has only marginal effect on the gameplay compared to previous title. It simply seems the developers did  not utilize full potential these changes offered. Examples would be, Your base is now instead of in the bunker on captured alien spaceship/supplybarge. Sounds cool? It is until you realize that it pretty much doesn't change a thing, now your base just moves around a map, thats about only effect it has. You also start out in undetected mode, giving you chance to sneak around the map and set ambushes, again that sounds good but you are only able to utilize this chance once every mission because once you spot the enemy units, they spot you and they get free move round. Onward from then the game plays exactly like Xcom. Things like this that were supposed to change the game turned out in the end to have very little effect on gameplay which is unfortunate in my opinion, it certainly doesn't ruin the game, the game is still fairly enjoyable, but it simply doesn't offer much new in gameplay. The Base building mechanic is still in the game but it does not offer much variety, or rather is very restrictive in options, you can choose from several types there are like 7 types that are mandatory and like 2 that are volunteer but you can win the game without them. So there is no reason to build any other than those that the game requires you to build so in the end, this aspect renders this mechanic pretty much useless.
There were some changes made to classes and their perks, here the changes are more obviuos and have much bigger effect on gameplay in my opinion. Overal I was happy with the changes, new perks/classes/specialisations, it made the game feel fresh and new. But then again here comes the point where the content offered in this game is smaller in comparison with for example Xcom EU. Whilst Xcom 2 offers some 4 + 1 classes Xcom EU has 1 or 2 more if I remember correctly. Now you might think that comparing basic game with full out stand alone expension pack isn't fair and you might be right but when simply thinking about value you get for your money Xcom EU comes out as winner. That being said I am sure we can expect some expansions comming our way even for this title and I am rather convinced that in the end the content offered in Xcom 2 will be at least the same as in Xcom EU.
In case of content as in items, weapons, armor, etc. The Xcom two again is very similar to basic Xcom, You have your 3 tiers of weapons and 3 tiers of basic armor with some special armor ment for working in synergy with certain class. What Xcom 2 does better than Xcom is character customization and it offers weapon upgrades which is excellent but just like previous points it comes with certain flaws. Menu for customization is little bit messy and requires player to click in and out of windows all the time in order to change pattern on armor and weapon and accessories and colour of gear which can get little bit annoying. Adding upgrades to weapons was great idea but since you can put max 2 and there are some 6 types of upgrades or so it just doesn't have that much depth, but still is nice perk to have in a game. What I really found cool though was that your soldiers have dabing based on the countries they are from... well at least those from major ones (American, British, Australian English, German, French, Spanish). This again is a nice little cherry on top, shame this is not included for most or all countries included in the game, would make so much more fun to listen to all the soldiers quotes in different languages. It is also shame some countries especially from developed world are missing. As I said in previous point in the end the value you get for your money is much lower than in case of Xcom EU, now I know this all may seem negative but I just want to let people know what to expect before they buy the game, because surely it is good game and I don't regret buying it for full price but someone with high expactations might so be aware.

Reducing beginner voice over hardly makes any difference. You also should get used to seeing enemies teleport and fall through the map. Often the pods with robots on a higher level than the rest of the map will just dissapear into the structures when engaged and stay out of the fight. Devs seriously need to fix their game instead of making a fool out of themselves with irrelevant DLC that has actually made the game run even worse somehow! Black Squad Early Impressions:
Here's a short little review that I decided to post up based on my early impressions on the game during its Early Access.
The game has a lot going for it that seperates it from other free FPS and for the matter, current paid FPS games like CS:GO. It leans towards the arcadey style shooter akin to the CoD series but brings good mechanics over from games such as Alliance of Valiant Arms and Counter Strike (such as strong, predictable gun recoil and control, attachable silences mid-game, lack of sprint, etc.)
It's a solid FPS experience that takes from good gunplay mechanics from the Counter Strike series but pairs it with good aim-down-sights action from CoD and blends it really well. Each and every weapon has its own unique recoil pattern and bring their own pros and cons to the table.
The game may seem to lack 'customization' options to weapons that seems to be trending on new FPS releases but in my opinion, this helps keep the game balanced as nearly every weapon has the same capabilities from fresh out the store (the guns already are decked out in 'tacticool' mods) and everyone is on the same playing field.
The game also does extremely well with its current Free to Play model which, let me stress, is 100% free to play and 0% pay to win. The only microtransactions that you can pay for are RNG boxes that contain skins of guns that you can otherwise unlock through either in game credits or this other currency called 'medals' which you get from doing daily quests. I only started playing today and I'm almost nearly on my way on getting a perm weapon from the medal store (1600 medals but I need 2500 medals for the purchase).
Oh, and all the guns in the in game store are for permanent purchase. No timed frills except for nades and event items.
On the server side of things, there's currently only 4 servers up for North and South America, Europe and Asia which is fine even though I play from Oceania. My ping is a playable 260 even in North America and I don't experience that bad of lag except for the 'no-regs' when I go up against a Sniper player who is quick enough to trade blows with me.
The one thing that I must take away from this game is that... the map designs are some of the worst I've ever encountered. Choke points on literally every map, on nearly every corner which strangles teams because there is no dynamic spawn system and follows more tradition T base, CT base style.
Despite this, the overall game is pretty damn good and hits the market hard as a strong F2P FPS contender.
Review Summary:
*Combat & Balance: 8.5/10 (+Extremely good gunplay with good weapon variety and damage models, -nades can be spammy at times)
*Customization: 7/10 (+Good system customizations, +Different characters, +a strong assortment of modern weaponry, -limited weapon customizations, -limited in depth customizations)
*Payment Model: 9/10 (+True free to play with no pay to win aspects, +Very easy to get cash by normally playing, +Methods of farming in game cash too, +Daily system is not intrusive, -Minor negative for those who don't like rng boxes)
*Servers: 7/10 (+Competent servers that work, -'Only' 4 regions)
*Map Design: 4/10 (+Lots of routes to take on maps, -Not competitively designed, -Terrible chokepoints, -Especially bad map design when you take into account nearly every gun comes pre-attached with a grenade launcher)
Overall Score: 7/10 - Black Squad is a solid F2P FPS to pick up if you're in the mood for a fast paced, arcadey, boots on ground FPS with a true free to play model that boasts a good assortment of guns coupled with extremely good gunplay.

This game will kick you in the face. Hard! So this game is for those looking for a challenge in dungeon crawler games. This is not your typical "hero group slays 1000 monsters without a scratch", no no no. Not only will you have to deal with challenging (or should I say difficult?) monster battles, but you have to worry about lighting torches, food, bleeding, disease, and the biggest killer of heroes, stress. If you have the right group of heroes you can keep your stress down to a minimum or on occasion, stress free. Let your stress go too high and your heroes will become insane and get afflicted with all sorts of phsycological disorders, and that stress, if left unattended, will make your heroes useless, or kill them outright.
I was drawn in by the Lovecraftian atmosphere of the game. The artwork is very well done to emphasize and accentuate the harsh realities of the game. For those who think the game is too difficult had better read the disclaimer at the startup screen. "THIS GAME IS ALL ABOUT MAKING THE BEST OF A BAD SITUATION. HEROES WILL DIE AND QUESTS WILL FAIL."
Personally I love the challenge presented by Darkest Dungeon. I love the music. The narrator tells the story so well it makes you want to go to his house, kick back some beers, and talk with him all night. Most of all. It's unique because it's not the same usual pattern that most other RPGs follow.
So I really recommend this game for those who want a real challenge. This has become my most favorite and addicting RPG of all time.

Let's keep it short.  This game is not fair.  The atmosphere is great and suitably unsettling and charming in a gothic, lovecraftian way, the management of heroes is interesting, and the gameplay, while simple, is very fun, but this is game leans heavily on RNG.  If that and hero permadeath are going to turn you off, steer clear.  I found that I could have some fun in the midgame spinning my wheels, but expect to drop a minimum of 20-40 hours trying to get through all the content and not all of it is fun.  By the time I got to end game content, the game was more stressful for me than fun and I had to quit.  This game will make you scream and tear out your hair, but it's deep and satisfying up to a point.  If you enjoy the grind and a feeling of progression to greater challenges, even if it's not going to be fair, then you will enjoy this game.
Also, shout out to Mark Brown who called out Darkest Dungeon for doing something really clever in a moral choice system that you may never see.  This game has an optimal way to play and a humane way to play, with no real incentive beyond your own personal beliefs for playing humanely.  This alone makes it very interesting because it will have you examine your values if you take the time to think about the heroes as people over digital avatars.
Worth playing through, even if you decide to never finish it.

My Original Review is below in qoutes and I think it's high time for an update. I have a shameful 500+ hours now in this game. I still recommend it highly.
The crew at ECG has done a great job with balance. It's not perfect, but it's constantly being adjusted. While we are on that subject let's discuss Pay to Win for a second. The game is NOT pay to win. I would describe it more as pay to look cool or decrease grinding. You still have to play the game to unlock things (though that might be going away soon) and even if you did not, the ships at the end of the skill tree are not by virtue better....they are just better at one specific thing. With that said you get the current three starter ships: the Pioneer, Venturer, Sentinal. These are all solid ships when played well. I have access to just about all the ships at this point (I have flown them all during alpha) and can tell you that my go-to ship for assault is STILL the pio; as one of my buddies put it "It's got 3 buttons for shootin em and 2 buttons for See'en em". The vent can self heal and area heal and WRECK your armor (this is a core skill). The Sentinal can kite, capture and dance around you while dishing out the murder. Give the three "starter" ships some seat time and you will be doing all right.
The learning curve is steep. I still learn new tricks and effects after a lot of play time. There are only a few ships that are bad (destroyer, currently my poor nerfed raven, ranger) and even those can be put to good use in the right situation. Take some time to learn the ranges of the ships. When in doubt use the tab menu in game to hover over any ability (enemy or friendly) and you get a summary of whet it does and how it works....start doing this early and the learning curve will be a lot easier for you.
The community is small and tight knit, the other day I was getting my hind end handed to me and had a guy on the enemy team ask me "Kilt....are you ok? I have seen you play better than this." THAT is a very cool thing to have in a hyper agressive setting like pvp. Don't be a jerk and we will get along fine. There are a few toxic guys in the game...ignore them, we pretty much all agree on who they are and devs are good about dealing with those who cross the line.
And now to my original review...funny how accurate my first sentance was.
"I have about 9 hrs. into this game as of the time of this writing. I plan for a lot more.
First, a warning for those planning purchase: If you are looking for frenetic action, you are in the wrong place. This is a tactical game with some one on one engagements lasting for minutes at a time. That might not seem like a lot, but think of how often you play a game and it's the same old "see an enemy, shoot enemy, repeat, die, repeat". I have had engagements that I knew the outcome of when the enemy is still 44km out (in that case I knew I was going to die while keeping most of the enemy occupied so the rest of my team could capture main base), that is not a fighter game.  Also if you expect to do well for the first few hours of the game, you might not have the patience for this. More seasoned captains are going to turn you to dust before you even start to learn a strategy that works for you...this steep learning curve would make a tutorial mission or two a welcome addition since I think it would help some players over that steep learning curve. Last word of warning, the game will punish you severely for leaving early (no xp, no credits, and a decrease in honor) so don't get into a game without 30 minutes to spare.
That being said, I love the mechanics of this game. At its heart it’s a big game of domination to see who can take the enemy base first. Pick a capital ship, learn its capabilities and try to achieve that objective. What hooked me about the game is just how much nuance they have built into each ship. For instance, the Hunter (my favorite ship to fly and to kill) has different levels of damage dealt out of its main cannons based on the orientation of the ship in relation to your target. Missiles fire from different sections of each ship...and a thousand other little details that make you have to out-think your opponent(s). That out thinking part is what makes the game great.
That being said, I would not mind seeing a few improvements since this is still in alpha.
--I think snipers are a bit overpowered. Lower the firing rate, slow them down...something.
--I would love some randomization to the station placement and the asteroid fields. This would add a bit more spice to each game
--while we are talking about station placement, everything is a bit too linear for what should be a space game. I would love to see more 3 dimensional maps.
--And I would LOVE to be able to control the pitch and roll of my ship. Especially when I have breached armor exposed to an enemy.
--Audible coms!!!!
--I would like to be able to friend, or stay on the same server for more than a game.
All that being said the devs are doing and have done a heck of a job making a game that has an altogether different pace than what you are used to playing. It's worth your time to take a look.

Yes, the controls take getting used to, but it honestly didn't take as long as I thought to have my bread doing air-flips.
One major issue that can't be ignored; the camera is not your friend. And in a game requiring such concentration and precission, that can be a right pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ (Likewise with Dark Souls.)
All in all, I tip my hat to the developers for originality, incredible detail, and amazing sound design. (The music gets repetitive quick, but the sound of physical objects is outstadning.)

An excellent follow-up to Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within.
Pros:
- Much more than just copy/paste gameplay from the prior title.
- Dynamic map generation (not subject to the same small set of maps like in the past)
- There's still room for the end-game 'victory lap', but alien objectives and 'timers' push you to move forward, and keep you from being able to indefinitely build up.
- Character classes and skills do a MUCH better job of synergizing, and really pull you to have a mix of soliders in your squad.  I've found myself trying all kinds of squad compositions, and never setting on exactly one mix.
- The game doesn't allow for the traditional play of slowly creep forward (on most missions).  Now, most missions include some kind of timer that is far less arbitrary than the prior Meld countdown, encouraging and sometimes forcing a much more aggressive playstyle.
- A good variety of new alien types and abilities to fight.
- Soldier customization is more intricate?  Not a selling point for me, but it's kinda neat, if you're into that.
Cons:
- Still going to have those rounds where your soldier misses a pair of 90% shots
- There are still some funky camera issues at times (watching a shot, trying to move a soldier between varying levels of elevation, etc...)
- Things are definitely still set up to quickly spiral out of control (escalations of losing entire squads, failing objectives, etc...)
Conclusion:
If you liked Enemy Unknown, and especially Enemy Within, you are going to want to pick this game up.  The minor frustrations you might experience with shot accuracy or failure escalation have really become known as the XCOM experience.  If you are ok with that, you're going to have a great time.

FPS genre started out with Id Software's Wolfenstein in 1992.
That same company later released Doom, and for quite a while most shooters were simply tagged as Doom Clones. Games like Quake, Duke Nukem, Shadow Warrior, Star Wars Dark Forces, Unreal were among them. These games lacked narrative and had a very maze like level design. It's very different from what we have today in our shooters.
Then in 1998, came Half Life. Love it or hate it, this game is the blueprint for all the shooters that come out these days. It was among the first shooters to have narrative. To account for the narrative, it had to make the level design more linear. The game is driven by the story, so to say. Level would be build around it, having set pieces here and there.
Games from the Doom era focused on you trying to avoid the incoming projectiles that are shot at you. They focused on mobility. Since they had a very maze like level design. They also would usually have a lot of secret places, where you could get better gear or ammo. Exploration was another thing that was focused on in older fps.
Half Life on other hand played differently from earlier FPS games. Accuracy wasn't something that was a thing back then, but with Half Life it was. You had a crosshair and you could not only look at x-axis, but also move your camera up and down (y-axis). All weapons in Half Life would also feature recoil on their guns.
You would also face enemies, with guns just like you. They would have cheater like accuracy. You wouldn't be able to dodge their incoming bullets. All you will be able to do is go behind cover.
I hope you find all this familiar.
That said, Half Life did feature elements from Doom games - mostly when encountering aliens. Headcrabs for example will jump at you. Vortigons would shot a green beam with a few seconds of delay. There are some that that spit corrosive fluid. All of these are dodge-able. The game also has Grunts, which are very big bullet sponges.
When encountering normal soldiers on other hand, it will play like today's shooter. Still, there is a fair amount of both in the game.
The game still has plenty of secret places with ammo and weapons stashes, so exploration isn't completely off the table.
Finally, it features a lot of puzzle solving and platforming, which is a bit unusual for an FPS. I personally found it very frustrating.
Back in the days, there was no story in FPS games. And even if there was, it would be delivered via cutscenes. Well, Half Life changed that. Like a said, a linear level design. Along that level, they would have friendly NPCs, with whom you could interact with, and cinematic set pieces. You would do more than just "run and gun".
Half Life story may not be unique, but it's about how they deliver it, that makes it so special. No one has ever done that, up till that point. They were the first.
Also, it may not look like it, but back then it was amazing. The game didn't even come to PS1 simply because the console couldn't handle the technology involved. Valve used GldSrc, which was based on Quake's engine. It's a groundbreaking game.
The only thing i want to complain about is the sounds. It really hurt my ears.

When a game that's 15 years old manages to be as fun as a current-gen game, it's ♥♥♥♥ing good. This is good. The gameplay is your regular, pretty hard good ol' shooter, but the story and atmosphere are superb. As I've said many times before, old games are masters of ambience, and Half-Life is master of masters. The best part about it is probably the eerily mysterious g-man, who you sometimes see calmly walking around an immense base, where, for reasons unknown, hell broke loose.
You play no part in the unleashing of hell. You are just some research assistant who is relatively new to the place and one day got caught up in this 'accident'. First you see this g-man walking around, obviously unaffected by the chaos, and you wonder what the ♥♥♥♥ he has to do with this mess. Later the military shows up trying to kill everybody involved, and you're just trying to figure out what the hell happened. Right now I'm getting messages from the Lambda Team (no idea who they are) and I've done them some favours. I am seriously eager to meet them and shake some answers out of them. I won't spoil much more, but I think it's clear that the story is sublime. And if you've enjoyed HL2 without playing this game, get ready to re-enjoy the crap out of HL2. I was kinda playing HL2:EP2 and this through eachother, but when Alyx randomly said: 'Prepare for unforseen consequences' shivers went down every single one of my bones. Damn, getting reminded of the hellish mess that is Half Life 1 is actually scary.

Fractured Space is an immense and at most times intense Space Ship shooter. As it is a team based "Control Point" style game you require team effort and support from other players on your side, tactics are an important part of the game and the worst thing you can do is follow your team into the enemy base and get yourself killed!
I'm going to do a serious review on this because I actually like this game!
is a team-based space combat game with a lot like the "Control Points" gamemode from TF2, the ships themselves in the game are based around
for example, Frigates, Cruisers, Battleships and the things you see a lot in
games. The ships feel large and weighty in space (even though there is no gravity) and they are slow to control, just like a large capital ship would feel like (If you catch my drift!) The aim of the game is to work as a team based fleet and capture control points A1/A2 or B1/B2 to make your way to the enemy base, though
The enemy will try to do the same, the combat in the game makes it epic and this game, though in early access is very promising and is definitely going in the right direction!
With 3 starting ships, you fight to earn XP and different Corporation style currencies to upgrade your ship or buy your own! (More on the 3 types of ship later)
Well that depends! If you like the sound of playing a space shooter based upon larger ships instead of fighters then
but if you don't fancy it then don't bother! Personally, I think you should buy this game, Perhaps £6.99 is a bit steep for some people but for me it seems perfectly reasonable.

When a game that's 15 years old manages to be as fun as a current-gen game, it's ♥♥♥♥ing good. This is good. The gameplay is your regular, pretty hard good ol' shooter, but the story and atmosphere are superb. As I've said many times before, old games are masters of ambience, and Half-Life is master of masters. The best part about it is probably the eerily mysterious g-man, who you sometimes see calmly walking around an immense base, where, for reasons unknown, hell broke loose.
You play no part in the unleashing of hell. You are just some research assistant who is relatively new to the place and one day got caught up in this 'accident'. First you see this g-man walking around, obviously unaffected by the chaos, and you wonder what the ♥♥♥♥ he has to do with this mess. Later the military shows up trying to kill everybody involved, and you're just trying to figure out what the hell happened. Right now I'm getting messages from the Lambda Team (no idea who they are) and I've done them some favours. I am seriously eager to meet them and shake some answers out of them. I won't spoil much more, but I think it's clear that the story is sublime. And if you've enjoyed HL2 without playing this game, get ready to re-enjoy the crap out of HL2. I was kinda playing HL2:EP2 and this through eachother, but when Alyx randomly said: 'Prepare for unforseen consequences' shivers went down every single one of my bones. Damn, getting reminded of the hellish mess that is Half Life 1 is actually scary.

The only game i've spent over a thousand hours on so far, most of them have been well spent. Unturned is heavily based around team survival, whether you're playing on a vanilla server or rocket server. It used to be more oriented to solo survival when bullet drop wasn't a thing as people would just camp the military base with their Grizzly, Timberwolf, insert military sniper here, until bullet drop was introduced. The team aspect of playing is really what makes unturned shine through as you depend on each other to finish someone off, watch your six and a better time than just getting shot up by that stacked six-man team camping the military base when trying to find a gun when your friend could've been holding one for you instead. However, surviving on your own holds its own perks. Going solo allows you to keep a lower profile , and if you're good enough with the right guns, you can wipe out whole teams. You also don't have to share supplies with anyone, either.
A long time ago, as in when Washington came out, Unturned ran way smoother on toasters like my HP 15 Inspiron Lagtop. Now a lot of my time is spent waiting for everything to load up at the start or having my screen constantly freeze up while playing on servers with even 50 m/s. With my specs I was once able to effectively run anything in Unturned with 30 frames, but in huge cities like Seattle or St. Petersburg, I only get a shoddy 7 frames per second. I don't know how Unturned got so laggy, but I still love playing it with an average of 17 frames per second. Hopefully Nelson gets this optimized before rolling out 4.0.
In conclusion, I definitely recommend this game, especially if you have really good specs or a nice handful of friends to play with. I can't express the gameplay enough but it speaks for itself with gunfights and LOOT, LOOT, LOOT.

Basically the whole game revolves around capital ship combat. Each ship has specific bonuses that allow players to have different playstyles. If you try to have a playstyle that doesn't fit your ship, it wont take too long to see it. Trial and error is one of your best friends in this game. Don't be worried about losing ships at the start. (However, each time you lose a ship in game increases the respawn time - up to a point) Also, don't worry about losing a game. No matter what, you gain experience and credits. Now there are also ship loadouts that you can modify, which also cost manufacturer experience to unlock, and credits to buy. I really REALLY like this game, and am excited to see where it's going to go. I like being able to see the development progress before my eyes and see the awesomeness unfold. Boiled down to its most basic, Fractured Space (FS) is a team game, where team composition, communication and tactics can really come into play.
:Game-play:
This is very much a team game, and really doesn't support lone wolves all to well. The objective is to capture the enemy home base. The map is split into five areas, each with their own bits for capping.
The first two are the team's home bases. These areas contain the home station (the win condition) and two mini-stations (I generally call these nodes to keep things clear).
The next two are the two main arena areas, Alpha and Beta. Each area contains two warp points (these are needed to be capped to jump into the enemy base) and three nodes, as well as asteroid based cover.
Lastly we have Gamma which is bang in the middle. It is warpable to from any area, but you can only jump to A/B warp points from there. There is only one structure here, the gas station, which is only cappable periodically. Capping it gives your fleet a huge boost to damage and recharge rates for about 2 minutes (or till death if they die before that time expires). Each time the station becomes available for capping, the bonus will be greater than the last.
Games are always 5v5. You enter the match with a pre-selected ship, however during warm-up or first entry, you can choose a different ship to better suit you team build. But once your ship is selected, that's it until the match is over.
:Mechanics:
Capping: Points are capped by entering their bubble of influence. Capping speed is determined by the amount of ship levels in the bubble versus the amount of opponent ship levels in the bubble (I'll explain levels next). I’m not sure at what multiples you have to be at to cap an area with enemy still in it, but you have to have significantly more levels than they do.
Levels and nodes: Maximum ship level is team wide, and is increased by capping nodes. Nodes generate points when capped, and when the points hit the right amount, your team levels up. You however do not automatically level up. Instead, you have to fly back to a capped warp station or home base. Levels increase damage, health and recharge rates, with each level growing exponentially (e.g. the jump between 5 and 6 will be far greater than 1 and 2).
Combat: The main feature of the game. Every ship has different ranges on it's guns, as well as some having optimal range before damage drop off. Many ships also rely on their facings for their weapons fire arcs. Whilst some ships can fight at any angle, some have to face certain ways to bring guns to bear.
Another aspect that is little often discussed is armour. Each ship has 6 different armour facings, being front, back, port, starboard, top, and finally bottom. As a facing gets repeatedly hit, the armour will take damage. Once it has taken enough, it will drop (represented by the facing burning) and any damage taken against that facing will increase.
All ships have abilities. This is what defines their tactics and play style with some ships able to generate different kinds of shielding, others have more support weapons, and mother with support drones or fighters/bombers. Each ship has three “class abilities” assigned on the 1, 2, & 3 keys, and “general abilities” on 4, 5, & 6. Your general abilities are Point defence(4), used for intercpeting missiles and hostile drone/attack craft, Warp to(5) for moving between locations, and Warp Home (6) which is a longer warp, but will always warp you to home base no matter the location (unless already home)
:Ships:
There are a multitude of ships to play with, each with their own unlocks to change out their equipment. Each ship will fit roughly into one of three categories, Defence, Support and Assault. All of which is pretty self explanatory. Composition of your team can be really important. Focused too much in one aspect can leave you woefully exposed, with certain ships being better on taking on different classes of ships. For example, the Assassin (A “Tier 3” unlock) is fantastic for taking out lighter ships and support ships, but will struggle against heavies and dedicated combat craft.
You start off with access to three different ships from the three different manufacturers (There is a fourth, but nothing has been released for them so far).
Flagship: One of the two heavies so far released. This is a defensive class ship, mainly due to its ability to tank huge amounts of damage. Despite having a short boost ability, it is very slow and with guns that are really focused on close range, it can feel really cumbersome.
Hunter: This is your first assault ship. It's nimble, it's guns are some what close range, and it has to be careful with it's facing. It can do micro-jumps to get it in range, can fire missiles for longer range and can detect nearby hidden ships. It has to keep a forward facing towards it's target or suffer huge DPS drop as it won't be able to bring it's other guns to bare.
Corvette: Your first support ship, and arguably the most useful. It's very light, meaning it's fast, but can't take to much damage. It is a dedicated healer however. It's main gun will have it's shots home towards your locked on enemy, allowing you to focus on your team mates. It's main features are it's repair beam and shield, allowing it to heal and block damage respectively.
My Summary:
I really do enjoy this game, however, as it's still in alpha, there will be a fair few changes in the future, as well as few bugs. I got it on the free steam weekend, but I would recommend it, even you just get it at it's cheapest price. I look forward to seeing what new features will be made for it. Bugs are currently few and far between, but can be very annoying, even match ruining if you come across one, but they do seem to be fixed pretty sharply. If you wished to hold out until it's more developed, I wouldn't blame you, but as it currently stands, the combat is nice and varied, with plenty of different ship types to keep matches interesting.

A great game in general, cool setting, epic music and so on. I really had fun the first 5-10 hours.
From a technical perspective it's fine as well (performance could be better, but I had no bigger bugs or crashes).
Why negative? I think it's just too stressful and frustrating. I played XCOM EU and all the old titles but this is the first time a XCOM-game is giving me too much pressure. I tried on veteran (should switch to Rookie maybe) and after some hours of playing I have the feeling my research and progress on the worldmap was not good enough and now game is over.
I'm forced to run across the map (time limit) and the enemies are getting stronger and stronger. No chance to plan an ambush, flank the enemy or so...just run and take the damage.
The result: All my soldiers are either dead, wounded for weeks or have penalities (shaken etc.). I need to recruit rookies to fill up the squad, what is not making things better. Now I have to save and load every single turn. Sniper missed? Load again! Run too far (into the next bunch of super aliens)? Load again!
And this is my point. It seems the game does not scale with your progress. If you're too slow (on the world map as well on the missions), bad luck. After 10 hours of playing you notice that the fun is gone, it's getting more and more difficult and every little mistake leads to a reload of the turn or restart of the mission. But this is just no fun anymore.
Maybe I'll have a new try on Rookie-Difficulty or use a mod to play without time limit...or maybe I'll just seek for another strategic game which is a bit less frustrating and gives the player a bit more space.

Excellent sequel that improves upon the original in many ways. I have not had any technical issue with the game so I can't comment. Only on the gameplay. As a huge XCOM fan (original 1990s version) + Xcom Enemy Unknown, I really enjoyed this one. However, there are some areas where it deserves criticism:
1. Timed missions - incredibly restrictive and ups the difficulty in an artificial, unnatural way. On higher difficulties it makes the missions crazy hard. There are mods that delay or remove timers.
2. Early/Mid-game feels short. This could be because of my experience but it does feel shorter than Enemy Unknown. You can rush tier 2 weapons (second tier) in just one month. It's often the best way to advance.
3. Mission variety. About the same number of types of missions as the first game, which for some of us might feel lacking. Also, the campaign missinos all feel rather similar and linear.
Now the good parts:
1. Customization  - They really heard us on this one. From the solider appearances to gun modifications and special weapons, this game has improved on the original ten-fold. Many more choices on how to equip soliders for a specific mission are availiable.
2. Gameplay - Same if not better than before. The best turn-based tactics game out there. Feel satisfaction everytime your solider hits that 50% chance shot. Feel the glory when that plasma grenade explodes on a group of three aliens.
3. New mechanics - Additions like armor, hacking, grenade launchers, or melee combat, all give the player more strategic options in every mission.
3. Enemy types - Again an improvement with some awesome enemy units that appear throughout the game.
So don't doubt it. If you liked the original XCOM, Enemy Unknown, or turn-based games in anyway this is a must-have.

I hear a lot of complaints aimed at the level of RNG in this game, to which I say learn how to game the system with buffs and debuffs.
I hear a lot of complaints about how punishing a failure can be, to which I say learn when to cut losses and turn tail. there is no shame in that.
I hear a lot of complaints involving how they just lost a 10 hours of work hero to a stupid mistake, to which I say learn from your mistake and keep a stiff upper lip.
I hear about an unfair moment where you did everything right, you gamed the system the best you could, you took every premesure you possibly could, you played as safe as you possibly can, and you still got annialated due to nothing more then bad rolls of the dice, to which I say thats the way this game goes.
This is the hardest of core. I've come to learn, and I respect that. there's no game these days quite like it. You are going to be put to the test in your levels of patience just as much, if not more then how your hero's are put to the test against stress. This game will ask a LOT of you. A LOT. I cannot stress this enough. you WILL loose hours, even days, weeks, months, in one case for me, a year's work to a bad roll of the die that you simply cannot have even a chance at preventing. I have seen formerly diehard fans who were part of the game since the kickstarter turn tail due how absolutely unfair and insaine this game can be in punishing you for things that are genuinly not your fault. I understand this. I respect this. This is not dark souls difficult, the hard but fair style. this is not I wanna be the guy difficult, with the tight manuvers you do over and over again through memorization till you get it. This is a game that will ask for pure, raw determination from you moreso then many things you will ever experiance in life, something not many people will have.
I'm 111 hours in as of writing. I still have yet to get a hero to level 6. 5, sure, but never 6, which is the max. I have yet to clear the first run of the Darkest dungeon, the endgame dungeon which has three layers to beat before you win the game. I HAVE beaten everything i've come across at least once through a lot of personal study, healthy preperation, and luck having never looked at a guide or wiki.
I'm nowhere near done despite the time I've sunk. It's rediculus. it's unfair. it's asking an unreasonable amount of time out of my life.
But it can be beaten. it can be slain.
In short, this is the ipitomy of a game not ment for everyone. This is not about machoistim, this is not about chalanging yourself, it is litterally just a time sink till you get that perfect run.
It is likely not for you, for which I say that I respect you for admiting that, if thats the case.
If you decide it is, I wish you the best of luck. Keep that torch lit when you need to, douse it if things are going really well and collect that sweet sweet extra loot. Learn what everything does as soon as you can, and keep your head up. remember that catastrophic, save ruining failures are going to happen, and be that spark of light in the overwhelming darkness.

This game has a very well designed turn based combat system with a lot of variation in character & enemy abilities. It is really fun to mix and match party and ability compositions and try them out against each dungeon's possible enemy compositions.
What makes it really special is the strategic resource management system wrapped around the tactical combat. The fact that it is impossible to avoid stress accumulation completely in every quest ensures that charecter availability is never 100% and you can’t roll through every dungeon with the optimal party. It makes risk/reward management interesting.
The art & music is top notch. And small touches like the character quotes in camp & behavior when they are afflicted add a lot to the atmosphere they create.
But the risk/reward balance at the champion level dungeons is a bit off though, it’s way too easy to lose characters to an unavoidable series of bad rolls and the cost of stress recovery is high at this level. This would all be fine if the rewards matched the costs, but they don't. High level dungeons end up being a net loss and the cost of replacing lost characters is ridiculously high (because of the cost of upgrades) which turns the late game to a bit of a grind. Despite this, I feel that overall the game is still very fun and worth playing.

In-game inventory shows in steam user arsenal, played this game about 4-5 years ago, got hit by nostalgia hammer and this is what I think...
I often played this game solo. Sometimes my pal would join me in, but it was too much of a grind fest for them.
My initial experience then was shock. An awe to the music, conept and art style. It really blew my mind how well made can a game be! It was era of Korean and Chinese grind-based mmo's which offered balance breaking p2w items or there were good, but p2p games. And there was Spiral Knights which had in-game transactions but overall, you, as a pleb poorfg player (like me), could actually catch up eventually with rich irl players.
Game had simple but well thoght story and lore. Player, as a inhabitant of a cog-based planet, need to delve into the deeps to git gud items and kill mighty bosses. It's got retro rpg flair but you can use swords, guns or bombs, play up to 4 people and do ride-like dungeons and score good loot.
Initially this made me soil my pants with excitement as it was trully a game I needed back then! It reminded me of Phantasy Star Online, which I spent countless hours playing on my Dreamcast console. Spiral Knights were great follow up to that at the time being.
But then I started to realize this game was just amazingly successful indie project which somehow got greenlit to steam (back then it wasn't taht easy to join the platform) and eventually Three rings software were devoured by SEGA, which again, at the time, made many questionable decissions to make the company alive and on the market.
Basically game was more and more becoming pointless grind. The key fun factor in games where you need to do the same thing over and over are: astonishing, super rare drops and challenging, sometimes very unfair bosses. Spiral Knight had none of these for me so, while still being rather scrub player, I left the game and quickly forget about it.
5 years passed.
So here I am. Still having those basic, in game items stocked up in my steam armory, flashing "Spiral Knights" logo everynoe and then it finally hit my soft spot and made me want to experience this game yet once more.
The game is very light, it's under 700mb and patches in 2-3 minutes. Still had my account on so I jumped into elevator and went for some fightin'.
Initial experience wasn't best to be honest. Game felt clumsy, control of the character wasn't that bad but I felt clearly this game is almost decade old.
Enemy AI is noneexistent. Either, creeps charge their power-ups so long you can kill them or shot orbs which aren't threat. Boss fights are a bit more challenging but it's not that punishing bullet hell so any Ikaruga or Touhou player could play it with their elbows while focusing on crosswords.
Inventory is old styled 30 or something bag so it gets full very fast. Same for the utility belt. They've added more NPC rtm sellers offering you actually decent items for ~5€ which could be grinded in one evening.
Bombs are useless at my low level but doubt they are any better later on. Damage output might be ok in team fights but overall for solo play it's lowest dps, 1/10th of sword-gun combo or worse.
Maps got few more objects on them and doesn't feel so empty now but fixed side camer is a bit annoying.
Music aged badly. Mixture of chiptune and keyboard-programmed orchestrals aren't bad but the compression/low quality of sounds itself and limited number fo tracks makes it annoying.
In the end, playing this game for about an hour made me realize how much it's just a shadow of much better, earlier mentioned PSO or any other mmo game actually.

Do you keep attacking while your own base is under attack or do you jump home and defend? Will you go for that point that let them jump for your base or do you continue to their base. Do you support your teammates, do you sneak off or do you fake a capture so that they jump away?
This game has found me hooked on a very simple but open gameplay in which teamwork is key and strategy comes forth in its best element. (TL;DR at bottom of review)
A game where skill actually is a factor in the development of your character. Social aspects like joining a guild with your RotMG friends make the game even better, which synergizes with the co-op feel of the game. Items are spread over the world from common items to rare treasures that come by only a several precious times a year. Hundreds and hundreds of monsters and bosses to fight definitely add an exciting touch to the game. The game overall has a creative, fantasy world that is not seen in any other MMOs today.
One broken thing about this game however is the pay-to-win process. In the spawn point of the Nexus there are in-game items sold for real-world currency. This point defeats the purpose of the game in the way that, one would start playing to acquire higher-tier loot, but would easily be able to obtain such high-tier loot through a simple, 5 dollar purchase.
Another is the frightening inconsistency of builds and releases. Through the course of playing this game for over 2 years, I have seen this game come through many changes. After the acquirement of this game by Kabam, development and build releases have been extremely lazy, drab, glitchy, and controversial to the overall structure of the game. In the past few months, however, builds have been more consistent, with less glitches and bugs.
TL; DR: The game boasts huge worlds with lots of monsters to fight. It's easy to meet friends and keep track of them by joining guilds with them. However, inconsistent builds and pay-2-win sales crumble away what otherwise would have been a solid, legendary game.

I ABSOLUTELY LOVE THIS GAME. I'm not a big fan of common multiplayer games like "CS" or "TF" (well, since I suck at them), very popular MMO-team based games like "World of Tanks" or "War Thunder" (because it's pay 2 win) and especially MOBA games (because they suck), but in Fractured Space I've found a perfect mixture of all these multiplayer games. It's a team based 5v5 multiplayer vehicle shooter there you PIERCE THE SKY on a gigantic spaceships. Unlike other spaceship shooters, ships here are not some crazy hyperspeed flying toasters, which you can't normally control and targeting the enemy's ship will make you puke. No, ships here are pretty slow, and that's really good. First - it's logical since they are really big and their size can be compared to some in-game asteroids. Second - because of this game is more based on a tactics like good teamplay and knowing ships' strong and weak points.
There are "tanks" like Flagship and Destroyer, fast attacking ships like Reaper, Hunter, Enforcer or Frigate, special ships like Sniper (the name says it all), Assassin (same here, stealth ship), Brawler (not so fast pretty strong attacking ship, but he can pull other ships right to him to destroy them at close range in a blink of an eye) and support ships like Corvette, Disruptor and Equalizer. There are a total of 12 ships for now and their number is growing as game development progressing. I haven't tried all of the ships yet, but judging on my game experience I can say that their balancing is very good. There are no "best" of "worst" ships here (although after progressing and getting new ships you will likely not to use some of the first ones) and every ship have his natural enemies. For example: enemy Sniper can make your team's life very hard, but good Brawler player can destroy that deadly, but porcelain beauty. So main goal here is to learn all ships' strong and weak points and choose your ship (that can be done only once in a match, so pay attention to enemy team's ships before match starts) and attack ships that have disatvantages to yours.
But this game is not only about killing other ships and getting frags - there are some MOBA-like capture the base elements. All map is divided into 5 star systems and you have to use hyperdrive jump to reach them. Each team has a Home Base with 2 Mining stations (they gather resources to level up during match). Center system is a Gas Station which gives a controlling team a lot of bonuses, but can be captured only three times in a match and during specific time. And side systems are Forward systems called Alpha and Beta which connects two teams bases and have 3 Mining Stations each. To get to the enemy's base you have to capture opposing forward base which is pretty hard, since enemy players will try to defend it. To understand game mechanic's you better watch a few gameplay videos, but I can tell you that it's well designed and really entertaining.
And main plus of this game is that it's not Pay2Win and developers say that they will not change this. It's still in Alpha stage of development and it's very stable and already has a lot of content to enjoy this game. I've picked it on Free Weekend and get it forever, but now you have to spent a few bucks to get the game with one of the Early Access packs. When development will reach stable phase devs will make this game Free2Play.
I recommend this game to every lover of team-based shooters and space games. Even though I've got this game for free I'll buy one of the Early Access pack to support game development.
