I remembered those days when I first found out about this game in 2013. I was amazed by everything in this game the characters, designs, platforms and much much more. I had a lot fun with this game because it was unlike anything I've played before in a F2P. During the first few ranks I've leveled up myself very quickly ( total ranks of 10) however when I got to the rank of "defender elite rank 8" everything went from a nice straight forward game to a total grindfest. Let me explain, in the old days of SK in 2012 all the gears are leveled up with heat and crafted wtih energy ( you find heat when you kill enemies and you obtain energy by waiting for hours to get the energy to regenerate) however in the new forge update in 2013 everything went downfall. They have slowed down our mission progress by adding fire crystals or orbs to level up and crafting your gears and weapons. What this means is that the energy regeneration is completely removed so you have to use orbs to craft new weapons.
Orbs are very rare so if you could not find 3 orbs to craft for a single gear or weapon then you are stuck on a rank and could not proceed to new missions until you buy it from the energy deposit ( shop ) or find it during tier runs. Heating is another problem, if you could not find fire crystals to level up your gear then all the precious hard earned heat is wasted.
Back then, the gear and weapons level up automatically so no fire crystals are involved to block progress.
Another problem in this game is its economy. Yes, you can still buy energy from the energy deposit as little as 11k crowns for 100energy nowadays. Crowns are ingame currency we use in SK you obtain them by killing off enemies. The energy price for 3 eternals orbs (highest ranked orbs) is 800energy. So 11 x 8 = 88, then you need 88k Crowns to craft one of the highest gear/Weapon in SK. It does not sound too bad did it? Well if you did 1 full run for tier 3 (total tiers 1, 2 and 3 being the highest) you get an average of 8k crowns. Took me 40 min on average to solo through the full tier 3 ( don’t bother looking to join a party, the game is pretty much dead and even if you do it would take you more time to complete a tier because you need to wait for other people ). So 40 x 11 = 440/60 = 7.3, then you need to take a total of 7hrs and 15 min to have the amount total of money to craft a single 5 star gear/weapon ( total stars 1-5). Pretty much you can find orbs in tier runs but they very rarely come by so you could be sitting and playing SK for months and still haven’t found a full set of 3 orbs.
The final problem is that the game is dead as I have mentioned earlier. The developers are constantly recolouring the themes of costumes (costumes are cosmetics and have no impacts on armor and stats, the purpose is to look good). Everyday, every week and every month of a year they don’t add new missions, new contents or new gears/weapons. I have to mention they did a gunner update of new gear and armor in 2014 and it was amazing not only that they added new missions. It went pretty well however from 2014-2016 they did not release anything new, just recoloured cosmetics and repeated events. I got to vanguard rank 10 in 2015 it was already boring me out when I’ve finished all the missions and got all the good gear. Lack of new content
I have much more to say about this game but I think I’ve given you a viewpoint of why I don’t recommend this game unless you like a big grindfest mate.

I tried this game and after losing a few missions in a row and running out of money I left it, but after a few months I had a craving to try it again and this time things started out a bit better and I really got into it. This is a great game and I enjoy playing it.
The things I like about it:
=================
- Theme and Art
The theme, artwork is really great and comes together nicely to make you feel like you're really exploring monster infested dungeons and clearing the lands of evil.
- Stategy
The turn based fighting is fun and engaging. At it's core its about chance and timing, but beating the different enemies requires one to know their strenghts and weaknesses and set up you characters, powers and trinkets to tip the odds in your favour. If you pull of a difficult mission it is very rewarding.
- Bosses
I like how there's a bunch of different bosses, each with their own story, strategy, strenghts and weaknesses.
Things I didn't like that much:
====================
- Lenght
I feel the game drags out a bit towards the end. I haven't actually finished yet, but thinking of taking a break for now.
- Cost of some of the town activities
I feel locking in skills cost to much, especially in the early parts of the game (and even after all the discount upgrades have been added in the late game). Since you'd rather spend money to upgrade character weapons and armour or cure and lower stress, the cost of locking in a positive quirk never outweighs the other upgrades. I also feel the trinket seller is also a bit to expensive. Since it's so easy to pick up trinkets in mission and you get one after each mission, you never feel the need to buy one.
- Character lines
Every now and then the characters decide to say something. I understand that it's to add to the theme, but mostly it just irritates me, since they sometimes say random things that don't always make sense or is informative or contributing to the story in the game. Also, you have to click to get the pop-up to go away and since I mostly navigate the dungeon with my keyboard it's not nice to have to wait for the pop-up to go away by itsself or to reach for the mouse to go on.
Very fun, great community. Playing with friends makes the experience 3x better.

Due to popular demand Ive decided to add a more ‘wholemeal’ first look review for people who like that sort of thing.
The game is essential qwop combined with the floor is lava. You navigate your slice of bread around various obstacles on a quest to get yourself nicely toasted (insert your own joke there). Encountering dirty items reduces your edibility and therefore your overall score, whilst getting smothered in tasty tasty jam boosts it.
The game controls exactly how you would imagine it does. Each corner is assigned a different button which when pressed holds that edge in place apparently regardless of the surface/physics. The mouse or thumb stick flicks the bread around of can be used to nudge it around for precise movements. Practiced or naturally skilled will surely be able to cartwheel their way onto the leaderboards quickly whilst people starting out will ultimately spend more time flailing around like a dying Magicarp. Your main opponent is your own frustration.
If the play style is sounding very familiar that’s because it is. Anyone who has already played Surgeon Simulator or Octodad will immediately recognise the pattern of destruction and failure. This means that behind its freshly baked exterior the game is likely to become stale fairly quickly. Like its sister games there is a big potential for fun workshop content but ultimately you cannot judge a game on what could possibly be made by fans later on.
It is worth pointing out that it is an early access game, meaning that it is essentially unfinished, although this game does feel a lot more complete than most. It is very much playable with the exception of a few minor bugs. Enabling the gif record mode makes the game basically unplayable and the music always seems to be coming out of a random corner of the room.
I think overall most people will have already made a decision about this game, and whatever your thoughts they are probably correct. It’s ultimately a casual iPad-destined meme-maker but it clean fun and will give most people a few laughs for less than the price of an average cinema ticket. If flinging a slice of bread around for a few hours is the sort of thing that will brighten your day, then this is probably for you.

while Blizzard is busy copying itself, Fractured Space is actually a Moba with a different feel and very unique playstyle.
Time to update.
let me give you a run down:
+ big arena
asteroids, bases, empty spaces. it has place for each ship to use its abilites and maneuverbility to
the fullest
+ new classes/abilities unlockable through earned experience
(having the massive, disproportionate Brawler coming up next to you for the first time is quite a
sight)
+ good balance for an Alpha built, each ship stands out on its own without any being overpowered
+ great graphics, running it on lower settings it is still more than enjoyable to see a flagship
desintegrate or explode
ship show damage, even though not yet detailed (but getting a full salvo on only one side will light
it on fire :) )
+ matchmaking is fast and uncomplicated, getting in game takes a minute
+ price, 10euro is a lot to ask for an early access game, but the 70 hours I got out of it alone are
worth it
+ community. still very friendly and helpful, but over time the servers have emptied, me included
+ atmosphere. getting chased by hunter only to have a flagship appear from underneath a base to
sweep in, guns blazing is a thing of pure joy and glory.
+ game is stable. 70 hours into the game I only experienced onlye a handful of crashes
+ rage quit no more. some one left your team? seat is open for new players to jump right in
- leveling is automated and levels and skill points are only applied while in base
while this might be great for less experienced Moba players, such as myself, the more veteran players might be turned off by this lack of control and customizability
- ships can be choosen by multiple players
never been a fan of seeing my player character out there a second or third time, even though it
makes a lot more sense here (Dota 2 does it right)
- controls. still clunky as hell, through several updates, but I seriously didn;t even try to change
anything :P take it with a grain of salt
- empty servers. while the matchmaking works fast it can take several minutes (up to ten, maybe
more) to fill a game. matches with less than 10 players have become common
Well, I can still only recommend the game to anyone with a love for spaceships, spaceship battles or who wants to find a different kind of challenging Moba.

I hear a lot of complaints aimed at the level of RNG in this game, to which I say learn how to game the system with buffs and debuffs.
I hear a lot of complaints about how punishing a failure can be, to which I say learn when to cut losses and turn tail. there is no shame in that.
I hear a lot of complaints involving how they just lost a 10 hours of work hero to a stupid mistake, to which I say learn from your mistake and keep a stiff upper lip.
I hear about an unfair moment where you did everything right, you gamed the system the best you could, you took every premesure you possibly could, you played as safe as you possibly can, and you still got annialated due to nothing more then bad rolls of the dice, to which I say thats the way this game goes.
This is the hardest of core. I've come to learn, and I respect that. there's no game these days quite like it. You are going to be put to the test in your levels of patience just as much, if not more then how your hero's are put to the test against stress. This game will ask a LOT of you. A LOT. I cannot stress this enough. you WILL loose hours, even days, weeks, months, in one case for me, a year's work to a bad roll of the die that you simply cannot have even a chance at preventing. I have seen formerly diehard fans who were part of the game since the kickstarter turn tail due how absolutely unfair and insaine this game can be in punishing you for things that are genuinly not your fault. I understand this. I respect this. This is not dark souls difficult, the hard but fair style. this is not I wanna be the guy difficult, with the tight manuvers you do over and over again through memorization till you get it. This is a game that will ask for pure, raw determination from you moreso then many things you will ever experiance in life, something not many people will have.
I'm 111 hours in as of writing. I still have yet to get a hero to level 6. 5, sure, but never 6, which is the max. I have yet to clear the first run of the Darkest dungeon, the endgame dungeon which has three layers to beat before you win the game. I HAVE beaten everything i've come across at least once through a lot of personal study, healthy preperation, and luck having never looked at a guide or wiki.
I'm nowhere near done despite the time I've sunk. It's rediculus. it's unfair. it's asking an unreasonable amount of time out of my life.
But it can be beaten. it can be slain.
In short, this is the ipitomy of a game not ment for everyone. This is not about machoistim, this is not about chalanging yourself, it is litterally just a time sink till you get that perfect run.
It is likely not for you, for which I say that I respect you for admiting that, if thats the case.
If you decide it is, I wish you the best of luck. Keep that torch lit when you need to, douse it if things are going really well and collect that sweet sweet extra loot. Learn what everything does as soon as you can, and keep your head up. remember that catastrophic, save ruining failures are going to happen, and be that spark of light in the overwhelming darkness.

This game starts off strong, from the very first mission the game is harder than EU... Also have to love the game for having mod support from the get go, I never thought I'd see the day where an xcom game would have the development kit released with the game, that was a great surprise and tons of the mods available are incredibly useful and game changing, which enriches the overall experience even more, plus you don't see the same map twice now, the maps are procedurally generated and you have to strategize as you uncover more of the map to find the best positions and act, I feel like the timed missions tons of people complain about are good, not every mission is timed, but the ones that are keep a good pacing, it doesn't ever feel like you're getting too rushed unless you get a streak of bad luck and have to make a break for the evac...
I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who has played enemy unknown/enemy within and enjoyed it, if you haven't this game is a tactical rpg of sorts where you give commands to your troops one at a time setting up positions for flanking and try to take out the enemy opposiiton while completing your objective, the visuals and representations of things are great, and the experience as a whole is truly amazing. I recommend playing ironman mode so you actually put thought into your choices, and when you take a loss of your best soldier you think back and reflect on what you could've done better in that mission, so on and so forth, to hell with savescummming!

SUBJECT: Half-Life
STATUS: Amazing
AWAITING FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS
All jokes aside, this game (and the entire franchise) is amazing, and is one of my favorite FPSes. There isn't much of a focus on the multiplayer, but the singleplayer campaign/story mode is great. You play as a theoretical physicist named Dr. Gordon Freeman, a badass nerd who loves kickin'♥♥♥♥♥and bashing crates. But he's all out of crates. He works at Black Mesa, a facility-science-company-thing where people do stuff. A lot of the work is with the military, so because of that they build devices such as turrets, weapons, etc. However, they also have a large focus on science and physics, and they are big competitors with Aperture Science (from Portal). Anyways, one day♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down and Freeman is right smack in the middle of it.
The Half-Life series as a whole is a great FPS experience. A lot of it involves taking advantage of your environments against your enemies. There's also a lot involving physics, especially in the second game with the Source engine.
Speaking of the Source engine, there's also another version of this game which runs on Source. It's mostly just a direct port, but if you play Garry's Mod, it's nice to have it so you can use it's resources in-game. However, this version (the original) has support for standalone mods, which HL:S doesn't.
If you're considering getting into the Half-Life series, the second game stands well on it's on without having to have played the first game to understand, but the original is still a great game and fun to play, so I highly recommend it. If you plan on getting this and aren't sure which one to get, then I recommend the Source version simply because it looks a little nicer and is a little more up to date, as long as you understand you can't get mods for it.
As for the multiplayer, well, the series doesn't have much of a focus on that, and since this runs on the GoldSrc engine (heavily modified version of the Quake engine), the multiplayer feels and plays very similar to Quake multiplayer, in terms of pace and gameplay. If you're mainly interested in the multiplayer, I recommend getting Quake III Arena, a multiplayer-only version of Quake which is pretty cool.
Also, if you're not a fan of FPS's and are very skeptical about this game, I'd like to go ahead and say that this game is amazing even if you're not that big of a fan of modern first-person shooters. I recommended this game to my friend Pokaymon, who played a lot of Portal, and even though he didn't have much interest in FPS's, he grew to like and enjoy this game. Speaking of Portal, this game takes place in the same universe as it. Portal initially started as a side-game to Half-Life when it launched with the Orange Box, but then it gained a lot of popularity so they made a sequel.
All in all:
If you aren't a fan of FPS's, I recommend trying this game or HL:S anyways if you're feeling open-minded.
If you're a fan of FPS's and are okay with a singleplayer experience with a lesser focus in multiplayer, I also recommend trying this game.
If you're a fan of multiplayer FPS's and don't care for singleplayer campaign, I recommend Quake III Arena or Half-Life Deathmatch: Source.

after many hours and finishing the game multiple times on normal and NG+ I finally decided to write a review for DD and maybe help few others which struggle with this game along the way as well.
DD is fantastic game with great atmosphere. If you like challenging game you will love this game as much as I do.
However I see many people here write nagative feedbacks about RNG and how it's screw them over.
Yes there is a RNG in the game and yes I lost many great heroes as well but lets be honest in 99% cases I lose them because I did not know enough about the game and / or was too greedy.
I will write few points below...
Most OP:
- character in game: Jester due to the huge stressheal
- ability in game: Scouting. With scouting you can see what to expext, quickly grab quest items or just simply avoid most (if not all) combats and go straight to boss fight with no stress or heal damage.
- trinket in game: Ancestor's map due to the scouting chance.
Learn:
-  to do night (tourchless) runs. Especially in early game night runs give you huge gold advantage due to the ++++ loot. Unfortunately there is the risk of meeting Shambler, however the chance is very low before Veteran / Champion levels.
- heroes abilities and which conbinations can create ultimate combos with good heroes setups.
- who to focus
- who to stun and when
- when to camp and what skills to use. Many heroes has OP camping skills like MAA has skills which boost the whole party or skills which bost Scouting. Also few heroes like PD remove multiple  diseases with one click saving you more golds.
- how to stressheal during combat. Trust me if you master this you you will end most of the runs with very low stress or not at all. This will save you huge amount of gold which you can then use to level your heroes instead. In my NG+ run I did not use the stress relief bilding at all which save me lot of herlooms as well. Simple leave  two weak mobs and keep them stunlock while stress healing your party. Jester is best for this but double HM combo works great too.
- what trinkets to use
-  to avoid short runs. Too much gold spend for what you can find. Also in long runs there is always secret room with 3 gems (2.5k gold each) or one of nice trinkets (2 of 3 are quite good).
- when to abandon a quest
- which Quirks to remove. Most of the Quirks can be ignored as long as you know your heroes and where to sent them...
- which Quirks to lock in on other hand
- which supply item to use on a Curios
- to use supplies such as Holy Water Medicinal herbs
- QUIT THE GAME AND STRESSHEAL YOURSELF
If you learn all the above and a bit more you will quickly realize that the game is not so hard after all. Just do not be greedy or love your heroes too much. Take them more as tools to save the world.

As someone fairly used to absurd RNG+grind (Warframe) and risk management (XCOM), this game, overall, was a fairly enjoyable experience.
However, after finishing the game, I can't in good conscience recommend it to anyone that isn't used to extreme levels of randomness in game design. Even when employing everything you can to minimize risks, at later levels your characters can die in the span of a single turn to plain bad luck.  And after sinking several hours worth of grind into a single elite-level character, losing one just because of poor luck feels like a punch in the gut, and unless you find grinding soothing, the lost time will be inexcusable to the average player.
The RNG really feels like its without any rhyme or reason, e.g. special items in the Warrens giving your characters traits for adventuring in the Ruins. Thankfully, most RNG checks seem to have a chance for a positive outcome as well, as characters gambling in the tavern can win new trinkets instead of just losing the ones you have.
Unless you are really averse for spoilers, I suggest watching
video review by Joseph Anderson to judge whether or not Darkest Dungeon will be worth your time.

TL;DR: dumbed-down dialogue, unimaginative story, lackluster DLC, paid mods. Better play something else.
Fallout is a fairly longstanding series, and it's only natural for players to have high expectations for games in it.
Fallout 3 was reasonably good. New Vegas was really good. I haven't played the first two games, but from what I've heard, they were amazing at their time.
I have played plenty of various RPGs in my time, all with different balance of role-playing, combat, and story. Fallout 4 is an RPG in the name only.
Sure, it has stats, it has skills, and it has perks. But what are those worth if the only thing they affect is combat? Dialogue and character interaction are at the heart of any competent RPG, and in Fallout 4, these elements were dumbed down to unbelievable levels.
You might remember how Fallout 3 and New Vegas had fairly large branching dialogue and potential for multiple endings, with a multitude of fairly consequential side quests? You won't see any of that here. Sure, you get four dialogue options. But they are not anything detailed, and tend to be mostly the same, with typical answers being "yes", "later", "yes, with sarcasm" and "yes, with joy". Sure, you get a few different endings, and for what it's worth, they are reasonably satisfying. But they basically boil down to picking a side in a conflict. The story isn't anything to write home about either. And the side quests... Why are you reading this, another settlement needs your help!
I don't think I'm in the full right to judge performance, as I have a fairly outdated GPU by modern standards, but I believe the game could have been better optimized. After all, there are still some new games that run perfectly well on my hardware.
I haven't played DLC either, but, from what I've heard, they are pretty mediocre too - at least I didn't feel like I wanted to buy any of them. In contrast, Skyrim had not one, but two high-quality DLC, and that house-building thing.
Does the game have any redeeming qualities? Sure. The combat is, if not amazing, at the very least competent. The environments are pretty and varied, even if they are mostly varying shades of brown. The modding scene is also reasonably good, which helps the longevity and replayability of the game a lot.
And, speaking of modding, Bethesda has found yet another way to ruin it. Or, rather, made a fresh attempt at one already failed tactic: paid mods. They have already tried it with Skyrim, and they failed. Now they are doing it again, but with a few "upgrades". They painted it as "AAA-quality DLC-sized expansions made by the community". Well, sure, the community is perfectly capable of producing that - I remember enjoying Falskaar in Skyrim. If Creation Club had been like that, with reasonable prices, I wouldn't have anything against it. But as it is, it is a blatant money grab. Horse armor for $5 and dinky little side quest to get it? Check. A shotgun for $4? Check. Pipboy reskin for $0.50? Check, check and check. An "AAA-quality DLC-sized expansion"? Nowhere to be found.
It might sound bad as it is, but it only gets worse. With free mods, you download only what you need. With Creation Club, you download all CC content (2GB as of now). And the it just sits there, taking up your disk space, jailed behind the paywall. Sure, 2GB isn't that much by modern standards, but it will only get worse as more armor reskins and questionable weapons are added.
Would I recommend playing it? It depends on what you're looking for in a game. If it's a thrilling story, detailed characters, interesting dialogue options and competent RPG elements - you might want to give Fallout 4 a pass. If you want some mindless action, Fallout lore, those sweet settlement mods, or a bit of world exploration - Fallout 4 might be just for you. Steam has an "Early Access" tag for a reason. That tag should still be all over this game.
Make no mistake, this game is in Alpha, with major changes still happening to core game concepts quite often.
The team behind this game is so completely lost, they're flailing around like that angry German kid we've all seen the vid of.
For those starting out, the game is likely fine but once you get to the higher (lvl/skill) end of the player base the problems start to pile up.
PvP includes playing against bots, where up to 40% of the captains present are controlled by (completely unbalanced) AI.
Complaints about this addition of AI to the PvP matches have been piling up and the developers have responded to this problem by eliminating 2 "players" from each team and closing nearly half of the usual map, turning the usual 5v5 into a 3v3... I'm not amused.
On top of this, the game regularly gets events which are focussed on PvE play.
All these changes have turned away a large section of the PvP-playerbase and continue to do so, leading to increased queue times.
And I would like to add that this game used to include sniper class ships. Too many newbies complained about these so now these ships have been overhauled completely turning them into some disgusting form of hybrid and again turning people away from the game who enjoyed specializing in these ships.
Weirdly enough, the developers had time to completely change 3 ships but fail to do any sort of balancing for any of the other ships, with most of them being completely unchanged for over a year if not more.
In short, if you like PvE, this game might still be fine.
For those of you who enjoy PvP, your experience will change on an update to update basis.
Seeing as this game has no early access tag, we will never know when this game finally comes out of early access.

Black Squad is a neat FPS Game, it is rather fun, and while it has very minimal pay to win elements, (better guns, and more selection). It is fairly well balanced, weapon wise despite the liberal distribution of gernade launchers (they have explosive free matches).
One thing that majorly detracts from this game, is in later matches after you have warmed up and the mm starts to put you with window lickers and high pingers, it gets pretty agrivating, the highpingers especially, they get a major first sight advantage when peaking due to the generous amount of interpolation, to the point that trying to peak against them is suicide unless you too have 2-300 ping, it breaks certain maps.
There is also liberal use of lag/packetloss switchess to make their charictar teleport from point to point, at times it is pretty broken.
They do have a great anticheat, only seen one person with an obvious wall/esp head baninging people behind crates and corners out of the blue, Battleeye the best in the buissness, but due to the developers lazy net coding, lag & packet loss is exploited to the extreme.
Maps are microsopic for the most part, there are a few game modes where it is reasonable for the game mode but for the most part way to small, I dont know if it is due to the engines limitiations or the developers willingness to tax the clients pc or their servers by making them larger.
Shooting mechanics are over simplified, shooting while running in sidestep for ex. if you are looking for something to kill an hour or two while you wait for something to cook or before work, sure it is fairly viable fresh experiance. but after a few hours of play, or to play as a main fps game it leaves to much to be desired for me to bother putting any money into it to support the developers.
TLDR:
Pros:
- Fast Paced
- classic fps, & counterstrike like game modes and elements
- some variety of characters and gear
- pay2win is not as ever preasent as in many other f2p games.
- could be a fun basic shooter game to play with friends, & clanmates.
- push buttion loadouts, (great idea)
- ballstic object penitration
- rather light resource wise (probably good for crappier computers)
- matchmaker seems reasonably fast.
Cons:
- Lag exploitation!
- Phone booth sized maps
- no actual customization of weapons (preset attachment loadouts)
- very slight P2W element in the weapon selection and capabiliy compaired to non premium weapons.
- high pingers are not kicked or seperated from people of <100 ping,
- a little to many gernade launches in game in general.
- very simple/basic shooting mechanics, rediculious run and gun side strifing is possible, head shots are also not 1 hit kill except for sniper rifles.
- limited selection of armor/character appearance.
- poor map design, TDM modes tend to devolve into spawn camping halway holding slaughters no matter what team you are on.
the one thing that prevents me from recomending this game above all else is the lag explotation, and bad net code. If it was less prevelant, or mm matched players aproprietly to ping I would have given it a recomend. but until then you should wait to see if they address these issues before diving in and potentially ruinging your experiance with the game long term.

I understand this is Early Access, but they are already headed in the wrong direction strategy-wise.
Pro:
I was expecting what might be a neat way to play with a Capital Ship in a MOBA setting. Going all out with your big ships without the risk of losing your "one-life" shiny ships in Eve or the trouble of finding a battle in other Open World games.
I was right. The fights were exciting, strategy and teamwork is needed. Graphics look good where they are finished and I expect the final version to look great.
Cons:
The support tier killed it for me. Other MOBA and even MMO games have dedicated support characters just like this game does and those characters make a difference (LoL, Eve...). If you play support in this game, well, you might as well not. The only support ship they have so far is highly underwhelming and useless by itself. Smart players will kill the support or force them to retreat first and easily finish off the remaining unsupported ships. It's no fun to have to run as soon as you are targeted, and often once targeted as support, there is no way to save yourself if there is more than one enemy. Fighting from afar isn't fun either as support. The worst part is the upgrades. They aren't even upgrades. From what I can tell each upgrade I purchased with points actually made the original support ship less effective. If they want this to be more than a run and gun game, and really have strategy, there needs to be support ships that matter. Otherwise have fun mashing your shoot button on the big gun ships.
Also the upgrades during battle. I was pretty confused about that. I go back to base and suddenly my ship is better? I don't know how or why it is better and I can't choose what these upgrades do.
I do look forward to how this game turns out, I know character balancing is a constant battle in any game.

Realm of the Mad God (ROTMG for short) is a top down MMO co-op bullet hell shooter. The goal is to reach the Mad God's kingdom and kill him, the act of doing this is extremely diffucult (for me anyway.) The game has a good progression system, you start with a wizard and unlock a new class at level 5, you then play as that class and unlock another when that one is level 5. This continues until you have 5 classes, then it starts to get a bit more complex.
The actual gameplay is pretty basic, it functions like any good top down shooter. Controls are very basic, left mouse for basic attack, space for special, and n for teleport back home. The special abilities are all fairly basic, your main attack with a bit more spread and damage. The enemies themselves don't provide much of a challenge, their numbers, however do. This game will throw wave after wave of enemies at you until you can't fight anymore. This game is A LOT easier when played with friends.
The in game community is non existent almost, or atleast I couldn't find it through all the spamming of chat channels. Gold sellers, and bots seem to be amiss in the main city. There are player-run guilds although I never had an opportunity to join one. While you level your character you'll come across some other players, most of which are luckily very generous. Lots of other players have given me gear they don't need.
All in all it's quite a fun game, I've put over 80 hours into it. I would reccomend it be played with friends rather than alone. On a scale of 1-10 this game would get a 7/10 it's very fun, although the classes and abilities seem quite basic, and the game play doesn't differ too hard from top down shooters.
I'm certainly more of a casual RTS player so cannot attest to how balanced and tactical this game is. It has a little nostaligia and for its age has a clean look and feel.

One of the great downsides of having a lightweight game with it's own launcher that people tend to play interspersed with other activities (read: procrastinating at work) is that if you forget to close the launcher aswell, Steam registers you with an obscenely high playtime.
Thus I found myself, with almost 100 hours logged on Starbound, but I still don't know what the f*ck I'm doing.
Personal melodrama aside, this is a pretty excellent game. Combining all the best elements of 2D explore-and-builds like Terraria, Starbound takes the random world generation to a whole new level. Each new planet is a new adventure, with new randomly generated wildlife (seriously, every planet's life is a different permutation.
Couple in variables of weather (nothing like an acid rain shower in the mornings to melt your bones), variable gravity, different atmospheres (the distinct lack of oxygen on some), tentacle worlds, lost outposts and vanished empires. It's all there, and Starbound is definitely a game to keep an eye out for.
The developers are also pretty keen on keeping devblogs up, so if you're the kind of person that likes to keep tabs on games in development that you're waiting for (if you're reading this, Space Station 13 devs, go f*ck yourselves) Starbound is an excellent candidate.

An excellent team based cap vs cap ship game that offers familiar roles to those of us who have partaken in at least one other team based arena combat game. The roles of medic, tank, scout (et all) are given in the form of different ships that have different specializations (for example the role of the medic is overseen by the Corvette that has by default a healing beam while on the flipside it has low hp and relatively lackluster weapons).
The "DLC" for this game is in actuality a monetary support option that unlocks skins and allows for bragging rights, it is not DLC in the traditional sense since Steam lacks a "donate" or "financially assist" option.
Spectacular "explosions" and epic space battles are the regular offering of this video game while varied and multiple different ships will satisfice any but the most die hard space opera fan. You begin at account creation with three different ships that correspond to the traditional roles of tank, scout and medic found in other team based arena games and earning XP and as well as credits goes towards unlocking weapons and new ship types.
The net code is impressive and optimized well (unlike many other multi player only games) with almost little noticeable lag and servers in all major regions (US, Asia, Europe) while on the player side graphic options are the standard fare with multiple resolutions and various other options that improve or decrease overall visual quality.
At the time of this review the game is in early access so do expect among others, missing features, some bugs (although I have not experienced any, that is other then the fighter swarms and leech drones I have launched at other players). The game also lacks a tutorial with said tutorial and introduction to the game being fulfilled by a series of Youtube videos.
As it is at the time of this review an early access title I cannot complain much with what has been accomplished so far I do however have hope that they will introduce additional maps and perhaps later down the line expand upon the lore and perhaps even introduce a single player component.

Darkest Dungeon is if Call of Cthulhu had a baby with Dungeons & Dragons, and that game was turned into a roguelike.  The setting is deeply Lovecraftian without being anywhere near haunted Arkham.  (Even the game studio's name is an obscure Lovecraft reference!)
The premise is very tabletop RPG:  There is allegedly both untold riches and unspeakable horrors beneath your ancestral estate.  You send various adventurers of about a dozen classes on expeditions in and around said estate, and can regroup back in the hamlet below.
Where other Lovecraft pastiches call
, Darkest Dungeon calls
.   When stress gets too high, party members' resolve is tested.  Most of the time, stress inflicts a negative Quirk, such as paranoia or hopelessness.  But you also can get a positive Quirk, such as courage or strength.  The hamlet has ways of elminating stress and Quirks, of course.
Party members can also show up with or develop Quirks that benefit or hamper how they handle stress, such as not being able to pray away the stress or only prayer can remove stress.  Or they are more or less stressed in one of the areas, or get bonuses or penalties versus a monster type.
Yes, there is permadeath in this game.  However, several features make this difficulty feel manageable, at least to start.
First, you're not going into battle yourself, so a full party death is not instant Game Over.  Second, there's always fresh meat coming on the stagecoach.  Third is the possiblity of retreat, both from battle and the dungeon itself, even if this inflicts some stress on your party.  And you get to retreat with the treasures you've already found.
Fourth is the Death's Door feature.  Once a health bar hits zero, that party member is announced as at Death's Door.  After this, there is often at least two rounds in which either status effects or an enemy blow can kill you, or you can heal.  Even a 1 HP healing resets the Death's Door count.  Meanwhile, a nearly-dead party member causes stress for the others.
As with all roguelikes, permadeath still becomes a problem.  You invest time and money in a character only to see them killed in the final room of a dungeon.  Then, with only a handful of seats on the weekly stagecoach and about a dozen classes, you may or may not easily find your favored classes to start over with.   Like D&D, the needed levels are few but rack up slowly, making a death all the more frustrating.
So Darkest Dungeon starts feeling grindy, or that you are spinning your wheels.  Any found treasures do count toward hamlet upgrades, though.
Another complaint is that you can never skip a game round without sending an expedition, so you cannot concentrate on a favorite team once you find it.  This adds to the feeling of grindy length.  Six hours in, and I've only gotten the "Congrats, you've passed the tutorial level," milestone achievement and have yet to face any of the laundry list of minibosses.
I wish Steam's review ratings were more granular than a simple up or down vote, because I would give this a tepid Yes recommendation.  You have to really, really,
like permadeath to go far in this game.
At the same time, the atmosphere is
, with great narrative voice acting and visuals, both in the game engine and the cutscenes.  Worth the price of admission if you like Lovecraftian horror or want to work out your PTSD issues.

I had dropped it as i was playing other games (mainly Elite: Dangerous), but i've come back to fractured space in the last couple weeks, and i must say that it's still as good if not better as when i started playing it.
There's been a lot of improvement, especially on the technical side. Long gone are the freezes one could ecounter when people where connecting to the match server or were respawning. And the same can be said of the rare crashes one could encounter while playing: not a single one in the last couple weeks of playing. There's now more variety between the maps.
The match maker might need some more work, but most battles seem quite balanced to me.
As far as gameplay goes, little has changed, and that's not a bad thing. Ships are still well balanced, and choosing a good team composition during the waiting screen is really important, as much as the strategy the team will choose.
Battles have just the right pace, not too fast and not too slow, just dynamic enough to keep everything interesting, while allowing for tactical play and decision making.
Another thing i like about this game is it's community. It has to be one of the most mature and polite communities i've encountered, so far. People are open to listen to commands and suggestions during matches, and i've never seen flaming or whining in a match, no matter how bad the losing side was doing. It makes the experience really, really enjoyable.
I got this game for free a year ago, when they ran one of the many free week-ends, and decided to drop 10€ on it to get the forerunner pack, as i thought the game deserved some support. I'm now really considering dropping some more money on Fractured Space, as i now think it deserves even more support, as the developers have shown they know what they're doing, and that they listen to the community (like with the recent revamp of the crew system and their response to the playerbase reactions). Fractured Space and it's developers are that good.
[[[Old Review (23/04/2015)]]]
This game is fun.
First of all, for an alpha stage game, Fractured Space is really stable. As of now, in 21 hours of playing, i've suffered a crash to desktop only two times, and just a handfull of minor issues. I'm yet to encounter any major issue, and this is something outstanding for a alpha release.
The gameplay is fluid, and, even thought there's only one match mode right now, it's really fun.
The ships are all well characterized, each one with it's own strenghts and flaw. Every ship has it's own set of weapons and abilities. As a result, a sniper ship will feast upon bigger, slower ships, but will be at a big disadvantage against smaller, faster ships designed for arrassing. Every class has its own counter, ensuring that, as long as the enemy team as the right ships, nothing is OP.
Also, graphics and sounds are really nice.
The only real problem as of now, is that some servers suffer from an heavy lag. But this is probably more related to the host, than to the game itself.
All in all, i give this game a 8/10. For an alpha it's outstanding, the devs are always in touch with the community, and the developing plan is public (they have it on trello, giving the players the opportunity to make suggestions on new features or tweaks), and the game is fun. It just needs more game modes, more reliable servers, and a revamp of the UI in some sections, and it would already be A LOT better than most early access games here on steam, and even better than many released games.

as a veteran of the RTS genre there are a few words I’d have for this game
lets start with what is good.
for a game made in 2005 it has very good graphics. And the way buildings fall apart when damaged is very satisfying. There are ALOT of choices for what units to build.
That being said there are far more negatives in my opinion
the controls are clunky at best and hot keys are far from intuitive or fast. The 'cards' add a level of complexity that is completely unnecessary. The units and their counters are so hard that there is almost no point to getting more then the other guy and if you don't have the perfect mix to take him down there is almost no chance to heavily damage his army let alone kill it. Field artillery is far over powered. Workers are absurdly expensive but I suppose that was a balance decision to make up for the fact the resource gathering and macro, if you can call it that, is so simple that it makes where to send your workers to gather minerals in starcraft seam arduous. Factions are far from balanced and not in the good way that promotes a healthy meta game. The computer AI if you can call it that is a joke and needs some serious attention. Battles even when they are at peak seam sluggish or everything is dead before any exchange has happened and micro is almost a joke.
In conclusion. Never buy this game when it's not on sale and your money would be far better spent buying age of empires two and it's expansion for cheaper

2. I am by no means saying this game is complete. It still needs ALOT of work. The community matters too and if they dont say anything, then the game suffers for it. I'll go ahead and be one of the many to tell you that this is a very good game. Steam unfortunately does not display the amount of time I sunk into this game during it's beta stages, but I can safely assume it's on par with my current time in steam. First of all, it does not appear that it would actually be very in-depth, but the devs have gone to incredible lengths to make the game appeal to many. Their semi-recent addition of the "Shadow Tower" gave players a sense of raiding in the game, and a feeling of the "end game" being legitimately difficult and requiring progression. The ability to be in multiple clubs (essentially the 'guilds' of Trove) is a unique feature I haven't seen in many other MMOs, but allows for the player to be a part of different communities. The building aspect of the game is streamlines, but in a way that it does not drop features. Cosmetic props are crafted out of recipes, and features like line-fills for building makes it actually very simple for anyone to start building stuff they would be proud of.
The collection system in the game is part of what ties everything in the game together. Unlocking new weapon or armor styles opens up cosmetic customization for the player, while all the various mounts, fishing rods, boats, and more would make any completionist excited. Rewarding the player for completing collections with mastery levels and bonuses to their account is a well-thought out system, and I found myself striving to collect more things even though I do not see myself as a completionist, especially when it comes to MMOs.
Everything in this game is easy to get the hang of, in truth. Classes only have a few skills each, meaning that complicated skill rotations aren't really a thing in this game. The trade skills (farming, runecrafting, ringcrafting, and fishing) are very simple, but with each of them having 250 levels to them, they provide plenty for the player to work towards. Runecrafting and Ringcrafting in particular tie in very well to a player's progression through ideally their first class, as the materials needed to further each become obtainable the higher the player gets in class levels, making a good progression.
The class system is implemented quite well. Classes are frequently released, and available for either microtransactions or through a currency the player can receive on a daily basis. There is no limit to how many classes you can buy, and they can be switched by simply pulling up a menu and selecting a different class to play as. Equipment for them is stored with the class itself, meaning that you don't need to haul around different armor sets or have different characters to play as different classes. Each class has it's own experience levels and gear levels, so players can "begin anew" with another class and progress through levels all over again, but at the same time still have their "main" class just a click away.
Content patches, my goodness. The devs livestream future updates and classes all the time, are constantly in communication with the playerbase, and love to introduce new content to the game. The community can contribute dungeons and weapon/armor styles, which I'm sure alleviates some stress from the Devs and allows them to focus on adding things like Shadow Tower, new classes, or the most recent addition of PvP.
Of course, there are some cons about the game, but these stem from the fact that Trove falls under the same curse that any MMO would: it sometimes gets repetitive. Trove is based around running dungeons in procedurally generated worlds, and, well, that can get old. Currently the only option for "end game" raiding is the Shadow Tower, and while it cycles through layouts (that are constantly being added to the game) being able to run each of the four floors for a reward only once a week makes it feel grindy. However, this all can only really be acknowledged, but not held against Trove, as "dailies" and "weeklies" have been a common staple for many MMOs.
Overall, Trove functions like an MMO-lite, in the fact that it's incredibly easy to pick up and get the hang of, while catering to everybody. It is nowhere near as complicated as big-name MMOs like WoW, TERA, Rift, etc., but that's part of it's appeal as well. You get the experience of playing with a playerbase on the scale of an MMO, but with a different fun, lighthearted, and lively feel to it.

Absolutely beautiful game. I loved XCOM EU and I was really excited to play XCOM 2. Then I saw some negative reviews and hesitated to buy it... I still ended up buying it and I'm so glad I did.  I started it off with a bitter taste in my mouth, because some of the reviews really sounded horrible, but even dispite that the game blew me away.
Pretty much everything XCOM EU did right, XCOM 2 does even better. The story is better, the classes and skills are better, the base building is better, the enemies are cooler, the researching and R&D is better.
Even things that some reviewers complained about I ended up really liking. The thing that worried me the most was that people said nearly every mission is a timed mission. I hated timed missions in XCOM EU, but in this game... I actually liked them! I'd say about 50% of the missions I play were timed, but to me it just felt right in this game. In XCOM EU the timers always felt too short, but in this game I feel they struck a perfect balance. You always have enough time to complete the mission, but you do have to hurry up a bit. I disagree with some people's complaint that it means you can't strategize because of it. I think you still have time to strategize, you just have to make razorsharp decisions about your strategy and have to "deal with it" if you made a wrong decision. You don't have time to sneak around in tiny moves just to be 100% on the safe side. The pace just feels right to me.
It's just a really really "epic" game to me.
Plus: The Steam Workshop inclusion is great. There are already so many cool things in the workshop. The voice packs people built add soooo much character to your soldiers. Really love it.
Only negative point I could find: The performance is terrible. I have a pretty decent gaming PC and I constantly have framerate drops and stuttering. Luckily this is a turn based game, so it doesn't matter that much (if this were an FPS it would be unplayable with the perfomance issues). I hope they fix this.

One of the great downsides of having a lightweight game with it's own launcher that people tend to play interspersed with other activities (read: procrastinating at work) is that if you forget to close the launcher aswell, Steam registers you with an obscenely high playtime.
Thus I found myself, with almost 100 hours logged on Starbound, but I still don't know what the f*ck I'm doing.
Personal melodrama aside, this is a pretty excellent game. Combining all the best elements of 2D explore-and-builds like Terraria, Starbound takes the random world generation to a whole new level. Each new planet is a new adventure, with new randomly generated wildlife (seriously, every planet's life is a different permutation.
Couple in variables of weather (nothing like an acid rain shower in the mornings to melt your bones), variable gravity, different atmospheres (the distinct lack of oxygen on some), tentacle worlds, lost outposts and vanished empires. It's all there, and Starbound is definitely a game to keep an eye out for.
The developers are also pretty keen on keeping devblogs up, so if you're the kind of person that likes to keep tabs on games in development that you're waiting for (if you're reading this, Space Station 13 devs, go f*ck yourselves) Starbound is an excellent candidate.

I'll go ahead and be one of the many to tell you that this is a very good game. Steam unfortunately does not display the amount of time I sunk into this game during it's beta stages, but I can safely assume it's on par with my current time in steam. First of all, it does not appear that it would actually be very in-depth, but the devs have gone to incredible lengths to make the game appeal to many. Their semi-recent addition of the "Shadow Tower" gave players a sense of raiding in the game, and a feeling of the "end game" being legitimately difficult and requiring progression. The ability to be in multiple clubs (essentially the 'guilds' of Trove) is a unique feature I haven't seen in many other MMOs, but allows for the player to be a part of different communities. The building aspect of the game is streamlines, but in a way that it does not drop features. Cosmetic props are crafted out of recipes, and features like line-fills for building makes it actually very simple for anyone to start building stuff they would be proud of.
The collection system in the game is part of what ties everything in the game together. Unlocking new weapon or armor styles opens up cosmetic customization for the player, while all the various mounts, fishing rods, boats, and more would make any completionist excited. Rewarding the player for completing collections with mastery levels and bonuses to their account is a well-thought out system, and I found myself striving to collect more things even though I do not see myself as a completionist, especially when it comes to MMOs.
Everything in this game is easy to get the hang of, in truth. Classes only have a few skills each, meaning that complicated skill rotations aren't really a thing in this game. The trade skills (farming, runecrafting, ringcrafting, and fishing) are very simple, but with each of them having 250 levels to them, they provide plenty for the player to work towards. Runecrafting and Ringcrafting in particular tie in very well to a player's progression through ideally their first class, as the materials needed to further each become obtainable the higher the player gets in class levels, making a good progression.
The class system is implemented quite well. Classes are frequently released, and available for either microtransactions or through a currency the player can receive on a daily basis. There is no limit to how many classes you can buy, and they can be switched by simply pulling up a menu and selecting a different class to play as. Equipment for them is stored with the class itself, meaning that you don't need to haul around different armor sets or have different characters to play as different classes. Each class has it's own experience levels and gear levels, so players can "begin anew" with another class and progress through levels all over again, but at the same time still have their "main" class just a click away.
Content patches, my goodness. The devs livestream future updates and classes all the time, are constantly in communication with the playerbase, and love to introduce new content to the game. The community can contribute dungeons and weapon/armor styles, which I'm sure alleviates some stress from the Devs and allows them to focus on adding things like Shadow Tower, new classes, or the most recent addition of PvP.
Of course, there are some cons about the game, but these stem from the fact that Trove falls under the same curse that any MMO would: it sometimes gets repetitive. Trove is based around running dungeons in procedurally generated worlds, and, well, that can get old. Currently the only option for "end game" raiding is the Shadow Tower, and while it cycles through layouts (that are constantly being added to the game) being able to run each of the four floors for a reward only once a week makes it feel grindy. However, this all can only really be acknowledged, but not held against Trove, as "dailies" and "weeklies" have been a common staple for many MMOs.
Overall, Trove functions like an MMO-lite, in the fact that it's incredibly easy to pick up and get the hang of, while catering to everybody. It is nowhere near as complicated as big-name MMOs like WoW, TERA, Rift, etc., but that's part of it's appeal as well. You get the experience of playing with a playerbase on the scale of an MMO, but with a different fun, lighthearted, and lively feel to it.
Well worth the cost.

A very difficult, atmospheric masterpiece of a game absolutely worth your time and money.
Unlike what a lot of other reviews say, I feel the real difficulty of this game doesn't come from RNG, but rather from its learning curve and understanding its mechanics. What I mean by this is the game punishes you hard for getting too comfortable and for making stupid choices, even though they may not seem like mistakes to you.
Don't be deterred by some of the negative reviews- the game is fair, and whenever you end up in a bad spot (which is often), it's almost never solely due to RNG, but because you made mistakes.
Let me say that again- THE GAME IS FAIR AND RNG IS VERY RARELY THE SOLE CAUSE OF YOUR PROBLEMS.
When you get party wiped, your heroes didn't die because you got unlucky or because the enemies are unfairly strong. You lost because maybe your team didn't have synergy with each other, or because you didn't bring enough stuns and heals, or because you used AOE instead of focusing down priority targets, or your trinket choices were weird and unoptimal.
When your heroes are overwhelmed by stress, it's not unfair or unlucky. Maybe you didn't bring enough backline damage to hit those stress casters. Maybe you took too many hits because your heroes are slow. Maybe you got greedy and didn't camp when you needed to.
When you're running low on cash, it's not because the game doesn't give you enough funds. Maybe it's because you buy too many provisions, or because you don't know what provisions activate certain curios, or because you make mistakes during dungeons and have to spend too much money on stress relief for your heroes.
Once you've learnt these important things (how to make good team comps, how to manage finances, how to upgrade the town, how to stall fights in order to maximise healing, and more), you'll be surprised how fair and manageable the game becomes. I recommend watching playthroughs of the game until you understand and can apply these concepts (FilthyRobot is an excellent player and his videos/streams are really good for learning)
And when♥♥♥♥♥♥does hit the fan (and it will), well, that's just the nature of the game and you have to remember that there is almost always something you could have done better to alleviate/prevent the situation.
The only negative thing I'd say about the game is that it does get a bit stale once you've learnt all these things, but then again you can always mod it for some variety- there are a lot of good class mods out there and Pitch Black Dungeon is a very, very hard overhaul of the game.
Overall, I practically cannot fault this game and highly recommend it, provided that you're willing to get your♥♥♥♥♥whooped while you're learning the ropes.

As it stands in alpha right now I wouldn't recommend it.
The progression is incredibly slow and there is no matchmaking system which means if you've only got the basics you'll be going in against not only veteran players but people who have far better gear and upgrades than you. I get frustrated when it feels like everyone on the battlefield hits you like freight train and no matter how you outmanuever or fire at what might be a weakspot you seem to do minimal damage. If the progression rate for your ship happened at a decent rate I could accept that BUT since it's so grindy you'll find yourself asking, why? Why should I continue to play and get my bell rung continuously feeling like it's not because of my skill but it's because the person I'm fighting has more time to play the game? So I can grind up to the next gun and THEN I can finally feel competitive? It's the Call Of Duty kicking puppies MM and it's something that I think definitely won't make this game accessible to players that don't have a lot of time on their hands.If they had a tiered matchmaker or skill based matchmaker to even things out I would be happy to continue to grind and fight to get to higher levels but as it stands I just don't like being abused because devs don't want to balance their game.
The game is objective based which is something I like and there is a constant sense of urgency to protect certain points and strategize to capture the enemy base. Unfortunately this also leads to problems in terms of teams not having a single ioda of map awareness which will more than likely get worse as the F2P crowd comes in looking for a space shootem up and find that they may actually have to switch on their brain. This leads to another point about the game that ultimately discourages me from playing. The matches ARE NOT reasonable in length. 30 minute matches are just way too long and take a lot of investment to play. IF they were balanced matches it might not be so bad BUT when you couple it with poor progression and no matchmaker, it results in a game that's just all around frustrating and sometimes just downright draining.
It's a shame because the actual game play aspects are really fun. The firing and accuracy feel pretty smooth, movement takes some getting used to but it works well enough, the abilities of each ship brings a different dynamic to each match and lets you find which playstyle works best for you. It's got a lot of really great elements that unfortunately are overshadowed.
Keep in mind it is still in alpha so things may change and I hope they do BUT as for now I'd rather move on to something fun to play.
Edit: After some discussion in the comments from the devs I think I've been able to come to a much better conclusion here than how my original viewpoints stand. While my original opinion of the game still stands in a lot of ways the comments from the devs have given me hope for this game's future. It is apparent to them as well that the matchmaking system needs work and I think that's ultimately the biggest underlying issue here. They have assured me that there will be a solution in the future to alleviate problems for new players.They've also sort of tackled the issue of progression, upgradeables and balance but I'm still not entirely satisfied with the answers given yet, we'll see in future updates and as the game progresses how big of an advantage these "side" upgrades are comparatively. They have taken the time to talk to just one consumer and that shows an immense level of care very few companies have and that alone almost warrants a purchase of this game. Keep up the good work Edgecase and while my feedback is negative right now that is likely to change in the future given your attention and care to the game.

I didn't know what to expect from Darkest Dungeon. Some of my friends love it, others hate it with passion. Well, most of the things you've heard are true. Darkest Dungeon has a terrific atmosphere, great narrative, good music, fun gameplay and also is pretty hard and feels unfair.
You've read all about the rng, You will yell at your screen. You'll feel everything's going to hell.
However the game is not unplayable, it's not impossible. You need to think before every party, every location you visit, every action. Stall for a turn in order to heal and it may be your last turn. Forget to get the right trinket or provision and you are dead. Pick the wrong class and each combat will seem extremely difficult. These are not the game's faults. These are your faults.
If you plan, if you look at the details, if you take good strategic decisions and yes, if you are a bit lucky, then you will do it. For people coming from an older gaming age (I'll not say old school), when games were more than QTE movies, this is your game. For people want to have a stress-free experience look elsewhere.
PROS:
- The narrator. You will love him.
- The gameplay, the skills, the trinkets
- The great artwork
- The atmsophere
CONS:
- Most people talk about the difficulty. The biggest problem is grinding. Up until you reach the 5th level everything is great. However later on you will need money, heirlooms and XP to go to level 6. You'll have to repeat the same things, especially after starting to lose your characters (and you will lose them). There is period in the game, that will server only for farming, looting and levelling. This period is too long. And if you make a couple of mistakes with TPKs, then it's even worse
- Vvulf. Town events are great, but this one is somewhat forced and comes a bit early.
- Darkest Dungeon (location). It's great but it's so different than the rest of the game, that becomes frustrating. I love the idea, but you will have to lose many characters (and most of all, hours of game and grinding) until you understand how it works. It's very harsh in the way it's implemented. Especially the fact that you need specific classes and you can't use again the same characters, makes you grind again from the start.
What a sad and disappointing move, instead of fixing their game they make you download a 2.1gb update of paid mods. Don't buy this game and waste your time go play Witcher 3.

Realm of the Mad God is a game that is completely unique in how it actually works. I have never seen a game that is similiar to this one. All the items are really cool, all the misc. items are unique, all the dungeons are insane fun. Overall, It is a well-done RPG but I have some things that I do not like in it. Even though the game is Free-to-play, it is also "Pay-to-win" if you know what I mean. You can still play and enjoy the game without giving any money, but if you want to play seriously and become a "pro" you will have to spend some money. For example, when you start off, you can have only one vault chest, which isn't enough for anything. It holds only 8 items. You need more storage than that. So you have buy more chest, each of which costs 500 gold coins, which are worth about 2.7 Euro. That is cheap, right? Considering you need at least 10-15 chests to store all of your UT's (Ultra Tiers) and all of your Stat Potions, there is no way of that being cheap. You also need more than one character. Each character slot costs 1200 gold coins. You can color your character, which of course also costs gold coins.
Dispite the fact that the game is "Pay-to-win", I still had an absolute HUGE ammount of fun with this game with my friends. Leveling up, killing gods, completing dungeons etc. The game is insane fun even if you do not pay any money.
I also have one more thing that annoys me. Server-side lag. My internet is really fast and I have no lag on other multiplayer games. But in RotMG sometimes because of the server-side lag I die, losing my character and all my hard-earned gear. That is something Kabam has to work on.
Final Rating: 7 / 10

Do I recommend this game? Yes and no is the simple answer. The more elaborated answer is a bit more... complicated.
Yes, I recommend it because:
+ The ultimate challenge for your patience
+ wonderful, playful music
+ nice graphics
+ excellent idea
But I don't recommend it because:
- It's way too hard and unforgiving for its own good (imho).
- Short soundtrack - all though lovely, I only played like 70 minutes, and I already got tired of the soundtrack
I want to comment a little bit more elaborated on the "too hard for its own good"-point here. I know this game is supposed to be hard, and I know it is the ultimate challenge. But in my opinion there are too many factors that makes you fail in order for this to be fun to play. Prior to ordering this game, I was just thinking that people were too bad gamers and soar loosers for down-voting this game due to its controls and being too hard. But now I understand them.
It is hard enough to master navigating the bread; but once you learn that it's quite simple. HOWEVER, what I cannot grasp is why the most difficult aspect of this game is to get into the God forsaken toaster??? You've just been through hell to get to the toaster, and then you simply cannot get into the bloody thing. On the first story mission I mastered my skills to get to the toaster in like 3 - 4 minutes, which is quite good considering I just bought the game. But then you are rewarded by having to spend another 5 minutes to get the bread to actually go into the toaster. And that blew a fuse for me.
The second thing that makes this game too difficult is how unforgiving it is; not only do you loose edibility (health), but also have a grip-counter which is way too short/small considering how you are sometimes supposed to hang above the floor infront of a grill in order to become toasted.
It is also not rewarding enough. The grading scale in the end is way too demanding, which more often than not sends out a vibe that "Hey, You suck ballz!". I mean, I don't expect an A-grading for completing a mission in 10 minutes, but a D when I lost no health at all? That is just mean.
So how to "fix" this game in my opinion? Make it a bit more forgiving; don't make it so difficult to get into the toaster after all the hell getting to the toaster, indicate WHAT is the toaster (it is difficult enough to get to it, you should not have to search for WHAT is the toaster), and make the toast more responsive to your controlls.
All in all: If you like to torture yourself, and/or have an incredible amount of patience, this game is for you. The concept is brilliant. But considering the immense difficulty of the game I would not recommend this for the weak-minded (I guess I am a weak-minded gamer in this sense).
My final verdict is a 7/10 for being a brilliant concept with good graphics and being a game that really stays true to its intended gameplay. But NO, I don't recommend this, unless you have some serious nerves of steel and is serious about sitting hours just to get through one or two levels of the game.

This one definitely builds upon the formula of XCOM: Enemy Unkown/Within, while taking the series even further in a different direction than the original X-COM games. The roles are reversed in this one, with you leading a small resistance group against the worldwide alien dictatorship that controls Earth. This game is definitely harder and has a lot more going on than the last one, too. There is a tight time/turn limit to get things done in almost every battle, counting down until aliens bring more reinforcements or lock down your objective, forcing you to be on the offensive more often than not. The geoscape has A LOT more going on, too, with tons of stuff to do and not enough time to do everything. There is a lot of customization options, and a ton of mods on Steam Workshop that add even more options for soldiers, which is nice. Your own soldiers, and the aliens, all have much more potent abilities than in the previous game, as well. While the more powerful abilities are cool and everything, it kind of makes the game about setting up your guys to insta-kill powerful aliens before they can get a turn to do massive damage.
I enjoyed the homages to the old X-COM games. Gauss weapons make a return (previously seen in X-COM Terror from the Deep and later in the Long War mod for XCOM). I think the final mission in particular felt like an interesting homage to the final missions in both Terror from the Deep and Apocalypse.
Compared to Enemy Within, it's basically more of the same, just with more everything. If you liked the last XCOM, you'll like this one.

The graphics style may not be to everyones liking, but I find it perfect for this game. It fits the atmosphere and the minimalistic animations really make this style pop. I love it, it's one of the more beautiful dungeon crawls I've seen released in a long time.
Sound design seems to mimic this as well with sounds being suitably meaty and punchy and instilling fear and doubt with a horror undertone. Definitely top notch work on this!
Having not gotten much further than Veteran quests, I'd say the enemy variety is decent, if not fantastic. You tend to run in to the same type of enemies a lot, even during a single run. However, even though this has happened a lot I don't feel like it hurts the game in any way, instead giving you an option to learn how to deal with the enemy types before encountering new ones. Each region also have their own unique set of enemies which helps spice things up.
Enemy difficulty varies wildly with some being absolute pushovers and posing no threat at all, while others can be potentially party-wipers on their own.
I find that the game has a competent tutorial system, but there is a lot that is not explained well at all. I've had multiple instances, even after 5+ hours of gameplay where I'm left scratching my head and thinking "what just happened?". There are a lot of these things that could be better explained, especially the speed stat, as I've had it happen more than once that the enemy party gets to act twice before I have a chance to react. Which leads us to the next point:
This is where people's opinions likely will diverge. Some find it perfectly fine that the game is stacked against you and completely unfair. I am however not one of those. I don't mind difficult games. Heck, I play roguelikes almost daily, I find Dark Souls to be one of the best action RPGs of today, and I'm an avid Dwarf Fortress fan.
What I don't like however is how utterly stacked this game is. I've had multiple parties wiped out without me even getting a chance to act. Enter combat, and even without "SURPRISED!", the enemy party acts first, stunning two members, and starts stacking stress. I've had instances where a party has started with near (>10) no stress and ended up at 150+ after a single battle. This in spite of me doing everything to stop the casters. Some enemy parties simply have too many casters, or too much protection for the casters, to be beatable with a lvl 2-3 party.
Then begins the downward spiral where the party, on its own, begins stacking stress, skipping turns, refusing healing all while the enemy party picks you apart one by one. Eventually you reach the point where you are so fed up with the fight that you say, "FINE, I'll retreat and call this a loss." But nope. You can't retreat, because it's the enemies turn right now, and you see they get to act three times before you do anything, in spite of having a SPD debuff on them and you having a SPD buff. So two of your party members go from 50% HP to dead in those three turns where you were not allowed to act, a third one dies to heart attack and at that point you just ragequit because you were never given a chance to properly act.
Yeah, there are likely people who will say "You didn't prepare", "You should've run earlier" or "git gud nub". But even with really stacked parties, such as high speed stunners, 1 HP healers (to prevent death blows) and high dodge stacking, you are still in the very end at the mercy of RNG, which is at least to me poor design. In addition, I've heard many people claim that you should "just read the wiki" to prepare for encounters. The big fun of games like these are to experience them blind on your first playthrough. If you cannot hope to win without resorting to a wiki, your game is designed poorly. Dark Souls is an example of this. Through careful observation, you can learn the patterns of any fight and beat it on your first attempt. Not many people do, but it's absolutely possible. In Darkest Dungeon, you have no hope of beating the Hag, for instance, on your first attempt unless you have the right team setup and strategy out of sheer luck.
I play games for fun and while DD definitely has a lot of fun in it, these moments where control is completely taken out of your hands, everything is stacked against you, the RNG gives you the finger and you wipe yet another party in a single battle even though you had good health and stress levels beforehand simply just make the game incredibly frustrating and unfair. That's also why I decided to not even bother anymore. I love for games to punish me for mistakes, lack of knowledge or simply doing something stupid. I don't love for games to simply say "Yeah, I know your party is OP and all, but you see today I'm just in a bad mood so here, have a loss." To me this is poor design, and something the devs should look to the roguelike genre for. There are horribad roguelikes out there as well, but in general those games will kill you only when you make mistakes or are taking risks. DD can kill you just out of spite (RNG being nasty).
If you find stacked odds and a lot of frustrating failiure to be fun, by all means, give DD a try because there's a lot to like here. The graphics and sound are great. The battle mechanics are, for the most part, really nice albeit a bit limited. It's just the endless frustration of knowing that the next battle could be the one that completely screws you over out of the blue. There is too much RNG in this game for my taste, and that puts it well beyond my control whether I win or lose.
