This one definitely builds upon the formula of XCOM: Enemy Unkown/Within, while taking the series even further in a different direction than the original X-COM games. The roles are reversed in this one, with you leading a small resistance group against the worldwide alien dictatorship that controls Earth. This game is definitely harder and has a lot more going on than the last one, too. There is a tight time/turn limit to get things done in almost every battle, counting down until aliens bring more reinforcements or lock down your objective, forcing you to be on the offensive more often than not. The geoscape has A LOT more going on, too, with tons of stuff to do and not enough time to do everything. There is a lot of customization options, and a ton of mods on Steam Workshop that add even more options for soldiers, which is nice. Your own soldiers, and the aliens, all have much more potent abilities than in the previous game, as well. While the more powerful abilities are cool and everything, it kind of makes the game about setting up your guys to insta-kill powerful aliens before they can get a turn to do massive damage.
I enjoyed the homages to the old X-COM games. Gauss weapons make a return (previously seen in X-COM Terror from the Deep and later in the Long War mod for XCOM). I think the final mission in particular felt like an interesting homage to the final missions in both Terror from the Deep and Apocalypse.
Compared to Enemy Within, it's basically more of the same, just with more everything. If you liked the last XCOM, you'll like this one.

The graphics style may not be to everyones liking, but I find it perfect for this game. It fits the atmosphere and the minimalistic animations really make this style pop. I love it, it's one of the more beautiful dungeon crawls I've seen released in a long time.
Sound design seems to mimic this as well with sounds being suitably meaty and punchy and instilling fear and doubt with a horror undertone. Definitely top notch work on this!
Having not gotten much further than Veteran quests, I'd say the enemy variety is decent, if not fantastic. You tend to run in to the same type of enemies a lot, even during a single run. However, even though this has happened a lot I don't feel like it hurts the game in any way, instead giving you an option to learn how to deal with the enemy types before encountering new ones. Each region also have their own unique set of enemies which helps spice things up.
Enemy difficulty varies wildly with some being absolute pushovers and posing no threat at all, while others can be potentially party-wipers on their own.
I find that the game has a competent tutorial system, but there is a lot that is not explained well at all. I've had multiple instances, even after 5+ hours of gameplay where I'm left scratching my head and thinking "what just happened?". There are a lot of these things that could be better explained, especially the speed stat, as I've had it happen more than once that the enemy party gets to act twice before I have a chance to react. Which leads us to the next point:
This is where people's opinions likely will diverge. Some find it perfectly fine that the game is stacked against you and completely unfair. I am however not one of those. I don't mind difficult games. Heck, I play roguelikes almost daily, I find Dark Souls to be one of the best action RPGs of today, and I'm an avid Dwarf Fortress fan.
What I don't like however is how utterly stacked this game is. I've had multiple parties wiped out without me even getting a chance to act. Enter combat, and even without "SURPRISED!", the enemy party acts first, stunning two members, and starts stacking stress. I've had instances where a party has started with near (>10) no stress and ended up at 150+ after a single battle. This in spite of me doing everything to stop the casters. Some enemy parties simply have too many casters, or too much protection for the casters, to be beatable with a lvl 2-3 party.
Then begins the downward spiral where the party, on its own, begins stacking stress, skipping turns, refusing healing all while the enemy party picks you apart one by one. Eventually you reach the point where you are so fed up with the fight that you say, "FINE, I'll retreat and call this a loss." But nope. You can't retreat, because it's the enemies turn right now, and you see they get to act three times before you do anything, in spite of having a SPD debuff on them and you having a SPD buff. So two of your party members go from 50% HP to dead in those three turns where you were not allowed to act, a third one dies to heart attack and at that point you just ragequit because you were never given a chance to properly act.
Yeah, there are likely people who will say "You didn't prepare", "You should've run earlier" or "git gud nub". But even with really stacked parties, such as high speed stunners, 1 HP healers (to prevent death blows) and high dodge stacking, you are still in the very end at the mercy of RNG, which is at least to me poor design. In addition, I've heard many people claim that you should "just read the wiki" to prepare for encounters. The big fun of games like these are to experience them blind on your first playthrough. If you cannot hope to win without resorting to a wiki, your game is designed poorly. Dark Souls is an example of this. Through careful observation, you can learn the patterns of any fight and beat it on your first attempt. Not many people do, but it's absolutely possible. In Darkest Dungeon, you have no hope of beating the Hag, for instance, on your first attempt unless you have the right team setup and strategy out of sheer luck.
I play games for fun and while DD definitely has a lot of fun in it, these moments where control is completely taken out of your hands, everything is stacked against you, the RNG gives you the finger and you wipe yet another party in a single battle even though you had good health and stress levels beforehand simply just make the game incredibly frustrating and unfair. That's also why I decided to not even bother anymore. I love for games to punish me for mistakes, lack of knowledge or simply doing something stupid. I don't love for games to simply say "Yeah, I know your party is OP and all, but you see today I'm just in a bad mood so here, have a loss." To me this is poor design, and something the devs should look to the roguelike genre for. There are horribad roguelikes out there as well, but in general those games will kill you only when you make mistakes or are taking risks. DD can kill you just out of spite (RNG being nasty).
If you find stacked odds and a lot of frustrating failiure to be fun, by all means, give DD a try because there's a lot to like here. The graphics and sound are great. The battle mechanics are, for the most part, really nice albeit a bit limited. It's just the endless frustration of knowing that the next battle could be the one that completely screws you over out of the blue. There is too much RNG in this game for my taste, and that puts it well beyond my control whether I win or lose.

Pros:

Events, many games have these, in this ones case, it's for new items, seasonal, christmas, halloween, valintines day, the usual.
Player made content, yes, that's right, this game DOES infact have this, not like TF2 or warframe where most you have to pay for, you just go out, and Find them! like any form of in game loot!

Stats, and this one i add just because, certain stats effect things like double jumps (Jump 16 times in the air!?), Run speed, health and energy regen, a few things you would expect and other's you would have never thought of! This one definitely builds upon the formula of XCOM: Enemy Unkown/Within, while taking the series even further in a different direction than the original X-COM games. The roles are reversed in this one, with you leading a small resistance group against the worldwide alien dictatorship that controls Earth. This game is definitely harder and has a lot more going on than the last one, too. There is a tight time/turn limit to get things done in almost every battle, counting down until aliens bring more reinforcements or lock down your objective, forcing you to be on the offensive more often than not. The geoscape has A LOT more going on, too, with tons of stuff to do and not enough time to do everything. There is a lot of customization options, and a ton of mods on Steam Workshop that add even more options for soldiers, which is nice. Your own soldiers, and the aliens, all have much more potent abilities than in the previous game, as well. While the more powerful abilities are cool and everything, it kind of makes the game about setting up your guys to insta-kill powerful aliens before they can get a turn to do massive damage.
I enjoyed the homages to the old X-COM games. Gauss weapons make a return (previously seen in X-COM Terror from the Deep and later in the Long War mod for XCOM). I think the final mission in particular felt like an interesting homage to the final missions in both Terror from the Deep and Apocalypse.
Compared to Enemy Within, it's basically more of the same, just with more everything. If you liked the last XCOM, you'll like this one.

I waited until the first "performance patch" was released (it didn't help) to write this review.  I haven't tried any of the mods.
tl;dr version: So many great ideas, but the execution and performance issues make XCOM2 unplayable.
Good:
- The aliens are incredibly interesting.  Most enemies are basically improvements from EU/EW.  Sectoids and Mutons receive massive upgrades from EU/EW, and there are several new enemies that make you really rack your brain on how you are going to combat them.
- New twists on some buildings.  The proving ground is fun.  It's mostly a random grab bag of weapons and armor.  The advanced warfare center gives you some pleasant surprises every now and then.
- Overwatch AI is improved.  No longer will 5 dudes on overwatch shoot at the dead alien the 1st guy killed.  All successful overwatch shots are useful.
- Everything looks pretty good.  The animation is much less cartooney than EU/EW.
- Dodge/Graze mechanic.  Pretty cool when it's in your favor, but heart-breaking when it burns you.
- Enemy reinforcements.  They will really screw up your game plan and make you recalculate.  Much improved over the drop-a-thin-man-in-there-and-put-him-on-overwatch paradigm from EU/EW.
- Weapon upgrades add another level to squad make-up.
- Psi-warriors are a unique class.  They are bad♥♥♥♥♥..  and probably even overpowered.  No longer just necessary to "take one for the team" in the final cinematic.
Neutral:
- Stealth ambushes were a good idea.  Triggering enemies with several squad members in overwatch commences a Boondock Saints-esque cascade of bullets.  However, overwatch is much less effective than EU/EW, and I end up following a procedure for conducting ambushes. *yawn*
- Lots of turn timers on mission.  They do add to the urgency and difficulty of missions, but generally force your hand most of the time.
- Mission types are basically the same as EU/EW.  Base assaults, terror missions, VIP rescue, destry the device.  A few new tricks, but they definitely took the don't-fix-what-ain't-broke approach.
- The Black Market.  It's an evolution of the Grey Market from EU/EW.  The Black Market can be useful, but I just don't get excited about it and it doesn't help out as much as the Grey Market did.
Bad:
- Performance.  Prior to the recent patch, I should have been able to play on max settings/resolution (including 4k) on both of my rigs as they are waaayyyy beyond the recommended specs.  However, max settings made the framerate drop to gamebreaking levels.  I was able to tweak the settings to make the game playable, but it never looked all that great.  I did not experience crashes before the patch.  THEN THE PATCH WAS BORN.  Post-patch, I experienced 1-3 crashes per hour of play (The last one I suffered occurred on the plane ride home from a terror mission on which only one civilian was killed).  The real insult is that the developer added an "auto settings detector" to help us all play at acceptable framerates.  The auto-detect simply dumbed down settings on my machines AND the framerate was much lower than pre-patch.  Just plain unacceptable
- Some missions seem pre-determined.  I loved the difficulty of Long War.  It was transparent and tactile.  You always knew why you were getting screwed, and were generally rewarded by living by the rules of XCOM.  But the rules of XCOM intermittently get flipped upside-down in XCOM2.  I have played several missions where there are a large number of improbable misses (> 85%) that lead me to fail the mission.  Even after save-scumming with an all-new approach, the overwhelming missed shots lead me to believe that the seed is choosing against me.  This leads to an unwanted side-effect of relying HEAVILY on 100% weapons (mainly grenades) and laughing when my guys miss three 90% shots in a row to end a turn.  It's insulting, and eliminates the fun of having a diverse squad.
Verdict: There is so much to like, but I can't enjoy it because the few things I hate are so very bad.

Half-Life 1 is a really nice game.
It got released in 1998 and so it looks really old but it can be a lot of fun. Half-Life is a classic.
You are a scientist called Gordon Freeman. One day you are involved in a critical test which goes terribly wrong and opens portals to the boarderland Xen. From that moment on, aliens invade earth and you find yourself in chaos and try to get out alive.
The singleplayer was revolutionary at the time because it has a continious story without cutscenes. I also like that there are a lot of enemy-types. The weapons are all really balanced (except gluongun) and fun to use. The story develops as you proceed in the game. It gets more and more mysterious and suspense.
In Half-Life you are mostly on your own and travel through many interessting environments. Sometimes the maps can be a bit confusing but in the end you will have a nice final and it feels great to finish the game.
In my opinion Half-Life's multiplayer is very very good. I played it a very long time and it has a great learning-curve. In Half-Life you have very dynamic gameplay with fast movement, air-control, excessive wallbanging and spawnkilling. It can be a really great feel to dominate and control the whole map. In Half-Life you can play many styles.. aggressive like a berserker but also slow and silent. It's possible to break the enemies advantage by clever ambushing and by hitting well aimed headshots. Since there are many different weapons you can always find different ways to deal with your enemy. Each weapon is very different and good in special situations. Also the maps are all very different to each other. Each map has it's own great design and unique gameplay.
Conclusion:
I recommend you to try Half-Life on LAN with friends, because it's a lot of fun to play against enemies of equal skill. Since it has a great learning-curve you have to get into the game a bit.
If you want to play online I recommend you to edit your config-file so you can have a field of view of 110 degrees and direct weapon-bindings. On most servers (Adrenaline Gamer Mod) you can use bunnyhop. Since they patched Half-Life you are no longer able to code bunnyhop-scripts in your config. So if you want a working bhop you have to use a macro programm like autohotkey or maybe your keyboard-driver. The other easier way to use bhop is to disable automatic updates and patch back half-life to an older version (still works online).
Half-Life has a lot of mods and there is a lot of custom content (player and weapon-models, maps, effects and hud-elements). I recommend you to install good visible custom crosshairs and use simple explosion sprites.
Regarding mods I can recommend you Adrenaline Gamer, Sven-Coop 3.0 (because it has the original Half-Life weapons and basicly is a coop mod for Half-Life), The Specialists (a Matrix-styled mod) and Frontline Force.
There are also a lot great singleplayer mods. I can recommend you Half-Life Invasion, Escape from the Darkness, Paranoia, Todesangst, ETC 1 and 2, Sweet Half-Life and a lot more.
Seriously there are a lot good mods out there..
All in all for me this game is a must have. So if you don't mind the old graphics and take some time to understand the game.. I think you will like it!

This is an edited review so bear that in mind.
Trove was a fun game for me, before the Mantle of Power update, I enjoyed it heavily because of the new stuff that it offered and the goal of getting radiant gear. It offered a gallery of item cosmetics designed by others that I enjoyed experimenting with to make each of the 12 or so classes I had unique. Doing the shadow towers was also a fun experience for a time. Clubs were also a large part of why I stayed as it allowed to meet other players to converse and help one another as well as to build in a sandbox world unique to that club. Crafting mounts and pets was very fun as well - I loved the variety.
However, these things only last a certain while. Over time I realised that this game was nothing but grinding. You would complete a dungeon out in the world in less than a minute to move on to the next one, and so on and so forth. Rinse and repeat 200 times a day.
I didn't mind the grinding part because it was removed in a sense by the time the marketplace came out where I could earn my fortune by buying and selling items on the market place for money to buy better gear and I could live with that.
Then, Mantle of Power. It's what turned this game into a grind fest. There's no avoiding it other than spending a large amount of money on gem boxes to increase your odds of ranking up gems. Gems, by the way, can only be earned from boxes that you get from a dungeon. They offer three varients of; common reward, lucky and rare. These correspond to the item rarities in game that gradually increases the higher level world you go to. This means that you'll spend hours grinding gems, upgrading them to only get an entire new set by the next world. It's ridiculously grindy. By the last level, it will take 70 boxes to get one rare gem- that can have awful stats- that you probably won't use. That's 70 dungeons, or 35 with premium. Oh. Did I mention that you'll have to do this for basically every class?
Without these gems, you can't progress in the shadow towers (that are like raids) as you need the highest level of gems to basically compete after normal difficulty. After you get the best gems possible the final boss in the entire game can die in a few seconds with other people at a similar level. Some classes are basically useless in this level of difficulty anyway.
Then, there are dragons. Dragons can be earned by completing challenges of doing dungeons in a specific biome every hour. You get boxes that allow a chance to get dragon souls and dragon coins. Now, considering you need 100 dragon souls for basically the full dragon collection, that's a lot of challenges. This would be okay if it was only a few dragons, but there are around 10 that do this. This gives mastery (a measure of your collection) that gives bonuses on its level. The dragons also give a buff that allows for magic find that is required to get even a chance of finding high level gear normally. Then, other dragons require 300 dragon coins which is a lot for one dragon, especially since there are so many of them now that all give the magic find buff. Other dragons need a dragon egg, or a few, as well as dragon coins. And 3 other dragons give a bigger buff and require a stupid amount of luck just to get the egg! It's too much for just that.
The premium function allows extra experience, less boxes needed for a guranteed rare and extra magic find, along with other benefits. The extra experience is handy since it will take literal weeks of constant grinding just to get to the max level of 30 in the highest difficulty. Less boxes needed for a rare basically sets you back by miles if you don't have premium as it'll take you twice as long just to get anything of value. The extra magic find is also needed; unless you don't have all of the dragons which is highly unlikely; to get a chance of finding higher level gear. Speaking of higher level gear, it's so easy to come by now, they may as well give it to you. The materials have dropped in price and can easily be gotten if you can handle the market place well.
I played this game a lot and enjoyed it for a while. The mixture of Minecraft and an MMORPG was incredibly enticing for me and the grind was more manageable back then. Now, there's no avoiding it. Either hours and hours put into it, or you get nothing. It's a shame. So no. There are too many things wrong to put into this modest review. Enjoy a few hours of the game if you want, but just be prepared for what's after.

Now that we've gotten the♥♥♥♥♥♥eating troglodyte cultists out of the way with that, let us proceed to the part intended to be read by real people. This is an extremely tough game to give a "not recommended" to, but I can't really do otherwise in its current state. Let us examine why.
1)

Let's start with the so-called hunger system, which has nothing to do with a mechanical representation of actual hunger, or bears any resemblance to the countless representations of hunger in other games. To sum up, the way hunger has worked since forever is a sort of invisible trap tile in a dungeon. To resolve the trap tile you need to spend 1 food per guy. If you do not have 1 food per guy, even if your entire party JUST
, you take starvation penalties. A thematic hunger system would in a simple implementation mechanically be a sort of health bar that decrements over time and that has to be filled up with food items
Legend Of Grimrock or countless other games. Nope, won't find anything like that here. Invisible traps that you have to waste one of your inventory slots to counter.
What's next? Let's talk about the Armor stat, or ARM. Yeah, your characters have none. Your ARMORED characters have 0 in this stat, even at the highest upgrade levels.
If you listen to bad design apologists, of which there are always hordes ready to counter any rational argument with a combination of slavish boot licking and suppression of their own cognitive dissonance, it's because giving ARMORED characters in half-plate any points in the ARMOR stat would "make the game too easy." Let that sink in for a moment. It's delicious. The result is that armored characters, totally contrary to being tanky, are incredibly squishy, and take MASSIVE amounts more damage than nible, evasion-heavy characters in light armor. So the thing to do is to tank with your nimble, thief-y characters, and have your ARMORED guy with the GIANT SWORD in the back acting as a support character.
2)
Yes, I understand the inventory is meant to be restrictive, as it would realistically be in a dungeon crawling scenario such as this. The way to implement a restrictive inventory that doesn't run face-first into the brick wall of what I call "throwing treasure away simulator" is a weight or encumbrance based inventory system. Think Long Dark, think Project Zomboid. Hell, think Eve Online, even. All of those games force you to make choices about what loot to carry back and what to put aside, and engage you in thematic inventory management gameplay. Does Darkest Dungeon?
Nope.
It's an extremely simplistic tile-based inventory of only 16 slots and, as usual, each stack of a given item type occupies one of these slots. The problem with this arrangement is that you cannot have item variety or the inventory gets choked to hell almost immediately. What does DD have, and what did every patch add? More item variety. Facepalm. I'll give you an example in the, what is it, six different kinds of gems you can pick up? Realistically the encumbrance value of these gems would be trivial, and their sale value high. Not here, boyo! Each separate gem type occupies its own inventory slot (reminder: you only have 16), so your tile inventory almost immediately get choked by the aforementioned item variety as you crawl through the dungeon. Did you bring some of the very attractively illustrated and seemingly useful supplies with you? You'll be throwing them away almost immediately as you proceed more than one or two rooms. So don't buy them. Apologists of bad design will call those "noob traps," which is the most asinine♥♥♥♥♥♥argument I've ever heard to excuse a fundamental failure on the designer's part. Excuse me for wanting an intuitive, immersive, atmospheric dungeon crawling experience.
Absolutely nothing to do with weight or encumbrance or anything remotely thematic. Nope, our party can only carry a limited
of items. In longer dungeon crawls, what this translates into is you throwing out most of the treasure you pick up, so... why are you doing longer dungeon crawls? Just do short ones and you come out with the exact same amount of treasure. It is incredibly frustrating to have to be throwing♥♥♥♥♥♥away not because your party is overburdened. No, but because they refuse to carry more than so many different types of gems on them.
Something that also plays into this is the way looting is handled. Let's say you enter a room with a chest, and the chest is guarded by a pack of skeletons. You kill the skeletons and you get some treasure. Now, what you might want to do is leave the loot on the skeletons, or arrange it in a neat pile in the middle of the room, add to it the loot from the chest, and then take your pick. Maybe if you don't pick something up you can leave it in the room and come back for it later when your packs are lighter and you don't have to cart all those supplies. Naturally, you can't do that. Any treasure you don't immediately pick up disintegrates. It's just gone. And no, you can't open the chest before resolving the loot from the pack of skeletons from that example. You have to disintegrate whatever loot the skeletons had before trying to resolve the chest loot. And again, you will hear the eternal refrain of "durrrrr the game would be too easy" from the game's many apologists if you criticize this sloppy mess of a system.
3)
When the game launched on SEA, the art style was nothing less than inspired and magical. Just incredible, incredible presentation, UI art. Clean, superbly tasteful, it was a delight to the eye. And then the "improvements" began. With nearly every update, they would slather on repulsive visual effects onto the beautiful 2D art, spoiling it.
For example, the clean and tasteful low fantasy inventory art got cheap glow effects reminiscent of something like World of Warcraft. Ugh! And they got worse and worse as the game went along. The only explanation I can think of for this total abandonment of the original visual concept and repeated lapse of good taste on the artist's part is burnout.
The UI art, I would argue, suffered most of all, receiving fugly animated effects and an art pass that replaced the crisp UI of old with something that looked out of a browser game. Bizarre colour choices. char limit
4)
This one is obviously more subjective than a statement about how the developers did not fulfill their KS promises (they technically did!), hence the asterisk. The perceived lack of completion comes from the continued presence of what I read as placeholder mechanics, such as the terrible hunger/food mechanic, or the perfect grid maps. Recall the KS trailer, which showed proper roguelike maps to crawl through. Where are those at, fellas? I understand this was never an explicit promise, but I've always felt this to be an implicit one, and so I feel a little tiny bit bait-and-switched to see it not just totally absent from the game's release, but never spoken about or hinted at in official communications.
==
To conclude, I think the time to have played this game was at the very beginning of its SEA phase, and I am very thankful to have been able to experience that little nugget of genius. Unfortunately, however, I feel the game's enormous potential has largely been squandered in virtually all subsequent "improvements," and it has degenerated into a near-abstract mess, presumably intended to appeal to the math jockey robots in the game's subreddit, in all the areas that the initial inspired builds were rock-solid. The only parts that remain of that absolutely magical game I played a few years back are the phenomenal voice acting/narration and a few scattered pieces of the original art.
Sometimes SEA games work out, and sometimes they don't.

Playing it in 2013 on this monster of a rig, I still found this a blast to play and I can still understand why it was so revolutionary at the time with my gaming history as a frame of reference. But even if I didn't have that frame of reference, Half-Life would still be a solid action game and brilliant shooter.
While it initially seems like a cookie-cutter FPS, it seems to do everything right; the AI holds up well; every gun feels satisfying to use; the map design is phenomenal, being interesting and encouraging exploration without ever getting you lost; the pacing of the gameplay is absolutely perfect, knowing when you're about to get bored and when you need to relax after some heavy action (and so on and so forth, I can go on forever).
There is one weakpoint. I notice that the Half-Life series is quite well known for its story. While the setting is brilliantly original and the game is very immersive as a whole, I think its story is well overrated. What the hell is up with the G-Man? It feels like he is someone they can drop in and out of the story whenever they like; he seems to have unlimited powers to change the game universe and that really erodes away the supernatural mechanics of the game's narrative. Furthermore, the story mostly consists of you going from point A to B, without really knowing what's going on. They could have dropped in a bit more characterisation to say the least.
But you know what? I will give it a pass on that point. They carried the setting very well and everything else fit well. Story is not the key draw of this game, and it taught me that you don't need a good story to make a highly immersive, sweeping adventure. So while it was less-than-satisfactory in this regard, I am willing to ignore it as it achieved the results of a good story without having a very good one at all; namely, a great deal of player immersion into the game's universe.
I admit I was sceptical coming to Half-Life, but by the end of it I realise why it was seen as a watershed for the FPS genre and a landmark for the history of video games at large. If there were one amazing FPS to define a genre, it would be Half-Life. Even today, it is still a good example of what we expect from a first-person shooter; and deservedly so.

I am Bread is a third Steam game by Bossa Studios who are known thanks to their crazy Surgeon Simulator. If you've already seen (or played) the game, you know it challenges players by having difficult controls that makes it frustrating but also hilarious to play. In this case, they did it in pretty similar way, with important difference: You will be in control of a slice of bread that wants to get toasted. (
)
Yes, it's a weird physics simulation game where you are trying to move bread towards a source of heat. Controls revolves around four buttons - a button for each bread's corner that makes it sticky. If you are now thinking about the movement, you have probably already thought out that all the movement is done by swinging and flinging on those stickied bread corners.
I can't say it would be unexpected after Surgeon Simulator, but it's still important to say that I am Bread is a difficult game. It has a high level of difficulty, you'll be raging a lot because while you'll be trying to get to get toasted (by toaster or table lamp, for example), you'll also have to dodge all dirty and wet areas and objects. Don't even think about touching ground! It's like the floor is lava, it makes you taste bad which leads up to the game over screen. And one more thing, you have limited "sticky timer". You can hold on some place swinging just for a moment, then you have to lay somewhere to regain your energy for being sticky.
While it's definitely a great game for skilled speedrunners, don't expect to get into it easily, you'll need a lot of practice to beat levels without getting dirty. Good thing is that the developers knew how begineers will suck at it, so after two times you lose a level, you'll get an option to remove the sticky timer and edibility meter (edibility is reduced by getting dirty).
The main story mode offers a classic level list with funny short story, delivered via medical reports, about a man who gets crazy because he thinks that a slice of bread is destryoing everything in his house. But there's more! There's also a cheese hunt, bagel race (probably the easiest game mode), rampage (where you have to destroy everything with baguette), zero-g (to make you even more frustrated), and free play mode.
It's worth mentioning that developers made a lot of free content for I am Bread later after release - Team Fortress 2 bread level, Goat Simulator mode (just change bread for goat) and Starch Wars mode, which is a kind of weird 3D space shooter with laser bread (referencing Star Wars, of course). Even if it's been done with the idea of cross brand marketing, I really appreciate that those updates came up for free!
The game supports keyboard and mouse or gamepad controls. While other players had problems with controllers, I played with Xbox 360 controller without any problem, haven't seen any lag through my gameplay sessions.
I am Bread is a perfect game for those who want something silly but difficult. It requires a lot of practice to get good at it, so depending on your perseverance, it can offer you many hours of entertainment and huge self-satisfaction in the end... or a lot of frustration. So it depends on your temper, but it's definitely worth buying.

WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD!
The predecessor XCOM: Enemy Unknown might have been difficult to mod, but that's probably the worst thing that could be said about it. Once modded the gameplay was amazing. Especially with the Long War mod.
Yes, there were still some things wrong with the predecessor, even after modding.
But to call XCOM2 'weak' would really be a shame.
Because that would waste the perfect application of the term 'abysmal' for this game.
Why?
1) The actual premise of shooting down UFOs (that's were the series came from, guys, it was originally called "UFO: Enemy Unknown") was totally and completely removed from the game.
No more figher planes, no more interceptors, nothing. Simply gone.
That's like taking city building out of Civilization. Stupid. Game breaking for me.
2) The premise of a small resistance group being able to do what it does in the game is totally ludicruous.
But hey, it's sci-fi, it doesn't have to follow logic, right?
Wrong.
For something that has turned into a terribly stupid economy- and turn-based-combat simulator the game logic is utterly ludicrous again.
EVERYONE on the combat map suddenly becomes visible if even ONE soldier is spotted makes for some totally immersion-breaking moments EACH AND EVERY COMBAT MISSION. Why would I keep someone back from the frontlines only to have him suddenly become a target when somebody else who is nearly a mile away is spotted is beyond me.
Because now there is NO CHANCE WHATSOEVER of leading the enemies on a wild goose chase by fleeing (visibly) with one soldier and dragging them behind me while the rest of the stealthed team moves in on the mission target. No chance for this basic maneuver. Due to some total balloney BS of a game logic.
Strategic map:
Yeah, ADVENT is in control of the world, we get it.
We don't know anyone around the world who opposes them except our own little group. But we were the greatest force to oppose the aliens 20 years ago. Now we are nothing but a powerless group of gimps trying to get a F'ING HUGE ALIEN SHIP to fly again. Yeah, great logic.
While we, as the resistance group on the 'strategic map' (hah, what is strategic about it, can anyone tell me?!?) can't simply broadcast on short-wave radio across the globe to simultaneously reach ALL resistance groups at once. Especially with a damn f'ing huge alien ship (where did it come from, anyway?) can't do a little radio building of our own.
Naaah, too logical. Nah, can't be done.
Sorry. Stupid logic does not trump sci-fi based logic.
This list could go on for quite a few pages.
3) A random number generator that generates a new roll every time the game is reloaded but still (and I checked) fails to come up with a number below 43% (which at that time was my chance to hack a heavy advent mec) after 50 (FIFTY) attempts is not a random number generator. Something is fixed there.
Or my four failed attempts to successfully apply a dead-eye shot with a final adjusted to-hit percentage of 94% with my plasma sniper rifle, a superior scope, the aiming PCS, and tracer rounds.
Yeah, very very likely, that chance.
Nuff said, otherwise I'm gonna go random on some developer's a$$.
4) A tech tree that is so shallow that you can have it finished after a mere two months game time?
Merely three weapon groups (basic, magnetic, plasma). No more laser, no more REASON to have different weapons. Once you reach plasma the end is reached. No more advancement, not even the slightest increment after that. No matter how many scientists you have. No chance to apply your possibly dozens of scientists to upgrading the clip sizes, or the ranges, or the damage, or... or... or...
Nothing.
Especially the ludicrous game logic of loading electorinic warfare bluescreen BULLETS into a PLASMA rifle.
Shouldn't the PLASMA rifle fire PLASMA?
Which is a super-heated stated of atomic nuclei stripped of their electrons (therefore being UNABLE TO BE A BULLET ANYMORE BECAUSE THERE IS NO MORE MOLECULAR COHESION?)
Still only ONE grenade for every soldier except the grenadier who can (hold your breath) carry at best FOUR grenades.
WOW! Now that is one hell of a grenadier, right? Especially as he carries an ancient ONE-SHOT grenade launcher design from around the 1940's. Wow, now that is really modern tech, isn't it?
Still only ONE ammo type for each soldier. No choices of changing ammo during the mission.
No mecs, no cyber-units. Upgrading of specified soldiers abilities of totally boring two choices each level.
No adjustability AFTER the fact.
Once you pick, you are stuck with it, even when the choice you made turned out to be totally useless (and trust me, there are quite a few really useless abilities in the game, such as all pistol skills for the snipers.)
No useful avenger upgrades except those 16 few vertical slots. Again, a flat side-view.
Scientists and engineers with as much personality as an Excel spreadsheet.
Who would have thought that the original UFO: Enemy Unknown would still have a better base building technique than a game 20 years younger? Not better graphics, no, butter a much more intersting premise.
Anyone still remember the 3d- building slots that allowed you to lay out your own base in the original game?
With defensive stations that actually did something useful instead of simply upgrading your theoretical defenses.
Especially because after the first UFO was evaded in this game I never ever saw another UFO again during my whole game. So what do I need those stupid defense stations for?
Boooooring. Snooze-fest!
5) A ranged game that has absolutely useless ranges for their weapons.
Many weapons have the problem of being barely able to clear a street -across, not lengthwise.
Sometimes you have problems of shooting across a room, as that already seems to be beyond the acceptable range for some weapons BECAUSE YOU ALREADY GAIN RANGE PENALTIES FOR IT!
Even the sniper rifle is barely able to shoot along a street, much less along a street block of three houses.
Come on, my slingshot at home has a greater range (and probably damage) than that stupid sniper rifle.
Dito for other classes.
The Ranger class that has amazing cinematographics for the first few times they strike down an enemy. After that the enemies become far too tough for that stupid useless toothpick of even the most advanced swordtype to do squat against virtually any enemy except the weakest. And the Ranger's shotgun requires the Ranger to be almost on top of the enemy.
Yeaaaah, great. Why not give me a spear and a sling with stones. Maybe I would actually get a better range with that than with my shotgun.
Psionic soldiers, errr operatives, that require a clear view of the enemy AND also nearly have to be up close and personal. Blaargh.
Nah, don't make me go into more detail.
The ranges and even the best upgrades in the tech tree totally suck.
6) Bugs and balancing issues still riddle this crash fest of a game.
I don't know how often the game crashed during my one play-thru. But I lost count at around 30.
When did Firaxis subscribe to the current gaming industry standard of releasing seriously unfinished and untested product?
7) And finally, an ending that was so anti-climactic that it nearly put me to sleep.
Oh boy, are you guys gonna be surprised the first time you see it.
It probably was one of the worst endings in the full UFO series I have ever seen.
Nah, not worth it.
Forget about this game. Maybe when, or rather IF, some of the Long War modders have finalized a full game overhaul of the complete logic then you might consider this game.
But only once this game has landed in the bargain bin of Steam.
Cause I wouldn't pay $10 for it in its currents state.
But even the most amazing mod won't bring interceptors back again.
Sad, sad state of afairs for the gaming industry.

XCOM 2 builds upon the idea that you failed miserably in XCOM: Enemy Unknown. And that is a damn good thing.
Where to start... Well, the concept of having a mobile base is very good, as you actually feel like you're on the run from the alien overlords and their grizzly genetically-altered army. You need to collect resources in order to survive, and the different things you can discover while searching are pretty standard, but varied enough for them to fit perfectly. The only thing about this is that early on you can get overwhelmed with the amount of areas you need to search, which can lead to a slow start that gives the aliens an early advantage.
The soldier customization puts most RPGs to shame and is easily the best part of the game. With the extensive modding community it is possible to create nearly any soldier you can think of. What other game can you have Halo's Spartans and the crew of Mass Effect's Normandy fighting side by side while the Gears of War decimate the aliens?
The combat feels mostly the same as it did in XCOM: EU, but with a twist. The new concealed mechanic allows you to ambush first. But you need to be careful as you can end up getting ambushed yourself if you get overconfident. I think my only gripe with this mechanic is that you can run into enemies in the most bull****y spots, and it can ultimately screw you over for the rest of the mission. Luckily if you're like me, you'll end up saving scum and reloading. Fortunately you won't have to sit through the aliens murdering your soldiers over and over like with Enemy Unknown. You can reload a save during their go at you. That said, where is the Restart Mission button?
Storywise, for my first playthrough I was intrigued with the way it was going. I liked the reveals, the twists, and the lore all the way through and it genuinely felt like the aliens were playing humanity like a flute. (damn you Speaker!) That said, the ending kind've feels the same as with Enemy Unknown in that it feels so ubrupt.
Ultimately, if you're a fan of the series, you'll love this game. If you're new to the series, you'll love this game. It's the best of the series and with the extensive modding community it's only going to get better.

Playing it in 2013 on this monster of a rig, I still found this a blast to play and I can still understand why it was so revolutionary at the time with my gaming history as a frame of reference. But even if I didn't have that frame of reference, Half-Life would still be a solid action game and brilliant shooter.
While it initially seems like a cookie-cutter FPS, it seems to do everything right; the AI holds up well; every gun feels satisfying to use; the map design is phenomenal, being interesting and encouraging exploration without ever getting you lost; the pacing of the gameplay is absolutely perfect, knowing when you're about to get bored and when you need to relax after some heavy action (and so on and so forth, I can go on forever).
There is one weakpoint. I notice that the Half-Life series is quite well known for its story. While the setting is brilliantly original and the game is very immersive as a whole, I think its story is well overrated. What the hell is up with the G-Man? It feels like he is someone they can drop in and out of the story whenever they like; he seems to have unlimited powers to change the game universe and that really erodes away the supernatural mechanics of the game's narrative. Furthermore, the story mostly consists of you going from point A to B, without really knowing what's going on. They could have dropped in a bit more characterisation to say the least.
But you know what? I will give it a pass on that point. They carried the setting very well and everything else fit well. Story is not the key draw of this game, and it taught me that you don't need a good story to make a highly immersive, sweeping adventure. So while it was less-than-satisfactory in this regard, I am willing to ignore it as it achieved the results of a good story without having a very good one at all; namely, a great deal of player immersion into the game's universe.
I admit I was sceptical coming to Half-Life, but by the end of it I realise why it was seen as a watershed for the FPS genre and a landmark for the history of video games at large. If there were one amazing FPS to define a genre, it would be Half-Life. Even today, it is still a good example of what we expect from a first-person shooter; and deservedly so.

Graphics, ship detail, game style, play experience, basically the whole premise is solid. The cons for me focus mainly around controls and overall physics. The ships (even the faster ones) are rather slow, cumbersome, and limiting in their movement. The best way to descibe the movement is like this...Space Submarines. Seriously, you could change the ship skins to submarines and put them in water and their movement would fit perfectly. The game assumes there is an up and down (which is relative in space) and orients your ship accordingly. It's impossible to roll (period) or change that standard up down orientation. And currently you can't rebind keys.
With that being said, I think this game is in a good spot for an alpha and has a ton of potential. And as a final thought for the developers, don't over do it with features, extras, and upgrades. The screen is already very busy. In my opinion, the better games have an easy to understand game play, easy primary and secondary action buttons (ie primary and secondary weapon), and a limited number of combination upgrades. TF2 did this perfectly in my opinion. Each class has it's own upgrades that can be bought or earned, but the number of upgrade combinations isn't completely overwhelming. In my opinion, the skill should be in the ability to outmanuever your opponent rather than in what souped up combination of weapons and abilities you have.

One of the most addictive games I've ever played.  I can't remember the last time I lost sleep because I couldn't pull myself away from the computer.  The game is split into 2 sections, the actual dungeon crawl, and then managing your characters at the town (kind of like the xcom base).  I'm always excited to enter a dungeon, but I'm just as excited to get back to my base to see what new recruits have arrived and what trinkets are available.
That all being said, this game will take the wind out of your sails eventually.  Just when you think you've figured things out, it turns out you haven't.  A lot of people complain about the supposed difficulty spike.  I don't actually think the difficulty spikes very much, it's just that in the early game, you don't have to play the game the way it was intended to be played:  You can go straight damage and ignore cc.
The game is almost too forgiving early on.  For the life of me I couldn't see the benefit of upgrading skills when all you got was a slight boost to accuracy, stuns seemed irrelevant and DoTs/debuffs seemed wasteful.
Level 5 dungeons require you to understand party composition, have your gear and skills upgraded, value cc and understand when DoTs and debuffs are necessary.  You don't need a guide for this, these are my tips for new players:
This game isn't easy, but it isn't cheaply difficult either.
A few minor changes I would like to see are faster turn resolutions, the delay between each characters turn starting is starting to be noticeable now that I know what I'm doing.  More chat bubble options would be nice, the text types too slowly for my tastes.  Some improvements could be made to the camping ui so you don't accidentally use a skill.  Trinket management is a bit clumsy.

If the player fails it should be due to his or her actions, not because the game decides to work against their inputs.
The humour of the game wears off quickly and it isn't enough to carry the frustration that comes from the core gameplay. Rampage mode is a nice option and serves as pure catharsis. I would actually be more interested in playing a fully-fleshed out Katamari Damacy style game with the rampage mechanics.
Overall, probably worth a try but I wouldn't pay full sticker price.

The game initially showed promise, but I quickly came to realise that it's so tied up in the designers' decisions for showboating and 'what-would-be-awesomes' that it isn't actually any
to play.
The core of the original XCOM game is there and they've added some really solid new features to it, such as the armour system and melee combat, but the bad decisions significantly outweigh the good. The amount of RNG (which on it's own is fine), combined with new status effects that essentially render your soldiers completely ineffective for a turn (and the sheer number the enemy can deploy them on you) can quickly render entire missions impossible to complete within the first turn of combat, potentially forcing you to reload the same mission over and over.
Animations in combat take forever and sometimes pause for a second or two afterwards for no clear reason, completely removing the sharp and snappy combat aesthetic they were aiming for and making battles take forever. The camera seems to snap all over the place for no good reason, even occassionally missing important enemy moves, and if I have to see that pointing animation one more time I don't know what I'll do.
The stealth system, while a nice addition, seems a bit ad-hoc and doesn't seem to explore its own potential fully. I'm not sure how I'd change it up but currently it just feels lacking.
The additions to the overworld gameplay are really fun and add a lot to the game, the more guerilla style warfare gives XCOM 2 a suitably refreshing style change from 1 and I think it's the overworld that's the strongest part of the game. However, that doesn't really translate to the battle gameplay.
Additionally, I'll be the first to admit my machine isn't top of the line (or even all that good anymore) but the amount of variation in the framerate, even with graphics settings dialled down from recommended only increase the frustration of trying to play this further.
In conclusion, a promising game sorely let down by some terrible design decisions for the battle system that would turn an otherwise fun game into a mess of frustration and disappointment. A real shame, as XCOM 1 is among my higher rated games.

As of 04/20/2015:
A 5 v 5 MOBA like game where huge capital ships clash in space, where you battle to control sectors a-la king of the hill, where the main objective is to sit your sexy battleship♥♥♥♥♥on the enemy team's base (HOME) long enough to capture and type "gg" before the system kicks you out to redo.
Basically, that's about it, and if you are into competitive pvp and spaceships that's pretty much all you need to know to love -and- hate every second of it.
Is it stable? Wow, much bugs?
For an alpha state game, I encountered little to no bugs per se, I did notice the occasional mass dissconnect but it never happened to me, and depending on the server you pick, lag is not bad, generall rule of thumb, pick the closest server location available, and the occasional massive kick for a maintenance here and there, that's good, if they are working they are caring.
Gameplay
At the start, and as you eventually realize the best use for each ship's skill, the game is pretty simple, pick a ship, warp to a sector and slowly push your ship forward into a enemy ship's range to  button mash their healthbar into oblivion before they do the same to yours, the learning curve is pretty smooth if you care to read your skill effects before getting into a game. There is real strategy into each ship's design and skillset, but you'll have to learn that yourself before you realize it was a mistake to whine in the main chat about how broken this or that ship is.
Content
THIS is where the problems start, even for an ALPHA version bla bla thing, the game is very very limited, you start with 3 different ships wich, through usage, give you points to unlock new models to then purchase, in total, 12 different ships all with it's uniqueish weaponery and capabilities, sounds okay, but you soon get bored after playing a few games with each class, only some come with unlockable weapon variations but they are uninspired and very similar to the main ones, basically, if one weapon does normally a lot of damage but in short range,  the variation may offer less or more range in exchange for more or less damage respectively.
EDIT: I have to be clear here, my problem is not the lack of ships, but it's delivery, the chained unlocking system feels like a chore and after you do get the new ship you feel dissapointed, not because the new ship is bad, contrary, the ships are surprisingly balanced enough that when going into battle in your hard earned new rig, you get pummeled by the starting ships even by new players that had a game or two on that ship, and ship mods give the same feeling, this are easily fixable and now that I know Game Devs are enough to read and reply to this beautiful nobody writing to you, I have high hopes they will fix this given time.
I also mentioned having only one map as a negative point, I have to put that out, come on, quality over quantity, map is kinda fun, and the matchmaking system feels bad probably because it's still growing gaming community, the chat system is a bit primitive if I may be so bold, though, and with the game ending in a quite abrupt score screen disconnecting everybody does feel a bit unfriendly,  surely a future fix, just please, please work on a friend system or a partying option, this kind of games are much much more fun with friends, if there actually IS such a way already, make it noticeable! I am no IT but I want to believe I'm not dumb enough to miss that feature that easily.
Graphics EDITED
After a surprisingly swift and polite reply from Game Dev. Stanith, I have to agree here, Ship models are indeed detailed and on it's own style, very well designed too, you will have to forgive my harsh judgement here mainly because the camera controls actually do not allow me to fully appreciate that,  smaller ships end up looking too far, and big ones like the infamous flagship are so large, the ship's tail actually gets in the way awkwardly, having the main weapon aiming permanently tied to the camera is a big factor here, you know you can't freely look around without risking the chance of losing precious DPS due to having to adjust your weapon positioning, I have to be fair here, it does seem complicated to favor both gameplay and aesthetics here, and it would be pretentious to punch them for that.
I was harsh on the game's detail and graphic state, game dev told me it was on a very early state, and, yes! I hve to agree with him on it, I was just a tad dissapointed here, I may have not paid for the game thanks to the weekend deal, but I had to review it as if I had, and for it's listed price I felt players could have been given something a bit richer, I know it will eventually be, but early access market is already stained as it is, so do forgive your humble player for expecting more for my money, the skin part on the other hand, seriously guys...
TL:DR Buy or No Buy? (EDITED)
I compared this game to Dreadnough, a very similar game in development that was announced not too long ago, Developer Stanith told me their game was in development was before Dreadnought's announcement, I have to say though, they surely were working on the game before they announced it, still, I would hate to raise controversy over something like that, I didn't mean to compare it in such a rude way, but Dreadnought being it's closest competitor, or competitor-to-be in my opinion, I foolishly gave the point to the game that looked to be on a more advanced state without digging in to facts, and with the benefit of the doubt in mind, I apologize.
You have to understand though, If I do compare it's not out of hate, I don't want this to be a watered down version of a bigger title, this game should have (and I believe it has) it's own soul and style, and if it's main difference over other titles is gonna be the price, sorry, at least in my case, some extra cash is worth for a richer experience
My review stays negative, as I had said, mainly for it's listed cost, if it had been a free title with the option to then decide to make the early purchase, my review would instantly be on the positive side, and if new features arrive soon as promised, I surely will even if the price is unchanged. But in an era where many of us are fed of early access titles that seem to enjoy the taste of income and simply appear to be so comfy in the pool to try to push forward, (no, seriously guys, you really think The Forest will ever make it out of alpha before they change to Unity 20?) I'll have to be mean on Fractured Space, why? Because I care.

The content creation club seems to have some of its heftiest items already be available elsewhere, I do believe horse armor at the very least had been available elsewhere, while the some of the other armors available can be obtained for free with superior versions by modders who decided to recreate them. This kind of creates a moral quandry, the official developers are making an inferior product that you have to pay for, one made after modders made the superior quality free ones, it would be in their best interest to take it down, however I have yet to see them do so. This is something to keep your eye on.
The content creation club also downloads any and all content to your disk, so it is in effect a sort of microtransaction system, unlocking items that is already in the game and downloaded to your computer. The big issue is in the future, when there had been plenty of creations made...will this make the game bloated? Many games end up struggling under the weight of its own content at times, sims 3 was a great example, ive seen the games performance chug due to all the expansions and even WORSE with shop items. This could end up making fallout require far more space to install while at the same time making it run worse.
At the end of the day, what is this going to be? They promised to sort of curate and pay modders to make content, however it has been since revealed that modders cant really do much with the limitations bethesda has put in place and with the saying of put your best foot forward, we have gotten skins, armor that already exists for free and HORSE ARMOR. Im not really sure why the hell they decided to release horse armor for the damn game considering its a reminder of their attempt to normalize DLC as a microtransaction, the same thing they are more or less trying to do, only with mods as microtransactions instead. They got a massive backlash back then, they got a massive backlash when the original paid mods released and they are getting a massive backlash now, if I were to make an observation, it really does not seem they learn. This is clearly not near the promises they made, as what they release just makes them out to be a laughingstock.
Addendum: Apparently, plenty of the creation club items offer statistical upgrades, such as an armor that lets you go invisible or backpacks that gives special bonuses based on how it is set up. Could an argument be made for pay to win singleplayer mods? Im not really sure about this, it does mean you may be paying bethesda to get better gear to progress easier. Its even more debatable with it being downloaded with the base game and purchasable with microtransactions.
Aside from that, fallout 4 is kind of a eh game anyways.
Its....at best, alright. But it has some of the same issues the core skyrim has, except mod support isnt really as developed to help fix some of the games core problems. The gunplay was most definitely improved but they kind of have been moving on a trend to make their games less about an RPG and more about an action game, the issue is that fallout 4 tries to be some hybrid of FPS and RPG but the RPG mechanics arent really there. They implemented a sort of procedural generation to weapons but lost out on actual depth to them. The perk system is for the most part just about making you stronger, as is the weapon upgrade system. In addition to radiant quests, ironically to this game less of a focus to quests than previous games and the game kind of being a little scattered with its content, often having certain characters in the story be far more fleshed out, as the story, aside from a split to choose a faction is linear.
Specifically, you cannot sequence break, you cannot kill important characters and dialogue in this purpose was mainly set up to act as a way to advance the plot forward rather than give options or unlock alternative ways of progressing. In many cases the "Four option" dialogue system results in choices that all effectively result in the same consequence or is otherwise saying the same things in different ways. The addition of a voiced protagonist hampers this further, as it meant that they have to record your character saying this for the entire game and also meant that the voice actor in question will have to be under a heavy load. This also means they have to pay more money for any sort of splits in dialogue or potentially worry about damaging the vocal cords of the voice actor. As a result this means that the questing experience is usually linear small stories, even admitted by the development team to be made not by their writers but by whoever had the coolest ideas.
I mean, just to cut this short, because I went on quite abit with my findings. The game is...okay, if you can get it on sale. I would instead recommend you to fallout new vegas as its a pretty well set up game made by some of the same people who created fallout 1 and 2 I believe. It kind of showcases what fallout can be when set up as an RPG and was really fun.

XCOM 2 builds upon the idea that you failed miserably in XCOM: Enemy Unknown. And that is a damn good thing.
Where to start... Well, the concept of having a mobile base is very good, as you actually feel like you're on the run from the alien overlords and their grizzly genetically-altered army. You need to collect resources in order to survive, and the different things you can discover while searching are pretty standard, but varied enough for them to fit perfectly. The only thing about this is that early on you can get overwhelmed with the amount of areas you need to search, which can lead to a slow start that gives the aliens an early advantage.
The soldier customization puts most RPGs to shame and is easily the best part of the game. With the extensive modding community it is possible to create nearly any soldier you can think of. What other game can you have Halo's Spartans and the crew of Mass Effect's Normandy fighting side by side while the Gears of War decimate the aliens?
The combat feels mostly the same as it did in XCOM: EU, but with a twist. The new concealed mechanic allows you to ambush first. But you need to be careful as you can end up getting ambushed yourself if you get overconfident. I think my only gripe with this mechanic is that you can run into enemies in the most bull****y spots, and it can ultimately screw you over for the rest of the mission. Luckily if you're like me, you'll end up saving scum and reloading. Fortunately you won't have to sit through the aliens murdering your soldiers over and over like with Enemy Unknown. You can reload a save during their go at you. That said, where is the Restart Mission button?
Storywise, for my first playthrough I was intrigued with the way it was going. I liked the reveals, the twists, and the lore all the way through and it genuinely felt like the aliens were playing humanity like a flute. (damn you Speaker!) That said, the ending kind've feels the same as with Enemy Unknown in that it feels so ubrupt.
Ultimately, if you're a fan of the series, you'll love this game. If you're new to the series, you'll love this game. It's the best of the series and with the extensive modding community it's only going to get better.

+ I love the idea of fighting huge battle cruisers.
+ I love the slightly slower pace of combat (compared to, e.g. CounterStike GO or Call of Duty).
+ basic controls are easy to pick up (WASD and point-and-shoot)
+ taking damage looks really impressive.
However:
- an FPS-like interface is easy, but it loses the feeling of flying in 3D space. This is a shooter with an invisible floor.
- the roles of the different battle ships are too close to shooters like Team Fortress or Call of Duty
- Due to the camera and the lack of frame of reference, these ships don't look especially big.
- weapons and gameplay are needlessly complicated
- visual clues are REALLY BAD. I know when I'm hit, and I know when I hit somebody else. That's about it. I sort of understand the base captures and the tug-of-war gameplay because I've seen it in other shooters, but I have NO idea why or when to capture the central resource/base/plant/whatever.
Also, you get some beta quirks:
- controls are not configurable (I guess they will be configurable before the game goes gold)
- animations look like they're static, not physics based and so they look like crap
- joining a game is awkward and offers me a choice I don't need to make. Either I want to jump into "any" game with a low ping, or I want to join a friend. Clans would be nice, too. There's very little sense in other choices as the games all play the same anyway.
All in all: don't pay for it unless you feel the need to be charitable to the developers.

Darkest Dungeon is a game that is prided on difficulty and being a unique experience. The lovecraftian horror elements add to the atmosphere, and the art style fits it perfectly. It admittedly does have a steep learning curve, and if you're not fond of RNG and randomness, this game is not for you, as that's where a decent amount of the difficulty stems from. A big part of the game is learning to deal with and mitigate the effects of RNG, and that isn't for everyone. This being said if you're into that, this game is great, and if you're into RPG's and/or lovecraftian horror, this game is excellent.
I will say this, do NOT, I repeat, do NOT buy this game if you're looking for a Rogue-Like, as this game is NOT a Rogue-Like, it's an RPG with RNG elements. The RNG is really as close to a Rogue-Like as this game is.
If you're into RPG's, Lovecraftian horror, and/or general difficulty, this game is right up your alley, otherwise, it might not be, but I still recommend giving it a shot.

I'm only 20 hours into game, so I will be speaking from that perspective.
I had some complaints about this game's unfrgiving and cruel design, until I realised that this game is supposed to be cruel and unforgiving. That it's not about making quick progress and levelling. This game is about giving you a particular experience. And everything is built around giving you that experience.
Now I play with a different approach. I don't play with the intent to play optimally and to beat it. I play to experience it. And if I ever manage to finish it, then it will be a bonus. So I don't mind that my heroes will die and many of my errands will end in utter failure. This is what I'm signing for. The stakes are set high and that makes the risk real. This is not about winning. This is about surviving and pulling through against all odds. And living with consequences of failure. And experiencing moments of horror but also, moments of hope, when you feel like all is lost, but a sudden lucky roll of dice allows for a narrow escape. If the game was fair and free of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, those moments would be meaningless.
It's an amazing and masterfully crafted game. but You need to know what you're getting yourself into before you ragequit with disappointment.
As for me, even if I stopped playing right now, after 20 hours I already got more from this game than my money's worth.

Since it's an Alpha build it's hard to judge it because it could change at any moment. Anyway 2015-04-15 comments.
Final verdict: I got to play it during the free weekend and it was quite enjoyable. If I had to pay full price to play it I'd probably wait for the developers to add more game modes and to see what kind of premium options the developers plan to offer in the in-game shop.
There were 3 ships instantly available and 9 more can be accessed by playing the game and unlocking them. So far only skins for ships seems to be cash only with the potential for Premium ships and crew members to be added to the shop later. So far it's too early to say if these premium options will be pay-to-win.
Each of the ships has a primary and a secondary weapon as well as some other weapons.
Primary weapons are mainly lasers but they vary in damage, speed, effective shooting angles (for some the target needs to be right in from of your ship) and other aspects (some do more damage with each hit so you need to be very close to make sure that you hit all your shots, while some are slower and effective at maximum range).
Secondaries and other weapons can vary greatly,they can allow you to teleport to another location, activate extra shields, fire repairing lasers at you teammates, disable your target's systems, activate a movement speed boots and so on.
So far it seems the ships can be only slightly customized by choosing from some pre-set options (faster+less damage or slower+more damage and so on), but I guess that is needed for balancing reasons.
So far the only game mode is a 5v5 Domination. The gameplay is mainly team oriented, but if you are playing against a not very coordinated team a single player can still carry his team to victory, but generally a balanced team composition and a coordinated team effort (of defending points and attacking) is needed.

XCOM 2 is a fantastic game, and it should be getting more praise than it is getting.  Yes every review of XCOM 2, the game is unoptimized, but does that mean you can't enjoy it.  I played half of XCOM 2 on 15 fps, and not a moment went by where I wasn't disappointed in the game.
My personal experience with XCOM was, despite the low fps, smooth.  No other bugs were encountered, and no other significant problem presented itself.  It was just pure fun for me.  Later on I changed the graphics to be set lower and I got 20-30 fps, but it the 15-20 wasn't really a big deal for me.
The gameplay is exactly what you'd expect from the past XCOM games, EU and EW, so no complaints there.  The weapons and armor are phenomenal to look at as well.  The art team did a really good job on this game,
The only problem I would say there is is the class system.  I am fine with the classes that are present in XCOM 2, alright, don't mess with them.  I am, however, disappointed with the way the classes, such as Psi and MEC class, were handled.  I can forgive the MECs not being present due to the fact that you're a resistance, not a military.  It would make sense not to have high tech military walkers, but when you need to have a PSI operative start from level 1, and you can't use your badass you've built up the entire game, that kind of makes me wonder why I even tried to get a PSI Operative in the first place.
As it is I would give XCOM 2 an 8/10.  Hopefully the DLC will add a new, interesting character class with new missions, weapons, armor, etc.

This game is awful. I picked it up because there were plenty of positive reviews but now that I've played it I realize there's nothing special here. The sound effects are HORRID. Someone could be standing two feet away from you and the gunshots will sound exactly the same as they do twenty feet away, or behind a wall, or across the map. On the topic of audio, the sound mixing is really atrocious. Every time you get a kill it plays an extremely loud stock gore sound effect which can't be turned down or disabled, this is aggravating to say the least. Every single gun is the exact same thing. You either take an accurate high rate of fire gun with no recoil (TAR-21), or a high damage low rate of fire gun with lots of recoil. (Any AK, HK14) The sniping is a joke because there is no scope sway if you move while scoped in. Shotguns are useless because they don't one shot and most rifles with kill you in 3 to 4 shots. The music is cringy, the ping is terrible, the translations are laughable (e.g. "It was too hard" is an actual voice line on defeat). The classes are groan-inducing and only available on the worst game mode, they're just in the game just so they can say it's a class based shooter. None of the weapons are purchasable for any time other than permanent. This wouldn't be a problem if they gave you more money, but after playing for a couple hours I only have enough for one very cheap gun and a rifle. (About 220,000 for both, all of which came from the money they start you with) and you get around 800 currency in a round where you did really well. The single redeeming feature of this game is the detailed gun models, which isn't even that big of a deal because you'll only be able to own two or three of these guns (besides the default three) before running out of currency and grinding TDM lobbies full of wall hackers and poor sports.
tl;dr This game is bad, play something else.

Final verdict: I got to play it during the free weekend and it was quite enjoyable. If I had to pay full price to play it I'd probably wait for the developers to add more game modes and to see what kind of premium options the developers plan to offer in the in-game shop.
There were 3 ships instantly available and 9 more can be accessed by playing the game and unlocking them. So far only skins for ships seems to be cash only with the potential for Premium ships and crew members to be added to the shop later. So far it's too early to say if these premium options will be pay-to-win.
Each of the ships has a primary and a secondary weapon as well as some other weapons.
Primary weapons are mainly lasers but they vary in damage, speed, effective shooting angles (for some the target needs to be right in from of your ship) and other aspects (some do more damage with each hit so you need to be very close to make sure that you hit all your shots, while some are slower and effective at maximum range).
Secondaries and other weapons can vary greatly,they can allow you to teleport to another location, activate extra shields, fire repairing lasers at you teammates, disable your target's systems, activate a movement speed boots and so on.
So far it seems the ships can be only slightly customized by choosing from some pre-set options (faster+less damage or slower+more damage and so on), but I guess that is needed for balancing reasons.
So far the only game mode is a 5v5 Domination. The gameplay is mainly team oriented, but if you are playing against a not very coordinated team a single player can still carry his team to victory, but generally a balanced team composition and a coordinated team effort (of defending points and attacking) is needed.

I love the XCOM series. Having played XCOM since 1994, I was really nervous when XCOM: Enemy Unknown came out in 2012, but it was an enjoyable reboot. It had its flaws and limitations but all in all was a fun game to play. I was blown away with XCOM 2, it is everything I wanted in a sequel.
Not only is this game worth paying full price for, it is also worth the inevitable hardware upgrade you're probably going to have to do to fully enjoy the game. I have an older gaming system, hardware is about 7 years old. I only had to upgrade system RAM from 4GB to 8GB and my video card from a GeForce GTX 260 to a GeForce GTX 750Ti 2GB, in order to run DirectX 11. All in all only about a $180 upgrade but it runs the game perfectly.
XCOM 2 take place a few decades after XCOM: Enemy Unknown (EU), but with a twist. Without having any spoilers for anyone who hasn't played XCOM: EU or XCOM 2 yet, the end of one does not match up completely with the beginning of the other. XCOM 2 is unlike most every other sci-fi sequel out there, and is much more enjoyable in my opinion.
PROS:
-Original Storyline.
-Fully Customizable Squad (ALL Squad specialties are useful, unlike previous Xcoms).
-Amazing Graphics.
-Tons of replay value.
-Computer AI is well done, unpredictable and fully uses the environment and weapon systems against you.
-Stays true to the core principles of XCOM.
CONS:
-Requires A LOT of hard drive space 45GB for basic install.
-Graphics Glitches that sometimes effects gameplay.**
-Smaller map size, not a lot of huge buildings to clear like XCOM: TFTD.
-Can have slow load times.
-Average game length.
**= Ghosting sometimes occurs and during graphics intensive segments (like catastrophic explosions) characters sometimes display incorrect actions afterward. (Like constant crouching or constriction after 'bladestorm' etc)
Probably my favorite turn-based strategy game of the last decade, and a must-have for any XCOM fan!
