The commander is back!  I had high expectations because I loved XCOM: Enemy Unknown and the Enemy Within expansion.  Usually when I let that happen, I am dissapointed.  But this is one of the few times where my expectations were exceeded (another notable mention being Borderlands 2).
The goal is the same: turn the aliens' weapons against them and break the foot of humanity off in their♥♥♥♥♥  However, this time the aliens are in control of earth.  You represent the xcom resistance, earth's last fighting force.  You aren't worried about the council, you are trying to pull together scattered resistance cells to get supplies.  The game does a lot to make you feel like the commander of a guerilla force.  You have a mobile base this time around, that you have to remove clutter from and fix up to make room for more facilities.  You start most fights in concealment, where you are hidden and must carefully choose when to strike.  Many missions are timed, requiring you strike hard and fast if you want to be able to evac your team in time.
Other new game elements include a separate psionic class with a host of abilities, the ability to call the skyranger and create and evac zone on some maps, and new skills and new takes on classes.  Assault is now Ranger, and includes skills focused on scouting and melee with a sword.  Snipers can now specialize in their pistols and be useful in close quarters.    Specialists can hack troublesome mechanical units.  I feel like there are a lot more hard to choose between skills, and lots of creative ways to build a squad.  A troop designer lets you create a pool of troops outside the main game, so you can create your x-com trooper friends once and use them for multiple games.
The story and atmosphere of the game are very engaging.  As the aliens research a secret avatar project, a progress bar will increase.  You must progress the story and assault bases to decrease it.  It's a visual indicator a your fight against time.  You can carry and evac downed squad members.  As I've stated, many missions require you to evac before the timer runs out and any remaining troops are cut off from escape.  There are many suprises  which I won't spoil, but I was caught off guard a few times.
As far as glitches, I've only run into one visual glitch in 40 hours of gameplay, it lasted for part of one mission and did not ruin gameplay.  I think EU had more, which they fixed quickly.
If you loved the first, you'll love this one.  If you like turn based strategy, blowing holes in buildings and storming them, hacking enemies' toys and blowing them up, mind controlling enemies and using them to blow up other enemies...so basically, if you want to go Mr.Torgue on some aliens, pick this up!

If I had reviewed this game when it had launched or in the patch prior to the Children of Anarchy DLC release, I would not have recommended this game to anyone except the die-hard loyalists of the franchise. But after I had tried to play the game again after the relase of the game's first DLC pack, I am happy to say that XCOM 2 is worth every penny of it's $59.99 price tag. The combat itself is more streamlined than in Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within, the storyline is very interesting, the customization options for XCOM's soldiers is almost limitless, and the mods help expand the experince greatly.
However, the game still suffers from framerate drops and slowdowns. The soldiers will disappear when you promote them right after the mission as well. Oh, and be careful when you use mods, because if you mix two mods that overwrite one of the required parameters for the game to run properly, you'll ultimately crash the game.
My final grade for the game would be an A or A+ if the slowdowns at graphics settings higher than Minimal and soldier dissapearing acts were fixed. But, for the time being, I'm giving it an A-.

I joined during the free weekend of this game, however after playing 25 matches I have found out what I consider what the good bad and ugly of this game are. Lets start with the ugly.
Ugly - Its in early access.... ya .... as we all know this means the game can change or be cancelled at any time with very little warning so I myself after the stomping lands, and cube world fiasco have held off on purchasing early access games. That being said the developers seem extremley into this game and fingers crossed looks like they will for along time coming. More ugly now. The leaderboards in the current state are kinda really crap lol, they are working on it to drastically improve them but currently they are simply just bad. The in game honor is calculated very weirdly and makes no sense in its current state. You can organize the leaderboard by everything except kill death ratio which makes no sense to me since that is in my opinion one of the most important things to sort by.
Bad- Now for the bad this is the stuff that the game could fix with a little bit of work. To start weakpoints..... for the love of god especially when flying the sniper ship at weak points on every ship that makes the gunplay far more balanaced. It makes it more balanced due to the fact that now as a corvette or other small ship and you run into any type of ship that has damage you literally have no chance. If you added a weak spot the little ship now has a chance to out manuever the bigger ship and take it out by  hitting the weak point. Another that goes  hand in hand with weak points is ships being effected by damage. currently you can be shot wherever and  have nothing happen. However i should be able to aim for the engines of the opposing ship and take them out he should lose alot of mobility makeing him way slower atleast for a short time till his engines are fixed. giving players a chance to be extremley tactical in their battles with opponents. remember this isnt stuff necessary for the game but i believe it would add to the game greatly. Another thing for  future would be more maps and even larger scale battle so  instead of 5 on 5 maybe 10 on 10 just to make battles even more epic this is space lol.
Good- Finally to the good. As is this game has absorbed 15 hours of my time already and its only been like 4 days so ya im a little obssesed.  This is essentialy a space ship moba everyship is unique in damage health and abilities so it takes a little bit to find out what gamestyle you like and can do best in. The way to unlock ships is to use a ship belonging to one of the three factions. every game you play with gains xp to unlock new loadouts for ships in that faction and new ships themselves. Also every game you play you get credits after you unlock things with xp you then use the credits to actually purchase the upgrades or ships themselves. The gameplay itself is very very easy to learn and master. after about my 5th game I have not had a game were i didnt get 10 plus kills 3 or less deaths and 7 or so base captures. if you have a nack for shooters the game is fairly easy to learn and your personal skills matters alot more than in other shooters that put too much reflex gameplay into the way you play. The visuals in this game are also very beautiful and keep the blankness of space interesting. Matches unlike most other mobas take about 15-30 mins to play I just had my longest match every at 46min which is about the average length of a match in most other mobas so this game is much easier to play if you only get 30 min to play here and there.

gameplay 9/10
graphics 8/10
audio 7/10
stats/leaderboards 5/10

You know that feeling when you are playing Rock, Paper, Scissors and the other player pulls "gun?" Yeah that's this game, and it makes that VERY clear when you start.
To Returning XCOM players:
This game will feel familiar to you, while still giving a variety of new mechanics to play around with. Believe me, it's not just a rehased Enemy Unknown. The difficulty has been ramped up in a variety of ways, including the new Avatar Project timer. Also, timed missions are much more common now, preventing the "sit back and kill everyone with overwatch" strategy.
To New Players:
You will get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked. Multiple times. Though it can be discouraging to fail a mission or lose your favorite soldier, you can't give up there. That is the enjoyment of the game. It's SUPPOSED to make you unhappy when you lose. Don't be surprised if you lose your first or second playthrough.
Overall, XCOM 2 is a magnificent sequel that, while feeling similar, gives you an entirely different experience, which will be much more prevelant with the new and large modding community. Because of the new mechanics, you will have to try new strategies and adjust to the new gameplay, which is fun in itself. The new emphasis on story can easily grasp you even if you don't realize it. You will not have the same experience in one playthrough that you got from another. An amazing work by the guys at Firaxis.
Good luck, Commander.

Have you ever imagined being the captain of your own starship, just like Captain Kirk or Captain Picard from Star Trek? Or even being in one of the countless space battles between 2 starcruisers seen in the Star Wars series? Well, this game will do that and much more.
Classified as a MOBA, it focuses on 5v5 matches. There are no ultimate abilities/skills for you to rely on, only your judgement, guile, ship, and squadron.
You'll start with 3 basic ships from 3 different manufacturers each(United Space Research[USR], Zarek Industries, and Titan Defense Systems[TDS]) for you to get your bearings.
You can purchase any ship and it's variety of weapon selections with in-game credits earned by playing, so you can customie your ship with a variety of loadouts based on your playstyle or team composition. From homing Smartguns, to Torpedoes, and different Engines, you'll find that each ship's indivuduality is highlighted with your choice of weapons and systems you put into them.
The only things that you could pay in-game is for cosmetic skins for the ships, similarly like in TF2.
Update Jun/29/2016: Game's gone F2P on June, manufacturer EXP will be removed on the July update.
Update Sep/29/2016: Game's left Early Access.

Want a challenge? Good.
Want a unforgiving game? Good.
No, it's not Dark Souls people. It's Darkest Dungeon, and with a little luck: You'll come to enjoy the unique challenge presented by this gem.
Darkest Dungeon is what Dark Souls is to Action RPGS: A game that rewards you for learning more and more about it's inner workings, while providing challenges that engage the player to make smart decisions, or even figure out different approaches to situations.
The game's rundown is essentially thus:
You pick from a select group of adventurers that have different classes, and send them on various expidition to recover your family's long lost treasures and heirlooms, while killing increasingly difficult enemies in the process.
Various factors come into play in this game though. It's not easy being an adventurer, and it's definitely not easy to stay sane when you're facing monster after monster. These poor wretches you've hired will go through hell and back...that is, if they're lucky to come out of it alive, or sane, for that matter.
From Traps, to Eldritch horrors: This game pits it all against you, and it's up to you to make a rag-tag group of fortune seekers force back the evil plague that's claimed your homeland...or die trying.

Dieses Spiel ist mein Lieblingsspiel schlechthin. Es hat tolle interessante Mechaniken und Helden die nicht alle strahlend sind, sondern auch echte Ecken , Macken und Kanten haben. Das Stress und Leichensystem lässt viel Spielraum zum Taktieren und um neue Strategien zu testen. Die Helden sind allesamt interessant und erlauben verschiedene Spielstile.
Da gibt es natürlich einige Sachen, die vielen sauer aufstoßen werden, wie z.b der Hohe RNG Faktor den man nicht beeinflussen kann, da kann es passieren, dass man von einem Skelett nunmal 4 mal hintereinander einen kritischen Treffer bekommt. Oder das ein Held trotz einer Deathblow Resistenz von 85% nach dem ersten Treffer das Zeitliche segenet. Hinzu kommt das man viel Grinden muss , sei es Gold oder Erbstücke die man für den Aufbau des Dorfes und den Ausbau der Helden benötigt.
Aber dennoch belohnt einem das Spiel mit einer dichten Atmosphäre einen großartigen Sprecher und interessanten Charackteren. Diese kann man noch zusätzlich anpassen und verändern, so kann man mit seinen Freunden in die Ruinen ziehen und den Ort von dem Bösen befreien. Es gibt nichts besseres als mit seinem letzten Helden, der völlig gestresst ist den letzten Lebenspunkt des Bosses zu rauben und dadurch noch den Kampf zu gewinnen.
Ich empfehle dieses Spiel allen, die eine hohe Frustresistenz haben, nix gegen Grinden haben und eine packende Atmosphäre zu schätzen wissen. Alle anderen die sich daran stören das es zuviel RNG  in diesem Spiel gibt und die es nicht mögen regelmäßig Helden zu verlieren, würde ich davon abraten das Spiel zu kaufen, oder mal reinzuschauen wenn es im Sale ist.
Pros +
-tolle Atmosphäre
- tolle Characktere
- tolles Artdesign
- toller Sprecher
- viele Spielstile möglich
- Stress Managment und Helden Managment bieteten viele stategische Aspekte
Cons -
- Viel Grinden

Pros:
+ Visual/Audio design is superb. Almost every action has a satisfying kick or flair to it. The art style and character designs are equally admirable.
+ It is enjoyably strategic, I feel like I appreciate turn based RPGs more because of it. The use of positioning, movement, and targeting makes you really think about how you compose your teams, especially at higher levels. "Dancing" parties, where characters are continually shuffling their position to allow others to attack, are especially fun. However, as the difficulty progresses, I felt that party compositions become a lot more restricted, which ruins some of the fun.
+ The lore is great, tying everything together, and an interesting take on the idea of the Eldritch Abomination. Each hero feels feels like a unique chracter, and I felt like I got to know their personalities, especially when they become Afflicted.
+ Ancestor's Portrait. Look at that ♥♥♥♥ing face, how can you not love it.
+ Wayne June.
Cons
- Don't be too alarmed by my hours played; it consists of at least 2 rage quit Hamlet deletions and many unnecessary hero grooming runs. However, this game still requires a lot of grinding, and I feel that a shorter, more focused experience would improve this game a lot, so that the climax at the end isn't a "♥♥♥♥ing finally. I swear to the Light if I got Calm-Creeping Cough on a hero again I'd knee the ♥♥♥♥ing screen".
- The RNG is... hmm. Losing a hero on the first death's door check is awful, but I have finished some bosses by critting so hard with a Leper that their mechanics never even factored into the battle. This makes the difficulty curve very inconsistent; many boss encounters are hard more because you get really unlucky rather than the bosses themselves being a threat. However, when RNGesus smiles upon you, you can really appreciate the outcome; the perfect crit, the Virtue right when you need it. I guess that the tone of the game is supposed to make it so these "Hero" moments stand out, while acquanting the player with the brutal nature of the game with a Treebranch Smackdown crit. Perhaps there was a way to make the RNG more feel more dire than frustrating, but in my opinion it leans more towards the latter, especially in Champion dungeons where getting Wryd Reconstruction's 0-Bleed special will get a hero killed.
- Perhaps it was because I grinded way too much before doing them, but I feel that the bosses outside of the Darkest Dungeon aren't as challenging as they could be. Lucky crits aside, I felt that I could just easily smack them until they died and deal with their gimmick with a designated hero (e.g. Arbalest for Swine Prince) or facetank/reduce their damage until they died. What I admire/dread about the Shambler fight is that it challenges you to deal with all of the threats of the boss as quickly as possible before they spiral out of control. I never got that sense of "kill them before they kill you" until the Darkest Dungeon.
While I have a lot more to say about the cons of this game, the good qualities of this game will become evident when you play it. If you don't mind committing to a game for a long time, Darkest Dungeon is a really captivating game.

As a big Dark Souls fan, it's probably not a huge surprise that I liked this game.
I found the gameplay to be very reminscient of X-Com games, in that you alternate between a "mission" phase and a "base building" (or town/hero upkeep in this case) phase.  The different classes are interesting, and while some are probably better than others, there is enough variability to add something to the game by mix and matching different character classes on missions.  In addition, the trinket system allows for just enough equipment customization on missions in a game where you are managing 20+ characters, but not too much.
In terms of negatives, the missions can get repetitive.  The first time you are levelling your characters, it's pretty fun.  But when you lose a couple characters or expand your roster and feel like levelling additional characters, it can be a bit monotonous to go through that process again.  There are a couple of ways to give new characters an xp boost, however unless a particular town event happens, you can't send high level characters on low level missions, so you can't speed things along by pairing your newbie with a team of maxed out characters.
In addition, while I found the difficulty to be challenging, but not too hard for the most part - this game can be frustrating at times.  Even if you know what you are doing, occasionally you'll have a mission that just goes bad.  One of your guys gets randomly focused by the enemy a bunch of times, or gets hit with a big crit a couple of times in a row and suddenly you've lost a guy that you spent a lot of time levelling up.  While this doesn't happen often, it does happen enough to be a bit of a pain.
Overall though, if you take the attitude that your heroes are all disposable and try not to get too attached to any in particular, the game plays smoothly for the most part and hero losses aren't that common once you learn the basics of the game.  Also, because there is no cost to recruiting new heroes, for all the talk of this being a hard game, the reality is that you can almost always recover from any disaster by just recruiting 4 new guys and sending them into a low level mission.  This in a way makes this game easier than the X-Com games because it's actually pretty difficult to mess up your game to the point where you can't just recover with a new team (unlike X-Com where you have to pay to hire new soldiers).  And the overall difficulty does not increase based on time spent, so there's really no penalty to doing this.
The level of challenge gives a nice feeling of accomplishment when the game is won and I'd recommend Darkest Dungeon to anyone who might like the gothic style of this game and doesn't generally play on easy mode.

A New Face for Early Access?
When most people hear "Early Access" in a game's description, what do they think?
"Shoddy, unfinished, unpolished, cash-grab."
Fractured Space is an Early Access game, and without a doubt it blows those stereotypes out of the water (or would that be asteroid belt?)
As an Early Access game, FS stands out with its beautifully polished content, but suffers from a lack thereof. What's in the game (as of the time of writing) is phenomenal, but one can't help shake the feeling that it's an empty frame - beautifully crafted - waiting for something to fill the void.
However, do not take this as a negative. The relatively small amount of content that exists in the game is still enough to keep a player occupied! Upgrade costs are balanced in such a way that players can look forward to tweaking their loadout with a new gimmick after every match, or hold out for a few more and get an entirely new ship.
With a pace that shifts from relaxed to blistering at a moment's notice, the game itself is stunning, breathtaking, and incredibly fun to play. There's something magical about drifting in calm silence to let your ship repair one moment, then warping in to a hurricane of shrapnel and broadside fire the next. Fractured Space truly captures the mix of nerve-wracking tactics and frenetic action that real space combat would be - and wraps it up in an intuitive, easy-to-learn package.
The assets are absolutely gorgeous and the atmosphere is incredibly well thought-out. Ship design seems to take cues from modern popular Sci-Fi as well as the classic Hard Science Fiction of the 20th century. The first time I clapped eyes on the game's "Flagship" heavy cruiser, I felt the spirit of Robert A. Heinlein become one with my own and we both giggled uncontrollably for several minutes from sheer glee.
Fans of War Thunder and other tactical vehicle-based team warfare games would be well-advised to pick this gem up ASAP.

Want a challenge? Good.
Want a unforgiving game? Good.
No, it's not Dark Souls people. It's Darkest Dungeon, and with a little luck: You'll come to enjoy the unique challenge presented by this gem.
Darkest Dungeon is what Dark Souls is to Action RPGS: A game that rewards you for learning more and more about it's inner workings, while providing challenges that engage the player to make smart decisions, or even figure out different approaches to situations.
The game's rundown is essentially thus:
You pick from a select group of adventurers that have different classes, and send them on various expidition to recover your family's long lost treasures and heirlooms, while killing increasingly difficult enemies in the process.
Various factors come into play in this game though. It's not easy being an adventurer, and it's definitely not easy to stay sane when you're facing monster after monster. These poor wretches you've hired will go through hell and back...that is, if they're lucky to come out of it alive, or sane, for that matter.
From Traps, to Eldritch horrors: This game pits it all against you, and it's up to you to make a rag-tag group of fortune seekers force back the evil plague that's claimed your homeland...or die trying.

Dieses Spiel ist mein Lieblingsspiel schlechthin. Es hat tolle interessante Mechaniken und Helden die nicht alle strahlend sind, sondern auch echte Ecken , Macken und Kanten haben. Das Stress und Leichensystem lässt viel Spielraum zum Taktieren und um neue Strategien zu testen. Die Helden sind allesamt interessant und erlauben verschiedene Spielstile.
Da gibt es natürlich einige Sachen, die vielen sauer aufstoßen werden, wie z.b der Hohe RNG Faktor den man nicht beeinflussen kann, da kann es passieren, dass man von einem Skelett nunmal 4 mal hintereinander einen kritischen Treffer bekommt. Oder das ein Held trotz einer Deathblow Resistenz von 85% nach dem ersten Treffer das Zeitliche segenet. Hinzu kommt das man viel Grinden muss , sei es Gold oder Erbstücke die man für den Aufbau des Dorfes und den Ausbau der Helden benötigt.
Aber dennoch belohnt einem das Spiel mit einer dichten Atmosphäre einen großartigen Sprecher und interessanten Charackteren. Diese kann man noch zusätzlich anpassen und verändern, so kann man mit seinen Freunden in die Ruinen ziehen und den Ort von dem Bösen befreien. Es gibt nichts besseres als mit seinem letzten Helden, der völlig gestresst ist den letzten Lebenspunkt des Bosses zu rauben und dadurch noch den Kampf zu gewinnen.
Ich empfehle dieses Spiel allen, die eine hohe Frustresistenz haben, nix gegen Grinden haben und eine packende Atmosphäre zu schätzen wissen. Alle anderen die sich daran stören das es zuviel RNG  in diesem Spiel gibt und die es nicht mögen regelmäßig Helden zu verlieren, würde ich davon abraten das Spiel zu kaufen, oder mal reinzuschauen wenn es im Sale ist.
Pros +
-tolle Atmosphäre

- toller Sprecher
- viele Spielstile möglich
- Stress Managment und Helden Managment bieteten viele stategische Aspekte
Cons -
- Viel Grinden
- Viel RNG

Pros:
+ Visual/Audio design is superb. Almost every action has a satisfying kick or flair to it. The art style and character designs are equally admirable.
+ It is enjoyably strategic, I feel like I appreciate turn based RPGs more because of it. The use of positioning, movement, and targeting makes you really think about how you compose your teams, especially at higher levels. "Dancing" parties, where characters are continually shuffling their position to allow others to attack, are especially fun. However, as the difficulty progresses, I felt that party compositions become a lot more restricted, which ruins some of the fun.
+ The lore is great, tying everything together, and an interesting take on the idea of the Eldritch Abomination. Each hero feels feels like a unique chracter, and I felt like I got to know their personalities, especially when they become Afflicted.
+ Ancestor's Portrait. Look at that ♥♥♥♥ing face, how can you not love it.
+ Wayne June.
Cons
- Don't be too alarmed by my hours played; it consists of at least 2 rage quit Hamlet deletions and many unnecessary hero grooming runs. However, this game still requires a lot of grinding, and I feel that a shorter, more focused experience would improve this game a lot, so that the climax at the end isn't a "♥♥♥♥ing finally. I swear to the Light if I got Calm-Creeping Cough on a hero again I'd knee the ♥♥♥♥ing screen".
- The RNG is... hmm. Losing a hero on the first death's door check is awful, but I have finished some bosses by critting so hard with a Leper that their mechanics never even factored into the battle. This makes the difficulty curve very inconsistent; many boss encounters are hard more because you get really unlucky rather than the bosses themselves being a threat. However, when RNGesus smiles upon you, you can really appreciate the outcome; the perfect crit, the Virtue right when you need it. I guess that the tone of the game is supposed to make it so these "Hero" moments stand out, while acquanting the player with the brutal nature of the game with a Treebranch Smackdown crit. Perhaps there was a way to make the RNG more feel more dire than frustrating, but in my opinion it leans more towards the latter, especially in Champion dungeons where getting Wryd Reconstruction's 0-Bleed special will get a hero killed.
- Perhaps it was because I grinded way too much before doing them, but I feel that the bosses outside of the Darkest Dungeon aren't as challenging as they could be. Lucky crits aside, I felt that I could just easily smack them until they died and deal with their gimmick with a designated hero (e.g. Arbalest for Swine Prince) or facetank/reduce their damage until they died. What I admire/dread about the Shambler fight is that it challenges you to deal with all of the threats of the boss as quickly as possible before they spiral out of control. I never got that sense of "kill them before they kill you" until the Darkest Dungeon.
While I have a lot more to say about the cons of this game, the good qualities of this game will become evident when you play it. If you don't mind committing to a game for a long time, Darkest Dungeon is a really captivating game.

A friend of mine bought this game for me and I hesitantly tried it with little-to-no expectations of it being a great game. Space MOBA? Ugh... Sounded like I might enjoy playing a game like &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Simulator 2.0" a bit more.
However, after getting in I grabbed a Corvette (one of 3 free starter ships) and went to town, supporting my team and picking off stragglers. Had a fun time doing it also. Not your traditional "healer/support class". It actually has some sharp teeth. Pleasantly surprised by the game.
The flight mechanics are fun and each ships movement feels unique. You can pilot a slow and clumsy tank, or an agile and rapidly boosting assault craft.
"Powers" are well thought out. There are a lot of abilites that are useful, nearly every ship has them. With 15 ships to choose from, that's a lot of combinations. Add to that, the crew system has a lot of potential in the future for min-maxers who wish to squeeze that last percentage point out of defense or dps and you have a game with a lot more depth than it appears on the surface.
The game looks good but in it's current early access I find that it may have syncing issues when players are coming in and out of the server or jumping from one place to another. It causes these "micro" hangups where everything freezes for a second or half a second. This might have been from free-weekend player fluxuation, but the game will likely need optimization for a successful future.
All in all I'll rank this a 7/10 with a bright future. Put on some fingerless gloves, your favorite workout clothes and man-up, this game is a good time.

Full thumbs up.  More difficult than the previous game Enemy Unknown/Within, and stays difficult longer.  That's a good thing.
XCOM has always had a reversed difficulty curve.  It starts out hard, and then gets progressively easier as you research tech.  In Enemy Unknown/Within, the first four missions on Impossible difficulty were brutal, but then the pressure dropped way off as long as you didn't screw up too badly.  XCOM2 keeps the pressure on for much longer, without resorting to arbitrary or underhanded tactics to keep it challenging.
Turn limits on missions are irritating, as is the Avatar timer that adds artifcial urgency to the pace.  They're tolerable due to being fairly generous with their limits, but if they're going to be that generous why have the timers at all?
Psionics and custom ammo are too powerful, could have been balanced a little better, but they primarily affect the second half of the game so it's not a big problem.
The re-designed Sectoid and the new Faceless and Andromedon enemies are very well done.  The new Sectopod is huge and intimidating, I love the look, but ultimately it's not that dangerous.  The enemy AI could be more aggressive with psionics as well, too often it just wastes its turn on tactically suicidal moves.
But the good far outweighs the bad.  Overall it's an incredible game.

Pros:
+ Visual/Audio design is superb. Almost every action has a satisfying kick or flair to it. The art style and character designs are equally admirable.
+ It is enjoyably strategic, I feel like I appreciate turn based RPGs more because of it. The use of positioning, movement, and targeting makes you really think about how you compose your teams, especially at higher levels. "Dancing" parties, where characters are continually shuffling their position to allow others to attack, are especially fun. However, as the difficulty progresses, I felt that party compositions become a lot more restricted, which ruins some of the fun.
+ The lore is great, tying everything together, and an interesting take on the idea of the Eldritch Abomination. Each hero feels feels like a unique chracter, and I felt like I got to know their personalities, especially when they become Afflicted.
+ Ancestor's Portrait. Look at that ♥♥♥♥ing face, how can you not love it.
+ Wayne June.
Cons
- Don't be too alarmed by my hours played; it consists of at least 2 rage quit Hamlet deletions and many unnecessary hero grooming runs. However, this game still requires a lot of grinding, and I feel that a shorter, more focused experience would improve this game a lot, so that the climax at the end isn't a "♥♥♥♥ing finally. I swear to the Light if I got Calm-Creeping Cough on a hero again I'd knee the ♥♥♥♥ing screen".
- The RNG is... hmm. Losing a hero on the first death's door check is awful, but I have finished some bosses by critting so hard with a Leper that their mechanics never even factored into the battle. This makes the difficulty curve very inconsistent; many boss encounters are hard more because you get really unlucky rather than the bosses themselves being a threat. However, when RNGesus smiles upon you, you can really appreciate the outcome; the perfect crit, the Virtue right when you need it. I guess that the tone of the game is supposed to make it so these "Hero" moments stand out, while acquanting the player with the brutal nature of the game with a Treebranch Smackdown crit. Perhaps there was a way to make the RNG more feel more dire than frustrating, but in my opinion it leans more towards the latter, especially in Champion dungeons where getting Wryd Reconstruction's 0-Bleed special will get a hero killed.
- Perhaps it was because I grinded way too much before doing them, but I feel that the bosses outside of the Darkest Dungeon aren't as challenging as they could be. Lucky crits aside, I felt that I could just easily smack them until they died and deal with their gimmick with a designated hero (e.g. Arbalest for Swine Prince) or facetank/reduce their damage until they died. What I admire/dread about the Shambler fight is that it challenges you to deal with all of the threats of the boss as quickly as possible before they spiral out of control. I never got that sense of "kill them before they kill you" until the Darkest Dungeon.
While I have a lot more to say about the cons of this game, the good qualities of this game will become evident when you play it. If you don't mind committing to a game for a long time, Darkest Dungeon is a really captivating game.

As a big Dark Souls fan, it's probably not a huge surprise that I liked this game.
I found the gameplay to be very reminscient of X-Com games, in that you alternate between a "mission" phase and a "base building" (or town/hero upkeep in this case) phase.  The different classes are interesting, and while some are probably better than others, there is enough variability to add something to the game by mix and matching different character classes on missions.  In addition, the trinket system allows for just enough equipment customization on missions in a game where you are managing 20+ characters, but not too much.
In terms of negatives, the missions can get repetitive.  The first time you are levelling your characters, it's pretty fun.  But when you lose a couple characters or expand your roster and feel like levelling additional characters, it can be a bit monotonous to go through that process again.  There are a couple of ways to give new characters an xp boost, however unless a particular town event happens, you can't send high level characters on low level missions, so you can't speed things along by pairing your newbie with a team of maxed out characters.
In addition, while I found the difficulty to be challenging, but not too hard for the most part - this game can be frustrating at times.  Even if you know what you are doing, occasionally you'll have a mission that just goes bad.  One of your guys gets randomly focused by the enemy a bunch of times, or gets hit with a big crit a couple of times in a row and suddenly you've lost a guy that you spent a lot of time levelling up.  While this doesn't happen often, it does happen enough to be a bit of a pain.
Overall though, if you take the attitude that your heroes are all disposable and try not to get too attached to any in particular, the game plays smoothly for the most part and hero losses aren't that common once you learn the basics of the game.  Also, because there is no cost to recruiting new heroes, for all the talk of this being a hard game, the reality is that you can almost always recover from any disaster by just recruiting 4 new guys and sending them into a low level mission.  This in a way makes this game easier than the X-Com games because it's actually pretty difficult to mess up your game to the point where you can't just recover with a new team (unlike X-Com where you have to pay to hire new soldiers).  And the overall difficulty does not increase based on time spent, so there's really no penalty to doing this.
The level of challenge gives a nice feeling of accomplishment when the game is won and I'd recommend Darkest Dungeon to anyone who might like the gothic style of this game and doesn't generally play on easy mode.

Look, I ain't going tell you this game is easy and I ain't going to tell you it's hard. I will tell you that depending on your ability to think ahead and adjust to the many curveballs this game will throw at you will decide the time spent and how much you will enjoy the game but the two are not mutually exclusive. You can spend very little time on the game and hate it or a very long time and love it, I am very much the latter. When I first heard about the game however many months ago, I was drawn in by its rogue art style, tactical turn-based combat, and its overall punishing, risk/reward gameplay I immediately knew I wanted the game, but not at twenty five bucks and certainly not on a console (PS4 for me as I own one) so when Steam did one of its numerous and fantastic sales and the price dropped to $15 I dropped the cash immediately and began playing even faster. There are so many pros about this game I don't have the time to go into every single one so you can watch some online review and see that for yourself but the cons are much, much more sparse and limited in that I will say there are times when it feels like the game is just "out to get you". I can't tell you how many times I'll go on a level 5 dungeon run and easily without any effort walk away with 20k gold and "ancestral" trinkets and on another run just as easily have everything go wrong, have a hero that I spent 5+hours to get to max rank one hit away from permadeath, and just overall have to abandon a dungeon run that I spent considerable resources and time to prepare for and I haven't even spent 5 minutes in. But don't get me wrong as much as I love this dungeon-crawling masterpiece there were a handful of times I couldn't look at this game and cursed it into the ground but usually by a weeks worth of time I always came back as the thought of beating that one mountain of a boss or obtaining that long sought after ancestral trinket was just too much for me to ignore. So if you're a masochist like myself and you know your way around a game like XCOM (or even Halo Wars) then whether you pick this game up for $25, $15 or even free you will enjoy it.

Best game on my list. The developers 1 year since release put out weekly patches for fixes and added much more content and character classes for free. The developer's choice to provide unwavering support for this game is an out-norm industry practice, risky but paid off incredibly well. It's well worth the money.
It's a turn based rogue-like rpg-like game where your entire party can whipe in a mission if your too greedy. Even if they are max level. It's unique difficult remained unscathed by your character progression without taking away from meaning behind character progression. The story is cthulu/poe inspired, if you like it you'll be a fan, I'm personally not a fan but the story is still okay for me.
I've spend weeks on this game building characters up only to have them gutted before I could make it to the final dungeon, I still haven't beaten it yet and taking my precious time. I've done more than 180 runs and yet touched the final level yet, I've still mostly experimented with character classes and how they combo with another, there are plenty so building your party for specific dungeons has incredible depth to them. The real progression is in the town, a home where your characters stay and build up and upgrade from plundering the dungeons, that's the only static progression in the game, all else can be whiped because character's die easily.
Most games will teach the player how to play the game and succeed. This one teaches you how to gracefully fail. The game teaches you everything you need to know but one thing which it clearly states you must learn if you ever want to complete the game, when do you call for retreat? How greedy can you get and at what cost? How far are you willing to go to get the job done? Half the time the Darkest Dungeon will leave you with choices you don't want to make but inevitably you must act.
It leaves the player with a stress or everlasting tension when playing this game, you will be at the edge of your seat constantly and rattled every time a enemy critically hits you. It will leave you with regret. The only way to play the game is on it's "True" difficulty, at the same time there is another difficulty preset in the game that you can choose to change any time; whether you run with a torch or not. If you run the gauntlet with no torches or light than the darker it gets the more powerful the enemies will spawn yet the greater the loot. I have a hard time not loosing characters with plenty of torches and I've run the dungeons in the dark as well. The difficulty is drastic but very fluid to change if your party is getting lucky and you want to maximize the loot from the raid, then snuff out the light.
There's been multiple times I've played this game losing characters and loot that I had to carry on and go for broke. I've party whiped many times all the consequence of not knowing when to retreat or ignoring so out of greed, there's been times where I've beat the boss of a dungeon with only one party member left alive, there was even a time when my party whiped and I beat the boss too but and passed the dungeon. This game really does make you exercise the distinct decision of knowing when to quit while your ahead that so that you could make that decision outside of the game.

There is a current trend among games on Steam: Microtransaction the ever-loving hell out of an Alpha release, then leave the game in perpetual Alpha state to cover the fact that the developers are raking in the dough, ever-more disinterested in actually publishing the game; result: a poorly designed, buggy game with enough financial backing to continue shoving it down your throat.
Fractured Space is NOT one of those games.
If you are unaware of what Fractured Space is, I'll sum it up: FS is a Capital Ship MOBA. I use the term "MOBA" loosely, however, as it is only a MOBA in [very general] terms of gameplay. New players will unltimately feel as though they are piloting a sluggish ship, mindlessly firing at other ships until one of them is destroyed. Beneath the surface, however, lies an intricate strategy game, backed with brief, albeit, intense battle. The strategy challenges you to know the strengths and weaknesses of each ship, and plan your attacks, positioning, posturing, and misdirections accordingly.
Some may argue that purchasing a game in such an early phase is a silly idea. I blow my nose at them! Fractured Space does what few Alphas have even bothered to bat an eye at; they give you completion! Now, before you grab your torches and pitchforks, allow me to explain. I understand that FS is nowhere NEAR a completed game, yet. There a re a lot of things to come with this game and countless directions it could take. That being said, what they HAVE given you works in its entirety. They have not provided a friend/buddy system yet, but they also didn't slap something together just to say that it's a present feature, without regard to its functionality. Any weapons that have not been implemented yet are labeled as such, so there is no question as to why it is there. At it's current state Fractured Space is a complete and functional, albeit simple, game. There's a lot of room for this game to become so much more than it already is.
I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the current trend of MOBA/RTSish/Shooting games that have been popping up on Steam. Hell, I'd say get the game just because its fun! But, if I am to be realistic, then I will say that not everyone will love this game. There's no specific reason as to why, except that no single game is ever for everyone.
To anyone who questions the purchaseable DLC, I say this: Do it if you want, or don't. there isn't much there and it
s not necessary at all. You can earn and play all the ships in realitvely short amount of time. The purchases do not grant, nor lend anyone to any form of pay-to-win. This game is solely skill-based.
TL;DR: a resounding YES! Buy this game. Revel in the fact that it works and is fun. Watch your small investment grow into an amazing game! Sneeze on haters!

This is the best F2P game I've played and even better it's a shooter!
I'll address some issues people have been mentioning in the negative reivews first.
Ping - Some people have complained about ping on the servers being too high, I've been playing on EU servers for about 2 weeks now and have never gone above 30 ping.
Hackers - I've yet to find a hacker in game but am often accused of being one.
People of other regions joining - There is a high ping auto kick system in place that doesn't allow this to happen.
Okay, now on to some of the pros.
Developers - The developers of the game from what I've witnessed have listened to the community and are often transparent through their patch streams on twitch.tv
Guns - The guns for the most part are balanced, you don't see everybody with the same assault rifles running around and each gun appears to have it's advantages and limittations.
Gameplay - I mainly play the 5v5 demolition as I've come from CS:GO, Insurgency and CoD. This mode I get the most enjoyment out of but they also have other game modes such as TDM and a protect the VIP as well as a 16 v 16 "battle mode" which I've tried and is actually really fun and unique. In terms of the 5v5 demolition the only thing I would change is the short bomb timer for the time the defending side has to defuse. It's around 45 seconds right now I believe which is very short especially if you're on the other side of the map.
Gun Mechanics - The gun mechanics feel like a mix between CS:GO and CoD. They're hard to describe in words but recoil with some guns can be a b**** and you might wanna learn to start popping heads.
Community - Overall the community within the game seems to be active with 5v5 clan wars ongoing. This being said I struggle to chat with my teammates with a lack of voice comms which should really be added into a game of this type.
Overall this game is fun, f2p, and definitely worth a shot. If you believe I left anything out of this review or wanna play sometime on EU servers feel free to add me!

Its the skyrim paid mod scandal, all over again. Only now its mixed in with microtransactions.
To note some negative factors that I learnt while researching this topic:
They removed the original skyrim from the steam store search, likely as to incentivize people buying the remastered edition for when they release paid mods for it.
Some things to note, I dont believe skyrim script extender has yet to work for the remaster and getting mods onto it was intentionally made more difficult in order to incentivize people using bethesdas propreity mod platform. In addition to being a bigger disk space product, less optimized(At least for me, I use an AMD), does not support old skyrim mods and does not support steam workshop, this product will be having paid mods implemented to it.
The content creation club seems to have some of its heftiest items already be available elsewhere, I do believe horse armor at the very least had been available elsewhere, while the some of the other armors available can be obtained for free with superior versions by modders who decided to recreate them. This kind of creates a moral quandry, the official developers are making an inferior product that you have to pay for, one made after modders made the superior quality free ones, it would be in their best interest to take it down, however I have yet to see them do so. This is something to keep your eye on.
The content creation club also downloads any and all content to your disk, so it is in effect a sort of microtransaction system, unlocking items that is already in the game and downloaded to your computer. The big issue is in the future, when there had been plenty of creations made...will this make the game bloated? Many games end up struggling under the weight of its own content at times, sims 3 was a great example, ive seen the games performance chug due to all the expansions and even WORSE with shop items. This could end up making fallout require far more space to install while at the same time making it run worse.
At the end of the day, what is this going to be? They promised to sort of curate and pay modders to make content, however it has been since revealed that modders cant really do much with the limitations bethesda has put in place and with the saying of put your best foot forward, we have gotten skins, armor that already exists for free and HORSE ARMOR. Im not really sure why the hell they decided to release horse armor for the damn game considering its a reminder of their attempt to normalize DLC as a microtransaction, the same thing they are more or less trying to do, only with mods as microtransactions instead. They got a massive backlash back then, they got a massive backlash when the original paid mods released and they are getting a massive backlash now, if I were to make an observation, it really does not seem they learn. This is clearly not near the promises they made, as what they release just makes them out to be a laughingstock.
Addendum: Apparently, plenty of the creation club items offer statistical upgrades, such as an armor that lets you go invisible or backpacks that gives special bonuses based on how it is set up. Could an argument be made for pay to win singleplayer mods? Im not really sure about this, it does mean you may be paying bethesda to get better gear to progress easier. Its even more debatable with it being downloaded with the base game and purchasable with microtransactions.
Aside from that, fallout 4 is kind of a eh game anyways.
Its....at best, alright. But it has some of the same issues the core skyrim has, except mod support isnt really as developed to help fix some of the games core problems. The gunplay was most definitely improved but they kind of have been moving on a trend to make their games less about an RPG and more about an action game, the issue is that fallout 4 tries to be some hybrid of FPS and RPG but the RPG mechanics arent really there. They implemented a sort of procedural generation to weapons but lost out on actual depth to them. The perk system is for the most part just about making you stronger, as is the weapon upgrade system. In addition to radiant quests, ironically to this game less of a focus to quests than previous games and the game kind of being a little scattered with its content, often having certain characters in the story be far more fleshed out, as the story, aside from a split to choose a faction is linear.
Specifically, you cannot sequence break, you cannot kill important characters and dialogue in this purpose was mainly set up to act as a way to advance the plot forward rather than give options or unlock alternative ways of progressing. In many cases the "Four option" dialogue system results in choices that all effectively result in the same consequence or is otherwise saying the same things in different ways. The addition of a voiced protagonist hampers this further, as it meant that they have to record your character saying this for the entire game and also meant that the voice actor in question will have to be under a heavy load. This also means they have to pay more money for any sort of splits in dialogue or potentially worry about damaging the vocal cords of the voice actor. As a result this means that the questing experience is usually linear small stories, even admitted by the development team to be made not by their writers but by whoever had the coolest ideas.
I mean, just to cut this short, because I went on quite abit with my findings. The game is...okay, if you can get it on sale. I would instead recommend you to fallout new vegas as its a pretty well set up game made by some of the same people who created fallout 1 and 2 I believe. It kind of showcases what fallout can be when set up as an RPG and was really fun.

IF I COULD REMAIN NEUTRAL ON THIS REVIEW I WOULD. I FEEL ITS GOOD BUT HAS MAJOR PROBLEMS.
Love/Hate relationship with this game. It does a lot of things well. The depth to the gameplay is fantastic. There are a variety of characters and classes in the game that are presented to you, all with very little explanation. You start off with a very weak group of heroes and if you are not careful bad luck will stab you in the back and you will lose your beloved characters. Luckily even if you lose a few heroes there is so much variety and depth to the game that it really keeps you coming back for more--even if a lot of the game is trial and error.
The problem is that after you get out of the zone where you feel like you are learning new things (generally towards the 60-80 hour mark) the game just becomes a tiresome slog. In Darkest Dungeon, you can be breezing through a dungeon and then a few unfortunate events transpire one turn after the next and you lose a character that you have long loved. Losing characters due to unfortunate circumstances grates on my nerves, and really does not feel like something you can analyze to fix for future trips through the various types of dungeons.
To further frustrate the player, the randomness is always in full effect. I have lost two characters of the same class back to back (which is bad, because there is luck involved in every aspect of this game) which becomes problematic because there are often certain heroes that work best with one another and if you lose the tank for said scenario you have to do your best with a lesser grouping.
If you do not want to brave a higher level dunegeon with a lesser group, you have to hope you have enough adventurers at a lower level to run lower level dungeons (which are less risky after you gather the right trinkets). Even then, you have to wait until after the dungeon to see if you can recruit a brand new level 3 hero fresh off the recruitment cart--the levels of characters that come off the cart are random and seemingly the level 3s are exceedingly rare. So there is a lot of hoping and praying involved in getting the right class and the right level combination at the right time.
You run into a lot of problems because of how random everything is. Lets say you have an abundance of crusaders and all that keeps popping up are a bunch of crusaders in the cart (which happens more than you would think), then you have to go through a dungeon, then randomly another non crusader dies due to bad luck, this then allows the problem to compound (this can happen with a variety of classes and then you are forced into compositions that are less than ideal all the time).
In my particular game, I have a problem where I need hellions, vestals, abominations, and plague doctors. Vestals and abominations refuse to group with one another so essentially I need 8 separate low level people just to hope to god I can get them up to level 6. I may be able to get by with a few less than 8, but people level up at different rates so one person can out level others and such...another fun part of the randomness of the game.
In my situation, i haven't seen a plague doctor above level 0 in about 60 dungeons (which is bad luck, and unbelievably annoying, and at this point its inhibiting my progress--and enjoyment--in the game). I am stuck trying to fight bosses with compositions that I know are not ideal because i do not have ~ 2 of each hero class. More like i have 3 of a hand full of classes and 0 of a bunch of other classes so instead of running the same tedious level 5 dungeons over and over and over (which have long since lost their luster and where i can no longer really get any trinkets of additional value) i try and finish out the dungeons with bosses (of which i only have a couple left) with a less than ideal group of characters. It doesn't work out great. But god knows I am tired of waiting for heroes of the correct class to show up in the cart.
It's very frustrating because when the gameplay is fair its a fun game. When the gameplay randomly screws you over--time and time again--it becomes frustrating. When it seems like the game has been conspiring against you for 60 turns it becomes even more abysmal.
Its a good game, but there are a lot of problems with it fundamentally. Its like progress just stops after the 80 hour mark unless you are lucky. Or unless you refuse to take risks. Or you enjoy replaying the same type of encounters 30 times to level up a new group of heroes (bear in mind you've probably already ran these dungeons ~500+ times at this point). I find tirelessly slogging through perfect dungeons with perfect comps unneccessarily boring after awhile so i would rather take risks which results in characters possibly dying, which makes me roll my eyes and further makes me want to stop enduring the game.
I'll undoubtedly try and get back into the game again, but at this point im about 100 hours into the game and am extremely frustrated. I still recognize the quality of the game and the depth but there is a lot of stuff that really gets in the way of an enjoyable strategic experience.
That's aside from the game randomly trying to literally stress you out with sudden jump scares and noises and stressful crap happening every 5 seconds in the game. I get that its part of the game, but it honestly gets tiresome when you're this deep in the game and just is another thing that makes you not want to play.
At this point i'm very in between recommending it and not recommending it. I like being able to finish games and this is ruining the entire experience.
P.S. After editing this review months later I found that I was getting stressed out just reading my own review of the game that I did essentially give up on. Maybe that's fair warning enough to anyone who would want to take on this game. May just be best to steer clear.

This is a really good game, but make no mistake, it's a really hard game too. There are a few casual games out there that are just really tough, and as a result, frustrating at times. The Binding of Isaac is a good example of that - no RNG love, no win - and yet the game is still great fun.
Well... Darkest Dungeon is that kind of game. It's in the title. It's also in the loading screen, where the devs warn you the sort of game it is. It's gritty. I'd imagine real dungeoneering is nothing short of hard, demoralising and ultimately soul-sapping. And that's what you have to deal with here - heroes that get stressed, and you need to manage that stress. You need to send them to a brothel to bang some random 'ho to unwind. You need to send them to the sanitarium to get psychological help to remove their hang-ups. In short, you have to have a steady stream of heroes so you can give them time out to rest.
Oh, and don't get too attached to them all - they'll die.
But why do I like it? Mainly because it's hard, and fun. There is great variety in the hero class skills, and finding good combinations is an absolute key to success. Also, knowing when to pull out is also really important... (do I take the joke, or just leave it???) But seriously, knowing when to leave the dungeon will actually save your team at times.
This is a game of experimenting. And yes, it's a game of RNG luck as well to an extent. So you will probably want to punch your screen at times. But frankly, it's addictive. It's rare for me to clock up 30 hrs on a casual game in 2 weeks.
About the only negative comment (apart from all the cursing I'm doing) is it's not as cheap as most casual-type games. Maybe get it on sale if possible...

Now, keep in mind this is an early access game, and I'm not much of a fan of MOBAs to begin with, so take everything in this review with a grain of salt...
Fractured Space is basically Dota, but in space. Also 3D. And there's only a handful of "characters" (read: ships) to choose from, though you can customize your ships with different unlockable equipment and crew. Minions and turrets have been replaced with capturable bases which provide some sort of bonus to your team's ships, though what those bonuses are isn't entirely clear; maybe I need to watch some more tutorials.
But the one thing that ruins it for me is the pacing. You know how in Dota, you can run up and attack someone, then run away if you take too much damage? Well, in Fractured Space, you can't really do that. Ships are so slow and ponderous that by the time you turn around and retreat, you're practically dead. And yes, you do have a hyperjump option, but if you use that, your ship is immobilized for a few seconds, during which time it takes massive damage (like, maybe 10 times?) from enemy attacks. So it's pretty much useless unless you somehow get lucky enough to be able to retreat with normal movement without the enemy tracking you down. Maybe I'm just not skilled enough, but it seems to me that this turns the game into basically a meat grinder where you attack, hope you don't die, if you die you wait to respawn, rinse and repeat. I know there's the strategic aspect of capturing the bases, but without decent combat mechanics, it doesn't really hold up. If the devs can fix this (maybe make the ships a bit more maneuverable, or add afterburners that have a limited amount of fuel) then I could see this being a good game, but as it stands, I'm just really not feeling it. <insert picture of Shulk here>
I do like the female Russian captain though. She reminds me of an older, ♥♥♥♥♥ier version of Captain Janeway. "We lost a ship! Oh well, we didn't need them anyway..."

God, I love so much about this game. Really, I love it. But it's soooo hard to recommend this game because I would like to keep my friends.
WOW, is it stressful. And that is the point, I get it...most things are challenging but a few things in the game are incredibly unfair (don't confuse the two).
On the one hand, I love that the game designers made a real challenge, but on the other hand they take full control way from the player. The actual gameplay is great! It's challenging, dark, has a lot of strategy, and it is a lot of fun 90% of the time. I loved the setting, the stories, the difficulty of the actual fights, and the upgrading system.
BUT there are THREE things in this game that make is just plain unfair. Pull-your-hair-out unfair. Like, “what were they thinking?!” unfair.
1. You can’t use your skills outside of combat. So no healing unless you’re being attacked. No mana bar, no healing potions either. This doesn’t make sense from a role-playing perspective. I get why it’s there, but it’s…frustrating. It's managable, but it takes control away from the player and breaks the fantasy immersion.
2. You don’t keep the items you buy! This drives me insane! You spend so much money on provisions every time you go on a quest and any left-overs just…vanish. It doesn’t make any sense! It's stupid. It’s just stupid. It’s here for the sake of being hard. No other RPG has this, and real life doesn't have it! Game designers: if you can see this, screw you for this one.
3. You have to bring food with you and that heals you a teeny bit when you eat..okay, fair right? But if you don’t eat it when the game tells you to...you lose HP. So you can’t eat early or you risk getting hungry…which again makes no sense! Everyone gets hungry at the same time even if they have eaten so you might as well never heal with food. And when you eat you gain 1-3 hp but lose 6-8 hp when you don’t!!! This is so stupid!
People who like this game…I like it to, I really do. I love Lovecraft, I want to keep playing, I want to enjoy it more, but every time I play it I get really stressed out and I need to de-stress like my characters. Games sholdn't feel like second jobs that are harder than your actual job.

Got to SFC Step 4 in 12 hours.  Was entertaining for a bit, but too arcadey for my personal taste.
It plays like Unreal Tournament with objectives, if you're playing Battle Mode, the best mode, which has a 4 classes, each with their own deal that cost skill points to use in Battle.
You get points in battle mostly by attacking enemy boxes (most people use knives for +12 points each quick swipe and not as much noise as weapon fire), which you spend on skills, like Claymore, UAV Recon, and some high-tier 1000 point skills like air strikes and artillery.
Doesn't seem like the Command's Helicopter Support is working at the moment, though.  It's mostly a 300 XP pinata right now.  Fortunately, Command has AT4, which can be a boon or a cancer, depending on if you're using it, or it's being used to one-shot you like the Quake Rocket Launcher: bunny-hop one-shots, often multi-kills, and accurate at all ranges, so you can shoot them at people and objectives, through windows etc.
You at least get warning when air strikes and artillery are coming at you, but there's no teamkill damage, so you can just fire at will with whatever support options you have, unless you frag or air strike yourself.
Teammates can block your shots, though.  Lost more than a few AT4 to people running right in front of it.  Ended up killing myself once this way: guy moved in front at the last second, he got hit in the back of the head, and I died from my own explosion.  Genius.
This game really needs teamkill damage.  Otherwise, there isn't much thought put into your skill use other than where to put it.  If your friendlies are in the air strike area right now: send it, they'll be fine.
Gunplay needs some work.  As is, submachine guns are super-accurate at any range you can get the shot on, and shotguns are obscenly powerful well past believable range, and bolt-action sniper rifles are capable of one-shotting people in the knee while the sniper is bunny-hopping.
Snipers are racking up the big scores right now, because Recon+bolt action tends to be like having an ESP hack with a one-shot weapon, so snipers are leading killboards each game.  I didn't even want to buy the bolt-action, because I was already an AT4/Shotty cancer player, and I didn't want to become a Claymore/Hellpike/Bolt Action cancer player, too.
The balance in this game needs more work, but it is in early access, so please leave feedback on wherever the devs are listening.
Overall, I enjoyed my time in, but I'll wait to see what happens as it develops after leaving my feedback on the issues I saw.

This game truly is a landmark, a new innovation within the Turn-Based Dungeon Crawler games.
The developers of this game introduced so many new things, and they got told that it would be terrible but they proved everyone wrong, showing that you can still innovate in this genre.
And they also added options to turn off some of the stuff that a lot of people dislike, one of which is that you can disable the feature that makes enemies leave behind corpses after they die.
This game is a dice-rolling game and I'm generally not a fan of games that include a ton of RNG but this game is different, it doesn't try to ♥♥♥♥ you over around literally every corner. But at the same time it's hard.
The game is centered around making the best out of a terrible situation.
The narrator for this game is a god-tier voice actor.
He adds so much to the atmosphere of the game and makes for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic moments when you do huge crits and stuff like that and the narrator jumps in with one of his epic lines.
Or when you're in a tide of sorrow and the voice actor reminds you of your situation.
The game supports modding and editing of game files(and doesn't punish players for doing so).
But be warned before you go into this game, you will fail.
You will face terrible situations and heart crushing losses in battle.
If you can't handle that, if you're the kind of person that quits a game right after you lose something big then there is no reason at all for you to buy this game.
You will fail many times as you start but you will also make epic victories which leave you with a feeling of hunger for more.
The game somehow manages to keep you addicted and coming pack despite your moments of frustration, loss and dismay.
The art style is amazing, a blend of gothic art, Lovecraftian art and all the like.
A negative thing I want to note about this game is the sheer length of it.
The developer claims that,
, it takes about 80 hours of play-time to complete the story, and that is a little bit too long for me.
And sometimes you have to question your sanity considering the hell your going through and then reminding your self that you're not even close to reaching the finish line.
But do not fear as the developers, as of posting this, have said they will add a shorter story mode which they claim will take,
, around 40 hours to complete.
As I said, this game is a stepping-stone in this category of games and is a must-buy.
Forever in our hearts!

There are a lot of improvements on this game that could make it more enjoyable than XCOM enemy unknown. Character custimization, weapon mods, melee combat, stealth mode and a cool story line for example.  However, the addition of so many timed missions completely ruin the game for me.  I really enjoyed xcom enemy unkown's turn based tactical shooting style and expected the same from this game. Every move of every turn required planning, for both that character and the squad as a whole.  Having a strategy to tackle the mission was essential along with the ability to adapt to unkown enemies that you didn't see.   Instead, the timed missions of XCOM 2, which seem to make up the overwhelming majority of missions, force you to play a blitz style game. This is a really good game, but make no mistake, it's a really hard game too. There are a few casual games out there that are just really tough, and as a result, frustrating at times. The Binding of Isaac is a good example of that - no RNG love, no win - and yet the game is still great fun.
Well... Darkest Dungeon is that kind of game. It's in the title. It's also in the loading screen, where the devs warn you the sort of game it is. It's gritty. I'd imagine real dungeoneering is nothing short of hard, demoralising and ultimately soul-sapping. And that's what you have to deal with here - heroes that get stressed, and you need to manage that stress. You need to send them to a brothel to bang some random 'ho to unwind. You need to send them to the sanitarium to get psychological help to remove their hang-ups. In short, you have to have a steady stream of heroes so you can give them time out to rest.
Oh, and don't get too attached to them all - they'll die.
But why do I like it? Mainly because it's hard, and fun. There is great variety in the hero class skills, and finding good combinations is an absolute key to success. Also, knowing when to pull out is also really important... (do I take the joke, or just leave it???) But seriously, knowing when to leave the dungeon will actually save your team at times.
This is a game of experimenting. And yes, it's a game of RNG luck as well to an extent. So you will probably want to punch your screen at times. But frankly, it's addictive. It's rare for me to clock up 30 hrs on a casual game in 2 weeks.
About the only negative comment (apart from all the cursing I'm doing) is it's not as cheap as most casual-type games. Maybe get it on sale if possible...
Dive in. Have fun. Die. Repeat.

God, I love so much about this game. Really, I love it. But it's soooo hard to recommend this game because I would like to keep my friends.
WOW, is it stressful. And that is the point, I get it...most things are challenging but a few things in the game are incredibly unfair (don't confuse the two).
On the one hand, I love that the game designers made a real challenge, but on the other hand they take full control way from the player. The actual gameplay is great! It's challenging, dark, has a lot of strategy, and it is a lot of fun 90% of the time. I loved the setting, the stories, the difficulty of the actual fights, and the upgrading system.
BUT there are THREE things in this game that make is just plain unfair. Pull-your-hair-out unfair. Like, “what were they thinking?!” unfair.
1. You can’t use your skills outside of combat. So no healing unless you’re being attacked. No mana bar, no healing potions either. This doesn’t make sense from a role-playing perspective. I get why it’s there, but it’s…frustrating. It's managable, but it takes control away from the player and breaks the fantasy immersion.
2. You don’t keep the items you buy! This drives me insane! You spend so much money on provisions every time you go on a quest and any left-overs just…vanish. It doesn’t make any sense! It's stupid. It’s just stupid. It’s here for the sake of being hard. No other RPG has this, and real life doesn't have it! Game designers: if you can see this, screw you for this one.
3. You have to bring food with you and that heals you a teeny bit when you eat..okay, fair right? But if you don’t eat it when the game tells you to...you lose HP. So you can’t eat early or you risk getting hungry…which again makes no sense! Everyone gets hungry at the same time even if they have eaten so you might as well never heal with food. And when you eat you gain 1-3 hp but lose 6-8 hp when you don’t!!! This is so stupid!
People who like this game…I like it to, I really do. I love Lovecraft, I want to keep playing, I want to enjoy it more, but every time I play it I get really stressed out and I need to de-stress like my characters. Games sholdn't feel like second jobs that are harder than your actual job.

This game truly is a landmark, a new innovation within the Turn-Based Dungeon Crawler games.
The developers of this game introduced so many new things, and they got told that it would be terrible but they proved everyone wrong, showing that you can still innovate in this genre.
And they also added options to turn off some of the stuff that a lot of people dislike, one of which is that you can disable the feature that makes enemies leave behind corpses after they die.
This game is a dice-rolling game and I'm generally not a fan of games that include a ton of RNG but this game is different, it doesn't try to ♥♥♥♥ you over around literally every corner. But at the same time it's hard.
The game is centered around making the best out of a terrible situation.
The narrator for this game is a god-tier voice actor.
He adds so much to the atmosphere of the game and makes for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic moments when you do huge crits and stuff like that and the narrator jumps in with one of his epic lines.
Or when you're in a tide of sorrow and the voice actor reminds you of your situation.
The game supports modding and editing of game files(and doesn't punish players for doing so).
But be warned before you go into this game, you will fail.
You will face terrible situations and heart crushing losses in battle.
If you can't handle that, if you're the kind of person that quits a game right after you lose something big then there is no reason at all for you to buy this game.
You will fail many times as you start but you will also make epic victories which leave you with a feeling of hunger for more.
The game somehow manages to keep you addicted and coming pack despite your moments of frustration, loss and dismay.
The art style is amazing, a blend of gothic art, Lovecraftian art and all the like.
A negative thing I want to note about this game is the sheer length of it.
The developer claims that,
, it takes about 80 hours of play-time to complete the story, and that is a little bit too long for me.
And sometimes you have to question your sanity considering the hell your going through and then reminding your self that you're not even close to reaching the finish line.
But do not fear as the developers, as of posting this, have said they will add a shorter story mode which they claim will take,
, around 40 hours to complete.
As I said, this game is a stepping-stone in this category of games and is a must-buy.

Pros:  Overall, they managed to make the game different, while keeping or expanding upon what makes Xcom one of my favorite games ever.
-Base-building is less annoying
-The new classes are interesting and cool
-Weapon mods and PCS were a good, interesting addition
-They removed the Scope which was too good and almost everyone used
-They took a note from Long War and allowed more varied items to be used early in the game
-The difficulties are imo done better
-Scientists and Engineers are less numerous and more significant, and they have their own appearances
-The modding scene has been great (turn off the timers instead of crying about it, but I think they're fine, and aren't as punishing as they were in timed EW/LW)
-You can re-spec troops
-More interesting options for grenades/armor
-Hacking is an enjoyable addition
-The Grappling hook is much cooler because it and many more things now DO NOT end your turn
-Instead of Interceptors and original-Gameboy-quality space battes, you get to travel around Earth and gather the nodes you think are most important
-This game is better than a 75% approval rating
Cons:
*The game runs far too poorly, so be aware (there are some fixes/recommendations available on the interwebz)
-The music is probably a little bit worse than in the other one
-The Mimic Beacon is overpowered
-You run out of research by the end of the game, which seems poorly balanced
-No MECS or gene mods yet (but they kinda still exist in other forms)
-A lot of the changes they made to the UI were imo downgrades
