If you loved XCOM: Enemy Unknown, you'll love XCOM 2; it's that simple.
They clearly listened to the fans and made a lot of little adjustments that get rid of little problems that occurred before (e.g. ammo is much easier to keep track of now, and upgraded armor takes effect on everyone), as well as establishing a new plotline that actually justifies a lot of the gameplay features that had some Fridge Logic before (e.g. "Why do we have so little funding?" and "Why are our soldiers mostly green recruits?"). They add enough new mechanics to keep it interesting (particularly Concealment), but few enough that it still feels like the same game.
The Grenadier and Sharpshooter classes will be largely familiar as variations on the old Heavy and Sniper, but the Ranger is radically different from the Assault and the Specialist is AMAZING and even better than the already-powerful Support class. Psionics are now more mutually exclusive from the other classes (and as a result I found myself not using them all that much).
The expanded character creation system is amazing, and allows you to even get attached to your soldiers ACROSS GAMES---if you save them to the character pool, the same names and faces will pop up on following playthroughs.
The biggest changes are twofold:
1. A lot more timed missions, which require a new style of play and annoyed a lot of people. Personally I like them, but find them a bit too hard; there are a couple of mods that recalibrate them by making the timers a bit longer or making them not activate until you break concealment, and with those on they're great.
2. The macro game has been totally revamped, and as a result takes some getting used to. The old "spam satellites like there's no tomorrow" has no equivalent, and you now want to reject a lot more missions---including Retaliation missions, the equivalent of Terror missions in the previous game. All the base structures work differently (even the power plants!). Engineers and scientists work differently---but also in a way that makes more sense. (You can no longer build structures to somehow magically acquire engineers.) The Avatar Project timer is terrifying, but not as bad as it looks---you can let the aliens get pretty close to finishing the project and still win if you complete enough story objectives or take out enough alien bases.
I still have some mixed feelings about the choices they made for the plot progression (especially the Codex); but in general it is a worthy successor to previous XCOM games and I look forward to DLC and maybe even expansions.

Despite the negative reviews claiming the RNG in this game is broken and/or skewed to be unfair to the player, I highly enjoy this game and would argue that the RNG is calculated how it should be.
Don't get me wrong - this game is BRUTAL. I've lost more heroes than I can count, lost a ton of gold, and almost cried when I barely managed to escape with one hero left and twice as much gold as I had to spend to start the quest. Yes, you will lose heroes. You'll lose your favorite ones, the ones you've babied since day 1, the ones you thought were your tanks, the ones you don't care about. You'll lose your money (a lot), and sometimes you'll get lucky.  When you get lucky, it's almost as relieving to the player as it seems to be for the characters in-game. (I can't tell you how many times I've almost had a heart attack when I wait for the reaction to max stress in the middle of a boss fight)
I've played a little bit of Dark Souls (and I'm garbage at it), and I'd say this is a comparable experience to it. It's brutal. It's painful. You're probably a masochist (or a sadist if you like watching them suffer repeatedly) if you play it for extended periods of time.  But it's still fun as hell.  If you're looking for an RPG/Dungeon Crawler style game that requires a little more effort than point, click, dead - you should give Darkest Dungeon a shot.
(Also shout-out to the devs, you guys have done so much work on it recently and it doesn't seem like you plan to stop anytime soon; love you devs ♥)

The Darkest Dungeon prides itself on its difficult and yet it doesn't realize that "difficuity" is the singluar reason why it fails as a game. Dark Souls might be hard but it is rewarding and doesn't erase hours of work by chance. This game doesn't realize that players don't want to be punished for trying out new rotations and left to rot because their team wasn't strong enough to stand against the over reliance of the game's RNG. While the beginning might be wonderful, but when the honeymoon is over the player will quickly realize that everything turns to a monochromatic grind for the sake of a one single team whose luck outlives the games whimsical system.
Do I recommand the Darkest Dungeon? Only to the people who likes grinding for chance of a lucky run and have the stomach of losing, repeativily, hours of work.
Edit 1: Just to clairfy this game has this weird thing where it likes to jump difficuity levels to keep you on your toes. That means when you've finally get a team to level 3 you have to directly jump into a level 3 dungeon. Level 2 dungeons don't exist therefore you can't even choose to play slowly and careful. The game makes you put your party in danger. So, if the run doesn't go well not only does your hours of hardwork to train the level 3 team go to waste in the best case scenario your game progress is impeded by a large margin. Therefore, prepare to grind mutiple teams to level 3 before you attempt a level 3 dungeon otherwise with one bad run, then your back to grinding level 1 dungeons.

This is ♥♥♥♥ing 2015 where players have to pay to test a product but Edge Case Games knows how valuable testers can be to your final product.
The free weekend is actually what got me into this game ^_^
Now I haven't spend many hours yet into this game but I will spend a lot more, because it is a very nice game. The graphics are neat, I can play everything at max settings (1080p) without the slightest performance drop in large battles.
The ships are a bit customizeable and you can choose in which you want your ship excell (for example blink distance over blink cooldown time).
It has a "skilltree" with at the moment 3 factions with each their own ships. To unlock a certain ship you'll have to spend a couple of battles in that corresponding faction.
The battle system is quite balanced as in the experienced players get with the newbies so it won't become pros vs noobs (haven't experienced it yet at least).So basically the teams have a fair chance at winning, because you can fight strong and weak opponents. There is also an assist counter which rewards funds and xp.
The interface is
easy to understand. There is no tutorial or whatsoever (or I might've skipped it accidently..) that explains the mechanics but through a couple of minutes of trial and error you will understand the basics.
It is fairly easy to attain goods for your ship(s) to unlock further upgrades/ships.
I haven't encountered major buggs that wrecks your gameplay so far, the only annoying bug that I found is a sound bug, when you close the reward screen before the counter is finished you will have that sound until you get to the same interface again.
Joining some servers that are too far away causes the client to crash, but there are enough servers out there to play on. In my situation, I can't go on US servers but I can join any UK servers.
So apart from the buggs and minor flaws this game is actually really dang good! But it is still in alpha so I won't critize every single small thing. The way they are heading is good, fingers crossed for a good finished product.

Great RTS.
Resources:
There are five resources: Food, Wood, Gold, Population, & Export. Food & Gold become no problem later game with buildings to supply an infinite amount (Mills & Plantations). Wood is the only true limited resource but only on some maps where the supply is smaller. Export is only for the Asian Civilizations. Population is maxed at 200 per player.
Pathfinding & Building Placement:
Pathfinding can be awful at times, escpecially when two groups are selected one of which is already at the destination if you send them to the destination the group already there will leave and meet the other group halfway then walk back to the destination as one group. There are pros and cons of this but more commonly than not it is a con.
Building placement is pretty good the only complaint is that it's a 3D game but you can't rotate buildings? You can supposedly get a mod for this but it's disappointing that it's not included with the game.
Balance:
There are some overpowered units in the game such as Covered Wagons (Germans) and the Organ Guns (Portuguese) but they're just ridiculous at killing their 1-2 types of units (Cavalry/Buildings & Infantry/Buildings respectively) but insanely weak against the others (Infantry & Cavalry respectively). So there is balance but if they catch you off-guard you're doom. Though I suppose that adds a higher level of competitiveness.
AI:
They're alright, but they are not different really than any other AI from other RTSs. Spam workers, pretend to be gathering resources but cheat all day and build whatever you want (based on difficulty level). They have very simple surrender-terms. They surrender on 2 conditions: 1) They have no villager producing buildings (Town Centers). 2) They have little to no Villagers.
Replayability:
They have cards that you receive once per level and you can use them in-game to receive various bonuses. (Some for your entire team). These also have tiers Lv. 10/25/40 (You start Lv. 10 unless you already have a 'HomeCity' of that civilization). These are nice to keep you playing but could be insanely better. Most are not really a choice, there are a few good picks but overall they lack in true-choice. Nevertheless, even if you find that you'd rather just continue playing and have all the cards from the start you can just go into the simple .xml file and give yourself all the cards that you want for every civilization.
Overall Rating:

Unfortunately I have to admit that it isn´t as much fun as I thought it would be. For me personally it is still quite a good game but the promise of a difficult game only holds up as far as the system oftentimes seems to be rigged against you. A false kind of difficulty if you will.
The amazing visuals and great animations together with a very clear menues and interfaces help you keep track of everything rather well (some negative points you will only find to be annoying later on but I´ll get to that). So it is easy enough to keep track of everything and pretty quickly (maybe 5 hours) you will have figured out how to play the game and will go on to think about more advanced strategies. The amazing voiceactor helps a lot keeping you going through the beginning as well.
That unfortunately is where I have to get to the negative points already.
After figuring out what is going on and how to deal with it to the best of your ability the main gameplay and a lot of the mechanics will get to be pain pretty quickly and be in a harsh contrast to how amazing everything felt in the beginning.
The biggest point is unfortunately the repetitiveness of it for the difficulty it hurls at you. Being the Dark Souls of it´s genre (whatever that means anyways) is fine when it would just be about the difficulty alone. But unfortunately you don´t have it in your hand, it increasingly will be a game of luck rigged against you. Your job of course is to figure out ways to eliminate risks or the % of them while letting your strenghts shine as often and reliably as possible. Think of it this way: You practiced backstabbing and countering blows in DS for the first 5 hours and now you are ready to go on to fight some stronger enemies in another area (aka Dungeon).
Good difficulty: You manage to eliminate enemies just as reliably with backstabs and counters as you did with the weaker ones before, but the game throws more enemies at you, some of which have faster movement sets or remain hidden until you engage in battle with another enemy or you find their hiding spot, so it is much harder to 1 vs 1 enemies. But if you are paying enough attention the game works just as smooth as you can play it.
Bad difficulty: Stronger enemies will have 50% chance to block and counter backstabs. Your weapons break quicker and you will constantly have to go and repair them because a broken weapon means 0 damage. More enemies will pop up out of nowhere once you are in battle, with a 30% chance a surprise attack will instantly kill you but of course there is no way to prevent that chance really (maybe 5% reduction with a good ring) because like said they just pop out of nowhere. Deaths btw. will lose you 2-3 hours of leveling.
Because I want to mention a few more details that aren´t important for the review itself for people just thinking about buying this game, you can skip my babbling to the last paragraph for the conclusion:
Here I want to mention some of the negative points that I noticed were diminishing my fun with the gameplay experience
(please do mind that this is after about less than 20 hours and with no warranty to be right, just some points that I want to mention specifically):
- A lot of times there is an aspect of "realism" like backtracking through dungeon parts you have already explored just to make it more challenging. I could very much do with a fog of war over the map until an exploration ability triggers and unveils the whole map and a smaller part of it in a detailed manner. Like it is now with so many goals stating "explore 90%" or "explore 100%" of the rooms in a dungeon and I walk into it seeing that I have to walk in two directions and the dungeon is split up pretty much 50/50 to each side, why can´t we sacrifice a little bit of that "realism" for convenience and give me a portal to drop somewhere before walking into a dead end and then having to backtrack all the way through almost empty rooms. It is also the wrong kind of difficult because my team will get more stressed out and require additional food when there is nothing I can do about it.
- Now I guess due to the limitations of being an "indiegame" founded on kickstarter this would just blow the budget and timelimitations out of the water but teams of five people would just be so much more fun. Not for the reason of making it less difficult, of course everything would need to be rebalanced but just the strategy aspect of building a team would be so much better when I can actually have one member free to say "I want to grind faster I will take another damage dealer" or "I lost too many ressources the last missions I will take someone to get me more loot" without constantly sacrificing another totally "must have" for it. Right now sure you can take a team with more damage, either through abilites or replacing a one spot with a slightly different member. But what I am talking about is one place where you can actually change the pace of the game, one spot that would allow for individuality in gameplay. But as said, I am very much aware that it is not possible as it stands now because of obvious limitations which is not the devs fault but it would up the fun I have with the game by a lot so I wanted to mention it.
- The grinding and repetivtiveness of it is in great but due to the slow exp gain. Especially for the beginning when one dungeon can get a hero to level 1 already I do wonder if it is absolutely needed that all new members are level 0 at first. I feel like with a bit of rebalancing (mainly in the gold department) giving a quicker start for new teams by having the caravarn already be at what is the first improvement state would help a get rid of a bit of the unnecessary grinding.
- I like the aspect of getting ambushed when you rest on a bonefire in enemy territory but when someone is scouting the area or there are teammembers with full health and no stress I feel like there should be a chance to prevent getting ambushed just as much as I would like to be less likely suprised by enemies when I already know that there will be a fight because of the scouting.
- Amulets should give some teambuffs, right now all I saw where individual buffs for the character that you equip it on but I would like more ways to have a team synergy
- more natural stressreduction
I personally do like the game still, there are a lot of negative points that I have made but I still played for almost 20 hours so far and will get to 30 eventually (but quite honestly I searched for something I could sink around 200 hours into which I certainly won´t). The thing is...I can´t recommend the game to my friends or others. The game is advertised as difficult and there is nothing wrong about that in itself. Unfortunately though the game is just too repetitive for how difficult it is, when the difficulties are not there to test my skill of the game but to keep me locked in mindless grinding missions. It is a timewaste unfortunately, whenever it sacrifies fun for difficulty just for the reason of getting it marketed like that and it becomes pretty obvious that the system they created could work very well but they chose to rig it against you. And some people seem to get it wrong: Frustration is not something that you want in your game as a developer, Difficulty should be a challenge aimed to question your decisions and strategies, not to create a barrier of frustration that needs to be overcome to go on (while it may sound very heroic it is a "game" after all). I personally am mature enough to admit that a loser-mode would be more of my style. It doesn´t have to be easygoing and everyone should have the option to play the game as difficult as it is intended to be played right now and get an archievement for that but I would rather sacrifice some of the "realism" and "difficulty" (when it isn´t there to test my skillset) aspects of it for the simple and blatant reason of just having fun with an otherwise great and well executed concept.

I don't know why they went into this direction that XCOM EU players had a hard time and gave up fighting for the Earth. It's like they tried Impossible Ironman started the game had all four rookies killed and just went with the message that the XCOM program has been cancelled.  And the aliens won and took over our planet. I felt like someone just decided to base the new XCOM 2 on those who thought the game was hard. If you want imppsible  play the original X-COM. I played over a thousand hours playing XCOM EU  because of its replayability. It is hard and frustrating at first but if you play ironman so many times you get used to it but then you get to learn how to really play.  I had to think of ways to play better and how to get the correct research to beat certain missions.  This XCOM 2 is so linear that after completing it once, I feel like I'm done. There is no fun in playing it again because it lack the variety.  It didn't give the players much option of how I should win the game. There was only one way to play the game And its the rush through and blow up as many bases as I can. I am a bit disappointed that the aliens did not try to intercept the Avenger as often as they should.  And why doesnt the avenger have space for two interceptors to engage who ever was attacking the avenger. And missions was limited to getting supplies, intel and guerilla operations only?  Honestly XCOM EU had way more missions.
This game should've been more like a DLC for those players who lost in XCOM EU. And for those who managed to win at XCOM EU, we should at least have a better game. You know something like Independence day 2 where we did win and we used alien technology to improve our defenses but the aliens came back bigger and stronger and we should've been able to import our old charactes from XCOM EU.  And maybe import the tech we did back then so that what ever research we did could be carried over to XCOM 2. Believe me it would be more fun if I can import my XCOM EU into XCOM 2. But since you guys didnt do that so we all start from scratch. One more thing, I want to see aliens on the missions and NOT Advent. Why have a picture of s sectoid on XCOM 2 if I meet more Advent than I meet umm say a Chrysallid, Muton or Sectoid. And seriously XCOM EU terror missions were harder than the terror missions now.
XCOM 2 for me was a a good game but not replayable. Graphics and customizations are awesome but I feel like they rushed the game and didnt think really hard about how they could make it better than last time. Did you ever wonder why X-COM back in the 1990's was memorable? Because of its replayability for players to try different ways to win. Some players take a long time to finish a UFO mission some are fast. Now everyone should just play it one way because of the timer. And the list of achievements are not that fun its only 50 compared to the 85 that XCOM EU had. Anyway it was a nice game, but I think I will go back XCOM EU and play it on Impossible Ironman and have my four rookies get killed and get the XCOM program cancelled ( I tried it and I still got completed it with three rookies remaining )so that I can follow the backstory for playing XCOM 2.

It's fun if you can deal with the slow pace. After all, you are flying a capital ship. If you chose the heavy class, you will be about as fast as a snail. You can upgrade your ship a bit to make it somewhat faster but....you'll still be very, very slow. With so many fast paced games out there, this can be very, very annoying and just too much to bear for quite a few gamers out there. I know this, because I was lucky enough to be able to listen to the whining, ehm, I mean the complaints of friends I tried to reel in during the free 2 play weekend . There are faster ships than the heavy cruisers that make it somewhat more bearable, but they also don't get to have a trillion HP.
It can get quite hectic once in a fire fight and the game also relies on you playing as a team. Fighting alone is a very stupid idea. No matter your ship type, aside from capturing points, one should never run off alone or one will most certainly be picked off by the enemy, since only support class ships have the speed to actually "run away" without warping to another system, which in turn makes you very vulnerable to dmg, as "in 2-3 hits dead" vulnerable.
The game has quite a bit of strategy to it, but nothing overly complicated. It's easy enough to grasp and after 1 or 2 matches you get the idea of what's going on and what you're supposed to be doing.
How a match plays out, as in what you should be doing to win, is a placeholder atm, according to a dev. Which is a good thing because at the moment, it's a bit soo simple and unbalanced. Still, you have quite a lot of ships for an Alpha that really play differently too, not just some skin changes with a novelty skill thrown in.
For example: There are 2 attack type ships I really enjoy. Attack ships need to get up close and personal and then devastate the opponent ship in a matter of moments. So how best to close in? One of them "blinks", like the protoss stalker units in SC2. It can teleport short distances. This not only teleports you right next to your foe, but also away from the line of fire, almost always confusing your attackers. Very cool to play as and to fight against. The other one has a harpoon. Yep, a harpoon in space. It's oddly satisfying pulling a heavy cruiser towards you and your mates from afar, or a sniper, or a weak support ship. Just don't make the mistake of pulling in an attack ship. You might win, but afterwards, you're always as good as dead.
There are others, like the sniper, assassin (cloak stealth), support ships (all can heal and have some additional support abilities) and quite a few more I haven't mentioned, since I haven't tried them out yet.
You'll have to unlock all ships first by playing the game. But it doesn't take too long. In 10 hours I unlocked about half of all the ships the game has to offer. I was able to play a new ship ever 2-3 matches, which kept me playing.
Again, it's fun if the premice seems interesting to you. Also, if you can accept the slow movement of the capital ships as a limitation that demands you play differently than you may be used to (no skirmishing, always know where you're going and why, pondering if you can get to point A in time to capture it or if you should rather settle for the closer point B and wait for reinforcements or warp out of danger) you'll probably be less annoyed with your ships speed.
This is one damn fine Alpha game. You should try it.

text:
In 2012, an old strategy franchise returned from the dead and showed the gaming community just what real difficulty and real pain is. That game was XCOM: Enemy Unknown, rebooted from a series once known as X-COM and it went on to win not just the pleasure of old fans but gain new fans as well.
XCOM 2 is the sequel to Enemy Unknown. Storywise, everything that happened in Enemy Unknown was a fake. The Commander was really a prisoner to the alien invaders and Earth has been conquered and ruled by the aliens with a faction of apparent human symphatizers called ADVENT. As the Commander, you're freed at the beginning of the game and once again, it's up to you to lead the forces of Earth against the aliens, only this time you'll be the attacker.
From a gameplay perspective, XCOM 2 is mostly the same. You try your best to keep your soldiers in the best cover you can find and launch attacks on your enemies. What changes is that this time, you start out in Concealment mode. The enemy won't know where you are until you attack or get spotted by them, so this is where strategy comes in as you'll have to pick a perfect opportunity to ambush the enemy. Sounds simple? Well, it wouldn't be XCOM if it was simple now, wouldn't it? This time, certain missions also feature a turn timer which shows how many turns you can take before you fail the mission. With that in mind, you have to get to an objective as quickly as you can while also keeping an eye on the timer. While it may seem like a rush, the timer is mostly fair. You do have enough time to get to an objective, you just need to make the most of Concealment mode. Another new element to the game is the more destructible environment. Putting all of your soldiers on top of a building may not always be such a good idea.
And stopping you from reaching those objectives would be the aliens now bolstered by ranks of so-called human volunteers. Some aliens make a return like the Sectoid and Muton but even the ones that returned have completely evolved or have been upgraded. Sectoids are no longer cannon fodder, Floaters have been upgraded to the angelic-looking Archons and the dreaded Sectopods return in a slimmer yet more powerful design. One way or another, the aliens are going to ruin your day, each of them with their own unique way.
All is not lost however. Your soldiers may be outnumbered and outgunned, but they're no pushovers. The classes are both similar and different from Enemy Unknown. Snipers now known as Sharpshooters not only make use of Sniper rifles but can learn to use pistols like a gunslinger from the Old West. A new class called the Ranger employs a high-risk, high reward combat style to slash the enemy with swords in melee combat. With the destructible environments, the Grenadier basically becomes the most powerful and valuable class you can have in your squad as you can blow enemies off buildings or those hiding behind cars and other explosive objects. Most importantly, you also can blow up walls and obstacles so that you can reach a objective faster. Rest assured, you're going to have a lot of fun doing that.
While XCOM 2 doesn't disappoint in its gameplay, it does in it's optimization. You'd think that having it as a PC-exclusive would make it easier for Firaxis to release a more polished game but nope, that didn't happen. The game is buggy like hell, at least it's mostly visual bugs  but still it can ruin the experience a little bit, especially for the last mission. There's also other weird problems like the aliens' turn taking too long, sudden framerate drops and the like but most players didn't experience anything game-breaking. Hopefully, Firaxis fixes the game soon.
All in all, XCOM 2 is a fantastic game and is a textbook example of what devs should do when making a sequel (not the bugs though). If you're one for great turn-based combat and you can stand the pain of watching your men and women die horribly in combat, then you'll love XCOM 2. Just remember when you miss a 95% shot, that's XCOM, baby.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown - the complete version is one of my most favorite games of the recent past. I played it on my PS3, PC/MAC, and my iPad. Hell, I still play it on my iPad. I then got into the Long War mod, and I couldn't play the base game anymore (except my iPad). XCOM 2 had some large shoes to fill. Did it?
I think it did. Let me first put a disclaimer up. I didn't experience any crashes or game ending bugs. I somehow missed all of those. Sure, I had some slowdowns and long loads, but no crashes. Very few bugs at all. I don't even have that great of a system, but that's besides the point.
I love XCOM 2. It took me a while to accept the timers, but when I did, I got over one of the few qualms I had with the game.
I love the new story. We lost to the Aliens. How refreshing. We are having to fight back and try to re-conquer our world. AWESOME. We have new mission types, and we use the hellicarrier from the Aveng....  er... floating alien transport ship instead.
We are a guerilla force out to exact revenge as we uncover the plot of the story. The unit rebalance and customization is great. The new gameplay is great. The timers... um, not so much. But then we have mods.
Oh the mods, the glorious mods. After downloading a dozen, I can't play the base game anymore. The modders are making this game even better.
How would I score this game? Hmm, I would certainly recommend it, but players need to accept that the RNG is brutal. Really brutal, and the game is harder than XCOM:EU was. Is it as hard as the LW mod? No, but it can be on the highest difficulty.
I have many more thoughts about it and if you are interested in reading them, here's a link:

Absolutely amazing. An experience everyone needs to go through (it's best if you go for the first game to begin your dark souls journey, but this one also works).
I consider it more like a big piece of art: the artwork is incredible, the story is amazing but meticulously hidden, so every detail you find makes you go "wow that makes sense!", the SOUNDTRACK is by far one the all-time top best that I've heard (to the point of making me have it in my playlists and walk around with songs stuck in my head) -and that may be an understatement-, the animations are very well polished (excluding some glitches or clippings but not enough to make an impact). This game you can sit back and admire for every step you make, like a piece of art.
Difficulty comes Dark Souls style, by now everyone should have an idea of what that means. But to clarify, it's a fair difficulty: if you remain calm and think about what you are doing good and wrong, the game becomes much, much easier, while still mantaining some level of challenge and entertainment.
Everything together makes up a really good, solid and unique game. But like I say to everyone that hasn't played: "It's not to be considered like a game, but more like an experience. One that it's very likely to change your view around games in general (and maybe even improving some aspects of your personality)". Of course this goes until you start actually re-playing the game and doing random stuff, and at this point yes, it can be considered like a game.
By this date, if you haven't played any Souls-like game (Dark Souls or Bloodborne in particular), I'm not sure what you're thinking or what you are doing with your life, but you should REALLY get your hands on a Souls and have a go at it, and strongly making sure you finish it.

The Darkest Dungeon prides itself on its difficult and yet it doesn't realize that "difficuity" is the singluar reason why it fails as a game. Dark Souls might be hard but it is rewarding and doesn't erase hours of work by chance. This game doesn't realize that players don't want to be punished for trying out new rotations and left to rot because their team wasn't strong enough to stand against the over reliance of the game's RNG. While the beginning might be wonderful, but when the honeymoon is over the player will quickly realize that everything turns to a monochromatic grind for the sake of a one single team whose luck outlives the games whimsical system.
Do I recommand the Darkest Dungeon? Only to the people who likes grinding for chance of a lucky run and have the stomach of losing, repeativily, hours of work.
Edit 1: Just to clairfy this game has this weird thing where it likes to jump difficuity levels to keep you on your toes. That means when you've finally get a team to level 3 you have to directly jump into a level 3 dungeon. Level 2 dungeons don't exist therefore you can't even choose to play slowly and careful. The game makes you put your party in danger. So, if the run doesn't go well not only does your hours of hardwork to train the level 3 team go to waste in the best case scenario your game progress is impeded by a large margin. Therefore, prepare to grind mutiple teams to level 3 before you attempt a level 3 dungeon otherwise with one bad run, then your back to grinding level 1 dungeons.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown - the complete version is one of my most favorite games of the recent past. I played it on my PS3, PC/MAC, and my iPad. Hell, I still play it on my iPad. I then got into the Long War mod, and I couldn't play the base game anymore (except my iPad). XCOM 2 had some large shoes to fill. Did it?
I think it did. Let me first put a disclaimer up. I didn't experience any crashes or game ending bugs. I somehow missed all of those. Sure, I had some slowdowns and long loads, but no crashes. Very few bugs at all. I don't even have that great of a system, but that's besides the point.
I love XCOM 2. It took me a while to accept the timers, but when I did, I got over one of the few qualms I had with the game.
I love the new story. We lost to the Aliens. How refreshing. We are having to fight back and try to re-conquer our world. AWESOME. We have new mission types, and we use the hellicarrier from the Aveng....  er... floating alien transport ship instead.
We are a guerilla force out to exact revenge as we uncover the plot of the story. The unit rebalance and customization is great. The new gameplay is great. The timers... um, not so much. But then we have mods.
Oh the mods, the glorious mods. After downloading a dozen, I can't play the base game anymore. The modders are making this game even better.
How would I score this game? Hmm, I would certainly recommend it, but players need to accept that the RNG is brutal. Really brutal, and the game is harder than XCOM:EU was. Is it as hard as the LW mod? No, but it can be on the highest difficulty.

Dark Souls for kids!
Spiral Knights has microtransactions and it pains me so.  This could have been a $19.99 game that goes on sale for $14.99 that takes you on a wild ride from start to finish with the only obstacles being your skill and your time investment.  Instead it's a free to play game that hurts you with in-game font telling you how much you're supposed to lose out of your wallet to keep going and progressing at the same time.  There are legitimate and genuine blockages inflicted on you in the form of rarities, which if you're a fan from long ago you might remember as energy.  Rarities are as they might sound - so ungodly rare that you might see them once in twenty levels.  You absolutely
have them to keep upgrading your weapons.  What they did with the forge and fire crystals is acceptable at best, if not frustrating beyond belief when you need the fifth and final tier of crystals.  When they told you that you need alchemical orbs to ascend weapons up a tier, I thought it was pretty neat.  The only downside is that they're the ultra rare rarities.  However, if you don't really care for THE GRIND, you can just give the developers dollars or euros for crispy access to what you're wanting.
The difference here is that in Dark Souls, if you wanted an item, you had to go get it.  Bust open a boss chest and just pick it up with your A button.  If you wanted to go get material to upgrade your weapons, you could go find where it's at and go snag it!  You might have to kick around a couple of enemies a few times, (slugs in blighttown gave 5 green titanite per drop) but there was never a forced grind to do anything.  In Spiral Knights, if you want an item, you have to run around in the dungeons and break boxes until your eyes fall out because it's not guaranteed at all.  Upgrade material is always just laying about, but the catch is that there's a hefty chance you won't ever see it.  See the difference? Dark Souls was a one-time payment of ~$20 or so, depending on when you bought it.  Spiral Knights is free to play since the very beginning tentatively stepping out with the free to play name keeping it tethered to safety.
What would I do?  Well like I was saying earlier, I would take Spiral Knights, give it a $19.99 price tag and maybe knock down all the cosmetic packs to $2.49 or so, with the expansion packs to $4.99.  Energy would be completely removed, doors requiring it in levels would be openable with a confirmation box.  Machines requiring energy would be powered by an in-game minigame, nothing too hard, probably connect A to B and don't hit the walls.  At the end of every level, there would guranteed be a box next to the elevator containing a dice roll of items.  You could either get that stratum's alchemical orb, a spark of life, a pile of that stratum's fire crystals (10 probably), or a hefty sum of crowns (100 up to 1000).  At the end of every stratum, there would guaranteed be a box in the rest stop zone containing two of that stratum's alchemical orbs, three sparks of life, and an even heftier sum of crowns (1000 to 2000 or so).  How would I nerf the farming?  You can only claim up to 9 alchemical orbs per strata each day, 30 sparks of life total each day from boxes.  Roadmap for future content?  Bigger, harder bosses with more difficult journeys to reach them.  Replace the Energy idea with a crown-investing stock market.  Fix the netcode, but it's not godawful enough to do right away.  What would happen to current users?  I love me some loyalty rewards, so everybody who had already dealt with the current rarities system would receive a care package containing 1 of each alchemical orb, 10 sparks of life, and a 1-journey Rarity Doubler, (which would make for a good microtransaction for this model) which allows you to collect double on your daily caps and double on all rarity pickups like orbs and fire crystals and lifesparks.  Anyone who had dealt with the legendarily frustrating energy system from way back when would get those rewards and a thank you note, as well as a collection of fantastic in-game cosmetic stuff like reusable badges and accessories.  It would be called Spiral Knights: Plunder of the Clockworks or maybe something with a better catch factor.
Anyways, none of this will ever be implemented, but I'm just the idea guy after all.  Funny how Spiral Knights is worth $19.99 but not worth the cost of free.  Dark Souls for kids, don't forget it.

This game is freaking terrible!  If you were a fan of the last reboot, and are wondering about whether or not to get this game, read this review!
You start most missions in concealed mode, which allows you to creep around the maps and set up an ambush. In this mode, Overwatch no longer has an aim penalty, so you could set all of your soldiers but one on Overwatch, and have the last one attack, or run out in the open to trigger a 'pod'. (Group of enemies that are just stood there) Once triggered, they will most likely run for cover, and your soldiers will shoot them.
Concealed mode is an interesting addition, but during the timed missions, where you are given 8 turns to complete the objective, or you fail the mission, you cant really be messing around slowly setting up an ambush to deal with the enemies. In this way, the game comes accross as having multiple personality disorder. Because of the new abilities the aliens have, you have to be very careful, running away and looking for cover. But because of the round timers that the developers have, you have to be very fast, making sure to get there on time. The developers also saw fit to remove the ability to 'dash' to a door or objective and activate it in the same turn. That means that you have to move there, and use your second action point to activate the objective, or dash there, and activate it on the next turn. Nearly all of the 8 turn missions I have attempted have been failed with one soldier standing right next to them, ready to activate it! FOR GOODNESS SAKES! I failed 8 missions in the campain, and completed 4, (some of them tutorial missions) on the easy difficulty, even though I have played the other game on impossible.
The aliens themselves have also been given much more power. Sectoids can now mind control, and appear just as early in the game as the last one. In the last game, only Sectoid Commanders could mind control, and you didn't encounter them until much later, when the research your scientists had done allowed you to manufacture advanced armours and weapons that leveled the playing field. Not only that, but Sectoids can also now raise the dead. So if one of your soldiers is unlucky (Literally, since the game is based around pseudo-random hit chances more than ever before...) not only does it hurt because you can attack the enemy once less per turn, but also it hurts because they can attack you once more per turn!  Killing the offending Sectoid will kill all the zombies as well though, but unfortunatly, it is rare that you encounter a Sectoid all on it's own. It is often accompanied by a pair of 'stun' troopers. These aliens are also encountered early in the game, and can dash AND melee attack your troops in the same move! Not only that, but they have a high chance to stun your troops, robbing them of their next move. It is hard to run away from these troops AND reach the objectives in time. Not only that, but while you run away for more cover, which is the only strategy in these Xcom reboots (everything else is random, positioning is the only certainty (and suppresion /explosives )...) you will invariably trigger another pod of deadly aliens, which will surely slaughter your entire team in the next go.
What is also poorly explained, and completely ruined, is the geoscape. In the last game, you were given clear goals of what to do next, or what decisions you could afford to make. In this game, Everything is random. There are 11 continental perks, but there are only 6 continents. The game randomly picks your starting position, randomly picks 6 perks out of the 11 in the game, and randomly gives each continent one of those perks. I started in New India, in Asia.
In the last game, you had a scan button, which would advance time. In this game, there are Scan buttons located all over the map. These buttons are essentially like bars, that get filled up as you choose to scan at that location, instead of another. once you have scanned it empty, you get the reward from it, what ever that was. Now, instead of monthly funding, every month, the funds you would have got are put down on the map somewhere, and need to be scanned for three days. You also need to build communications centers in your base to be able to contact more regions, and the regions are contacted in linear order.
Research and base management works the same, with a list of upcomming events that get completed as you scan in the map. Manufacturing works similarly, but now once you have manufactured certain items (Like armour or weapons) You only need to manufacture one, and every troop can have one.
There are certain missions in the game which advance the 'Advent' bar until completed, which when full, ends the game.  These missions don't disapear after a day like the others, and can be attacked at anytime. But only if you have contact with the continent that it is located in. So if you dont have access to that mission, you will have to build a communications center. But if you don't have enough power, you will need to build a power plant. But if you don't have enough money to do that, you will need to scan around to get some. While scanning, there is a risk a pick two, or pick three mission will pop up. You can choose to ignore it if you want, but there are 2 or 3 negatives associated with each of those missions, such as all enemies will have armour for the next month, or your funding will be cut in half next month. You can only pick one of those missions, and the other two negatives will happen anyway. But it will be difficult to beat those missions, with the new timer mechanics, and unfair enemy powers. If you dont have enough time to wait for all the building either way, then you will lose the game.
There is no way to play the game like the last one in my opinion. Now, instead of being able to start a new playthrough and put on Ironman/Impossible, and follow through with a certain strategy you have been working on, the game does everything
randomly, making it so you go in blind everytime. The old rules still apply to a deggree, elevation is good, blow up their cover, run away if you can to a more secure location, focus fire etc etc.
But all of those rules go out of the window randomly. You rely on cover? Well what about if one of the humans running around on the map randomly turns into a giant monster, that can walk up to your soldier on a balcony, and swipe it's claws, and completely destroy the building your team is stood on, in one move? You always know you can run away from the aliens to secure a much better environmental advantage, like higher cover or a vantage point? Aww, well, too bad, you got a mission that expects you to kill 10 aliens and hack the box in 8 turns, with four rookies, and devastating consequences for failure.
There are some positives though:
They fixed the mouse lag, making for a much more enjoyable user experience. The game also runs well for me on my old rig, so I don't know why some users are reporting performance issues, but it may be a driver issue or something. The game looks pretty good as well. The game features well done randomly generated maps. The designs, the music, the sound are all great! One great moment I recall was a grenade knocking a soldier into a train, only to have a 'BANG' play, as his body hit the metal train! xD The game is also much more snappier than before, it's very responsive and less time-wastie to give orders and pan the camera. The game world and designs ooze atmosphere also.
The tactical randomness lets the game down imo. You shouldn't have to mod the game to give you one or two more turns, that's something the developers should have anticipated.

BUY/SALE/PASS:  Sale - Wait for a sale price
About ten years ago, there came along a budget title out of Japan named Katamari Damacy.  In the tiny feet of a diminutive prince, players were tasked with picking up whatever random crap was strewn around a room/house/neighborhood/city/planet as fast as you can.  It was strange, yet strangely compelling; an oddity of video games that came out of nowhere and has since been milked dry as a concept; even the original creator has distanced himself from the series.  Weird games slowly drift by the wayside as video games break way into the mainstream, and things become normal.
Then, in 2015, players were tasked with playing as a slice of bread.
Bossa Studios, the creators of Surgeon Simulator 2013, bring us yet another bizarro creation.  As a single slice of bread, your mission in I am Bread is to get toasted by any means necessary.  Gripping the surfaces and objects around you with the corners of your bread slice (somehow…), you must traverse the various rooms of a house to find that sweet embrace of heat that will get you nice and crispy.  But don’t land anywhere gross or linty!  Otherwise you’ll end up inedible, and what will even be the point of being toasted?  The horror of such a thought!
I am Bread is utter nonsense baked into a bizarre, fluffy bun.  Yet the gameplay is so fun and goofy, oftentimes creating some of the best accidentally funniest moments of any game released this year.  Purposefully frustrating controls leave the player pulling out their hair one moment and laughing the next.  There’s no escaping it.  You are bread.  And you will be toast, one way or another.  Delightful music, fun gameplay, funky concept, all worthy of a sale price purchase.

Trove, true to it's name, is a game full of wonderous little things. I honestly tried it out with little to no expectations, and I was very pleased.
Quite simply, Trove is an MMORPG with simple but fun beat-em-up controls and Minecraft elements, like randomly-generated world, lots of things to explore, and building through crafting and blocks.
The entire game is very charming and intuitive. The UI is especially well designed, and new players should have little problems getting the hang of things.
This game is great as a single-player experience, but appears more fun as a multiplayer experience. There are just so many different dungeons to explore, monsters to fight and places to visit! It always feels fresh.
I recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of MMORPGs, but is looking for a simpler and more intuitive system. Fans of Minecraft who wants a free-to-play version to play with friends should also try this game.
However, if the visual style isn't your cup of tea, or the controls seem weak to you, steer clear.

Expansion updated review.
The range of missions is pretty limited and the locations often feel too much like dejavu.  The expansion has added a bit to this and it has helped a great deal in this regard with some welcome diversity..
At last! You can now limit some of the verbose and annoying comments throughout battle.
I do very much like the progression and the way it is balanced in many respects and the expansion adds more variation to this to good effect..
There are moments where a key piece of research finishes and you get certain weapons and armour which do feel very satisfying.  However, it is still a little too predictable to the point of monotony, no matter which choices you make, you will get an entirely predictable response from the game.  It all feels way too scripted and constrained and a bit unsatisfying at times.   This general linear feel and avatar project system is the most irritating aspect of a game I would have really liked much better without it.  The constant constraints are infuriating.  However, the expansion offers more ways to counter the Avatar nonesense and just (barely) enough variety to make it more interesting.
Pacing should be an under the hood sort of game dynamic you are not really aware of.  In XCom 2 it is over and instrusive.
The classes  were pretty obvious and fun to play but pre expansion they were a little too limited in diversity however, the expansion adds something to this with faction heroes with their own expandability and options which open a new paradigm.
Weapons are satisfying once researched and there are less obvious issues with the aim and miss system which at launch were utterly bizarre with regular misses at ridiculously high percentages killing immersion. Research is fun and the weapons etc are interesting and keep you wanting more.
It is, on balance, alright, just but not worth buying because it is exactly the same as every other game they made with exactly the same deep flaws.  After all this time, its unforgivable.
1.  The game itself has been limited and controlled to the point of being nauseatingly linear.  It tries to give the illusion of freedom but it doesnt work.
2.  The UI still has the same glaring flaws it always had. You think you commanded a solider to hit one thing, it goes ahead and hits something else. Particularly with Rangers.
3.  Being a hard fight would be fine.  But the way it is balanced is always such that you never get to enjoy your achievements in any way.  It isnt fun.  You never get a good moment where you feel you achieved something because the moment you do, the game balances that achievement to the point you are still disadvanted.  Perhaps this is intended, it is incredibly unsatisfying.
4.  The exapansion adds factions. For people fighting for survival they seem to lack commitment to anything and with one exception, they seem utterly useless anyway.  No wonder they are winning, I want to annihalate them myself.  If only there was a nuke faction option. Now that would be satisfying.

After coming back to this game, I can say I am thoroughly disappointed. All the ships are so overdetailed that they blend together. It's hard to see wether you're picking a small attack ship or a tank with some of the factions (manufacturers?)
Not to mention that they went with the horrid League of Legends monetization setting, where you earn tiny amounts of currency (400 from a random match) to purchase a ship with sky high costs (1.9 mill)
I do not regret leaving this game.
-----
This is so brutally unfinished. I had to dig deeply into the research tree to figure out why was I dealing zero damage to the enemy -- turns out my flak cannon had a super limited range, and the turrets' positions are somehow not important enough to mention.
HOWEVER
The placement of your spaceship's hardpoints (not customizable) is crittical when you're attempting to broadside. In the wrong ship at the wrong angle, you'll be firing one cannon, or maybe none.
Range on the enemy ships is a tiny, TINY font inside the lock-on window.
And would someone be so kind as to explain to me why distance wn't let me target a ship I'm clearly looking at?
Team balancing is utterly screwed. It may autobalance at the beginning of the match, but if someone on your team decides to drop out, you're out of luck.
There is absolutely no matchmaking. You gotta pick one of several servers which may or may not let you in.
There will be absolutely no control about who you jump into a game with. You could have your very first match against a full team of veterans... Good luck then!
There are levels, but there is absolutely no indication of what do you get as you level.
The ships are divided by manufacturer. Playing a ship from a particular manufacturer gives you exp with that MFer and that one only. You use the veterancy accumulated to unlock parts and then -then- you STILL gotta pay to get the part, with generic credits, nonetheless.
This leads to a dark place where you're likely to have countless tech unlocks, but no credits to get any of them. Yet another instance of grinding.
I don't wanna freaking grind! It's a PvP arena game, I wanna jump in and fight other people! Having so many different currencies affecting the same thing seems little more than a bottleneck.
Anyway, before I go into full-on-rant mode, I'll conclude that trying out this game merely primed me for Greybox / Yager's Dreadnought. I'm gonna keep an eye out for that instead, while praying to all known gods (and some made-up ones) they don't screw it up and add yet another micropayment system.
(Which this game already has, but is just not active yet.)
I know it's in early access, and I can see how woefully, horribly unfinished it is, but I still gotta give it a thumb down, mostly because i'm figuring out with my limited playtime that it is likely to become a cash-grab, using unreal engine 4 to distract us from it.

XCOM2 is an interesting plot twist, allwing to turn the tables and become the hit-and-run attacker.
I like the graphics, the rich customization and the modding possibility from day 0.
I liked very much the tatical features of concealment and the new importance of overwatch in the own turn.
The newly introduced element of hacking is increasingly powerful and adds interesting tactical options.
On the downside I agree that the ever-present turn limit is not making the experience richer and displaced in this setup. However, at least if you play casually, it is doable.
I was more set aback by the thin degrees of freedom the strategic game offers, it is quite a laid-out story and the player seldom has a real choice of action.
Overall, I can and do recommend the game, not only for fans of the old series but also for people that bnever played any XCOM game. It is a rich diversification from the usual game scene.

Overall a decent game worth a try, however the abysmal 3rd person camera, inconsistent visual detail and iffy physics killed most of the enjoyment I felt I would get from this game.
I played SS previously and that was a pretty fun gem, yet it did have some quirks and an excessive amounts of clipping. Bread, I don't feel, is anywhere near as good as SS.
Bread's friendship with Goat Simulator sort of reduced my minimal respect for such an original game, that is Bread. GS is an extremely buggy game that thrives off of bugs, glitching and clipping, all are annoyances of mine. Labeling weak coding and QC as an aspect of gameplay doesn't cut it for me. I felt Bread went down that route a little bit, which I don't like.
Performace of Bread is questionable. I get huge frame rate drops when the Goat destruction levels start up and also every time I break that jar of jam with the bread. Speaking of the jam, the glass containers in this game look like something from a 2005 title. They are a huge eye sore, and they are everywhere. Technology exists today that makes glass look realistic... please use it. This is a 2015 title. Even with it being from a small developer, they still have enough money to get some decent looking glass going on. 21st Century Fox is a partial owner of Bossa, there's tons of money there to get some better graphics and coding. Hopefully they go down this route as Bossa becomes more popular. I hear they're working on a MMO open-world title right now... yikes. That's a huge jump.
Speaking of graphics, it's hit or miss in each level. The few levels towards the end are the worst, visually. It doesn't make sense why this is even happened other than laziness, or they ran out of time. The game has a gradual decline in graphics the further you progress. I see tons of low res textures, a very poor sky box, background visuals look like they're from the 80's, etc. Graphics aren't everything, but they are important.
Some visuals are cartoony, some are more heavily detailed.... don't mix this sh**, pick one and go with it for the whole game.
The third person camera... Christ. Yes, many games suffer from third person camera issues, especially those old GTA games, but lets get this sh** cleaned up, guys. It jumps around everywhere, clips through everything, hinders those bagel racing levels like crazy, and is poorly optimized. It pisses me off. Unity can do better.
Iffy physics. Props and movable objects sometimes do move around in a natural manner when you grab them or push them, but not all of the time. It's inconsistent, like the visuals. I've gotten stuck on props many times, and have had myself, and different objects bounce unnaturally in different directions, before saying to myself "wtf is this sh**, seriously?"
Negatives aside, Bread does have its moments. I'm glad the 0 gravity mode is back from SS. It is very difficult to control, but is rewarding when you beat it. The humor is nice. The game is fun to watch. The concept is fresh. Like SS, the controls and movements have a steep learning curve, but is awesome when you get it down.
Like I said previously, maybe give the game a whirl, it's pretty unique. Like SS, it requires a lot of patience. As for the questionable overall quality, Bossa: talk to Fox and get some heavy funds rolling in, hire a few more devs (get some people from big triple-A companies), get some Unity pros to work with ya'll--Unity can accomplish so, so, so much more.
Thanks.

This is my first ever game review so bear with me... I was originally sceptical when I saw this game in my steam library for free but i decided to try it out. It was very easy to get into the game look over the controls and enter a match, and I had a great time with it. The concept is that you have a 5v5 match with players controlling large capital ships which try to take over different points throughout the map. These points are in different zones which players can warp into. Capturing these points gives your team resources which build toward upgrades that increase your teams stats.
The ships in the game are completely badass in appearance and the game is beautiful. As I was playing after their promotion there were no shortages of people to play with and talk to. The ship customization currently isn't all that great as you can only get a couple upgrades for a few of the ships but each ship in itself is completely unique in the way it plays its role.
If you want to be a long range sniper you can, if you want to sneak up on people and try to one shot them thats cool too, or even if you just want to pester the enemy there are ships for that as well. One thing I do enjoy is that progressing to different types of ships is not all that difficult and in 20 hours i have all but 3 of them. The game requires a great deal of cooperation with team-mates in order to not only play but to select the right ships for the job. A good strategy is the difference between an easy win and a quick loss in many circumstances.
Overall I think this is probably one of the best alpha games I have played in a while and I can't wait to see what they will be adding into the game in the future.

So, XCOM 2 is a PC exclusive. This confuses me, a lot, just because this game is basically XCOM 1 all over again. Sure, there are some new things here and there, but at the same time, it's mostly the same thing. There's a lot of PROS I could list, but I'd just be describing XCOm 1. So... Let's focus on what's different.
PROS (aka what's different than the first, but better:
+It's XCOM again! The turn based combat returns and, like before, is amazing. Instead of having a base, you're a ship. It works out and, instead of hunting UFOs, UFOs hunt you!
+Instant workshop support for mods. This is a big win. In fact, I'd say this game is worth it just for the fact that the modding is so much easier to install and get working.
+The story is set 20 years in the future after humanity loses the war. I like this, but... Umm... That's about it! It works well with the new system.
MIXED (aka what's new but may or may not appeal or half-works):
+/-The new aliens are nice! But... Some of them are obviously phoned in, or are reskins of previous enemies. I'd rather just have the old ones.
+/-The concealment benefits that the player can get in certain missions is really nice. There's always a point where you need to break stealth and go loud. It's nice, especially since I was able to sneak into a base, position myself mere inches away from the aliens, and proceed to ♥♥♥♥ their day up, plant a bomb, and get out. However, once you're discovered, you can't restealth. This isn't too great, considering when you find other enemies, they act surprised to see you.
CONS:
- Let's talk more about the bloody stupid "Enemies see you, then move" thing when you encounter them on the battlefield. It's annoying and really adds more ragequit to the game. The fact that this is still in the game confuses me since concealment was added. I can't tell you how many times my last move for the squad ended with my last member noticing the shadow of an alien that triggers the attack. This wouldn't be much of an issue, but many of the new aliens are so powerful they can instantly kill the most prepared squad member with full health. There's a difference between challenging gameplau and unfair design choices.
-The game, at least when it came out since I haven't played too much since the last patch, does not run well. I don't know how this is possible since the first game ran flawlessly, and it was also featured on the consoles! Why is this a PC exclusive yet it runs horrible?! Typically, since you don't need to produce the game on the consoles, you can uses THAT extra beta testing/bug fixing money on the PC version.
-The % chance is broken. Sure, it says 80%, but it won't hit.
CONCLUSION:
If you want more of XCOM 1, this game is for you! Just remember to mod the hell out of the game.

The game is a very flawed but yet beautifull jewel. With that i mean: even though it has an enormous flaw i will still continue to play it and certain people will absolutely love it but i can sadly not recommend the game to people as it is the most rage inducing game i have ever played.
1. Intro
The game revolves around one sentance 'make the best of bad situations' and you really get that feeling. Almost every decision will have an upside and a downside thus you have to weight the options. As i said, the entire game revolves around this.
2. The Problem
The game is portraied to be very hard, which it is. Good right? -Yes and no, not really to be honest
The game relies solely on RNG to make it harder. Almost every decision you make is subject to a dice roll. Even when you did everything you could to stack the odds in your favor you can still lose the roll, this happens far too much to make it feel rewarding when you made a good play.
Eventually you learn that the game wants you to think of your heroes as 'disposable'. Once you learn this you have taken a HUGE step towards becoming better. Awesome. -Yes!
After I progressed through the game I started see a pattern. I was simply recruiting heroes to slam them against a wall hoping it would break. Didn't break? -Recruit new ones and slam them against the wall once more.
You start looking for certain types of heroes with certain traits. Which is also 100% subject to RNG. You can get your entire dream party in once day or you can wait 20 years for the right hero with the right traits to pop up.
You can do your best to stack the odds in your favor which helps tremendously but even then it is still based on dice rolls.
Some more examples of RNG:
Exploration
The game features a 'Torch' mechanic which is fairly straightforward: The brighter the torch the easier yet lower rewards, the dimmer the torch the harder yet greater rewards. It also ties in with the 'Surprise' mechanic:
Depending on your torch's light level you can surprise or get surprised. To put it short, the surprised party is in a severe disadvantage. Or so it seems, this is where the combat comes in.
Combat
The party consists of 4 heroes. You can assign each of them to a certain location, this is vital if you wish to succeed as all skills require a certain position within the party to be used.
If your party is surprised all your heroes are scattered and the enemy gets to attack you for free. Of course, they get 2-3 free rounds as you are usually still re-positioning your party because otherwise you can barely fight back. Meanwhile the enemy is hitting away at your party.
If you are taking care of your torch you will have a lower chance of getting surprised but it is still possible.
CONCLUSION
The game starts out awesome and ramps up the awesomeness very quickly. After a short while the fatal flaw becomes visable and you start realising that no matter how much effort you put in, things can still go morbidly wrong.
-Yes, i know this is the entire purpose of the game. The problem is that the way they executed and designed it makes the entire game more and more rage inducing.
Tip: If you really like the game, play it in short bursts.

This game is great. You start with two adventurers going to the town and from there you get a score of new classes, (and I guess you call the abomination a race.) You take your adventurers throughout dungeons, fighting monsters and gaining xp, similar to Wizards of the Coast's Dungeons and Dragons. On the way, your adventurers gain stress, and if you let the stress get too high, it'll reach the point of affliction. They can gain negative personality traits such as abusive, or selfish, or they could gain virtues, such as courageous, or focused. If the stress gets too high, they have a heart attack. Also, the only way to get rid of afflictions is to lower their stress to 0/200, by letting them drink in the Tavern, or pray in the Abbey. The turn-based battling, and the loot you can find is all interesting. Once I found the head of one of my dead adventurers. I love how you can upgrade town buildings to look nicer, and your characters are upgradable, too. The eerie soundtrack and unsettling noises in the dungeons really add to the game's dark, hopeless atmosphere, as your adventurer's fight for their lives against Prophets, madmen, necromancers, skeletons, fish people and even killer pigs. Watch out for the pigs, because they can make your adventurers diseased. Diseases can only be treated in the sanitarium, back in the Hamlet (the town). Overall the games combat, exploration and dark atmosphere make for an awesome playthrough. I reccomend it to casual gamers and hardcore gamers alike. This game is definitely a good experience, and is totally worth every penny.

Expansion updated review.
The range of missions is pretty limited and the locations often feel too much like dejavu.  The expansion has added a bit to this and it has helped a great deal in this regard with some welcome diversity..
At last! You can now limit some of the verbose and annoying comments throughout battle.
I do very much like the progression and the way it is balanced in many respects and the expansion adds more variation to this to good effect..
There are moments where a key piece of research finishes and you get certain weapons and armour which do feel very satisfying.  However, it is still a little too predictable to the point of monotony, no matter which choices you make, you will get an entirely predictable response from the game.  It all feels way too scripted and constrained and a bit unsatisfying at times.   This general linear feel and avatar project system is the most irritating aspect of a game I would have really liked much better without it.  The constant constraints are infuriating.  However, the expansion offers more ways to counter the Avatar nonesense and just (barely) enough variety to make it more interesting.
Pacing should be an under the hood sort of game dynamic you are not really aware of.  In XCom 2 it is over and instrusive.
The classes  were pretty obvious and fun to play but pre expansion they were a little too limited in diversity however, the expansion adds something to this with faction heroes with their own expandability and options which open a new paradigm.
Weapons are satisfying once researched and there are less obvious issues with the aim and miss system which at launch were utterly bizarre with regular misses at ridiculously high percentages killing immersion. Research is fun and the weapons etc are interesting and keep you wanting more.
It is, on balance, alright, just but not worth buying because it is exactly the same as every other game they made with exactly the same deep flaws.  After all this time, its unforgivable.
1.  The game itself has been limited and controlled to the point of being nauseatingly linear.  It tries to give the illusion of freedom but it doesnt work.
2.  The UI still has the same glaring flaws it always had. You think you commanded a solider to hit one thing, it goes ahead and hits something else. Particularly with Rangers.
3.  Being a hard fight would be fine.  But the way it is balanced is always such that you never get to enjoy your achievements in any way.  It isnt fun.  You never get a good moment where you feel you achieved something because the moment you do, the game balances that achievement to the point you are still disadvanted.  Perhaps this is intended, it is incredibly unsatisfying.
4.  The exapansion adds factions. For people fighting for survival they seem to lack commitment to anything and with one exception, they seem utterly useless anyway.  No wonder they are winning, I want to annihalate them myself.  If only there was a nuke faction option. Now that would be satisfying.

Bias warning: I grew up in the 90ies playing the original XCOM series.
Therefore I was quite intrigued by the remakes and I found XCOM:EU really a well-made remake that was taking the good parts of the old game into a modern frame. So I was positively thirelled to hear a dark voice say "welcome back, commander".
XCOM2 is an interesting plot twist, allwing to turn the tables and become the hit-and-run attacker.
I like the graphics, the rich customization and the modding possibility from day 0.
I liked very much the tatical features of concealment and the new importance of overwatch in the own turn.
The newly introduced element of hacking is increasingly powerful and adds interesting tactical options.
On the downside I agree that the ever-present turn limit is not making the experience richer and displaced in this setup. However, at least if you play casually, it is doable.
I was more set aback by the thin degrees of freedom the strategic game offers, it is quite a laid-out story and the player seldom has a real choice of action.
Overall, I can and do recommend the game, not only for fans of the old series but also for people that bnever played any XCOM game. It is a rich diversification from the usual game scene.

I love this game.  It's almost everything that I've wanted from Counter-Strike that it doesn't deliver.
The graphics are gorgeous, highly detailed, with wonderul special effects.  Yes, they aren't current generation graphics, but compared to Counter-Strike?  They look amazing, and are exactly what I dream of when I think of Counter-Strike with better graphics.
The sound is raw and gritty and supremely satisfying.  The sound of headshots is gory and rewarding, making me really cherish them.  And sound design is expertly done, focusing on clear and conise noises that clearly indicate where and what is going on.
The gunplay is tight, but quite forgiving.  This is basically a somewhat easier Counter-Strike, where your friends that lack First Person Shooting skills could still pick up some kills if they use a Sub Machine Gun, but will still lose to more skilled players due to superior recoil control, movement, etc.
And the most key factor for me, matches only take 20-30 minutes as opposed to Counter-Strike's mostly hour long matches.
And to top all of this off, the game is free and actually fair.  There's only one currency you can purchas with money, and you can't purchase any advantages with it.  The only "advantage" you can buy is either a $25 DLC that gives you a weapon and an exclusive skin for said weapon, or a $30 DLC that gives you 7 weapons.  All those weapons can be acquired in game and they also offer a 2 free DLCs that allow you to try two different sets of 7 weapons for 15 days each which can help you make informed purchase decisions.
All in all, I hope this game succeeds and continues to grow and build an audience and improve itself.

This game is great. You start with two adventurers going to the town and from there you get a score of new classes, (and I guess you call the abomination a race.) You take your adventurers throughout dungeons, fighting monsters and gaining xp, similar to Wizards of the Coast's Dungeons and Dragons. On the way, your adventurers gain stress, and if you let the stress get too high, it'll reach the point of affliction. They can gain negative personality traits such as abusive, or selfish, or they could gain virtues, such as courageous, or focused. If the stress gets too high, they have a heart attack. Also, the only way to get rid of afflictions is to lower their stress to 0/200, by letting them drink in the Tavern, or pray in the Abbey. The turn-based battling, and the loot you can find is all interesting. Once I found the head of one of my dead adventurers. I love how you can upgrade town buildings to look nicer, and your characters are upgradable, too. The eerie soundtrack and unsettling noises in the dungeons really add to the game's dark, hopeless atmosphere, as your adventurer's fight for their lives against Prophets, madmen, necromancers, skeletons, fish people and even killer pigs. Watch out for the pigs, because they can make your adventurers diseased. Diseases can only be treated in the sanitarium, back in the Hamlet (the town). Overall the games combat, exploration and dark atmosphere make for an awesome playthrough. I reccomend it to casual gamers and hardcore gamers alike. This game is definitely a good experience, and is totally worth every penny.
