Spiral Knights had so much going for it, but now stands as a glorious monument to repeatedly poor developer decisions eating away at the core of a game like an infection. Money-grubbing Ubisoft you might expect this from, but it's a bit disheartening to see yet another misguided indie dev fall for the 'costume & cosmetics' trap at the expense of gameplay. Mind you, Hello Games just might've punctured that particular indie goodwill bubble once and for all.
That being said! If you have no problems with eternal grinding, don't mind being stuck on the gear treadmill and like the look of the game world, then don't let this review stop you. There's plenty of good in Spiral Knights, and given the generous price of $0, you could do a lot worse than trying it out.
Let's start with the good: Spiral Knights looks the business, with a cutesy blocky aesthetic that meshes well with the light tone of the game. The customisation options are plentiful, and it's satisfying the collect cool weapons, armour and gear while progressing through the story. The only problem is the immense, mountainous grind that infests everything in this game world. Even the early game is tainted somewhat, but the cracks split into crevasses before you even spot the endgame on the horizon. Every level will need to be rerun many, many times for currency and rare drops; in some games this isn't a problem at all, but Spiral Knights remains a relatively simple game at heart. It's an entry-level game in the genre, and so combat and exploration are highly simplistic...meaning that repetition follows, and no amount of customisation can salvage it.
The OST is nice, no two ways about it; touching at times, intense at others. The story is a little light, quite whimsical but ultimately engaging enough. And the dungeon-running is pretty neat when you first emerge from your escape pod, particularly if you have a few friends to accompany you through the Clockworks. It's just that there's no longevity to the fun, and things get insanely repetitive very rapidly. Even the midgame content recycles assets to a significant degree, let alone the endgame where the majority of the grinding will be done. You have quite a few weaponry options in combat, but few moves to utilise - it gets dull pretty fast. Diminishing returns set in quickly.
As I said before, if you don't mind a huge grind then don't let my review deter you - there are certainly far worse options out there. Quite a few of the complaints of long time players may not apply to new adventurers, and given that Spiral Knights is now FTP, it can't hurt to try it out. Just don't hesitate to bail out if it all wears a bit thin; it saddens me that for all the obvious charm therein, I don't see myself playing this one again.

In 2012, Firaxis released Xcom Enemy Unknown which helped breathe new life into the genre and successfully rebooted the classic UFO defense franchise. Now, 4 years later, Xcom 2 hopes to improve on all of the elements of its predecessor.
Taking place roughly 20 years after where the first game left off, and in an unusual sense for a sequel, Xcom 2 assumes you failed Enemy Unknown as it now takes place in a dystopian future where the aliens have conquered earth. Rather than defending the planet from UFOs, you’re tasked with bolstering resistance cells across the globe with your mobile, flying fortress; the avenger. This functions in the same way as your underground base from the first title, as you can upgrade it, add new facilities, as well as recruit soldiers while managing research and production.
The core concepts are similar to Enemy Unknown and you’re faced with a constant race against the clock since the aliens are developing something called the Avatar project. Certain missions will act to delay the progress of the project, but it's game-over upon its completion. There’s also dark events which can provide random modifiers and buffs to the aliens you encounter. Occasionally you’ll be prompted to complete guerilla missions which allow you to prevent a dark event but you’re unable to stop them all, as you’ll typically have to pick and choose which event is most pressing.
The world map functions similarly to Enemy Unknown. You’ll set up a base and will be able to scan the map for certain points of interest. Building radio relays in countries will increase your monthly budget, and continental bonuses make a return, adding some elements of strategy and planning. Upon scanning the map, you’ll frequently be interrupted to go on missions, which are all randomly generated with varying objectives. These objectives range from escorting an NPC, saving civilians, eliminating a target or killing every alien in an area.
The turn-based combat is what you’d come to expect from an Xcom game, death is permanent and your soldiers can still possibly miss a point-blank shot which otherwise has a 97% success rate. Stealth has been added, which can allow you to strategically place your soldiers and set up ambushes with overwatch, but a lot of the time you’ll feel rushed as there isn’t much time to complete the objectives in most cases. Taking one extra step is sometimes enough to alert enemies to your presence, so you really have to balance between moving cautiously and completing a mission as fast as possible. That element of randomness can be a detriment, as sometimes a civilian could block a ladder and thus seal off the only way up to a rooftop extraction, or a ridiculous amount of enemies could spawn directly on top of a transmitter you’re otherwise supposed to protect. Which leads to one major issue with Xcom 2, it’s extremely luck based and these random factors can cause you to fail a mission with very little control. You can recover from failed missions, but it does feel a little unfair and can be a major downer for ironman playthroughs in which you only have one save file.
The soldier classes feel a lot more fleshed out and distinct from one another as they all kind of blurred together in the previous installment. For example the Ranger is equipped with a sword which can absolutely devastate enemies in melee combat while the specialist has a drone that can hack hostile robotic units or support squad mates from anywhere on the map. The scientists and engineers play more of a role now as well. They’re actually named and can be individually assigned to different projects.
Xcom 2 also completely expands on the level of customization, giving a lot more appearance options for your soldiers. You’re also able to modify your soldiers’ weapons with various attachments as well as give them performance enhancing implants. While all of these customization options were quite welcomed, this resulted in some completely broken and overpowered combinations. For example, I had given one of my soldiers a superior repeater which gave him a 15% chance to instantly execute whatever target he was shooting at and as a result I was able to one-shot the hardest enemy in the game. The difficulty in general is kind of spiky, while the game initially starts off as challenging; it quickly becomes too easy upon developing certain technologies. Some better pacing would have greatly alleviated this issue because as it stands, it can switch from being so easy that it’s tedious to frustrating with little warning.
At first, there seems to be a greater variety of enemies present in Xcom 2. The majority of enemies you face are Advent troopers, human-like soldiers that support the alien regime, while more familiar aliens such-as sectoids function as lieutenants and are actually a greater threat than the previous games. The other aliens have also evolved over the twenty year gap between Enemy Unknown. Unfortunately you hardly fight them in the latter half of the game as you pretty much always face the same enemies over and over again at that point.
I also had some issues with the world map. It gives you so many optional areas to scan for additional supplies and personnel but you’re interrupted every two seconds to take part in another randomly generated mission. There are very few actual story missions, and the random stages can really get tedious in the latter half of the game. There’s also very little rhyme or reason going into the appearance of a stage. You could accept a mission in Africa only for there to be pine trees and snow on the ground, making no sense whatsoever. There are a lot of bugs present in the game as well. From graphical glitches, laggy animations and the odd crash.
Xcom 2 promised re-playability with its use of random stages but I would’ve honestly preferred handcrafted levels with more of a narrative. There’s also extra mod support this time around but most of the mods available currently are cosmetic or the odd weapon, which doesn’t really add anything significant to the gameplay.
The multiplayer from Enemy Unknown makes an appearance again but it’s even more of a throw-away mode this time around. You’re given even less customization options than before as you’re no longer able to choose the rank and loadout of human soldiers. The turns don’t play out simultaneously and can take an extremely long time as there’s quite a bit of additional lag between them. That combined with crashes and random disconnects make this mode barely playable.
The soundtrack is well done and changes to match the mood of the battle as well as the enemies you encounter. Unfortunately, there isn't much variety between tracks and it isn't as memorable as Michael Mccann’s soundtrack from Enemy Unknown who was probably too busy working on Deus Ex Mankind Divided.
Ultimately, Xcom 2 makes a very strong first impression but it was all downhill from there though, and towards the end of the game, I couldn’t wait to be done with all the randomly generated filler content. That coupled with an overall lack of pacing made it a bit of a disappointment. It’s an improvement over Enemy Unknown in some areas but a step-back in others. Xcom 2 is by no means a bad game, and will most likely improve with time; I was just expecting a lot more.
+	Strong Turn Based Tactical Combat
+	Increased Customization Options
+	Interesting Premise
+	Soldier classes and base management are more refined.
-	Repetitive Gameplay and Filler Content
-	Numerous Bugs
-	Lackluster Multiplayer
-	Not enough of an improvement over Enemy Unknown

I love the idea of a space combat shooter, so Fractured Space is definitely my kinda of thing.  Unfortunately, the thing I've always loved most about space games is full freedom of movement. You can float upwards or downwards, but your orientation never actually changes.  This means no banking around an asteroid, no complex evasion to shake targetting, and no fun feeling (for me) of being in space.  This game feels far more like a game of submarines than a game of giant space warships.
I can't really recommend Fractured Space, and I doubt the reason for my objection will change as they exit Early Access.  I want something more like Freespace + multiplayer, and I don't think that's a direction the devs plan to go.

Hiding behind the moniker of "Hard" doesn't hide all the bad game design.

Upgrade the wagon to get as many heroes as possible, send those heroes into dungeons without provisions, run away before they die, collect loot.  Dismiss stressed heroes and repeat ad naseum.
The game just stacks the deck too far against you.  Hell you get stress at random for just walking down the hall.  You get stress for basically everything, but you cant really easily remove the stress.  You get no attachment to your heroes because they are all disposable meat until you are done the grind.
Does this sound fun to you?  It certainly wasn't for me.  Uninstalling and disappointed.  It's a shame too, as the art style is awesome and the core game play is interesting.  But the design decisions just crush you under their grindy weight.  Some people enjoy being punished and accomplishing miniscule steps forward, I certainly am not one of these people.  I enjoy challenging games like Rogue Legacy and Dark Souls 1/2/3, but this is not one of those titles.

Ok, I love the idea of this game and enjoyed most of the gameplay. This has been something I have been waiting for. I congradulate the developers of this game for getting the feel of this game done right. Though as it is in Early Access and in "Live Alpha" as it says in-game, there are a few problems.
1. Balancing for the ships is nowhere to be seen. Yes, there are classes that are designed to deal with a particular craft, but what are you going to do when the entire enemy team is just flagships? Oh and dont mention that they captured the entire map just to show up on your front door as Level 5 ships while your just now getting to Level 2 with your own ship that is outgunned and has way less HP than a flagship. Also, flagships can hit you with disable and your just a sitting duck. Try to warp out of the battle? Take 30x more damage and die faster.
2. It's not really a pay to win game(which is a good thing) and is more of a play to win, but the "boosters" that are available allow someone to gain access to better craft like, say, the Assassin or Sniper class right off hand. And for those that dont buy boosters, you're stuck with basic everything. No extra's, no XP boosts, or any Credit boosts of any kind. I do understand that the Devs need to make money somehow but that's not my issue. My issue is the lack of matchmaking. Matchmaking that allows you to play with those of your skill level. In 2012, Firaxis released Xcom Enemy Unknown which helped breathe new life into the genre and successfully rebooted the classic UFO defense franchise. Now, 4 years later, Xcom 2 hopes to improve on all of the elements of its predecessor.
Taking place roughly 20 years after where the first game left off, and in an unusual sense for a sequel, Xcom 2 assumes you failed Enemy Unknown as it now takes place in a dystopian future where the aliens have conquered earth. Rather than defending the planet from UFOs, you’re tasked with bolstering resistance cells across the globe with your mobile, flying fortress; the avenger. This functions in the same way as your underground base from the first title, as you can upgrade it, add new facilities, as well as recruit soldiers while managing research and production.
The core concepts are similar to Enemy Unknown and you’re faced with a constant race against the clock since the aliens are developing something called the Avatar project. Certain missions will act to delay the progress of the project, but it's game-over upon its completion. There’s also dark events which can provide random modifiers and buffs to the aliens you encounter. Occasionally you’ll be prompted to complete guerilla missions which allow you to prevent a dark event but you’re unable to stop them all, as you’ll typically have to pick and choose which event is most pressing.
The world map functions similarly to Enemy Unknown. You’ll set up a base and will be able to scan the map for certain points of interest. Building radio relays in countries will increase your monthly budget, and continental bonuses make a return, adding some elements of strategy and planning. Upon scanning the map, you’ll frequently be interrupted to go on missions, which are all randomly generated with varying objectives. These objectives range from escorting an NPC, saving civilians, eliminating a target or killing every alien in an area.
The turn-based combat is what you’d come to expect from an Xcom game, death is permanent and your soldiers can still possibly miss a point-blank shot which otherwise has a 97% success rate. Stealth has been added, which can allow you to strategically place your soldiers and set up ambushes with overwatch, but a lot of the time you’ll feel rushed as there isn’t much time to complete the objectives in most cases. Taking one extra step is sometimes enough to alert enemies to your presence, so you really have to balance between moving cautiously and completing a mission as fast as possible. That element of randomness can be a detriment, as sometimes a civilian could block a ladder and thus seal off the only way up to a rooftop extraction, or a ridiculous amount of enemies could spawn directly on top of a transmitter you’re otherwise supposed to protect. Which leads to one major issue with Xcom 2, it’s extremely luck based and these random factors can cause you to fail a mission with very little control. You can recover from failed missions, but it does feel a little unfair and can be a major downer for ironman playthroughs in which you only have one save file.
The soldier classes feel a lot more fleshed out and distinct from one another as they all kind of blurred together in the previous installment. For example the Ranger is equipped with a sword which can absolutely devastate enemies in melee combat while the specialist has a drone that can hack hostile robotic units or support squad mates from anywhere on the map. The scientists and engineers play more of a role now as well. They’re actually named and can be individually assigned to different projects.
Xcom 2 also completely expands on the level of customization, giving a lot more appearance options for your soldiers. You’re also able to modify your soldiers’ weapons with various attachments as well as give them performance enhancing implants. While all of these customization options were quite welcomed, this resulted in some completely broken and overpowered combinations. For example, I had given one of my soldiers a superior repeater which gave him a 15% chance to instantly execute whatever target he was shooting at and as a result I was able to one-shot the hardest enemy in the game. The difficulty in general is kind of spiky, while the game initially starts off as challenging; it quickly becomes too easy upon developing certain technologies. Some better pacing would have greatly alleviated this issue because as it stands, it can switch from being so easy that it’s tedious to frustrating with little warning.
At first, there seems to be a greater variety of enemies present in Xcom 2. The majority of enemies you face are Advent troopers, human-like soldiers that support the alien regime, while more familiar aliens such-as sectoids function as lieutenants and are actually a greater threat than the previous games. The other aliens have also evolved over the twenty year gap between Enemy Unknown. Unfortunately you hardly fight them in the latter half of the game as you pretty much always face the same enemies over and over again at that point.
I also had some issues with the world map. It gives you so many optional areas to scan for additional supplies and personnel but you’re interrupted every two seconds to take part in another randomly generated mission. There are very few actual story missions, and the random stages can really get tedious in the latter half of the game. There’s also very little rhyme or reason going into the appearance of a stage. You could accept a mission in Africa only for there to be pine trees and snow on the ground, making no sense whatsoever. There are a lot of bugs present in the game as well. From graphical glitches, laggy animations and the odd crash.
Xcom 2 promised re-playability with its use of random stages but I would’ve honestly preferred handcrafted levels with more of a narrative. There’s also extra mod support this time around but most of the mods available currently are cosmetic or the odd weapon, which doesn’t really add anything significant to the gameplay.
The multiplayer from Enemy Unknown makes an appearance again but it’s even more of a throw-away mode this time around. You’re given even less customization options than before as you’re no longer able to choose the rank and loadout of human soldiers. The turns don’t play out simultaneously and can take an extremely long time as there’s quite a bit of additional lag between them. That combined with crashes and random disconnects make this mode barely playable.
The soundtrack is well done and changes to match the mood of the battle as well as the enemies you encounter. Unfortunately, there isn't much variety between tracks and it isn't as memorable as Michael Mccann’s soundtrack from Enemy Unknown who was probably too busy working on Deus Ex Mankind Divided.
Ultimately, Xcom 2 makes a very strong first impression but it was all downhill from there though, and towards the end of the game, I couldn’t wait to be done with all the randomly generated filler content. That coupled with an overall lack of pacing made it a bit of a disappointment. It’s an improvement over Enemy Unknown in some areas but a step-back in others. Xcom 2 is by no means a bad game, and will most likely improve with time; I was just expecting a lot more.
+	Strong Turn Based Tactical Combat
+	Increased Customization Options
+	Interesting Premise
+	Soldier classes and base management are more refined.
-	Repetitive Gameplay and Filler Content
-	Numerous Bugs
-	Lackluster Multiplayer
-	Not enough of an improvement over Enemy Unknown

In this review I'm not just going to say "This game is terrible, rip off of CS:GO." I'm going to list my pros and cons for this game. Either way, its a free game. Its not like you're spending $60 on this game and the reviews are going to determine whether you buy it or not. If you think you'd like it, play it.
That being said, I can't recommend this game. Putting 16 hours into this game I've found some things I really don't enjoy.
Starting off with the good stuff. The ability to buy guns without paying real money. This is a good concept to keep the game from being pay to win. Also, the daily rewards and rewards for ranking up are a nice addition, so it won't take that long to get the gun you wanted. Possibly only 5-6 rankups.
While I did have a lot of fun with this game, it isn't because of the game itself. Playing this with friends is like watching a movie that isn't terrible, but you laugh about its noticable flaws.
Some guns have little to no recoil, meaning you just hold mouse one and you can kill someone. Only select guns have noticable recoil (such as the AKs). This isn't good for a game that is already considered finished and an esport in some countries. Also, the damage is horrendous. You can unload 20 bullets into someone's chest from 5 feet away and they'll still be alive. I've experienced this many times myself. Snipers are too easy. There doesn't seem to be any penalty for missing a shot, because you can just crouch while locking in another bullet, and pop up and instantly shoot someone because there isn't any penalty for shooting while standing up. Also a lot of the snipers are one hit kills. Now you may say that "It's just like the AWP in CS:GO  I don't see your problem," but in CS:GO at least you get punished for sniping while moving, uncrouching, jumping, ect. In CS:GO your movement speed is slower when you have an AWP. In Black Squad, there isn't that much of a speed difference. Hitreg seems really bad as well. You can be aiming right at someone and the bullet or knife won't hit, even if you are right in front of the person. People can join any server region they want so you need to deal with someone over 200 ping stuttering around the map. Please make dedicated servers so people won't join servers and have over 200 ping. Lastly, the community is so toxic. It seems like you can't join a 5v5 game and just have fun without someone being toxic on your team, or the other team. I know that the game devs can't do anything about this, but still, beware that people are very toxic on this game.
TL:DR This game has potential, but in its current state I can't recommend it. There are too many bugs and things that are just bad, like the gun mechanics and that isn't good, considering its out of early access and an esport in other countries. If you want to try this game, get it, its free, but I can't recommend it myself.
EDIT: Also forgot to add about how loud the game is, how slow the sensitivity is, and how weird the controls are during the tutorial, and you can't change them until you finish the tutorial. M3 doesn't seem to be a good key for spriting in my opinion.

One of the few games I ever had the drive to 100%. The only thing that sucks about DS3 is PvP. I mean seriously, some covenants are basicaly broken after you reach a certain point in the game, specifically the Watchdogs of Farron and the Darkmoon Blades. Search up "proof of concord kept" on Youtube and you'll find ways to FARM it, or people saying how unbalanced the game is. These are supposed to be given to you when you finish a quest for the Darkmoon Blades, and you only need 30 to complete the covenant. The summon rate for this covenant is abysmal, and it stops nearly completely if you are medium to high level, making farming the only way to complete an otherwise great covenant. Finishing the covenants centered around Invasions are notoriusly awful, as 9 times out of 10 you'll get a group of Co-Opers or gankers who team up to kill you. This seriously hampers the multiplayer aspect, causing players to spend AGES farming for covenant items or climbing the PvP ladder.
Co-Op is not nearly as wonky-- Any pair of friends (or enemies), regardless of level, can play together using a password system, with the higher level player being nerfed to a realistic level in everything but damage. The Co-Op in Dark Souls 3 is better than any other Souls game, hands down. The DLC also adds a considerable amount to the game, albeit not to the extent DS2 did with the Crown trilogy.
What makes Dark Souls 3 stand out, however, is
the expansion of the Infusion system. You can make a weapon scale in damage better based on if you use Dex or Strength, you can convert it to static elemental damage, have scaling elemental damage, you name it. You can also have a weapon scale based on your Luck stat!
While leaving some things about the previous games unchanged, for better or worse, Dark Souls 3 brings enough to the table to stand alone, and fixes many of the issues in the previous games. 8 out of 10.

Hiding behind the moniker of "Hard" doesn't hide all the bad game design.
The front end difficulty curve is obscene, bordering on stupid.  Read any experienced guide and you will see what I mean.  You aren't supposed to follow the initital advice of the game.  Don't cure your characters, hell don't even provide provisions for them.
Upgrade the wagon to get as many heroes as possible, send those heroes into dungeons without provisions, run away before they die, collect loot.  Dismiss stressed heroes and repeat ad naseum.
The game just stacks the deck too far against you.  Hell you get stress at random for just walking down the hall.  You get stress for basically everything, but you cant really easily remove the stress.  You get no attachment to your heroes because they are all disposable meat until you are done the grind.
Does this sound fun to you?  It certainly wasn't for me.  Uninstalling and disappointed.  It's a shame too, as the art style is awesome and the core game play is interesting.  But the design decisions just crush you under their grindy weight.  Some people enjoy being punished and accomplishing miniscule steps forward, I certainly am not one of these people.  I enjoy challenging games like Rogue Legacy and Dark Souls 1/2/3, but this is not one of those titles.

Black Squad is a F2P 'competitive' multiplayer shooter that claims to hit alot of high marks, toting 'amazing netcode', 'great shooting mechanics' and 'absolutely no pay to win', ending with it's statement as the best F2P shooter on the market. In my experience it was less than stellar and doesn't live up to most of what it says.
To start, the mechanics are pretty standard fare. After a recommended tutorial explaining the basic controls, you're dropped into one of various gamemodes which include TDM, Assassination which is a VIP protection mode with an AI VIP for some reason, and Battle, which is a 32 player objective focused mode. These are just the ones I played, but there's a handful of other modes like one-life hardcore modes or modes that only allow specific weapons like sniper rifles, knives, etc. Pretty basic and not really anything unique in that aspect, Battle probably being the most original, but it suffers in it's own way, which I'll get back to in a bit.
In terms of weapons and inventory the game is indeed not Pay 2 Win. Any stuff that can be bought with IRL money is strictly cosmetic as of the time of writing this, and the only way to get other firearms is through "Gold" (the generic currency you get through playing) or "Medals" (A special currency you only obtain through things like level ups, daily/weekly challenges). There's an okay assortment of weapons to choose from, from assault rifles to sniper rifles, SMGs and LMGs. Secondaries too, though they're only obtained through medals rather than gold. Though, curiously, the grenade equippables you get are on a trial timer. You can get them through opening cases that are microtransaction boxes. Thankfully the box grenades come out of can be bought via gold.
So why do I not recommend the game? It has a plethora of underlying issues that turn an 'okay' generic shooter into a significantly less enjoyable experience.
Remember that 'amazing' netcode? I can't tell if it really is amazing, because even though I search for a game in an NA server, I'm still getting placed with and against players with 250-400 ping. The game has no region locking or filtering as far as I can tell, and because of this it ends up in alot of frustrating moments where I'll get shot through cover, a decent chunk of time after I've left my opponent's view. Lag and such is an issue in pretty much every online game that's ever existed, but this game handles ping differences in a very poor fashion, especially when there's no failsafe in place like a ping checker/limiter during matches. I wouldn't list this except it's happened in
every match I played that I can remember playing with my time spent on the game.
While the game may not be Pay 2 Win, the gun balance is questionable at times. Most weapons are fine tuned in terms of balance, offering a good compromise of damage/recoil/fire rate etc, or filling a specific niche (more accuracy and less recoil for less damage, for example). However, the starter sniper rifle
But then there's a bolt action sniper rifle you can buy with gold that will instantly kill, even on a bodyshot. There are also an AK series of rifles, namely the AK12 and AK47, which not only possess underbarrel grenade launchers (something certain rifles have including gold ones), but can one tap you with a headshot. If I've poked through the game correctly they're the only rifles that have this ability to one tap. You can argue that they have less fire rate so it rewards careful aiming ala CSGO style, but the only way to achieve these AKs inparticular is through those medals currency I mentioned. You can get other rifles and the sniper rifle I mentioned through standard gold, but the AKs, as an example, are medal locked, which brings me to my next point.
There is most certainly a grind to this game. Assault rifles cost 120k gold. Sniper rifles are 192k gold.  LMGs are 92k with shotguns and one SMG clocking in at 96K. The grenades on a timer? 3.5-5k gold, to use grenades for
There's been a booster going for the gold and XP you earn, but doing fairly well in game I was earning anywhere from 700 gold to around 1k when I did exceptionally good. That's with a 20% boost, mind you. Once you beat the tutorial it starts you off with a little over 200k gold, which is good to buy around two rifles/SMGs or one sniper rifle, but after that it's back to grinding your money. Thankfully you get around 15k gold just for logging in per day and extra gold/medals for each week you login, but that's assuming you'll stick around long enough to play. That's over a week of just signing in to get one firearm that you may not even like, since there's no way to test them except for one-time DLCs you can get from the store page that give you 15 days of use on the weapons, I don't think it covers all firearms in game but I haven't actually checked, to be fair. Medal specific weapons? Those AK and other medal-specific rifles cost you 2500 medals each, and all secondary pistol firearms are medal locked as well, at 1.5k medals per and knife reskins for the same amount. There's one SMG for 2k medals, and a sniper rifle for 3.2k. If I'm correct it starts you with 500 medals, and awards up to 100 a day for winning X amount of times, plus weekly challenges for playtime. Leveling up grants 100 medals per level, I believe. While the medal-restricted weapons certainly aren't overpowered by definition, I have to wonder why the one-tap rifles are strictly for people who only stick around, and in the end it feels more like a grindfest to potentially get a leg up on everyone.
The grind, and overall playability, seems hampered to me because the game is so shallow. It has nothing unique going for it. It lacks the tension and strategy of tactical shooters like CSGO or Rainbow Six Siege, but the core run-and-gun feeling also isn't fluent or satisfying enough to be something like CoD or arena-esque shooters for example. It has a handful of various modes like I mentioned, which are all either "Do X objective like kill/defend this area/VIP" (or kill the other team to end the round prematurely) or just straight up kill in TDM. Battle mode is the 32 player mode which has you destroying 5 caches of the other team, located around the map. The catch is that you have 'classes' that have access to special abilities. Triggering an ability uses points that you re-earn by killing players and damaging the caches. This is easily the most unique mode, except it's very messy because there's no limit to how many players of each kind of class there can be. Being a class doesn't really affect your weapons (unless you activate one of it's special abilities like pulling out a grenade/rocket launcher), and certain class abilities aren't particularly useful. Supports for example have a medkit, that they can drop one of at a time, but that's if anyone sees it to run over it before they die. The Command class also gets an attack helicopter to assist- except, since there can only be one at a time, you could have a handful of Command users who are unable to use it and whoever mashes their activate key first gets to use theirs.
In total the game just feels watered down and as if it's trying to be multiple games. Like it's trying to capture the hardcore, tactical and tense gameplay of high-profile shooters like CSGO, or the fast paced twitch shooter gameplay of CoD/arena shooters, but it ends up being a washed out mix of both that doesn't accomplish what it sets out to do. Pair that with the grind for new firearms and ping issues, and how repetitive and lifeless it is and you just have a game that's acceptable at best. That is, till you realize what faults it has underneath it's surface. It's even harder to recommend when you have better quality F2P shooters like Dirty Bomb, or even TF2. (Despite it seemingly being on life support, it's still kicking a bit)

A year later and it's time for a real review.
XCOM 2 is a game of potential that fell short.  It just isn't as replayable as the first game, as the flaws just become more apparent each time through.
First, the maps aren't as procedural as we were led to believe. The result being that all the maps feel the same with slight differences instead of a unique map each time. Map packs help slightly, but I've not found too many of those that make it better.
Timed Missions - I get what they were trying to do by having these, giving you a high octane mission where escape is the priority instead of long drawn out battles. However, I want long battles where I'm working my team around the flank to take out enemies. Even the in game explanations of some of the timers don't make sense. (Advent laptops and data vaults have a nasty tendency to self destruct when XCOM comes in stealthed.)
The DLC, while adding some really good story bits, didn't impress me with their rewards. Finish them too early and you'll have 3 overpowered soldiers, finish too late and and it doesn't have much of an impact. Finding the perfect place for Goldylocks is difficult.
On to stuff I liked:
Character customization. making your team of badasses look awesome is super easy to do. With all the mod packs for more things for your soldiers to wear make it even better.
Weapon mods and customization. While I would have preferred more variety it's awesome to have.
The story is actually pretty good, with Shen and Tygan having a more colorful history than Old Shen and Vahlen.
All in all, it isn't a bad game. I got my money's worth at launch full price, but I've gotten so much more out of the first game and Long War.

Got in on this during the free weekend, and have to say I'm deeply impressed.
It's a nice refreshing change of pace from the usual hero-based MOBA to be able to pilot big spaceships and start blasting the enemy.  There's a decent variety of ships with their own strengths and weaknesses, and each has some customization options (I.E. Balanced cannon vs rapid fire short range cannon vs high power slow speed long range cannon) that opens up some capacity to tailor the ship to your personal playstyle.  (Note that as of this writing several ships have very few options, though it looks like they're working on them)  In terms of a good spaceship combat game this is extremely satisfying.
There's only one major downside with the game right now, and that's the lobby system.  To join a game you have to manually choose a server, and there is no capacity to set up a group to play with.  For getting one friend in on your team it's managable with a bit of coordination, but trying to get in any more is largely impossible.  The game is still only alpha though, so that's forgivable, though I'd like to see fixing this made a priority.  It'll be a lot easier to convince my friends to get in on it when we call all play together. :3

Ive had this game for a while and keep wanting to post a review. Do you like the art of Mike Mignola? Great, because even though he doesn't do the art for this game, its an homage to his style. Do you like dark, eldritch settings? Great, because thats exactly what Darkest Dungeon has.
This is a game about losing. You start off fighting a losing battle in dungeons that are too hard, with heroes that are too weak, and a town that is not developed. You might be mistaken in thinking that your characters are the main point of development in this game, but really its the town. Your adventurers will slowly bring back enough stuff to upgrade the town to make it better and attract better and more adventurers. Adventurers are your currency that you use and eventually lose. Some die. Some go crazy from the stress. Literally. Your characters gain stress in each dungeon as they see and do things, and develop quirks like only drinking in town, or always needing to be the first to open chests (for good or ill). Sometimes they become afraid of certain types of monsters, become masochistic, or even just afraid of the dark. Given enough time and money, you could cure these quirks in town at the church or the tavern or the brothel. But eventually it becomes too costly and you can let them die or let them leave.
This is a dark and fun RPG about trying to find victoory in every loss and fight a constant losing battle. It looks great, is easy to understand, and is difficult while not giving you a game over screen when your party of aventurers die. If they do, just go back to town and pick up more for the meat grinder.

Before I start this review, keep in mind that this is my personal opinions of this game, and you can differ as you wish.
XCOM 2 is the sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within, which back then I loved- in fact, I still love. XCOM 2 might be good, but it's not perfect, that much I can say.
For starters, I found the story to be a bit bland and plain. It's like every other game: "Find the bad guy! Shoot the bad guy! You win!" Now, I've nothing against that, but it's a bit of creative space wasted.
Graphics? I liked 'em to some degree. There was no real artstyle that catched my eye, which again is a shame. I was expecting the enviorments to be more... What's the word? Alien. ADVENT and their troops are alien. Yes, this planet is inhabited by humans, but it still doesn't justify the artstyle.
Gameplay? It's good. Your typical XCOM game. You maintain everything as the 'commander' of the XCOM project- or what is now 'The resistance', meaning you're in charge of R&D, taking on operations, etc. However, I do find the amount of supplys they give you to be a bit annoying after ops. I want to finish my scans one by one, not delay the story! It's a minor thing, but it can be quite annoying to me.
Characters: Oh my god, did I love this feature. The introduction of character pools and customization was the best decision Firaxis ever made. I'm a frequent roleplayer, and I keep track of my characters, no less. Being able to make them as well as the system would let me felt like it was more rewarding than it should've.
Performance Issues: Now, I'm not saying I didn't get a lag spike here and there, but I didn't really see the fuss of all the lag and performance issues. Mind you, these are thoughts before the performance patch. I run a lower-end PC, no less, so I should be the one lagging more frequently, but it seems to be a opposite world.
Overall, the game is quite solid on some aspects, whilst having no ground on others. If you don't mind having a plain narrative and artstyle, you better pull out that $59.99, as this game is for you.

RotMG is a very unique MMO. It manages to combine teamwork, bullet hell, and dungeon crawling in one neat package. Hope right in and watch as you quickly level up and gain power, then suddenly be killed and lose it all, then hop in again and get it all back! Server strain is a big issue, but as long as they aren't full you should be able to manage. Maxing out your class of choice is quite a challenge, and should keep you entertained for quite a while. The aforemented Mad God is also quite satisfying when you do get to attack it. The hilarity of watching a whole server scramble through his punishing dungeon is very memorable indeed.
If I had to say what this games biggest flaw is, it would be the turn towards pay-2-win it has taken. This unfortuantely was not always a problem; realm gold (the game's premium currency) used to just be good for buying cosmetic dyes and pets, or extra storage space. Now, with all sorts of high-tier gear being offered for it, the game feels more hollow and less rewarding. The adventure is still there, but it seems redundant when you can bypass it with the wave of a credit card. This is what personally keeps me from getting back into the game (along with technical difficulties with connecting to my Kongregate account), but if you're fine with it, don't let me stop you! It's still a wonderful game, and i'd recommend at least giving it a shot. It's free, after all; what have you got to lose?

Overall - Good vanilla, much better with mods / gameplay tweaks. The game did have quite a few issues at launch though, released a bit too early.
Gameplay - 2 major ways XCOM 2 differs from XCOM:EW
XCOM 2 is guerilla warfare (Hit and run). Most missions are on a turn timer and you'll have to secure a package/V.I.P before having to extract / kill the remaining enemies. Think meld containers, but mandatory.
Higher enemy offensive / mobility power. They can do such things as pull you from up to twelve tiles away, full-move dash attacks or even smash through walls. Its basically kill the enemies the turn you activated them or suffer greatly, not much hunkering down / skirmishes / long fights.
Atmosphere - Can be a bit less serious compared to XCOM: EW. Renegade grandpa's with pink t-shirts and laser swords, aliens angrily shake their fists at you and the camera loves their butts, snake breasts, etc. Not necessarily bad, just a different tone than expected.
DLC - Same opinion as the community
Resistance warrior - Negative (Overpriced): (Small amount of cosmetics)
Anarchy's children - Negative (Different): (See above "Atmosphere", cosmetics too off theme)
Alien Hunters - Mixed (Leader Mechanics):  (Being balanced for the War of the Chosen DLC,)
Shen's last Gift - Positive: (Mech being upgraded (Accuracy and attachments) in War of the Chosen DLC)
----Reinforcement pack is just a bundle of packs excluding Resistance warrior----
Modding - Community is fantastic, especially Long War Studios (Now called Pavonis Interactive) who also made an unofficial (But amazing) XCOM:EW Expansion (Long War) as well as XCOM 2: Long War.

Like Jake Solomon, XCOM: UFO Defense was the epiphany that opened the doors of perception of my teenage video game consciousness. Creepy late nights fearing cyberdisks and chryssalids, grays doing mind control. It's the symbol of my junior year of high school and the most terrifying, strategically deep game I have ever played.
That said, XCOM 2 is also a perfect 10.
The Good:
The best part of the new game was the decison--a bit daring--to turn XCOM on its head and make it a guerilla army. This was always how it felt--a ragtag group of soldiers, struggling to scrap together the cash to buy a couple grenades. And now this theme is deployed perfectly. By being on the losing side of history, the stakes in a way feel higher--not just to preserve the status quo as in XCOM 1994 and XCOM EU, but rather to create a worldwide revolution against an unjust social order. THAT ALONE makes this experience mind-blowing for me.
However, the next thing, and not too many critics focus on this, is that XCOM 2 deepens the strategy layer of XCOM EU, which let's admit, was dull. The strategy layer was actually quite engaging in the original 1994 XCOM UFO Defense. This alone is a godsend, as you have choices of how to pass time now. Do you want to pick up some more cash or go to get another engineer? The cash takes longer, but it could help you upgrade to better armor if you get it before the next terror mission, which you now know is coming "imminently." Choosing certain missions counters "dark events" and advances on the part of the aliens, so now the "here are three missions choose one" makes sense, as you can only develop a plan to sabotage one place. Additionally it's now a nonlinear experience in which your choice of how to get resources, develop your base, and trade on the black market all feel much more open-ended and up to your player preferences. Want a psi lab after a month? Done. Want to sell all your intel (so you can't contact more resistance fighters) to buy physical upgrades for your soldiers? You can do that instead. Want to get good armor instead of pursuing the main plot or spending your money on a laboratory? You can do that instead. XCOM EU felt like there was an optimal pattern. Now that is gone and thank god.
Along those lines, the changes to the strategy layer, in which the avenger must now pick up resources (as well as soldiers, engineers and scientists) adds tension, as you hope to get these bonuses before the next battle crops up. Additionally it plays perfectly into the theme of the guerilla nature of XCOM in an occupied world. We must scavenge whatever resources we can coverlty and then escape, but if an alien attack breaks out, we have to abandon our quest for more supplies to fend off the immediate threat.
As if that wasn't enough, the move and overwatch ad infinitum of XCOM 1 is now gone, replaced by ambushing tactics and a risk taking demanded by a countdown timer. This means you either a.) run up to and strike an unsuspecting pod (awesome!) or b.) MUST run up and trigger a pod even if you're not in a perfect position. Overwatch is still powerful but not overpowered as it was in part one. Additionally the new classes, especially as they approach Major become AWE-INSPRIING. This is counterbalanced by some very strong and very resistant enemies. It's not a case of make the enemies average and make the soliders average. Toward the end it's amazing squad vs. amazing enemies.
Procedurally generated maps make for a great experience, as nothing ever looks too similar (through one playthrough and part of another). I didn't even see a snowy one as I beat it in July. Next, the addition of experimental armor, grendaes and weapons adds variability to each playthrough, as some times you might have acid grenades, other times you get a hazmat suit.
Finally, I love character customization and the modding community has really added to my experience. I wanted a Nicaraguan solider with a beret and spiders on his armor. I got exactly that. Customization helps you have a tie to your soldiers, so when they die it's all the more painful.
The Not so Good:
Some good new enemies characters, but I didn't see some of them very often, perhaps cause I beat it "early" (this was on veteran). I also often felt more annoyed than terrified of some of the characters (Codex anyone?) and the sense of terror wasn't there. Hopefully my Commander playthough will have more of that. Andromedons and Gatekeepers felt kinda faceless and almost robotic to me, not organic. I am also a big XCOM 1994 fan and felt some of the new enemies weren't quite in the spirit of the original, but this is a minor gripe.
Some things are not clear for new players: like the Advanced Warfare Center speeds up your healing! (Shouldn't this be an Advanced Clinic for thematic reasons?). Regardless, this is not a gripe so much as just a word to new players to expect some confusion on the first playthrough (I abandoned mine after three or four months because I stupidly didn't realize the research route I needed to develop armor)
Some confusing plot points, but to some extent I accept these as they allow for wild and diverse speculation.
The Bad:
Just the bugs, framerates, inability to move to certain floors on buildings. Nothing gamebreaking. This game is actaully an 11, so the bugs simply push it down to a 10.
Viva XCOM! And viva Chrysallids, sorry, I really like them...

Ah yes, XCOM 2 the long awaited sequel to XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within by Firaxis. Does it live up to the hype that Enemy Unknown (a remake of the original UFO Defense) had especially with the Long War mod? Well that answer is a little complicated, it is yes and no.
XCOM 2 is a remake of not the 2nd game in the original X-COM series but in actuality the 3rd, X-COM: Apocalypse. In XCOM 2 you play as not a group that is defending their home world from the invading aliens but in fact the world actually ended up losing to the aliens and conquered Earth. 20 years after the events of Enemy Unknown, Officer Bradford (command) came upon intelligence that found where the ADVENT (the alien government) was hiding you, the commander, all this time. Once the commander is back XCOM is back and operational can commence the operation to find out ADVENT's true intentions and to overthrow the alien government. Spoiler alert: The aliens are actually being bad, SURPRISE!!!
Enemy Unknown/Within's main story missions were very unique in that they set up various challenges and felt completely different from the defense or rescue missions on the side. For example the Newfoundland Mission in Enemy Within was an absolutely hard and fun mission but those are no where to be found in XCOM 2. Most of the missions in XCOM 2 are, go here, defend this or attack that or save these civilians. Occasionally you'll have a mission where you'll attack an Advent facility to prevent the Advent project but those themselves aren't entirely memorable either. With the exception of the missions where a UFO shoots down your ship or the final mission, nothing was incredibly memorable about the campaign itself.
XCOM 2 is much like its original in that it is a squad turn based strategy game where your team of 4-6 soldiers try to complete different objectives. There are five classes that are fairly similar to Enemy Unknown with a few new skills. Those classes include Ranger (close quarters), Grenadier (machine gun and grenades), specialist (robot hacking and healing), sharpshooter (sniper) and the Psi Op who uses various psionic powers as you train them in the Psi Lab.
As you progress through the game your objective will to be not only to discover how to defeat the Advent Project but to also make contact with other resistance cells in order to gain resources and intel to combat the ADVENT. The missions that appear on the world progress as you make contact with more resistance locations and the maps themselves during your missions are procedurally generated making no mission location to seem like the same. Though that does have a strange habit of making Siberia seem like it is in a desert location though that might have been a bug originally when I played.
While you are progressing in making contacts and that mad XCOM money you are able to purchase and research new armor and weapons that can further help your team survive out in the field. Along with the money you also get intel for completing different missions. This intel allows you to purchase different things from the black market and allows you to make contact with other resistance locations throughout the world.
Much like Enemy Unknown, you can't just dillydally around the map. If you take too much time, depending on how many Advent facilities are in the world the Advent Project will progress where if it fills up you lose the game. On top of that the Advent have different resistance retaliation time periods where they will attack different resistance locations causing resources to slow down and if you don't stop them at all either by not going there or failing the mission you can lose contact with that area all together and have to re-establish said contact. Another combat against you going slowly is over time the ADVENT will acquire abilities that change various things in game. Whether those be a UFO searching around for you, progress on the Advent Project, stronger armor, slower research, less intel or several others. These can hurt you but I noticed that they don't change the game too much. Obviously they didn't want to make the game impossible but it seems like the advent events could have been a little more impactful.
Let's talk about the difficulty of this game for a bit. I know some found the RNG (Random Number Generator) a little harsh, missing a 90% chance to hit, but over the course of the game it will end up balancing out. I understand that sometimes it feels like those misses come at the most inopportune times but with the way you can get around the aliens from even being able to hit you with grenades, overwatch, the over powered mimic beacon there is always a way to keep the balance on your side. I would argue that this game is too easy and it doesn't truly get hard until the last mission in the game that has no escalator in difficulty. In Enemy Unknown the missions ramped up in difficulty all the way until the final mission on the alien ship. In XCOM 2 the missions are all fairly simple, especially when your soldiers are properly equipped, until that last mission that throws a whole bunch of problems your way including mind controlling avatars at the end.
Also a problem I had with this game was it didn't really feel like it was a step up from Enemy Unknown. Sure there are new classes and the new concealed mode but for all Firaxis's talk about Enemy Unknown being a tutorial for the Long War mod, they seemed to not take any hints and try to add features that the Long War made better in EU. With that said however, Firaxis did allow for mods in the beginning include the vast steam marketplace that already existed just one week after the game launched. I have no doubt the Long War guys will make another or some other group of modders will make this game even better.
Graphics wise XCOM 2 is much better than its predecessor despite it running the same engine, albeit it is running on Unreal 3.5 opposed to Unreal 3. There is a lot of customization of your soldiers too, allowing you to make your gameplay unique and different. There have been reports of problems that I noticed myself however if you had vsync and FXAA on however that might be fixed soon in a patch. On top of the graphics, the soundtrack is also a huge plus on this game. I found myself singing along during a lot of the songs because they were extremely catchy and enjoyable despite them being replayed a lot during the game.
Overall XCOM 2 despite all its flaws is still a game I absolutely had a blast to play. Not many games make me want to sit all week and do nothing but play it but XCOM 2 definitely does such. There are problems with the lack of content and difficulty along with some early performance issues and a lackluster story but that doesn't discount how much fun it is.

I read alot of reviews before I bought this game, and mostly heard things about how it was unnecessarily unfair. These reviews turned me off to the game (which I'd been interested in for awhile). I finally picked it up, and I wish I'd never listened to a bulk of those reviews. Most reviews went on about how the game was brutally relentless, hating the player at every turn and ALWAYS stacking the odds against you. However, upon having played the game myself, I say this is a pro rather than a con. The thing about Darkest Dungeon is that the game wants you to loose (there is even a warning message every time you start the game). And not just in the aspect of RNG. Of course, everything in actual combat is stacked against you. Powerful enemies with powerful moves call for planning at every encounter, and even then, RNG will still bite you. But beyond this, the game is designed to hurt you in the long run. From negative quirks and diseases your heroes pick up, to over stressed heroes, to a lack of funds, to a lack of valid heroes, etc. This sorts of things are meant to build up over time and will lead you to lose unless legitamte effort is put into compensating for the things you will run into. But that's not the whole of Darkest Dungeon. The challenge Darkest Dungeon presents is that no matter how well you play this game, the previously stated difficulties WILL catch up to you. They will hurt you, kill you heroes, and possibly make you lose your playthrough. I think this is why Darkest Dungeon recieves the criticism it recieves. Most gamers nowadays expect a "right way" to play their games, to maximize the good and minimize the bad. Darkest Dungeon firmly throws that idea into the pits, and says, "You are going to suffer, then lose. You will continue to do so, until you win at immeasurable cost." If this is something you can accept, and are willing to take on, then you should give Darkest Dungeon a shot.

Overall - Good vanilla, much better with mods / gameplay tweaks. The game did have quite a few issues at launch though, released a bit too early.
Gameplay - 2 major ways XCOM 2 differs from XCOM:EW
XCOM 2 is guerilla warfare (Hit and run). Most missions are on a turn timer and you'll have to secure a package/V.I.P before having to extract / kill the remaining enemies. Think meld containers, but mandatory.
Higher enemy offensive / mobility power. They can do such things as pull you from up to twelve tiles away, full-move dash attacks or even smash through walls. Its basically kill the enemies the turn you activated them or suffer greatly, not much hunkering down / skirmishes / long fights.
Atmosphere - Can be a bit less serious compared to XCOM: EW. Renegade grandpa's with pink t-shirts and laser swords, aliens angrily shake their fists at you and the camera loves their butts, snake breasts, etc. Not necessarily bad, just a different tone than expected.
DLC - Same opinion as the community
Resistance warrior - Negative (Overpriced): (Small amount of cosmetics)
Anarchy's children - Negative (Different): (See above "Atmosphere", cosmetics too off theme)
Alien Hunters - Mixed (Leader Mechanics):  (Being balanced for the War of the Chosen DLC,)
Shen's last Gift - Positive: (Mech being upgraded (Accuracy and attachments) in War of the Chosen DLC)
----Reinforcement pack is just a bundle of packs excluding Resistance warrior----
Modding - Community is fantastic, especially Long War Studios (Now called Pavonis Interactive) who also made an unofficial (But amazing) XCOM:EW Expansion (Long War) as well as XCOM 2: Long War.

This game... THIS game... I honestly thought that this game would be of no interest to me whatsoever, I mean, why would it? Minecraft failed to hold my interest, despite its endless moddability (I still like it, though!). Terraria peters out after you finish the latest content. Starbound is... that's right, dead. Honestly, my first thought when seeing this was, "Oh god, another stupid block-building game that just so HAPPENS to be free to play." and yes, it was another stupid block-building game that just so HAPPENS to be free to play... but as I delved into it, I began to see behind it, and by god, out of all the block-building open world adventure games out there, this one practically takes it for me.
So, what is Trove? Simple, it's a game where you pick one of the many classes available and just go on out there into the open world(s), gathering treasure, building blocks and equipment, it's really just what would happen if Minecraft decided to steal from Terraria's book and add classes while they're at it. And shockingly, it works. Also, the story is nothing to write home about, it really feels like an excuse plot at this point, although, mind you, I haven't really gotten into the super End-Game content yet so I cannot say for certain that this changes.
It's like Minecraft with guns.
Now, classes, these make up the abilities and weapons that your character is capable of, from throwing frost bolts to fae blasts to shooting people in the face and throwing boomerangs at them, every class has their own unique skillset, along with pros and cons. For instance, I made the
of playing an Ice Sage, a class that has a magical shield that protects them from harm and an ult that freezes everyone in an area around them and deals delayed damage to them, pretty hard to use while solo but when I'm running a dungeon by myself and a random player bursts in, I can see the Ice Sage's true strength shine through. Of course, not every class is going to be on equal footing, some are clearly stronger than others and while there are some that are super strong on paper (Fae Tricksters come to mind) but are somewhat borderline in practice. Every class can contribute something, however, and that's fine with me.
Classes are good, allows for multiple playstyles, some slight imbalance with some but overall they feel balanced.
Not entirely impressive, to say the least, but the blocky nature of the graphics lends it to a lot of its cartoonish charm, which is especially prevalent in the Candy zones of the world (yes, candy, don't question it.) and the buildings that are placed by default by the game are, well, actually really darn impressive considering the simplicity of it all, and the dungeons are all thematically built according to what zone you're in so, like,  a Fae dungeon can be a tree or a storybook or an Everfrost dungeon can be a crying Mammoth stuck in the ice, I feel there's a good bit of variety to at least slow down the tedium of dungeon grinding.
Now, about the building part itself, you've got a few avenues, you can build directly onto the world (although considering the temporal nature of the worlds why would you unless you're cheesing something.) or build in a designated zone named a Cornerstone. Cornerstones are like portable housing, and they're scattered across the map, it's where you can build and design whatever your heart desires within a small limitation though. But if you're not happy about the limitations of the portable houses, you can join (or make) a club and go into a Club World where you can build to your heart's content (permission pending). The tools for building is rather simple, in build mode you have two functions, left click places and right click mines, simple as that, placement is actually really cool as you can click and drag to where you want to place a line of blocks down, which makes some of the tedious parts of building much more bearable. It can be a bit finicky, though, with the third person camera but it works!
Graphics are simple, yet somehow, they manage to look really good. Building is not as tedious as anticipated.
Yes, it's not a Free to Play game without the cash shop, a F2P game without a cash shop is a free game without a... erm... hmm... I'll get back to you on that one but I digress, yes, there's a cash shop, you can buy things in there from ores to costumes to packs to new mounts (although, mind you, the default mount serves most purposes well) and some other miscellaneous stuff like name changes, flasks, emblems, and what have you. The emblems and flasks are pretty cheap compared to the rest of the shop and the free currency can be easily acquired by simply doing stuff in game... or you can open up your wallet for the premium currency to get them. Only cosmetics will ever be locked behind a paywall, as far as I know. Mounts, on the other hand, I'm not too sure on, but I'm certain they're not Pay-2-Win.
There's also a patron thing that I'm iffy about as it grants some advantages to the players who buy it like extra jumps (which, surprisingly, is a big deal in this game), extra magic find, 50% more experience, and more. Is it Pay2Win? I'm going to let you be the judge of that...
Cosmetics are mostly paid for with premium currency, game uses a freemium system where you can acquire free currency to spend on certain perks. Patron remains a concern.
I feel that this is quite a solid  game despite its drawbacks, it can get grindy and repetitive in due time, the classes are stuck with their limited skillset and gathering blocks to craft and build with can be a bit of a chore early game, but all in all, I feel that Trove is pretty good for a free to play game... sure, I feel there may be some aspects that would trigger some P2W alarm bells but for me, personally, I'm perhaps willing to look over it... although keeping a careful eye on it to make sure it doesn't go out of control. Also, if you're ever going to be playing this for the first time, it might be best to drag some friends along to make the initial voyage more palatable as soloing can be a bit dull.

Well, it has been many months since I posted my original review, and I now have close to 150 hours in Fractured Space. I definitely reccomend the game--it has many good MOBA-like aspects, but it puts an entirely new and orignal spin on the very concept of a MOBA.
Like other MOBAs, there are some skins and certain resources that can only be acquired through real-world currency, but for the most part, the game rewards and encourages playing matches to earn resources; a great example of this are the Missions. There are 3 sets of missions that a player can strive to complete at any time, and the rewards, while somewhat randomized, are usually worth the effort. These missions require the player to achieve certain accomplishments within PVP or quickplay (vs robots) matches, within the Mission's time-limit (for example, a mission may ask you to get 36 kills with a "Heavy" ship). The point is, these missions have set up a fun and motivating mechanic to encourage and reward frequent and SKILLED play.
The ships themselves, as well as the environment in which games take place, are well-balanced, creatively designed, and STUNNINGLY beautiful. Graphics requirements are not too demanding, and server latency is generally good.
As for gameplay?
Spaceships. Shooting. Other. Spaceships.
It's every bit as amazing as it sounds.
Addendum:
Though I still reccomend this game wholeheartedly, and I have greatly enjoyed it (250 hours and counting as of this addition), I feel I should warn potential players that, depending on your location and what time of day you choose to play, you MAY have trouble finding a game. And, during these periods of time when few players are online, you MAY be matched with players far above and below your skill-level. This can be frustrating for obvious reasons--imagine a League of legends matching diamond players with Bornze players.
But, it doesn't happen every game, and as long as you try to learn and play intelligently, the community will happily help you get better at the game. **The Fractured Space official Discord channel is an especially useful and friendly resource to meet other players, get advice, and learn about the game**.

Like Jake Solomon, XCOM: UFO Defense was the epiphany that opened the doors of perception of my teenage video game consciousness. Creepy late nights fearing cyberdisks and chryssalids, grays doing mind control. It's the symbol of my junior year of high school and the most terrifying, strategically deep game I have ever played.
That said, XCOM 2 is also a perfect 10.
The Good:
The best part of the new game was the decison--a bit daring--to turn XCOM on its head and make it a guerilla army. This was always how it felt--a ragtag group of soldiers, struggling to scrap together the cash to buy a couple grenades. And now this theme is deployed perfectly. By being on the losing side of history, the stakes in a way feel higher--not just to preserve the status quo as in XCOM 1994 and XCOM EU, but rather to create a worldwide revolution against an unjust social order. THAT ALONE makes this experience mind-blowing for me.
However, the next thing, and not too many critics focus on this, is that XCOM 2 deepens the strategy layer of XCOM EU, which let's admit, was dull. The strategy layer was actually quite engaging in the original 1994 XCOM UFO Defense. This alone is a godsend, as you have choices of how to pass time now. Do you want to pick up some more cash or go to get another engineer? The cash takes longer, but it could help you upgrade to better armor if you get it before the next terror mission, which you now know is coming "imminently." Choosing certain missions counters "dark events" and advances on the part of the aliens, so now the "here are three missions choose one" makes sense, as you can only develop a plan to sabotage one place. Additionally it's now a nonlinear experience in which your choice of how to get resources, develop your base, and trade on the black market all feel much more open-ended and up to your player preferences. Want a psi lab after a month? Done. Want to sell all your intel (so you can't contact more resistance fighters) to buy physical upgrades for your soldiers? You can do that instead. Want to get good armor instead of pursuing the main plot or spending your money on a laboratory? You can do that instead. XCOM EU felt like there was an optimal pattern. Now that is gone and thank god.
Along those lines, the changes to the strategy layer, in which the avenger must now pick up resources (as well as soldiers, engineers and scientists) adds tension, as you hope to get these bonuses before the next battle crops up. Additionally it plays perfectly into the theme of the guerilla nature of XCOM in an occupied world. We must scavenge whatever resources we can coverlty and then escape, but if an alien attack breaks out, we have to abandon our quest for more supplies to fend off the immediate threat.
As if that wasn't enough, the move and overwatch ad infinitum of XCOM 1 is now gone, replaced by ambushing tactics and a risk taking demanded by a countdown timer. This means you either a.) run up to and strike an unsuspecting pod (awesome!) or b.) MUST run up and trigger a pod even if you're not in a perfect position. Overwatch is still powerful but not overpowered as it was in part one. Additionally the new classes, especially as they approach Major become AWE-INSPRIING. This is counterbalanced by some very strong and very resistant enemies. It's not a case of make the enemies average and make the soliders average. Toward the end it's amazing squad vs. amazing enemies.
Procedurally generated maps make for a great experience, as nothing ever looks too similar (through one playthrough and part of another). I didn't even see a snowy one as I beat it in July. Next, the addition of experimental armor, grendaes and weapons adds variability to each playthrough, as some times you might have acid grenades, other times you get a hazmat suit.
Finally, I love character customization and the modding community has really added to my experience. I wanted a Nicaraguan solider with a beret and spiders on his armor. I got exactly that. Customization helps you have a tie to your soldiers, so when they die it's all the more painful.
The Not so Good:
Some good new enemies characters, but I didn't see some of them very often, perhaps cause I beat it "early" (this was on veteran). I also often felt more annoyed than terrified of some of the characters (Codex anyone?) and the sense of terror wasn't there. Hopefully my Commander playthough will have more of that. Andromedons and Gatekeepers felt kinda faceless and almost robotic to me, not organic. I am also a big XCOM 1994 fan and felt some of the new enemies weren't quite in the spirit of the original, but this is a minor gripe.
Some things are not clear for new players: like the Advanced Warfare Center speeds up your healing! (Shouldn't this be an Advanced Clinic for thematic reasons?). Regardless, this is not a gripe so much as just a word to new players to expect some confusion on the first playthrough (I abandoned mine after three or four months because I stupidly didn't realize the research route I needed to develop armor)
Some confusing plot points, but to some extent I accept these as they allow for wild and diverse speculation.
The Bad:
Just the bugs, framerates, inability to move to certain floors on buildings. Nothing gamebreaking. This game is actaully an 11, so the bugs simply push it down to a 10.
