Ah yes, XCOM 2 the long awaited sequel to XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within by Firaxis. Does it live up to the hype that Enemy Unknown (a remake of the original UFO Defense) had especially with the Long War mod? Well that answer is a little complicated, it is yes and no.
XCOM 2 is a remake of not the 2nd game in the original X-COM series but in actuality the 3rd, X-COM: Apocalypse. In XCOM 2 you play as not a group that is defending their home world from the invading aliens but in fact the world actually ended up losing to the aliens and conquered Earth. 20 years after the events of Enemy Unknown, Officer Bradford (command) came upon intelligence that found where the ADVENT (the alien government) was hiding you, the commander, all this time. Once the commander is back XCOM is back and operational can commence the operation to find out ADVENT's true intentions and to overthrow the alien government. Spoiler alert: The aliens are actually being bad, SURPRISE!!!
Enemy Unknown/Within's main story missions were very unique in that they set up various challenges and felt completely different from the defense or rescue missions on the side. For example the Newfoundland Mission in Enemy Within was an absolutely hard and fun mission but those are no where to be found in XCOM 2. Most of the missions in XCOM 2 are, go here, defend this or attack that or save these civilians. Occasionally you'll have a mission where you'll attack an Advent facility to prevent the Advent project but those themselves aren't entirely memorable either. With the exception of the missions where a UFO shoots down your ship or the final mission, nothing was incredibly memorable about the campaign itself.
XCOM 2 is much like its original in that it is a squad turn based strategy game where your team of 4-6 soldiers try to complete different objectives. There are five classes that are fairly similar to Enemy Unknown with a few new skills. Those classes include Ranger (close quarters), Grenadier (machine gun and grenades), specialist (robot hacking and healing), sharpshooter (sniper) and the Psi Op who uses various psionic powers as you train them in the Psi Lab.
As you progress through the game your objective will to be not only to discover how to defeat the Advent Project but to also make contact with other resistance cells in order to gain resources and intel to combat the ADVENT. The missions that appear on the world progress as you make contact with more resistance locations and the maps themselves during your missions are procedurally generated making no mission location to seem like the same. Though that does have a strange habit of making Siberia seem like it is in a desert location though that might have been a bug originally when I played.
While you are progressing in making contacts and that mad XCOM money you are able to purchase and research new armor and weapons that can further help your team survive out in the field. Along with the money you also get intel for completing different missions. This intel allows you to purchase different things from the black market and allows you to make contact with other resistance locations throughout the world.
Much like Enemy Unknown, you can't just dillydally around the map. If you take too much time, depending on how many Advent facilities are in the world the Advent Project will progress where if it fills up you lose the game. On top of that the Advent have different resistance retaliation time periods where they will attack different resistance locations causing resources to slow down and if you don't stop them at all either by not going there or failing the mission you can lose contact with that area all together and have to re-establish said contact. Another combat against you going slowly is over time the ADVENT will acquire abilities that change various things in game. Whether those be a UFO searching around for you, progress on the Advent Project, stronger armor, slower research, less intel or several others. These can hurt you but I noticed that they don't change the game too much. Obviously they didn't want to make the game impossible but it seems like the advent events could have been a little more impactful.
Let's talk about the difficulty of this game for a bit. I know some found the RNG (Random Number Generator) a little harsh, missing a 90% chance to hit, but over the course of the game it will end up balancing out. I understand that sometimes it feels like those misses come at the most inopportune times but with the way you can get around the aliens from even being able to hit you with grenades, overwatch, the over powered mimic beacon there is always a way to keep the balance on your side. I would argue that this game is too easy and it doesn't truly get hard until the last mission in the game that has no escalator in difficulty. In Enemy Unknown the missions ramped up in difficulty all the way until the final mission on the alien ship. In XCOM 2 the missions are all fairly simple, especially when your soldiers are properly equipped, until that last mission that throws a whole bunch of problems your way including mind controlling avatars at the end.
Also a problem I had with this game was it didn't really feel like it was a step up from Enemy Unknown. Sure there are new classes and the new concealed mode but for all Firaxis's talk about Enemy Unknown being a tutorial for the Long War mod, they seemed to not take any hints and try to add features that the Long War made better in EU. With that said however, Firaxis did allow for mods in the beginning include the vast steam marketplace that already existed just one week after the game launched. I have no doubt the Long War guys will make another or some other group of modders will make this game even better.
Graphics wise XCOM 2 is much better than its predecessor despite it running the same engine, albeit it is running on Unreal 3.5 opposed to Unreal 3. There is a lot of customization of your soldiers too, allowing you to make your gameplay unique and different. There have been reports of problems that I noticed myself however if you had vsync and FXAA on however that might be fixed soon in a patch. On top of the graphics, the soundtrack is also a huge plus on this game. I found myself singing along during a lot of the songs because they were extremely catchy and enjoyable despite them being replayed a lot during the game.
Overall XCOM 2 despite all its flaws is still a game I absolutely had a blast to play. Not many games make me want to sit all week and do nothing but play it but XCOM 2 definitely does such. There are problems with the lack of content and difficulty along with some early performance issues and a lackluster story but that doesn't discount how much fun it is.

was able to finally join and play a few rounds.  I really want this game to be something good, but as it stands right now, it's just not.  There is no real way to coordinate team play, people just show up in random ships, so it's hard to develop an overall strategy, especially since you are pretty much guaranteed to be playing with strangers.  Ship balance is just not good.  These are supposed to be capital ships, and they die sometimes in less than 10 seconds, from maybe one or two other ships.  Sorry, but if these ships are huge powerful ships, they should have some staying power, which would add a great tactical element.  Also, allowing only one (maybe two at the most) titans per team would also provide more strategic and tactical depth.  Maneuvering the ships is straightforward but cumbersome.  Targeting needs to have some serious work...Most ships are relying on projectile weapons with no tracking capabilites, and missiles or lasers.  There's not a lot of variety.
Respawning sometimes takes over 60 seconds.  What's up with that?
The best thing about this game seems to be that the devs are actively involved in forums and might actually take player feedback into consideration.
I might come back and check this game out again if it makes it to a good beta stage, but right now, there's just no compelling reason to keep playing.

This game is very difficult. The game opens up telling you that. The beginning and middle portions are fair and the end game portions are where the games difficulty ramps up to  ridiculous levels. But it's fun. Everything from building up and leveling your army is extremely enjoyable and time will fly by without you even realizing it. Like with any very difficult roguelike, there will be points when you will get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's gonna happen. But when you succeed it's that much more fulfilling. There is a lot of stuff at the beginning that will kick you while you're down, but everything from the diseases and quirks, to equipment will become accessable once you start building up your estate, which is an enjoyable thing in and of itself. The art style and lovecraftian atmosphere is wonderful, and to be honest I'm a total sucker for it. Red Hook is going to be implementing features to make it more accessible to those who aren't a glutton for punishment so maybe wait for that? Also new DLC will be coming to the game soon to add even more to this already robust game.
The RNG at times seems like it's just not in your favor, but you learn whats going on, on the backend, when an action is happening and you will build your characters strengths to fight against the bad rolls. I have yet to find a part of this game that is just unmanageable, and I feel heeding the words of those who've played the game for ~7 hours and then get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and write a bad review is a bad way to go. The game isn't for everyone, which can be said about a lot of games of this type. What I recommend is watch some lets plays of it, get an idea of what the game is all about and then buy it, especially while it's on sale.
All in all it's fantastic game, that I look forward to playing again the moment I turn it off.

This game... THIS game... I honestly thought that this game would be of no interest to me whatsoever, I mean, why would it? Minecraft failed to hold my interest, despite its endless moddability (I still like it, though!). Terraria peters out after you finish the latest content. Starbound is... that's right, dead. Honestly, my first thought when seeing this was, "Oh god, another stupid block-building game that just so HAPPENS to be free to play." and yes, it was another stupid block-building game that just so HAPPENS to be free to play... but as I delved into it, I began to see behind it, and by god, out of all the block-building open world adventure games out there, this one practically takes it for me.
So, what is Trove? Simple, it's a game where you pick one of the many classes available and just go on out there into the open world(s), gathering treasure, building blocks and equipment, it's really just what would happen if Minecraft decided to steal from Terraria's book and add classes while they're at it. And shockingly, it works. Also, the story is nothing to write home about, it really feels like an excuse plot at this point, although, mind you, I haven't really gotten into the super End-Game content yet so I cannot say for certain that this changes.
It's like Minecraft with guns.
Now, classes, these make up the abilities and weapons that your character is capable of, from throwing frost bolts to fae blasts to shooting people in the face and throwing boomerangs at them, every class has their own unique skillset, along with pros and cons. For instance, I made the
of playing an Ice Sage, a class that has a magical shield that protects them from harm and an ult that freezes everyone in an area around them and deals delayed damage to them, pretty hard to use while solo but when I'm running a dungeon by myself and a random player bursts in, I can see the Ice Sage's true strength shine through. Of course, not every class is going to be on equal footing, some are clearly stronger than others and while there are some that are super strong on paper (Fae Tricksters come to mind) but are somewhat borderline in practice. Every class can contribute something, however, and that's fine with me.
Classes are good, allows for multiple playstyles, some slight imbalance with some but overall they feel balanced.
Not entirely impressive, to say the least, but the blocky nature of the graphics lends it to a lot of its cartoonish charm, which is especially prevalent in the Candy zones of the world (yes, candy, don't question it.) and the buildings that are placed by default by the game are, well, actually really darn impressive considering the simplicity of it all, and the dungeons are all thematically built according to what zone you're in so, like,  a Fae dungeon can be a tree or a storybook or an Everfrost dungeon can be a crying Mammoth stuck in the ice, I feel there's a good bit of variety to at least slow down the tedium of dungeon grinding.
Now, about the building part itself, you've got a few avenues, you can build directly onto the world (although considering the temporal nature of the worlds why would you unless you're cheesing something.) or build in a designated zone named a Cornerstone. Cornerstones are like portable housing, and they're scattered across the map, it's where you can build and design whatever your heart desires within a small limitation though. But if you're not happy about the limitations of the portable houses, you can join (or make) a club and go into a Club World where you can build to your heart's content (permission pending). The tools for building is rather simple, in build mode you have two functions, left click places and right click mines, simple as that, placement is actually really cool as you can click and drag to where you want to place a line of blocks down, which makes some of the tedious parts of building much more bearable. It can be a bit finicky, though, with the third person camera but it works!
Graphics are simple, yet somehow, they manage to look really good. Building is not as tedious as anticipated.
Yes, it's not a Free to Play game without the cash shop, a F2P game without a cash shop is a free game without a... erm... hmm... I'll get back to you on that one but I digress, yes, there's a cash shop, you can buy things in there from ores to costumes to packs to new mounts (although, mind you, the default mount serves most purposes well) and some other miscellaneous stuff like name changes, flasks, emblems, and what have you. The emblems and flasks are pretty cheap compared to the rest of the shop and the free currency can be easily acquired by simply doing stuff in game... or you can open up your wallet for the premium currency to get them. Only cosmetics will ever be locked behind a paywall, as far as I know. Mounts, on the other hand, I'm not too sure on, but I'm certain they're not Pay-2-Win.
There's also a patron thing that I'm iffy about as it grants some advantages to the players who buy it like extra jumps (which, surprisingly, is a big deal in this game), extra magic find, 50% more experience, and more. Is it Pay2Win? I'm going to let you be the judge of that...
Cosmetics are mostly paid for with premium currency, game uses a freemium system where you can acquire free currency to spend on certain perks. Patron remains a concern.
I feel that this is quite a solid  game despite its drawbacks, it can get grindy and repetitive in due time, the classes are stuck with their limited skillset and gathering blocks to craft and build with can be a bit of a chore early game, but all in all, I feel that Trove is pretty good for a free to play game... sure, I feel there may be some aspects that would trigger some P2W alarm bells but for me, personally, I'm perhaps willing to look over it... although keeping a careful eye on it to make sure it doesn't go out of control. Also, if you're ever going to be playing this for the first time, it might be best to drag some friends along to make the initial voyage more palatable as soloing can be a bit dull.
Could be fun with friends.

As someone looking primarily for a single-player RTS, I have to say I was disappointed. There are some interesting ideas and designs to this game, but as a single player experience I don't think either the campaign or the skirmish mode measure up, and I'd say in many ways inferior to games that came out 2-3 years earlier (Age of Myth, Rise of Nations, Warcraft III, etc.).
What I liked:
As a concept, the home city idea was very interesting. As a practical measure, I found myself using basically the same combo of cards every playthrough. It did make for occasional surprises (to be attacking an enemy city when they suddenly cashed in a bunch of units in your midst), but by and large, it became routine pretty quickly.
-Graphics are good, though some framerate issues even without settings maxed
What I didn't like:
-AI is terrible. In most of the campaign, you'd have to make a pretty major mistake to actually lose. I didn't really have any need to learn the unit counters until the last scenario in Act II (which can largely be won by exploiting a single counter).  By the same token, your own units will wander off and get themselves killed more often than you'd like.
-Unit control isn't great. And sad that a 2005 release doesn't let you put units in multiple groupings. Want a group for all artillery for and a subgroup for just cannons for combat precision?  Too bad!
-Reward for advancing ages was implemented better in the earlier 'Age of Mythology.' There the rewards represented actual tactical choices with pros/cons. Here the proper choice is often a given. "Let's see - do I want a boat reward on this map with no water or whatever option B is?"
Maybe this game is great for multi-player, I can't say. But as single-player goes, it was disappointing.  Honestly I can't say it would even make my RTS top 10, despite the few things it does do well.

Age of Empires III is, without a doubt, an RTS classic. Though perhaps not as popular or widely played as its predecessor, AoE3 deserves recognition for its gutsiness and charm.
Gameplay is comparable to other RTS titles with the notable exception of the home city and experience mechanics. Prolonged games and even campaigns will accrue experience points that grant resource, tech, and military benefits to players based on their customized home cities. The ability to level up one's supply support and farm experience through side objectives and battles adds an entirely new dimension to the economic and military struggles that have typically comprised RTS experiences.
Aesthetically, the game is quite enjoyable. While it is a tad old, the textures and visual resources manage to be reasonable (though cutscenes are frequently laughable in quality). The ability to zoom in and out on the game has made a return from Age of Mythology, making combat engagements easier to watch and enjoy up close. The soundtrack is iconic and will get stuck in your head after only a few games.
The campaigns are what make the complete collection really shine. While deathmatches and skirmishes are entertaining, the at-times-poorly-written-but-still-enjoyable story of the Black family over six generations establishes a sort of epic within the game that players will find themselves driven to progress through. Lovable and hateable characters such as the black family, Billy Holme, Kanyenke, Major Cooper, and more color the games often cheesy but still fantastic story. The relative historical accuracy of the game makes is engaging and watching characters such as George Washington, Simon Bolivar, and General Custer being woven into the story is quite amusing. An expectation emerges as to who the story will involve next. Once players get bored with the stories of the Black family (in the original game and the War Chiefs expansion), they can turn their eyes to several shorter stories of Japanese, Chinese, and Indian heroes in the Asian Dynasties expansion, allowing for a whole new Age of Empires experience.
Most faults within the game are fairly minor and don't impede playing extensively. The most irritating problem comes with managing large groups of units and selecting individual soldiers out of said groups. This can be accomplished much easier with hotkeys, but it's a lot of effort for such an activity. Unit speeds, managing artillery, and certain little ticks with targeting, action queueing, and attack orders are also frustrating at times, though not game breaking. The pacing of the Japanese campaign in the Asian Dynasties expansion is also notably broken, although it arguably allows for a wider range of deck and home city customisation.
Age of Empires III is, in brief, yet another respectable and pleasant RTS game from Ensemble Studios. The gameplay echoes older titles while incorporating novel elements to breath new life into the series, and the story is engrossing and captivating in much the same way that Age of Mythology (and, to an extent, not Age of Empires II) was. AoE3's knack for good storytelling and gameplay that is quick and easy to pick up overcomes its small mechanical faults and sometimes poor campaign pacing to present an enchanting and memorable game that is definitely worth playing, and the variety of campaigns provided by the various expansions will ensure the player does just that for a considerable amount of time. Welcome to the New (or perhaps the old, as is the case with Morgan Black and the Japanese campaign) World!

This game is very difficult. The game opens up telling you that. The beginning and middle portions are fair and the end game portions are where the games difficulty ramps up to  ridiculous levels. But it's fun. Everything from building up and leveling your army is extremely enjoyable and time will fly by without you even realizing it. Like with any very difficult roguelike, there will be points when you will get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's gonna happen. But when you succeed it's that much more fulfilling. There is a lot of stuff at the beginning that will kick you while you're down, but everything from the diseases and quirks, to equipment will become accessable once you start building up your estate, which is an enjoyable thing in and of itself. The art style and lovecraftian atmosphere is wonderful, and to be honest I'm a total sucker for it. Red Hook is going to be implementing features to make it more accessible to those who aren't a glutton for punishment so maybe wait for that? Also new DLC will be coming to the game soon to add even more to this already robust game.
The RNG at times seems like it's just not in your favor, but you learn whats going on, on the backend, when an action is happening and you will build your characters strengths to fight against the bad rolls. I have yet to find a part of this game that is just unmanageable, and I feel heeding the words of those who've played the game for ~7 hours and then get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and write a bad review is a bad way to go. The game isn't for everyone, which can be said about a lot of games of this type. What I recommend is watch some lets plays of it, get an idea of what the game is all about and then buy it, especially while it's on sale.
All in all it's fantastic game, that I look forward to playing again the moment I turn it off.

After 35h of playing + watching some lets plays, I really have to compliment the developers for improving upon XCOM EU significantly. Sure, the game may have its weak points, but to me, first and foremost, XCOM 2 is a game with well-designed game mechanics, great presentation, and, like its predecessor, a shining example of how a replayable campaign can be interwoven with extremely atmospheric story telling.
Pro:
+ soldier customisation increases your attachment to your soldiers and makes each decision, each mistake more emotionally impactful
+ incredible catalogue of available mods, shortly after release
+ sympathetic set of story characters
+ more tense game play due to the timers on many of the missions; to me this is a plus because of the scenario in which you are inferior at most times
+ the procedurally generated maps (made from hand-crafted pieces afaik) offer a lot of replayability, especially when compared to XCOM:EU
Con:
- riddled with bugs right now. Most of them are minor, but having the level objective that you are supposed to protect be set on fire on turn one by some clumsy sectopod is quite frustrating. i reloaded and replayed this mission a number of times, each time the objective got destroyed after turn 5 or 6, and it died having almost half of its health bar, even when i had aggro'd all enemy groups...
- late strategy game feels too easy (not true for the late tactical game)
- after the first 10h of playing the game, the rather long character animations start becoming annoying; but that can be remedied with mods (i think the now built-in zip-mode does not speed up enough of the animations)
- item- and soldier management seems a bit more cumbersome than it needs to be
- aiming grenades is still a mess like in EU. Why? Just show me the tiles i can target and which ones i cant. Searching for the right cursor position and having the explosion area jump around because of the grenate bouncing off some part of the level is very ... cumbersome.
- it seems that the game does not communicate well a lot of gameplay-relevant facts. For how long will my soldier be poisoned? Does this action break concealment? Does this action trigger from concealment (looking at you, overwatch)?
Despite those flaws - most of which I hope will soon be patched out - i can still wholeheartedly recommend XCOM 2 to lovers of the turn-based tactical genre.

- Ranger: so much fun to use both with the shotgun and the sword; beautiful kill animations
- Sharpshooter:  not overpowered as many snipers are in other games... good times to be had with the pistols too!
- Psi Operative: some great new abilities that are interesting and worth using.  The one weird element for me is how these powerful mentalists are unable to conceal themselves and will be detected by an advent soldier 20 blocks away who is facing the wrong way... maybe its the smell!
- Grenadier: I am not a fan of grenades and blowing everything up so I probably misuse these guys but this is I enjoy fighting my battles
- Specialists:  see hacking section below
Negatives:
- Strategy layer is way too busy looking and that globe looks awful.  I actually found the trick midway thru: dont bother with the globe at all, forget 90% of the screen and focus only on the "taskbar" at the bottom.  You have icons for your missions on the left and your facilities on the right.     Nice work here Firaxis!
- "Bradford, shut your face!"  Everybody who has played xcom 2 has said that exact sentence a minimum of 14 times... so much narration, so much useless commentary, so much awful advice, so much time wasted...

Allright, if you want it to take more space in the base, thats fine, give me the purple room but dont force me to go back to the main screen to go between the 2 research labs!  Why can I not see my soldiers in the infirmary??  Why is the infirmary not connected to the living quarters??
I found the reason why when I finished the game in less than 30hrs: its because without all that time wasted navigating the base, this game would be less than 20hrs for sure.   so much time wasted

After flying off the bathroom mirror, I managed to grab onto to the wall only to fall to a sogy doom in the toilet. Knowing the end is rye, I quickly try to grab the seat, but fail, falling straight into the bowl, ending my dream of becoming toast. This, along with some frustration, is what you can expect to find in I Am Bread. So why am I recommending this game? Because despite some wonky controls, this game is fun, and well worth purchasing. In what other game are you able to crawl across someone's bedroom just to toast yourself on a light bulb?
I will admit that the controls are hard, and the situation is made worse by the fact that there's a limited amount of time you can hold onto to something, but if you can get used to the controls the game is actually fun, and hilarious. I've had fun just trying to find out how many ways I can toast myself. I've managed to toast myself on everything except the toaster oddly enough. There are other game modes as well, incuding a time trial mode and a zero gravity mode, so beyond the hilarity of being bread, there is a actual game here. Top it off with jam, butter, a graet soundtrack, and the magical marmalade that let's you crawl across the floor, and you've got yourself a pretty tasty treat. So overall, I give it a score of 9/10. The controls are a bit hard, and there aren't as many toasting levels as I would have wanted, but overall a solid...uh...adventuring puzzle(?) game.

I used to play this game back in 2012. It used to be pretty fun, and the community was great. Lots of people willing to give you a hand if you need it in a mission, and the grinding was fair (unless you're aiming for an expensive costume or furniture, which would then take some time). I even created my own guild in this game, and our guild was pretty well-known amongst the older members of the community. But if the game was that good, then why did I give it thumbs down?
First, notice the past tense, "was". I don't deny the game was fun in the past, and I still visit this game from time to time purely due to nostaligia. But, to sum it up, this game really lacks development. In these 4 years I've been playing, there have not been much new content. Money was not an issue to the devs, but the devs just became money craving maniacs. To be fair to them, it wasn't always like that. But after the update where the forging system was introduced, elevator fee removed, and battle sprites came out (about 2 years ago approximately), the devs basically stopped pushing out any new content. Instead, they went for the "costume hype" and reskinned tons of costumes just so that people are more willing to spend their money in this game. Barely any of that money went into the game however. The levels were the same, and the grinding becomes increasingly more and more boring. In the meantime, while more and more older members of the community leaves the game due to boredom, the community becomes worse and worse as a result. Now no one's willing to help out a poor guy who just needs some help on a boss unless they pay up. The game just doesn't feel the same anymore as a result.
About a year ago, the devs might've finally sensed that their game is going down the drain, and finally released some new content, the mysterious core itself. However, I can't help but express my disappointment. While the storyline might finally be "complete", the levels themselves were just a reuse of old things. Same level designs, same textures, even the monsters are just copied from shadow lairs. In other words, the devs did absolutely nothing except piecing together a few new levels from pre-exisiting levels. Even the ending of the game is just like the ending of a shadow lair run, which was introduced way before this update was pushed out.
In the meantime, the prices and the grinding in the game reaches the point of insanity. It bores me to the point where I'd rather go and "play" Cookie Clicker than spending another hour just to do another "vana run" just to get those radiant crystals. You can argue that everyone will eventually be bored by these grinding type of games, but at least they're fun with friends. This game achieves the extraordinary, in that you'll find these vana runs boring even if you're with your friends. Why? Because the grinding is real. Be prepared to run Vanaduke 100 times if you want to heat your 5 star weapon from level 1 to 10 fail-proof. 30 would probably be the minimum if you're lucky enough to get the level up on the 30% success forges (they rarely succeed, I really doubt if it's 30% at all). Since each run takes an hour give or take, be prepared to spend 50-100 hours just to heat ONE piece of 5 star equipment. Please note that your knight have at least 4 5 star equipments you need to heat before you can become a Vanguard.
So if you're not the kind of guy who want to spend 500+ hours in this game grinding your head off, then I recommend you don't waste your time on this game. I wasted 1500 hours on this game total (including my time on my old Steam account), and I must say I seriously regret it. Don't be like me.
2/10, would not grind again.

"Early Access" is definitely the proper term for it.  It took us how long to get into a state where the entire thing wasn't being wiped every week or so?
Honestly, in the six months it has been since public beta release (if not longer for original backers, though I've found no reference as to how that was handled for us), there has been very little positive change.  So many mechanics are reworked, changed again, and then altered to the point where over about 8 characters I've yet to progress much beyond the first boss for how inconsistent things are.
This wouldn't be an issue if the game were internally consistent as well.  Levels feel arbitrary, difficulty and resource sparcity is all over the map, and your luck of actually finding reasonable equipment is something of a tongue-in-beak joke, to say nothing of how "dungeons" provide little to no challenge or reason for exploration (unless you want some new furnishings for your space ship).
I can forgive some of the broken promises -- they're a reality of development that stuff gets cut when a studio finds them to be too great a challenge or too taxing.  But honestly?  I've expected a lot more than what has happened in these intervening months, and all I've really seen is just "Terraria the Space Opera."
(At least in v1.0 Terraria I could progress naturally with crafting and resource gathering.)
I still must praise the art direction, though.  The appearance of the game is wonderful and nostalgic, even if the optimization is horridly lackluster (and the GL version even more so), and there's something deliciously campy about swinging a huge laser axe at weird aliens.
As a time-waster, I'd say it's absolutely worth it.  As a game?  I can't recommend it.  Not in its current incarnation at least.
Somewhere down the road I'll pick it back up and see what's beneath all the dust.  I want to enjoy this game, but it needs a little more time in the proverbial development oven.
----
Well, I picked it back up, and let me tell you, at first I was truly amazed how far we had come!  Gameplay that did not grind to a halt because weather was happening, monsters that did not instantly kill me because I entered an unbalanced biome, and an actual STORY that didn't feel thrown in to test a boss encounter!
All in all it felt like a proper, true progression -- the kind you'd expect in a game about traveling the stars and exploring the universe.  Linear, but not bad.
Only, it's not so much linear as "copy, paste, repeat."
The story is, quite simply, a bit of a joke.  You and you alone are perhaps the last surviving wielder of the might SPACE CROISSANT, which just so happens to be recognized by the plot-convenient grandmother of the game who ALSO just so happens to be the primary quest-giver.  Very convenient.  Kind of like having a special space station to keep all the critical NPCs in.
In
Starbound, your primary objective is to fetch the MacGuffins which will seal away The Big Space Evil with a name like the "Destroyer" or something very generic.  I have admittedly
defeated it myself, but between a friend and I, every chapter has been viewed in one form or another.
And every chapter is the same:
1). Go scan some things with your fancy new SPACE CROISSANT scanning mode (press the N key for "No, not again, why must I scan things").
2). But scan only the Green ones (Colored For Your Convenience).
3). Go to the racially-themed sandbox map that involves fighting and / or puzzling your way to a boss encounter!
4). Kick its butt or try again.
5). Collect shiny.
And that's it.
Once you have all six of the Very Shiny Objects of Destiny, your Space Journey is complete.
And for those of you like myself who have spent more time doing the side quests in an effort to get the biggest (and best decorated) ship possible, only to realize that now you have a bunch of chuckle-heads wandering around your majestic Space Pyramid that keep letting the damned fluffalo out of hydroponics lab, well ... you've probably spent forever scouring the surfaces of planets to scan everything imaginable to decorate with / pixel-print / loot-for-unspecified-reasons-but-mostly-collection, and also probably all the highest level equipment you can craft.
Because there's really not that much crafting anymore.  In fact, it seems like half of the equipment is purchase- / loot-only, and vendors are everywhere but seem to have very abysmal stock for supposedly space-faring colonies across the stars.  Seriously, does nobody send a care package anymore?
That was about the time I'd also come to realize I had managed to see every biome and explorable area in the game; they were ... repeating.  Near-identical copy-paste delves, outposts, and subterranean mish-mosh that eventually I couldn't get far enough away from my starting quadrant to find a map that felt all too familiar.
It was a fun 50 hours or so, but it's also supposed to be a giant sandbox ... in space.  Only the sandbox ended up being my ship and I've run out of things to do in it.
Hopefully we'll see a patch in the future that adds back a lot of the cut content, like the unique monsters (I think we're down to maybe 30 now, of which you'll see about 15 frequently).  Though personally, I'd settle for more planet and star variance.  Only 4 "tiers" of exploration feels pretty redundant in a universe with literal billions of stars.

Like many people I have my doubts about games in early access especially space games considering controversial games like Star Citizen are on the brink of being "the next big thing." This game has a lot of potential and is the first game I have put my faith in the devs for early access, I signified this by my purchase of Vanguard during the free weekend play on 4/18/15. One of the final factors in my decision to support this came from the fact the devs gave the game for free to anyone who played it on this weekend, on top of that they encountered server overloads due to the new players and within a day it was fixed and running again, they also keep monthly patch notes listed as soon as you log onto the game so you can see where the progress is taking place and what they are doing to improve the game.
This game in short is a space MOBA (think League and Dota but without the hostile community). Upon looking at the reviews I happened to come across one negative review that summarized ships aren't really different and it's just point and shoot. Please do note that, yes, some ships are more point and shoot as that is their role, but in order to survive when you aren't a heavy class you must move around and utilize your ablities effectively, I'd also like to go on the record and say this game is in EARLY ACCESS, there are still balancing issues they are attending to and tweaking. I do not understand how someone puts only 2-3 hours in the game and says ships are all the same and it's point and shoot. As someone who has put a fair amount of hours in compared to other reviewers I can say for a fact that there are times I've won 1v3 engagements in an Assassin/Phantom class due to using my ship's abilities well and opponents simply sitting there like ducks.
TL;DR This game is tons of fun in early access and possesses a lot of potential, if you like space fights and MOBA style games, look no further as this is the forerunner. Please do not be discouraged by some reviews where people only put in a handful of time and complain about typical alpha/early access problems, good devs deserve to be supported!

I read alot of reviews before I bought this game, and mostly heard things about how it was unnecessarily unfair. These reviews turned me off to the game (which I'd been interested in for awhile). I finally picked it up, and I wish I'd never listened to a bulk of those reviews. Most reviews went on about how the game was brutally relentless, hating the player at every turn and ALWAYS stacking the odds against you. However, upon having played the game myself, I say this is a pro rather than a con. The thing about Darkest Dungeon is that the game wants you to loose (there is even a warning message every time you start the game). And not just in the aspect of RNG. Of course, everything in actual combat is stacked against you. Powerful enemies with powerful moves call for planning at every encounter, and even then, RNG will still bite you. But beyond this, the game is designed to hurt you in the long run. From negative quirks and diseases your heroes pick up, to over stressed heroes, to a lack of funds, to a lack of valid heroes, etc. This sorts of things are meant to build up over time and will lead you to lose unless legitamte effort is put into compensating for the things you will run into. But that's not the whole of Darkest Dungeon. The challenge Darkest Dungeon presents is that no matter how well you play this game, the previously stated difficulties WILL catch up to you. They will hurt you, kill you heroes, and possibly make you lose your playthrough. I think this is why Darkest Dungeon recieves the criticism it recieves. Most gamers nowadays expect a "right way" to play their games, to maximize the good and minimize the bad. Darkest Dungeon firmly throws that idea into the pits, and says, "You are going to suffer, then lose. You will continue to do so, until you win at immeasurable cost." If this is something you can accept, and are willing to take on, then you should give Darkest Dungeon a shot.

Spiral Knights is a top-down TLoZ inspired MMO, where you go floor to floor down the Clockworks, the source of the worlds power. There are many different presets for floors, where you will find several different species of monsters ranging from slimes, wolves, robots, and Gremlins to kill and take their Crowns (currency), Heat (used to upgrade your gear), and materials. There are 3 different Clockwork tiers, with the difficulty and loot increasing as you get deeper and deeper into it. At first, you will only be able to go to the first tier and be forced to go back as you reach small towns in the Clockworks, as they serve as gates for the different tiers. As you progress in the story and upgrade your gear you will be able to access these towns and move on, with there being vendors along the way to sell you useful upgrade blueprints you cant get anywhere else. There are 4 main bosses in the game, with each of them giving tokens once you beat them, and when you get enough you can trade them for very good and useful gear, which very well may make up your arsenal when you approach endgame.
The PvP is a control point mode, where you fight off the other team to take hold of 3-7 points for the longest amount of time. There are 3 different "classes" in PvP, Striker, Stealth, and Shield. Striker removes your shield for a jet boost which can get you from area to area very quickly. Stealth makes you invisible when shielding, with a small radar around you when you get close to someone. Shield amplifies your shield, making it reach around you, shielding your teammates inside it. Unfortunately you are not given any kind of gear for it, and there are not restrictions on what gear you can and cannot use. This means that those who have an extreme amount of money will use items with ungodly stats, which most can only hope to get withing a few months. The PvP is split into 3 tiers like the Clockworks, with each tier corresponding to your gear. Good luck finding a match with anything less than tier 3 Gear however, as it is extremely rare to see anyone not in the tier 3 matchmaking. Technically, this mode is not P2W, as you can buy all these items with Crowns, but it will take so long you might as well not even try. The meta is also quite bad, with only a few specific items being good, mainly a few of the Boss items, and status inflicting mist bombs. While it is possible to do well without these items, without health boosting trinkets, and ungodly unique variant weapons, you will have a tough time.
Unless you have a friend or two who are already well off and have played for a good amount of time and is willing to play with you, I wouldn't even bother with this game. The devs have stopped caring about it completely, with all new content being simple reskins of cosmetic items. If you want to play Spiral Knights by yourself, be prepared to do most of it solo, and whatever you do, do NOT pay any money for energy, the games higher tier currency. This is a F2P MMO, so it only makes sense that there will be grind walls inciting you to pay real money (which unfortunately I fell trap to). The community is decent, however 90% of everyone you're going to see is people who have spent hundreds, even thousands of hours on this game from years back, who still feel obligated to "play" (aka sit in Haven (the hub world), for hours on end stalking the auction house).

Do I regret putting so much time and energy into this game? I wouldn't say so, as it has brought me many hours of enjoyment and a few short term friends along the way. However, at the current state it is in, I can't recommend playing it right now. Even now, I only ever boot up the game (which can take up to HOURS as the game doesn't update on its own, and only starts updating when you run the game, something that should have been fixed years ago) to check up on any season events going on. If you are new to this game, the first time you boot up the see Haven at dusk, covered in Halloween garb, or in a snowy wonderland at Christmas time, it is quite magical, and I've had some of the most fun just fooling around in Haven during then. For now though, stay away from this game. The population is dying and any friends you make will most likely be gone in only a few days, never to be seen again. If you do wish to play however, I can only hope you have a fraction of the fun I've had in my early days, and I wish you luck.

After 35h of playing + watching some lets plays, I really have to compliment the developers for improving upon XCOM EU significantly. Sure, the game may have its weak points, but to me, first and foremost, XCOM 2 is a game with well-designed game mechanics, great presentation, and, like its predecessor, a shining example of how a replayable campaign can be interwoven with extremely atmospheric story telling.
Pro:
+ soldier customisation increases your attachment to your soldiers and makes each decision, each mistake more emotionally impactful
+ incredible catalogue of available mods, shortly after release
+ sympathetic set of story characters
+ more tense game play due to the timers on many of the missions; to me this is a plus because of the scenario in which you are inferior at most times
+ the procedurally generated maps (made from hand-crafted pieces afaik) offer a lot of replayability, especially when compared to XCOM:EU
Con:
- riddled with bugs right now. Most of them are minor, but having the level objective that you are supposed to protect be set on fire on turn one by some clumsy sectopod is quite frustrating. i reloaded and replayed this mission a number of times, each time the objective got destroyed after turn 5 or 6, and it died having almost half of its health bar, even when i had aggro'd all enemy groups...
- late strategy game feels too easy (not true for the late tactical game)
- after the first 10h of playing the game, the rather long character animations start becoming annoying; but that can be remedied with mods (i think the now built-in zip-mode does not speed up enough of the animations)
- item- and soldier management seems a bit more cumbersome than it needs to be
- aiming grenades is still a mess like in EU. Why? Just show me the tiles i can target and which ones i cant. Searching for the right cursor position and having the explosion area jump around because of the grenate bouncing off some part of the level is very ... cumbersome.
- it seems that the game does not communicate well a lot of gameplay-relevant facts. For how long will my soldier be poisoned? Does this action break concealment? Does this action trigger from concealment (looking at you, overwatch)?
Despite those flaws - most of which I hope will soon be patched out - i can still wholeheartedly recommend XCOM 2 to lovers of the turn-based tactical genre.

Half-Life, a game from the late 90's, and still a great game.
Gordon Freeman, a scientist from the Black Mesa Research Facility, has to fight against aliens and the military after an experiment has gone wrong, creating a rift between dimensions. Using the H.E.V. Suit and whichever working weapons he finds, he will have to go to the world between dimensions named Xen and fight the leader of the alien riot. To do so, he has to navigate through a destroyed Black Mesa, going through the railway, the laboratories, and the surface, heavily guarded by the military aiming to kill the ones who made the supposed experiment, that including Gordon Freeman himself, and reach the Lambda Complex. By this description, it may sound like a short game. But it actually has quite the challenges. You'll need to crouch through tight areas, jump over hazardous liquids, and shoot everything you see. I consider this game to be a Shooting-Platformer, due to the amount of challenges required to take alternative routes through destroyed rooms requiring jumping skills.
Oh, and it also has a Multiplayer mode. I haven't played on it much, but it seems pretty good. Hence why there's also a mod for HL mainly based on Multiplayer, which is Counter-Strike. So good that it was even released as it's own game and sequels.
If you don't like the old-fashioned models, there is also a Free-to-download HD Pack.

I like hard games. I grew up on Wizardry where the game was 'out to get you' and all that. The NES was my system of choice for years. Dark Souls and Bloodborne are extremely challenging yet fair. But this game- And I DO like it- the thing is just unfair in a lot of ways. This isn't another "TEH RNG IS SUXXS" complaint, it's a design choice complaint on the part of the devs.
For starters, why when you finally clear an area you have a bonus chance to.. get another disease or terrible quirk? That's
reward for finally making it through isn't it? Which leads to this point: You can quickly amass so many negative quirks and diseases IN ONE DUNGEON yet you can only potentially cure one of them back at town- for exorbant prices, I might add. My crusader somehow picked up a drinking problem while looking at a book (because that makes sense) and upon returning to town with tons of stress I see that the questmaster NPC is in the bar. So that's pretty fair too..
The inventory space is way too small for the amount of supplies you have to take with you in order to survive, and that means you have a tiny amount of space left for things to bring back to town and sell. You know, to afford those super high prices for stress relief and disease-away. Trinkets (aux items for your characters' 2 inventory slots) are good but almost all of them have a penalty, further handicapping your hopeless heroes in a game that's set up to dole out more penalties than an Oakland Raiders game.
And sometimes when I go to click on a 4th slot / rear position monster my guy will attack somebody else. These kind of bugs should have been picked up on and fixed long before release.
I like this game a lot. I think that's why it pains me when bad design choices like these run all through it. I really hope there'll be a Darkest Dungeon 2 someday where these design flaws won't exist, because I'll be the first in line to buy it.
Pretty graphics and a cool aesthetic can only go so far, ultimately I have to not recommend buying this unless it's on sale and you're curious what the fuss is about.

Darkest Dungeon is arguably one of the best games I have played during this decade. Make no mistake, this is one of the hardest games too, but it is so fun to fight monsters, explore caverns, fight more monsters, equip your heroes, build up the town and manage the stress levels of your heroes that you quickly get over the obscene frustration you may feel at times.
It isn't all that hard to play to begin with, just use the heroes correctly and you will be fine, but once you start to get to the higher tier dungeons, there is so much management and so many things to take into consideration, like using a specific trinket or consumable that increases the damage you deal to the type of monster in that dungeon or decreases your damage taken or using a bottle of holy water to purify a corrupted shrine that buffs your party, all the while ensuring you don't overcommit to a specific team since having one team at level 4 and all your other heroes at level 0 is a surefire way to lose yourself the game.
You have to plan for the worst case scenario and make the best of your situation, which is what the whole thing is about. You are attempting to reclaim your land from evil creatures that destroyed and overtook it during the absence of your ancestors. This is a game about forcefully taking back your home from a horde of evil creatures that drove your family out, perhaps in the process, avenging your ancestors.
With a dark, brooding storyline and mysterious atmosphere, this game will keep you up all night slamming your fists into your desk, swearing at your screen and furiously murdering hordes of undead, beasts and eldritch horrors from the depths of madness from dusk until dawn.

Unless you have a friend or two who are already well off and have played for a good amount of time and is willing to play with you, I wouldn't even bother with this game. The devs have stopped caring about it completely, with all new content being simple reskins of cosmetic items. If you want to play Spiral Knights by yourself, be prepared to do most of it solo, and whatever you do, do NOT pay any money for energy, the games higher tier currency. This is a F2P MMO, so it only makes sense that there will be grind walls inciting you to pay real money (which unfortunately I fell trap to). The community is decent, however 90% of everyone you're going to see is people who have spent hundreds, even thousands of hours on this game from years back, who still feel obligated to "play" (aka sit in Haven (the hub world), for hours on end stalking the auction house).

Do I regret putting so much time and energy into this game? I wouldn't say so, as it has brought me many hours of enjoyment and a few short term friends along the way. However, at the current state it is in, I can't recommend playing it right now. Even now, I only ever boot up the game (which can take up to HOURS as the game doesn't update on its own, and only starts updating when you run the game, something that should have been fixed years ago) to check up on any season events going on. If you are new to this game, the first time you boot up the see Haven at dusk, covered in Halloween garb, or in a snowy wonderland at Christmas time, it is quite magical, and I've had some of the most fun just fooling around in Haven during then. For now though, stay away from this game. The population is dying and any friends you make will most likely be gone in only a few days, never to be seen again. If you do wish to play however, I can only hope you have a fraction of the fun I've had in my early days, and I wish you luck.

Oh Darkest Dungeon. My bittersweet companion. That sums it up pretty well but there's so much that goes into it to make it such an absorbing experience.
You begin as an outsider to the bleak affairs of your newly inherited Hamlet; a wretched place where nothing is gleeful, the buildings are ruined and the surrounding environs are corrupted. Four places, the Ruins themselves, the Warrens, the Cove and the Weald, each with their own flavours of unnatural taint. Each requiring specific preparations and favouring different explorers. The wide assortments of classes make up your 4 person party, each baring significantly different contributions to the parties strength and assembling them to compensate for one another's weaknesses, or to compliment one another's strengths makes for an interesting dynamic between different combinations.
Lets take a step back. Gameplay is divided into two parts; plumbing the four aforementioned areas (and a fifth much later) with a small party in order to advance and to loot, and managing the hamlet they return to and your roster as a whole. All the while described by the disembodied voice of the ancestor that caused all the unholiness in the first place and then killed himself, leaving you to piece this broken place back together, in probably one of my favourite pieces of game narration I've ever encountered, it truly adds something to every scenario with his old, affected voice overlaying them.
Delving into the dark places puts you in one of two situations, exploring and fighting, combat is turn based, with each fighter having their own initiative to determine the order of turns, various status effects and weaknesses specific to certain areas make preparation key, as you can only bring a certain amount of limited supplies with you, and how much you can take back as loot is limited by what you have filled your inventory with in the first place. You will not know what will be useful until you have experimented, or guessed, and taking risks is your only option. Combat, despite sounding impersonal in description is made visceral by simply focusing on the combatants. Assaults upon your explorers will not only be physical, but psychological; for each fighter's mind has a breaking point, and deciding whether to focus upon the impacts of physical harm or insanity will never be easy. Exploring you will have the chance to interact with various hazards around these places, using items discerningly can grant you great boons, not doing so can cause great trauma, but loot must be taken, or else you will be returning empty handed. Both aspects of this dungeon delving are unforgiving, and sacrifices will have to be made. Each area eventually presents two powerful enemies that must be hunted down, to cleanse these places and to discover more of your ancestor's dark secrets, each one being hugely different, the Gibbering Prophet who hides behind the pews of an old church to protect himself from the slashes of your melee warriors, or the Alluring Siren who may charm one of your mercenaries to fight alongside her and summons wretches of the sea to do much the same. Each one presents a unique threat.
If and when your explorers return to the hamlet, they will only carry the weight of their mental ailments back with them, a huge variety of afflictions, or strengths, may change not only the way they fight, but the way they act, sometimes outside of your control. The hamlet provides oppotunity for respite, whether by faith, by revelry, or by medicine, to care for your ailing mercenaries. How successful you were outside will determine how much you can improve your hamlet, or indeed restore your warriors. It also provides places to train your warriors, hire new mercenaries and to enhance their equipment, the capacities of each again improves by how much you were able to loot. Again, outside of this place you must choose whether to press your warriors into further danger in order to return with greater, much needed, treasure, or to make a timely retreat whilst you still can.
The atmosphere of the entire world you have entered is crafted to crush and destroy your spirit, the hand drawn art style is flawless in creating a dark impression of even the holiest of things, every sound gives more and more to the grim nature of it all. The lost diaries of previous explorers, the memoirs of your ancestor, the horrific deeds done in his name, the encounters with unique otherworldly terrors like the Collector all come together in blood stained, disease ridden, unholiness like a mixing pot of all that damns.
To take a step back and be less theatrical about it; this game is fantastic, it is challenging, it is absorbing, it is compelling. It has life unlike any other, twisted though it may be.
Right onto the short part of this review; complaints, in fact, it might just be 'complaint'. Singular.
Bosses are repeated three times. Not in immediate succession of course, but of all the bosses in the four primary areas, they are all faced three separate times at heightening levels of difficultly. I personally don't have a problem with this as it's made more interesting by changes in mechanics, addition of more moves to the bosses and new memoirs unlocked after each, however I can see how it might annoy someone less patient.
It also does become hugely difficult towards the end, the fifth area, the Darkest Dungeon itself, is pig-headedly unforgiving. Bring bandages and prepare to be bled.
However, all in all, this game recieves my heartiest of recommendations, and I don't hesitate to say it's the best indie game I have played this year, quite possibly the best game I have played this year overall. Darkest Dungeon you are a 10/10. Red Hook, have my children. It's been roughly two years since I've reviewed Starbound on Early Access, and boy, has this game gone through a ton of iterations.  Some of them good, some of them bad.  But since it's finally been officially released, I figured it was time to give the game an up-to-date, proper review.
First off, yes, it's pretty much Terraria IN SPACE!  Heck, with the exception of the space combat/travel segments, you could also say that Starbound is essentially what No Man's Sky should've been when exploring planets.  And unlike No Man's Sky, you can actually meet and interact with other players!
You can travel from the many, many worlds and sectors, each one having their own little secrets and unique mini-biomes to discover though, and that's a great deal of the charm with this game.  And yes, each world is roughly the same size as the worlds you'd find in Terraria, the underground included, meaning that you are going to have a LOT of places to explore.  That part hasn't changed one bit.
However, the exploration process has been streamlined significantly, mostly to make things less frustrating for new players and easier to get into.  That means less grindy chores, less ridiculous resource requirements or vague quest tasks (well, mostly... I'll explain more in a moment), no starting planets that get hammered by huge♥♥♥♥♥asteriods outta nowhere and destroys your starting home (GOD THAT WAS ANNOYING), no starting planets with lava or toxic pools instead of water, less unbalanced enemy encounters, etc.  It certainly makes like easier for the most part, but it does remove a bit of the challenge and that feel of beating the odds when they're stacked against you.
The streamlining does have a fault, though.  Whereas in Terraria you could find over-powered gear and items if you knew where to look, were willing to brave the more dangerous regions, or simply lucked out, you'll rarely encounter situations where it feels like you've 'gamed' the system or discovered an awesome piece of gear.  With the exception of the consumable items and wearable gear, all of your equipment is randomly generated, with stats matching the worlds your on and rarely exceeding it.  There isn't as much variety in the gear either, so don't expect as much esoteric equipment as you'd find in Terraria.
The game now has a campaign to complete.  The unique story missions certainly stand out, both because of how large they are, and how much detail you realize must've gone into designing each mission.  The undersea Hyotl library was the most memorable, if only because I was left admiring how much effort went into designing the whole place, and more importantly, how it's theoretically possible for me to reconstruct it... provided, if I had mastered the wiring system, had infinite construction resources, and no life to speak of.  But the sidequests on the other hand are mostly randomly generated, often have vague instructions, and quickly become repetitive.  The vagueness of certain objectives cannot be stated enough - several times I had to defer to online guides in order to figure out just what did the quest giver mean or where to find and craft the ingredients.  You'll eventually find yourself burning out on any of the sidequests not given on the Space Outpost, possibly only endulging them for the sake of obtaining a new crew member for your starship.
Sadly, the game still has issues with engine optimization.  The issues no longer affect me (unless I'm visiting one of the more crowded settlements or in a big fight), but I've been hearing lots of chatter from other players complaining that the game has a terrible framerate, crashes frequently, or can't even be booted up.  Thus, make the best out of that 2 hour grace period you have after purchase to figure out if the game can even run on your system, or else you might be stuck with a dud for awhile longer.  There are also other glitches abound, but the fact that I can't remember them off the top of my head probably speaks to how minor most of them are.
SUMMARY:
Ultimately, my recommendation is still the same as it was two years ago.  Starbound's gameplay can indeed be fun building your own little town and upgrading your starship, doubly so with some of the higher quality mods out on Steam.  But the game still does feel partially incomplete for some reason.  Perhaps it has to do with the fact that I was one of the earliest players and remember what the original version played like, faults and all, or how many things were significantly altered or even removed.  Remember the tentacle biome, or some of the original bosses?  Or even better, the original quick-inventory system, or how you could actually pause the game when playing alone? Perhaps they'll appear in a future update, perhaps not.
But for now, it's a good game overall, and if you enjoyed Terraria or other similar games, I'm pretty sure you'll enjoy Starbound.

This has been one of my most satisfying yet equally intimidating challenges. Aesthetically speaking it's sublime, but it has a nuance in it's stillness that brings back the fledgling terror I had as I stared at enemies from a distance in Dark Souls. You craft a team of four soldiers from your barracks which can be bolstered after each excursion. Then you navigate one of five instance dungeon venues given a varying map and mission, occassionally interrupted by turn-based combat scenarios or curious interactable prompts that offer you a small level of influence. Combat is deceptively simplistic, four of eight skills per character usually selected by yourself before the mission. The most devastating synergies are quietly left unsaid as opposed to forced down your throat with the promise of survival, while still giving success plausibility in non-climatic endeavors through a multitude of playstyles. Consumables are purchased before each trek, in anticipation of the interactables as well as status conditions. There's a level of resource management that helps add frustration and tension in the best of ways as decision making leaves lasting repurcussions for your escapades without quite holding your progress hostage, but still promotes infinitely deeper foresight and creativity.
It's easy to start on a whim but can alternatively be played for hours given the varying instance lengths, and accordingly each tier of longevity offers a different due reverence for every location. Camping Skills demand scrutiny and tactics. Consumable space becomes less abundant. Anticipating danger and knowing when to rest become a balancing act between pesimisstic over-preparation and damning optimism from experience.
To call this a self-destructive dance with risk assesment and management with cold, efficent decision making would be an understatement.
To call that a bad thing would be a lie.

Dark Souls III was my first Dark Souls game, or even my first entry into the "Souls-like" genre of  games. I had tried Dark Souls before in years past, but threw down the controller in a fit of disgust within a couple of hours. When I sat down with Dark Souls III, I told myself that I'd give the series another shot. Am I glad that I did.
DS3 has allowed me to mature as a gamer. The game is difficult, and will kill you over and over and over. But most of all, it's fair. It rewards skill. It sometimes rewards daring, risky behavior. But most times, it punishes it. That Hollow that comes out of an alcove and stabs you? He's always going to be there. Nothing changes from death-to-death. Bosses don't change up their movesets. Dark Souls teaches you how to beat it by teaching you to be vigilant and to not give up. There's nothing like fighting a boss five, ten, twenty times, only to see yourself get progressively farther along in the fight. It gave me that thrill like progression raiding in an MMO back in the day, knowing that bit-by-bit, you were getting better.
I'm no Dark Souls master. Far from it. I'm still a sword-and-shield scrub. I may never get to the level of guys running around naked with two Ultra Greatswords. But having played that, I can respect those that do. Those that have mastered the genre. Those that never, ever, gave up, even after thousands of deaths. Dark Souls isn't easy, but it is worth it.

I like hard games. I grew up on Wizardry where the game was 'out to get you' and all that. The NES was my system of choice for years. Dark Souls and Bloodborne are extremely challenging yet fair. But this game- And I DO like it- the thing is just unfair in a lot of ways. This isn't another "TEH RNG IS SUXXS" complaint, it's a design choice complaint on the part of the devs.
For starters, why when you finally clear an area you have a bonus chance to.. get another disease or terrible quirk? That's
reward for finally making it through isn't it? Which leads to this point: You can quickly amass so many negative quirks and diseases IN ONE DUNGEON yet you can only potentially cure one of them back at town- for exorbant prices, I might add. My crusader somehow picked up a drinking problem while looking at a book (because that makes sense) and upon returning to town with tons of stress I see that the questmaster NPC is in the bar. So that's pretty fair too..
The inventory space is way too small for the amount of supplies you have to take with you in order to survive, and that means you have a tiny amount of space left for things to bring back to town and sell. You know, to afford those super high prices for stress relief and disease-away. Trinkets (aux items for your characters' 2 inventory slots) are good but almost all of them have a penalty, further handicapping your hopeless heroes in a game that's set up to dole out more penalties than an Oakland Raiders game.
And sometimes when I go to click on a 4th slot / rear position monster my guy will attack somebody else. These kind of bugs should have been picked up on and fixed long before release.
I like this game a lot. I think that's why it pains me when bad design choices like these run all through it. I really hope there'll be a Darkest Dungeon 2 someday where these design flaws won't exist, because I'll be the first in line to buy it.
Pretty graphics and a cool aesthetic can only go so far, ultimately I have to not recommend buying this unless it's on sale and you're curious what the fuss is about.

Darkest Dungeon is arguably one of the best games I have played during this decade. Make no mistake, this is one of the hardest games too, but it is so fun to fight monsters, explore caverns, fight more monsters, equip your heroes, build up the town and manage the stress levels of your heroes that you quickly get over the obscene frustration you may feel at times.

You have to plan for the worst case scenario and make the best of your situation, which is what the whole thing is about. You are attempting to reclaim your land from evil creatures that destroyed and overtook it during the absence of your ancestors. This is a game about forcefully taking back your home from a horde of evil creatures that drove your family out, perhaps in the process, avenging your ancestors.
With a dark, brooding storyline and mysterious atmosphere, this game will keep you up all night slamming your fists into your desk, swearing at your screen and furiously murdering hordes of undead, beasts and eldritch horrors from the depths of madness from dusk until dawn.

EDIT 4: The game has changed quite a lot since I made this review. Some really nice things that they now have, are upgrades that gear your ship into a specific direction. The three you can upgrade into are Defense, Utility and Offense. Currently, defense is kinda useless.
There's lots of new ships, although I'd say the balancing has gone down since I last played. There are a few ships that just have too much, a big one being the Guardian.
EDIT 3: Ofcourse, things I talk about are subject to change.
EDIT 2: Well, it's working now. The game so far has been really fun. It's a bit like a MOBA having 'lanes' (Large sectors of space you can jump to), 'towers' (Capturable stations, although they don't provide defense) and a central 'nexus' that when captured, wins the game. The combat is great, and even with a high latency you won't experience many problems. It's a bit like World of Tanks, where moving will make your shots less accurate, represented by a circle that changes size, and more accurate when still. But there's none of those shots in WoT where point blank, your shell feels like completely avoiding the tank. Out of the ships i've played, most are well balanced. Each has their own role and can support the team in some way, with the exception of the destroyers. They do great even solo, and your team is more or less supporting you. The only ship I really see a problem with is the Corvette. It's role is to heal, but you don't get any exp/credits for healing, and if you're near the combat to get assists/damage in, you get focused and die near instantly.
I'd have to say my only problem with this game, which I think is being changed in the future, is lack of items/upgrades that you can buy ingame, like all MOBAs have. As of right now, over time you earn upgrades which just up your stats. Health, armor, firerate, damage. It just gets increased. No cool things that let you build your own items/upgrades. If that does happen, bonus points if they change how your ship looks :v.
There isn't much grind, which depending on who you ask, is good or bad. Personally, I think the game is to easy. 4-5 matches and you unlock a new ship.
The optimization is kinda bad, but it runs on my potato, so nothing I can say about that. It's playable, i'm happy.
Overall, I have to say this game is worth it. It's core gameplay is fun and addictive, even without all the features on the side. All ships have their role in the team, just some *cough*corvette*cough* have more trouble grinding to new ships, but the grind isn't that much anyway. The devs are competent, and they're not out for your money and nothing else, which you can't say about many early access games, and they listen to the community. Buy the game and play it guis
