Review Update 4/17/2015
I decided to add a brief summary for clarification of my negative review. Seems there is some confusion.
1. I bought this title very soon after it was made available on steam.
2. The benefits of early-access purchase were described differently - as being "access to all current ships and new ships as they are released." I decided to spend money to support the development of this f2p title because that sounded like a good benefit for my investment.
3. The description has changed since then and I no longer have access to those ships. Regardless of progression system development, what was advertised to me was not provided to me.
All further negative things I have to say about this game may be fixed at some point in the future. Take that into account when reading my analysis of game mechanics. I would not have even posted this analysis if it wasn't for the issue of false advertisement/deceptive business practices. TL;DR Ships don't feel strong or different enough. Devs falsely advertised title when it was first released and still won't admit it, might not be trustworthy.
Review Update 4/13/15:
I have since had the opportunity to play this game live with actual people. I played several rounds.
Since this is an ALPHA title, anything here is subject to change. My one major concern about the direction this game is heading in is in terms of tactical and mechanical diversity of gameplay.
Currently, ships only seem to be able to utilize a single primary weapon type during a match. It appears as though some ships have other unlockable weapon types, but you cannot utilize more than one type of primary weapon on a ship at a time. Despite these weapons ostensibly having different tactical applications, they end up feeling rather homogenous in actual gameplay. Ships seem defined by their constraints rather than their capabilities - This one is slow, that one is fragile, that one is short range, that one does less damage, etc. Ships also have definitive abilities like a short-range teleport or a beam that disables target movement temporarily, and often some kind of alternative "secondary" abilities like missiles or defensive shields.
Actual gameplay boils down to watching your ship approach to within your weapon's effective range and holding down the mouse button until either they die or you die. You might have missiles, a group of fighters, or a defensive cooldown to execute. Despite the fact that most of these abilities have long cooldowns, they do not seem to be particularly impactful on outcomes of fights with exception of some very powerful defensive abilities that some ships possess. You press your buttons and cross your fingers while you watch your HP bars race to zero. Ship movement is more like "Space whales" than "Space ships" but any sense of size lent by the slow-paced movement is mitigated by the homogenous and unimpressive weaponry each ship possesses. For example, you would think a 1-km long flagship would have more than a single piddly wing of fighters that appears to next to no impact on the outcome of a fight, and more than a single weapon turret. For how long cooldowns are and how little difference the abilities seem to make in many cases, the majority of gameplay involves watching your single weapon type gradually pound away at the enemy's hull why they do the same to you.
Considering there are other titles in the works that are in pre-Alpha development with conceptually similar premises, but with far greater polish and tactical diversity, multiple weapon types and in greater numbers on each ship, and far more "active" gameplay mechanics - AND considering the questionable deceptive business practices affecting the earliest purchasers of this title - I would not recommend investing in this title unless it changes dramattically over the course of future development.
TRUST:
The economy of a F2P title is trust-based and thus it is highly important for developers of F2P games to correctly and accurately describe to customers exactly what they are purchasing and its implications for their game experience. Customers who spend their money on your title must walk away feeling that it was worthwhile to do so, because your game survives on continued purchases from its largest fans.
This means being honest and transparent and making sure your customers get their expected value from their purchase.
When I purchased this Early Access for a free-to-play title, the description for the product indicated that by purchasing this title in it's very early stages I would be receiving access to "all ships released going into the future". Thus I considered my purchase to be an investment in a title that looked very promising and offered interesting gameplay potential. However the description was changed on the store page AFTER I purchased it, and now describes the benefits of early access as a "Permanent XP boost." I also find that all ship types that I previous had access to are now unavailable and locked behind a progression system.
Locking ships that were explicitly described as being included in the content pack that I purchased and re-defining the product that I purchased AFTER I paid for it is not an ethical business practice and hence I cannot recommend to anyone that they invest their time or their money into this F2P title.

One of the best new features in AoEIII is unfortunately also the one that keeps me from enjoying it as much as I have enjoyed other games in the series. The introduction of the Home City was a pretty radical departure for the series, introducing persistent leveling to your favorite civilizations, with immediate and powerful gameplay modifications tailored by you to enhance and compliment your playstyle. On the one hand, this feature works great and is very enjoyable, as you pick and choose 'cards' before going into each match, which might upgrade your units, or your production, or they might give you free units, or unlock abilities. On the other hand, you'll quickly realize that each civilization has its own Home City and you have to play each and every one of them for dozens of matches if you want to competitively play all of them. If you have one or two favorite civs that you'll be playing all the time then that's no problem; you can focus on your favorites and be happy as a clam. If you enjoy playing them all though, and are a fan of the Random Civ option from previous games, then the removal of that feature and the introduction of persistence may irritate you.
Other than that, all I'd have to say is that this is a great RTS, with good campaigns, good civilization variety, artwork, music, sound design, gameplay, and scenario editor. Highly recommended.
